# Sūrah al-Muʾminūn (Chapter 23) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Introduction to the Sūrah

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Chapter Named for the People It Describes**

Sūrah al-Muʾminūn, "The Believers," takes its name from its very first word after the divine oath-like opening: *qad aflaḥa al-muʾminūn* — "Truly the believers have prospered." It is a Makkan sūrah of 118 verses, revealed in the later Makkan period according to the majority of scholars, at a time when the small community around the Prophet ﷺ was enduring boycott, ridicule, and the slow attrition of hope, and needed to be told with certainty who they were and where their road ended. The chapter answers that need at once. Before it argues with anyone, before it narrates a single prophet's story, it holds up a portrait of the successful human being — humble in prayer, turned away from idle talk, generous, chaste, trustworthy, punctual before God — and then announces the inheritance of Firdaws, the highest garden of Paradise. Everything that follows in the sūrah is a widening of that first picture: what these believers believe, why they believe it, who opposed such believers before, and what becomes, at the very end, of those who mocked them.

**Place in the Qur'anic Order and the Meaning of Its Sequence**

In the written muṣḥaf al-Muʾminūn follows Sūrah al-Ḥajj and precedes Sūrah al-Nūr. The classical scholars of *munāsabah* — the science of thematic connection between sūrahs — noticed that al-Ḥajj closes with a command and a promise: *"So establish the prayer and give the alms and hold fast to God; He is your Protector — and how excellent a Protector, and how excellent a Helper!"* (22:78). Al-Muʾminūn opens by describing precisely the people who did that: those who are humble in prayer, who give the alms, and who guard their prayers. The end of one sūrah gives the instruction; the beginning of the next shows the instruction lived. Sūrah al-Ḥajj also spoke of the human embryo's stages as a proof of resurrection (22:5); al-Muʾminūn returns to the same argument with greater precision (23:12–16), so that the reader who moves from one chapter to the next hears the argument twice, first briefly and then in full.

**The Architecture of the Sūrah**

The sūrah has a clear and beautiful design, which the commentary that follows will trace verse by verse. It moves in seven broad movements:

1. **The portrait of the successful believers (vv. 1–11):** seven qualities, framed at the beginning by the word "prosperity" and at the end by the word "Firdaws."
2. **The signs of God in the human body and the natural world (vv. 12–22):** the embryo, death and resurrection, the seven heavenly paths, rain stored in the earth, gardens of dates and grapes, the olive of Sinai, cattle and ships.
3. **The history of the messengers (vv. 23–50):** Noah and his ark; an unnamed generation destroyed by the Cry; the chain of messengers sent in succession; Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh; Jesus and Mary given refuge.
4. **The single community of the messengers and the splitting of their followers (vv. 51–56):** God's address to all messengers as one brotherhood, the tearing of their unity into factions, and the false confidence of the wealthy.
5. **The second portrait of believers, and the arguments with the deniers of Makkah (vv. 57–92):** the anxious, hurrying, God-fearing believers contrasted with the heedless rich; the six questions ("Have they not contemplated…? Do they not know their Messenger…?"); the argument from ownership of the earth, the heavens, and all dominion; and the rational proof against multiple gods.
6. **The Prophet's own supplications (vv. 93–98):** the prayer not to be among the wrongdoers, the command to repel evil with what is better, and the refuge from the whispering of devils.
7. **Death, the barrier, the Trumpet, the scales, and the final dialogue in Hell (vv. 99–118):** the last plea to be returned, the barzakh, the weighing of deeds, the exchange between God and the condemned, the recollection of the believers who were mocked, the compressed sense of earthly time, the question "Did you suppose We created you in vain?", and the closing prayer for forgiveness and mercy.

The chapter opens with *qad aflaḥa al-muʾminūn* — "the believers have prospered" — and closes, two verses from its end, with *lā yufliḥu al-kāfirūn* — "the disbelievers will not prosper" (23:117). The same root, *f-l-ḥ*, brackets the whole sūrah. The reader who notices this understands the sūrah's single thesis: there are two ways to live, and only one of them ends in flourishing.

**When Heaven Opened: Reports About the Sūrah's Revelation**

A well-known report transmitted by Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Ḥākim, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, describes the physical intensity that sometimes accompanied revelation and links it to the opening of this sūrah. ʿUmar said:

> *"When revelation descended upon the Messenger of God ﷺ, a sound like the humming of bees could be heard near his face. One day revelation came upon him, and we waited for a while; then it was lifted from him, and he faced the qiblah, raised his hands, and said: 'O God, increase us and do not decrease us; honor us and do not humiliate us; give to us and do not deprive us; prefer us and do not prefer others over us; be pleased with us and make us pleased.' Then he said: 'Ten verses have been revealed to me — whoever establishes them will enter Paradise.' Then he recited: 'Truly the believers have prospered…' until he completed ten verses."* (Aḥmad, Musnad; al-Tirmidhī 3173; al-Ḥākim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ on the criteria of Muslim)

Whatever the precise grading of this chain (al-Tirmidhī noted an irregularity in it, though al-Ḥākim authenticated it), the report's content is confirmed by the sūrah itself: the ten opening verses are a program of life, and the Prophet ﷺ treated them as a promise of the Garden to whoever fulfilled them. It is also transmitted that when ʿĀʾishah was asked about the character of the Prophet ﷺ, she replied, "His character was the Qur'an," and then recited *qad aflaḥa al-muʾminūn* through the tenth verse, saying, "Thus was the character of the Messenger of God" (al-Nasāʾī, *al-Sunan al-Kubrā*; cf. Muslim 746 for the shorter form). The opening of al-Muʾminūn was therefore understood by his own household as a description of the man himself.

**Why This Sūrah Matters Today**

The situation into which al-Muʾminūn was revealed is not remote from ours. A small number of people had accepted a demanding truth in a society that was wealthy, confident, mocking, and convinced that its comfort was proof of divine approval. The sūrah dismantles that confidence with unusual patience: it asks its opponents to concede that God owns the earth, the heavens, and all dominion (23:84–89), and then asks how, having conceded that, they can be "bewitched" into denying His right to be obeyed and His power to raise the dead. It refuses to let prosperity be read as blessing: *"Do they reckon that, on account of the wealth and children We have provided them, We hasten unto good for them? Nay, but they are unaware!"* (23:55–56). It defines success not by what a person has but by what a person is. And it ends in a courtroom in which the mockers are silenced and the mocked are vindicated — a scene that every believer who has ever been laughed at for praying, fasting, dressing modestly, or refusing a dishonest deal is meant to carry in his heart as the true ending of his story.

**How to Read What Follows**

The commentary treats each of the 118 verses as a complete, independent discourse. Where the source commentary groups verses (6–7, 10–11, 15–16, 21–22, 27–28, 33–34, 45–46, 48–49, 55–56, 60–61, 64–65, 66–67, 73–74, 80–81, 82–83, 84–89, 93–95, 99–100, 102–103, 105–106, 112–114), each verse has been separated and given its own full treatment, as the method requires. For every verse the reader will find the Arabic key terms explained simply; the classical interpretations of al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī, and the Companions and Successors from whom they transmit; authentic Prophetic reports with their collections named; the logical structure of the verse's argument; and its bearing upon the moral and psychological life of a person living now. Nothing has been shortened because the chapter is long. The sūrah's own first lesson — that the believer is one who is *not hurried* in prayer and who *turns away* from what is idle — has been taken as the rule for reading it: unhurried, and attentive only to what matters.

## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:1

> **Truly the believers have prospered,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Verdict Announced Before the Trial**

The sūrah does not begin with a command, a question, or a narrative. It begins with a verdict: *qad aflaḥa al-muʾminūn* — "Truly the believers have prospered." The Arabic particle *qad*, placed before a past-tense verb, does not merely mark the past; it confirms and emphasizes that something has really, certainly, happened. The believers have not merely *hoped* to prosper or *begun* to prosper; the matter is settled. The Arabic grammarians observe that *qad* with the perfect tense conveys *taḥqīq* — verification — as when one says "the caravan has *indeed* arrived." God speaks of an outcome that lies in the future for the believers as though it were already accomplished, because whatever God decrees is, from the standpoint of His knowledge, already done. This is a familiar Qur'anic device: *"The command of God has come, so do not seek to hasten it"* (16:1), spoken while the Hour is yet to arrive. The believer who hears verse 1 is therefore being told: the end of your road is not uncertain. Before the sūrah lists a single condition of belief, it announces that whoever meets those conditions has already, in God's decree, succeeded.

**What "Prospering" Means in Arabic**

The verb *aflaḥa* comes from the root *f-l-ḥ*, whose most concrete meaning is to split or cleave. The farmer who breaks open the earth to plant is a *fallāḥ*, and the word for the cultivator survives with that meaning in Arabic to this day. From this image the word came to mean success and flourishing, because the one who splits the hard soil, sows, waters, and waits eventually reaps. *Falāḥ* is therefore not the luck of the lottery winner; it is the harvest of the one who labored patiently through seasons when nothing visible was growing. The Arabs also used the word for remaining and enduring, so *falāḥ* carries the sense of a good that lasts, as opposed to a pleasure that vanishes. When the caller to prayer cries *ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ* — "Come to prosperity!" — five times a day, this is the prosperity meant: the durable, cultivated success of a person who has broken open the hard soil of his own soul and planted what God commanded.

The lexicographers add that *falāḥ* is the attainment of what one desires together with deliverance from what one fears. Both halves are essential. A man who gains everything he wanted but is destroyed by what he feared has not prospered; a man who escapes every danger but never attains what he hoped for has not prospered either. The believer, the verse says, gets both: the Garden he hoped for and safety from the Fire he dreaded. This is why al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī defined it as *al-ẓafar wa idrāk al-bughyah* — victory and the reaching of the goal — and divided it into worldly and otherworldly kinds, of which the second is *"an everlasting existence without extinction, a wealth without poverty, an honor without abasement, and a knowledge without ignorance."*

**The Word the Qur'an Reserves for the Truly Successful**

The Qur'an uses this root with striking consistency to separate two categories of human beings, never applying "prosperity" to the wrongdoer. When it describes the reverent at the opening of Sūrah al-Baqarah it concludes: *"Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and it is they who are the prosperous"* (2:5). When it describes those who command good and forbid evil it says: *"and it is they who are the prosperous"* (3:104). When it speaks of the wrongdoers it says flatly: *"Indeed, the wrongdoers do not prosper"* (6:21), and of those who fabricate lies about God: *"Indeed, those who fabricate lies against God do not prosper"* (10:69). In this very sūrah the two poles meet: the first verse says *"the believers have prospered"* and the second-last verse says *"the disbelievers will not prosper"* (23:117). The entire chapter is suspended between those two statements like a bridge between two pillars.

The word also anchors the Qur'an's teaching on the purification of the self. In Sūrah al-Shams, after eleven oaths, the divine conclusion is: *"He has prospered who purifies it (the soul), and he has failed who buries it"* (91:9–10). And in Sūrah al-Aʿlā: *"He has prospered who purifies himself, and remembers the Name of his Lord and prays"* (87:14–15). Notice that the very deeds mentioned here — purification, remembrance, prayer — are the deeds al-Muʾminūn goes on to list. The Qur'an's vocabulary is internally consistent: *falāḥ* is always the fruit of *tazkiyah* — the cleansing and growth of the soul.

**Who Are "the Believers"?**

The word *al-muʾminūn* is the plural active participle of *āmana*, "to believe," from the root *a-m-n*, which carries the meanings of security, safety, and trust. The believer is literally "one who has entered into security," or "one who grants security" — he has found safety with God and, as the Prophet ﷺ said, others are safe from his harm. Both meanings are alive in the word. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"The Muslim is he from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe, and the believer (al-muʾmin) is he whom people trust with their lives and their property."* (al-Nasāʾī 4995; al-Tirmidhī 2627; the first clause in al-Bukhārī 10 and Muslim 41)

The definite article *al-* on *al-muʾminūn* is significant. It is not "some believers" or "believers in general," but *the* believers — those known and characterized by belief, those whose faith has become their identity. Al-Ṭabarī explains that the reference is to those who *"affirmed the oneness of God and His Messenger and acted upon what He commanded them,"* and then notes that God Himself immediately defines the term by listing their attributes in the following verses. In other words, verse 1 makes a claim, and verses 2 through 9 supply the definition of the subject of that claim. One cannot read verse 1 in isolation and conclude that mere verbal profession secures the harvest; the verse is the heading of a list.

**A Report on the Making of Paradise**

Al-Ṭabarī and others transmit a report from Kaʿb al-Aḥbār and from Abū al-ʿĀliyah that when God created the Garden of Eden, He looked upon it and said, "Speak," and it said, *"Truly the believers have prospered"* — as though Paradise itself, on seeing its own beauty, could find no better words to describe the good fortune of those who would inhabit it. Another version of the report says that God created Adam with His Hand, wrote the Torah with His Hand, planted the Garden of Eden with His Hand, and then said, *"Truly the believers have prospered."* These are not Prophetic ḥadīths but *isrāʾīliyyāt* and reports of the early generations, and the classical scholars cite them with due care. Their value is not as history but as commentary: they express the early Muslims' sense that this verse is the caption written upon Paradise. Ibn Kathīr, discussing verse 11, transmits the sounder Prophetic version of this idea: that Firdaws is the Garden's center and summit and that God planted it Himself, which we will examine there.

**Why God Begins with the Reward Rather Than the Work**

There is a pedagogy in beginning with the verdict. Human beings work better when they can see the end of their labor. A student who knows that a degree awaits her at the end of four years endures the examinations; a laborer who has been shown the finished house does not resent carrying the bricks. God, who created the human heart, opens this program of demanding disciplines — humility in prayer, restraint of the tongue, giving away wealth, chastity, honoring every trust, punctuality in worship — by first showing the finished house. Then the list of bricks follows, and finally the house is named again in verse 11: Firdaws. The demands of verses 2–9 are framed on both sides by the reward, so that the believer never reads a command without its promise in view.

There is also a matter of certainty. The Makkan Muslims in the year this sūrah descended did not look prosperous. Some were slaves being tortured in the sun; some had lost their trade and family; the Prophet ﷺ himself had been driven from Ṭāʾif with stones. To these people God did not say "you may prosper if things improve." He said "you have prospered," using the grammar of a completed fact. Faith, the verse teaches, is not a bet on future good fortune; it is the possession of a good already secured in the decree of the One who cannot fail.

**The Logic of Success Redefined**

The verse quietly overturns the definition of success that every society naturally holds. The Makkans, like people everywhere, measured prosperity by wealth, sons, and standing, and the sūrah will later quote them thinking exactly this way: *"Do they reckon that, on account of the wealth and children We have provided them, We hasten unto good for them?"* (23:55–56). Against this the sūrah establishes a different metric. Success is measured at the end of the journey, not at the midpoint; it is measured by what a person becomes, not by what accumulates around him; and it is measured by the only Judge whose verdict is final. A traveler is not called successful because he has a comfortable seat on the train; he is successful when he arrives at the right station. The Qur'an states this principle plainly elsewhere: *"Whoever is removed from the Fire and admitted into the Garden has certainly prospered; and the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion"* (3:185).

**Living the Verse Now**

Read personally, the verse is a question before it is a comfort. The reader is invited to ask: am I among *al-muʾminūn* as God defines them in the next verses? The verse then becomes a mirror held up throughout the following nine verses. Read communally, it is a source of dignity: believers are not to think of themselves as the poor cousins of a prosperous world, but as people who have already won what the world is still chasing. And read spiritually, it teaches a habit of the heart the Prophet ﷺ described when he said that the affair of the believer is *"all good; if something pleasant befalls him he gives thanks, and that is good for him, and if something harmful befalls him he is patient, and that is good for him"* (Muslim 2999). Such a person cannot lose, because both outcomes feed the harvest. That is what it means to say the believers *have prospered* — in the past tense, before the story is even told.

## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:2

> **who are humble in their prayers,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Brick: Not Prayer, but a Quality of Prayer**

After announcing that the believers have prospered, the sūrah begins to define them, and its very first characteristic is not "who pray" but "who are humble *in* their prayers": *alladhīna hum fī ṣalātihim khāshiʿūn*. The choice is deliberate and instructive. Prayer itself is assumed — no one enters the category of "believer" without it — so the verse moves past the fact of prayer to its inner quality. It is as though a physician, asked to describe a healthy heart, did not say "it beats" but "it beats with the right rhythm." The verse teaches that the presence of prayer distinguishes the Muslim from the non-Muslim, but the presence of *khushūʿ* within prayer distinguishes the prosperous believer from the merely observant one.

The grammar reinforces this. The sentence is a nominal one built on a pronoun, *hum* ("they"), followed by the prepositional phrase *fī ṣalātihim* ("in their prayers") placed *before* the predicate *khāshiʿūn* ("humble"). In Arabic, fronting the prepositional phrase produces emphasis and specification: it is *in their prayer*, precisely there, where their humility is found and proven. The use of the active participle rather than the verb also indicates a settled, habitual state rather than an occasional act — they are *characterized* by humility, not merely humble once in a while.

**The Root of Khushūʿ: Lowered Eyes and a Bowed Land**

The word *khāshiʿūn* comes from the root *kh-sh-ʿ*, whose basic sense is lowness, stillness, and submission. The Qur'an uses it for the physical world as well as for people. Of the earth before rain it says: *"And among His signs is that you see the earth khāshiʿah (barren and still); then when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells"* (41:39). Of the Day of Judgment it says that people will emerge from their graves *khushshaʿan abṣāruhum* — "their eyes humbled" (54:7) — and that faces on that Day will be *khāshiʿah* (88:2), and voices will be *khashaʿat* — hushed — before the Merciful so that *"you hear nothing but a whisper"* (20:108). The word, then, gathers together the ideas of lowered gaze, stilled limbs, hushed voice, and a heart that has stopped resisting — the whole posture of a creature that knows it stands before its Master.

From this the classical commentators drew a distinction that became standard: *khushūʿ* has an inner seat and outer effects. Its seat is the heart; its effects appear in the limbs. Al-Ṭabarī summarizes the early views as humility, fear, and stillness, and adds that the humility of the heart shows itself in the lowering of the eyes and the quieting of the body. Al-Rāzī states that *khushūʿ* in relation to the inward state is *"an attitude of self-effacement and obedience,"* while in relation to the outward it is the stillness of the limbs and the lowering of the gaze. Ibn al-Qayyim expressed it memorably: *"Khushūʿ is the standing of the heart before the Lord with humility and brokenness."* When the heart stands like that, the body cannot fidget.

**A Report About Where the Eyes Go**

Several commentators, including al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī, record that before this verse was revealed some of the Companions would raise their eyes toward the sky while praying, and that after it descended they lowered their gaze to the place of prostration. Whatever the precise chronology, the practice is firmly established by the Prophet's own severe warning against raising the eyes in prayer. Al-Bukhārī records from Anas ibn Mālik:

> *"What is the matter with people who raise their eyes toward the sky in their prayer?" He spoke so strongly about this that he said: "They will surely stop doing that, or their sight will be snatched away."* (al-Bukhārī 750)

And Muslim records from Jābir ibn Samurah:

> *"Let people stop raising their eyes toward the sky in prayer, or their sight will not return to them."* (Muslim 428)

The Prophet ﷺ also disliked turning the face during prayer; when ʿĀʾishah asked about it he said, *"It is a snatching which Satan snatches from the prayer of a servant"* (al-Bukhārī 751). These reports show that the *outer* stillness is not a trivial matter of etiquette: the wandering eye is the outward symptom of a wandering heart, and the Prophet ﷺ treated it as a theft.

**The Hadiths al-Rāzī Cites on the Empty Prayer**

The source commentary preserves two sayings that al-Rāzī quotes to illustrate the difference between the prayer that is performed and the prayer that is *received*. The first:

> *"How many a worshipper stands to pray whose share of it is only toil and weariness."* (Cited by al-Rāzī; a parallel wording concerning fasting and night prayer is in Ibn Mājah 1690 and Aḥmad, from Abū Hurayrah: "Perhaps a person who fasts gets nothing from his fast except hunger, and perhaps a person who stands at night gets nothing from his standing but sleeplessness.")

The second, transmitted as a saying of the early generations and sometimes attributed to the Prophet ﷺ:

> *"The servant has of his prayer only that which he understood (or was present for) of it."*

The Prophet's authentic words carry the same teaching in a quantified form. Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī record from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir:

> *"A man may finish his prayer and nothing is written for him of it except a tenth of it, a ninth, an eighth, a seventh, a sixth, a fifth, a quarter, a third, or a half."* (Abū Dāwūd 796; graded ḥasan)

The logic here is that the prayer has a body and a soul. The body is the sequence of standings, bowings, and prostrations; the soul is *khushūʿ*. A body without a soul is a corpse — it may be complete in every limb and still be lifeless. The believer described in this verse is the one whose prayer is alive.

**The Prayer That Brings Forgiveness**

The Prophet ﷺ described the reward attached to a prayer performed with this attentive humility. Muslim records from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān that he performed ablution and then said, I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ perform ablution like this, and he said:

> *"Whoever performs ablution like this ablution of mine, then stands and prays two units of prayer in which he does not speak to himself (lā yuḥaddithu fīhimā nafsahu), his past sins are forgiven."* (al-Bukhārī 159; Muslim 226)

The condition — "in which he does not talk to himself" — is *khushūʿ* described from the inside: the inner monologue silenced, the mind not conducting business, replaying quarrels, or planning dinner while the mouth recites. The scholars explain that this refers to the voluntary, sustained wandering of thought, not the involuntary flicker that the believer notices and dismisses; the latter is unavoidable and forgiven, while the former is the real thief.

**Why Humility Is Placed at the Head of the Portrait**

Why should *khushūʿ* in prayer be the very first quality of the prosperous, before charity, chastity, or honesty? Because prayer is the root, and the other virtues are its branches. The Qur'an says: *"Indeed, prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing"* (29:45) — but a prayer without presence restrains no one, as everyday experience proves in the person who prays and then cheats. The prayer that reforms conduct is the humble prayer, because a person who has actually stood before God for a few minutes with awareness finds it harder to forget Him in the marketplace an hour later. The sequence of the sūrah thus mirrors a causal order: humility in prayer *produces* the avoidance of idle talk (v. 3), the generosity (v. 4), the chastity (v. 5), and the trustworthiness (v. 8) that follow. The spiritual commentators, as the source notes from Ibn ʿAjībah, insisted that *khushūʿ* inside prayer cannot be maintained without practicing the virtues outside it; the relationship runs in both directions. A person who spends the day in backbiting will not find stillness when he raises his hands for prayer, and a person who finds stillness in prayer will find backbiting distasteful.

**The Psychology of a Distracted Prayer**

Anyone who has prayed knows the experience: the mouth reaches the second sūrah and the mind is already in tomorrow's meeting. Modern psychology calls this "mind-wandering" and has measured that the untrained mind drifts nearly half its waking hours. The Prophet ﷺ described its cause in the language of the unseen: a devil named Khinzab who *"comes between a man and his prayer and confuses him,"* against whom the remedy is to seek refuge in God and spit dryly three times to the left (Muslim 2203, from ʿUthmān ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ). The two descriptions do not compete: the Qur'an speaks of both the whispering of Satan and *"what the soul whispers"* (50:16), and the believer trains against both.

The training has practical steps that the scholars distilled from the Sunnah: praying as though it is one's last prayer (*"Pray the prayer of one bidding farewell,"* Ibn Mājah 4171); praying in the state of *iḥsān* described by Gabriel's ḥadīth, *"that you worship God as though you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you"* (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8); understanding the meaning of what is recited; pausing at each verse of the Fātiḥah in awareness of God's answer to each (Muslim 395); not praying while food is served or while needing the toilet (Muslim 560), because the body's insistent demands defeat the heart's stillness; and removing visual distractions — the Prophet ﷺ once removed a decorated garment because *"its markings distracted me in my prayer"* (al-Bukhārī 373). None of this is mysterious. A person who wanted to listen carefully to a beloved voice would turn off the television, silence the phone, and face the speaker. *Khushūʿ* is applying to God the courtesy we routinely extend to people we respect.

**An Analogy: Stillness as a Sign of Attention**

Consider how attention shows itself in ordinary life. When a child is genuinely absorbed in a story, her body goes still, her eyes fix on the storyteller, her hands stop moving. When a defendant hears the judge begin to read the verdict, the courtroom falls silent and no one shifts in his seat. Stillness is the body's natural response to significance. The Qur'an's insistence on *khushūʿ* is therefore not an arbitrary ritual requirement; it is the demand that prayer be treated as what it is — the most significant appointment of the day — and that the body confess this by its stillness and the heart by its presence. A restless prayer betrays a heart that has judged the meeting unimportant.

**Khushūʿ and the Loss of the Age**

There is a sober warning in the tradition that *khushūʿ* will be the first thing lifted from this community. Al-Ṭabarānī and others transmit from Abū al-Dardāʾ: *"The first thing to be lifted from this ummah will be khushūʿ, until you will see no one with khushūʿ."* (al-Ṭabarānī; Ibn al-Mubārak in *al-Zuhd*; the meaning is supported by the general decline of religion foretold in authentic reports). This is why the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge from *"a heart that does not humble itself (qalbin lā yakhshaʿ)"* (Muslim 2722). Humility in prayer is not a bonus feature for the spiritually ambitious; it is a defense against a specific and foretold spiritual disease.

**Where This Verse Leaves the Reader**

The first attribute of the prosperous is an interior one that no observer can fully verify — only God knows who is truly present before Him. This teaches, at the very threshold of the portrait, that the prosperity of verse 1 is not won by appearances. It also gives every believer an immediately actionable task: the next prayer. Nothing needs to be purchased, no journey undertaken; the believer needs only to lower his gaze, still his limbs, silence the inner talker, and remember Who is listening. If he does, he has laid the first brick of the house that verse 11 will name.

## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:3

> **and who turn away from idle talk,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Prayer Mat to the Tongue**

The second attribute of the prosperous believers moves from the inner posture of prayer to the outer conduct of speech and attention: *wa alladhīna hum ʿan al-laghwi muʿriḍūn* — "and who turn away from idle talk." The sequence is not accidental. The one who has stood humbly before God cannot descend from that station and immediately plunge into vain chatter without feeling the contradiction. The verse thus describes what the person of *khushūʿ* looks like when he leaves the mosque. Al-Rāzī noted that this arrangement is itself an argument: humility in prayer is the root, and turning away from what is idle is its first fruit.

Once again the grammar carries emphasis. The prepositional phrase *ʿan al-laghw* ("from idle talk") is placed before the predicate *muʿriḍūn* ("turning away"), specifying the object of their aversion. And *muʿriḍūn* is an active participle, denoting a stable trait rather than a single act. They are people whose *settled disposition* is to turn from what is vain.

**The Meaning and Range of Laghw**

The word *laghw* derives from the root *l-gh-w*, which describes speech that has no worth, no benefit, and no consequence — the chatter of birds, the babble of a crowd, words that do not count. In Arabic law an oath made without intention is called *laghw al-yamīn*, an "idle oath," which the Qur'an says God does not hold against a person (2:225; 5:89), precisely because it is empty of purpose. The word therefore covers, at its widest, anything that is void of good.

The commentators differed over how broadly to draw the boundary. Al-Ṭabarī gathers the views: some said it means *shirk* and every act of disobedience; some said the abusive talk of the idolaters who used to insult the Prophet ﷺ; some, like Ibn ʿAbbās, said falsehood (*al-bāṭil*) generally. Al-Rāzī reports the three tiers noted in the source: speech that is forbidden, speech that is disliked, and speech that is permissible but unnecessary. He records that some scholars limited the verse strictly to what is forbidden, while others extended it to the merely useless. Al-Ṭabarī's own preference is characteristically comprehensive: *laghw* is *"every falsehood, obscenity, and vain thing, and everything in speech that God has disliked,"* and the believers turn away from it all.

The strongest reading, therefore, is that *laghw* is a spectrum. At one end lies clearly sinful speech — lying, backbiting, slander, mockery, obscenity, disputing about God without knowledge. In the middle lies speech that is not sinful but wastes what is precious: hours of gossip, argument for its own sake, pointless entertainment. At the far end lies the faint but real *laghw* of the person who, having nothing sinful to say, still says a great deal that accomplishes nothing. The prosperous believer, the verse says, is *turning away* — moving in the opposite direction — along this entire spectrum, not merely avoiding its extreme.

**Turning Away Rather Than Merely Abstaining**

The verse does not say the believers *do not speak* idly; it says they *turn away* from it. The image is of a person who, when *laghw* is presented to him — a rumor, a quarrel, a crude joke, an invitation to a useless argument — physically and morally turns his face in another direction. This matches the Qur'an's portrait of the servants of the Merciful: *"and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity"* (25:72), and of the sincere among the People of the Book: *"And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, 'To us our deeds and to you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant'"* (28:55). Notice in that last verse the manner of turning: not with contempt, but with peace. The believer who leaves the idle conversation does not deliver a lecture; he says, in effect, "peace," and moves on to what matters. This is also the meaning of the Qur'an's command: *"Take what is given freely, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant"* (7:199).

**The Prophetic Teaching on the Tongue**

The Prophet ﷺ made the guarding of speech a hinge of religion. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent."* (al-Bukhārī 6018; Muslim 47)

This ḥadīth is the verse's most direct commentary: the believer has only two options, beneficial speech or silence; there is no third category of "harmless chatter" recognized as a right. Al-Tirmidhī records the Prophet's definition of a person's Islam being beautiful:

> *"Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him."* (al-Tirmidhī 2317; Ibn Mājah 3976; graded ḥasan)

And Muʿādh ibn Jabal, having asked the Prophet ﷺ about the deed that would admit him to Paradise, received a long instruction that ended with the Prophet taking hold of his own tongue and saying, *"Restrain this."* Muʿādh asked, "O Prophet of God, will we be held accountable for what we say?" He replied:

> *"May your mother be bereft of you, Muʿādh! Is there anything that throws people on their faces — or he said, on their noses — into the Fire except the harvests of their tongues?"* (al-Tirmidhī 2616; Ibn Mājah 3973; graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ)

The phrase "harvests of their tongues" is remarkable in light of the root *f-l-ḥ* in verse 1: the tongue too is a field, and it can be planted with a crop that ruins the farmer.

**Why Idle Talk Is So Dangerous: The Logic of the Verse**

Why would the Qur'an place the avoidance of *mere* idle talk — not only of lying or slander — among the seven qualities of those who inherit the highest Paradise? Several reasons stand out.

First, time. A human life is a fixed number of breaths, and the believer has been told that he will be asked *"about his life, how he spent it"* (al-Tirmidhī 2417). Idle talk is the most common way in which life leaks away unnoticed. No one decides to waste ten years; but ten minutes here, an hour there, an evening of chatter, and the years are spent. The believer who turns away from *laghw* is defending his capital.

Second, the slope. Idle talk rarely stays idle. Conversation that begins with nothing to say drifts toward the interesting, and the most interesting subject is other people, and speech about other people becomes backbiting — which the Qur'an compares to *"eating the flesh of one's dead brother"* (49:12). Al-Ghazālī observed that most sins of the tongue begin as innocent conversation that had no anchor. The believer who leaves the room before the drift begins has avoided the slope altogether.

Third, the heart. Speech is not neutral to the speaker. What the tongue repeats, the heart absorbs. Hours of trivial talk produce a trivial heart, one that finds the Qur'an heavy and the gossip column light. The scholars of the soul called this the "hardening" that follows much talk without remembrance, and the Prophet ﷺ warned: *"Do not talk excessively without remembrance of God, for much talk without remembrance of God hardens the heart, and the person farthest from God is the one with a hard heart"* (al-Tirmidhī 2411). The connection to verse 2 is now complete: *laghw* hardens the heart, and a hard heart cannot achieve *khushūʿ*. The two verses describe a single condition from two sides.

**The Modern Ocean of Laghw**

No generation has faced *laghw* on the scale of the present one. The seventh-century Arab could be idle only with the people physically around him; today a device in the pocket offers an endless stream of talk, images, disputes, and entertainment engineered by experts to seize attention and never release it. Much of it is not sinful in itself; nearly all of it is *laghw* in the precise sense of this verse — content that has no consequence for one's Hereafter and little for one's worldly good. The verse's command to *turn away* has therefore become newly demanding and newly liberating. A believer who learns to close the application, to leave the comment thread, to decline the pointless argument, is practicing verse 3 with a discipline his ancestors were never asked for. The Qur'an's portrait of the successful is, in this respect, more countercultural now than when it descended.

**Paradise as the Land Without Laghw**

There is a beautiful correspondence between this verse and the Qur'an's descriptions of the Garden. Of Paradise it says: *"They will hear therein no idle talk, only peace"* (19:62); *"They will hear therein no idle talk and no sinful speech, only the saying: Peace, peace"* (56:25–26); and *"They will hear therein no idle talk nor lying"* (78:35). Paradise is defined, in part, as the place where *laghw* does not exist. The believer who turns away from idle talk in this world is therefore already living, as far as he can, in the atmosphere of the world to come; he is rehearsing the speech of the people of the Garden. This is the deep reason the trait belongs among the qualities of those who inherit Firdaws: they have begun to speak its language here.

**Practical Discipline**

The application of this verse is concrete. Before speaking, the believer can ask three questions the scholars derived from the Sunnah: Is it true? Is it beneficial? Is it necessary now? Silence passes this test more often than speech. In gatherings, he may learn to steer conversation toward what benefits — knowledge, encouragement, planning good, remembering God — and to excuse himself gracefully when it cannot be steered. In private, he may audit his consumption of others' *laghw* as strictly as his production of his own, for the ear that listens to idle talk is a partner in it. And in all of this he may remember that the turning away is not sullen or superior; it is the natural preference of a heart that has tasted something better in prayer and finds, quite simply, that idle talk no longer satisfies.

## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:4

> **and who give the alms,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Quality: From the Tongue to the Hand**

The portrait of the prosperous now moves from what the believer withholds — idle speech — to what he gives: *wa alladhīna hum li'l-zakāti fāʿilūn* — literally, "and who are, for the zakāh, doers." Having described a person whose prayer is humble and whose tongue is guarded, the sūrah turns to his hand. The order is again meaningful. A person can achieve stillness in prayer and silence in company while remaining, at the level of possessions, entirely self-centered. Islam does not permit faith to stop at the boundary of the wallet. As the Qur'an repeatedly pairs prayer with alms — *"establish the prayer and give the zakāh"* appears more than two dozen times — so this sūrah, having begun with prayer, immediately anchors it to giving.

**An Unusual Phrase: "Doers of Zakāh"**

The wording of this verse is distinctive. Everywhere else the Qur'an says the believers *give* (*yuʾtūn*) the zakāh. Here alone it says they are *fāʿilūn* — "doers," "performers" — *for* the zakāh. The classical scholars paused over this choice, and their explanations open up the verse.

Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī suggest that *zakāh* here may denote not only the payment itself but the *act* of purification, and that one "does" an act rather than "gives" it. That is, the verse is describing people who *actively bring about* zakāh — who perform the deed of purifying their wealth and their souls. A second explanation is that *fāʿilūn* emphasizes exertion and initiative: they do not passively wait for the collector; they are *agents* of zakāh who seek it out, calculate it, and deliver it. A third, offered by some commentators, is that the phrase is broader than the legal alms and covers every act by which a person purifies himself, as in the Qur'an's usage: *"He has prospered who purifies himself (tazakkā)"* (87:14). This last explanation resonates with the sūrah's opening word *aflaḥa*, since the same root *f-l-ḥ* is paired in 87:14 with *tazakkā*.

The construction with the preposition *li-* ("for the zakāh") adds a further nuance. It suggests dedication or purpose: they act *for the sake of* zakāh, or they are people *devoted to* zakāh. The grammar thus paints not a grudging taxpayer but a person whose relationship to his wealth is oriented toward giving.

**The Two Meanings of Zakāh and the Makkan Context**

The word *zakāh* comes from the root *z-k-w*, which means both to grow and to be pure. Cultivated crops that flourish are said to *zakā*; a soul that is cleansed is *zakiyyah*. The Islamic institution of zakāh carries both meanings at once. It purifies the giver of greed and the wealth of the claims of others, and it causes both the wealth and the soul to grow — the wealth through divine blessing, the soul through the habit of detachment. The Qur'an states this dual function explicitly when it commands the Prophet ﷺ: *"Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow (tuṭahhiruhum wa tuzakkīhim)"* (9:103).

Because this sūrah is Makkan, and the detailed legal rates of zakāh (the *niṣāb* thresholds, the two-and-a-half percent on savings, the tenth on rain-fed crops) were fixed in Madinah, the commentators note that *zakāh* here refers to the general obligation of purifying charity that was already binding in principle from the beginning of revelation, and which the Madinan legislation later specified. Ibn Kathīr writes that most scholars hold zakāh to have been made obligatory in Madinah, while its *principle* existed in Makkah, and he cites 6:141 — a Makkan verse — *"and give its due on the day of its harvest."* Thus the believers praised here are those who, even before the detailed law, were already giving from what they had. That is consistent with the sūrah's use of *fāʿilūn*: they were "doing zakāh" before there was a formal collector, out of the inner compulsion of faith.

**Zakāh as a Pillar and a Test**

The Prophet ﷺ placed zakāh among the five pillars upon which Islam is built (al-Bukhārī 8; Muslim 16), and the Qur'an makes it, alongside prayer and repentance, the condition of brotherhood in faith: *"But if they repent, establish the prayer, and give the zakāh, then they are your brothers in religion"* (9:11). After the Prophet's death, when certain tribes proposed to pray but withhold zakāh, Abū Bakr fought them, declaring: *"By God, I will fight whoever separates prayer from zakāh, for zakāh is the due of wealth"* (al-Bukhārī 1400; Muslim 20). The first Caliph understood what this verse teaches: prayer and alms are not separable qualities of the believer; the humble prayer of verse 2 and the given alms of verse 4 are two limbs of a single body.

The Prophet ﷺ also described the fate of the one who withholds it, in words that make the reason for the verse's severity plain:

> *"Whoever is given wealth by God and does not pay its zakāh, his wealth will be made to appear to him on the Day of Resurrection as a bald-headed venomous snake with two black spots over its eyes. It will encircle his neck and bite his cheeks and say: 'I am your wealth; I am your treasure.'"* Then he recited: *"Let not those who withhold what God has given them of His bounty think it is good for them; rather, it is bad for them. Their necks will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection"* (3:180). (al-Bukhārī 1403)

**Why Giving Belongs Among the Marks of Prosperity**

There is an apparent paradox in listing *giving away wealth* among the signs of *prosperity*. The world defines prosperity by accumulation; the Qur'an lists distribution. The resolution lies in understanding what wealth does to the human heart when it is held and when it is released.

Held wealth tends to become a master. The Qur'an describes the human being as *"intense in his love of wealth"* (100:8) and warns that *"your wealth and your children are only a trial"* (64:15). The person who never gives never tests whether he owns his money or his money owns him. Zakāh is the periodic proof of ownership: by giving a fixed portion away, the believer demonstrates — to himself above all — that his hand can open. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Charity does not decrease wealth"* (Muslim 2588), and the reason is not only divine replenishment but that the person who gives has lost nothing of what actually matters; he has instead gained a freedom the hoarder never tastes.

Released wealth, moreover, builds the society in which the believer must live. Zakāh is not private charity distributed at whim; it is a right (*ḥaqq*) belonging to the poor, the needy, and the other categories God named in 9:60. The Qur'an says of the righteous: *"And in their wealth was a recognized right for the beggar and the deprived"* (70:24–25). By calling it a right, the Qur'an removes the giver's sense of superiority — he is not being generous; he is paying what he owes — and removes the recipient's shame — he is not begging; he is receiving his due. No secular welfare system has so precisely protected the dignity of both parties.

**The Psychology of the Open Hand**

Modern research on well-being has repeatedly found what this verse implies: people who give regularly report greater happiness, lower anxiety about money, and a deeper sense of meaning than those with equal income who do not. The believer does not need the studies, but they illustrate the Qur'an's claim that giving *is* prospering, not its opposite. The miser lives in fear of loss; the giver lives in trust of the Provider. The Qur'an names this transaction plainly: *"Whatever you spend, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers"* (34:39) — the very title, *khayr al-rāziqīn*, that this sūrah will apply to God in verse 72.

An analogy the scholars used: wealth is like water. Stagnant water in a closed pool becomes foul; running water stays clean and gives life wherever it flows. Zakāh is the channel that keeps a person's wealth running. The name of the institution, with its meaning of *growth*, is not a euphemism; it is a description of what happens to wealth, and to the person, when the channel is opened.

**Zakāh and the Sūrah's Larger Argument**

Later in this sūrah, the disbelievers will boast of *"the wealth and children We have provided them"* and imagine that God is thereby *"hastening good to them"* (23:55–56). Verse 4 has already answered them. The believer's relationship to wealth is not to possess as much as possible but to purify what he has and let it flow. The mark of divine favor is not the size of the treasury but the openness of the hand. When the sūrah later says that the believers *"give what they give while their hearts quake with fear"* (23:60), it returns to this same trait at a deeper level: not only do they give, they give without self-satisfaction, anxious whether their gift is accepted. Verse 4 establishes the practice; verse 60 will describe its inner spirit.

**Living the Verse**

For the believer today, verse 4 asks for something specific and measurable. He should know what he owns, know what he owes, calculate it honestly each lunar year, and pay it promptly to those entitled. Beyond the obligation, the spirit of *fāʿilūn* — being an active *doer* of purification — invites him to look for what else in his life needs the cleansing that giving provides: the grudge that generosity dissolves, the anxiety that trust in the Provider calms, the isolation that the recipient's gratitude bridges. The person who has learned to be humble before God (v. 2), to guard the tongue (v. 3), and now to open the hand (v. 4) is building, brick by brick, the character that verse 11 will crown.

## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:5

> **and who guard their private parts,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fourth Quality: Guarding What Is Most Private**

The portrait now touches the most intimate domain of human life: *wa alladhīna hum li-furūjihim ḥāfiẓūn* — "and who are guardians of their private parts." The sequence of the sūrah has moved from the heart (humility in prayer), to the tongue (turning from idle talk), to the hand (giving alms), and now to the body's most powerful appetite. The believers described here are those who have brought even this drive, the one most resistant to reason, under the authority of God's law. This is not a peripheral virtue. The Qur'an lists it alongside prayer and charity, and the Prophet ﷺ made it a condition of his personal guarantee of Paradise.

**The Language of Guarding**

The verb *ḥafiẓa*, from which *ḥāfiẓūn* derives, means to preserve, protect, and keep watch over something. It is the word used for memorizing the Qur'an (*ḥifẓ*), for the angels who record deeds (*ḥāfiẓīn*, 82:10), and for God's own attribute *al-Ḥafīẓ*, the Preserver. It implies vigilance against loss or violation. One guards a treasure, a border, a trust. The verse therefore frames chastity not as a repression or denial of the body, but as an act of *guardianship* — the careful keeping of something valuable that must not be squandered or exposed to harm.

The word *furūj* (singular *farj*) literally means an opening or a gap, and by extension the private parts of the body. The Qur'an uses this same root for the openings in the sky (*furūj*, 50:6) and for the private parts of both men and women (24:30–31; 33:35). The use of the plural with the possessive "their" — *furūjihim* — and, once more, the fronting of the prepositional phrase before the predicate, produces the emphatic specification that characterizes the whole passage: it is precisely *their private parts* that they are guardians of.

As with the previous verses, *ḥāfiẓūn* is an active participle. It describes a permanent disposition, a standing watchfulness, rather than an occasional restraint. Guarding is not something the believer does once; it is what he *is*.

**What Guarding Includes**

The primary and unanimous meaning, as the source commentary states, is abstaining from unlawful sexual relations — *zinā* in all its forms. But the classical scholars drew out the wider implications from the word's choice. *Ḥifẓ al-farj* includes, according to al-Qurṭubī and others: guarding against unlawful intercourse; guarding against unlawful exposure — covering the *ʿawrah* before those not entitled to see it; and guarding the paths that lead to the sin — the gaze, the touch, the private seclusion with a non-relative. The Qur'an connects the gaze and the private parts explicitly in the verse that legislates modesty: *"Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them"* (24:30), and the same for believing women (24:31). Al-Qurṭubī observes that guarding the eye is mentioned *before* guarding the private parts because the eye is the messenger of the heart, and every fall into unchastity begins with a look that was not restrained.

The Prophet ﷺ described this progression precisely. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"God has written for the son of Adam his portion of zinā, which he will inevitably encounter. The zinā of the eye is the look; the zinā of the tongue is speech; the soul wishes and desires; and the private parts confirm all this or deny it."* (al-Bukhārī 6243; Muslim 2657)

The ḥadīth teaches that guarding the private parts is the final gate of a fortress whose outer walls are the eye, the tongue, and the imagination. The believer who guards only the final gate while leaving the outer walls open has made his task nearly impossible.

**The Two Ḥadīths of Guarantee**

The Prophet ﷺ attached to this quality a personal guarantee of Paradise. Al-Bukhārī records from Sahl ibn Saʿd:

> *"Whoever guarantees for me what is between his jaws and what is between his legs, I guarantee for him Paradise."* (al-Bukhārī 6474)

This ḥadīth is a commentary on verses 3 and 5 together: what is between the jaws is the tongue (v. 3), and what is between the legs is the private parts (v. 5). The Prophet ﷺ identified these two as the decisive fronts. And when asked what most causes people to enter Paradise, he answered: *"Taqwā of God and good character."* When asked what most causes people to enter the Fire, he said: *"The two hollow things: the mouth and the private parts"* (al-Tirmidhī 2004; Ibn Mājah 4246; graded ṣaḥīḥ by some). The Qur'anic portrait and the Prophetic warning converge on the same two organs.

**Why the Qur'an Elevates This Virtue**

Why should the control of a bodily appetite rank with prayer and alms among the marks of those who inherit Firdaws? The answer lies in what unchastity does to the individual, the family, and the society, and in what chastity protects.

For the individual, the sexual drive is the appetite most capable of overruling reason. The Qur'an calls unlawful intercourse *"an indecency and an evil way"* (17:32), and the person who habitually yields to it has demonstrated that, in the decisive test, his desire governs him rather than God. Chastity, by contrast, is the clearest possible proof that a person's will is sovereign over his impulses — the same sovereignty required for *khushūʿ* in prayer, for restraining the tongue, and for releasing wealth. The believer who cannot guard this has not, in the Qur'an's estimation, yet learned to guard anything.

For the family, unchastity is corrosive at the root. The Islamic family is built on the certainty of lineage and the exclusivity of the marital bond; *zinā* destroys both. Children of uncertain parentage, spouses betrayed, homes broken — the Qur'an's severity toward *zinā* is proportional to the damage it inflicts on the most basic unit of human life. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the prohibition protects *"the lineages, the honor, and the wealth"* — for illegitimate offspring also confuse inheritance.

For the society, the normalization of unchastity produces exactly what the modern world exhibits: the collapse of marriage, the loneliness of the unattached, the commodification of the human body, and the vast industries that profit from unregulated desire. The Qur'an's insistence on guarding is not prudery; it is the recognition that a society that cannot regulate this drive will eventually be regulated *by* it.

**The Positive Vision Behind the Guarding**

It would be a misreading to hear this verse as hostility to the body. The very next verse (23:6) will make the lawful exceptions explicit — "save from their spouses" — and declare that in those relationships the believers *"are not blameworthy."* Islam does not ask the believer to extinguish desire but to channel it into the bond that God has blessed. The Prophet ﷺ described marital intimacy itself as an act of charity that earns reward (Muslim 1006), and he rebuked those Companions who wished to renounce marriage, saying: *"I marry women; whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me"* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401). Guarding the private parts, then, is a guardianship *for* something: for the spouse to whom one's intimacy is promised, for the children who deserve certainty about their parents, and for the dignity of one's own soul.

The Qur'an's own analogy is that of a garment: *"They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them"* (2:187). A garment covers, protects, warms, and beautifies. Chastity is the discipline that makes this mutual covering possible; unchastity is the tearing of the garment.

**Practical Guarding in a Culture of Exposure**

The believer today lives in an environment engineered to defeat this verse. Images that the seventh-century Muslim could encounter only rarely are now delivered continuously and deliberately. The Qur'an's strategy remains the same, but its application has become more demanding. Guarding the private parts begins with guarding the eye, as 24:30 teaches; guarding the eye in the present age means controlling the screen. It includes guarding the imagination, which the ḥadīth above calls "the soul wishing and desiring"; the scholars recommend remembrance of God, fasting, and useful occupation as the remedies. The Prophet ﷺ prescribed to the young: *"O young people, whoever among you can afford to marry, let him marry, for it lowers the gaze and guards the private parts; and whoever cannot, let him fast, for it is a shield for him"* (al-Bukhārī 5065; Muslim 1400). Marriage is the lawful channel; fasting is the training of the will when the channel is not yet available. Neither is a mere suggestion; both are the Prophet's practical program for fulfilling verse 5.

It also includes avoiding seclusion with those one could be tempted by — *"No man is alone with a woman but that Satan is the third of them"* (al-Tirmidhī 2165) — and avoiding the environments in which the outer walls fall. The believer who understands the fortress analogy does not wait to defend the last gate.

**The Reward of Those Who Guard**

The Qur'an lists the guarding of the private parts among the qualities of those for whom God has *"prepared forgiveness and a great reward"* (33:35), and in the same list places *al-ḥāfiẓīna furūjahum wa'l-ḥāfiẓāt* — men and women alike. The Prophet ﷺ named among the seven whom God will shade on the Day when there is no shade but His: *"a man whom a woman of position and beauty invites, and he says, 'I fear God'"* (al-Bukhārī 660; Muslim 1031). The fact that this act of guarding, alone among private struggles, earns a place among the seven suggests how heavy God has weighed it. Yūsuf, peace be upon him, is the Qur'an's supreme example: invited by his master's wife behind locked doors, he said *"I seek refuge in God"* (12:23) and chose prison over sin. The verse before us is, in a sense, the doctrine of which Yūsuf's story is the illustration.

**Where the Verse Stands in the Portrait**

Verse 5 completes the first half of the portrait of the prosperous. The believer has been shown as humble before God, restrained in speech, generous with wealth, and now sovereign over his strongest appetite. The next two verses will clarify the lawful boundaries of that sovereignty, so that no one misreads guarding as prohibition of what God has permitted.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:6

> **save from their spouses or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Exception That Defines the Rule**

Having praised those who guard their private parts, the sūrah immediately clarifies the lawful domain in which that guarding is set aside: *illā ʿalā azwājihim aw mā malakat aymānuhum fa-innahum ghayru malūmīn* — "except with their spouses or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are not blameworthy." This verse is essential to the correct understanding of the previous one. Without it, "guarding the private parts" might be mistaken for celibacy or asceticism. With it, the Qur'an establishes a principle that runs through all of its sexual ethics: the drive itself is not evil; its *misdirection* is. Within the boundaries God has set, there is no blame — indeed, there is blessing and reward.

The structure of the exception is telling. It does not say the believers "occasionally" or "reluctantly" have relations with their spouses; it says that in this domain they are *ghayru malūmīn* — "not blamed" — a phrase that removes the shadow of guilt entirely. This is a direct refutation of the view found in some religious traditions that sexual union, even in marriage, is a concession to weakness or a lesser state. Islam declares the marital bond a place of complete moral freedom within the wider structure of restraint.

**The Word "Spouses" and Its Balance**

The word *azwāj* (singular *zawj*) means "pairs" or "mates" and is used in the Qur'an for both husbands and wives. Its root meaning conveys the idea of two things joined into one — a pair, a couple. The Qur'an uses the word for the pairs of every created thing (*"And of everything We created pairs,"* 51:49), and for the spouses of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers. The term therefore emphasizes complementarity and union rather than possession or hierarchy. When the verse says "their spouses," it is describing a bond in which two halves complete each other, as the Qur'an says elsewhere: *"He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy"* (30:21).

Because the address in this sūrah is grammatically masculine plural — which in Arabic includes both men and women unless context restricts it — the ruling applies to both husbands and wives. The same principle appears in Sūrah al-Maʿārij (70:29–30) in identical words. Women guard their private parts from all but their husbands; men from all but their wives; both are blameless within the bond.

**"Those Whom Their Right Hands Possess"**

The second category, *mā malakat aymānuhum*, refers to female slaves or bondwomen owned by a man, with whom lawful relations were permitted under specified conditions. This phrase requires honest and careful treatment. The Qur'an was revealed into a world in which slavery existed on every continent and had for millennia. It did not create the institution; it inherited it and set about regulating, restricting, and progressively dismantling it. Relations with a bondwoman were permitted only to her owner (not to anyone else, and never to a woman with her male slave); she could not be shared, lent, or forced into prostitution — *"Do not compel your slave girls to prostitution when they desire chastity"* (24:33); if she bore her master a child she became *umm walad*, could not be sold, and was freed upon his death, and her child was free and legitimate from birth. The Qur'an's overriding thrust was toward freedom: it made the freeing of slaves an expiation for numerous sins (4:92; 5:89; 58:3), a category of zakāh expenditure (9:60), and an act of the highest righteousness — *"the freeing of a neck"* is placed at the head of the steep ascent in 90:13. The Prophet ﷺ freed every slave he was given and said: *"Whoever frees a believing slave, God will free from the Fire, for every limb of his, a limb of the one who freed him"* (al-Bukhārī 6715; Muslim 1509).

The source commentary directs the reader to 4:24 for the fuller discussion. What must be said here is that this clause describes a historical circumstance, not a permanent ideal. With the abolition of slavery — which Muslim jurists across the world have affirmed as binding under contemporary treaties and as consonant with the Sharīʿah's own objective (*maqṣad*) of freedom — the category has no living application, and the verse's operative content for the believer today is the first clause: the marital bond.

**The Principle of Lawful Fulfillment**

The verse establishes a principle whose wisdom deserves reflection. Human beings have appetites. A law that simply forbade appetite would be unlivable and would produce, as history shows, hypocrisy and secret vice. A law that permitted every appetite without limit would produce, as history also shows, the collapse of family and society. The Qur'an chooses the middle road: it identifies the lawful channel and opens it fully, while closing every other. The Prophet ﷺ embodied this balance. When three men came to his house intending to renounce marriage, food, and sleep out of zeal, he corrected them: *"By God, I am the most fearful of God among you and the most conscious of Him, but I fast and I break my fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me"* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401).

Muslim records the astonishing exchange in which the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions that in each person's marital intimacy there is a charity. They asked, "O Messenger of God, does one of us fulfill his desire and receive a reward for it?" He replied:

> *"Do you not see that if he were to place it in the forbidden, he would have sinned? Likewise, if he places it in the lawful, he has a reward."* (Muslim 1006)

This ḥadīth is verse 6 in practical form. The same act that is a grave sin outside the bond is an act of reward inside it. What determines its moral weight is not the act but the boundary.

**Not Blameworthy: The Removal of Guilt**

The phrase *ghayru malūmīn* — "not blamed" — is stronger than mere permission. The Qur'an could have said *"it is lawful for them"* (ḥalāl); instead it says that no blame attaches to them at all. This removes not only legal penalty but the psychological burden of guilt. Believers are not to feel that their marital life is a spiritual weakness to be apologized for. On the contrary, the Prophet ﷺ described a loving marriage as half of religion: *"When a servant marries, he has completed half of his religion; let him fear God in the remaining half"* (al-Bayhaqī, *Shuʿab al-Īmān*; graded ḥasan by some). And he said: *"Of this world, women and perfume have been made beloved to me, and the coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer"* (al-Nasāʾī 3939; Aḥmad). The man of *khushūʿ* in prayer (v. 2) and the man of lawful marital love (v. 6) are the same man.

**Why the Boundaries Protect Love**

The verse teaches that restraint outside the bond and freedom inside it are two sides of one principle. What makes marital intimacy valuable is precisely its exclusivity. A gift given to everyone is worth little to anyone; a bond that can be entered and left casually offers no shelter. By guarding the private parts from all others (v. 5), the believer makes his gift to his spouse meaningful (v. 6). The Qur'an's imagery of spouses as "garments" for each other (2:187) depends on this: a garment shared with the whole street is not a garment. The boundaries are what turn desire into love, and love into the *sakīnah* — tranquility — that 30:21 promises.

There is also a matter of trust. The following verse 8 will praise those who *"keep their trusts and their covenant."* Marriage is described by the Prophet ﷺ as a covenant of extraordinary weight: *"You have taken them by the trust of God and made their private parts lawful by the word of God"* (Muslim 1218, from the Farewell Sermon). Chastity within marriage is the keeping of that trust; verses 5–6 and verse 8 are therefore intimately linked.

**Practical Guidance**

For the believer, this verse carries several practical lessons. First, marriage should be made easy and honored, not delayed by inflated dowries and social pretensions, since it is the divinely appointed channel that makes verse 5 achievable; the Prophet ﷺ said: *"The most blessed marriage is the one with the least burden"* (Aḥmad; al-Bayhaqī). Second, within marriage the spouses should attend to each other's rights with generosity, since neglect on either side weakens the fortress the verse protects; the Prophet ﷺ said: *"The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family"* (al-Tirmidhī 3895; Ibn Mājah 1977). Third, believers should reject both the ascetic error that treats marital love as impure and the libertine error that treats every desire as a right. The verse's phrase "not blameworthy" defends against the first; the next verse's phrase "transgressors" will defend against the second.

**A Verse of Mercy Within a Verse of Discipline**

Verse 6 is, finally, an expression of divine mercy. God did not create human beings with desires and then forbid their fulfillment. He created the desire and the lawful means of satisfying it, and He declared the believer who uses that means to be entirely free of blame. This is the Qur'an's characteristic balance: *"God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship"* (2:185). Guarding the private parts is demanding, but it is not cruel, because the Guardian of the law has provided the door through which the guarded treasure may be lawfully shared.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:7

> **and as for those who seek beyond that, it is they who are transgressors—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Closing the Door That Verse 6 Opened**

Verse 6 opened a lawful door: within marriage, and within the historical category of bondwomen, there is no blame. Verse 7 immediately closes every other door: *fa-man ibtaghā warāʾa dhālika fa-ulāʾika hum al-ʿādūn* — "but whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors." The two verses form a single legal sentence: the exception and its limit. The Qur'an, having named the permitted, does not leave the boundary implied; it states explicitly that everything outside that boundary is transgression. The precision is typical of the Qur'an's method with matters of the appetites: clear permission, clear prohibition, and no ambiguous middle ground for desire to exploit.

**The Word "Seek" and the Word "Beyond"**

The verb *ibtaghā*, from the root *b-gh-y*, means to seek, desire, or pursue something — often with intensity. The same root produces *baghy*, oppression or the overstepping of limits, which hints at the moral quality of what is being described: the seeking here is a seeking that oversteps. The verse targets not merely the act but the *pursuit*, the orientation of desire toward what lies outside the lawful. This is consistent with the ḥadīth cited under verse 5, in which "the soul wishes and desires" is counted as part of the progression toward the forbidden.

The word *warāʾa* means "behind" or "beyond." Its use here is vivid: the lawful relationships are a defined territory, and *warāʾa dhālika* — "beyond that" — is everything on the far side of its fence. The verse does not enumerate what lies beyond; it does not need to. Everything not included in verse 6 is, by definition, included in verse 7. This is the exegetical principle that the classical jurists drew from the pair: the permitted is defined by inclusion, the forbidden by exclusion, so that no new form of sexual relationship can claim legitimacy simply because it was not specifically named.

**Who Are "the Transgressors"?**

The word *al-ʿādūn* comes from the root *ʿ-d-w*, which means to run, to pass beyond, to overstep, and hence to be hostile or to transgress. The related noun *ʿudwān* means aggression; *ʿaduww* means enemy. The transgressor, in this Qur'anic sense, is one who has run past the boundary God drew. The Qur'an uses the same root when it warns: *"These are the limits (ḥudūd) of God, so do not transgress them (fa-lā taʿtadūhā); and whoever transgresses the limits of God, it is they who are the wrongdoers"* (2:229). The image is spatial and consistent: God has drawn lines; the believer stays within them; the transgressor crosses.

The sentence structure — *fa-ulāʾika hum al-ʿādūn*, "it is *they*, they who are the transgressors" — uses the emphatic pronoun *hum* and the definite predicate to produce a restrictive, categorical judgment. It does not say "they have done something wrong," but "they are *the* transgressors," identifying them with the category. This mirrors the sūrah's earlier emphatic constructions praising the believers, and it will be echoed in verse 10: *"It is *they* who are the heirs."* The rhetoric of the sūrah repeatedly draws sharp lines between the two groups by using the same emphatic grammar for each.

**What the Verse Prohibits**

The classical scholars derived from the verse the prohibition of every sexual outlet outside marriage (and, historically, lawful concubinage). This includes fornication and adultery (*zinā*), homosexual acts, and, according to the majority of jurists, other forms of sexual gratification outside the bond. Al-Qurṭubī records that the verse was used by many scholars as a proof text against solitary gratification, since it lies "beyond" the two lawful relationships named; some jurists, including some Ḥanbalīs, allowed it as a lesser evil in cases of fear of falling into *zinā*, but the verse's plain scope favors the majority position. The temporary marriage (*mutʿah*) practiced in pre-Islamic Arabia was likewise held by the Sunni schools to fall under this verse once the Prophet ﷺ prohibited it permanently at Khaybar and again at the Conquest of Makkah (al-Bukhārī 5115; Muslim 1406–1407).

The verse's breadth is its strength. The forms that unlawful desire can take are endless, and human ingenuity in devising them is inexhaustible. Rather than chase each form with a separate prohibition, the Qur'an defines the lawful narrowly and declares all else transgression. Whatever new arrangement any age invents, the believer already knows where it stands: is it marriage, or is it *warāʾa dhālika*?

**The Logic of a Bright Line**

Why does God draw the boundary so sharply, without gradation? Because in this domain gradation is precisely what desire exploits. A person who accepts a "little" transgression as harmless has already lost the argument, since the appetite will always petition for a little more. The Prophet ﷺ described this dynamic with the image of the boundary and the pasture:

> *"The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that many people do not know. Whoever guards against the doubtful matters has protected his religion and his honor, and whoever falls into the doubtful matters falls into the unlawful — like a shepherd who grazes his flock around a protected sanctuary and is on the verge of entering it. Truly every king has a sanctuary, and the sanctuary of God is His prohibitions."* (al-Bukhārī 52; Muslim 1599)

Verse 7 marks the sanctuary's edge. The believer who wishes to fulfill verse 5 — guarding the private parts — cannot graze along the fence; he must keep his flock well inside the lawful territory of verse 6.

There is also a social logic. Sexual boundaries are among the few limits that, if allowed to erode gradually, erode completely. Societies that began by tolerating small deviations have almost always ended by abandoning the concept of transgression altogether. The Qur'an's refusal to admit degrees is an act of foresight: it anticipates the slope and forbids the first step.

**The Word "Transgressor" as a Moral Diagnosis**

Note the moral vocabulary the verse chooses. It does not call such people "sinners" or "the lustful"; it calls them *transgressors* — boundary-crossers. This diagnosis is more penetrating than it first appears. The problem with unlawful sexuality, in the Qur'an's analysis, is not primarily that it involves pleasure, but that it involves *taking what has not been given*. The lawful spouse has been given by God's word and by contract; the unlawful partner has not. The transgressor's fundamental error is thus a refusal to accept limits set by a higher authority — the same error, at root, as every other sin. This is why the Qur'an can move from a discussion of chastity directly to a discussion of trusts and covenants in the next verse: both are about respecting what has and has not been entrusted to one.

**Mercy Within the Severity**

The verse is severe, but the Qur'an's severity toward this sin is always accompanied by the open door of repentance. In the same breath that it commands the punishment of *zinā*, it says: *"But if they repent and reform, then leave them alone; indeed, God is ever Accepting of repentance and Merciful"* (4:16). And in the description of the servants of the Merciful, after condemning those who commit *zinā*, it says: *"except for him who repents, believes, and does righteous work; for them God will replace their evil deeds with good"* (25:70). The believer who has crossed the line and returned is not permanently branded a transgressor; the verse describes a condition, not a life sentence. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"The one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin"* (Ibn Mājah 4250). The door of verse 7 closes on the act, not on the person who turns back.

**Applying the Verse Today**

In the contemporary world, the sharpest challenge to this verse is not the temptation to commit particular acts but the wholesale redefinition of transgression itself. The prevailing culture holds that consenting adults may do as they wish and that the very idea of a boundary "beyond" which lies transgression is oppressive. The believer must understand that the verse is asking him not merely to abstain from certain acts but to hold a different *map* of reality — one in which the lines are drawn by God, not by consent or preference. Holding that map in an environment that mocks it requires the same quality the sūrah began with: *khushūʿ*, the humble recognition that one stands before a Lord who has the right to command.

Practically, the verse invites the believer to be honest about the "beyond" in his own life — the glance that lingers, the message that should not have been sent, the content consumed in private — and to bring it back inside the boundary. It invites parents to teach their children the map early and clearly, since the boundary is more easily kept by those who grew up knowing where it lies. And it invites the community to make the lawful door of marriage accessible, since a boundary is easiest to respect when the legitimate way is open.

**The Pair Completed**
