Verses 6 and 7 together are a small masterpiece of legal drafting: total freedom inside a defined space, total prohibition outside it, and no gray zone for desire to negotiate. Having completed the discussion of the body's most powerful appetite, the sūrah will turn in verse 8 to a virtue that governs all human relationships: the keeping of trusts and covenants.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:8

> **and who keep their trusts and their covenant,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fifth Quality: Reliability**

After the intimate domain of chastity, the sūrah turns to the social domain of reliability: *wa alladhīna hum li-amānātihim wa ʿahdihim rāʿūn* — "and who, for their trusts and their covenant, are keepers." The believer has been described as humble before God, restrained in speech, generous with wealth, and sovereign over his desires. Now he is described in his dealings with other people: he can be relied upon. What is placed in his keeping is safe; what he promises, he performs. This verse, almost word for word, appears again in Sūrah al-Maʿārij (70:32), which suggests that it was regarded as a fixed and indispensable component of the believer's character.

The placement is again logical. Chastity (vv. 5–7) is itself the keeping of a trust — the marital covenant; verse 8 generalizes from that specific trust to all trusts. Al-Rāzī notes that the sequence moves from the believer's relationship to his Creator (prayer), to his own soul (guarding tongue and body), to his wealth (zakāh), and now to his fellow human beings (trusts and covenants). The portrait is systematically complete.

**Amānāt: The Plural and Its Reach**

The word *amānāt* is the plural of *amānah*, from the root *a-m-n* — the same root as *īmān* (faith) and *muʾmin* (believer). This etymological kinship is not coincidental; the Arabs understood that faith and trustworthiness are one thing seen from two sides. *Amn* is security; *amānah* is that which is deposited with someone on the assumption of security; and the *muʾmin* is both one who has found security in God and one with whom others' trusts are secure. The Prophet ﷺ made the connection explicit:

> *"There is no faith (īmān) in one who has no trustworthiness (amānah), and there is no religion in one who does not keep his covenant."* (Aḥmad, Musnad 12383; al-Bayhaqī; graded ḥasan)

The plural *amānāt* signals the wide variety of trusts. The commentators enumerate: property deposited for safekeeping; secrets confided; responsibilities of office; the rights of family; the body and faculties God has lent each person; knowledge that must be conveyed accurately; and above all the religious obligations themselves. Ibn Kathīr writes that *amānah* here includes *"all that God has entrusted to His servants of His commands and prohibitions, and all that people have entrusted to one another."* The Qur'an itself uses the word for the primal trust of moral responsibility that the heavens and earth declined and the human being accepted: *"Indeed, We offered the Trust (al-amānah) to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains, and they declined to bear it and feared it, but the human being bore it"* (33:72). Every smaller trust is a fragment of that great one.

**ʿAhd: The Singular Covenant**

Notice that *amānāt* is plural but *ʿahd* — covenant — is singular. Al-Rāzī and others observe that the singular may be used because *ʿahd* is a generic noun encompassing every covenant, or because the primary covenant is one: the covenant between the servant and God, of which all human agreements are extensions. The Qur'an speaks of the covenant taken from the children of Adam before they were born: *"Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we bear witness"* (7:172), and of the covenant with each community through its prophets. It also uses *ʿahd* for the ordinary promises people make: *"And fulfill the covenant; indeed, the covenant will be questioned about"* (17:34). The believer who keeps his word to a neighbor is, in the Qur'an's understanding, practicing the same fidelity he owes to God.

**The Word "Keepers": Rāʿūn**

The predicate *rāʿūn* is the active participle of *raʿā*, which means to tend, to shepherd, to watch over. The shepherd (*rāʿī*) is the one who guards the flock from wolves, leads it to pasture, and answers for every sheep. The Qur'an's choice of this word for the keeping of trusts is precise: a trust is not something one merely avoids betraying; it is something one actively tends, like a living animal that will die if neglected. The famous ḥadīth on responsibility uses the same word:

> *"Each of you is a shepherd (rāʿin), and each of you is responsible for his flock. The ruler is a shepherd and responsible for his flock; the man is a shepherd over his family and responsible for them; the woman is a shepherd over her husband's house and children and responsible for them; the servant is a shepherd over his master's property and responsible for it."* (al-Bukhārī 893; Muslim 1829)

The verb *raʿā* thus links verse 8 to the whole Islamic ethic of stewardship. The believer is a shepherd of everything entrusted to him — his office, his family, his wealth, his knowledge, and his word.

**Betrayal as a Sign of Hypocrisy**

The Prophet ﷺ placed the violation of trusts and covenants among the defining marks of the hypocrite — the very opposite of the believer this sūrah describes. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"The signs of the hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies; when he promises he breaks his promise; and when he is entrusted he betrays."* (al-Bukhārī 33; Muslim 59)

And in another version from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr: *"...and when he makes a covenant he acts treacherously"* (al-Bukhārī 34; Muslim 58). Two of the three (or four) signs concern exactly the two things this verse names: promises/covenants and trusts. The believer and the hypocrite are thus distinguished, in the Prophet's own diagnosis, precisely by verse 8. A person may pray and fast, but if his word is worthless and his hands are not safe, he carries the marks of the hypocrite regardless of his outward practice.

The Prophet ﷺ also gave the loss of trustworthiness as one of the signs of the Last Hour. When a Bedouin asked him when the Hour would come, he said: *"When the trust is lost, await the Hour."* The man asked, "How will it be lost?" He said: *"When authority is given to those unfit for it, await the Hour"* (al-Bukhārī 59). And Ḥudhayfah related the Prophet's prophecy that trust would be gradually withdrawn from hearts until *"people will trade with one another and hardly anyone will fulfill a trust, so that it will be said: 'Among such-and-such tribe there is a trustworthy man'"* (al-Bukhārī 6497; Muslim 143). The scarcity of the trustworthy is, in the Prophet's telling, the mark of a decaying age.

**The Trustworthy One: The Prophet's Own Title**

Before he was known as a prophet, Muḥammad ﷺ was known throughout Makkah as *al-Amīn*, "the Trustworthy." The Quraysh, even while persecuting him, continued to deposit their valuables with him; and when he emigrated to Madinah, he left ʿAlī behind specifically to return every deposit to its owner (Ibn Hishām, *Sīrah*). This is one of the most extraordinary facts in the biography of the Prophet ﷺ: his enemies trusted him with their property while plotting to kill him. Verse 8 describes a quality that the Prophet ﷺ possessed to a degree his opponents themselves testified to, and the sūrah will invoke this later: *"Or do they not know their Messenger, and so deny him?"* (23:69). The man they called *al-Amīn* was the man they called a liar; the contradiction condemned them.

**Why Reliability Is a Pillar of Prosperity**

Why does keeping trusts and covenants belong among the seven qualities of those who inherit Firdaws? Consider what a society becomes when this virtue is absent. Every contract must be enforced by force; every deposit must be guarded against the guardian; every promise must be doubted. The cost of distrust is enormous — economists now measure "social capital" and find that societies where people can rely on one another are wealthier, safer, and happier. The Qur'an knew this without the measurements. A community of believers who *keep* trusts and covenants can function on a basis of confidence rather than surveillance, and this confidence is a form of prosperity that no wealth can buy.

Consider also what betrayal does to the betrayer. The person who breaks a trust once finds the second breach easier; the person who breaks his word habitually loses the ability to believe his own promises. He becomes, in the Prophet's diagnosis, a hypocrite — a person whose inner and outer selves have separated. The believer who keeps trusts is preserving his own integrity in the literal sense: his wholeness, the correspondence between what he says and what he does. That wholeness is a precondition for the *khushūʿ* of verse 2, since a divided self cannot stand whole before God.

**Types of Trust the Believer Must Tend**

The scholars organized the trusts a person carries into concentric circles, and the arrangement is useful for self-examination.

The trust between the servant and God: the prayer, the fast, the zakāh, the avoidance of what He forbade — all performed even when no human being is watching. Ibn Masʿūd said: *"The first thing you will lose of your religion is trustworthiness, and the last is the prayer."*

The trust of one's own body and faculties: the eye, the ear, the tongue, the mind — lent by God and to be used as He directed. The Qur'an says: *"Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — all of those will be questioned"* (17:36).

The trust of family: the spouse's rights, the children's upbringing, the parents' care. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"It is sufficient sin for a person to neglect those he is responsible for"* (Abū Dāwūd 1692).

The trust of office and work: doing the job one is paid for honestly, refusing bribes, not exploiting position. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever we appoint to a task and provide for, whatever he takes beyond that is embezzlement (ghulūl)"* (Abū Dāwūd 2943).

The trust of speech: the secret confided, the counsel sought. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"When a man tells you something and then looks around, it is a trust"* (Abū Dāwūd 4868; al-Tirmidhī 1959). And: *"The one consulted is entrusted"* (al-Tirmidhī 2822).

The trust of property: deposits, loans, borrowed items, and the funds of others one manages. The Qur'an commands: *"Indeed, God commands you to render trusts to whom they are due"* (4:58).

**Covenants Even with Enemies**

One of the most striking features of the Islamic ethic of covenant is that it binds the believer even toward those who do not share his faith or wish him well. The Qur'an commands fulfillment of treaties with the polytheists as long as they keep them (9:4, 9:7). The Prophet ﷺ honored the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah even when its terms were painful and returned Abū Jandal to the Quraysh because he had given his word. Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān and his father, having been made to promise the Quraysh that they would not fight at Badr, were told by the Prophet ﷺ: *"Go. We will fulfill their covenant and seek God's help against them"* (Muslim 1787). Verse 8 does not say "their covenants with believers" — it says "their covenant," absolutely.

**Practical Application**

The believer today can audit his life against this verse in a few plain questions. Do people get back what they lend me, on time and undamaged? Do I arrive when I said I would arrive? Do secrets stay with me? Do I do the work I am paid for when no one is checking? Do I keep the promises I made to my children, which they remember far longer than I do? Do I fulfill the covenant with God — the prayer at its time — that no one else can verify? Each "yes" is a stone in the house of verse 11; each "no" is a mark, in the Prophet's own words, of the hypocrite. The verse asks the believer to become a person about whom it can be said, as it was said of the Prophet ﷺ before his mission: *al-Amīn* — the one who can be trusted.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:9

> **and who are mindful of their prayers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Portrait Closes Where It Began**

The seventh and last quality of the prosperous believers returns to the subject of the first: prayer. Verse 2 said they are *humble in* their prayers; verse 9 says *wa alladhīna hum ʿalā ṣalawātihim yuḥāfiẓūn* — "and who, over their prayers, keep guard." The list opens and closes with the same act. This ring structure is deliberate and deeply instructive. Prayer is the frame within which every other virtue — the guarded tongue, the open hand, the chaste body, the honored trust — is set. Al-Rāzī observes that beginning and ending with prayer signals its rank as *"the most important of all the acts of obedience,"* and that the two mentions are not redundant, since each names a different aspect of the same act. The first concerns the *quality* of the prayer while one is in it; the second concerns the *constancy* of the prayer across the days of a life.

**Two Words for Two Dimensions: Khushūʿ and Muḥāfaẓah**

The distinction between verse 2 and verse 9 lies in the two verbs. *Khushūʿ* (v. 2) is an inner state during prayer: humility, stillness, presence. *Muḥāfaẓah* (v. 9), from the root *ḥ-f-ẓ* — the same root as *ḥāfiẓūn* in verse 5 — is guardianship over the prayer as a whole: preserving it from being missed, delayed, curtailed, or performed carelessly. The form *yuḥāfiẓūn* (Form III) implies sustained, continuous effort — the way one *maintains* a building or *keeps* a watch — rather than a single act. One can imagine a person who is deeply humble in the prayers he performs but who frequently misses prayers; and one can imagine a person who never misses a prayer but is rarely present in any of them. The sūrah requires both: humble *within* each prayer, and vigilant *over* all of them.

Notice also a small grammatical change. In verse 2 the word was *ṣalātihim* — "their prayer," singular. In verse 9 it is *ṣalawātihim* — "their prayers," plural. The commentators found this significant. Humility (v. 2) is one quality that applies to prayer as a genus; guarding (v. 9) applies to each individual prayer — the dawn, the noon, the afternoon, the sunset, the night — as a distinct appointment that must not be missed. The plural insists that the believer cannot be selective, keeping the convenient prayers and neglecting the inconvenient.

**What Guarding the Prayers Means**

The classical scholars, as the source commentary reflects from al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī, gathered several meanings under *muḥāfaẓah*, all of which are true simultaneously.

First, praying each prayer at its appointed time. This is the most emphasized meaning. The Qur'an declares: *"Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times"* (4:103). When ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd asked the Prophet ﷺ which deed is most beloved to God, he answered: *"The prayer at its time"* (al-Bukhārī 527; Muslim 85). The person who habitually delays prayer until the last moment, or beyond it, has failed to *guard* it even if he eventually performs it. The Prophet ﷺ described the delayed and hurried prayer as *"the prayer of the hypocrite: he sits watching the sun until, when it is between the two horns of Satan, he stands and pecks out four units, remembering God only a little in them"* (Muslim 622).

Second, performing the prayer with its full conditions — ablution, purity, facing the qiblah, covering, and the complete performance of each standing, bowing, and prostration. The Prophet ﷺ called the one who did not complete his bowing and prostration *"the worst thief — the one who steals from his prayer"* (Aḥmad; al-Ḥākim; graded ṣaḥīḥ). Guarding the prayer means not stealing from it.

Third, continuity. The Prophet ﷺ said that the most beloved deeds to God are *"the most consistent, even if small"* (al-Bukhārī 6464; Muslim 783). Guarding implies that the prayer is never abandoned, in travel or illness, in ease or hardship. The Qur'an teaches the prayer of fear for the battlefield (4:102) precisely so that no circumstance is allowed to cancel it.

Fourth, the guarding of the prayer's outer supports: performing the Sunnah prayers that surround the obligatory ones, praying in congregation, and attending to the prayer's etiquette. Ibn Kathīr writes that *muḥāfaẓah* covers *"performing them constantly at their times, as Ibn Masʿūd and Masrūq said."*

**The Prayer as the Boundary of Faith**

The severity with which the Prophet ﷺ treated the neglect of prayer explains why guarding it is the seal of the portrait. Muslim records from Jābir:

> *"Between a man and polytheism and disbelief is the abandonment of the prayer."* (Muslim 82)

And al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī record from Buraydah:

> *"The covenant between us and them is the prayer; whoever abandons it has disbelieved."* (al-Tirmidhī 2621; al-Nasāʾī 463; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The Companions understood this. ʿAbdullāh ibn Shaqīq said: *"The Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ did not consider the abandonment of any deed to be disbelief except the prayer"* (al-Tirmidhī 2622). Whatever the juristic details of the ruling on the one who neglects prayer — and the schools differed over whether the abandonment is disbelief that removes one from Islam or a grave sin short of it — the consensus is that prayer is the boundary line of the community. The person who guards it stands inside; the person who abandons it stands at the edge, at best. This is why the portrait of the prosperous cannot end without returning to it.

**The First Question on the Day of Judgment**

The Prophet ﷺ taught that the prayer is the first deed to be examined:

> *"The first of his deeds for which a servant will be held to account on the Day of Resurrection is his prayer. If it is sound, he has succeeded and prospered (aflaḥa wa anjaḥa); and if it is defective, he has failed and lost. If something is deficient in his obligatory prayer, the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, will say: 'Look whether My servant has any voluntary prayers,' and the obligatory will be completed from them. Then the rest of his deeds will be dealt with in the same way."* (al-Tirmidhī 413; Abū Dāwūd 864; al-Nasāʾī 465; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The words are exact: *aflaḥa* — the very verb of verse 1. The Prophet ﷺ described the outcome of the first question in the vocabulary of this sūrah's opening. The one whose prayers were guarded is the one who "has prospered." Verse 9 is the door through which the promise of verse 1 is entered. The ḥadīth also illuminates the fourth meaning of *muḥāfaẓah* mentioned above: the voluntary prayers are the reserve from which deficiencies in the obligatory are repaired, and the person who guards his prayer builds that reserve.

**Why the Frame Is Prayer**

There is wisdom in making prayer both the opening and the closing of the believer's portrait. Prayer is the one act that recurs five times daily, structuring time itself. Every other quality in the list is practiced intermittently: one gives zakāh yearly, keeps trusts when entrusted, guards chastity when tempted, turns from idle talk when it arises. Prayer alone is a fixed rhythm, independent of circumstance, and it is this rhythm that keeps the other qualities alive. The Prophet ﷺ compared it to a river:

> *"Do you think that if there were a river at the door of one of you in which he bathed five times a day, any dirt would remain on him?" They said: "No dirt would remain." He said: "That is the likeness of the five prayers; God erases sins by them."* (al-Bukhārī 528; Muslim 667)

The person who bathes five times daily in that river returns, each time, to the humility of verse 2, and leaves, each time, better able to guard his tongue, his wealth, his body, and his word. Prayer is not one virtue among seven; it is the engine of the other six. That is why the list begins and ends with it.

**An Analogy: The Guard Who Never Leaves His Post**

The word *muḥāfaẓah* evokes a sentry who keeps watch through the night. A sentry who is alert for an hour and then sleeps has not guarded the camp; a sentry who stands at his post the whole night has, even if the hours were tedious. The believer who prays only when he feels spiritual, or when it is convenient, or when others are watching, is the sleeping sentry. The believer who rises for Fajr in winter, who leaves the meeting for Ẓuhr, who pulls the car over for Maghrib on the road, is the sentry who kept his post. The verse honors constancy more than intensity — not because intensity is unimportant (verse 2 demanded it) but because a life is made of ordinary days, and guarding the prayers on ordinary days is what carries a person to the Garden.

**Practical Steps**

Guarding the prayers in the modern day requires deliberate structures. The believer should know the prayer times of his location and arrange his schedule around them rather than the reverse — the Prophet ﷺ described the believer who *"guards"* the prayers as one who prays them *"at their beginning times"* whenever possible. He should treat the prayer as an appointment more binding than any meeting, since it is an appointment with God. He should use the voluntary prayers as insurance, as the ḥadīth above indicates. He should pray in congregation when he can, since the Prophet ﷺ said the congregation prayer is *"twenty-seven degrees"* better than the individual (al-Bukhārī 645; Muslim 650). And he should remember that the guarding is mutual: the Prophet ﷺ transmitted from his Lord that *"whoever guards them will have a covenant with God to enter him into Paradise"* (Abū Dāwūd 1420; al-Nasāʾī 461).

**The Portrait Completed**

With verse 9 the description of the prosperous believer is complete. Seven qualities have been named: humility in prayer, turning from idle talk, giving alms, guarding chastity (with its lawful exception and its limit), keeping trusts and covenants, and guarding the prayers. The list is bracketed by prayer, structured to move from God to self to wealth to others and back to God. The next two verses will pronounce the verdict on those who possess these qualities — the inheritance that awaits them.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:10

> **It is they who are the heirs,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict Pronounced**

The seven qualities have been listed; now the sentence is passed: *ulāʾika hum al-wārithūn* — "Those — they are the heirs." The verse is brief, but its grammar is charged. The demonstrative *ulāʾika* ("those") points back to everyone described in verses 2–9, gathering all seven qualities into a single referent. The separating pronoun *hum* ("they") between subject and predicate produces exclusivity: *they* — and no one else — are the heirs. And the definite article on *al-wārithūn* ("*the* heirs") completes the restriction: not "heirs" among others, but *the* heirs, the true and rightful ones. The same emphatic construction appeared in verse 7 for the transgressors (*ulāʾika hum al-ʿādūn*) and appears in 2:5 for the reverent (*ulāʾika hum al-mufliḥūn*). The sūrah sets the believers and the transgressors face to face using the same grammatical form, so that the hearer understands there are two definite categories and no third.

**The Language of Inheritance**

The word *al-wārithūn* is the plural of *wārith*, "heir," from the root *w-r-th*, which means to inherit — to receive property or position from one who has passed on. God Himself is called *al-Wārith*, the Inheritor, because He remains after all things pass and to Him everything returns: *"Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritor"* (15:23). The verse's choice of this word for the believers' relationship to Paradise is arresting. One might have expected "those are the winners" or "those are the rewarded." Instead the Qur'an uses a term from the law of succession. Why?

The classical commentators offered several complementary explanations. First, inheritance is the most secure form of ownership: an inheritor does not have to purchase, negotiate, or compete; the estate comes to him by right, as a settled matter. By calling the believers heirs, the verse conveys that Paradise is theirs by a title as firm as any heir's title to his father's house. Second, inheritance implies that something is received without having been earned by equivalent exchange — the heir did not build the house. This preserves the Qur'anic teaching that Paradise is ultimately a gift of divine mercy, not a wage precisely proportioned to human work. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God envelops me in His mercy"* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816). The deeds of verses 2–9 are the conditions of heirship, not the price of the estate.

Third, and most remarkably, there is a Prophetic explanation that gives the word a literal application. Ibn Mājah and others record from Abū Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> *"There is none of you but has two abodes: an abode in Paradise and an abode in the Fire. When he dies and enters the Fire, the people of Paradise inherit his abode; and that is the meaning of God's words: 'It is they who are the heirs.'"* (Ibn Mājah 4341; a similar report is in al-Bukhārī 6569 without the verse citation: "No one enters Paradise but he is shown his place in the Fire had he done evil, so that he may be more grateful; and no one enters the Fire but he is shown his place in Paradise had he done good, so that it may be a source of regret for him.")

According to this explanation, every human being was created with a potential place in the Garden. Those who forfeit it by disbelief leave their portion vacant, and the believers inherit it, so that the Garden is filled and nothing is wasted. The believers are "heirs" in the fullest legal sense: they receive an estate left behind by those who died without claiming it. Ibn Kathīr cites this ḥadīth in explaining the verse and considers it the most direct interpretation. It also gives a sober meaning to the sūrah's later verses: the mockers who laughed at the believers (23:110) will discover in the Hereafter that the believers now possess what could have been theirs.

**Inheritance and the Qur'an's Wider Usage**

The Qur'an uses the language of inheriting Paradise in several places, and reading them together enriches this verse. The people of the Garden, when they enter, are told: *"And it will be called out to them: 'This is the Garden which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do'"* (7:43). Abraham prayed: *"And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss"* (26:85). And at the close of Sūrah al-Zumar the people of Paradise say: *"Praise be to God, who fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the earth (of Paradise), that we may settle in the Garden wherever we will"* (39:74). In each case the word conveys the settled, permanent, rightful possession of the heir who has come into his estate.

The Qur'an also speaks of the righteous inheriting the *earth*: *"Indeed, We have written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants"* (21:105). Some commentators read this as a promise of worldly authority to the community that fulfills the conditions of verses 2–9; others read it as the earth of Paradise. Both readings converge on the principle that the qualities of the believer are not merely private virtues but the very conditions of stewardship — of inheriting whatever God chooses to entrust.

**Why the Verdict Precedes the Naming of the Estate**

The verse says the believers are heirs but does not yet say what they inherit; that is left to verse 11. This delay is rhetorically effective. The listener hears "heirs" and immediately asks, "Heirs of what?" — and the answer, when it comes, is the highest word in the Qur'an's vocabulary of reward: Firdaws. The suspense of a single verse magnifies the estate. The technique also mirrors the structure of the whole passage: verse 1 announced prosperity without defining it; verses 2–9 defined the prosperous; verse 10 declares them heirs; verse 11 names the inheritance. Promise, conditions, verdict, reward — the sūrah's opening is a complete legal and spiritual transaction.

**The Psychology of Being an Heir**

There is a difference between how a hired worker and an heir relate to the future. The worker fears dismissal; the heir waits with confidence for what is already his. The Qur'an's choice of "heir" is meant to shape the believer's inner state. The person who has the seven qualities is not to live in anxious uncertainty about whether God will "hire" him into Paradise; he is to live as an heir — grateful, expectant, and careful not to forfeit the estate. This matches the sūrah's opening in the perfect tense (*qad aflaḥa*, "they *have* prospered"): the believer's success is spoken of as accomplished.

At the same time, the verse guards against complacency, because an heir can be disinherited. The Qur'an warns those who were given the Book before and then *"inherited the Book"* only to take the goods of this world (7:169). The qualities of verses 2–9 are not a one-time qualification but a continuing state, as the active participles of each verse showed. The heir keeps his title as long as he remains the person described. This balance — confidence without complacency, hope without presumption — is exactly the equilibrium the Prophet ﷺ described when he said that if the believer knew the full extent of God's punishment he would despair of Paradise, and if the disbeliever knew the full extent of God's mercy he would not despair of it (Muslim 2755).

**A Modern Reflection: What Is Truly Inherited**

In the modern world, inheritance is one of the few forms of wealth that people receive without earning, and it is often the source of family conflict, envy, and legal battle. The Qur'an takes this universally understood concept and redirects it. The greatest inheritance is not the estate a parent leaves, which is divided, diminished by taxes, and eventually spent, but the estate God has prepared, which is *"a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth"* (3:133), undivided, undiminished, and eternal. The person who spends his life scheming for the first inheritance while neglecting the conditions of the second has, in the Qur'an's estimation, misjudged which estate is worth having. The believer, by contrast, invests in the qualities of verses 2–9 with the composure of someone who knows that his true inheritance is secure and awaiting him.

**The Verse as a Turning Point**

Verse 10 is the hinge of the sūrah's opening. Before it, the text describes; after it, the text rewards. The seven qualities have been laid down like the conditions of a will. Now the will is read: those described are the heirs. The next verse will name the estate, and with it the opening of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn will be complete — a portrait, a verdict, and a Garden.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:11

> **who shall inherit Paradise, abiding therein.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Estate Named**

The suspense of verse 10 is resolved: *alladhīna yarithūna al-firdawsa hum fīhā khālidūn* — "those who will inherit al-Firdaws; they will abide therein forever." The heirs have been identified; now the inheritance is named, and it is not simply "the Garden" (*al-jannah*), the Qur'an's general term for Paradise, but *al-Firdaws* — a word the Qur'an uses only twice, here and in Sūrah al-Kahf, where it is likewise the reward of *"those who believe and do righteous deeds"* (18:107). The sūrah began with the general promise of prosperity (v. 1) and ends its opening passage with the most specific and exalted reward in its vocabulary. This is the summit of the portrait.

**The Word Firdaws and Its Meaning**

The word *firdaws* entered Arabic from an older Iranian source; the Old Persian *pairidaēza* meant a walled enclosure or garden, and it passed into Greek as *paradeisos* and thence into English as "paradise." The source commentary rightly notes the shared etymology. The Arabs used *firdaws* before Islam to mean a garden that contains grapevines and every kind of tree, and the lexicographers (as al-Qurṭubī records) defined it as *al-bustān alladhī fīhi al-karm* — the garden with vines — or, more broadly, a garden that gathers every desirable plant. Al-Ṭabarī transmits from Mujāhid that Firdaws in the Roman (Greek) tongue is *al-bustān*, the garden; from Kaʿb that it is *"the garden in which are grapevines"*; and from others that it is the highest and best part of Paradise. Whatever its linguistic origin, the Qur'an appropriated the word and gave it a technical meaning that the Prophet ﷺ defined with precision.

**The Prophet's Description of Firdaws**

The most important commentary on this verse is the Prophet's own instruction on what Firdaws is and how to ask for it. Al-Bukhārī records from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"Whoever believes in God and His Messenger, establishes the prayer, and fasts Ramaḍān, it is a right upon God to admit him to Paradise, whether he fought in the way of God or sat in the land in which he was born." They said: "O Messenger of God, shall we not give the people the good news?" He said: "In Paradise there are a hundred degrees which God has prepared for those who strive in His way; between each two degrees is a distance like that between the heaven and the earth. So when you ask God, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middlemost of Paradise and the highest of Paradise, and above it is the Throne of the Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth."* (al-Bukhārī 2790)

Three facts about Firdaws emerge from this authentic report. It is the *middle* of Paradise (*awsaṭ al-jannah*), which in Arabic idiom means its best and most excellent part, as one says "the middle of the necklace" for its finest jewel. It is the *highest* of Paradise (*aʿlā al-jannah*), directly beneath the Throne of the Merciful. And it is the *source* of Paradise's rivers, which flow downward from it to every other garden. Everything else in Paradise, in other words, is watered from the estate the believers of verses 2–9 inherit.

Al-Tirmidhī and others record a parallel from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit in which the Prophet ﷺ adds: *"Paradise has a hundred degrees... and Firdaws is the highest of them; from it the four rivers of Paradise gush forth, and above it is the Throne. So when you ask God, ask Him for Firdaws"* (al-Tirmidhī 2531). The Prophet ﷺ did not tell his community to aim low. Having described the loftiest place, he commanded: *ask for that*.

**Firdaws Planted by God's Hand**

There is also a report, transmitted by al-Ṭabarī and cited by Ibn Kathīr, in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"God planted the Garden of Firdaws with His Hand"* — and some versions add that He then said: *"Truly the believers have prospered"* (23:1). The version that reaches the Prophet ﷺ is contested in its chain, but the meaning is supported by the general Qur'anic and Prophetic teaching that Firdaws is the choicest portion of Paradise. It connects verse 11 back to verse 1 and completes the ring: the sūrah began with God's declaration of prosperity and ends its opening with the garden that, in this report, occasioned that declaration.

**A Companion's Mother and the Word Firdaws**

Al-Bukhārī records a moving report that shows how the first Muslims heard this word. When Ḥārithah ibn Surāqah was killed by a stray arrow at Badr, his mother came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of God, you know the place Ḥārithah held in my heart. If he is in Paradise I will be patient and hope for reward; but if it is otherwise, you will see what I do." The Prophet ﷺ replied:

> *"Woe to you — or, have you lost your mind? Is it one Garden? They are many gardens, and he is in Firdaws al-Aʿlā (the Highest Firdaws)."* (al-Bukhārī 2809)

The answer teaches two things. First, Paradise is not a single undifferentiated place; it is many gardens in ascending degrees, and Firdaws is the summit. Second, a young man who had fulfilled the conditions of this sūrah — belief, prayer, and giving his life in the way of God — was placed by the Prophet's own testimony in the very estate verse 11 names. The word was not an abstraction to the Companions; it was where they hoped to find their sons.

**"Abiding Therein": The Meaning of Khulūd**

The verse ends with *hum fīhā khālidūn* — "they, in it, are abiding forever." The word *khālid* comes from the root *kh-l-d*, which means to remain, to endure, to be permanent. Its opposite is everything the human being knows: the flower that wilts, the house that crumbles, the body that ages, the pleasure that fades. The Qur'an emphasizes eternity in nearly every description of Paradise because the human heart cannot rest in a good it knows will end. A vacation is shadowed by its last day; a beautiful season by the approach of winter. Firdaws is the good without a last day.

The Prophet ﷺ described the moment when this permanence is announced:

> *"When the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, death will be brought in the form of a ram and made to stand between Paradise and the Fire. It will be said: 'O people of Paradise, do you know this?' They will look and say: 'Yes, this is death.' It will be said: 'O people of the Fire, do you know this?' They will look and say: 'Yes, this is death.' Then it will be slaughtered, and it will be said: 'O people of Paradise — eternity, and no death; O people of the Fire — eternity, and no death.'"* Then he recited: *"And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be decided"* (19:39). (al-Bukhārī 4730; Muslim 2849)

And Muslim records the caller who will announce to the people of Paradise: *"It is for you to be healthy and never fall ill, to live and never die, to be young and never grow old, and to enjoy bliss and never be miserable"* (Muslim 2837). The word *khālidūn* in this verse is the promise of that announcement.

Again the pronoun *hum* is used — "*they* in it are abiding" — with the same emphasis as the previous verses. The believers' possession of Firdaws is exclusive and their permanence in it is settled. Nothing about the transaction is provisional.

**Why Firdaws Is the Fitting Reward for These Seven Qualities**

There is a proportion between the conditions and the prize. The seven qualities of verses 2–9 are demanding precisely because they touch every area of life — worship, speech, wealth, desire, relationships — and because they require constancy (the active participles of every verse). A reward that touched only one area, or that lasted only for a time, would be no fit return for a whole life so ordered. Firdaws — the *center*, the *summit*, the *source* — matches a life in which God was made the center, the highest concern, and the source of every motive. The Qur'an states the principle of proportion elsewhere: *"Is the reward for excellence (iḥsān) anything but excellence?"* (55:60).

There is also a logic in the sūrah's *ordering*: the highest garden is named *after* the list of deeds, not before. God does not dangle the reward and then extract the price; He describes a certain kind of human being, and then reveals that such a human being has, by becoming that, already come into an estate. The reward is less a payment than a destination that the character itself was traveling toward.

**The Verse as an Instruction to Aim High**

The most practical lesson of verse 11 comes from the Prophet's command: *"When you ask God, ask Him for Firdaws."* The believer is not to be satisfied with the minimum — with merely escaping the Fire or entering the lowest garden. He is to set his sights on the summit. This has an immediate effect on ambition. The person who aims at Firdaws will not be content with a distracted prayer, an occasional charity, a mostly-guarded tongue. He will pursue the seven qualities with the seriousness of someone competing for the highest prize. The Qur'an commands this competitiveness: *"And for this let the competitors compete"* (83:26); *"So race to the good"* (2:148). Verse 11 tells the believer what is at the finish line.

**The Opening Passage as a Whole**

With verse 11 the sūrah's first movement is complete. It has told us who succeeds (v. 1), what they are like (vv. 2–9), what they are (v. 10), and what they receive (v. 11). The passage is a miniature of the entire Qur'anic message: faith, character, and destiny bound together in a single sentence eleven verses long. The Prophet ﷺ, according to the report of ʿUmar cited in the introduction, said of these verses: *"whoever establishes them will enter Paradise."* And ʿĀʾishah, asked about his character, recited them and said: *"Thus was the character of the Messenger of God."* The reader who has followed these eleven verses now possesses a description of the man to whom they were revealed and of the destination he was promised.

The sūrah will now change register. Having shown the believers and their reward, it will turn in verse 12 to the origin of the human being from clay, and lay before the reader the evidence — in his own body, in the sky, in rain and fruit and cattle — of the God whose Garden has just been described.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:12

> **And indeed We created man from a draught of clay.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A New Movement: From the Destination to the Origin**

The sūrah has just described the believer's destination — Firdaws, the highest garden, forever. Now it turns abruptly to his origin: *wa laqad khalaqnā al-insāna min sulālatin min ṭīn* — "And indeed We created man from an extract of clay." The movement from verse 11 to verse 12 spans the entire arc of human existence, from the loftiest end to the humblest beginning. The juxtaposition is purposeful. Having promised the heir a kingdom, God reminds him what he is made of. The person who has just heard that he may inherit the summit of Paradise is told, in the next breath, that he began as a filtrate of mud. The lesson is at once humbling and exalting: the raw material was clay, and the destiny is the Throne's shadow; the distance between them is the measure of divine generosity.

There is also an argumentative purpose. Verses 12–16 lay out the stages of human creation and conclude with death and resurrection. The sequence is one of the Qur'an's most frequent proofs of the Hereafter: the One who brought a thinking, feeling, speaking creature out of clay and a drop of fluid can bring him again out of dust. The sūrah will later quote the deniers asking, *"When we are dead and are dust and bones, shall we be resurrected?"* (23:82). Verse 12 has already answered them before they speak: you were dust once, and here you are.

**The Oath-Like Opening: Wa Laqad**

The verse begins with *wa laqad* — "and indeed, certainly" — a combination of the emphatic particle *la-* and the confirming *qad*. The *lām* here is often understood as the *lām* of an implied oath ("By God, We have certainly..."). The Qur'an uses this opening to introduce truths it wishes the listener to receive as established beyond dispute. Six of the following verses (12, 17, and the beginning of the Noah narrative at 23) open with this same emphatic formula, so that the sūrah's second movement is a series of solemn affirmations laid down one after another like foundation stones.

**Who Is "Man" Here?**

The word *al-insān* — "the human being" — is definite and generic. The commentators, as the source notes from al-Ṭabarī, differed over its reference. Some, including Qatādah and Mujāhid as al-Ṭabarī transmits, held that *al-insān* here is Adam specifically, since only he was created directly from clay; the subsequent verses (*"Then We made him a drop"*) would then refer to his descendants, the pronoun shifting from Adam to his progeny. Others held that *al-insān* refers to every human being, since every person is ultimately from clay through Adam, and since the food that becomes the reproductive fluid grows from the earth. Al-Rāzī records the view that the clay is itself a reference to Adam, so that the verse means: "We created the human being from an extract drawn from Adam, who was of clay."

The most satisfying reading holds both together. Adam was created from clay directly; every descendant is created from clay indirectly, through the chain of nourishment that begins in soil and ends in the drop. The word *sulālah* — "extract" — supports this comprehensive reading, as we will see. The Qur'an elsewhere addresses all humanity with the same fact: *"O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop..."* (22:5), where "you" is plainly every listener.

**The Word Sulālah: What Is Drawn Out**

The word *sulālah* is derived from the root *s-l-l*, which means to draw something out gently from something else — as a sword is drawn from its sheath (*salla al-sayf*), or as a hair is pulled from dough. The form *fuʿālah* in Arabic denotes the product or residue of an action: *qulāmah* is what is pared from a fingernail, *kunāsah* what is swept up, *ṣubābah* what remains in the cup. *Sulālah* is therefore "that which is drawn out" — the extract, the quintessence, the fine filtrate obtained by drawing the essential from the gross. Al-Zamakhsharī defines it as *"the pure essence that is extracted from a thing."* Ibn ʿAbbās, as al-Ṭabarī transmits, glossed it as *ṣafwat al-māʾ* — the pure part of the fluid — and others as *khulāṣat al-ṭīn*, the purified essence of clay.

The precision of this word rewards attention. God does not say He created man "from clay" simply, as He does in other verses (e.g., 6:2; 7:12; 38:71), but "from an *extract* of clay." The word implies a process of selection and refinement: from the whole mass of earth, a fine portion was drawn out; from that portion, the human body was fashioned. Whether one reads this of Adam, whose clay was, in the reports, gathered from all the earth and refined, or of his descendants, whose bodies are built from the finest nutrients extracted by digestion from food grown in soil, the word captures the same reality — the human being is the distilled essence of the earth.

**Clay in the Qur'an's Vocabulary of Creation**

The Qur'an describes the original substance of the human being with a family of related words, each highlighting a different stage or aspect. It is *turāb*, dust (3:59; 22:5); *ṭīn*, clay — dust mixed with water (6:2; 7:12; 32:7); *ṭīn lāzib*, sticky clay (37:11); *ḥamaʾ masnūn*, dark altered mud (15:26, 28, 33); and *ṣalṣāl ka'l-fakhkhār*, dried clay like pottery that rings when struck (55:14). These are not contradictory; the commentators understood them as the successive states of a single material: dry dust, moistened into clay, kneaded until sticky, left until it darkened, and finally dried until it rang. The verse before us uses *ṭīn*, clay, and adds *sulālah* to indicate that it was the refined part of that clay.

The Qur'an also names the *other* origin, the drop of fluid — *nuṭfah* (16:4; 36:77), *māʾ mahīn*, a despised fluid (32:8; 77:20), *māʾ dāfiq*, a gushing fluid (86:6). Verses 12 and 13 of this sūrah set the two origins side by side: clay for the species, the drop for the individual. Ibn Kathīr comments that the verse *"refers to Adam, whom God created from an extract of clay,"* and then explains that the following verse moves to his offspring.

**Why God Reminds Us of Clay**

The Qur'an returns to the human origin from clay repeatedly, and it does so for reasons that touch both belief and character.

For belief: the argument from origin is the Qur'an's most accessible proof of resurrection. Every listener knows he did not exist, then existed. The material of his body was, not long ago, soil in a field; through plants and animals it entered him and became eye, brain, and hand. If that transformation happened once — demonstrably, before our eyes, in every child born — the claim that it can happen again after death is not a leap but an inference. The Qur'an makes this explicit: *"He who created you the first time will bring you back"* (17:51), and: *"Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time"* (36:79).

For character: the memory of clay is the antidote to arrogance. Iblīs's original sin was contempt for clay — *"I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay"* (7:12) — and every human arrogance repeats his error in miniature. The person who remembers that he is filtered mud does not look down on another person who is filtered mud. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"God has removed from you the arrogance of the Age of Ignorance and its boasting about ancestors. People are of two kinds: a righteous believer who is dear to God, or a wicked sinner who is worthless to God. People are all the children of Adam, and Adam was from dust"* (al-Tirmidhī 3955; Abū Dāwūd 5116). Verse 12 is the theological basis of human equality: one origin, one substance, one Maker.

**The Marriage of Humility and Honor**

Notice how the verse holds two truths in balance. On one side, the material is lowly: clay, earth, the stuff one walks on. On the other side, the agent is God Himself — *khalaqnā*, "*We* created," in the majestic plural — and the product is *al-insān*, the being whom God honored, to whom He taught the names of all things, before whom He commanded the angels to prostrate. The verse does not say "man is mere clay"; it says God *created* man *from* clay. The preposition *min* ("from") marks the starting point, not the identity. A cathedral is built *from* stone, but it is not merely stone; a symphony is made *from* vibrations of air, but it is not merely noise. The lowliness of the material glorifies the Maker and should humble the made — but the making itself confers a dignity that the material never had.

**The Spiritual Reading: Clay and the Receptive Heart**

The spiritual commentators drew a further lesson from the choice of clay. Clay is the most receptive of materials: it takes whatever shape the potter gives it, and it is fertile — seeds planted in it grow. The human being is likewise the most receptive of creatures, able to be shaped by revelation and to bring forth fruit. But clay that becomes too dry cracks and cannot be worked, and the Qur'an describes hardened hearts as *"like stones, or even harder"* (2:74). The believer who remembers his origin in *moist* clay — *ṭīn*, not *ṣakhr* — asks God to keep his heart soft enough to be shaped. The sūrah's opening verses described exactly such a heart: humble in prayer, turning from what is idle, giving, guarding, keeping trust.

**A Reflection for the Present Age**

Modern science has confirmed, in its own terms, what this verse states: the human body is built from the same elements found in the earth's crust — oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus, and the rest — assembled through nutrition from soil-grown food. No element in a human being is foreign to the clay. The believer does not need this confirmation to accept the verse, but he may notice that the more precisely the origin of the body is understood, the more exactly the Qur'an's words fit. What science cannot supply is the *khalaqnā* — the Agent who drew the extract from the clay and made it a person. That is the verse's true subject, and it is the subject to which the next two verses will return with increasing wonder as they trace the drop, the clot, the lump, the bones, and finally "another creation."

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:13

> **Then We made him a drop in a secure dwelling place.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Species to the Individual**

Verse 12 described the origin of the human race from an extract of clay; verse 13 describes the origin of every individual human being: *thumma jaʿalnāhu nuṭfatan fī qarārin makīn* — "Then We placed him as a drop in a firm lodging." The connecting word *thumma* ("then") marks a sequence, and the pronoun "him" carries forward the *insān* of the previous verse. If verse 12 spoke of Adam, verse 13 speaks of his descendants, each of whom begins not from clay directly but from a drop. If verse 12 spoke of the species collectively, verse 13 narrows the lens to the single life, the one conception, the one womb. Either way, the transition is from the general fact of human createdness to the intimate history of *you*, the listener.

The verb also changes. Verse 12 used *khalaqnā*, "We created"; verse 13 uses *jaʿalnā*, "We made" or "We placed." *Khalq* is bringing into being; *jaʿl* is the assignment of a state, a function, or a place. The drop is not a new creation from nothing; it is the human material *assigned* to a new form and *placed* in a new location. The verb quietly asserts that even at this microscopic stage, when the future person is a fluid invisible to the eye, a divine act of placement is at work.

**The Word Nuṭfah**

*Nuṭfah* comes from the root *n-ṭ-f*, which means to drip or to trickle. A *nuṭfah* is a small quantity of liquid, a drop, or what remains of water in a bucket. The Arabs used it for the seminal fluid, and the Qur'an adopts it throughout its accounts of human origin (16:4; 18:37; 22:5; 35:11; 36:77; 40:67; 53:46; 75:37; 76:2; 80:19). Two of these passages add qualifying words: *nuṭfah amshāj*, "a drop of mingled fluids" (76:2), which the commentators understood as the mixture of the male and female contributions; and *nuṭfatin idhā tumnā*, "a drop when it is emitted" (53:46). In 75:37 the Qur'an asks: *"Was he not a drop of fluid emitted? Then he was a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned."* The word thus designates the very first stage of an individual's existence — the humble, tiny, fluid beginning that no one remembers and few contemplate.

The Qur'an chooses this word deliberately to provoke reflection on origins. In 80:17–19 it rebukes the arrogant human being: *"Cursed is man; how ungrateful he is! From what did He create him? From a drop He created him and proportioned him."* And in 36:77: *"Does man not see that We created him from a drop — and behold, he is a clear adversary!"* The one who argues against God about the Resurrection is invited to recall that he himself was, not long ago, a drop.

**The Secure Dwelling Place: Qarār Makīn**

The drop is placed *fī qarārin makīn* — "in a firm, secure resting place." The word *qarār* comes from the root *q-r-r*, which means to settle, to become fixed, to be at rest. A *qarār* is a place where something comes to rest and remains — the bottom of a vessel where liquid settles, a settled abode. *Makīn* comes from the root *m-k-n*, which conveys firmness, establishment, and security; it is related to *makān*, place, and *tamkīn*, empowerment or firm establishment. The two words together describe a location that is both a *resting place* and *firmly secured* — a lodging that holds its guest safely.

The commentators unanimously identified this as the womb (*al-raḥim*), and the Qur'an confirms the identification in Sūrah al-Mursalāt: *"Did We not create you from a despised fluid, and place it in a firm lodging (qarārin makīn) for a known term?"* (77:20–22). The same phrase, the same referent. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī explain that the womb is called *makīn* because it is protected in the deepest part of the body, shielded from injury and disturbance, and because God has made it firm enough to hold and nourish the growing child until birth.

**Why the Qur'an Praises the Womb**

The description of the womb as a *secure dwelling* is not merely anatomical; it is an act of directing the listener's attention to a marvel he habitually ignores. Consider what the phrase implies. The drop is the most fragile of substances. Placed anywhere else — on the ground, in the open air — it perishes within moments. God has prepared for it a place that is dark, warm, moist, cushioned, and hidden; a place where it is protected from light, cold, impact, and infection; a place that nourishes it without its asking and holds it without its clinging; a place designed *before* the drop arrives, prepared by cycles that the woman herself does not consciously direct. The Qur'an calls attention to this in the phrase *"in three darknesses"* (39:6), which the commentators understood as the abdominal wall, the womb, and the membranes that enclose the child. The security of the *qarār makīn* is therefore threefold, and its architecture is entirely God's work.

There is also a psychological point. Every human being alive today, including the most powerful and the most proud, spent the first months of his existence in total dependence within this secure lodging. He did not choose it, build it, or defend it. He was placed there by a hand not his own, and kept there by a mercy he did not earn. The Qur'an reminds him of this so that he may recall, in his adulthood, the same dependence. The believer who understands verse 13 does not imagine himself self-made.

**The Prophet's Account of the Womb's Stages**

The Prophet ﷺ described the drop's journey in the womb in a ḥadīth recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd:

> *"Indeed, the creation of each of you is gathered in his mother's womb for forty days as a drop (nuṭfah), then he is a clinging clot (ʿalaqah) for a like period, then a lump of flesh (muḍghah) for a like period. Then the angel is sent to him and breathes the spirit into him, and he is commanded with four words: to write his provision, his lifespan, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed."* (al-Bukhārī 3208; Muslim 2643)

Muslim also records from Ḥudhayfah ibn Asīd that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"When forty-two nights have passed over the drop, God sends to it an angel who shapes it and creates its hearing, sight, skin, flesh, and bones; then he says: 'O Lord, male or female?' And your Lord decrees what He wills, and the angel writes"* (Muslim 2645). These reports show that the *qarār makīn* is not merely a passive container; it is the theater of a supervised process, in which the drop is watched, shaped, and inscribed with a destiny while still invisible to human eyes. The security of the dwelling place includes the security of divine attention.

**The Argument the Verse Is Building**

Verse 13 is the second step in a proof that runs from verse 12 to verse 16. The argument may be stated plainly. Premise one: you began as clay (v. 12). Premise two: you were then a drop, placed by God in the womb (v. 13). Premise three: from that drop, God fashioned, stage by stage, a complete human being (v. 14). Conclusion one: you will die (v. 15). Conclusion two: you will be raised (v. 16). The logical force lies in the *observed* transformations. Everyone concedes that a drop became a person; that is not a matter of faith but of biology. If the greater wonder — a person from a drop — is a fact, then the lesser wonder — a person from his own remains — cannot be dismissed as impossible. The Qur'an makes this inference explicit elsewhere: *"Does man think that he will be left without purpose? Was he not a drop of emitted fluid? Then he was a clinging clot, and He created and proportioned, and made of him two kinds, male and female. Is not that One able to give life to the dead?"* (75:36–40). Verse 13 supplies the "drop" premise of that argument.

**Humility Drawn from a Drop**

The Qur'an's insistence on this origin has a moral aim: to dismantle the arrogance that comes from forgetting where one came from. The sūrah will later portray the *malaʾ* — the wealthy notables — who despised the messengers as mere men "eating what you eat" (23:33), and the Pharaoh who regarded a whole people as "slaves we possess" (23:47). Every such arrogance rests on forgetting verse 13. The notable and the slave, the Pharaoh and the Israelite, began identically: a drop in a secure lodging, unable to feed or protect themselves, entirely at the mercy of the One who placed them there. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said: *"What has the son of Adam to do with pride? His beginning is a drop and his end is a corpse, and between the two he carries filth."* The verse is the Qur'anic root of that saying.

**Gratitude Drawn from Security**

Alongside humility, the verse plants gratitude. The phrase *qarār makīn* invites the listener to recognize that his first home was prepared for him by God through his mother, and this recognition is one of the Qur'anic foundations of the duty to parents: *"And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents; his mother carried him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship"* (46:15). The secure lodging was secure for the child at a cost to the one who provided it. The believer who ponders verse 13 finds within it a reason to honor his mother and a reason to thank the God who made her womb a refuge.

**A Modern Note**

Contemporary embryology has described the womb's protective functions in detail — the implantation of the embryo into the prepared uterine wall, the amniotic fluid that cushions it, the placenta that feeds it and filters harm, the muscular wall that holds it. Every one of these features is a specification of the two words *qarār makīn*: a resting place, firmly secured. The Qur'an did not need to supply the details; it named the reality with a precision that the details confirm. The believer's response is not to marvel at the coincidence but to recognize the Speaker. The One who described the lodging is the One who built it, and He is the One who, in the next verse, will describe what He did within it.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:14

> **Then of the drop We created a blood clot, then of the blood clot We created a lump of flesh, then of the lump of flesh We created bones and We clothed the bones with flesh; then We brought him into being as another creation. Blessed is God, the best of creators!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Longest Verse of the Passage and Its Six Stages**

Verse 14 is the center of the sūrah's meditation on human origins and one of the most detailed embryological statements in the Qur'an. It carries the drop of verse 13 through five further transformations and concludes with a doxology — a burst of praise — that is unique in the Book. The verse reads as a chain, each link introduced by *thumma* ("then") or *fa-* ("and so"): drop → clinging clot → lump of flesh → bones → bones clothed with flesh → "another creation." Then, as though the Speaker Himself pauses in wonder at what He has described, comes the exclamation: *fa-tabāraka Allāhu aḥsanu al-khāliqīn* — "So blessed is God, the best of creators!"

The stages are the same as those in 22:5 and in the ḥadīth of Ibn Masʿūd (al-Bukhārī 3208; Muslim 2643) quoted under the previous verse. But here they are laid out with a syntactic care that the commentators treasured, and each stage deserves its own examination.

**Stage One: The ʿAlaqah**

*Thumma khalaqnā al-nuṭfata ʿalaqah* — "then We created the drop into an *ʿalaqah*." The word *ʿalaqah* comes from the root *ʿ-l-q*, whose core meaning is to cling, to hang, to attach. From this root come *ʿalaq*, the leech (which clings), *ʿalaqa*, to be attached, and *taʿalluq*, attachment or dependence. The classical translation "blood clot" reflects one of the word's senses — a clot of thick blood that clings — and this is how al-Ṭabarī and most early commentators glossed it: *dam ʿabīṭ*, fresh thick blood. But the root meaning is broader, and modern readers have noticed that the embryo at this stage literally *clings* to the wall of the womb and resembles, in shape, the leech that the same root names. The Qur'an's first revealed verses used this very word: *"Recite in the name of your Lord who created; created man from an ʿalaq"* (96:1–2). The word thus has a special place in the Muslim memory — it was the first description of the human being that the Prophet ﷺ ever received.

Note the verb: *khalaqnā*, "We created." The drop did not *become* a clinging thing on its own; God *created* it into that form. Each stage is a distinct creative act. The Qur'an does not describe an automatic unfolding but a series of divine interventions, each producing something the previous stage did not contain.

**Stage Two: The Muḍghah**

*Fa-khalaqnā al-ʿalaqata muḍghah* — "and We created the clinging thing into a *muḍghah*." *Muḍghah* comes from the root *m-ḍ-gh*, to chew, and denotes a piece of flesh the size of a mouthful, of the kind one might chew. Al-Zamakhsharī and others explain that it is called a *muḍghah* because it is a small lump of flesh about the size of what one places in one's mouth. The Qur'an in 22:5 adds a qualifier: *muḍghatin mukhallaqatin wa ghayri mukhallaqah* — "a lump, formed and unformed" — which the commentators understood as the stage at which the features of the body begin to be differentiated, some parts already taking shape while others remain undifferentiated. Some modern readers have also observed that the embryo at this stage bears surface markings resembling teeth impressions, though the classical meaning is simply the chewable-sized lump.

Once more the verb is *khalaqnā*. The lump is *created*, not merely grown.

**Stage Three: The Bones**

*Fa-khalaqnā al-muḍghata ʿiẓāman* — "and We created the lump into bones." From the shapeless lump emerges structure — the skeleton, the framework upon which the body will be built. The word *ʿiẓām* is the ordinary plural of *ʿaẓm*, bone. The classical commentators noted the order: bones *before* flesh. This is the order of construction that any builder would recognize: the frame first, then the covering. The Qur'an describes it as a distinct creative act, because the transformation from a soft lump into a structure that will bear weight and give shape is a qualitative leap, not a mere quantitative increase.

**Stage Four: Bones Clothed with Flesh**

*Fa-kasawnā al-ʿiẓāma laḥmā* — "and We clothed the bones with flesh." Here the verb changes from *khalaqnā*, "We created," to *kasawnā*, "We clothed" or "We dressed." The metaphor is that of a garment: the bones are the body, and the flesh is the clothing placed upon them. Al-Rāzī pauses on the aptness of this image. Clothing fits the wearer, covers what would otherwise be exposed, protects it, and gives it a pleasing appearance; flesh does all this for the skeleton. Moreover, clothing is applied *after* the body exists, which reflects the order the verse establishes. The commentators saw in this verb evidence of divine artistry: God does not merely assemble; He dresses His creation with care, as a tailor fits a garment.

The image also anticipates death and resurrection. In the vision of Ezekiel-like dry bones that the Qur'an alludes to in 2:259 — *"look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh (naksūhā laḥmā)"* — the same verb appears. The God who clothed bones with flesh in the womb will clothe them again in the grave. The verse is quietly preparing the argument of verse 16.

**Stage Five: Another Creation**

*Thumma anshaʾnāhu khalqan ākhar* — "then We brought him forth as another creation." The verb changes a third time: not *khalaqnā*, not *kasawnā*, but *anshaʾnā*, from the root *n-sh-ʾ*, which means to originate, to raise up, to bring into being something that did not exist. The object is *khalqan ākhar*, "another creation," "a different creation." The verse marks this stage off from everything that preceded it by the change of verb, by the word *thumma* (indicating a longer pause or greater interval than *fa-*), and by the description "another." What was this new creation?

The commentators, as the source records, offered several views, and al-Ṭabarī reports them: the breathing of the spirit (*rūḥ*) into the body, so that what was a form becomes a living, sensing person — this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others, and al-Ṭabarī judges it soundest; the emergence of the child from the womb into the world as a new being; the growth of teeth and hair, or the transition through infancy to youth, to adulthood, to old age. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī include the interpretation that it refers to the full maturation of the human being's faculties — reason, speech, discernment — the flowering of the person into a rational, morally responsible creature. Ibn Kathīr, following the majority, explains: *"That is, We breathed the spirit into him, and he became a creature of a different kind, possessing hearing, sight, perception, movement, and disturbance."*

These readings need not compete. Each is a moment at which something categorically new appears — life where there was form, personhood where there was tissue, reason where there was instinct. But the deepest reading is the first, and it is the one supported by the ḥadīth of Ibn Masʿūd: after the stages of drop, clot, and lump, *"the angel is sent to him and breathes the spirit into him."* The body, however perfectly assembled, is not yet a human being. The *khalq ākhar* is the arrival of the soul — the moment the clay-born structure becomes a *person*, a "you," capable of knowing God. This is the single most important fact about human beings, and the verse marks it with its most emphatic verb.

**The Doxology: "Blessed Is God, the Best of Creators"**

Having recounted these stages, the verse concludes with *fa-tabāraka Allāhu aḥsanu al-khāliqīn*. The verb *tabāraka*, from the root *b-r-k*, conveys abundance, permanence, and exaltation; it is used in the Qur'an only of God, and it means that He is the source of all blessing, exalted above every deficiency, and abundant in good. The particle *fa-* ("so") links the praise to what preceded: *because* He did all this, blessed is He.

The phrase *aḥsanu al-khāliqīn*, "the best of creators," raised a theological question that the commentators addressed with care. Does it imply other creators? The answer, as al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and Ibn Kathīr explain, is that the Arabic *khalaqa* has a general meaning of "to fashion, to measure out, to shape" — a carpenter "creates" a chair, a poet "creates" a verse — and in this loose sense human beings are "creators." But only God creates in the true sense: bringing into being from nothing, and giving life. The Qur'an itself uses the word for the shaping done by Jesus with God's permission: *"I create for you from clay the form of a bird"* (3:49). So God is "the best of creators" because His fashioning alone is original, complete, and living, while every human fashioning merely rearranges what He already made. Mujāhid said: *"They fashion (yaṣnaʿūn) and God fashions, and God is the best of fashioners."*

**The Story Behind the Doxology**

There is a famous report, transmitted in the *Sīrah* and tafsīr literature, concerning this phrase. When the verse was being revealed and the Prophet ﷺ dictated it to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (or, in other versions, the scribe reached the words *khalqan ākhar*), ʿUmar exclaimed spontaneously, *"Fa-tabāraka Allāhu aḥsanu al-khāliqīn!"* — and the Prophet ﷺ said that the verse had been revealed with exactly those words. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr mention this among the instances of ʿUmar's "concurrences" (*muwāfaqāt*) with the revelation. The report illustrates the naturalness of the doxology: any believer who follows the stages of the verse to their conclusion is moved to say what ʿUmar said. The praise is not tacked on; it is the only fitting response to what has been described.

(A related report concerns ʿAbdullāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ, a scribe who is said to have made the same exclamation and, when told it matched the revelation, to have apostatized in confusion; he later returned to Islam at the Conquest of Makkah and died a Muslim. The classical scholars treated this report with reservation because of weaknesses in its chain, and it should not be allowed to obscure the sounder point: the doxology is the natural climax of the verse.)

**Why the Stages Are a Proof**

The verse's argumentative purpose is the same as that of 22:5 and 75:37–40: the stages of human creation are an *observed* miracle that establishes the *possibility* of the resurrection. But verse 14 adds something to the argument by its detail. It shows that human creation is not a single act but a sequence of acts, each of which produces what the previous stage did not contain. A drop does not "contain" a clinging clot; a lump does not "contain" bones; bones do not "contain" a soul. At each step, God brings forth something new. The one who watches this sequence — and every parent has watched at least its result — cannot coherently claim that God is unable to bring forth life from bones a second time, since He brought forth bones from a lump and life from bones the first time.

The verse also answers a deeper philosophical objection. The deniers of resurrection often argued from *continuity*: how can the same person be restored after his substance has scattered? The verse replies that personal identity never rested on the continuity of substance in the first place. The person who is now reading this verse shares almost no material with the drop he once was; his cells have been replaced many times over; yet he is the same person. The "other creation" — the soul — is what makes him himself, and God who joined that soul to a body once can join it to a body again.

**Ethical Fruit: The Sanctity of the Unborn**

The verse's description of the embryo's stages became the foundation of Islamic law's protection of unborn life. The jurists derived from the ḥadīth of Ibn Masʿūd that the spirit enters at one hundred and twenty days, and they treated the destruction of the fetus after ensoulment as a form of homicide requiring blood-money (*ghurrah*); many restricted abortion even before that point to cases of genuine necessity. Whatever the details of the juristic debate, the principle is clear: what God is *creating* stage by stage in the *secure lodging* is not tissue but a person in formation, and the verse's reverence for that process — culminating in "blessed is God" — forbids treating it lightly.

**A Verse to Live With**

For the believer, verse 14 is a meditation to return to. It invites him to look at his own hand and see in it clay, drop, clot, lump, bone, flesh, and soul — six divine acts, each one gratuitous, none of which he requested or deserved. It invites him, when he looks at another human being, to see the same six acts and to honor them. It invites him, when he holds a newborn, to say what ʿUmar said. And it invites him, when he doubts the resurrection or fears death, to recall that the God who did all this in the darkness of the womb, without his knowledge or consent, has promised to do it again in the darkness of the grave, and that He who has done the harder thing will not fail at the easier. *Blessed is God, the best of creators.*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:15

> **Then indeed you shall die thereafter.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence That Follows Every Life**

The previous verse ended in a burst of praise for the God who fashioned the human being through six stages of creation. Verse 15 delivers, without transition or softening, the next fact in the sequence: *thumma innakum baʿda dhālika la-mayyitūn* — "Then indeed, after that, you will surely be dead." The verse is short, but every word in it is emphatic. *Thumma*, "then," continues the chain of *thumma*s that structured verse 14; death is simply the next link. *Inna*, "indeed," asserts certainty. *Baʿda dhālika*, "after that," refers back to the whole marvelous process just described. The *lām* of emphasis on *la-mayyitūn* — "you will *surely* be dead" — adds a further layer of assurance. And the active participle *mayyitūn*, rather than the verb *tamūtūn* ("you will die"), describes death not merely as an event that will occur but as a state that awaits — you are, in effect, already the dying.

There is also a change of address. Verses 12–14 spoke of "man" and "him" in the third person; verse 15 turns to the listener directly: *innakum* — "*you*." The Speaker is no longer describing a species; He is addressing each person who hears the verse, telling him what will happen to him. The shift makes the verse impossible to hold at arm's length. The reader who admired the embryology of verse 14 as a description of humanity in general is now told: this is *your* story, and its next chapter is your death.

**Why Death Follows Immediately Upon Praise**

The placement of this verse is one of the sūrah's most powerful rhetorical moves. Verse 14 built up a crescendo of creative acts and crowned it with *"Blessed is God, the best of creators."* One might have expected the passage to linger there, in wonder. Instead, the very next word is death. Why?

First, honesty. The Qur'an never flatters its listener. Having shown him the extraordinary care with which he was made, it does not allow him to conclude that he is therefore permanent. The masterpiece of creation is mortal; the being God shaped through six stages will be laid in a grave. The juxtaposition guards against the arrogance that admiration of one's own design might produce.

Second, argument. The sequence creation → death → resurrection is a single proof, and death is its middle term. The commentators note that the verse cites 7:25 as its parallel: *"He said: 'Therein you shall live, and therein you shall die, and from it you shall be brought forth.'"* Life, death, and resurrection are three acts of one Agent. By inserting death between the creation of verse 14 and the resurrection of verse 16, the sūrah shows that death is not the negation of God's creative work but a stage within it — as much a divine act as the drop and the clot. The Qur'an states this explicitly: *"He who created death and life to test you"* (67:2). Death is *created*; it is something God makes, not something that escapes His making.

Third, urgency. The seven qualities of verses 2–9 and the inheritance of Firdaws in verse 11 are not to be pursued at leisure. The listener has a deadline. Verse 15 reminds him that the window in which humility, restraint, charity, chastity, fidelity, and prayer can be practiced is closing.

**The Certainty of Death in the Qur'an**

No fact is asserted in the Qur'an with more uniformity than death. *"Every soul shall taste death"* (3:185; 21:35; 29:57). *"Indeed, you are mortal and they are mortal"* (39:30) — addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself. *"Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you were in lofty towers"* (4:78). *"Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you; then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the seen"* (62:8). The Qur'an calls death *al-yaqīn*, "the certainty" (15:99), because it is the one future event about which no human being can entertain a rational doubt. Everything else — wealth, health, marriage, children, success — is uncertain; death alone is guaranteed.

The Prophet ﷺ described its inevitability with the image of a shadow: *"Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him"* (al-Bukhārī 6507; Muslim 2683), and he taught the Companions to say when passing a grave: *"Peace be upon you, O abode of a believing people; and we, God willing, shall join you"* (Muslim 249). The "God willing" in that greeting is not about *whether* but about *when* and *in what state*; the joining itself is certain.

**Why Death Is Called "The Certainty" Yet Is So Rarely Faced**

The verse's heavy emphasis — *inna*, *la-*, the participle — is directed against a peculiar human blindness. Everyone knows he will die; almost no one lives as though he knows it.
