The Prophet ﷺ diagnosed this precisely when he said: *"The hearts of the children of Adam are all heedless of death, though they see the dead"* — a saying transmitted in the wisdom literature — and when he described the human being as one who *"grows old, and two things in him remain young: greed for wealth and greed for life"* (al-Bukhārī 6421; Muslim 1047). Death is the fact we know best and think about least.

The Qur'an's remedy is the frequent, deliberate remembrance of death, which the Prophet ﷺ prescribed in unmistakable terms:

> *"Remember often the destroyer of pleasures — death."* (al-Tirmidhī 2307; al-Nasāʾī 1824; Ibn Mājah 4258; graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ)

He called death *hādhim al-ladhdhāt*, "the destroyer of pleasures," because the thought of it cuts through every worldly indulgence and restores proportion. The person who remembers that he will *surely* be dead does not sell his Hereafter for a bribe, does not hold a grudge for decades, does not postpone repentance, and does not pray as though he had a thousand more prayers to perform. Ibn ʿUmar said the Prophet ﷺ took him by the shoulder and said: *"Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveler passing through"* — and Ibn ʿUmar used to add: *"When evening comes, do not expect the morning; and when morning comes, do not expect the evening. Take from your health for your sickness and from your life for your death"* (al-Bukhārī 6416).

**The Wisdom of Being Made Mortal**

Why did God make the being He fashioned so carefully subject to death? The Qur'an gives several answers, and reflecting on them turns the verse from a threat into an explanation.

Death is the condition of the test. *"He who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed"* (67:2). A test with no end is no test; the examination must close for the paper to be graded. Death is the closing of the examination room.

Death is the door to the reward. The believers of verses 2–9 inherit Firdaws (v. 11), but Firdaws lies on the other side of death. The Prophet ﷺ described the believer's death as *"a gift"* and taught that *"the believer's soul, when it departs, is met by angels who say: 'Come out, O good soul that was in a good body; come out praised, and receive glad tidings of rest and provision and a Lord who is not angry'"* (Aḥmad, from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib; Abū Dāwūd 4753). For the one who has fulfilled the conditions of the sūrah's opening, death is not an end but an arrival.

Death is the great equalizer and the proof of divine sovereignty. Kings and slaves, the notables who mocked the prophets and the poor who followed them, all pass through the same door. The sūrah will later show the wealthy deniers boasting of their possessions (23:55–56) and crying out when the punishment comes (23:64–65). Death is the moment at which their wealth becomes irrelevant and the believer's poverty becomes irrelevant, and only the seven qualities count.

**An Analogy: The Season That Must End**

A farmer who has planted knows that the growing season is finite. He does not resent the approach of harvest; he prepares for it. The whole meaning of his labor depends on the fact that the season ends — if summer lasted forever, nothing would ripen and nothing would be gathered. The Qur'an's opening word in this sūrah, *aflaḥa*, comes from the root of cultivation. Verse 15 tells the cultivator when his season ends: after the six stages of his making, he will die. The believer who understands this does not fear the harvest; he fears arriving at it with an empty field.

**Death and the Architecture of the Sūrah**

Verse 15 also prepares the ground for the sūrah's ending. In verses 99–100 the sūrah will depict the disbeliever at the moment of death crying, *"My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I left behind"* — and the answer: *"No. It is only a word he says; and behind them is a barrier until the Day they are raised."* Verse 15 is the plain statement of the fact that verses 99–100 dramatize. The person who takes verse 15 seriously now will not have to utter the plea of verse 99 later.

**A Practical Discipline**

The classical scholars developed concrete practices around the remembrance of death, and each is a way of living verse 15. Visiting graves, which the Prophet ﷺ permitted precisely because *"they remind you of the Hereafter"* (Muslim 976). Attending funerals and helping to wash and bury the dead. Writing a will promptly, since the Prophet ﷺ said: *"It is not right for a Muslim who has anything to bequeath to pass two nights without his will written beside him"* (al-Bukhārī 2738; Muslim 1627). Reconciling with those one has wronged before the account is closed. And, most simply, ending each day with the awareness that one might not see the morning, as the Prophet ﷺ taught in the sleeping supplication: *"In Your name, my Lord, I lay down my side, and by You I raise it. If You keep my soul, have mercy on it; and if You release it, protect it as You protect Your righteous servants"* (al-Bukhārī 6320; Muslim 2714). Sleep itself, the Qur'an says, is a nightly rehearsal of death (39:42).

**The Verse Is Not the Last Word**

Finally, it must be stressed that verse 15 is not the end of the sequence. It is followed immediately by verse 16: *"Then indeed you will be raised on the Day of Resurrection."* Death in the Qur'an is never the final fact; it is the penultimate one. The believer reads verse 15 with sobriety but not with despair, because he knows what the next verse says. The person who made him from clay and a drop, who brought him forth as "another creation," and who will bring him to death, has one more act to perform — and that act is the subject of the verse to come.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:16

> **Then surely you shall be raised up on the Day of Resurrection.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Link in the Chain**

The sequence that began with clay in verse 12 reaches its conclusion: *thumma innakum yawma al-qiyāmati tubʿathūn* — "Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised." Six creative stages (v. 14), then death (v. 15), then this. The verse is the destination toward which the entire passage has been traveling. Everything before it — the extract of clay, the drop in its secure lodging, the clot, the lump, the bones, the flesh, the soul, the death — has been assembled as evidence for this single claim, which was the most contested claim of the Prophet's mission in Makkah: that the dead will rise.

The verse's construction parallels verse 15 exactly. *Thumma*, "then"; *innakum*, "indeed you"; a temporal specification; and a verb. The parallelism is deliberate. By stating resurrection in the same grammatical form and with the same emphasis as death, the Qur'an places the two on the same footing of certainty. The listener who accepts verse 15 — and no one can deny it — is being told that verse 16 stands on identical ground. The particle *inna* asserts both with the same force. If you are certain of your death, the sūrah says, be equally certain of your rising.

**The Word Tubʿathūn: Being Sent Forth**

The verb *tubʿathūn* is the passive of *baʿatha*, from the root *b-ʿ-th*, which means to send, to dispatch, to rouse from sleep or rest, to raise up. The Qur'an uses the same root for the sending of prophets — *"We sent (baʿathnā) among every community a messenger"* (16:36) — and for the raising of the dead. The shared root is illuminating: resurrection is a *sending forth*, a dispatching of the human being from the stillness of the grave into the activity of judgment, just as a messenger is dispatched from private life into public mission. The Arabs used *baʿatha* for rousing a camel that had knelt, or waking a sleeper. Death, in this vocabulary, is a kneeling or a sleep, and resurrection is the command to rise.

The passive voice — "you will *be* raised" — is significant. The human being does not raise himself; he is raised by an Agent. This corresponds to the passive voice that the Qur'an uses throughout its descriptions of the Last Day: the Trumpet *is blown*, the earth *is shaken*, the graves *are overturned*. The one who was passive in his creation (he did not choose to be a drop, or a clot, or to receive a soul) will be equally passive in his resurrection. Both are acts of God upon him.

**The Day of Standing**

The phrase *yawm al-qiyāmah* — "the Day of Resurrection" — literally means "the Day of Standing," from the root *q-w-m*, to stand. It is named for the moment when all human beings rise from their graves and stand before their Lord. The Qur'an says: *"The Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds"* (83:6). The word captures the posture of the creature at judgment: upright, present, attentive — the posture of the servant before the Master, or the defendant before the Judge. It is also, notably, the posture of prayer. The believer who *stood* (*qāma*) in prayer five times a day, with the *khushūʿ* of verse 2, has rehearsed the standing of this Day; the one who never stood will find the Day's standing strange and terrible.

The Qur'an gives this Day many names, each highlighting one aspect: the Day of Reckoning (*yawm al-ḥisāb*), the Day of Judgment (*yawm al-dīn*), the Day of Gathering (*yawm al-jamʿ*), the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain (*yawm al-taghābun*), the Day of Regret (*yawm al-ḥasrah*), the Overwhelming (*al-ghāshiyah*), the Striking Calamity (*al-qāriʿah*). *Yawm al-qiyāmah* is the most frequent, occurring some seventy times. It is the name that emphasizes the *fact* of the event before any of its consequences: the dead will stand.

**Why the Argument Works**

The passage from verse 12 to verse 16 is one of the Qur'an's tightest arguments, and its logic deserves to be spelled out because the sūrah will later confront the deniers directly (23:35–38, 82–83).

The deniers' objection was always the same: *"When we are dust and bones, shall we be raised?"* (23:82). The objection assumes that a body once dissolved cannot be reconstituted. The Qur'an's reply, laid out in verses 12–16, has three parts.

First, the argument from the first creation. You were not; then you were. The material of your body was clay and a drop, both of which are further from being a person than dust and bones are. If God brought a person out of a drop, the claim that He can bring a person out of dust is not extraordinary. The Qur'an makes this inference in the same words the deniers use: *"Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?"* (19:67); *"He says: 'Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?' Say: 'He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knowing of all creation'"* (36:78–79).

Second, the argument from the stages. Creation was not a single act but a series of transformations, each producing what the previous stage did not contain (v. 14). A God who performs categorical transformations as a matter of routine — lump into bone, bone into a sensing person — is manifestly capable of the transformation from dust into a living body. The deniers admit every earlier transformation because they have witnessed it; they deny only the last, which they have not witnessed. But the earlier transformations are, if anything, more remarkable.

Third, the argument from death. Death is itself a divine act (v. 15) — the withdrawal of the soul from the body at God's command. The One who withdraws the soul knows where He has put it and can return it. The Qur'an says: *"God takes the souls at the time of their death... then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others until a specified term"* (39:42). Sleep is the nightly proof: the soul is taken and returned every night. The morning is a small resurrection.

The Prophet ﷺ made this last point tangible in the morning supplication he taught: *"Praise be to God who gave us life after He caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection (nushūr)"* (al-Bukhārī 6312). Every believer who says these words on waking is affirming verse 16 with the evidence of his own night.

**The Hadith of the Tailbone**

The Prophet ﷺ described the physical mechanism of resurrection in a report recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"Between the two blowings of the Trumpet there will be forty." They asked: "Forty days?" He said: "I decline to say." They asked: "Forty months?" He said: "I decline to say." They asked: "Forty years?" He said: "I decline to say." Then he said: "Then God will send down water from the sky, and they will sprout as vegetation sprouts. There is nothing of the human being that does not decay except one bone: the tailbone (ʿajb al-dhanab); from it creation will be assembled on the Day of Resurrection."* (al-Bukhārī 4814; Muslim 2955)

The image is again agricultural — the dead "sprout" as seeds sprout after rain — and it connects verse 16 back to the root of the sūrah's first word, *aflaḥa*, the cultivator's success. Resurrection is the harvest of the human crop; the earth, watered from heaven, yields its dead as it yields its grain. The Qur'an uses the same comparison: *"And We send down from the sky blessed water, and We bring forth by it gardens and grain for harvest... and We give life thereby to a dead land. Thus will be the emergence (al-khurūj)"* (50:9–11). The next verses of this sūrah (17–22) will turn precisely to rain, gardens, and harvest — so that the natural signs that follow verse 16 are themselves further proofs of what verse 16 asserts.

**Why Resurrection Is Necessary, Not Merely Possible**

The passage establishes that resurrection is *possible*. The sūrah's closing verses will establish that it is *necessary*: *"Did you suppose that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?"* (23:115). The two arguments are complementary. Possibility answers the objection "It cannot happen"; necessity answers the objection "Why should it happen?" And the answer to the second is justice. The seven qualities of verses 2–9 are demanding, and many who practice them die poor, mocked, and unrewarded in this world; many who violate them die rich and honored. If there were no resurrection, the moral order would be a fiction and the sūrah's opening promise — *"the believers have prospered"* — would be false. Verse 16 is the guarantee that the promise of verse 1 will be kept. Without it, the portrait of the believer would be a portrait of a fool; with it, the portrait is of the wisest of human beings.

**The Psychology of Believing in the Rising**

Belief in resurrection transforms a person's relationship to time, suffering, and injustice. The person who believes he will be raised does not need to win every argument now, avenge every wrong now, or taste every pleasure now. He can be patient, because the account is not closed at death. He can forgive, because the Judge will judge. He can give, because what he gives is not lost but sent ahead. And he can face his own death — the certainty of verse 15 — without the despair that grips those for whom death is annihilation. The Qur'an describes the believer's calm at the end: *"O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing"* (89:27–28). That tranquility is the fruit of verse 16.

Conversely, the denial of resurrection produces exactly what the sūrah will describe in the deniers: the conviction that *"there is nothing but our life in this world; we die and we live, and we will not be raised"* (23:37), and therefore the pursuit of wealth and status as the only goods (23:55), the mockery of those who live for another world (23:110), and the terrible awakening when the truth arrives (23:99–100, 106–108). The whole moral drama of the sūrah turns on whether verse 16 is believed.

**Living Toward the Standing**

For the believer, verse 16 is a compass. It tells him where he is going, and therefore how to travel. The Prophet ﷺ summarized the practical response in a single sentence when a man asked him about the Hour: *"What have you prepared for it?"* (al-Bukhārī 6171; Muslim 2639). The right response to the certainty of the Day of Standing is not speculation about its date but preparation for its standing. The seven qualities of the sūrah's opening are that preparation; Firdaws is what awaits the prepared.

With this verse the sūrah's meditation on the human being's own body — from clay to the grave to the standing — is complete. In the next verse, the lens widens dramatically: from the microcosm of the womb to the macrocosm of the seven heavens above.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:17

> **And indeed We created above you seven paths, and We were not heedless of creation.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Womb to the Heavens**

Having traced the human being from a drop in the darkness of the womb to his standing on the Day of Resurrection, the sūrah now lifts the listener's gaze upward: *wa laqad khalaqnā fawqakum sabʿa ṭarāʾiq wa mā kunnā ʿan al-khalqi ghāfilīn* — "And We have certainly created above you seven tracts, and We are never unmindful of creation." The transition is from the smallest scale to the largest. The same *wa laqad* — "and indeed, certainly" — that introduced the creation of man in verse 12 now introduces the creation of the heavens, so that the two are presented as parallel proofs of the same divine power. The One who fashioned you in stages also built what is above you in layers, and He is heedless of neither.

The address remains in the second person: *fawqakum*, "above *you*." God is not describing an abstract cosmos; He is pointing to what is directly over the listener's head as he stands on the earth. The verse invites him to look up.

**The Word Ṭarāʾiq: Paths, Layers, and Things Laid One Upon Another**

The word *ṭarāʾiq* is the plural of *ṭarīqah*, from the root *ṭ-r-q*. The root has several related meanings that the commentators drew upon. Its most familiar sense is a way or path — *ṭarīq* is a road, and *ṭarīqah* a way of doing things, a method, a course. But the root also carries the meaning of striking or beating, as in *ṭaraqa al-bāb*, to knock on a door, and from this comes *miṭraqah*, a hammer. And, as the source commentary notes, the verb *ṭāraqa* means to lay one thing upon another — to layer, as a sandal-maker layers leather (*naʿl muṭāraqah*), or as armor is layered in plates.

From these meanings the commentators derived their interpretations. The majority, including al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, and Ibn Kathīr, understood *sabʿa ṭarāʾiq* as the seven heavens, and they explained the word *ṭarāʾiq* in two complementary ways. First, the heavens are called *ṭarāʾiq* because they are layered one above another — *ṭibāqan*, as the Qur'an says elsewhere: *"Who created seven heavens in layers (ṭibāqan)"* (67:3), and: *"Have you not considered how God created seven heavens in layers?"* (71:15). Second, they are called *ṭarāʾiq* because they are the *paths* of the angels — the routes by which the angels ascend and descend, and by which revelation and command travel between heaven and earth. Al-Ṭabarī transmits from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, from Ibn ʿAbbās: *"seven heavens"*; and from Mujāhid and Qatādah the same. Al-Rāzī mentions the further view that *ṭarāʾiq* may refer to the orbits of the celestial bodies — the paths along which the sun, moon, and five visible planets travel — since each moves along a fixed *ṭarīqah*, or to the celestial spheres of traditional astronomy.

These readings converge on the essential point: above the human being is a structured, ordered, layered creation, with fixed paths and courses, of a magnitude beyond his comprehension. Whether one thinks of seven heavens, seven orbits, or seven layers, the verse describes a cosmos that is *architected* — not a random scatter but a building with floors.

**Why "Seven"?**

The number seven recurs throughout the Qur'an's description of the heavens: seven heavens (2:29; 17:44; 41:12; 65:12; 67:3; 71:15; 78:12), and correspondingly seven earths in one verse (65:12). The classical scholars took the number literally, as a report of seven distinct heavens through which the Prophet ﷺ ascended on the Night Journey, meeting a prophet at each (al-Bukhārī 3887; Muslim 162). Some also noted that seven in Arabic usage can connote completeness or abundance, as in *"seven ears of grain"* (2:261) or *"seventy times"* (9:80). The two readings do not conflict: there may be seven heavens in fact, *and* the number may signify a complete and perfect structure. What matters for the verse's argument is that the heavens are *many*, *ordered*, and *above* — a vast construction whose existence testifies to a Builder.

Al-Rāzī notes an interpretive current, reflected in the source, that the "seven paths" have a spiritual application: the veils of ignorance and vice over the heart, which must be lifted so that the rain of divine knowledge (v. 18) can reach it. This allegorical reading, associated with Ibn ʿAjībah and the Sufi commentators, does not replace the literal but adds to it: as there are seven layers between the earth and the Throne, there are layers between the heart and its Lord, and the believer's work is to become transparent to what descends.

**"And We Were Not Heedless of Creation"**

The second half of the verse is one of the sūrah's most profound theological statements: *wa mā kunnā ʿan al-khalqi ghāfilīn* — "and We have never been, and are not, heedless of creation." The word *ghāfil*, from the root *gh-f-l*, means unmindful, inattentive, neglectful — the state of a person whose attention has lapsed. The verse denies this state of God absolutely. The verb *kunnā* with the negative *mā* ("We were not") in Arabic idiom denies a quality permanently: not "We were not heedless at that time," but "It has never been Our way to be heedless."

The word *al-khalq* here admits two meanings. It may mean *the act of creating* — God did not create the seven heavens carelessly, but with precision and purpose. Or it may mean *the created things* — God has not created the heavens and then abandoned them and their inhabitants to run on their own, unwatched. Both readings are true and both are Qur'anic. The first corresponds to the Qur'an's insistence on the *precision* of creation: *"You will not see in the creation of the Merciful any inconsistency; so return your vision — do you see any breaks?"* (67:3). The second corresponds to its insistence on God's *continuous attention*: *"He arranges every matter"* (10:3); *"Every day He is in some affair"* (55:29); *"His footstool extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation tires Him not"* (2:255).

The classical commentators emphasized the second meaning particularly, because it answers a specific error. Some ancient philosophers held that God created the world and then withdrew, leaving it to natural laws, uninvolved in the details of human life — a view that has modern descendants in deism. The verse refutes this: the One who built the seven heavens above you has never, for a moment, been unmindful of what lies beneath them. He knows the drop in the womb (v. 13) and the deed of every person (v. 51: *"I know what you do"*). Al-Ṭabarī explains: *"We were not heedless of what We created; rather We preserve it and manage it."* Ibn Kathīr adds that the heavens' preservation from falling is itself a sign of this attention: *"Indeed, God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease"* (35:41).

**The Logic of the Verse: Structure Implies Attention**

The two halves of the verse are connected by a quiet inference. A structure as vast and ordered as the layered heavens does not maintain itself. Orbits are kept; the sky does not fall; the seasons return; the constellations hold their positions across millennia. This constancy is either uncaused — which no rational person accepts of any other order — or it is the continuous work of a Sustainer. The verse names the Sustainer and denies that His attention ever lapses. In the language of a modern analogy: the greater the complexity of a system, the more constant the attention required to maintain it; the heavens are the most complex system a human being can perceive, and they are maintained without interruption; therefore the One who maintains them is never inattentive.

The verse also bears on the argument for resurrection that verses 12–16 concluded. A God who is not heedless of creation will not allow it to end in nothing. The deniers' assumption was that human life is unobserved and unaccounted for — that one dies and that is the end. Verse 17 replies that nothing under the seven heavens is unobserved. The theme will return at the sūrah's end: *"Did you suppose that We created you in vain?"* (23:115). Verse 17's denial of divine heedlessness is the seed of that final question.

**Why This Matters for the Human Heart**

Consider the emotional weight of the verse's second half. The human being, standing beneath the immensity of the sky, can feel one of two things: insignificance ("I am nothing in all this") or belonging ("the One who made all this knows me"). The Qur'an directs him firmly to the second. The vastness above is not evidence that he is forgotten; it is evidence of the capacity of the One who has not forgotten him. The Prophet ﷺ taught the Companions to gaze at the sky and recite the closing verses of Āl ʿImrān: *"Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for those of understanding, who remember God standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying: 'Our Lord, You did not create this in vain'"* (3:190–191; al-Bukhārī 4569; Muslim 763). The reflection is meant to produce the words *"not in vain"* — the same conviction verse 17 states from God's side: *"We were not heedless."*

There is also a warning folded into the comfort. The God who is not heedless of the heavens is not heedless of the person who thinks himself unobserved. The sūrah's opening described believers who guard their private parts and keep trusts — acts performed largely in private. Verse 17 assures them that their unseen fidelity is seen; it also warns the one who sins in secret that his secrecy is only from other creatures. The Qur'an says: *"Do not think that God is unaware (ghāfil) of what the wrongdoers do; He only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare"* (14:42). The same word, *ghāfil*, denied of God in both verses.

**An Analogy: The Architect Who Stays**

Imagine an architect who designs a seven-story building of extraordinary complexity — every floor supported by the one below, every system balanced — and then, instead of leaving, remains permanently in residence, attending to every room, aware of every occupant, maintaining every beam. This is the picture verse 17 paints of God's relationship to the heavens and to us. The building is the seven paths above; the residence is the phrase "We were not heedless." No human architect does this; the divine Architect does nothing else.

**The Verse in Its Place**

Verse 17 opens a short catalogue of natural signs (vv. 17–22): the heavens, rain, gardens, the olive, cattle, and ships. Each is introduced as a divine act and each is a proof of the same three things — God's power (He made it), God's care (He made it *for you*), and God's attention (He is not heedless). The catalogue follows the argument from human creation and precedes the histories of the prophets, so that the listener is confronted with three kinds of evidence in succession: his own body, the world around him, and the record of those who denied. After verse 17's sweeping upward gaze, the next verse will bring the eye back down along the path of falling rain.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:18

> **And We sent down water from Heaven in due measure, and settled it in the earth, and We are able to make it disappear.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Heights to the Ground: The Descent of Water**

Verse 17 pointed upward to the seven layered heavens; verse 18 follows the path by which the heavens touch the earth: *wa anzalnā min al-samāʾi māʾan bi-qadarin fa-askannāhu fī al-arḍi wa innā ʿalā dhahābin bihi la-qādirūn* — "And We sent down from the sky water in measure, and We settled it in the earth; and indeed We are able to take it away." The verse describes a complete cycle: descent, measurement, storage, and the ever-present possibility of removal. Of all the natural signs the Qur'an cites, water is the most frequent, because nothing makes the dependence of life upon God more obvious. Every human being, every animal, every plant, exists only because water falls from above and stays below. The verse names the three facts about that water which most deserve reflection: it comes *in measure*, it is *stored* for us, and it can be *taken away*.

**"Water from the Sky": The Gift That Descends**

The verb *anzalnā*, "We sent down," is the same verb the Qur'an uses for the sending down of revelation. The parallel is not accidental; the classical and spiritual commentators both noted that rain and revelation are twin descents from heaven, one giving life to the earth and the other to the heart. The Qur'an itself makes the comparison: *"He sends down from the sky water, and valleys flow according to their measure (bi-qadarihā)"* (13:17) — a verse the commentators read as a parable of revelation received by hearts according to their capacity. Verse 18 uses the same phrase, *bi-qadar*, "in measure," which invites the same reflection: as rain is measured to the earth's need, revelation is measured to the heart's capacity.

The word *al-samāʾ* — "the sky" — in this context means the clouds or the region above, from which rain falls. The verb's direction matters: water comes *down*. The human being does not manufacture it or summon it; it arrives from above his head, from a source he does not control, at times he cannot fix. The Qur'an presses this point when it asks: *"Have you seen the water that you drink? Is it you who sent it down from the clouds, or are We the senders? If We willed, We could make it bitter; so why are you not grateful?"* (56:68–70). Verse 18 is the affirmative form of that question.

**"In Due Measure": The Precision of Provision**

The phrase *bi-qadar* — "in measure," "according to a determined quantity" — is the theological center of the verse. The word *qadar* comes from the root *q-d-r*, which means to measure, to determine, to have power over; it is the root of *qudrah* (power) and of *qadar* in the sense of divine decree. The Qur'an states as a universal principle: *"Indeed, all things We created with measure (bi-qadar)"* (54:49), and: *"There is nothing but that its treasuries are with Us, and We do not send it down except in a known measure (bi-qadarin maʿlūm)"* (15:21). Water is the most tangible instance of this general law.

What does "in measure" mean for rain? The commentators explain it in several dimensions. First, quantity: enough to give life, not so much as to destroy. Too little rain is drought; too much is flood. The Qur'an mentions both as punishments — the drought years of Pharaoh's people (7:130) and the deluge of Noah's (23:27). Ordinary rain is the mercy between these extremes, calibrated to what the earth and its creatures need. Al-Rāzī notes that if the measure were slightly altered in either direction, life would be impossible. Second, distribution: rain falls where it is needed, in seasons, according to a rhythm that allows planting and harvest. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that no year has more rain than another, but God distributes it as He wills (al-Ṭabarī, on 25:50). Third, quality: the water is sweet and usable — *"and We give you to drink of sweet water"* (77:27) — whereas most of the earth's water is salt.

The measured character of rain has an argumentative purpose. Measure implies a Measurer. Randomness does not produce sustained precision. The listener who admits that rain comes "in measure" — and every farmer knows that it does — has admitted the existence of One who measures. Verse 18 asks him to draw the inference.

**"And We Settled It in the Earth": The Hidden Storage**

The second act in the verse is *fa-askannāhu fī al-arḍ* — "and We caused it to settle (or dwell) in the earth." The verb *askana*, from the root *s-k-n*, means to cause to be still, to make dwell, to lodge; it is the root of *sakīnah*, tranquility, and *maskan*, dwelling. Rain does not merely fall and run off; it is *lodged* in the earth — absorbed into soil, stored in aquifers, held in springs and wells, retained as snow and ice on mountains, released gradually in streams. Without this settling, every rainfall would be a flash flood followed by drought; the earth would drink nothing and keep nothing.

Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, and others explain that this refers to the springs, wells, and rivers that hold water after the rain has passed, so that people may drink and irrigate in seasons when no rain falls. Ibn Kathīr writes: *"He made it dwell in the earth as springs and wells and rivers, storing it for people's benefit throughout the year."* The Qur'an refers to the same fact elsewhere: *"Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky and makes it flow as springs in the earth?"* (39:21). The phrase "settled it in the earth" thus names the entire hidden infrastructure of groundwater on which civilization has always depended — the wells of the desert, the springs of the oasis, the rivers of the valley.

There is also a moral dimension in the choice of the verb *askana*. The word describes a *dwelling*: the water is given a home in the earth, as the human being was given a home in the *qarār makīn* of the womb (v. 13). The same Provider who prepared the secure lodging for the drop prepared the underground lodging for the rain. The pattern is consistent: God does not merely create; He *houses* what He creates.

**"And We Are Able to Take It Away": The Threat Behind the Gift**

The verse ends on a note of warning: *wa innā ʿalā dhahābin bihi la-qādirūn* — "and indeed, We are surely able to take it away." The grammar is intensely emphatic: *inna* ("indeed"), the *lām* of emphasis on *la-qādirūn* ("*surely* able"), and the fronting of the phrase *ʿalā dhahābin bihi* ("over its removal") before the predicate, which produces the sense: "over its removal — over that specifically — We have complete power." The word *dhahāb* means going away, departure, vanishing.

Why end a verse about mercy with a reminder of its possible withdrawal? Because a gift that is never threatened is never valued. The listener who has grown up with wells that never dried and rivers that never failed treats water as a fact of nature rather than a daily act of God. The Qur'an corrects this in the sharpest terms: *"Say: Have you considered, if your water were to sink into the ground, who could bring you flowing water?"* (67:30). The verse is the last in Sūrah al-Mulk, and its placement as the sūrah's closing word gives some idea of the weight the Qur'an places on this question. The water that is *settled* in the earth could be *sunk* beyond reach; the water that is *sent down* could be *withheld*. Both have happened in human history, and both are the Qur'an's illustrations of how completely a proud civilization depends on what it did not make.

The commentators noted that the removal can occur in several ways: the rain may cease, as in drought; the groundwater may sink beyond the reach of wells; the water may become undrinkable; or the earth may cease to retain it. In every case, the human being discovers that his prosperity rested on a condition he never controlled. Al-Rāzī observes that this is why the verse follows the assertion of measured provision: the measure is a favor, and the possibility of removal is what makes the favor visible.

**The Logic and the Lesson**

The verse teaches through a three-part structure that has a clear logic. Descent: the water comes from above, not from you. Measure and storage: it comes in exactly the quantity that sustains life, and it is kept for you in the earth. Removal: all of this could stop. The conclusion the listener is meant to draw is gratitude and humility — gratitude for the measured gift, humility before the One who could withdraw it. The Qur'an states the intended response after a parallel catalogue of provisions: *"So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?"* (55:13, refrain).

There is also an argument for resurrection folded into the water. The Qur'an repeatedly compares the revival of dead land by rain to the revival of the dead: *"And you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every beautiful kind. That is because God is the Truth, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things competent"* (22:5–6). The water that verse 18 describes is the agent of the annual resurrection of the earth, and the sūrah has just concluded its argument for the resurrection of the body (v. 16). The listener is meant to connect them: the One who raises the crop from the dead soil every spring will raise the sleeper from the dead soil at the Trumpet.

**The Spiritual Reading**

The source commentary notes the allegorical reading that the spiritual commentators applied to verses like this one: the earth is the receptive heart, the water is the knowledge and mercy that descend from God, and the settling of the water is the taking root of faith in the heart. Ibn ʿAjībah and others develop this: as the earth must be soft and open to receive the rain, the heart must be humble (v. 2) to receive guidance; as water settles in the earth and emerges later as springs, knowledge settles in the heart and emerges as wisdom and good deeds; and as God can withdraw the water, He can withdraw guidance from a heart that has hardened. This reading does not displace the literal — the verse is first about rain — but it illustrates the Qur'an's habit of describing the physical world in words that also describe the spiritual, so that the observer of nature learns something about his own soul.

**A Modern Reflection**

The hydrological cycle that verse 18 summarizes — evaporation, precipitation, infiltration, storage, discharge — is now measured with great precision, and the measurements reinforce the verse's emphasis. The total amount of fresh water accessible to human beings is a tiny fraction of the earth's water, and it is kept usable only by the continuous operation of a cycle that human beings did not design and cannot replace. Modern societies that have depleted their aquifers have discovered the meaning of *"We are able to take it away"* not as a religious threat but as a hydrological fact. The verse asks the person who turns on a tap to remember what he is receiving, from Whom, and on what conditions. The believer who says *al-ḥamdu lillāh* after drinking, as the Prophet ﷺ taught (al-Tirmidhī 1816), is enacting verse 18 in a single breath.

**Toward the Gardens**

The water that descends in verse 18 will, in verse 19, become gardens of dates and grapes. The sūrah's catalogue of signs moves as the water moves: from sky, to earth, to fruit. The next verse will describe what grows from the measured, settled gift.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:19

> **And thereby We brought into being for you gardens of date palms and grapevines, wherein you have many fruits and whereof you eat,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**What the Water Becomes**

The water that descended in measure and settled in the earth (v. 18) now appears in its fruit: *fa-anshaʾnā lakum bihi jannātin min nakhīlin wa aʿnāb, lakum fīhā fawākihu kathīratun wa minhā taʾkulūn* — "Then We produced for you by it gardens of palm trees and grapevines, in which for you are many fruits, and from which you eat." The connective *fa-* ("then, and so") ties this verse tightly to the previous one; the *bihi* ("by it") refers to the water. The logic of the catalogue is causal: the sky gives water, the water is stored in the earth, and from that stored water gardens grow. Each verse depends on the one before, as each stage of the embryo (v. 14) depended on the previous stage. The sūrah is teaching the listener to see the world as a chain of divine acts, not a collection of unrelated facts.

**The Verb Anshaʾnā Again**

The verb *anshaʾnā* — "We produced, We brought into being" — is the same verb used in verse 14 for the "other creation" (*anshaʾnāhu khalqan ākhar*), the moment the embryo became a living person. Its reuse here is significant. The Qur'an describes the growth of a garden from rain with the same verb it used for the ensouling of a human being, because both are acts of bringing forth what did not previously exist. The seed does not "contain" the palm; the vine cutting does not "contain" the grape cluster. Something new emerges, and the emergence is God's. The believer who learns to say *anshaʾnā* over a garden learns to see origination where the heedless see only process.

**"For You": The Grammar of Gift**

Twice in this short verse the word *lakum* — "for you" — appears: *"We produced for you... in which for you are many fruits."* The repetition is emphatic. The gardens are not merely produced; they are produced *for the human being*. This is one of the Qur'an's most frequent notes: creation is described as *musakhkhar*, subjected and made serviceable, to mankind. *"And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth — all from Him"* (45:13). The phrase *lakum* transforms the natural world from a neutral environment into a table spread by a Host. The person who eats a date has been *given* the date; the verse insists on this by naming the recipient twice.

This has moral consequences that the sūrah's opening already anticipated. If provision is a gift, then hoarding it is ingratitude and sharing it is the natural response — hence the "doers of zakāh" of verse 4. If provision is a gift, then the boasting of the wealthy in verses 55–56 is absurd, because they are boasting of what was handed to them. The word *lakum* quietly reorients the whole human relationship to wealth.

**Date Palms and Grapevines: Why These Two?**

The verse names two plants specifically: *nakhīl*, date palms, and *aʿnāb*, grapevines. The Qur'an pairs them repeatedly (2:266; 13:4; 16:11, 67; 17:91; 18:32; 36:34; 80:28–29), and the pairing was not arbitrary. To the Arab listener, these two were the aristocrats of cultivated plants — the staples of the oases of Arabia and of the gardens of Ṭāʾif and Syria, the most prized fruits, the most valuable orchards, and the most reliable sources of both immediate food and stored sustenance.

The date palm was, and remains, the tree of Arabian life. Every part of it was used: the fruit for food fresh and dried, the pit for fodder, the fronds for roofing and baskets, the fiber for rope, the trunk for beams. The Prophet ﷺ compared the believer to it: *"There is a tree among the trees whose leaves do not fall, and it is like the Muslim; tell me what it is." The Companions thought of the trees of the desert, and Ibn ʿUmar thought it was the date palm but was shy to speak. The Prophet ﷺ said: "It is the date palm."* (al-Bukhārī 61; Muslim 2811). The believer, like the palm, is constant in every season, and every part of him benefits others. The Qur'an's parable of the good word is likewise a tree *"whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky, producing its fruit at all times by permission of its Lord"* (14:24–25), which many commentators identified as the palm. Dates were also the food of the Prophet's household for months at a time, and he said: *"A house with no dates in it — its people are hungry"* (Muslim 2046).

The grapevine represents a different kind of bounty: the fruit that is both eaten fresh and preserved as raisins, that yields juice and vinegar, and that in pre-Islamic times yielded wine — which the Qur'an would later forbid, while retaining the vine's status as a sign of blessing. The Qur'an mentions grapes among the fruits of Paradise (78:32) and among the blessings of this world, and it uses the garden of vines as the setting for its parable of the two men in Sūrah al-Kahf (18:32–43), where the ungrateful owner's garden is destroyed — a warning that bears directly on the "We are able to take it away" of verse 18.

By naming these two, the verse names the best of what the listener knew, so that his gratitude would be concrete rather than abstract. A modern reader may substitute the staples of his own land — wheat, rice, olives, citrus — without altering the verse's meaning; but he should notice that the Qur'an spoke to its first audience in the language of their own orchards.

**"Many Fruits": Abundance Beyond the Named**

After naming the two plants, the verse widens: *lakum fīhā fawākihu kathīrah* — "in which for you are many fruits." The word *fawākih* (singular *fākihah*) denotes fruits eaten for pleasure and refreshment rather than mere sustenance — the delicacies of the table. The adjective *kathīrah*, "many," signals that the gardens contain far more than dates and grapes; the two named are examples of a general abundance. The commentators note that "gardens of palms and vines" would, in the Arab experience, also contain figs, pomegranates, and other fruits growing beneath and between the larger trees. The verse thus moves from the specific to the general: here are two fruits you know; here also are many more.

The word *fākihah* introduces an important theme. God did not provide only what is necessary for survival. He provided *delight*. The Qur'an lists among the provisions of the earth not only *"grain"* but *"fruits and herbage, as provision for you and your animals"* (80:27–32), and it describes the orchards of this world as a foretaste of the gardens of the next. The believer is meant to enjoy the sweetness of fruit as a sign of the generosity of the Giver — and the Qur'an rebukes those who forbid what God has made lawful of such enjoyments: *"Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?"* (7:32).

**"And From Which You Eat": The Last Link**

The verse closes with *wa minhā taʾkulūn* — "and from which you eat." This is the final step in the chain that began in the sky. Water descended, was stored, produced gardens, which produced fruit, which the human being eats. The verse ends with the act of eating because that is the point at which the divine provision enters the human body and becomes, in time, the "extract of clay" (v. 12) that becomes the drop (v. 13). The circle is closed: the human being was made from the earth's extract; the earth's extract reaches him through fruit; the fruit is grown by water; the water is sent by God. Every meal is a link in the process by which God continues to "create" the human being from the earth.

The commentators also noted the partitive *min* — "*from* which you eat" — implying that not all of the garden is for eating; some is for other benefits (shade, wood, trade, beauty) and some is for other creatures. The Qur'an elsewhere balances human eating with the provision of animals: *"Eat and pasture your cattle"* (20:54). Verse 19 focuses on the human portion; verses 21–22 will turn to the cattle.

**The Argument in the Verse**

Like every verse in this catalogue, verse 19 is doing two things at once: it is inviting gratitude and it is proving a point. The point concerns the deniers of resurrection, whose objection the sūrah has already anticipated (v. 16) and will quote (vv. 35–38, 82–83). The dead land brought to life by rain and yielding fruit is the Qur'an's standing image of resurrection: *"And He it is who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy, until when they have carried heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land and send down water by it and bring forth by it every kind of fruit. Thus will We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will be reminded"* (7:57). The garden of verse 19 is the earth resurrected. The listener who watches a palm grove rise from land that was barren in the dry season has watched, in miniature, what verse 16 promised.

**The Spiritual Reading**

The commentators who read the earth as the heart and the rain as revelation (see v. 18) carried the allegory through to the fruit: the gardens are the virtues and good deeds that grow in a heart watered by guidance, and the "eating" is the believer's own enjoyment of the fruits of his faith — the sweetness of prayer, the peace of trust in God, the contentment of gratitude. The Prophet ﷺ spoke of *"the sweetness of faith"* (al-Bukhārī 16; Muslim 43) as something tasted. Verse 19, on this reading, describes the orchard of the soul, and the seven qualities of verses 2–9 are its date palms and vines.

**Gratitude in Practice**

The practical application of the verse is the discipline of eating with awareness. The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to name God before eating (al-Bukhārī 5376), to praise Him after (al-Tirmidhī 3458), and to say when tasting the first fruit of the season: *"O God, bless us in our fruits and bless us in our city"* (Muslim 1373). He taught that God is pleased with the servant who *"eats a morsel and praises Him for it, or drinks a sip and praises Him for it"* (Muslim 2734). These small practices are verse 19 lived: they insert the *lakum* — the awareness of gift — into the ordinary act of eating, so that no date or grape is consumed without a moment's recognition of the chain that brought it from the sky.

**Toward the Olive**

The catalogue continues in the next verse with a single tree singled out for special mention — the olive of Sinai, whose oil was light and food to the whole ancient world.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:20

> **and a tree issuing forth from Mount Sinai that produces oil and a seasoning for eating.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**One Tree Set Apart**

After the gardens of dates and grapes, the catalogue of provisions pauses on a single tree: *wa shajaratan takhruju min Ṭūri Saynāʾa tanbutu bi'l-duhni wa ṣibghin li'l-ākilīn* — "and a tree that emerges from Mount Sinai, which grows producing oil and a relish for those who eat." Grammatically, "a tree" (*shajaratan*) is joined to the "gardens" of verse 19 as a further object of *anshaʾnā* — "We produced for you... and a tree." But the verse treats this tree differently from the gardens: it is singular, it is located, and its products are named. The Qur'an does not name the tree, but the commentators are unanimous, as the source records from al-Qurṭubī, that it is the olive (*al-zaytūn*). Why should the olive be singled out from all the trees of the earth and given its own verse?

**The Olive's Place in the Qur'an**

The olive is mentioned by name six times in the Qur'an (6:99, 141; 16:11; 24:35; 80:29; 95:1) and once more, as here, by description. In Sūrah al-Tīn God swears by it — *"By the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinai, and this secure city"* (95:1–3) — pairing it, as this verse does, with Mount Sinai. Most memorably, in the Verse of Light, the olive is the source of the oil that illuminates the parable of divine light: *"...lit from a blessed tree, an olive, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it — light upon light"* (24:35). The olive is thus the Qur'an's *blessed tree* (*shajarah mubārakah*), and the Prophet ﷺ confirmed the description:

> *"Eat the oil (of the olive) and anoint yourselves with it, for it is from a blessed tree."* (al-Tirmidhī 1851; Ibn Mājah 3319; graded ṣaḥīḥ)

The singling out of the olive in verse 20 is therefore consistent with its standing throughout revelation. It is the tree of light, of blessing, of Sinai, and of the oil that fed and lit the ancient world.

**"Issuing Forth from Mount Sinai"**

The phrase *takhruju min Ṭūri Saynāʾ* — "emerging from Mount Sinai" — locates the tree. The word *ṭūr* means mountain, and *Saynāʾ* is Sinai; the Qur'an uses both *Ṭūr Saynāʾ* (here) and *Ṭūr Sīnīn* (95:2), the two being variant forms of the same name. This is the mountain on which God spoke to Moses, and the region in which the olive has been cultivated since antiquity. The commentators offered two readings of why the olive is tied to this mountain. Some, including al-Ṭabarī, took it as the olive's *origin*: the tree first grew in the region of Sinai and spread from there to the Levant and the Mediterranean, so that "emerging from Sinai" describes its geographic source. Others took it as a matter of *prominence*: the olive is associated with Sinai because the mountain's slopes and surrounding lands were famous for their olive groves, and naming a thing by its most notable location is common Arabic usage — as one might say "the dates of Madinah" without denying dates elsewhere.

There is also a symbolic depth. Sinai is the mountain of revelation, where the fire that Moses saw was in a tree (28:30) and where God spoke directly to a prophet. The olive that grows from Sinai is a tree of *light* — its oil literally illuminated lamps for millennia — growing from the mountain of light. The Verse of Light would later make this association explicit by placing the olive's oil in the lamp of God's light. In verse 20, the association is quieter but present: the tree of Sinai produces the oil of lamps and the food of the table. Revelation and sustenance descend from the same mountain.

**The Debate Over "Saynāʾ"**

The source commentary preserves an interesting linguistic dispute. Some early authorities read *saynāʾ* not as a proper name but as an adjective meaning "blessed" or "beautiful," so that *Ṭūr Saynāʾ* would mean "the blessed mountain" or "the beautiful mountain." Al-Ṭabarī transmits this from some of the Successors but rejects it, arguing that there is no such adjective in the Arabic language; *saynāʾ*, he holds, is simply the name of the mountain, which the Qur'an pronounces in two forms. Al-Qurṭubī records both views and notes that the mountain is also said to derive its name from the *sīnā*, the stones or trees of the region. Whatever the etymology, the two readings agree on the essential: the tree comes from a blessed and sacred mountain, and the Qur'an is directing the listener's attention to a place where God's word and God's provision meet.

**"Producing Oil": The Wealth of the Olive**

The verse says the tree *tanbutu bi'l-duhn* — "grows with oil" or "produces oil." The word *duhn* means oil or grease, and the olive's oil was the most valuable vegetable oil of the ancient world: it was food, fuel for lamps, ointment for the skin and hair, medicine for wounds, and a commodity of trade. The verb *tanbutu* ("grows") with the preposition *bi-* has been read in two ways by the grammarians: "grows *bringing* oil" (the *bāʾ* of accompaniment — the tree grows and its oil grows with it) or "grows *by means of* oil" (the tree is nourished by its own oil). Both express the marvel that a tree draws water from the earth and produces from it not water but oil — a substance categorically different from what it took in. The commentators saw in this the same wonder that verse 14 found in the embryo: the emergence of something that the raw material did not contain. Rainwater goes into the olive tree; oil comes out. No chemist standing at the root could deduce the oil from the water. The tree is an alchemist, and the alchemy is God's.

**"And a Seasoning for Those Who Eat"**

The final product named is *ṣibgh li'l-ākilīn* — "a relish (or condiment) for eaters." The word *ṣibgh* comes from the root *ṣ-b-gh*, whose primary meaning is to dip or to dye; the same root gives *ṣibghah*, dye or coloring, used in the phrase *ṣibghat Allāh*, "the coloring of God" (2:138), and in Christian Arabic for baptism (immersion). *Ṣibgh*, as the source notes, denotes a condiment into which bread is dipped — olive oil, vinegar, or similar — the simplest and most ancient form of seasoning. The image is of the Arab meal: bread torn and dipped into a dish of oil. The Prophet ﷺ himself ate this way; Muslim records that he said, *"What an excellent condiment vinegar is"* (Muslim 2052), and the ḥadīth quoted above commands eating olive oil.

The mention of *ṣibgh* alongside *duhn* distinguishes two uses of the same oil: as a substance in itself (for lamps, anointing, medicine) and as a relish for food. The verse thus describes the olive's complete usefulness: it lights, it heals, it beautifies, and it flavors. Few plants serve so many human needs from a single fruit. The Qur'an's choice to devote a whole verse to it is a lesson in noticing — in recognizing that the most ordinary elements of a meal are extraordinary provisions.

**Why the Olive Deserves Its Own Verse**

The catalogue of provisions in verses 17–22 moves from the vast (the seven heavens) to the intimate (the dish of oil on the table). The olive stands at the intimate end. It teaches that God's signs are not only in the cosmos but in the kitchen, and that the believer's gratitude should be trained on small things as well as great. There is a Prophetic model for this: the Prophet ﷺ gave thanks for a sip of water and a morsel of food (Muslim 2734), and the Qur'an rebukes those who overlook the small provisions when it lists *"and We caused to grow therein grain, and grapes and herbage, and olives and palm trees"* (80:27–29) — a list very close to the one in this sūrah — and concludes: *"as provision for you and your grazing animals"* (80:32).

There is also, once more, an argument. The olive's transformation of water into oil, like the embryo's transformation of a drop into a person and the rain's transformation of dead earth into gardens, is a categorical change that human beings observe constantly and cannot replicate. The verse invites the deniers of resurrection to explain how a tree does what they claim God cannot do. If a tree can make oil from water, can the Maker of the tree not make a body from dust?

**The Olive and the Light Within**

The spiritual commentators, following the Verse of Light, read the olive as a symbol of the illumined heart. The olive's oil "would almost glow even if no fire touched it" (24:35) — a description of a heart so pure that it nearly shines before revelation reaches it, and blazes when it does. The tree "neither of the east nor of the west" is the balanced heart, not swayed to any extreme. Verse 20's olive, growing from the mountain of revelation and producing both light and nourishment, is a picture of the believer described at the sūrah's opening: rooted in the sacred, producing light for others and sustenance for himself. Ibn ʿAjībah and others develop this reading; it does not replace the literal olive, but it explains why the Qur'an returns to this tree with such reverence.

**A Practical Reflection**

The believer today can recover the awareness this verse teaches through a simple exercise: to trace, occasionally, the origin of what is on his plate. The oil in the dish came from a fruit, which came from a tree, which drew water from the earth, which came from the sky, which came from God. The same exercise applied to bread, to fruit, to meat, would reveal that every meal is a convergence of divine acts. The Prophet's instruction to name God before eating (*bismillāh*) and to praise Him after is the compressed form of this exercise — a way of acknowledging, in two words, the chain that verse 20 spells out.

**Toward the Cattle**

The catalogue moves in the next verse from plants to animals: from the tree that produces oil to the cattle that produce milk, and from the food of the table to the transport of the road.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:21

> **And truly in cattle there is a lesson for you: We give you to drink from that which is in their bellies, and in them you have many uses, and some of them you eat.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From the Garden to the Herd**

The catalogue of signs turns from the plant kingdom to the animal: *wa inna lakum fī al-anʿāmi la-ʿibrah, nusqīkum mimmā fī buṭūnihā wa lakum fīhā manāfiʿu kathīratun wa minhā taʾkulūn* — "And indeed, for you in the cattle is a lesson: We give you drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat." Once again the verse is framed by the grammar of gift — *lakum*, "for you," appears twice, as in verse 19 — and it follows the same structure as the verse on gardens: a general benefit, then "many" benefits, then eating. The parallelism teaches the listener to see plants and animals as two chapters of a single book of provision, each written for him.

**The Word Anʿām**

The word *anʿām* is the plural of *naʿam* and denotes livestock — specifically camels, cattle, sheep, and goats, the eight kinds in four pairs that the Qur'an enumerates in Sūrah al-Anʿām (6:143–144), the chapter named for them. The root *n-ʿ-m* is the root of *niʿmah*, blessing or favor, and of *naʿīm*, bliss. The Arabs called their livestock *anʿām* because they were the very embodiment of blessing: wealth, food, drink, clothing, transport, and status all flowed from the herd. To name the animals with the word for "blessing" is already to make a theological point, and the Qur'an builds on it: *"And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat. And for you in them is beauty when you bring them in for the evening and when you send them out to pasture"* (16:5–6).

**"A Lesson": The Meaning of ʿIbrah**

The verse says that in cattle there is *la-ʿibrah* — "surely a lesson." The word *ʿibrah* comes from the root *ʿ-b-r*, which means to cross over, to pass from one side to another — as one crosses a river (*ʿabara al-nahr*) or as a dream is "crossed" from image to meaning in interpretation (*taʿbīr*). An *ʿibrah* is therefore something that enables the mind to cross from what is seen to what is unseen, from the observed fact to the truth it points to. The Qur'an uses the word for the histories of destroyed nations (*"Indeed in that is a lesson for those who fear,"* 79:26) and for the alternation of night and day (24:44). Here it is applied to livestock: the person who looks at a cow correctly is meant to *cross over* from the cow to its Creator.

The *lām* of emphasis on *la-ʿibrah* insists that the lesson is real and present, not a matter of pious imagination. The verse then specifies exactly where the lesson lies.

**The Marvel of Milk**

The first and most emphasized benefit is drink: *nusqīkum mimmā fī buṭūnihā* — "We give you to drink from what is in their bellies." This is milk, and the Qur'an describes its production more fully in the parallel passage of Sūrah al-Naḥl: *"And indeed, for you in the cattle is a lesson: We give you drink from what is in their bellies — from between excretion and blood — pure milk, palatable to drinkers"* (16:66). The *ʿibrah* of milk lies in its origin. The animal eats grass and drinks water; within its body these become blood and waste; and from between these two — from a system that is processing filth and circulating blood — emerges a substance that is white, sweet, nourishing, and clean. Al-Rāzī pauses on this: the same digestive process that produces excrement produces milk, and the two are separated in the animal's body so completely that no trace of the one taints the other. He calls this one of the clearest proofs of a wise Maker, since no blind process would sort the pure from the impure with such precision.

The verb *nusqīkum* — "*We* give you to drink" — attributes the act directly to God. The cow does not give milk; God gives milk *through* the cow. This is the Qur'an's consistent way of speaking about secondary causes: they are real, but they are instruments, and the Agent is God. The believer who drinks milk is receiving it from the same Hand that sent the rain (v. 18). The Prophet ﷺ taught a specific supplication for milk that acknowledges this: *"O God, bless us in it and give us more of it,"* explaining, *"for nothing suffices in place of both food and drink except milk"* (al-Tirmidhī 3455; Abū Dāwūd 3730). Milk, in other words, is the one provision that is complete in itself — a fact the Prophet ﷺ noted as a reason for a special prayer.

**"Many Benefits"**

The verse continues: *wa lakum fīhā manāfiʿu kathīrah* — "and for you in them are many benefits." As in verse 19, the word *kathīrah*, "many," signals that the named benefit (milk) is one among a multitude. The commentators enumerate: wool, hair, and fur for clothing and tents (16:80); hides for leather; bones and horns for tools; dung for fuel and fertilizer; the labor of plowing and threshing; the carrying of loads; the breeding of more animals; the wealth and trade they represent; and the beauty and dignity they confer (16:6). The Qur'an sums up the wider list in 16:80: *"And God has made for you from your homes a place of rest, and made for you from the hides of the cattle tents which you find light on your day of travel and your day of encampment; and from their wool, fur, and hair is furnishing and enjoyment for a time."*

The word *manāfiʿ* (singular *manfaʿah*) is the ordinary word for benefits or uses. Its breadth teaches that the *ʿibrah* is not confined to one product: the whole animal, in every part and function, is arranged for human use. The person who considers how completely a single sheep serves human needs — food, drink, clothing, shelter, tools, fuel — has considered a design whose thoroughness no human engineer has matched.

**"And From Them You Eat"**

The verse closes as verse 19 closed: *wa minhā taʾkulūn* — "and from them you eat." Meat is the last-named benefit, and the partitive *min* again signals that only *some* of them are eaten — the camel and sheep and goat are eaten; and even of these, not all, since some are kept for breeding, milk, and labor. The Qur'an elsewhere sets the rules for this eating: the animal must be slaughtered in God's name (6:118), certain animals and states are forbidden (5:3), and the eating is to be with gratitude. The permission to eat meat is thus a bounded permission; the animals are given for human benefit but not for human cruelty, and the Prophet ﷺ taught: *"God has prescribed excellence (iḥsān) in all things; so when you kill, kill well, and when you slaughter, slaughter well; let each of you sharpen his blade and spare the animal suffering"* (Muslim 1955).

**The Lesson Within the Lesson: Dependence**

Verse 21's deepest teaching lies in a fact the listener may overlook: the human being cannot make milk, wool, or meat. He can only receive them from creatures that he did not create and whose inner workings he does not control. The Qur'an presses this in Sūrah Yā Sīn: *"Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have made, cattle, so that they are their owners? And We have tamed them for them, so some of them they ride and some they eat"* (36:71–72). The word "tamed" (*dhallalnā*) names a further mercy: the animals could have been wild and useless, or dangerous; God made them docile enough for a child to lead. A camel, many times a man's strength, kneels for him to mount. This docility is not the human being's achievement; it is a subjection God imposed on the animal for the human being's sake. The believer who mounts a horse or milks a goat is exercising a dominion that was *granted*, and the grant can be recalled.

**The Argument to the Deniers**

Like every sign in this catalogue, cattle carry an argument. The sūrah's opponents denied the resurrection and, in practice, gave God partners — idols who neither created cattle nor gave milk. The Qur'an asks them in the parallel passage of Sūrah al-Naḥl: *"Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then be reminded?"* (16:17). The one who gives milk from between blood and waste, wool from skin, and strength from grass, is the only one deserving of worship. Verse 21's *ʿibrah* is a crossing not only from the cow to the Creator but from the many gods to the One. And the transformation within the animal — grass into milk — is, once more, a categorical change of the kind that proves the possibility of the final transformation, dust into living body.

**The Spiritual Reading**

The commentators who read the natural signs allegorically saw in cattle the lower self (*nafs*) that must be tamed. The animal soul in the human being — its appetites and strength — is like the camel: dangerous if wild, immensely useful if disciplined. The seven qualities of verses 2–9 are the discipline by which the believer tames his own *anʿām* and draws from them the milk of good deeds. The person who has subjected his appetites to God's law finds in them, as the verse says of cattle, *"many benefits"*; the person who has not is dragged by them.

**Gratitude Made Concrete**

The Prophet ﷺ taught his community to see cattle as this verse teaches. He told the man who complained of poverty to seek out the milk of his neighbors' animals, and he counted among the marks of a blessed household the presence of a sheep or two. He taught that the animals themselves have rights: to be fed, watered, not overburdened, and not tormented — *"A woman entered the Fire because of a cat she tied up, neither feeding it nor letting it eat of the vermin of the earth"* (al-Bukhārī 3318; Muslim 2242). The *ʿibrah* of verse 21 is thus not merely a matter of admiration but of conduct. The believer who takes the lesson treats the animal as a divine provision and its Provider as the object of thanks.

**Toward the Roads and the Seas**

The next verse will complete the catalogue by naming the last great benefit of cattle — transport — and pairing it with a benefit of the sea: ships. From the bellies of animals, the sūrah will move to the backs of camels and the decks of vessels.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:22

> **And upon them, and upon ships, are you carried.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Catalogue's Last Sign: Movement**

The catalogue of natural signs that began with the seven heavens closes with a short verse about transport: *wa ʿalayhā wa ʿalā al-fulki tuḥmalūn* — "and upon them (the cattle) and upon the ships you are carried." After the drink, the many benefits, and the meat of verse 21, the verse names one final use of cattle — bearing human beings across the land — and pairs it with the vessel that bears them across the sea. The sūrah has moved from the sky (v. 17), through rain (v. 18), gardens (v. 19), the olive (v. 20), and cattle (v. 21), to the two means by which the human being crosses the two great surfaces of the earth: dry land and water. The verse is brief because it completes rather than begins; it is the last note of a chord.

**"Upon Them": The Camel as Ship of the Desert**

The pronoun *ʿalayhā* ("upon them") refers to the *anʿām* of the previous verse — the livestock — and specifically to those among them that are ridden: camels, horses being counted separately in the Qur'an (16:8), and, in other lands, oxen and donkeys. For the Arab listener, the reference was above all to the camel, which the Arabs themselves called *safīnat al-barr*, "the ship of the land." Without it the deserts of Arabia would have been impassable; with it, caravans linked Yemen to Syria, and the Quraysh grew wealthy on *"the journey of winter and summer"* (106:2). The camel carried people, goods, water, and tents; it endured thirst and heat; it converted the scrub of the desert into strength; and it knelt to receive its rider. The Qur'an singles it out for contemplation: *"Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?"* (88:17).

The verb is passive: *tuḥmalūn*, "you are carried." The human being does not carry himself; he is *borne* by a creature God tamed for him. This echoes verse 21's *nusqīkum* ("We give you drink") and the Qur'an's general habit of describing the human being as the *recipient* of provision, not its author. The Qur'an makes the point explicit in Sūrah al-Zukhruf: *"...and made for you of ships and cattle those which you ride, that you may settle yourselves upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you have settled upon them and say: 'Glory to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have done it by ourselves (wa mā kunnā lahu muqrinīn); and indeed, to our Lord we shall return'"* (43:12–14). This verse of al-Zukhruf is the perfect commentary on verse 22: it names both cattle and ships, it uses the same idea of being carried, and it tells the rider what to say.

**The Supplication of Riding**

The Prophet ﷺ made the teaching of 43:13 a practice. Muslim and Abū Dāwūd record from Ibn ʿUmar that when the Prophet ﷺ mounted his camel to travel, he would say *Allāhu akbar* three times and then:

> *"Glory to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have done it by ourselves; and indeed, to our Lord we shall return. O God, we ask You on this journey of ours for righteousness and piety, and for deeds that please You. O God, make this journey easy for us and fold up its distance for us. O God, You are the Companion on the journey and the Guardian of the family. O God, I seek refuge in You from the hardship of travel, from a sorrowful sight, and from an evil return in wealth and family."* (Muslim 1342)

Every Muslim who recites these words on mounting a vehicle — a camel then, a car or plane now — is enacting verse 22. The words convert the act of being carried into an act of remembrance. The phrase *"we could not have done it by ourselves"* is the exact confession that verse 22's passive verb demands: the strength of the camel, the buoyancy of the ship, the engine of the car, are all beyond the rider's own power; he sits upon them by a subjection God imposed.

**"And Upon Ships": The Sea Made Passable**

The second half of the verse names *al-fulk* — ships. The word *fulk* is used in the Qur'an for both a single ship and ships in general, and it is the word used for Noah's ark, which this very sūrah will describe in verses 27–28. The mention of ships here is thus a bridge to the narrative that follows: the ship as a sign of mercy (v. 22) leads directly into the ship as the instrument of salvation from the Flood (vv. 27–29). The sūrah's transitions are never accidental.

The Qur'an lists the ship among God's signs more than twenty times, and always with the same emphasis: the sea is vast, deep, and dangerous; the ship is a fragile assembly of wood; and yet, by God's law, the ship floats, the wind drives it, and human beings cross the uncrossable. *"And of His signs are the ships in the sea like mountains; if He wills, He stills the wind and they remain motionless on its surface"* (42:32–33). *"Do you not see that the ships sail through the sea by the favor of God, that He may show you of His signs? Indeed in that are signs for everyone patient and grateful"* (31:31). And: *"Your Lord is He who drives the ship for you through the sea that you may seek of His bounty; indeed, He is ever Merciful to you"* (17:66).

The ship is a sign in a way slightly different from the camel. The camel is a living creature God tamed; the ship is a human artifact. Yet the Qur'an attributes the ship's sailing to God, because the *conditions* that make it possible — the density of water, the buoyancy of wood, the winds, the stars by which sailors navigate (6:97), the human intelligence that builds hulls and sails — are all God's provision. The human being builds the ship; God built the sea, the wind, the wood, and the builder. Verse 22 credits the carrying to God without denying the craft to man.

**The Human Being as a Traveler**

There is a deeper reason why the catalogue of signs ends with transport. The human being is, in the Qur'an's understanding, a traveler. He is on a journey from the drop (v. 13) to the grave (v. 15) to the standing (v. 16), and every earthly journey is a small image of the great one. The Prophet ﷺ told Ibn ʿUmar: *"Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveler passing through"* (al-Bukhārī 6416). The camel and the ship carry the traveler across land and sea; but the same God who provides those carriers provides the carriers of the final journey: *"the Day the earth will be changed into another earth"* (14:48). The person who is carried across the desert by a camel he did not create, and across the sea by winds he does not command, should recognize that he is carried through *all* of life by a power not his own. Verse 22's passive verb is a description of the human condition.

The source commentary notes that seafaring functions in the Qur'an as a symbol of the human spiritual state, and this is developed most sharply in the passages that describe the sailor in a storm. When the waves rise like shadows, the Qur'an says, people *"call upon God, sincere to Him in religion; but when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate, and some deny"* (31:32; cf. 10:22–23; 29:65). The ship exposes what prosperity hides: the human being's true dependence, which he remembers when the sea is angry and forgets when it is calm. Verse 22 names the ship as a blessing; the storm verses name it as a test. Both are true, and the sūrah's opening believers — who are *"in awe for fear of their Lord"* even on land (23:57) — are those who remember at sea what they knew on shore.

**The Completed Catalogue and Its Structure**

With verse 22 the sūrah's second movement — the signs of God in creation — closes. It is worth seeing the whole in outline. The passage began with the human being (vv. 12–16), traced from clay to resurrection. It then turned outward to the cosmos (v. 17), the rain (v. 18), the plants (vv. 19–20), the animals (v. 21), and finally the means of human movement across the earth (v. 22). The order is meaningful: it moves from the human being's own body, which he cannot deny, to the heavens above him, to the water that comes down from them, to the fruit that grows from the water, to the animals that eat the fruit's kin, to the human uses of those animals and of the sea. Every element depends on the one before, and every element is *"for you."* The catalogue is a single argument: you are surrounded, above and below and within, by evidence of a Creator who provides with measure, who is not heedless, and who can withdraw what He gave.

**The Response the Verse Seeks**

The Qur'an tells the listener how to respond to verse 22 in the parallel verses already cited: *"remember the favor of your Lord... and say: Glory to Him who has subjected this to us"* (43:13). The right response to being carried is not pride in one's vehicle but gratitude to the One who made the carrying possible. In the modern world, where the camel has become the automobile and the ship the aircraft, the verse's meaning is unchanged. The engineering is human; the physics, the materials, the intelligence, and the safe arrival are God's. The believer who says the traveling supplication before starting the engine is training himself in the awareness the verse teaches, and the believer who arrives safely and says *al-ḥamdu lillāh* has understood that the arrival was not guaranteed.

**Toward Noah**

The mention of ships in verse 22 prepares the ear for what follows. Having laid out the signs of God in the human being and the world, the sūrah will now turn to history — to the record of those who saw these signs and denied them, beginning with the first great prophet of warning, Noah, and the ship that saved the believers when the water God had measured (v. 18) was released without measure.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:23

> **And We indeed sent Noah to his people, and he said, “O my people! Worship God! You have no god other than Him. Will you not be reverent?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn from Signs to History**
