The sūrah has laid out its evidence: the human body (vv. 12–16) and the created world (vv. 17–22). Now it turns to what human beings have done with that evidence: *wa laqad arsalnā Nūḥan ilā qawmihi fa-qāla yā qawmi uʿbudū Allāha mā lakum min ilāhin ghayruhu a-fa-lā tattaqūn* — "And We certainly sent Noah to his people, and he said: 'O my people, worship God; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?'" The same emphatic *wa laqad* that introduced the creation of man (v. 12) and the heavens (v. 17) now introduces the sending of the first great messenger. The three *wa laqad*s tie the three sections together: We created you; We built the world for you; and We sent messengers to tell you what it all means.

The transition has a specific logic. The signs of verses 12–22 are, in principle, sufficient for a thinking person to infer a Creator. But the Qur'an knows that signs alone are not enough; human beings need a *messenger* to articulate what the signs imply and to command the response they require. Noah is the first such messenger of whom the Qur'an gives a detailed account, and his message is the message the signs were pointing to: *worship God alone*.

**Why Noah Comes First**

Noah is the first of the five "messengers of firm resolve" (*ulū al-ʿazm*, 46:35) and the first prophet sent to a people who had fallen into idolatry. The Prophet ﷺ described him as *"the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth"* (al-Bukhārī 3340; Muslim 194, in the ḥadīth of intercession, where humanity will say to Noah: "You are the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth"). Before Noah, the commentators explain, humanity was on a single religion of monotheism; idolatry arose in his time, and he was sent to confront it. Ibn ʿAbbās explained the origin of that idolatry in a report al-Bukhārī records: the idols of Noah's people — Wadd, Suwāʿ, Yaghūth, Yaʿūq, and Nasr (71:23) — were originally righteous men whose statues were set up after their deaths as memorials, and whom later generations came to worship (al-Bukhārī 4920). Noah's mission was thus the first great confrontation between revealed monotheism and human-invented religion, and every subsequent messenger repeated it.

Noah's relevance to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah was direct. Noah preached for nine hundred and fifty years (29:14) to a people who mocked him, called him mad, and threatened him — precisely what the Quraysh were doing to Muḥammad ﷺ. The sūrah tells Noah's story to tell the Prophet's: the opposition you face is not new; it is the oldest pattern in human history, and it always ends the same way.

**"We Sent": The Meaning of Irsāl**

The verb *arsalnā*, "We sent," from the root *r-s-l*, is the root of *rasūl*, messenger. A *rasūl* is one sent with a message from another; the word implies both the authority of the sender and the fidelity of the bearer. By saying *"We sent Noah,"* God establishes at the outset that Noah's words are not his own opinion but a commission. This matters for what follows: when Noah's people reject him, they are rejecting the One who sent him. The Qur'an makes this explicit of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God"* (4:80). The messenger's authority is derivative, and therefore absolute within its scope.

**"O My People": The Voice of Kinship**

Noah's address begins *yā qawmi* — "O my people." The possessive "my" is tender. Noah does not address them as "O idolaters" or "O sinners" but as *his* people, his kin, those to whom he belongs and who belong to him. Every prophet in the Qur'an speaks this way to his own nation — Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, Moses — and the phrase carries a whole ethic of preaching. The messenger is not an outsider condemning strangers; he is a member of the family pleading with his family. This is why the Qur'an says the messengers were sent *"from among themselves"* (23:32; 2:151): a message delivered by a stranger can be dismissed; a message delivered by one's own brother, whose honesty one has known for decades, cannot so easily be. The sūrah will later use this fact against the Quraysh: *"Or do they not know their Messenger, and so deny him?"* (23:69).

**"Worship God; You Have No God Other Than Him": The Core Message**

The heart of Noah's message is two sentences: *uʿbudū Allāha* — "worship God" — and *mā lakum min ilāhin ghayruhu* — "you have no deity other than Him." The first is a command; the second is the reason for it. The command uses the imperative *uʿbudū*, from *ʿ-b-d*, the root of *ʿabd*, servant. To worship is to make oneself a servant — to submit, obey, love, fear, and hope in the One served. The second sentence uses the strongest form of negation in Arabic: *mā... min... ghayruhu* — "there is not, of any deity, other than Him." The *min* before *ilāh* is the *min* of comprehensive negation: not a single deity, of any kind, exists besides Him. This is the sentence that every prophet was sent to deliver, as the Qur'an states: *"And We sent no messenger before you except that We revealed to him: There is no deity except Me, so worship Me"* (21:25).

The source commentary points out that this precise refrain — *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him"* — recurs in this sūrah in verse 32, on the lips of the unnamed messenger to the next generation, and in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf and Sūrah Hūd on the lips of Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, and Shuʿayb in succession (7:59, 65, 73, 85; 11:50, 61, 84). The repetition is a deliberate literary and theological device. It shows that the message of every messenger was *identical* — not merely similar, but word for word the same — and therefore that the religion of God is one across history. The sūrah will state this explicitly: *"Indeed this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me"* (23:52). Verse 23 is the first instance of that unity.

**"Will You Not Be Reverent?": Taqwā as the Response**

Noah's address closes with a question: *a-fa-lā tattaqūn* — "Will you not then be God-fearing?" The verb *tattaqūn* is from *taqwā*, the central Qur'anic virtue, whose root *w-q-y* means to guard oneself, to protect against harm. *Taqwā* is the state of a person who walks carefully because he knows there is danger — like a traveler on a narrow path with thorns on either side, gathering his garments and watching his step. Noah's question thus means: knowing that there is no god but God, and that He will hold you to account, will you not guard yourselves? Will you not take care?

The question form is rhetorical but not merely so. It is an appeal to reason. Noah has stated a fact (there is no other god) and now asks his people to draw the obvious practical conclusion. If the fact is true, reverence is the only rational response; the question exposes the irrationality of hearing the fact and remaining careless. The particle *fa-* in *a-fa-lā* ("will you not *then*") marks this inference: *given* what I have said, will you not *therefore* fear? The whole sūrah is built on such inferences — from the signs of verses 12–22 to the worship of verse 23; from the concession that God owns everything (vv. 84–89) to the question *"how then are you bewitched?"* (v. 89).

**The Logic of Noah's Message**

Noah's three sentences form a complete argument that deserves to be spelled out because it is the argument of the entire Qur'an. First: worship God. Second: because there is no other god. Third: therefore, guard yourselves. The middle premise is the foundation. If there were other gods, worship might be divided; if there were none at all, worship would be pointless. But if there is exactly one God — the One who made you from clay, sends the rain, grows the gardens, gives the milk, and holds the seven heavens — then to worship anything else is to worship what did none of this, and to worship nothing is to ignore the One who did all of it. The rationality of monotheism lies in its correspondence to reality: there is one Source, and the intelligent creature aligns himself with it.

The message also implies a moral order. *Taqwā* — guarding oneself — presupposes that there is something to guard against: a reckoning, a consequence, a Judge. Noah's question assumes that his people know, at some level, that their idolatry has consequences. The sūrah will confirm this assumption when it shows the deniers conceding God's ownership of everything (vv. 84–89) while refusing its implications. Noah's people, like the Quraysh, did not lack knowledge; they lacked the will to act on it. *A-fa-lā tattaqūn* is addressed to that will.

**Noah's Method: The Pattern of Prophetic Preaching**

The Qur'an records Noah's preaching at greater length in Sūrah Nūḥ (71:5–20), and reading it alongside verse 23 fills out the portrait. Noah preached *"night and day"* (71:5), *"openly and in secret"* (71:9); he promised forgiveness, rain, wealth, children, and gardens to those who repented (71:10–12); he argued from creation — *"Do you not see how God created seven heavens in layers, and made the moon a light and the sun a lamp? And God caused you to grow from the earth"* (71:15–17) — the very signs this sūrah has just enumerated. His people responded by *"putting their fingers in their ears, covering themselves with their garments, persisting, and being arrogant"* (71:7). Noah is thus the model of the patient preacher who uses every method — reason, promise, warning, persistence, gentleness — and who is rejected not for lack of evidence but for the hardness of his hearers.

**The Verse's Bearing on the Believer**

For the believer, verse 23 establishes several things. It establishes that his religion is the religion of Noah — the oldest religion on earth, not an innovation of the seventh century. It establishes that the core of that religion is a single sentence, *"there is no god but God,"* and a single response, *taqwā*. It establishes that preaching that religion means addressing people as "my people," with kinship and patience, and asking them to reason. And it establishes that rejection is not evidence of failure: the greatest of preachers preached for nearly a millennium and was believed, the Qur'an says, by *"only a few"* (11:40).

For the modern reader, Noah's question remains the question. The signs of verses 12–22 are more precisely understood now than at any time in history — the embryo's stages, the water cycle, the chemistry of milk. The response the signs call for is unchanged: *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then guard yourselves?"* The reply of Noah's people, which the next verse records, is the reply that every generation has been tempted to give.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:24

> **But the notables who disbelieved among his people said, “This is only a human being like yourselves, desiring to set himself above you. And had God willed, He would have sent down angels. We heard not of this from our fathers of old.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The First Recorded Rejection**

Noah has delivered the simplest message in the world: worship God alone, and guard yourselves. Verse 24 records the reply — the first reply of a people to a messenger that the sūrah quotes at length: *fa-qāla al-malaʾu alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi mā hādhā illā basharun mithlukum yurīdu an yatafaḍḍala ʿalaykum wa law shāʾa Allāhu la-anzala malāʾikatan mā samiʿnā bi-hādhā fī ābāʾinā al-awwalīn* — "But the chiefs who disbelieved among his people said: 'This is nothing but a human being like you who wishes to gain superiority over you. And if God had willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our forefathers.'" Four objections are packed into this single verse, and every one of them would be repeated against every subsequent prophet, including Muḥammad ﷺ. The verse is thus not merely a historical record but a catalogue of the standard arguments of unbelief.

**Who Spoke: The Malaʾ**

The speakers are identified as *al-malaʾ alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi* — "the *malaʾ* who disbelieved among his people." The word *malaʾ*, from the root *m-l-ʾ*, "to fill," denotes the assembly of chiefs, the notables, the leading men who "fill" the council and whose presence "fills the eye" with their status and wealth. As the source notes, the Qur'an uses this word for the ruling elites in nearly every prophetic story: the *malaʾ* of Pharaoh (7:109; 23:46), of the Queen of Sheba (27:29), of the Quraysh (38:6), of the people of Hūd (7:66), of Shuʿayb (7:88), and of the king in Joseph's story (12:43). The pattern is unmistakable and the sūrah's introduction has already noted it: the opposition to prophets comes first and most bitterly from the *powerful*. The poor and the weak are the first to believe — the Qur'an records that Noah's followers were called *"the lowest of us"* (26:111) and *"those who are the most abject among us, at first thought"* (11:27) — while those who have the most to lose from a leveling message are the first to resist it.

The qualifier *alladhīna kafarū min qawmihi* — "who disbelieved among his people" — is a precise restriction. Not all the notables disbelieved; not all his people were notables. The verse names a specific faction: the powerful who chose disbelief. The Qur'an is careful not to condemn whole classes; it condemns choices.

**Objection One: "Only a Human Being Like You"**

The first objection is *mā hādhā illā basharun mithlukum* — "this is nothing but a human being like you." The construction *mā... illā* ("nothing but") is dismissive: Noah is reduced to his species. The word *bashar* denotes the human being in his physical, visible aspect — from the root meaning skin, surface — as opposed to *insān*, which emphasizes his social and rational nature. To call Noah "a *bashar* like you" is to say: he has skin like yours, eats like you, sleeps like you; what could such a creature have to do with God?

The objection assumes that a messenger of God must be something other than human. The Qur'an answers it repeatedly and from several angles. First, a human messenger is *necessary*: only a human can be a model for humans, can be imitated, can be understood. *"Say: If there were on the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from heaven an angel as a messenger"* (17:95). Second, every messenger before was human: *"And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed"* (16:43; 21:7). Third, the messenger's humanity is precisely what makes his miracle a miracle — a man who could not read brought a Book; a man like them spoke words they could not match. The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say exactly this: *"Say: I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God"* (18:110). The very phrase the notables used as an objection, God commanded His Prophet to use as a confession.

**Objection Two: "He Wishes to Set Himself Above You"**

The second objection is *yurīdu an yatafaḍḍala ʿalaykum* — "he wishes to gain superiority over you." The verb *yatafaḍḍala*, from *faḍl* (excellence, favor, surplus), means to seek to be preferred, to raise oneself above others in rank. The notables interpret Noah's message as a bid for power: he claims prophethood in order to rule.

This objection reveals more about its speakers than about Noah. The *malaʾ* were men whose whole lives were organized around rank; they could not conceive of a man speaking except to gain rank. They projected their own motive onto the prophet. The Qur'an exposes this projection by recording Noah's actual position: he asked for no wage — *"O my people, I ask you for no wealth for it; my reward is only from God"* (11:29) — and he refused to drive away the poor believers to please the rich (11:29–30; 26:114). A man seeking superiority does not embrace the lowest and refuse payment. The sūrah will later put the same defense on the lips of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Or do you ask them for a wage? The wage of your Lord is better"* (23:72). The messengers' refusal of payment is the standing refutation of the charge of ambition.

The psychological insight is sharp and durable. When people cannot answer a message, they attack the messenger's motives — and the motive they attribute is usually their own. The one who loves money accuses the preacher of greed; the one who loves power accuses him of ambition; the one who loves fame accuses him of vanity. The *malaʾ* wanted superiority, and so they saw superiority-seeking in the man who threatened theirs.

**Objection Three: "Had God Willed, He Would Have Sent Angels"**

The third objection is *wa law shāʾa Allāhu la-anzala malāʾikatan* — "and if God had willed, He would have sent down angels." Here the notables invoke God against His messenger. They do not deny God's existence; they claim to know how He would act if He wished to communicate: He would send angels, not a man.

The objection is a form of argument from personal expectation: "This is not how *I* would have done it, therefore it was not done." It recurs throughout the Qur'an: *"Why was an angel not sent down to him?"* (6:8); *"Why was an angel not sent down with him to be a warner alongside him?"* (25:7); *"If your Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels; so indeed we disbelieve in what you have been sent with"* (41:14). The Qur'an's reply is threefold. If an angel had been sent, it would have had to appear as a man in order to be seen and followed, and the same confusion would have resulted (6:9). If an angel had been sent in its true form, the matter would have been decided and no respite for repentance would remain (6:8). And the demand itself is a refusal to be guided by evidence: Noah's people had the message, its reasonableness, and the man's known integrity; they wanted a spectacle instead of a truth.

There is also a subtle theological error in the objection. By saying "had God willed, He would have sent angels," the notables invoke God's will as though they knew it — while rejecting the actual expression of that will, which was Noah. The Qur'an will later show the Makkans doing the same (23:84–89): conceding God's sovereignty in words while refusing it in practice.

**Objection Four: "We Never Heard This from Our Forefathers"**

The fourth and final objection is *mā samiʿnā bi-hādhā fī ābāʾinā al-awwalīn* — "we have not heard of this among our earliest forefathers." This is the argument from tradition: what our ancestors did not know cannot be true. It is the most common of all objections to the prophets in the Qur'an. The people of Hūd said it (7:70); Pharaoh's people said it (28:36); the Quraysh said it repeatedly — *"Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps"* (43:22–23); *"Rather, they say: We found our fathers upon a way, and we are guided by their footsteps"* (43:22).

The Qur'an's response to this argument is one of its most important contributions to human thought: *"Even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?"* (2:170); *"Even if I bring you better guidance than what you found your fathers upon?"* (43:24). Tradition, the Qur'an teaches, is a *fact* about the past, not an *argument* about the truth. That one's ancestors believed something proves that they believed it; it proves nothing about whether it is so. The notables' fourth objection is a refusal to think — a decision to let the dead decide for the living. Ibn Kathīr comments that this objection reflects *"their blind imitation of their ancestors without proof."*

The irony, which the Qur'an elsewhere exposes, is that the notables' own idolatry was itself a departure from *their* ancestors' religion: as Ibn ʿAbbās explained (al-Bukhārī 4920), the idols of Noah's people were memorials to righteous men that later generations turned into gods. The tradition the *malaʾ* defended was an innovation; the message they rejected as novel was the original faith. Those who appeal to "our forefathers" rarely go back far enough.

**The Structure of the Verse: A Portrait of Denial**

The four objections form a complete psychology of rejection, and they are still the four objections one hears today. The first (he is only human) is *contempt for the messenger*. The second (he seeks superiority) is *suspicion of motive*. The third (God would have sent angels) is *the demand for a different kind of evidence*. The fourth (our fathers never heard this) is *the refuge in tradition*. None of the four engages the actual content of Noah's message — that there is one God who created them and will hold them to account. The notables attack everything about the message except the message. This is the signature of denial in every age: when the argument cannot be answered, the arguer is discredited, his motives impugned, the form of the proof rejected, and the authority of custom invoked.

**Why the Qur'an Records the Objections**

The Qur'an does not hide the arguments of the prophets' enemies; it quotes them in full and answers them. This is itself a lesson. A message confident of its truth does not fear the objections against it; it states them fairly and replies. The believer who reads verse 24 is being trained to recognize these objections — in others and in himself — and to see through them. He is also being comforted: the Prophet ﷺ heard every one of these four objections from the Quraysh, and the verse tells him that Noah heard them first, four thousand years before, and that they did not prevent the Flood.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Argument**

Verse 24 also serves the sūrah's larger design. The opening described believers marked by humility (v. 2); verse 24 describes the notables marked by arrogance. The opening described people who "keep their covenant" (v. 8); the notables break the primal covenant with God. The signs of verses 12–22 were addressed to reason; the notables reply with contempt, suspicion, spectacle-seeking, and tradition — everything except reason. The sūrah is drawing, in parallel columns, the two kinds of human being it announced in verse 1 and will announce again in verse 117: those who prosper and those who do not. The *malaʾ* of Noah's people are the first full portrait of the second kind. The next verse will complete their speech with an insult and a threat.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:25

> **He is but a man possessed. So wait concerning him, for a time.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Argument to Insult**

The notables' speech, which began in verse 24 with four objections dressed as arguments, ends in verse 25 with a diagnosis and a dismissal: *in huwa illā rajulun bihi jinnatun fa-tarabbaṣū bihi ḥattā ḥīn* — "He is nothing but a man in whom is madness; so wait concerning him until a time." The movement from verse 24 to verse 25 is the movement from debate to contempt. Having failed to answer Noah's message, the chiefs declare that it needs no answer: the man is insane. This is the last refuge of those who cannot refute — to declare the speaker unworthy of refutation.

**"Nothing But a Man": The Diminishing Formula Again**

The verse opens with the same construction as the first objection of verse 24: *in huwa illā* — "he is nothing but." The particle *in* here is a negative (equivalent to *mā*), and *illā* means "except"; together they produce an exclusive, reductive claim: he is *nothing more than* the following. In verse 24 the reduction was to *bashar*, a human being; in verse 25 it is to *rajul bihi jinnah*, a man with madness in him. The notables have moved from "merely human" to "less than a sane human." The escalation is deliberate: contempt, once begun, grows.

**"In Whom Is Madness": The Meaning of Jinnah**

The phrase *bihi jinnah* — literally "in him is *jinnah*" — is the verse's key expression. The word *jinnah* comes from the root *j-n-n*, whose basic meaning is concealment or covering. From this root come *jinn* (the hidden beings), *janīn* (the fetus, hidden in the womb), *jannah* (the garden, hidden by dense foliage), *junnah* (a shield, which covers), and *majnūn* (the madman, whose reason is covered). *Jinnah* is madness, insanity — the state of a person whose intellect has been veiled. As the source notes, the word is related to *majnūn* and evokes the pre-Islamic belief that madness was caused by possession by *jinn*. Both terms can mean simply "insane," without reference to the supernatural, and the notables may have intended either sense: that Noah was literally possessed by a spirit, or simply that he had lost his mind.

The accusation of madness is the most frequent charge against the prophets in the Qur'an. It was made against Noah here and in 54:9 (*"they said: A madman!"*); against Moses by Pharaoh (26:27: *"Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad"*); and against the Prophet ﷺ repeatedly (15:6; 37:36; 44:14; 51:52; 68:51; 81:22). The Qur'an notes the pattern explicitly: *"Likewise, there came to those before them no messenger except that they said: 'A magician or a madman.' Did they suggest it to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people"* (51:52–53). The uniformity of the accusation across centuries and continents, the Qur'an suggests, is itself evidence that it is not an honest diagnosis but a reflex of rejection.

**Why "Madness" Is the Charge**

Why did the notables choose insanity rather than, say, deceit? The choice is psychologically precise. A liar must be argued with, because a liar has a purpose; a madman need not be argued with, because a madman has no reason to appeal to. By declaring Noah insane, the *malaʾ* excused themselves from engaging his message at all. The charge is also socially effective: it mobilizes pity and fear rather than curiosity. People do not investigate the claims of the mad; they avoid them. The chiefs were not trying to prove Noah wrong; they were trying to make him unhearable.

There is a further irony that the Qur'an draws out elsewhere. The content of Noah's message — worship the One who made you, the sky, the rain, and the gardens — is the most rational proposition available. The content of the notables' position — worship statues of dead men, deny any accounting, obey ancestors who understood nothing — is, by any measure, the less rational. The Qur'an turns the charge around in the case of the Prophet ﷺ: *"Your companion is not mad"* (81:22), and: *"By the grace of your Lord, you are not mad"* (68:2), and then it describes the true madness: *"Have you seen the one who takes as his god his own desire?"* (25:43). The man who follows evidence to its Source is called mad by men who follow their appetites and their fathers. The sūrah will later put the charge against the Prophet ﷺ in exactly these words — *"Or do they say: In him is madness?"* (23:70) — and answer it: *"Rather, he has brought them the truth."*

**"So Wait Concerning Him Until a Time"**

The second half of the verse is the notables' policy: *fa-tarabbaṣū bihi ḥattā ḥīn* — "so wait concerning him for a time." The verb *tarabbaṣa* means to wait expectantly, to bide one's time, to watch for an outcome. The phrase *ḥattā ḥīn* — "until a time" — is deliberately vague: until some while has passed, until things change.

The commentators understood this counsel in two ways. First, as a counsel of patience: wait until he dies, or until his madness passes, or until people lose interest, and the problem will solve itself. Al-Ṭabarī explains: *"Wait for him until death comes to him and relieves you of him."* Second, as a counsel of observation: watch him for a while and see whether what he says comes true. Both readings share a strategy — do nothing, engage nothing, simply outlast him. It is the policy of those who cannot win an argument but believe they can wait it out.

The Qur'an notes the same strategy among the Quraysh toward the Prophet ﷺ: *"Or do they say: A poet, for whom we await the calamity of time?"* (52:30) — that is, let us wait until he dies as other poets have died. And the Qur'an's answer: *"Say: Wait, for indeed I am with you among those who wait"* (52:31). The messenger, too, is waiting — but for a different outcome. In the case of Noah, the outcome was the Flood.

**The Irony of "Until a Time"**

There is a profound irony in the notables' words that the sūrah will unfold. They said: wait until a time. The Qur'an later says of Noah's people: *"So the Cry seized them in truth"* (23:41, of the next generation), and of Noah's: *"And they were drowned"* (23:27). The *ḥīn* — the "time" — came, but it was not the time they expected. They waited for Noah's death; God sent the deluge. The notables imagined that time was on their side; the sūrah teaches that time is on the side of the truth. *"No community can hasten its term, nor delay it"* (23:43). The disbelievers' "wait" and God's "term" (*ajal*) are two different clocks, and only one of them is real.

**The Verse as a Warning to the Believer**

There is a lesson here for the believer who is himself tempted to "wait" — to postpone commitment, to observe from a distance, to see how things turn out before deciding. The notables' policy was fatal not because it was hostile but because it was passive: they treated the greatest question of their lives as something to be deferred. The Qur'an's constant counsel is the opposite: *"And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord"* (3:133); *"Race to the good"* (2:148). The person who waits "until a time" to take religion seriously often discovers that the time was shorter than he supposed — which is precisely what the sūrah's closing verses will depict: *"Until, when death comes to one of them, he says: My Lord, send me back"* (23:99).

**What the Believer Learns from Being Called Mad**

The verse also prepares the believer for a specific experience: being considered irrational by those who reject his faith. In every age, the person who prays five times daily, fasts a month a year, gives away a portion of his wealth, guards his chastity, and orders his life around an unseen God will be thought, by some, to have lost his reason. The sūrah teaches him to recognize the charge as the oldest in history, to notice that it was leveled at the most rational men who ever lived, and to respond as Noah responded — not with anger but with continued preaching and, when the preaching is exhausted, with prayer (v. 26). The Prophet ﷺ was called mad, magician, poet, and soothsayer; he answered with the Qur'an and with patience. The charge of madness is not a verdict; it is a sign that the message has struck something that cannot be argued with and must therefore be dismissed.

**The Speech Concluded**

With verse 25 the notables' speech is complete. Two verses have contained five objections and a policy: he is only a man; he wants power; God would have sent angels; our fathers never heard of it; he is mad; wait him out. Not one word addresses whether there is one God who made the world. The Qur'an has set the entire case for unbelief before the reader and shown that it consists of everything except an answer. Noah's response, in the next verse, is not another argument. He has made his arguments for nine hundred and fifty years. He turns to his Lord.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:26

> **He said, “My Lord! Help me, for they deny me.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**When Argument Ends, Prayer Begins**

The notables have spoken: Noah is only a man, an ambitious man, a madman; God would have sent angels; the ancestors knew nothing of this; wait him out. Noah's reply is not addressed to them at all. It is addressed to God: *qāla rabbi unṣurnī bimā kadhdhabūn* — "He said: 'My Lord, help me because they have denied me.'" Seven words in Arabic, and they mark the turning point of the story. Everything before this verse was Noah speaking to his people; everything after it is God acting. The prayer is the hinge between the age of preaching and the age of judgment.

The brevity of the prayer is itself instructive. Noah does not deliver a long complaint, does not rehearse the nine hundred and fifty years of mockery, does not name the notables or list their crimes. He says three things: *my Lord*; *help me*; *they have denied me*. The economy reflects a heart that has said everything it needs to say to people and now needs only to say one thing to God.

**"My Lord": The Address of Intimacy**

Noah begins with *rabbi* — "my Lord." The word *rabb* denotes the one who owns, nurtures, sustains, and brings to completion; a *rabb* is not merely a master but a caretaker, the one responsible for the growth of what he owns. The possessive *-ī* ("my") makes the address personal. Noah does not say "O God" (*Allāhumma*) or "O Lord of the worlds"; he says "*my* Lord" — the One who has cared for me, who sent me, who has watched every day of this long mission. This is the address of the prophets in their extremity: Zechariah's *rabbi* (19:4), Job's *rabbi* (21:83), Jonah's cry from the belly of the fish, Moses's *rabbi* at the burning bush and after his flight from Egypt (28:24). The word carries the whole relationship: I am Yours; You have raised me; I turn to You.

**"Help Me": The Request**

The request is a single imperative: *unṣurnī* — "help me," "grant me victory." The root *n-ṣ-r* means to aid, to support, to give victory to one against an opponent. It is the root of *anṣār*, the Helpers of Madinah, and of *naṣr*, the victory that the Qur'an promises the messengers: *"Indeed, We will support (la-nanṣuru) Our messengers and those who believe in the life of this world and on the Day the witnesses will stand"* (40:51). The word implies a contest with two sides and a request that God take one's side.

What kind of help did Noah ask for? The commentators read the request in light of what followed and of Noah's fuller prayer in Sūrah Nūḥ: *"My Lord, do not leave upon the earth of the disbelievers a single inhabitant; indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and beget none but wicked disbelievers"* (71:26–27). Noah's request for help was, in the end, a request for judgment — for God to decide between him and his people, since they had made clear that they would never decide for themselves. In Sūrah al-Qamar the same prayer is quoted in slightly different words: *"So he called upon his Lord: I am overpowered, so help (fa-ntaṣir)"* (54:10). "I am overpowered" — *annī maghlūb* — is the confession that lies beneath verse 26: I have done all that a man can do; now only You can act.

**"Because They Have Denied Me": The Reason**

The grounds for the request are given in three words: *bimā kadhdhabūn* — "because of their denying me." The *bāʾ* is causal: help me *on account of* their denial. Noah does not say "because they have wronged me" or "because they have insulted me" — though they had — but "because they have *denied* me." The verb *kadhdhaba* (Form II of *k-dh-b*, to lie) means to call someone a liar, to reject his truthfulness. The wound Noah names is not the personal insult of being called mad but the rejection of the *message*: they have declared the truth to be a lie. His prayer is for the vindication of the truth, not for the soothing of his feelings.

This is a subtle and important point. Prophets do not pray for revenge on those who mock them personally. The Prophet ﷺ, bleeding at Ṭāʾif, prayed: *"O God, guide my people, for they do not know"* (a report in al-Bukhārī 3477 records this prayer for a prophet struck by his people; the Prophet ﷺ made the same prayer). Noah's prayer comes after nine and a half centuries and after God Himself had revealed that *"none of your people will believe except those who have already believed"* (11:36). The prayer of verse 26 is the prayer of a man who has been told by God that the door is closed and who now asks God to do what only God can do. It is submission, not vengeance.

**The Pattern of the Prophets' Prayers**

Verse 26 is echoed almost word for word in verse 39, where the unnamed messenger of the next generation prays: *"My Lord, help me, for they have denied me."* The repetition establishes the prayer as the *standard* recourse of the messenger when preaching has been exhausted. The Qur'an records the same turn in Moses (*"My Lord, indeed I do not control except myself and my brother, so part us from the defiantly disobedient people,"* 5:25), in Lot (*"My Lord, help me against the corrupting people,"* 29:30), and in Shuʿayb (*"Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth,"* 7:89). The sequence is always the same: call, patience, rejection, prayer, judgment. The believer who sees this pattern understands that prayer is not the abandonment of effort but its completion — the last step of a process that began with the first word of preaching.

**Why Prayer, and Not Despair or Force**

The notables' rejection left Noah with three logical options: despair (give up, conclude the mission was futile), force (compel belief, or attack the deniers), or prayer (turn the matter over to God). The Qur'an shows him choosing the third, and the choice teaches the theology of the whole Book. Despair is excluded because *"none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people"* (12:87). Force is excluded because *"there is no compulsion in religion"* (2:256) and because the messenger's task is only to convey: *"Upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance"* (24:54). What remains is the recognition that hearts belong to God and outcomes belong to God, and that the servant's part ends where the Master's begins. The Qur'an tells the Prophet ﷺ: *"Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills"* (28:56). Noah's prayer is the enacted form of that verse.

There is also a psychological wisdom here. The person who has labored for years and been rejected is tempted either to bitterness or to self-blame. Noah's prayer avoids both. He does not curse his people (in this verse) and he does not accuse himself of failure. He states the fact — they denied — and hands it to the One who sent him. This is the emotional discipline that the Qur'an teaches to every believer who calls to good and is refused: your job was the calling; the result was never yours.

**God's Answer**

The next verse begins *fa-awḥaynā ilayhi* — "So We revealed to him" — and the *fa-* ("so, then") links the answer directly to the prayer. Noah asked for help; help came in the form of a command to build the Ark. This immediacy is the Qur'an's testimony to the power of the prayer of the wronged. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Beware the supplication of the oppressed, for there is no veil between it and God"* (al-Bukhārī 2448; Muslim 19). Noah was the most patiently oppressed man in history, and when he finally raised his hands, the answer was the greatest intervention in the history of the earth before the last Day.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 26 gives every believer a model of what to do when he has done everything he can. He has advised, argued, been patient, been mocked; the people have not changed. The verse teaches him to say: *rabbi unṣurnī* — my Lord, help me. It teaches him to name the real injury (denial of the truth, not wounded pride), to ask for God's help rather than his own revenge, and to trust that the *fa-* of the answer will follow. The help may not come as a flood; it may come as patience, as a change in circumstances, as the guidance of one heart among many, as vindication on a Day the believer will not see on earth. But the verse promises that it comes: *"And Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers: that they would be those given victory"* (37:171–172). The same root, *n-ṣ-r*, in the promise and in Noah's prayer.

**The Story Turns**

With this verse the narrative of Noah passes from the human to the divine. The people have said their last word (v. 25); Noah has said his (v. 26); now God speaks (v. 27). The next verse contains the longest divine speech in the sūrah's account of Noah — the command to build the Ark, the sign of the gushing oven, the instruction about who may board, and the prohibition against pleading for the wrongdoers.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:27

> **So We revealed unto Him, “Build the Ark before Our eyes and by Our Revelation. Then when Our Command comes and the oven gushes forth, place therein two of every kind, and thy family except those against whom the word has already gone forth. And address Me not concerning those who did wrong; surely they shall be drowned.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer to the Prayer**

Noah prayed, *"My Lord, help me"* (v. 26). Verse 27 is the answer, and it opens with the particle of immediate consequence: *fa-awḥaynā ilayhi* — "So We revealed to him." The help Noah asked for does not come as a thunderbolt against his enemies but as a set of instructions to Noah himself. This is characteristic of how God answers the prayers of His servants: not usually by removing the difficulty at once, but by giving the servant something to *do* within it. Noah asked for victory; he received a shipbuilding commission. The victory would come, but through his own labor under divine direction.

The verse is the longest in the sūrah's account of Noah and contains five distinct elements: the command to build; the sign that will signal the Flood; the instruction to load the Ark; the exception concerning his family; and the prohibition against interceding for the wrongdoers. Each deserves attention.

**"Build the Ark Before Our Eyes and by Our Revelation"**

The command is *iṣnaʿ al-fulka bi-aʿyuninā wa waḥyinā* — "construct the Ark under Our eyes and by Our revelation." The word *fulk* is the same word verse 22 used for ships in general; now it names the one specific ship that mattered most in human history. The verb *iṣnaʿ*, from *ṣ-n-ʿ*, means to craft, to manufacture, to make with skill; it implies labor and technique. Noah was not told to pray for a ship; he was told to build one.

The phrase *bi-aʿyuninā* — "under Our eyes" — is one of the Qur'an's expressions of God's attribute of sight, and the classical scholars of creed affirmed it as God has stated it, without asking how and without likening it to creaturely sight. Its meaning in context is protective and intimate: build it while We watch over you, guard you, and guide your hands. Al-Ṭabarī explains: *"under Our observation and Our protection"* — no one will be able to harm you or the Ark while you work. The same phrase is used of Moses: *"that you might be brought up under My eye"* (20:39), and of the Prophet ﷺ: *"for indeed you are under Our eyes"* (52:48). In each case the expression conveys that the servant is not laboring alone or unseen but under the direct care of his Lord. For Noah, who was about to spend years building a ship on dry land while his people jeered — *"whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they ridiculed him"* (11:38) — the assurance that God's eyes were upon him was the sustenance of the work.

The phrase *wa waḥyinā* — "and by Our revelation" — indicates that the design and method of the Ark were divinely instructed. Noah did not invent shipbuilding; he was taught it. The commentators note that the Ark's dimensions, materials, and construction — *"planks and nails,"* as 54:13 says — were revealed. This is consistent with the Qur'an's teaching that useful crafts were originally taught to human beings by God: David was taught the making of armor (21:80), and the first human being was taught the names of all things (2:31).

**"When Our Command Comes and the Oven Gushes Forth"**

The second element is the sign: *fa-idhā jāʾa amrunā wa fāra al-tannūr* — "then when Our command comes and the oven gushes forth." The word *amr* here means the decree, the divine order for the Flood to begin. The sign of that decree is *fāra al-tannūr* — the *tannūr* boiled over, gushed, erupted with water.

The word *tannūr* denotes the clay oven used for baking bread, still called by that name across the Muslim world. The commentators, as the source records, offered several interpretations. The majority — including Ibn ʿAbbās according to one report, Mujāhid, and al-Shaʿbī — took it literally: a specific oven, in Noah's house or in a designated place, from which water began to gush, and this was the sign to board. Al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī transmit this view. The sign was fitting in its improbability: water erupting from the place where fire should be is a sign no one could mistake, and it symbolized the reversal of nature that the Flood would be. Other views: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said that *tannūr* means the break of dawn — "the lightening of the morning" — so that the phrase means "when the dawn breaks"; and others said it refers to the surface of the earth generally, which "gushed" from every side, as 54:12 says: *"And We caused the earth to burst with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed."* Al-Ṭabarī records that some said *tannūr* refers to the highest and most noble place on earth. The plainest reading remains the literal oven, and it is the one Ibn Kathīr favors.

Whatever the precise referent, the meaning is clear: a specific, unmistakable signal was appointed, and Noah was to wait for it. He was not to guess or hurry; God would tell him when.

**"Place Therein Two of Every Kind"**

The third element is the cargo: *fa-sluk fīhā min kullin zawjayni ithnayn* — "then take into it of every kind two, a pair." The verb *salaka* means to insert, to make enter, to lead along a path. The phrase *zawjayni ithnayn* — "two mates, two" — is emphatic: a pair, male and female, of each kind of animal. In Sūrah Hūd the same instruction is given (11:40). The purpose was the preservation of the animal kinds through the Flood, so that the earth could be repopulated. The instruction shows that God's judgment on Noah's people was not a judgment on the earth itself or its creatures; the animals, innocent of the idolatry, were to be saved along with the believers. The Ark was thus a vessel of mercy inside an act of justice.

**"And Your Family, Except Those Against Whom the Word Has Gone Forth"**

The fourth element is the human cargo: *wa ahlaka illā man sabaqa ʿalayhi al-qawlu minhum* — "and your family, except those among them against whom the word has already gone forth." Noah was to bring his household — but not all of it. The exception refers, as the parallel in Sūrah Hūd makes clear, to two persons: Noah's wife, who betrayed him (66:10: *"God presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot; they were under two of Our righteous servants but betrayed them"*), and his son, who refused to board and was drowned (11:42–43). *"The word has gone forth"* means that God's decree of their punishment had already been issued because of their persistent disbelief.

The exception teaches a truth that cuts against every human instinct: kinship does not save. Noah, the greatest of preachers, could not save his own wife and son, because salvation is not by blood but by faith. The Qur'an states this principle at the sūrah's end: *"And when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day"* (23:101). The Prophet ﷺ told his own family the same: *"O Fāṭimah, daughter of Muḥammad, ask me for whatever you wish of my wealth, but I cannot avail you anything before God"* (al-Bukhārī 2753; Muslim 206). Verse 27 establishes this at the beginning of prophetic history: the Ark carried believers, not relatives.

**"And Address Me Not Concerning Those Who Did Wrong; They Shall Be Drowned"**

The fifth element is a prohibition: *wa lā tukhāṭibnī fī alladhīna ẓalamū innahum mughraqūn* — "and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned." The verb *khāṭaba* means to address, to speak to, to petition. God forbids Noah in advance from interceding for the wrongdoers once the Flood begins.

This prohibition is one of the most solemn in the Qur'an, and it must be read with care. It does not mean that Noah was forbidden to pray at all; it means that the matter of the wrongdoers was closed, and that no plea could reopen it. The source commentary rightly connects this to 11:46, where Noah, seeing his son drowning, cries, *"My Lord, my son is of my family, and Your promise is true"* — and God answers: *"O Noah, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work was other than righteous. So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge. I advise you, lest you be among the ignorant."* Verse 27 is the advance warning that made that later rebuke just. Noah had been told: do not address Me about them. The paternal cry escaped him anyway, and God's response was gentle correction rather than punishment, and Noah immediately repented (11:47).

The source also connects the prohibition to 9:113–114, where the Prophet ﷺ and the believers are forbidden to seek forgiveness for the idolaters once it has become clear that they are people of the Fire, and where Abraham's prayer for his father is explained as having been made only until *"it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God."* Together these verses establish a limit on the reach of a believer's compassion: he may pray for the guidance of anyone living, but he may not petition God to reverse a judgment God has declared final. The reason is not that compassion is wrong but that it must be governed by knowledge — *"do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge."*

**The Word "Wronged" and the Word "Drowned"**

The wrongdoers are called *alladhīna ẓalamū* — "those who did *ẓulm*." *Ẓulm* means to place something where it does not belong; its greatest form is *shirk*, placing worship where it does not belong: *"Indeed, shirk is a great ẓulm"* (31:13). Noah's people were wrongdoers not primarily because they mistreated Noah but because they gave God's right to idols. And their sentence is stated in a single word with the emphatic *inna*: *innahum mughraqūn* — "indeed, they are the drowned." The passive participle presents the drowning as already settled; from the standpoint of the decree, they are already under the water.

**Why the Flood Was Just**

A reader may ask how the drowning of an entire people can be just. The Qur'an's answer is embedded in the story's structure. Noah preached for nine hundred and fifty years (29:14) — longer than any warning in human history. He used every method (71:5–20). God informed him that no more would believe (11:36). The people themselves demanded the punishment: *"O Noah, you have disputed with us and prolonged the dispute; so bring us what you promise us, if you are truthful"* (11:32). The judgment came only after every avenue of mercy was exhausted and refused. The Qur'an's principle is: *"And never would your Lord have destroyed the cities until He had sent to their mother city a messenger reciting to them Our verses; and We would not destroy the cities except while their people were wrongdoers"* (28:59). The Flood was the enforcement of a warning that had been given for nearly a millennium.

**The Ark as a Symbol**

The classical and spiritual commentators saw in the Ark an image that outlasts the story. The Ark was built on dry land, by instruction, amid mockery, over years, before any water was visible; it was the only safety when the water came; it was entered by faith, not by lineage; and it carried its passengers to a blessed landing. Every element applies to the life of faith. The believer builds his Ark — prayer, charity, chastity, fidelity, the seven qualities of verses 2–9 — in the dry season, while others laugh, on the word of a revelation he trusts; and when the water comes, as verse 15 promised it would, the Ark is the only vessel afloat. The Prophet ﷺ used the image himself: *"The likeness of my household among you is the likeness of Noah's Ark: whoever boards it is saved, and whoever stays behind is drowned"* — a report transmitted by al-Ḥākim and others with disputed chains, but with a meaning that the Qur'an itself supports.

**God's Instructions and Human Labor**

Finally, the verse teaches something about how divine help works. Noah's prayer was answered not by the removal of his difficulty but by a plan, a sign, a cargo list, an exception, and a prohibition — in short, by *instructions*. The help of God, in the Qur'an, is rarely a substitute for human action; it is the direction of human action toward a goal that human action alone could not reach. Noah had to build. God would send the water. The believer who prays *"help me"* should expect, as Noah did, to be given work to do under the eyes of the One who heard him.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:28

> **And when thou mountest the Ark, thou and those with thee, say, ‘Praise be to God, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people.’**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Instructions for the Moment of Salvation**

The divine speech that began in verse 27 continues, and it now moves from the building and loading of the Ark to the moment of boarding: *fa-idhā istawayta anta wa man maʿaka ʿalā al-fulki fa-qul al-ḥamdu lillāhi alladhī najjānā min al-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — "And when you have settled, you and those with you, upon the Ark, say: 'Praise be to God, who has saved us from the wrongdoing people.'" God does not merely tell Noah what to do; He tells him what to *say* at the moment of deliverance. The verse is therefore a lesson in the etiquette of salvation — what the tongue of the rescued should utter when the danger has passed and the vessel is afloat.

**"When You Have Settled Upon the Ark"**

The verb *istawayta*, from the root *s-w-y*, means to become level, to settle firmly, to be established in a position. It is used in the Qur'an for the settling of the Ark itself upon Mount Jūdī (11:44: *"and it settled — wa istawat — upon al-Jūdī"*) and for the settling of a rider upon his mount (43:13: *"that you may settle — li-tastawū — upon their backs"*). The choice of this verb, rather than simply "when you board," conveys a moment of *completed* embarkation: when you and your company are safely aboard and settled, when the boarding is done and the vessel bears you. The moment of praise is the moment of secured safety.

The phrase *anta wa man maʿaka* — "you and those with you" — is inclusive. The instruction is not for Noah alone but for the whole company of believers aboard. The praise is communal. Noah is to lead it, but every rescued soul is to share in it. This anticipates the Qur'an's picture of the people of Paradise, whose *"last call will be: Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds"* (10:10) — a communal praise from all the saved together.

**"Say: Praise Be to God"**

The words prescribed begin with *al-ḥamdu lillāh* — the same words that open the Qur'an's first sūrah, the same words a Muslim says on waking, after eating, after sneezing, at every turn of good. *Ḥamd* is praise with love and gratitude; it is directed at the praised one's qualities and at his favors. *Lillāh* — "to God" — with the definite article on *al-ḥamd* means that *all* praise, by right, belongs to Him.

Why is praise the prescribed response to salvation? Because salvation is an act of God, and the recognition of a favor's source is the first duty of the one favored. The alternatives are instructive. Noah could have been told to say "We have survived" (attributing the outcome to fate), or "We built well" (attributing it to his own skill), or "We were right" (turning the moment into vindication over enemies). Instead he is told to say: *Praise be to God, who saved us.* The verse redirects the natural reaction to rescue — relief, pride, triumph — into gratitude toward the only true Rescuer. The Ark was Noah's labor, but the safety was God's gift; the verse insists on the distinction.

**"Who Has Saved Us from the Wrongdoing People"**

The specific favor named is *najjānā min al-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — "saved us from the wrongdoing people." The verb *najjā* (Form II of *n-j-w*) means to deliver, to rescue, to bring to safety; *najāh* is salvation. Notice that the rescue is described as being *from the wrongdoing people*, not merely from the water. The Flood was the instrument; the deliverance was from the *society* of the wrongdoers — from their oppression, their mockery, their corruption, and the judgment that fell on them. The believers were saved not only from drowning but from the company of those whose rejection had made the earth unbearable for the truth.

This teaches something about what salvation is. The Qur'an frequently describes it as separation: God separates the believers from the wrongdoers, physically (as in the Ark, or the Exodus) and finally (on the Day of Judgment: *"And be separated today, O criminals,"* 36:59). To be saved is to be taken out from among those who have chosen destruction. The Ark's passengers, praising God for salvation *from the wrongdoing people*, are the pattern for the believers of the sūrah's opening, who will be separated from the mockers at the end (23:108–111).

**The Prophet's Practice: Praise at Deliverance**

The Prophet ﷺ made the etiquette of verse 28 a regular part of the believer's life. When he mounted his riding animal to travel, he said *al-ḥamdu lillāh* three times after the words of 43:13 (Muslim 1342, cited under v. 22). When he returned from a journey, he said: *"Returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord"* (al-Bukhārī 1797; Muslim 1344). When he saw someone afflicted, he taught the believer to say: *"Praise be to God who has spared me from what He afflicted you with and preferred me over many of those He created"* (al-Tirmidhī 3431). When something pleased him he said: *"Praise be to God by whose favor good things are completed,"* and when something displeased him: *"Praise be to God in every circumstance"* (Ibn Mājah 3803). The habit of turning to *al-ḥamdu lillāh* at every deliverance, large or small, is the habit verse 28 instituted at the boarding of the Ark.

**A Noteworthy Feature: The Prayer Is Taught in Advance**

Observe that God tells Noah what to say *before* the event, while he is still building. The praise is scripted in advance. Why? Because the moment of rescue is a moment of overwhelming emotion, and human beings in such moments do not always find the right words — or find any words at all. By teaching the prayer beforehand, God ensures that the first words spoken aboard the Ark will be the right ones. This is the wisdom behind the Prophet's teaching of specific supplications for specific moments: on waking, on sleeping, on entering the mosque, on hearing thunder, on seeing the new moon, on receiving good news. The prescribed words carry the believer through the moment with the correct orientation even when his own heart is too full or too scattered to compose one.

There is also a matter of confidence. God's teaching Noah the prayer of salvation before the Flood is an implicit promise that the salvation will happen. Noah is being told, in effect: you will board; you will be safe; and here is what you will say. The instruction is itself a reassurance to the man who had just prayed *"help me"* (v. 26).

**The Believer Aboard His Own Ark**

The spiritual commentators read verse 28 as an instruction for every believer who is delivered from any of the "floods" of life — a danger passed, an illness healed, a temptation resisted, a corrupt environment escaped, a period of trial ended. The correct response is not self-congratulation, not relief alone, and not gloating over those who did not escape, but *al-ḥamdu lillāh alladhī najjānā* — "Praise be to God who saved us." The word *us* is significant: the believer praises God for the salvation of his companions with him, not for himself alone. And the phrase "from the wrongdoing people" reminds him what he was saved from: not merely a circumstance but a company.

In the modern context, the verse speaks to the believer who has been kept from the mockery, corruption, and heedlessness of a surrounding culture — who has found himself, by God's grace, on the deck of faith while the water rises around a society that laughed at the shipbuilder. His prescribed response is humility and gratitude, not superiority. He did not build the Ark unaided; he built it *"under Our eyes and by Our revelation"* (v. 27), and he boarded it because God saved him.

**From Praise to Petition**

Verse 28 prescribes praise for the salvation already granted. The next verse (v. 29) will prescribe a petition for what is still to come — a blessed landing. The order is a lesson in the etiquette of supplication: praise first, then request. This is the order of the Fātiḥah (praise in its first half, petition in its second), the order the Prophet ﷺ taught for all supplication (*"When one of you prays, let him begin by praising his Lord and extolling Him, then send blessings on the Prophet, then ask what he wishes,"* al-Tirmidhī 3477; Abū Dāwūd 1481), and the order in which Noah is instructed aboard the Ark. The believer who has learned verse 28 says *al-ḥamdu lillāh* before he says *rabbi anzilnī*.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:29

> **And say, ‘My Lord! Harbor me in a blessed harbor, for Thou art the best of harborers.’**

**Expanded Commentary**

**After Praise, Petition**

Noah was told first to praise God for the salvation already accomplished (v. 28); now he is told to ask for what lies ahead: *wa qul rabbi anzilnī munzalan mubārakan wa anta khayru al-munzilīn* — "And say: 'My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, for You are the best of those who bring to land.'" The two verses together form a complete supplication in the classical shape: gratitude for the past, then request for the future, both directed to the same Lord. Aboard a vessel adrift on a world-covering flood, with no land in sight and no map, Noah is taught to pray not for the water to recede — that is God's affair — but for a *good arrival*. The prayer is about the destination.

**The Root n-z-l and Its Range**

The verse turns on a single root repeated three times: *anzilnī* ("cause me to descend/land"), *munzalan* ("a landing place" or "a landing"), and *al-munzilīn* ("those who bring to land"). The root *n-z-l* means to come down, to alight, to descend from a mount or vessel, and — in its causative form — to bring down, to lodge, to give hospitality. The Arab host who receives a guest is said to *anzala* him: to bring him down from his camel and lodge him. From this comes *nuzul*, the provision offered to a guest, a word the Qur'an uses for the hospitality of Paradise (18:107: *"gardens of Firdaws as a lodging — nuzulan"*). The root also gives *manzil*, a house or station, and *nuzūl*, the descent of revelation.

So the prayer *rabbi anzilnī munzalan mubārakan* carries a layered meaning. On the plainest level, as the source notes from al-Qurṭubī, it means: "Cause me to disembark in a blessed place" — bring the Ark to rest on good ground and let me step off onto it. On a second level, it means: "Lodge me as a guest is lodged" — receive me, provide for me, give me hospitality in the new world after the Flood. The word *munzalan* may be read as a noun of place (a landing site) or as a verbal noun (the act of landing); the reciters transmit both *munzalan* (with *ḍammah*, from the causative, "a landing given by another") and *manzilan* (with *fatḥah*, "a dwelling place"), and both meanings are embraced.

**"A Blessed Landing": The Word Mubārak**

The landing Noah is to ask for is *mubārak* — "blessed." The root *b-r-k* denotes abundance, permanence, and increase; the *birkah* is the pool where water gathers and stays; *barakah* is the divine increase that makes a little go far and a thing endure. To ask for a *blessed* landing is to ask for more than a safe one. Safety is the absence of harm; blessing is the presence of good — growth, provision, and permanence. Noah asks that the place where the Ark comes to rest be a place where life can begin again and flourish. The Qur'an confirms that the prayer was answered: *"It was said: 'O Noah, disembark in peace from Us and blessings (barakāt) upon you and upon nations from those with you'"* (11:48). The very word Noah asked for — *barakah* — is the word God used in granting it.

The word *mubārak* also appears in the sūrah's own catalogue of provisions: the water sent down from heaven was described as *"blessed"* in a parallel verse (50:9), and the olive of verse 20 is the *"blessed tree"* of 24:35. Noah's prayer asks that the earth after the Flood be the kind of earth verses 18–20 described — watered, fruitful, and blessed.

**"You Are the Best of Those Who Bring to Land"**

The prayer closes with a reason: *wa anta khayru al-munzilīn* — "and You are the best of those who bring to land / who give lodging." This closing phrase is of a type the Qur'an uses often, and the sūrah has already used one: *"the best of creators"* (v. 14). It will use others: *"the best of providers"* (v. 72) and *"the best of the merciful"* (vv. 109, 118). In each case the construction is *khayr* + a plural participle, and in each case it means that while others may perform the action in a limited or derivative way — human hosts lodge guests, human parents "create" children in a loose sense — God performs it perfectly, originally, and without limit.

To call God *khayru al-munzilīn* aboard the Ark is to make a specific confession. A human sailor might bring a ship to shore, but he cannot make the shore blessed; a human host might lodge a guest, but he cannot guarantee the lodging's safety or permanence. God alone can bring the Ark to rest on a mountain He has chosen, cause the waters to recede, and make the drying earth bring forth again. The praise is not decorative; it is the ground of the request. Noah asks for a blessed landing *because* the One he asks is the best of those who grant landings. This is the logic the Prophet ﷺ taught for supplication: to call upon God by the Name that corresponds to the need — to ask the Provider for provision, the Forgiver for forgiveness, and, here, the Lodger for a lodging.

**The Ark's Landing in the Qur'an**

The Qur'an records where the prayer was answered: *"And it was said: 'O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold.' And the water subsided, and the matter was accomplished, and it settled on al-Jūdī"* (11:44). Al-Jūdī is a mountain that the commentators located in the region of the upper Tigris (in what is now southeastern Turkey or northern Iraq); the important point for verse 29 is not the geography but the fact of a *chosen* landing. The Ark did not drift to rest at random; it *settled* (*istawat*, the same root as verse 28's *istawayta*) where God brought it. The blessed landing was an act of the best of those who bring to land.

**The Deeper Journey: The Believer's Landing**

The classical commentators, and especially those who read the Ark as a figure of faith, saw in verse 29 a prayer that reaches beyond Noah's ship. Every believer is aboard a vessel — his own life — crossing waters he does not control, toward a landing he cannot see. The journey ends in death (v. 15) and the standing (v. 16), and the believer's landing is his grave and then his abode in the Hereafter. Verse 29 gives him the words to pray for that landing: *My Lord, bring me to a blessed landing, for You are the best of those who lodge.* The Prophet ﷺ described the believer's grave as a *"garden from the gardens of Paradise"* (al-Tirmidhī 2460) — a blessed landing — and the Qur'an describes Firdaws as the *nuzul*, the guest-lodging, prepared for the believers (18:107). The root is the same: the believer asks the Lodger of the Ark to lodge him in the Garden.

There is a further application, gentler and nearer. The believer who migrates — from a home, a city, a country — for the sake of his faith or his family's safety is on Noah's water, and verse 29 is his prayer. The Prophet ﷺ made the greatest migration in Islamic history, from Makkah to Madinah, and the Qur'an gave him a prayer of the same shape: *"My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority"* (17:80). Every emigrant, every traveler, every person stepping into an unknown place, can say with Noah: *rabbi anzilnī munzalan mubārakan*.

**The Prophet's Own Use of the Root**

The Prophet ﷺ taught his community a supplication for arriving at any new place, which is verse 29 in practice: *"Whoever alights at a place and says: 'I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He has created,' nothing will harm him until he departs from that place"* (Muslim 2708). The verb used in the ḥadīth is *nazala* — the very root of verse 29. The believer who stops at a roadside, checks into a hotel, moves into a new house, or camps in a field, and says these words, is asking for what Noah asked: that his landing be safe and blessed. The Prophet ﷺ also taught, on entering a town: *"O God, Lord of the seven heavens and what they shade, Lord of the seven earths and what they carry... we ask You for the good of this town and the good of its people, and we seek refuge in You from its evil and the evil of its people"* (al-Nasāʾī in *ʿAmal al-Yawm wa'l-Laylah*; al-Ḥākim). The structure — praise of the Lord of the heavens, then request for a blessed arrival — mirrors verses 28–29 exactly.

**Order and Composure in the Face of the Unknown**

Consider the emotional situation of verse 29. Noah is aboard a vessel on a flood that has destroyed the world he knew. His wife and son are among the lost. There is no shore in sight and no certainty of one. In this situation, God teaches him to pray not in panic but in order: first praise (v. 28), then a specific, hopeful, forward-looking request (v. 29). The prayer assumes that there *will* be a landing; it asks only that it be blessed. This is the composure of faith: the believer on the flood does not doubt that God will bring him somewhere; he asks that where He brings him be good. The Qur'an's teaching that *"with hardship comes ease"* (94:5–6) is enacted in the sequence of these two verses — the Ark, the praise, the petition, the landing.

**The Close of the Divine Speech**

Verse 29 is the last line of the speech that God addressed to Noah beginning in verse 27. The speech commanded the building, gave the sign, ordered the cargo, excepted the condemned, forbade intercession, prescribed the praise, and taught the prayer. The next verse steps back from the story and tells the reader why it was told: *"Indeed in that are signs, and indeed We were testing."*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:30

> **Truly in that are signs, and truly We put [mankind] to the test.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Narrator Steps Forward**

The story of Noah, told in seven verses (23–29), closes with a comment from the Narrator: *inna fī dhālika la-āyātin wa in kunnā la-mubtalīn* — "Indeed in that are signs, and indeed We were surely testing." The verse is short and its function is interpretive: it tells the listener what he has just heard and why he heard it. The Qur'an often does this after a narrative — *"Indeed in that is a sign"* (26:8, 67, 103, and elsewhere) — and the practice is a lesson in how to read scripture. A story in the Qur'an is not told for entertainment or even primarily for information; it is told because it contains *āyāt*, signs, and because it illustrates a principle. Verse 30 names the principle: God tests.

**"Indeed in That Are Signs": Reading the Story Correctly**

The demonstrative *dhālika*, "that," gathers the whole account — Noah's call, the notables' rejection, the prayer, the Ark, the Flood, the salvation, the landing. In all of it, the verse says, are *āyāt*, "signs." The word *āyah* (plural *āyāt*) means a sign, a mark, a token that points beyond itself to something else; it is the same word used for the verses of the Qur'an and for the phenomena of nature (as in the catalogue of verses 17–22). The story of Noah is thus placed in the same category as the rain and the cattle and the verses of the Book: it is *evidence*, something that a thinking person reads and from which he draws conclusions.

What are the signs in the story? The commentators enumerate them, and each corresponds to a theme of the sūrah. The story is a sign of God's *power*: He drowned a world and saved a ship. It is a sign of His *justice*: the punishment came only after nearly a thousand years of warning. It is a sign of His *mercy*: He saved the believers and the animals, and He taught Noah what to say. It is a sign of the *truthfulness of the messengers*: Noah said the Flood would come, and it came. It is a sign of the *pattern of history*: the powerful reject, the humble believe, and the end vindicates the humble. And it is a sign of *resurrection*: the earth that the Flood covered was brought back to life, as the drowned will be. Every one of these is a sign in the precise sense: a visible event that points to an invisible truth.

The plural *āyāt* and the emphatic *la-* insist that there is not merely one lesson but many, and that they are real. The listener who hears the story of Noah and takes from it only a tale of an ancient ship has not read it.

**"And Indeed We Were Testing": The Central Principle**

The second half of the verse is the more profound: *wa in kunnā la-mubtalīn* — "and indeed We were surely putting to the test." The particle *in* here is the lightened form of *inna* (affirmation), and the *lām* on *la-mubtalīn* is the *lām* of distinction that marks it as such; together they produce strong emphasis: "We *certainly were* testing." The word *mubtalīn* is the active participle of *ibtalā*, from the root *b-l-w*, which means to test, to try, to examine — originally, to wear something out by use in order to discover its quality. A *balāʾ* is a trial; *ibtilāʾ* is the act of testing.

Whom was God testing? The source commentary records the classical answers: Noah's people, whom God tried by sending them a messenger and watching how they would respond; and, by extension, every people to whom a messenger comes. Al-Qurṭubī explains that God *tried* the previous peoples by sending them prophets, so that their obedience or rejection would become manifest. Al-Ṭabarī adds that the purpose of mentioning this to the Prophet ﷺ was to show him that other prophets experienced what he was experiencing, and that the rejection he faced was itself the substance of the test his people were undergoing.

But the verse's grammar is open: it does not name the object of the testing. The omission is significant. God was testing Noah's people by the message; He was testing Noah by their rejection and by the long years of labor; He was testing the believers who boarded by the mockery they endured; and He is testing the *listener* — the Makkan, and every reader since — by telling the story. Would the hearer take the sign, or would he, like the notables, say "we never heard this from our fathers"? The story is itself part of the test.

**The Doctrine of Testing in the Qur'an**

Verse 30 states in a single word a principle that the Qur'an develops everywhere. Human life is a test. *"He who created death and life to test you (li-yabluwakum) as to which of you is best in deed"* (67:2). *"And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss of wealth and lives and fruits — but give good tidings to the patient"* (2:155). *"Do people think that they will be left to say 'We believe' and not be tested (lā yuftanūn)? But We have certainly tested those before them"* (29:2–3). The test is not an occasional feature of life but its structure; the sūrah's own opening presupposed it, since the seven qualities of verses 2–9 are precisely the passing marks of the examination.

The testing takes two forms, and the story of Noah shows both. There is the test of *hardship*: the believers were mocked, persecuted, and made to build a ship on dry land. There is the test of *ease*: the notables had wealth, power, and centuries of security, and the sūrah will later say of such people, *"Do they reckon that, on account of the wealth and children We have provided them, We hasten unto good for them? Nay, but they are unaware"* (23:55–56). The Qur'an states the dual test plainly: *"And We test you with evil and with good as a trial"* (21:35). Noah's people failed the test of ease; Noah's followers passed the test of hardship.

**Why God Tests**

A natural question arises: if God knows everything, why does He test? The answer, given by al-Rāzī and the theologians generally, is that the test is not for God's knowledge but for the manifestation of the creature's choice. God knows what a person will do; the person does not know until he does it, and neither does anyone else. The test makes the hidden actual. It gives the human being the dignity of *becoming* what he is through his own choices, rather than merely being declared so. It also establishes justice: no one is rewarded or punished for what he *would* have done but only for what he did. Noah's people were not drowned for the disbelief God foreknew; they were drowned for the disbelief they enacted over nine hundred and fifty years of warning.

There is also a purifying function. The word *ibtalā* was used for testing gold in fire — the fire does not create the gold's purity but reveals and separates it from dross. The believers on the Ark had been refined by centuries of mockery into a company that God described as *"few"* (11:40) but pure. The Qur'an says: *"God would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He separates the wicked from the good"* (3:179). The Flood was the separation.

**The Verse and the Prophet's Situation**

The commentators emphasize that verse 30 was addressed, in its first hearing, to a specific man in a specific difficulty. The Prophet ﷺ in Makkah was being called mad, ambitious, and merely human; his people invoked their fathers and waited for his death. Verse 30 tells him: this is a test — the same test Noah faced — and the story of Noah is the sign of how such tests end. The consolation is not sentimental; it is structural. The Prophet ﷺ is being shown the *shape* of his own story in the story of his predecessor, and being assured that the shape ends in vindication. The Qur'an states this purpose explicitly elsewhere: *"And each story We relate to you from the news of the messengers is that by which We make firm your heart"* (11:120).

**The Verse and the Believer's Life**

For the ordinary believer, verse 30 is a lens through which to read his own experience. When he is mocked for his faith, he is being tested, as the Ark's passengers were. When he is comfortable and untroubled, he is being tested, as the notables were. When he preaches and is refused, he is being tested, as Noah was. When he sees the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer, he is being tested in his trust that the account is not yet closed. The verse teaches him to ask, in every circumstance, not "why is this happening to me?" but "what is being tested in me, and how do I pass?"

The Prophet ﷺ described the test's severity and its logic: *"The most severely tested of people are the prophets, then the next best, then the next best. A man is tested according to his religion; if his religion is firm, his test is increased"* (al-Tirmidhī 2398; Ibn Mājah 4023). Noah, the first messenger, bore the longest test in history. The believer who is tried should understand that trial is not a sign of God's displeasure but of the seriousness with which He regards the one tried.

**A Closing Analogy**

An examination is not the enemy of the student; it is the means by which his study becomes a qualification. A student who was never examined would never graduate, however much he learned. The Qur'an presents life as an examination whose questions are the circumstances God sends and whose answers are the choices the human being makes.
