The story of Noah is the record of one examination: the questions were a messenger's call and a thousand years of patience; the notables answered with contempt and the believers with faith; and the results were published by the Flood. Verse 30 tells the reader that his own examination is in progress, and that its questions are of the same kind.

**The Narrative Moves On**

With the principle stated, the sūrah turns in the next verse to the generation that followed Noah — a people who received the same message, made the same objections, and met a different but equally decisive end. The test, the verse has told us, did not end with the Flood; it was repeated, and the next verses show the repetition.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:31

> **Then after them We brought into being another generation.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**History Continues After the Flood**

The account of Noah is complete and its lesson stated. Now the sūrah moves forward in time: *thumma anshaʾnā min baʿdihim qarnan ākharīn* — "Then We produced after them another generation." The verse is brief — a single sentence marking a transition — but its brevity carries meaning. History does not end with a judgment; it continues, and the same test is administered again. The Flood cleared the earth of one generation, and God immediately brought forth another, to whom the same message would be sent and from whom the same response would be demanded. The verse reminds the listener that the story of Noah was not unique; it was the first performance of a drama that would be staged again and again.

**The Verb Anshaʾnā: A Third Time**

The verb *anshaʾnā*, "We produced, We brought forth, We raised up," appears here for the third time in the sūrah. It was used for the ensouling of the embryo (v. 14: *"We brought him into being as another creation"*), for the growth of gardens from rain (v. 19: *"We produced for you by it gardens"*), and now for the rise of a new generation after the Flood. The repetition is not accidental. The Qur'an uses the same verb for the origination of a person, a garden, and a civilization, because all three are acts of the same Originator. A generation does not "arise" of its own accord any more than a garden grows itself or a soul creates itself. The peoples of history are *brought forth* by God, as the sūrah's next verses will show that they are also *ended* by Him (v. 41).

There is a further parallel. Verse 14 spoke of *khalqan ākhar*, "another creation"; verse 31 speaks of *qarnan ākharīn*, "another generation." The adjective *ākhar* ("another, other") links the two. As the individual human being passes through successive stages, each one "another" than the last, so humanity as a whole passes through successive generations, each one "another" than the last. The sūrah is teaching the listener to see history as it taught him to see embryology: as a sequence of divine acts, each raising up something new from what preceded.

**The Word Qarn**

The word *qarn* is rich in meaning. Its root, *q-r-n*, means to join, to pair, to link — a *qarīn* is a companion, and *qarn* is also the horn of an animal (paired on the head). Applied to human beings, a *qarn* is a generation: the people who are "joined" together in a single age, contemporaries who live and die together. By extension it means a century or an epoch — the span of a generation's life. The Qur'an uses it, as the source commentary lists, in many passages about the peoples of the past: *"Have they not seen how many a generation We destroyed before them?"* (6:6); *"And how many a generation have We destroyed after Noah!"* (17:17); *"And how many a generation before them did We destroy who were greater in power?"* (50:36).

The Prophet ﷺ used the word for the generations of his own community: *"The best of people are my generation (qarnī), then those who follow them, then those who follow them"* (al-Bukhārī 2652; Muslim 2533). The word thus carries the sense of a people bound by a shared time, a shared culture, and — in the Qur'an's usage — a shared test and often a shared fate.

**Which Generation?**

The verse does not name the new generation. The source commentary records that some interpreters speculated: some said it was ʿĀd, the people of Hūd, who are described in the Qur'an as the successors of Noah's people (*"And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah,"* 7:69); others said Thamūd, the people of Ṣāliḥ, because the punishment described in verse 41 — the Cry (*ṣayḥah*) — matches the punishment of Thamūd in other passages (11:67; 54:31). Al-Qurṭubī, as the source notes, observes that the verse gives no explicit identification, and this restraint is itself instructive.

Why leave the generation unnamed? Because the point is not *which* people but *what kind* of people. The sūrah is drawing a pattern, and a pattern is clearer when the particulars are stripped away. The unnamed generation stands for every generation: it receives a messenger from among itself (v. 32), it objects that he is only a man who eats and drinks (v. 33), it denies the resurrection (vv. 35–37), it accuses the messenger of lying (v. 38), the messenger prays (v. 39), and the judgment falls (v. 41). The reader who hears this account without a name is invited to supply his own generation's name, and to ask whether the pattern fits.

**The Logic of Succession**

The verse also carries a quiet argument. God brought forth a new generation *after* the destruction of the old. This shows that the destruction was not a failure of the divine plan, nor the end of God's dealings with humanity, but a stage within a continuing purpose. The earth was not abandoned after the Flood; it was repopulated, and the test was renewed. This is consistent with the Qur'an's picture of God as continuously active — *"Every day He is in some affair"* (55:29) — and with verse 17's assertion that He is *"never heedless of creation."* The succession of generations is the visible form of divine attention across time.

The succession also carries a warning. Each generation inherits the earth from one that was removed, and each is therefore standing on ground that previous occupants forfeited. The Qur'an says to the Quraysh: *"Do they not travel through the earth and see how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength, and they cultivated the earth and built it up more than these have built it up"* (30:9). The generation that forgets it is a successor forgets that it, too, can be succeeded. Verse 31's *"after them"* — *min baʿdihim* — is a phrase that every generation should hear as addressed to itself: you came after others; others will come after you.

**The Sūrah's Structural Pattern**

Verse 31 begins the second of three prophetic accounts in the sūrah's historical section (Noah, vv. 23–30; the unnamed generation, vv. 31–41; and the summary of successive messengers, vv. 42–44, followed by Moses and Jesus, vv. 45–50). The three accounts are arranged in decreasing detail and increasing generalization: Noah's story is told with names and specifics; the second generation is anonymous but its dialogue is quoted; the third section compresses many messengers into a single sentence. The effect is to move the listener from the particular to the universal — from one man's story to the law of history. Verse 31 is the first step of that movement.

**The Verse for the Reader**

For the believer, the verse teaches several things. It teaches that God's purpose is not defeated by human rejection: after the Flood, another generation; after every failure of a people, another people. It teaches humility about one's own generation's place: we are one *qarn* among many, neither the first to be tested nor the last. And it teaches attention to the pattern: the next verses will show the unnamed generation repeating the errors of Noah's, and the reader is meant to recognize that the repetition is possible in his own time. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"You will follow the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit"* (al-Bukhārī 3456; Muslim 2669). The verse invites the reader to break the pattern rather than repeat it.

**Toward the Message Repeated**

The next verse will show what God did with the new generation: He sent them, as He sent Noah's people, a messenger from among themselves, with a message identical to Noah's, word for word. The test is renewed, and the sūrah will show whether the new generation answered it differently.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:32

> **And We sent among them a messenger from among themselves, [saying], “Worship God! You have no god other than Him. Will you not be reverent?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Same Message to a New People**

The generation that God raised up after the Flood (v. 31) did not go unwarned: *fa-arsalnā fīhim rasūlan minhum an uʿbudū Allāha mā lakum min ilāhin ghayruhu a-fa-lā tattaqūn* — "And We sent among them a messenger from among themselves, saying: 'Worship God; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?'" The reader who has followed the sūrah will recognize the last three clauses instantly: they are, word for word, what Noah said to his people in verse 23. The sūrah quotes the identical sentence to make an unmistakable point — the message did not change. A new generation, a new messenger, the same words. Whatever else differs between the ages, the religion of God is one.

**"We Sent Among Them a Messenger from Among Themselves"**

Two prepositional phrases frame the messenger: *fīhim*, "among them," and *minhum*, "from among them." The first indicates location — the messenger lived in their midst, not in a distant land; the second indicates origin — he was one of them, of their stock, their tongue, their known families. Together the phrases describe the Qur'anic principle that every messenger is sent to his own people as one of their own. *"And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, that he might make clear to them"* (14:4). *"Indeed, God conferred a favor upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from themselves"* (3:164).

The wisdom of this principle is manifold, and the commentators drew it out. A messenger from among a people speaks their language and knows their customs, so the message reaches them without the barrier of translation or foreignness. His character is known to them from childhood, so they can judge his honesty by decades of observation rather than by his claims. He shares their conditions — their food, their climate, their hardships — so his example is imitable; a foreign or angelic messenger could set no standard a human being could follow. And his kinship with them removes the excuse that an outsider has come to dominate them; he has no foreign power behind him and nothing to gain but their good. The sūrah will make this last point against the Quraysh: *"Or do they not know their Messenger, and so deny him?"* (23:69).

**The Irony the Verse Prepares**

Yet it was precisely this quality — being *from among them* — that the people would turn into an objection. The next verse records the notables saying: *"This is only a human being like you, eating what you eat and drinking what you drink"* (23:33). What God intended as a mercy (a messenger you can understand and follow), the deniers treated as a disqualification (a messenger no better than ourselves). The verse sets up this irony by emphasizing *minhum* before the objection is voiced. The reader is meant to see that the objection attacks the very thing that made the message accessible. It is as if a patient rejected a physician because he spoke the patient's language.

**The Messenger Left Unnamed**

Like the generation itself (v. 31), the messenger is not named. He is simply *rasūlan* — "a messenger." The source commentary's tentative identifications (Hūd to ʿĀd, or Ṣāliḥ to Thamūd) remain speculation, and al-Qurṭubī's caution holds. The anonymity serves the sūrah's method: by leaving the messenger unnamed, the text makes him the *type* of all messengers, and his message the type of all messages. Whoever he was, he said what Noah said and what Muḥammad ﷺ said. The name is unnecessary because the function is universal.

**The Message Itself, Word for Word**

The three clauses of the message were examined under verse 23, but their repetition here invites a further observation. The Qur'an could have written "and he called them to what Noah had called his people." Instead it quotes the sentence again in full. Why?

First, because repetition is how the Qur'an teaches unity. The source commentary notes that this exact refrain — *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him"* — is placed on the lips of Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, and Shuʿayb in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf (7:59, 65, 73, 85), and of the last three in Sūrah Hūd (11:50, 61, 84). The reader who encounters the same words in the mouths of prophets separated by centuries and continents learns, without being told, that prophethood is a single office with a single message. The sūrah will state the conclusion in verse 52: *"Indeed this, your community, is one community."* Verses 23 and 32, with their identical wording, are the evidence for that verse.

Second, because repetition exposes the deniers. If the message had varied — if each messenger had brought a different doctrine — the deniers' rejection might have been excused as confusion. But the message was always the same, always simple, always the same three clauses. Its rejection was therefore never a matter of complexity but of will. The people of the second generation could not claim that the message was unclear; they had the same sentence that Noah's people had, and the Flood as a demonstration of its seriousness.

Third, because repetition consoles the Prophet ﷺ. He, too, was saying exactly these words in Makkah: *"Say: I am only a warner, and there is no deity except God, the One, the Prevailing"* (38:65). Verse 32 tells him that his sentence is the sentence of every messenger before him — that when he says *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, he is saying what was said after the Flood and before it.

**"Worship God": The Command Analyzed Once More**

The command *uʿbudū Allāh* — "worship God" — deserves a note on its scope. The word *ʿibādah* in Arabic is not limited to ritual acts. The classical definition, given by Ibn Taymiyyah, is *"a comprehensive term for everything God loves and is pleased with, of words and deeds, outward and inward."* Worship includes prayer and fasting, but also honesty in trade, kindness to parents, justice in judgment, and the guarding of the tongue and the private parts that the sūrah's opening described. To "worship God" is to orient the whole of life toward Him. The messengers' command was therefore not merely "perform rituals for God instead of for idols" but "make God the center of everything." This is why the command is followed by the reason — *"you have no god other than Him"* — and by the appeal to *taqwā*: because He alone is God, the whole of life belongs to Him, and the whole of life should be guarded accordingly.

**"Will You Not Be Reverent?": The Question Renewed**

The closing question — *a-fa-lā tattaqūn* — asks the new generation what it asked the old: given that there is no god but God, will you not guard yourselves? The question assumes the listener has the capacity to answer yes. It is not addressed to stones. Every messenger asked it because every people could, in principle, have said yes. The second generation, as the next verses show, said no — but the question's presence in the verse is the record that they were given the chance.

**The Test Renewed**

Verse 30 said that God was *"testing."* Verse 32 is the test administered to the second generation: a messenger from among them, a message they could understand, a question they could answer. The following verses will record their answer, and the reader — who has already heard Noah's people's answer — is invited to notice whether history repeats itself. It does; and the sūrah's method of quoting the identical message is what makes the repetition visible. The same words in, the same words out: the message was constant, and so, tragically, was the response.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:33

> **And the notables of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and unto whom We had given luxury in the life of this world, said, “This is but a human being like you, eating of what you eat, and drinking from what you drink.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Same Speakers, More Fully Described**

The new messenger has spoken; now the reply comes, and it comes from the same class that replied to Noah — the *malaʾ*, the notables. But this time the Qur'an describes them with three qualifications before quoting them: *wa qāla al-malaʾu min qawmihi alladhīna kafarū wa kadhdhabū bi-liqāʾi al-ākhirati wa atrafnāhum fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — "And the chiefs of his people, who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter and whom We had given luxury in the life of this world, said..." Three descriptors: they *disbelieved*; they *denied the meeting of the Hereafter*; and they had been *given luxury* in this world. The verse tells us who they were before it tells us what they said, because the three facts explain the speech.

**Descriptor One: They Disbelieved**

*Alladhīna kafarū* — "who disbelieved." The root *k-f-r* means to cover; the *kāfir* is one who covers the truth he knows, or covers the favor he has received (ingratitude). The word appeared in verse 24 for Noah's notables and it appears again here, establishing continuity. The chiefs of the second generation were not ignorant of God; the sūrah will show later that such people conceded God's existence and ownership of everything (23:84–89). Their disbelief was a covering-over of what they knew, not an absence of knowledge.

**Descriptor Two: They Denied the Meeting of the Hereafter**

*Wa kadhdhabū bi-liqāʾi al-ākhirah* — "and denied the meeting of the Hereafter." This is a new detail, not stated of Noah's notables in verse 24. The phrase *liqāʾ al-ākhirah* means "the meeting of the Hereafter" — the encounter with God and with one's deeds on the Last Day. To deny this meeting is to deny that life has an accounting. The verse identifies this specific denial as the root of the notables' position, and the following verses will bear this out: their central objection (vv. 35–37) will be precisely that the dead do not rise.

The placement of this descriptor is diagnostic. The Qur'an teaches that the denial of the Hereafter is the psychological foundation of nearly all moral corruption. If there is no meeting, no account, no consequence beyond the grave, then the only rational policy is to maximize pleasure and power in this life — which is exactly what the third descriptor shows the notables doing. The Qur'an makes the connection elsewhere: *"Indeed, those who do not expect the meeting with Us and are satisfied with the life of this world and feel secure in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs — for those, their refuge will be the Fire"* (10:7–8). Denial of the meeting produces satisfaction with the world; satisfaction with the world produces heedlessness of the signs.

**Descriptor Three: They Were Given Luxury**

*Wa atrafnāhum fī al-ḥayāti al-dunyā* — "and We had given them luxury in the life of this world." The verb *atrafa*, from the root *t-r-f*, means to give someone ease, affluence, and the soft life; the *mutraf* (plural *mutrafūn*) is the person who lives in luxury, pampered by wealth and unaccustomed to hardship. The word carries a connotation of the moral softening that affluence produces — the loss of seriousness, the indifference to others' suffering, the assumption that one's comfort is one's right.

The Qur'an uses this root with striking consistency as a marker of the opponents of the prophets. *"And We did not send into a city any warner except that its affluent ones (mutrafūhā) said: Indeed we, in that with which you were sent, are disbelievers"* (34:34). *"And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones (mutrafīhā), and they defiantly disobey therein, so the word comes into effect upon it, and We destroy it with complete destruction"* (17:16). The source commentary notes the parallels in 11:116 and 21:13, and this sūrah will return to the *mutrafūn* in verse 64: *"until, when We seize their affluent ones with the punishment, at once they cry out."* The luxurious are the sūrah's recurring villains — not because wealth is evil, but because unexamined affluence, combined with denial of the Hereafter, produces a specific spiritual disease: the conviction that this life is all there is and that one is already winning it.

Notice the verb's subject: *atrafnāhum* — "*We* gave them luxury." God is the giver of their affluence. This is significant in two ways. It removes any suggestion that the notables earned their position by merit; their wealth was a provision, and, as verse 30 said, a test. And it sets up the sūrah's later argument (vv. 55–56) that the affluent misread their affluence as divine approval, when it was in fact the very substance of their trial. The luxury God gave them was the examination they failed.

**The Speech: "Only a Human Being Like You"**

Having described the speakers, the verse quotes them: *mā hādhā illā basharun mithlukum* — "this is nothing but a human being like you." This is exactly the first objection of Noah's notables in verse 24, repeated word for word. The sūrah's method continues: as the message was identical (vv. 23 and 32), so the rejection is identical. The generation changed; the reflex did not.

But then the second generation's notables add a detail that Noah's did not: *yaʾkulu mimmā taʾkulūna minhu wa yashrabu mimmā tashrabūn* — "he eats from what you eat and drinks from what you drink." The objection is made more concrete, more physical. The messenger is disqualified not merely for being human but for the most ordinary evidences of humanity: he eats bread, he drinks water. The Quraysh would say the same of the Prophet ﷺ: *"What is this Messenger who eats food and walks in the markets?"* (25:7), and the Qur'an's answer was: *"And We did not send before you any of the messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets"* (25:20).

**The Logic of the Objection Examined**

The objection that a messenger cannot be someone who eats and drinks is worth dissecting, because its absurdity is instructive. The argument runs: God's messenger should be exalted; eating and drinking are lowly; therefore one who eats and drinks cannot be God's messenger. The flaw is in the second premise. Eating and drinking are not lowly; they are the condition of every living human being, including the notables making the argument. The objection therefore amounts to: "He cannot be a messenger because he is alive in the same way we are." But a messenger who did not eat or drink would not be a human being at all, and would therefore be useless as a guide to human beings — which is precisely the Qur'an's reply (17:95). The notables demand a messenger they could not follow and reject the one they could.

There is also a revealing inversion in the objection. The notables consider themselves superior because of their luxury — their fine food and drink. When the messenger eats ordinary food, they consider him inferior. But the messenger's ordinary eating is the mark of his solidarity with the people he was sent to; the notables' luxurious eating is the mark of their separation from them. The very thing the notables scorn is the messenger's credential.

**What the Three Descriptors Explain**

The verse's structure — three descriptors, then the speech — teaches how to read opposition to the truth. The objection "he is only a man who eats and drinks" is not a conclusion reached by reasoning; it is the *expression* of a prior condition. People who have covered the truth (descriptor one), who have decided there is no accounting (descriptor two), and who are comfortable in this world (descriptor three) will find *some* objection to any message that threatens the arrangement. The specific objection is almost incidental; if it were not "he eats," it would be something else. The Qur'an teaches the believer to look past the surface argument to the condition that produces it. This is not to dismiss all objections — the Qur'an answers them in detail — but to understand that answering them will not always persuade, because the objection was never the real reason.

**The Verse and the Believer's Self-Examination**

The three descriptors also function as a mirror. The believer is invited to ask: Is there any covering of known truth in me? Do I *live* as though I will meet God, or only *say* so? Has comfort softened my seriousness? The sūrah's opening believers were marked by the opposite of the third descriptor: they "give what they give while their hearts quake" (23:60) — affluent, perhaps, but not *mutraf*, because their wealth had not made them heedless. The line between provision and luxury, in the Qur'an's usage, is not the amount but the effect: does it make one grateful and generous, or forgetful and contemptuous? Verse 33 shows what the second effect looks like.

**The Speech Continues**

The notables' speech does not end here; it runs through verse 38, escalating from the objection about eating and drinking to a warning against following the messenger (v. 34), to mockery of the resurrection (vv. 35–37), to the final accusation of lying (v. 38). The next verse gives their practical conclusion: if you obey a man like yourselves, you will be losers.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:34

> **So if you obey a human being like yourselves, then surely you will be losers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Description to Threat**

The notables have described the messenger as a mere man who eats and drinks (v. 33). Now they draw the practical conclusion for their audience: *wa la-in aṭaʿtum basharan mithlakum innakum idhan la-khāsirūn* — "And if you should obey a human being like yourselves, indeed you would then be losers." The speech has moved from assessment to warning, from "look what he is" to "look what will happen to you if you follow him." This is the rhetoric of the elite when it feels its authority threatened: it does not merely argue against the challenger; it warns the people of the consequences of defection.

**The Grammar of Certainty**

The verse is heavily emphatic. It opens with *la-in* — the *lām* of oath combined with the conditional *in* — which in Arabic introduces a condition whose consequence is sworn to: "By God, if you obey..." The apodosis is introduced by *innakum* ("indeed you"), reinforced by *idhan* ("in that case, then"), and sealed with another *lām* of emphasis on *la-khāsirūn* ("*surely* losers"). The notables are not expressing an opinion; they are pronouncing a certainty with all the grammatical weapons the language provides. This intensity is itself a sign of anxiety. Those who are secure in their position do not swear oaths about the ruin of those who might leave it.

**"A Human Being Like Yourselves": The Objection Repeated a Third Time**

The phrase *basharan mithlakum* — "a human being like yourselves" — appears now for the third time in the sūrah (vv. 24, 33, 34). The repetition within the notables' own speech shows how central this objection was to them. They could not see past the messenger's humanity. And the phrase's third use reveals its underlying logic more clearly than the first two: to *obey* a human being like yourselves is, in the notables' view, a humiliation. The word *aṭaʿtum* ("you obey") is the key. The notables did not object to *listening* to a man; they objected to *obeying* one — to submitting their conduct to the direction of someone who had no claim to rank over them.

This exposes the real issue. The notables were accustomed to being obeyed. In their social order, obedience flowed upward toward wealth and lineage. A messenger from among the ordinary people — one who ate what they ate — inverted this order: he demanded that the notables obey the message he carried, and that the people obey God rather than the chiefs. The notables' warning to the people is therefore also a defense of their own position: if you obey *him*, you stop obeying *us*. The Qur'an exposes this dynamic repeatedly, most sharply in the mouths of the followers on the Day of Judgment: *"Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our masters and our great ones, and they misled us from the way"* (33:67).

**"You Will Be Losers": The Word Khāsirūn**

The consequence the notables threaten is *khusrān* — loss. The root *kh-s-r* is the root of commercial loss: the merchant whose venture returns less than he invested has *khasira*. The word is one of the Qur'an's most important terms, and it is almost always used by God to describe the *disbelievers*: *"Indeed, the losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection"* (39:15); *"Say: Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well"* (18:103–104). The entire Sūrah al-ʿAṣr is built on it: *"By time, indeed mankind is in loss (khusr), except those who believe and do righteous deeds..."* (103:1–3).

Here, the word is turned around. The notables use God's own vocabulary against God's messenger: they tell the people that *following* the messenger will make them losers. This is a precise inversion of the truth, and the sūrah's structure exposes it. The sūrah began, *"Truly the believers have prospered"* (23:1) — *aflaḥa*, the opposite of *khasira*. It will end, *"Indeed, the disbelievers will not prosper"* (23:117). And in between, it will show exactly who the losers are: *"And those whose scales are light — it is they who have lost their souls, abiding in Hell"* (23:103). The notables' threat, "you will be losers if you obey him," is answered by the whole architecture of the chapter: no, you will be losers if you do *not*.

**The Psychology of the Threat**

Why did the notables frame their opposition as a warning about *loss*? Because loss is what people fear most, and because the notables understood what kind of loss their audience would fear. Following the messenger would mean losing the notables' patronage, losing social standing, losing the security of the tribe, perhaps losing wealth and safety — the losses that the early Muslims in Makkah actually suffered. The notables were not lying about these costs; they were lying about their significance. They presented the temporary losses of this world as total loss, and concealed the permanent loss of the Hereafter that their own path led to. The Qur'an's response to this manipulation is to redefine loss on a longer timescale: *"Whoever is removed from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has attained success"* (3:185) — and whoever is not, has lost, whatever he kept in this world.

The threat also works by a familiar mechanism: it makes the *followers* feel that obedience to the messenger would be a kind of self-degradation. "Obey a man like yourselves? You, who are free men?" This appeal to pride is subtle and effective. It recasts submission to God's message as submission to a social equal, and it exploits the natural human reluctance to be led by someone who is "no better than I am." The Qur'an's answer is that the messenger is not asking to be obeyed *as a man*; he is conveying a command from God, and obedience to him is obedience to God (4:80). The notables deliberately conflate the two in order to make faith look like servility.

**The Irony of "Like Yourselves"**

There is a deep irony in the notables' phrase. They warn the people against obeying "a human being like yourselves" — and yet they themselves demand obedience, and they are also human beings like the people. The notables' whole position rests on the people obeying *them*, men who eat and drink exactly as the messenger does. The objection, taken seriously, would dissolve the notables' own authority. What the notables really meant was: do not obey a human being *like yourselves* — obey human beings *above* yourselves, namely us. The word *mithlakum* ("like you") is the tell: the notables did not consider themselves "like" the people; they considered themselves superior. The messenger's ordinary humanity threatened not the people's dignity but the notables' claim to be extraordinary.

**How the Qur'an Answers**

The Qur'an's response to verse 34's threat is distributed through the sūrah, but it can be gathered. First, obedience to a human messenger is not humiliation but the only possible path to guidance, since only a human can convey God's word to humans (17:95). Second, the messenger's ordinariness is a mercy and a proof, not a defect (25:20). Third, the true measure of loss and gain is the Hereafter, not the social calculus of this world (23:102–103). Fourth, those who make this threat will themselves discover, at the end, who the losers were: *"And they will say: Had we but listened or reasoned, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze"* (67:10).

**The Verse for the Believer Today**

The notables' threat is not confined to ancient generations. Every believer who takes his faith seriously in a secular or hostile environment hears a version of it: "If you follow this, you will lose — your career, your reputation, your friends, your place in society." The threat is sometimes accurate about the worldly costs. The sūrah teaches the believer to hear it for what it is: the voice of those who have denied the meeting of the Hereafter (v. 33), for whom worldly loss is the only loss imaginable. The believer measures on a different scale. He has already been told that *he* is the one who has prospered (v. 1), and that the heirs of Firdaws are those who possess the seven qualities (vv. 2–11), not those who kept the notables' favor. The question the verse leaves him with is simple: whose definition of loss does he accept?

**The Speech Escalates**

Having warned the people against obeying the messenger, the notables now turn to the content of his message, and specifically to the doctrine they find most ridiculous: that the dead will be raised. The next three verses are their mockery of the resurrection.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:35

> **Does he promise you that when you are dead and are dust and bones, you shall indeed be brought forth?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Real Objection Surfaces**

The notables have dismissed the messenger as a man who eats and drinks (v. 33) and warned the people against obeying him (v. 34). Now they name the doctrine that most offends them: *a-yaʿidukum annakum idhā mittum wa kuntum turāban wa ʿiẓāman annakum mukhrajūn* — "Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought out?" Verse 33 had already told us that these notables *"denied the meeting of the Hereafter."* Verse 35 shows that denial in action. Everything before this — the contempt for the messenger's humanity, the warning about loss — was preliminary. The resurrection is the point at which the notables' rejection becomes explicit and their mockery begins.

**The Rhetorical Question**

The verse is a question, but it is not a request for information. The interrogative *a-* ("does he...?") introduces a question of incredulity and derision — the tone of someone who repeats an absurd claim in order to expose its absurdity. "Does he *really* promise you *that*?" The notables address the people, not the messenger; they are performing the messenger's message for the crowd in a voice designed to make it sound ridiculous. This is a classic technique of mockery: state your opponent's position in the most literal, physical terms and let the audience laugh.

**"Does He Promise You": The Word Yaʿidu**

The verb *yaʿidu*, "he promises," from the root *w-ʿ-d*, is used for both promises of good and threats of evil (though Arabic often distinguishes *waʿd*, promise, from *waʿīd*, threat). The notables' use of it here is contemptuous: the messenger "promises" them something — as though he were offering a gift — and the gift is that they will be dug out of their graves. The word also carries an implication of futurity that the notables exploit: a promise concerns what has not yet happened and cannot be verified. The messenger is asking them to believe in something none of them has seen. The sūrah has already answered this implicit objection in verses 12–16, where the unseen future resurrection was grounded in the seen past creation; but the notables did not attend to that argument.

**"When You Have Died and Become Dust and Bones"**

The heart of the objection is the physical description: *idhā mittum wa kuntum turāban wa ʿiẓāman* — "when you have died and become dust and bones." The notables choose the most vivid image of decay available: not merely death, but the reduction of the body to its most inert remnants. *Turāb* is dust, dry earth — the substance from which verse 12 said the human being was created. *ʿIẓām* is bones — the framework that verse 14 said God created from the lump and clothed with flesh. The notables, without knowing it, are naming the very materials the sūrah has already identified as the raw stuff of God's creative work. They intend "dust and bones" as an argument *against* resurrection; the sūrah has already made "dust" and "bones" arguments *for* it.

This is the objection's fatal weakness, and the Qur'an exposes it wherever the objection appears. The notables assume that dust and bones are the *end* of a process; the Qur'an has shown that they are its *beginning*. *"Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?"* (19:67). *"He says: 'Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?' Say: 'He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knowing of every creation'"* (36:78–79). The person who was made *from* dust is in no position to say that he cannot be made from dust again.

**"You Will Be Brought Out": The Word Mukhrajūn**

The claim the notables mock is *annakum mukhrajūn* — "that you will be brought out." The word is the passive participle of *akhraja*, to cause to exit, to bring forth. As the source notes, the literal meaning is "caused to leave" — brought out of the earth in which the dead lie. The Qur'an uses this same root for the resurrection in several places, and always with the same image of *emergence*: *"Thus will be the emergence (al-khurūj)"* (50:11), spoken after the description of rain reviving dead land; *"the Day they will emerge (yakhrujūna) from the graves rapidly"* (70:43); *"and from it We will bring you out (nukhrijukum) another time"* (20:55).

The image is agricultural, and this connects the verse to the sūrah's own catalogue of signs. Verse 19 spoke of gardens that God *"brought into being"* from water sent into the earth; the resurrection is described with a related image — the dead brought *out* of the earth as plants are brought out of it. The notables use *mukhrajūn* as a term of ridicule; the Qur'an uses it as a term of botany. The seed goes into the ground as an inert thing and comes out as a living plant; the body goes into the ground as dust and bones and comes out, at God's command, as a living person. The notables laughed at a process they watched every spring.

**The Repetition of Annakum**

A grammatical detail: the word *annakum* ("that you") appears twice in the verse — once after *yaʿidukum* and once before *mukhrajūn* — with the long conditional clause between them. This repetition is not redundancy; Arabic grammarians explain that when a clause is long, the *anna* is repeated to reconnect the predicate with its subject after the interruption. But the repetition also serves the notables' mockery: it emphasizes the "you" — *you*, dead, dust, bones — *you* brought out. The rhetorical effect is to make the audience picture themselves as skeletons and then imagine being told they will walk again. The notables want the image to seem grotesque.

**The Objection Across the Qur'an**

The source commentary notes that this objection is the standard form of the denial of resurrection throughout the Qur'an: 17:49 and 17:98 (*"When we are bones and crumbled particles, will we be resurrected as a new creation?"*); 23:82 in this very sūrah, where the Quraysh will repeat the second generation's words almost exactly; 37:16 and 37:53; 56:47 (*"When we die and become dust and bones, are we indeed to be resurrected?"*); and 79:11 (*"Even when we are decayed bones?"*). The uniformity is the point. The sūrah quotes the second generation's objection here and the Quraysh's objection in verse 82 in nearly identical words, so that the reader sees the Quraysh as merely the latest generation to say what every generation of deniers has said. The sūrah will make this explicit in verse 81: *"Rather, they say the like of what the former peoples said."*

**Why the Resurrection Is the Sticking Point**

Why, of all the messenger's teachings, was the resurrection the one the notables mocked? Because it is the doctrine on which everything else depends. If there is a resurrection, there is an accounting; if there is an accounting, the notables' luxury (v. 33) is not a reward but a responsibility, their contempt for the poor is a crime, and their rejection of the messenger is a debt that will be called in. The resurrection is the doctrine that makes morality binding. The notables understood this — which is why they attacked it, and why they attacked it with mockery rather than argument. One cannot argue that the future will not happen; one can only make the claim look silly. Mockery is the tool of those who fear a proposition they cannot refute.

**The Believer's Response**

For the believer, verse 35 is both a warning and a preparation. It is a warning that the objection to the resurrection will always be framed as an appeal to "common sense" — dust is dust, bones are bones, the dead do not walk. It is a preparation because the sūrah has already supplied the answer in verses 12–16: the argument from the first creation. The believer who has absorbed those verses can meet the notables' question without embarrassment. "Does he promise you that when you are dust and bones you will be brought out?" Yes — by the One who brought you out of dust and a drop the first time, when you were nothing at all. The question that was meant to be ridiculous is, on reflection, the question that most deserves a serious answer, and the sūrah has given it.

**The Mockery Intensifies**

The notables' question in verse 35 is followed, in the next verse, by an exclamation that dismisses the very possibility of what they have described: "Far, far away is what you are promised!" The rhetorical question becomes a rhetorical dismissal.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:36

> **Far-fetched, far-fetched is that which you are promised.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Shortest Verse and the Loudest Scorn**

Having posed the resurrection as a ridiculous question (v. 35), the notables now answer it themselves with an exclamation: *hayhāta hayhāta limā tūʿadūn* — "Far, far away is what you are promised!" The verse is among the shortest in the sūrah and among the most expressive. It contains no argument, no evidence, no reasoning — only a doubled word of dismissal. It is the sound of scorn, preserved in the Qur'an so that every generation could hear what the rejection of resurrection actually sounds like when stripped of its pretensions: not a counter-argument, but a snort.

**The Word Hayhāt**

*Hayhāt* is what Arabic grammarians call an *ism fiʿl* — a "verbal noun" or "noun of action," a word that carries the force of a verb without being conjugated. It means "how far!" or "far removed is..." and it is used to declare that something is remote, unlikely, or out of the question. The source commentary rightly renders it "far-fetched, far-fetched" and notes that al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī explain it as signifying distance in the sense of improbability or impossibility. The word is used in classical Arabic poetry for things hopelessly beyond reach — the beloved who will never return, the youth that is gone. When the notables apply it to resurrection, they are placing it in the category of the impossible dream.

The word's very form is expressive. It is an exclamation, not a proposition; it belongs to the register of emotion, not logic. One cannot rebut *hayhāt* with a syllogism any more than one can rebut a sneer. This is precisely the notables' intention: to remove the resurrection from the domain of things one argues about and place it in the domain of things one laughs at.

**The Doubling**

The word is said twice: *hayhāta hayhāta*. Arabic uses repetition for emphasis, and the doubling here intensifies the dismissal to the maximum: not merely far, but far, far — impossibly, absurdly, unthinkably far. The commentators note that the repetition conveys the notables' total confidence in their position. They are not expressing doubt; they are expressing certainty that the thing is impossible. And the Qur'an, by preserving the doubling, preserves the *tone* — the sense of men throwing back their heads and laughing at the very idea.

The doubling has a further effect for the reader who knows how the story ends. The notables said "far, far" about the resurrection; five verses later they will be seized by the Cry and reduced to debris (v. 41). Their confident repetition becomes, in retrospect, the measure of their blindness. The thing they declared doubly impossible was, in fact, doubly certain — as certain as their death (v. 15), as certain as their rising (v. 16), both of which the sūrah had already asserted with the same doubled emphasis (*inna... la-*). The two emphatic pairs — God's *innakum la-mayyitūn... innakum tubʿathūn* and the notables' *hayhāta hayhāta* — stand against each other across the sūrah, and only one of them was true.

**"What You Are Promised"**

The object of the dismissal is *limā tūʿadūn* — "what you are promised" or "what you are threatened with." The preposition *li-* here is explained by the grammarians as attaching to *hayhāt* to specify what is far away; some read it as "far away *for* what you are promised," meaning "how far is the realization of what you are promised." The verb *tūʿadūn* is passive: "you are promised" — by the messenger. The notables refer to the resurrection not by name but by the vague "what you are promised," which is itself a form of contempt: the thing is not worth naming; it is merely "that promise of his."

The passive also subtly shifts the address. In verse 35 the notables asked, "Does *he* promise *you*?" Here they say, "what *you* are promised." The messenger has dropped out of the sentence; only the people and the promise remain. The notables are now speaking directly to the people's own sense of plausibility: *you* have been promised this; look how far-fetched it is.

**Why Scorn Rather Than Argument**

The Qur'an's decision to record this verse — pure scorn without content — is instructive. It shows that the denial of resurrection, when pressed, has no argument behind it. The notables have not shown that resurrection is impossible; they have declared it impossible. And the declaration rests on nothing but the feeling that dead bodies do not rise — a feeling derived from the observation that, within the ordinary course of nature, they do not. But the messenger never claimed that they rise within the ordinary course of nature; he claimed that God will raise them. The notables' *hayhāt* is therefore an answer to a claim no one made. They dismiss the natural impossibility of a thing that was only ever asserted as a divine act.

This reveals the structure of the objection. Behind "far, far away" lies an unstated premise: that nothing can happen except what happens by itself. The notables have, in effect, denied that God acts — while, as the sūrah will show (vv. 84–89), conceding in words that God created and owns everything. The incoherence is total: they admit that God made the heavens and the earth, and they scoff at the suggestion that He can remake a body. Al-Rāzī points out this contradiction in his discussion of the deniers: they affirm the greater and deny the lesser.

**The Distance Inverted**

There is a profound irony in the word *hayhāt*, "far." The notables use it to say that resurrection is far from possibility. The Qur'an elsewhere uses the vocabulary of distance to say the opposite: *"Indeed, they see it as far (baʿīdan), but We see it as near (qarīban)"* (70:6–7). What the deniers call distant, God calls near. And the sūrah's closing verses will show just how near: the person who said *hayhāt* about the resurrection will, at the moment of death, be crying *"My Lord, send me back"* (23:99), and will find that the barrier (*barzakh*) between him and the world is absolute, and that the Day he called far has arrived. The distance was never in the event; it was in the notables' willingness to see it.

**The Sound of Every Age**

*Hayhāt hayhāt* has been said in every generation. It was said by Noah's people, by the second generation, by the Quraysh (who, the sūrah says in v. 81, *"say the like of what the former peoples said"*), and it is said today in more sophisticated vocabulary: "unscientific," "wishful thinking," "a fairy tale." The vocabulary changes; the content does not. It remains a declaration of impossibility unsupported by any demonstration of impossibility — an emotional verdict dressed as a rational one. The believer who recognizes the ancient *hayhāt* beneath its modern costumes is not intimidated by it. He knows it was said before, with equal confidence, by men who were "made into debris" (v. 41).

**What the Believer Takes from This Verse**

The verse teaches the believer to distinguish between two things that are often confused: the *feeling* that something is impossible and the *demonstration* that it is. The notables had the feeling; they did not have the demonstration, and they could not have had it, because the resurrection is not a claim about what nature does but about what God will do. The believer, faced with *hayhāt* in any form, should ask the questioner one question: "Did the One who made you from dust need your permission the first time?" If the questioner concedes a Creator — and the sūrah will show that the notables did — then *hayhāt* collapses. If he does not, then the argument must begin further back, with verses 12–22, and not with the resurrection at all.

The verse also teaches the believer something about his own speech. Scorn is easy, and it feels like strength; but it is the tool of those who have run out of arguments. The believer who wishes to defend the truth should not imitate the notables' method — mockery without content — but the sūrah's method: evidence patiently laid out, from the embryo to the rain to the record of history. *Hayhāt* is what people say when they cannot say anything else.

**The Speech Continues**

The notables' dismissal is followed, in the next verse, by their positive creed — the only doctrine they affirm: "There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and we will not be raised." The scorn of verse 36 becomes the dogma of verse 37.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:37

> **There is naught but our life in this world: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Creed of the Deniers**

After the scorn of *hayhāt hayhāt* (v. 36), the notables state their positive belief: *in hiya illā ḥayātunā al-dunyā namūtu wa naḥyā wa mā naḥnu bi-mabʿūthīn* — "It is nothing but our worldly life: we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected." This is the only affirmative doctrine the notables hold, and it is the creed of materialism in every age, stated with a compression that no modern formulation has improved upon. Three clauses: there is only this life; the cycle of death and life is all that happens; and there is no rising. The verse is the complete theology of a person who has denied the Hereafter, and the Qur'an preserves it so that its shape can be seen clearly.

**"It Is Nothing But Our Worldly Life"**

The first clause uses, once again, the exclusive construction *in... illā* — "it is nothing but." The pronoun *hiya* ("it") refers to life, existence, the whole of what there is. The notables reduce all reality to *ḥayātunā al-dunyā* — "our lower/nearer life." The word *dunyā* is the feminine of *adnā*, meaning "nearer" or "lower"; the Qur'an calls this world *al-ḥayāt al-dunyā*, "the nearer life," always in implicit contrast with *al-ākhirah*, "the later/further life." By adopting the Qur'an's own term while denying its counterpart, the notables' speech contains a hidden incoherence: they call this life "the nearer life" while denying that there is any further one. The very word they use presupposes what they deny.

The possessive *-nā* ("our") is also revealing: "*our* worldly life." The notables speak of life as a possession — as something that is theirs. This proprietorship is the root of their error. The sūrah has already established that life is not a possession but a gift and a test (vv. 12–16, 30); the human being was *created* from clay, *placed* as a drop, *brought forth* as another creation, and will be *caused to die* and *raised*. None of these are things he does; they are things done to him. To say "*our* life" as though it were self-owned is to have forgotten every verse of the sūrah's second movement.

**"We Die and We Live"**

The second clause, *namūtu wa naḥyā* — "we die and we live" — is the one the source commentary singles out as the distinctive addition of this verse compared with its parallel in 6:29. The order is striking: death first, then life. The commentators offered two readings, both recorded by al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī. First, the phrase may describe the succession of generations: some of us die and others are born to replace them; the species continues, but the individual does not return. This is the reading al-Ṭabarī prefers: *"some of us die and others live,"* meaning the cycle of birth and death continues on earth indefinitely, without any personal resurrection. Second, the phrase may be a *hysteron proteron* — an inversion of natural order for rhetorical effect — meaning simply "we live and we die," the whole of existence being the span between birth and death.

Both readings express the same worldview: existence is a closed cycle with no exit and no destination. The notables acknowledge death; they acknowledge life; they deny that either has a meaning beyond itself. This is the "eternal return" of the materialist — generation after generation, born and dying, and nothing more. The Qur'an quotes the same creed from the Quraysh: *"And they say: There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time"* (45:24), adding there the attribution of everything to *dahr*, time or fate.

**"And We Will Not Be Resurrected"**

The third clause is the denial proper: *wa mā naḥnu bi-mabʿūthīn* — "and we are not going to be raised." The construction is emphatic: *mā... bi-* with the passive participle *mabʿūthīn* is the strongest available negation of a future state. The word *mabʿūthīn* is from the same root as *tubʿathūn* in verse 16 (*"you will be raised"*). The notables negate, in the same vocabulary, exactly what God affirmed. The two verses face each other across the sūrah: God's *innakum... tubʿathūn* and the notables' *mā naḥnu bi-mabʿūthīn*. The reader is left in no doubt about the precise point of contradiction.

**The Logical Structure of Materialism**

Verse 37 deserves examination as an argument, because it is presented as one. The notables move from an observation (people die and others are born) to a conclusion (there is no resurrection). But the observation does not support the conclusion. That people die and are replaced is a fact about this world; it says nothing about whether there is another. The notables have confused *"we have not seen the dead rise"* with *"the dead will not rise"* — a confusion between the absence of evidence within one domain and the evidence of absence in all domains. It is as if a person who had never left his village concluded that there were no other villages.

The sūrah has already exposed the flaw from another direction. Verses 12–14 showed that each person has *already* undergone a transformation more radical than resurrection: from clay to drop to person. The notables accept this transformation because they see its results daily; they reject the resurrection because they have not seen it. But if the criterion is "what I have seen," they should reject their own embryonic development too, since none of them saw *that*. The argument from observation, applied consistently, undermines itself.

**The Moral Consequence of the Creed**

The Qur'an's concern with verse 37 is not merely intellectual. The creed "there is only this life" has consequences, and the sūrah shows them in the notables' own conduct. If there is only this life, then luxury (v. 33) is the highest good and its pursuit the only rational aim. If there is no meeting with God (v. 33), then the messenger's call to worship and *taqwā* (v. 32) is pointless and even harmful, since it diverts effort from the only life there is. If there is no resurrection, then the poor who follow the messenger are indeed "losers" (v. 34), because they have sacrificed the only goods that exist. The notables' contempt, their warning, and their mockery all follow logically from verse 37. The creed is the root; the conduct is the fruit.

This is why the Qur'an treats the denial of the Hereafter as the most dangerous of errors — more dangerous, in its practical effects, than many forms of theological confusion. A person who believes in a distorted God but expects an accounting will still restrain himself; a person who believes in no accounting has no reason, beyond social convenience, to restrain anything. The Qur'an says of such people: *"They know what is apparent of the worldly life, but they, of the Hereafter, are unaware"* (30:7) — and that unawareness governs everything else.

**The Psychology Behind the Creed**

Why would anyone *want* to believe verse 37? On its face, it is a bleak creed: no meaning beyond the cycle, no justice beyond the grave, no reunion, no rest. The answer the Qur'an gives is that the creed is not adopted for its attractiveness but for its convenience. *"Rather, man desires to continue in sin. He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?"* (75:5–6). The person who wishes to live without restraint finds the denial of accounting congenial, and constructs or accepts a creed that licenses it. The notables were affluent (v. 33); the creed of verse 37 told them that their affluence was the whole prize and that no one would ask how they used it. It is not hard to see why they preferred it.

**The Verse in the Modern World**

Verse 37 is the most contemporary verse in the sūrah, because its creed is now the default assumption of much of the developed world. "This is the only life we have" is said as though it were a discovery of science, when it is in fact an ancient dogma that the Qur'an quoted from the mouths of Bronze Age chiefs. The believer should notice this. The materialism that presents itself as modern and rational is the oldest and least examined of human creeds, and it rests today on exactly what it rested on then: the feeling that dust does not rise, and the desire that it should not. The believer meets it as the sūrah met it — not with contempt, but with the questions of verses 12–22 and the history of verses 23–44.

**The Speech Concludes**

The notables have one sentence left. Having reduced reality to this life and denied the resurrection, they draw the inevitable inference about the messenger: if there is no resurrection, then the man who promises it is a liar. The next verse records that final accusation.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:38

> **He is but a man fabricating lies against God, and we do not believe him.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Charge**

The notables' speech, which began in verse 33, reaches its conclusion: *in huwa illā rajulun iftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban wa mā naḥnu lahu bi-muʾminīn* — "He is nothing but a man who has invented a lie against God, and we will not believe in him." The speech has moved through five stages: he is only a man who eats and drinks (v. 33); obeying him means loss (v. 34); his promise of resurrection is absurd (vv. 35–36); there is only this life (v. 37); and now — therefore — he is a liar and we reject him. The final verse is the logical terminus of everything before it. If there is no resurrection, then the man who promises it in God's name has invented something and attributed it to God. The accusation of fabrication is not an additional insult; it is the conclusion the notables' premises require.

**"Nothing But a Man": For the Fourth Time**

The verse opens with the notables' favorite construction: *in huwa illā rajulun* — "he is nothing but a man." This is the fourth time in the sūrah that a messenger has been reduced by this formula (vv. 24, 25, 33, 38). The repetition across two generations shows how fixed the reflex was. The notables could not think about the messenger except by first diminishing him. In verse 25 the formula introduced "a man in whom is madness"; here it introduces "a man who has invented a lie." The two charges — madness and lying — are the twin accusations leveled against every prophet, and they are logically incompatible: a madman does not calculate lies, and a liar is not mad. The Qur'an notes this incoherence in the Quraysh's accusations against the Prophet ﷺ, who called him at once a poet, a soothsayer, a madman, and a sorcerer — categories that exclude one another. The notables of the second generation were no more consistent; they called their messenger mad (implied in the parallel to Noah) and now call him a deliberate fabricator.

**"Who Has Invented a Lie Against God"**

The charge is *iftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban* — "he has fabricated a lie against God." The verb *iftarā*, from the root *f-r-y*, means to cut, to fashion, and hence to invent, to forge — originally, to cut leather into a shape. To *iftarā* a lie is to manufacture a falsehood deliberately, as an artisan manufactures a product. The phrase *ʿalā Allāh* — "against God," "upon God" — specifies the gravest form of lying: not a lie about a man, but a lie attributed to God, a claim that God said what He did not say.

The irony of this charge, as the source commentary notes, is total. The notables accuse the messenger of lying about God, when it was they who had fabricated a religion of idols and denied what God had actually revealed. The Qur'an makes the reversal explicit throughout: *"And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie about God or denies His signs?"* (6:21; 7:37; 10:17). The verse names two kinds of injustice — inventing lies about God and denying His signs — and the notables were guilty of the second while accusing the messenger of the first. The Qur'an also states who the real fabricators are: *"Say: Have you seen what God has sent down to you of provision, and you have made of it lawful and unlawful? Say: Has God permitted you, or do you invent (taftarūna) lies about God?"* (10:59). The people who declared the resurrection impossible and their idols real were the ones who had "invented against God."

**The Structure of the Accusation**

The accusation of fabrication rests entirely on the notables' prior denial. Consider the reasoning: (1) There is no resurrection (v. 37). (2) The messenger says God has promised a resurrection. (3) Therefore the messenger has attributed to God a falsehood. The argument is valid, but its first premise is the thing in question. The notables have not shown that there is no resurrection; they have asserted it with a scornful *hayhāt* (v. 36). Everything else follows from an assertion. This is what the classical logicians called *muṣādarah ʿalā al-maṭlūb* — begging the question. The notables convict the messenger of lying by assuming the falsehood of the very thing he was sent to announce.

The Qur'an's response to this circularity is to break it with evidence outside the circle: the first creation (vv. 12–14), the natural signs (vv. 17–22), the history of previous deniers (vv. 23–41), and, at the sūrah's end, the concessions the deniers themselves make about God's power (vv. 84–89). The notables' accusation cannot be answered on its own terms because it has no terms; it can only be answered by widening the discussion to the evidence they refused to consider.

**"And We Will Not Believe in Him"**

The verse and the speech close with a declaration: *wa mā naḥnu lahu bi-muʾminīn* — "and we are not going to believe in him." The construction is the same emphatic negation used in verse 37 for the resurrection (*mā naḥnu bi-mabʿūthīn*). The parallel is exact: "we will not be raised" and "we will not believe." The two negations are linked; the second follows from the first. And the phrase is not a statement of present opinion but of settled future policy: we will *not* believe — the door is closed.

This finality is what distinguishes the notables from an honest doubter. A doubter says, "I am not convinced"; the notables say, "we will not believe." The first leaves room for evidence; the second announces that no evidence will be considered. It is this closure that the Qur'an identifies as the essence of *kufr*: not the absence of belief but the refusal of it. *"Indeed, those who disbelieve — it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe"* (2:6). The notables have arrived at that state by their own declaration.

The word *muʾminīn* — "believers" — is the same word that gives the sūrah its name and opens its first verse. *Qad aflaḥa al-muʾminūn* — "the believers have prospered." The notables declare themselves the opposite: *mā naḥnu... bi-muʾminīn* — "we are not believers." They have, in their own words, excluded themselves from the category the sūrah promised prosperity to. The sūrah does not need to pronounce judgment on them; they have pronounced it on themselves.

**The Speech as a Whole**

The notables' speech (vv. 33–38) is now complete, and it repays reading as a single composition. It begins with the messenger's body (he eats and drinks) and ends with his character (he is a liar). In between, it warns the people, mocks the resurrection, and states the materialist creed. Not one sentence engages the actual content of the message — that there is one God who created them and to whom they will return. The speech attacks the messenger's humanity, threatens the people's interests, ridicules the Hereafter, and asserts a dogma; it never asks whether the message is *true*. This is the Qur'an's portrait of how rejection works: it circles the message without ever entering it.

**The Source's Insight: Acknowledging God While Denying His Relevance**

The source commentary makes a valuable observation on this verse: the notables, like the Arab idolaters, did not deny God's existence. They accused the messenger of lying *about God* — which presupposes that God exists and can be lied about. Their error was not atheism but the confinement of God to irrelevance: He exists, but He has no claim on human life beyond this world, no accounting, no resurrection. This is, the source notes, precisely the position of the Quraysh, who *"worshipped idols and acknowledged the existence of God"* while denying the Hereafter. It is also, one might add, the practical position of many in the modern world who profess belief in God while living as though verse 37 were true. The notables' creed is not "there is no God"; it is "God does not matter." The sūrah's later argument (vv. 84–89) will be built precisely on this: you admit He owns everything — how then can you deny that He can raise you and will judge you?

**The Messenger's Response**

The notables have said their last word. As with Noah (v. 26), the messenger's reply is not addressed to them. He has heard himself called a mere man, a threat to the people's interests, a promiser of absurdities, and a liar against God. The next verse records what he says, and to whom.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:39

> **He said, “My Lord! Help me, for they deny me.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prayer Repeated Exactly**

The unnamed messenger has been called a mere man, a threat, a promiser of absurdities, and a fabricator of lies. His reply is the same seven Arabic words that Noah spoke in verse 26: *qāla rabbi unṣurnī bimā kadhdhabūn* — "He said: 'My Lord, help me, for they have denied me.'" The sūrah's method of exact repetition reaches its most poignant instance here. The message was identical (vv. 23 and 32); the rejection was nearly identical (vv. 24–25 and 33–38); and now the prayer is identical, letter for letter. Two messengers separated by generations, facing two peoples, end their preaching with the same breath.

Because the words were examined in detail under verse 26, this commentary will not repeat that analysis but will ask what the *repetition itself* teaches, and what is different about the prayer in its second setting.

**Why the Same Words?**

The Qur'an could have written "and he prayed as Noah had prayed." Instead it quotes the prayer again in full. The choice makes several points at once.

First, it establishes the prayer as *the* prayer of the messenger in extremity — not a personal idiosyncrasy of Noah but a form that belongs to the office. When a messenger has exhausted every means of persuasion and been met with a closed door, this is what he says. The sūrah is teaching the Prophet ﷺ, and through him every caller to God, the words for that moment.

Second, it emphasizes the *unity of the prophets' experience*. The message was one (v. 52 will say so explicitly); the opposition was one (v. 81 will say the Quraysh repeat "what the former peoples said"); and the recourse was one. The prophets form a single brotherhood — the Prophet ﷺ said, *"The prophets are paternal brothers; their mothers differ but their religion is one"* (al-Bukhārī 3443; Muslim 2365) — and the sameness of their prayer is the audible form of that brotherhood.

Third, the repetition creates a rhythm of *inevitability*. The reader who has followed the sūrah knows what happened after Noah's prayer: the Ark, the Flood. When the second messenger prays the same words, the reader expects the same kind of answer — and the next verses deliver it (vv. 40–41). The repetition is thus a literary device that builds dread: the deniers have said what the earlier deniers said; the messenger has prayed what the earlier messenger prayed; the pattern is complete, and the reader knows what completes it.

**What Is Different in the Second Setting**

Although the words are the same, the situation has a different texture, and the difference is instructive.

Noah's prayer came after nine hundred and fifty years and a divine revelation that no more would believe (11:36). The unnamed messenger's duration is not given; the sūrah compresses his story into a single exchange. The effect is to show that the prayer is not tied to a particular length of trial. It is the response to a *state* — the state in which the people have declared "we will not believe" (v. 38) — not to a *duration*. When the door is shut, the prayer is appropriate, whether the shutting took a millennium or a season.

Noah's people had rejected him with contempt and a policy of waiting (vv. 24–25). The second people rejected their messenger with a fully articulated creed of materialism and a charge of lying against God (vv. 33–38). The second rejection is more developed, more doctrinal, and in a sense more culpable: these people had the Flood behind them as a warning and still constructed a theology of denial. The messenger's prayer, though verbally identical, therefore carries a different weight: it is the prayer of a man whose people rejected not only him but the lesson of history.

**"For They Have Denied Me": The Charge Returned**

The reason the messenger gives — *bimā kadhdhabūn*, "because they have denied me" — has an added resonance in this setting. The notables' final word (v. 38) was *iftarā ʿalā Allāhi kadhiban* — "he has fabricated a *lie* (*kadhib*)." The messenger's prayer uses the same root: *kadhdhabūn* — "they have called me a *liar*." The two uses of *k-dh-b* face each other. The notables said: he lies. The messenger says to God: they call me a liar. He does not defend himself to them; he reports the charge to the One who knows the truth. This is the discipline of the prophets: when accused of lying about God, they do not argue their honesty before men but place the matter before God, who *"knows the secret and what is more hidden"* (20:7). The Qur'an instructs the Prophet ﷺ in the same discipline: *"And if they deny you, say: My deeds are mine and your deeds are yours; you are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do"* (10:41).

**The Prayer as the Boundary of Human Effort**

Both Noah's prayer and this one mark the same boundary: the point at which human effort ends and divine action begins. The messenger has done everything within his power — he has called, explained, warned, endured. What remains is beyond his power: the hearts of the people, and their fate. The prayer is the recognition of that limit. It is not an admission of failure but of the *division of labor* between servant and Lord. The Qur'an states this division repeatedly to the Prophet ﷺ: *"Upon you is only the conveyance, and upon Us is the account"* (13:40). The messenger conveyed; he now hands the account to God.

For the ordinary believer, this boundary is equally real and equally freeing. A parent who has taught, a friend who has advised, a teacher who has explained, a caller who has called — each reaches a point at which the other person's choice is not within reach. At that point the believer can either torment himself with what he might have done differently or say, with Noah and the second messenger, *rabbi unṣurnī*. The prayer transfers the weight of the outcome from the shoulders that cannot bear it to the One who holds all outcomes. It is the remedy for the exhaustion of the sincere.

**The Answer Comes Faster**

There is one more difference between the two prayers, visible in what follows each. After Noah's prayer, God's answer was a long instruction (vv. 27–29): build, wait for the sign, load, board, praise, pray. After the second messenger's prayer, God's answer is a single sentence (v. 40): *"In a little while they will surely become regretful."* The compression reflects the sūrah's method of moving from the detailed to the general, but it also reflects a shortening of divine patience with a people who had a precedent to learn from and refused it. Noah's people had no Flood behind them; the second generation had. The Qur'an says: *"And how many a generation have We destroyed after Noah!"* (17:17). The prayer was the same; the answer came more swiftly.

**The Verse as a Mirror**

Verse 39 holds up a mirror to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah and to every believer since. The Prophet ﷺ was being called exactly what the second messenger was called — a man, a liar against God, a promiser of absurdities. The sūrah tells him: two messengers before you heard this and said these words; say them too. And the believer who calls others to good and is met with the notables' answers — "you are only a person like us; following you would cost us; your Hereafter is a fairy tale; you are making it up" — is told the same. The seven words of verse 39 are not a historical curiosity. They are a prayer the Qur'an has placed in the believer's mouth for the day he needs it.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:40

> **He said, “In a little while they shall become remorseful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God's Reply in a Single Line**

The messenger prayed, *"My Lord, help me, for they have denied me"* (v. 39). God's answer is a single sentence: *qāla ʿammā qalīlin la-yuṣbiḥunna nādimīn* — "He said: 'After a little while they will surely become regretful.'" Where Noah received a long set of instructions (vv. 27–29), the second messenger receives a promise and a timeline. The compression is deliberate. The sūrah is moving toward generalization, and the answer to this prayer is stated in the most general form possible: the deniers will regret, and soon.

**"After a Little While": ʿAmmā Qalīl**

The phrase *ʿammā qalīl* is composed of *ʿan* ("after, from"), the redundant *mā* (which the grammarians say adds emphasis, as in *ʿammā qalīl* = "after only a little"), and *qalīl* ("a little, a short time"). The whole means "in a very short while," "before long." The word *qalīl* is the same word the Qur'an uses for the believers who boarded the Ark — *"and none believed with him except a few (qalīl)"* (11:40) — and for the worldly enjoyment of the deniers — *"a little enjoyment (matāʿ qalīl), then their refuge is Hell"* (3:197). It is a word of smallness, and here it measures the remaining time of a people who thought they had all the time in the world.

Recall the notables' policy toward Noah: *"wait concerning him for a time (ḥattā ḥīn)"* (v. 25). They thought time was their ally; they would outlast the messenger. God's answer to the second messenger reverses the calculation: it is *they* who have only *a little* time. The two temporal phrases — the notables' *ḥattā ḥīn* and God's *ʿammā qalīl* — face each other across the sūrah, and only one of them measured time correctly. The deniers' "wait a while" is answered by God's "a little while." Their delay was His deadline.

**"They Will Surely Become Regretful": The Grammar of Certainty**

The predicate is *la-yuṣbiḥunna nādimīn*. The verb *yuṣbiḥu* means literally "to enter the morning" and by extension "to become," with a connotation of a sudden new state — as one wakes to find things changed. The *lām* of emphasis and the heavy *nūn* of emphasis (*-unna*) together produce the strongest form of future assertion in Arabic: "they will *most surely* become." The certainty with which the notables said *hayhāta hayhāta* (v. 36) about the resurrection is matched, and exceeded, by the certainty with which God says *la-yuṣbiḥunna* about their regret.

The predicate noun is *nādimīn* — "regretful," "remorseful." The root *n-d-m* denotes the pain of wishing one had acted otherwise — the specific sorrow of a person who sees, too late, that his choice was wrong. As the source notes, the word appears in the story of Cain, who after killing his brother *"became among the regretful (nādimīn)"* (5:31), and in the story of Thamūd, who after hamstringing the she-camel *"became regretful"* (26:157). In both cases the regret came after the irreversible deed and could not undo it. Verse 40's *nādimīn* carries the same quality: this is not the productive regret of repentance (*tawbah*), which can still change the future, but the sterile regret of those who see the consequence arriving and can no longer avert it.

**What Regret Is and Why It Is the Promised Outcome**

Why does God name *regret* as the outcome, rather than destruction or punishment directly? The choice is psychologically precise. Regret is the inner event that accompanies the outer punishment; it is the moment when the denier's own mind turns against him and admits what he refused to admit. The punishment falls on the body; the regret falls on the soul.
