And regret is, in a sense, the worse of the two, because it is the recognition that the punishment was avoidable — that the message was true, that the warning was sincere, that the door was open and one chose to keep it shut.

The Qur'an gives this regret a name in its descriptions of the Last Day: *yawm al-ḥasrah*, the Day of Regret (19:39), and it describes the disbeliever's cry: *"Oh, my regret over what I neglected in regard to God!"* (39:56). The sūrah will stage this regret at length in its closing verses: *"My Lord, send me back, that I might do righteousness in what I left behind"* (23:99–100); *"Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"* (23:106). Verse 40 is the earliest announcement, in the sūrah, of the emotion that its ending will dramatize.

There is a further reason regret is the named outcome. The notables had accused the messenger of lying (v. 38). Regret is the internal confession that he was telling the truth. God does not merely destroy the deniers; He causes them to *know*, before the end, that they were wrong. This knowledge is a form of justice: the truth they suppressed is forced back into their awareness. *"On the Day when their faces are turned about in the Fire, they will say: Oh, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger!"* (33:66). The regret vindicates the messenger in the only court that matters — the conscience of his accusers.

**The Timing: Why "Soon"?**

The word *qalīl* raises a question: how soon? The answer, given in the next verse, is: soon enough that the same generation that mocked witnessed the Cry. The regret was not deferred to the Hereafter alone; it came in this world, at the moment of the punishment. This is characteristic of the Qur'an's accounts of the destroyed nations: the punishment fell within the lifetime of those who had denied, so that the deniers themselves — not their descendants — saw the truth of what they had called a lie.

But the phrase also has a wider application. From God's perspective, *every* human span is "a little while." The Qur'an describes the Day of Judgment as *"near"* (70:7) and the life of this world as *"an hour of a day"* (10:45), and the sūrah itself will conclude by having the deniers say they lived *"a day or part of a day"* (23:113). Whatever the length of a person's life, the moment of regret is *ʿammā qalīl* — after a little while — because the whole of life is little. The word is thus both a specific prediction about the second generation and a general truth about the human condition.

**The Verse as Consolation to the Messenger**

Verse 40 is addressed to the messenger, and it is, in the first place, a consolation. He prayed "help me"; God replied, in effect, "the matter is already decided, and soon." The messenger is not told to do anything further — no ark to build, no sign to await. He is told only to wait, as the deniers had told the people to wait, but with the opposite expectation. This is the consolation that the Qur'an gives the Prophet ﷺ repeatedly: *"So be patient; indeed, the promise of God is truth"* (30:60); *"And do not be grieved by them, and do not be in distress over what they conspire"* (16:127). The messenger's part is done; the outcome is guaranteed and imminent.

For the believer who has been mocked, dismissed, or accused of lying for his faith, the verse offers the same consolation in the same form. He is not promised that his opponents will be converted; he is promised that they will *regret*. He does not need to see the regret to trust the promise; God has said *la-yuṣbiḥunna*, and the emphasis is God's, not his.

**A Warning to the Reader**

The verse also functions as a warning, because every reader is a potential *nādim*. The regret God promised the second generation is the regret every person will feel who neglected what he knew he should have done. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"There is no one who dies but regrets."* They asked: "What does he regret, O Messenger of God?" He said: *"If he was a doer of good, he regrets that he did not do more; and if he was a doer of evil, he regrets that he did not desist"* (al-Tirmidhī 2403). The verse invites the reader to choose which regret he will have — the small regret of the righteous who wished they had done more, or the total regret of those who denied and were seized.

**The Promise Fulfilled**

Verse 40 is a promise; verse 41 is its fulfillment. The "little while" passes in the space between two verses, and the Cry comes.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:41

> **So the Cry seized them rightly, and We made them into dross; so away with the wrongdoing people!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The "Little While" Ends**

God promised the messenger that his deniers would soon regret (v. 40). Verse 41 records the fulfillment: *fa-akhadhat-humu al-ṣayḥatu bi'l-ḥaqqi fa-jaʿalnāhum ghuthāʾan fa-buʿdan li'l-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — "So the Cry seized them in truth, and We made them as debris; so away with the wrongdoing people!" The verse contains three movements linked by the particle *fa-*, "so, and then": the seizure, the reduction, and the dismissal. Each *fa-* marks an immediate consequence of the last; there is no interval, no negotiation, no appeal. The people who said *"we will not believe"* (v. 38) and *"far, far away is what you are promised"* (v. 36) are, in the space of a single verse, seized, pulverized, and cursed.

**"The Cry Seized Them": The Ṣayḥah**

The instrument of the punishment is *al-ṣayḥah* — "the Cry," "the Shout," "the Blast." The word comes from the root *ṣ-y-ḥ*, to shout or scream; a *ṣayḥah* is a single, overwhelming sound. As the source commentary records, the classical scholars understood it in several ways: al-Rāzī mentions that it was the literal shout of the angel Gabriel, so terrible that it stopped the hearts of all who heard it; others took it as a violent quaking or thunderous blast that accompanied the destruction; and some took it as a general term for the sudden, sound-borne death that God sent. The Qur'an uses *ṣayḥah* for the destruction of Thamūd (11:67; 54:31), of the people of Shuʿayb (11:94), of the people of Lot (15:73), of the people of al-Ḥijr (15:83), and of the people of the town in Sūrah Yā Sīn (36:29: *"It was not but one Cry, and immediately they were extinguished"*). It is also the word used for the Trumpet blast of the Last Day (36:49, 53; 50:42). The Cry is thus the Qur'an's recurring image of a punishment that comes as *sound* — instantaneous, inescapable, and total.

The verb *akhadhat* — "it seized" — is significant. The root *a-kh-dh* means to take, to grasp, to seize; the Qur'an uses it for God's seizure of the wrongdoers in many verses: *"Thus is the seizure (akhdh) of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong; indeed, His seizure is painful and severe"* (11:102). The Cry did not merely strike them; it *took* them, as a hand takes what it grips. The notables who thought themselves in possession of "*our* worldly life" (v. 37) were themselves possessed by the punishment.

**"In Truth": Bi'l-Ḥaqq**

The Cry seized them *bi'l-ḥaqq* — "in truth," "rightly," "justly." The phrase is a moral qualification, and it is essential. The destruction was not arbitrary, not excessive, not the whim of an angry power; it was *ḥaqq* — the right thing, the just thing, the true thing. As the source notes from al-Rāzī, *bi'l-ḥaqq* indicates that the punishment was deserved. The people had received a messenger from among themselves (v. 32), had heard the clear message (v. 32), had been warned by the precedent of Noah's people (vv. 23–30), had mocked the resurrection (vv. 35–37), had called the messenger a liar (v. 38), and had closed the door with "we will not believe." Every condition of a just punishment was met: knowledge, warning, opportunity, and persistent refusal. The Cry came *bi'l-ḥaqq* because the people had chosen it *bi'l-bāṭil* — through falsehood.

The word *ḥaqq* also carries the sense of *reality*, as opposed to illusion. The notables' creed (v. 37) was a false picture of reality: this life only, no resurrection. The Cry was reality arriving. The thing they called "far, far away" came *bi'l-ḥaqq* — as the truth they had denied. There is a grim symmetry: those who rejected the *ḥaqq* were seized by the *ḥaqq*.

**"And We Made Them as Debris": Ghuthāʾ**

The second movement is *fa-jaʿalnāhum ghuthāʾan* — "and We made them *ghuthāʾ*." The word *ghuthāʾ*, as the source explains, denotes the scum, froth, dead leaves, and broken twigs that a torrent carries on its surface and deposits along its banks when it recedes — the worthless debris of a flood. The Qur'an uses the same word in Sūrah al-Aʿlā: *"and He who brings out the pasture, then makes it black debris (ghuthāʾan aḥwā)"* (87:4–5), describing green vegetation that dries, blackens, and is swept away. The image is one of complete worthlessness and complete passivity: *ghuthāʾ* has no life, no shape, no value; it goes where the water takes it and is discarded where the water leaves it.

The choice of this word for the notables is devastating in its irony. These were the *malaʾ* — the men who "filled the eye," the affluent (v. 33), the ones who warned the people against loss (v. 34). God made them *ghuthāʾ* — flotsam. Everything that constituted their importance — wealth, rank, confidence — was stripped away, and what remained was the debris left behind by a receding torrent. The Prophet ﷺ used this very word to warn his own community against a different but related fate: *"The nations are about to call one another against you as diners call one another to a dish."* They asked, "Is it because we will be few?" He said: *"No, you will be many, but you will be ghuthāʾ like the ghuthāʾ of the torrent; and God will remove fear of you from the hearts of your enemies and cast weakness (wahn) into your hearts."* They asked what *wahn* was, and he said: *"Love of the world and hatred of death"* (Abū Dāwūd 4297; Aḥmad). The connection is exact: what made the second generation *ghuthāʾ* was precisely love of the world (v. 33's luxury, v. 37's "only our worldly life") and denial of what lies beyond death.

**"So Away with the Wrongdoing People": Buʿdan**

The third movement is a dismissal: *fa-buʿdan li'l-qawmi al-ẓālimīn* — "so away with the wrongdoing people!" The word *buʿdan* is a verbal noun in the accusative, functioning as an imprecation or a declaration of distance: "let them be far removed," "perdition to them," "away with them." The root *b-ʿ-d* means distance, and the phrase declares that the wrongdoers have been removed — from life, from mercy, from any further concern. Al-Ṭabarī explains it as *"perdition and distance from the mercy of God."*

The word *buʿdan* echoes, with terrible precision, the notables' own *hayhāta hayhāta* (v. 36) — which also meant "far, far." They had said that the resurrection was far; God says that *they* are far. They used the vocabulary of distance to dismiss the truth; God uses it to dismiss them. The reader who notices the echo understands the sūrah's justice: each people is answered in its own words.

The Qur'an uses this formula of dismissal for the destroyed nations in several places: *"Away with Thamūd!"* (11:68); *"Away with Madyan, as Thamūd was done away with!"* (11:95); and, in this sūrah, again at verse 44: *"So away with a people who do not believe!"* The repetition marks the formula as the standard verdict on those who reject the messengers after clear warning.

**"The Wrongdoing People": The Charge Named**

The people are called *al-qawm al-ẓālimīn* — "the wrongdoing people." *Ẓulm*, as noted under verse 27, is the placing of a thing where it does not belong; its gravest form is *shirk*, placing worship where it does not belong. The second generation's wrongdoing was comprehensive: they placed idols where God belonged, placed contempt where honor belonged (toward the messenger), placed luxury where gratitude belonged, and placed denial where the resurrection belonged. Their punishment is the removal of everything they had misplaced.

**Why the Verse Is Brief**

Noah's story was told across seven verses; the second generation's punishment is told in one. The compression reflects the sūrah's movement toward generalization, but it also reflects something about the nature of the event. The Cry was instantaneous. There was no Ark to build, no forty days of rain, no gradual rising of waters. One sound, and it was over. The verse's brevity mirrors the punishment's speed. The notables had a whole lifetime to consider the message; their end took a single moment. This asymmetry — long opportunity, sudden close — is the Qur'an's consistent picture of divine patience followed by divine decision: *"And I granted respite to the disbelievers, then I seized them; and how was My reproach!"* (22:44).

**The Lesson for the Reader**

Verse 41 completes the second of the sūrah's historical accounts and delivers its verdict. For the reader, the lesson is threefold. First, the promise of verse 40 was kept, and kept quickly; God's "soon" is not the deniers' "someday." Second, the punishment was *bi'l-ḥaqq* — just — and every element of the story shows why. Third, the outcome of denial is *ghuthāʾ* — the reduction of all human importance to debris — and *buʿd* — distance from mercy. The sūrah's opening promised that the believers "have prospered" and will inherit Firdaws; verse 41 shows what the alternative is. The two destinies are placed side by side so that no one can claim the choice was unclear.

The Prophet ﷺ was hearing this verse in a city whose notables were saying what the second generation had said. The verse told him — and tells every believer surrounded by confident mockery — that confidence is not evidence, that "we will not believe" is not a permanent refuge, and that the torrent, when it comes, leaves only debris of those who thought themselves permanent.

**The Pattern Continues**

Having recounted two generations and two judgments, the sūrah will now generalize: other generations followed (v. 42), each had its fixed term (v. 43), messengers came in succession and were denied in succession (v. 44). The pattern that two stories established, the next three verses will state as a law.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:42

> **Then after them We brought into being other generations.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Pattern Becomes Plural**

After the destruction of the second generation, the sūrah moves forward once more: *thumma anshaʾnā min baʿdihim qurūnan ākharīn* — "Then We produced after them other generations." The verse is almost identical to verse 31, which introduced the second generation, with one decisive difference: there the noun was singular — *qarnan ākharīn*, "another generation" — and here it is plural — *qurūnan ākharīn*, "other generations." The sūrah has moved from one story (Noah), to a second (the unnamed generation), and now to *many*. The shift from singular to plural is the shift from narrative to law. The reader has seen the pattern twice; now he is told that it repeated itself across many peoples, too numerous to narrate individually.

**The Verb a Fourth Time**

The verb *anshaʾnā* — "We produced, brought forth, raised up" — appears now for the fourth time in the sūrah (vv. 14, 19, 31, 42). It was used for the ensouling of the embryo, the growth of gardens, the rise of the second generation, and now the rise of many generations. Each use reinforces the same theology: what comes into being — a soul, a garden, a people, a civilization — comes into being by God's act. The generations of history are not accidents of demography; they are *produced*, as a gardener produces a crop. And what God produces, He may also remove, as the previous verse showed. The rhythm of *anshaʾnā* (v. 42) following *jaʿalnāhum ghuthāʾan* (v. 41) — "We raised up" following "We made them debris" — is the rhythm of history as the Qur'an sees it: God raises, tests, and, when a people fails finally, removes and raises again.

**"After Them": The Ground Beneath Every Generation**

The phrase *min baʿdihim* — "after them" — repeats from verse 31, and its repetition drives home a truth every generation forgets: it stands on ground vacated by a predecessor. The generations of verse 42 arose after the second generation was made debris; the second generation arose after Noah's people were drowned. Every people inherits the earth from a people that lost it. The Qur'an makes this point to the Quraysh, who lived among the ruins of ʿĀd and Thamūd and passed them on their trade routes: *"And indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night; will you not then use reason?"* (37:137–138). The ruins were the *ghuthāʾ* of earlier generations; the Quraysh walked over it daily without reading it.

The word *baʿd* also implies a *sequence*, and sequence implies a *direction*. History in the Qur'an is not cyclical in the sense of repeating without purpose; it moves toward an end — the Day of Standing (v. 16) — and each generation is a stage on that road. The "other generations" of verse 42 are not merely more of the same; they are further steps toward the Hour, each one given its chance, each one adding to the record that will be opened at the end.

**"Other Generations": The Unnamed Multitude**

The generations are *ākharīn* — "other," unspecified. Who were they? The commentators mention the candidates that the Qur'an names elsewhere: ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the people of Madyan, the companions of al-Rass, the people of Tubbaʿ, and others. The Qur'an lists several of these together in Sūrah Qāf: *"The people of Noah denied before them, and the companions of al-Rass and Thamūd, and ʿĀd and Pharaoh and the brothers of Lot, and the companions of the thicket and the people of Tubbaʿ. All denied the messengers, so My threat was justly fulfilled"* (50:12–14). And it states that there were many more of whom no record was given: *"And messengers We have mentioned to you before, and messengers We have not mentioned to you"* (4:164). Verse 42's *qurūnan ākharīn* gathers all of these — the named and the unnamed — into a single phrase.

The anonymity is again purposeful. As in verses 31–32, the sūrah is more interested in the *type* than in the *instance*. By not naming the generations, the verse allows every generation — including the reader's own — to see itself in the plural. The question the verse poses is not "which generations were these?" but "is mine among them?"

**The Compression as Argument**

There is a rhetorical logic in the sūrah's progressive compression. Noah's story: seven verses. The second generation: eleven verses. Many generations: one verse. The decreasing length does not mean decreasing importance; it means the pattern has been established and no longer needs elaboration. Once a reader has seen the same message (vv. 23, 32), the same objections (vv. 24–25, 33–38), the same prayer (vv. 26, 39), and the same kind of end (vv. 27, 41), he does not need to be shown the pattern a third and fourth and fifth time. He needs only to be told that it *was* repeated. Verse 42 tells him, and verses 43–44 will state the law that governed each repetition.

This is a lesson in how the Qur'an teaches. It does not overwhelm with data; it establishes a pattern with a few clear cases and then invites the mind to generalize. The believer who has understood Noah and the second generation has understood the fate of every denying people, because the structure is invariant. The Qur'an says so explicitly: *"[This is] the established way (sunnah) of God with those who passed on before, and you will not find in the way of God any change"* (33:62).

**The Persistence of Divine Purpose**

Verse 42, like verse 31, teaches that God's purpose is not defeated by human failure. Two generations were destroyed; God raised up others. The destruction of a people does not mean the abandonment of humanity. The Qur'an expresses this persistence in a striking image: *"And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people; then they will not be the likes of you"* (47:38). The earth is never left without a people, and no people is left without a messenger (35:24: *"And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them"*). Verse 42's "other generations" are the proof of this constancy: God kept raising peoples, and, as verse 44 will say, kept sending messengers to them.

**A Reflection for the Present**

Every generation believes itself to be the culmination of history — the generation that finally understands, that has outgrown the errors of its predecessors, that will not be swept away. The generations of verse 42 believed this too. Each was "other" than the one before, and each thought its otherness was progress. The Qur'an's judgment is that the otherness was superficial: they said what the former peoples said (v. 81), and they met what the former peoples met. The believer reads verse 42 as a corrective to the illusion of generational uniqueness. His generation is one *qarn* among many; it will be judged by the same standard; and the only way to be truly "other" than the destroyed generations is to answer the messenger differently.

**Toward the Law of Terms**

The verse has said that other generations arose. The next verse will state the law that governed each of them: no community can hasten its appointed term or delay it. The plural generations of verse 42 are about to be placed under a single, inflexible rule.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:43

> **No community can hasten its term, nor delay it.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Law Beneath the Stories**

After naming the succession of generations (v. 42), the sūrah states the law that governed every one of them: *mā tasbiqu min ummatin ajalahā wa mā yastaʾkhirūn* — "No community precedes its term, nor do they delay it." The verse is a principle, not a narrative. It steps back from the particular peoples and their particular ends and declares what was true of all of them: each had an appointed term, and none could move it in either direction. The verse explains, in retrospect, why Noah's people were not drowned in the first century of his preaching nor spared in the tenth; why the second generation was seized "after a little while" (v. 40) and not sooner or later. Every judgment fell at its *ajal* — its fixed moment — neither early nor late.

**The Word Ajal**

The word *ajal* means an appointed time, a fixed term, a deadline — the end-point set for something in advance. As the source notes, it most often refers to the term of a person's life, the moment of death: *"And for every person We have fixed a term"* (cf. 6:2: *"He decreed a term, and a specified term is with Him"*). But the Qur'an also applies it to communities: *"And for every nation is a term; when their term comes, they will not remain behind an hour, nor will they precede it"* (7:34; also 10:49; 16:61). Al-Rāzī, as the source records, notes that the *ajal* here may refer to the period a people is allotted on earth — the span of its civilization — as well as to the moment of its destruction. Both are appointed, and both are unmovable.

The concept of *ajal* is one of the Qur'an's central teachings about time. Time is not an open field in which anything may happen at any moment; it is a structured sequence in which events have their assigned places. The rain falls *bi-qadar*, "in measure" (v. 18); the drop stays in the womb *"for a known term"* (77:22); the nations rise and fall at their *ajal*. Nothing is early, nothing is late, from the standpoint of the One who fixed the terms.

**"No Community Precedes Its Term"**

The first clause, *mā tasbiqu min ummatin ajalahā*, uses the verb *sabaqa*, "to precede, to outrun, to get ahead of." The negation with *min* before *ummatin* is comprehensive: not a single community, of any kind, gets ahead of its term. The image is of a race in which no runner can cross the finish line before the appointed moment; however fast a people rushes toward its end — however deep its corruption, however loud its demand for the punishment (as Noah's people demanded: *"bring us what you promise us,"* 11:32) — the end does not come until its hour.

This clause has a specific relevance to the Prophet's situation and to the psychology of the deniers. The Quraysh mocked the delay of the punishment they were warned of: *"And they say: When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"* (10:48; 21:38; 27:71; 34:29; 36:48). They took the delay as evidence that the warning was empty. Verse 43 answers: the delay is not the absence of a term but the not-yet-arrival of it. A people cannot bring its judgment forward by taunting; the term is fixed.

**"Nor Do They Delay It"**

The second clause, *wa mā yastaʾkhirūn*, uses the verb *istaʾkhara*, "to seek delay, to fall behind, to be late." When the term comes, no power can postpone it: not wealth, not fortifications, not numbers, not repentance offered at the last moment when the punishment is already visible (as Pharaoh's was, 10:90–91). The second generation of this sūrah could not delay the Cry by a single breath.

Note the grammatical shift within the verse: the first clause has a singular feminine verb (*tasbiqu*) agreeing with *ummah*, "community"; the second has a plural masculine verb (*yastaʾkhirūn*), agreeing with the *people* who make up the community. The commentators observed that this shift moves from the community as an abstract entity to its members as individuals: the community as a whole cannot hasten its term, and its people, individually, cannot delay it. No one escapes by being part of a group, and no one escapes by being an individual within it.

**The Two Directions and Their Meaning**

Why does the verse deny *both* hastening and delaying? Because each direction corresponds to a different human error. The denial of hastening answers the *scoffer* who says "if the punishment were real, it would have come by now." The denial of delaying answers the *procrastinator* who says "there is still time; I will repent later." Both assume that time is elastic — that the term can be stretched or compressed by human attitude. The verse denies both. The scoffer will find that the term arrives exactly when appointed, regardless of his scoffing; the procrastinator will find that it cannot be pushed back, regardless of his intentions. The Qur'an addresses both directly: to the scoffer, *"They urge you to hasten the punishment; and God will never fail in His promise"* (22:47); to the procrastinator, *"And God will never delay a soul when its time has come"* (63:11).

**The Theology of the Fixed Term**

The doctrine of *ajal* is often misunderstood as fatalism, and the misunderstanding must be corrected. The verse does not say that a community's *conduct* is fixed; it says that its *term* is fixed. What a people does with its allotted time is its own choice, and that choice determines what the term brings — mercy or judgment. Noah's people had nine hundred and fifty years; they could have believed at any point, and the term would then have been a term of blessing, not drowning. The fixity of the term is not the fixity of the outcome; it is the fixity of the *deadline*. And a deadline, far from removing responsibility, intensifies it. The student who knows the exam is at a fixed hour studies harder, not less.

There is also comfort in the doctrine. The believer who knows that terms are fixed by God does not live in terror of enemies who cannot advance his end by a moment, nor in false confidence that he can postpone it. The Qur'an says: *"Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you were in lofty towers"* (4:78) — and also: *"And it is not for a soul to die except by the permission of God at a decree determined"* (3:145). Both verses are verse 43 applied to the individual. The result is a peculiar freedom: since the term cannot be moved, the believer is free to act rightly without calculating whether right action will shorten or lengthen his life. The Companions marched into battles with this freedom; Khālid ibn al-Walīd, who had sought death in a hundred fields and died in his bed, is reported to have said: *"There is no part of my body without the mark of a sword or spear, and here I die on my bed like a camel — may the eyes of cowards never sleep!"*

**Why the Verse Sits Here**

The verse's placement between the plural generations (v. 42) and the succession of messengers (v. 44) is exact. Verse 42 said many generations arose; verse 43 says each had a fixed term; verse 44 will say that messengers came to each and were denied, and each followed the others into destruction. The three verses together form a compact philosophy of history: peoples arise (42), each has a deadline (43), each receives a messenger before the deadline and is judged by its response (44). Verse 43 is the hinge — the law of time that makes the sequence just. Because each people had a fixed term, each had a fixed opportunity; because the term could not be hastened, each had the full opportunity; because it could not be delayed, none could evade the account.

**The Verse in the Believer's Life**

For the individual believer, verse 43 is the community-scale version of a truth he must apply to himself. His *ajal* is fixed. He cannot hasten it by recklessness or delay it by caution beyond what God has decreed. What he *can* do is fill the time before it with the seven qualities of the sūrah's opening. The Prophet ﷺ taught the community to see the fixed term as a reason for urgency, not passivity: *"Take advantage of five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your wealth before your poverty, your free time before your busyness, and your life before your death"* (al-Ḥākim; al-Bayhaqī; graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Ḥākim). Each of these is a term that will arrive at its appointed moment and cannot be delayed. The believer who understands verse 43 does not wait.

**Toward the Succession**

Verse 43 has stated the law of terms. The next verse will show the law in operation across the whole span of prophetic history: messengers sent one after another, each denied, each people following the last into the record of stories told as warnings.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:44

> **Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Whenever there came unto a community its messenger, they would deny him. So We caused them to follow one another, and made them the objects of stories. So away with a people who believe not!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Whole of Prophetic History in One Verse**

Verse 44 is the summary toward which the sūrah's historical section has been building. Noah's story (vv. 23–30) was told in detail; the second generation's (vv. 31–41) in less; the many generations (v. 42) in one line; and now the entire pattern is stated as a law of history: *thumma arsalnā rusulanā tatrā, kullamā jāʾa ummatan rasūluhā kadhdhabūhu, fa-atbaʿnā baʿḍahum baʿḍan wa jaʿalnāhum aḥādīth, fa-buʿdan li-qawmin lā yuʾminūn* — "Then We sent Our messengers in succession. Every time there came to a community its messenger, they denied him. So We made them follow one another, and We made them tales; so away with a people who do not believe!" The verse contains four movements: the sending, the denying, the destroying, and the dismissing. Together they compress thousands of years into a single sentence.

**"We Sent Our Messengers in Succession": Tatrā**

The first movement is *arsalnā rusulanā tatrā* — "We sent Our messengers *tatrā*." The word *tatrā* is rare and precise. It comes from the root *w-t-r*, which gives *witr* (odd, single) and *tawātur* (the successive transmission of a report by so many chains that its authenticity is certain). *Tatrā* means "one after another," "in a continuous series," "successively, with intervals between." The commentators explain that it describes messengers coming one after another, each following the one before, not simultaneously but in an unbroken chain across time. Al-Ṭabarī glosses it: *"one following another."*

The word conveys two things at once: *continuity* and *interval*. There was never a time without a messenger's teaching available to humanity — *"there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them"* (35:24) — yet the messengers did not come all at once; they were spaced across history, each sent when needed. This is the divine method: persistent, patient, never abandoning humanity, never overwhelming it. The Prophet ﷺ described himself as the last brick in a building whose walls were made of all the messengers before him (al-Bukhārī 3535; Muslim 2286) — a perfect image of *tatrā*: one brick after another, in sequence, until the structure was complete.

The source commentary connects *tatrā* to the sequential arrangement of the prophetic stories in Sūrahs 7 and 11, where Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, and Shuʿayb appear in order with identical messages. The word names the pattern those sūrahs display.

**"Every Time a Messenger Came to a Community, They Denied Him"**

The second movement is *kullamā jāʾa ummatan rasūluhā kadhdhabūhu* — "every time its messenger came to a community, they denied him." The word *kullamā*, "every time, whenever," establishes the regularity. This was not the occasional response; it was the *typical* one. The phrase *ummatan rasūluhā* — "a community, its messenger" — with the possessive emphasizes that each community had its *own* messenger, from among itself (v. 32), speaking its language, known to it. And still: *kadhdhabūhu*, "they denied him."

The regularity is a sobering fact about human nature. The Qur'an does not conceal it: *"Alas for the servants! There did not come to them any messenger except that they used to ridicule him"* (36:30). Why should the response be so uniform? Because, as the sūrah has shown twice, the objections were always the same — he is only a man, he threatens our position, his Hereafter is absurd, our fathers never heard of this — and these objections arise not from the specifics of any message but from the permanent features of the human situation: pride, attachment to the world, fear of change, and the desire not to be accountable. The messengers changed; the human heart they addressed did not. The Qur'an says of the Quraysh what verse 44 says of all: *"Did they suggest it to one another? Rather, they are a transgressing people"* (51:53) — the sameness of the response across unconnected peoples is explained not by conspiracy but by a shared condition.

The verse is careful, however, not to say that *everyone* denied. It says *"they"* — the community as a body, led by its notables — denied. Within every community there were believers: Noah's few, the second generation's unmentioned followers, and the "group of My servants" whom the sūrah will recall at its end (23:109). The pattern of denial was the pattern of the majority and the powerful; it was never total.

**"So We Made Them Follow One Another"**

The third movement is *fa-atbaʿnā baʿḍahum baʿḍan* — "so We caused some of them to follow others." The verb *atbaʿa* means to make one thing follow another; the phrase means that God caused the denying communities to follow one another *into destruction*. As Noah's people were drowned, the next generation was seized by the Cry, and the next met its own end, each people "followed" the one before into the same fate. The word *atbaʿnā* echoes the *tatrā* of the messengers: the messengers came in succession, and the deniers *fell* in succession. The two sequences run in parallel — a chain of warnings and a chain of ruins — and the sūrah presents them as cause and effect.

Al-Rāzī, as the source notes, reads *"We caused them to follow one another"* as referring to their destruction in sequence. The verse thus states, as a general law, what verse 43 implied: each community reached its term and was removed, and the next inherited its place, and the process continued.

**"And We Made Them Tales": Aḥādīth**

The fourth movement within the third is *wa jaʿalnāhum aḥādīth* — "and We made them *aḥādīth*." The word *aḥādīth* is the plural of *ḥadīth* — a report, a story, a thing spoken of — or, as the source notes from al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī, of *uḥdūthah*, a tale told with wonder or as a lesson. God made the destroyed peoples into *stories*: they ceased to be living communities and became things that later generations talked about. The Qur'an uses the same expression for the people of Sheba: *"So We made them tales (aḥādīth) and dispersed them in total dispersion"* (34:19).

The phrase carries a specific kind of humiliation. The notables of these communities had been the *subjects* of history — the men who decided things, whose names were feared. God made them the *objects* of history — the cautionary examples that travelers pointed to, that poets lamented, that mothers frightened children with. Al-Qurṭubī observes that this is not a positive sense of being remembered: they became bywords for ruin, as one says "the fate of ʿĀd" to mean total destruction. The Qur'an itself is the great repository of these *aḥādīth*: every story of a destroyed nation in the Book is a fulfillment of verse 44. The peoples who denied the messengers are now, precisely, *stories* — told in a Book they never expected, to a community they never imagined, as warnings they never heeded.

There is a further irony. The notables had accused the messengers of bringing *"fables of the ancients"* (*asāṭīr al-awwalīn*, 23:83). God made the notables themselves into the *aḥādīth* of the ancients — real stories with real lessons, unlike the fables they had invoked to dismiss revelation. The people who called the truth a tale became the tale.

**"So Away with a People Who Do Not Believe"**

The verse closes with the formula of dismissal: *fa-buʿdan li-qawmin lā yuʾminūn* — "so away with a people who do not believe!" The same *buʿdan* that dismissed the second generation in verse 41 now dismisses every denying people at once. But there is a shift in the description. In verse 41 they were *al-qawm al-ẓālimīn*, "the wrongdoing people"; here they are *qawmin lā yuʾminūn*, "a people who do not believe." The two descriptions name the same people from two angles: their wrongdoing (the placing of things where they do not belong) and its root (the refusal of faith). The root is named last, as the sūrah's final diagnosis: what destroyed every one of these peoples was, at bottom, *lā yuʾminūn* — they did not believe. And the sūrah is named for the opposite: *al-Muʾminūn*, those who did.

**The Verse as a Philosophy of History**

Verse 44 offers a complete account of how history works, and it is worth stating plainly because it differs sharply from the accounts most modern readers have absorbed. History, in this verse, is not driven primarily by economics, technology, or the clash of powers; it is driven by the response of peoples to the messengers sent to them. Nations rise by God's production (v. 42), receive a warning (v. 44), are judged by their response, and either continue or become tales. The fixed term (v. 43) ensures that each has a full opportunity; the succession (*tatrā*) ensures that none is left without a warner; the destruction (*atbaʿnā*) ensures that denial has consequences; and the tales (*aḥādīth*) ensure that later peoples can learn from earlier ones. It is a moral philosophy of history, in which the decisive variable is faith.

**The Verse for the Reader's Own Time**

The reader of verse 44 stands, like every reader before him, in the sequence it describes. The messengers came *tatrā*, and the last of them was Muḥammad ﷺ; there is no further messenger to await. The reader has the *aḥādīth* — the stories of every destroyed people — collected in the Qur'an for his benefit. The only question the verse leaves open is the one it has always left open: will this community, this generation, this person, be among *qawmin lā yuʾminūn*, or among *al-muʾminūn* who have prospered? The verse does not decide; it lays out the record and the law, and leaves the choice where it has always been.

**The Section Closes; Two Prophets Remain**

With verse 44 the sūrah has completed its general account of prophetic history. But it will now add two specific cases that stand apart from the pattern of destroyed nations: Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh (vv. 45–49), and Jesus and Mary (v. 50). These two accounts introduce something new — a scripture given (v. 49) and a sign made of a mother and child (v. 50) — and they lead to the sūrah's declaration that all the messengers were one community (vv. 51–52).

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:45

> **Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and a manifest authority**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Anonymous Generations to Named Prophets**

The sūrah has compressed the history of many peoples into a single law (vv. 42–44). Now it returns to specifics, and to the most frequently told story in the Qur'an: *thumma arsalnā Mūsā wa akhāhu Hārūna bi-āyātinā wa sulṭānin mubīn* — "Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and a clear authority." The word *thumma*, "then," places this sending in the sequence of *tatrā* (v. 44) — Moses is one of the messengers sent "in succession" — but the naming of him, after the anonymity of verses 31–44, signals that his case will illustrate something the pattern alone did not show. Two features distinguish it: the opponent is not a diffuse "notables" but a single tyrant, Pharaoh; and the outcome includes not only a destruction (v. 48) but the giving of a Book (v. 49).

**"Moses and His Brother Aaron"**

The verse names two messengers, not one. Moses is mentioned in the Qur'an more than any other prophet — some one hundred and thirty-six times — and his story is told in more sūrahs than any other; but the Qur'an is careful, here and elsewhere, to name Aaron beside him. Aaron's inclusion was Moses's own request: *"And appoint for me a minister from my family — Aaron, my brother. Increase through him my strength and let him share my task"* (20:29–32). God granted it: *"We will strengthen your arm through your brother"* (28:35). The phrase *akhāhu Hārūn* — "his brother Aaron" — with the word "brother" emphasized, points to the human bond at the center of this mission. Moses did not want to face Pharaoh alone, and God did not send him alone.

The two-messenger structure has a lesson the commentators drew out. Aaron was, according to the Qur'an, more eloquent than Moses (28:34), and Moses asked for him specifically to *"confirm me, for I fear they will deny me"* (28:34). The mission to Pharaoh thus modeled a principle of cooperative effort: the prophet who is strong in resolve is paired with the prophet who is strong in speech, and together they present what neither could alone. The Qur'an says the two were addressed together and commanded together: *"Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in My remembrance"* (20:42). The believer who calls to God is not required to have every gift himself; he is permitted — encouraged — to seek a brother whose gifts complete his own.

**"With Our Signs": The Āyāt of Moses**

The two were sent *bi-āyātinā* — "with Our signs." As the source notes from al-Rāzī, these are the miracles given to Moses: the staff that became a serpent (7:107; 20:20), the hand that came forth white without harm (7:108; 20:22), and the nine signs sent against Egypt — the years of drought, the shortfall of crops, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood (7:130–133), together with the parting of the sea. The Qur'an speaks of *"nine clear signs"* given to Moses (17:101). The word *āyāt* is the same word used for the natural signs of verses 17–22 and for the verses of the Qur'an itself. Moses's miracles were *signs* in the exact sense: visible events that pointed to an invisible truth — that the God who sent Moses was the God who controlled nature, and that Pharaoh, who claimed lordship, controlled nothing.

The signs were also *evidence*. The Qur'an presents Moses's miracles not as spectacles but as proofs presented to a court: Moses says to Pharaoh, *"I have come to you with a clear evidence (bayyinah) from your Lord"* (7:105), and Pharaoh's response is to summon his magicians for a public contest of evidence (7:111–126). The signs were meant to persuade, and they did persuade the magicians, who prostrated on the spot (7:120). What they did not do was persuade Pharaoh — and that failure, the next verse will show, was not a failure of the evidence.

**"And a Manifest Authority": Sulṭān Mubīn**

The verse adds a second thing to the signs: *sulṭānin mubīn* — "a clear authority." The word *sulṭān* comes from the root *s-l-ṭ*, which conveys power, dominion, and mastery; a *sulṭān* is authority, and later, the one who holds it. In the Qur'an, *sulṭān* often means a *proof* or *warrant* — the authority that a demonstration confers on a claim: *"Bring your proof (sulṭānakum)"* (21:24); *"They follow nothing but assumption... no authority (sulṭān) has God sent down for it"* (53:23). *Mubīn* means clear, manifest, self-evident. The phrase *sulṭān mubīn*, as the source notes, refers to the clarity and persuasive force of Moses's signs — the authority they carried with them, such that any fair observer would recognize them as coming from God.

Why does the verse mention both *āyāt* and *sulṭān*? Al-Rāzī and others explain that the signs are the miracles themselves and the *sulṭān* is their evidentiary power — the fact that they were not merely strange events but *compelling* ones, leaving no rational room for denial. The distinction matters because it locates Pharaoh's rejection precisely: he did not lack signs, and the signs did not lack authority. He rejected what he *knew* to be true. The Qur'an says so explicitly: *"And they rejected them, while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance"* (27:14). The *sulṭān mubīn* was so clear that it convinced even those who rejected it; the rejection was of the will, not of the mind.

The phrase appears elsewhere in the same connection: *"And We had certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority to Pharaoh and his establishment"* (11:96; 40:23). And 4:153 speaks of *"a clear authority"* given to Moses. The consistency of the phrase across sūrahs shows that the Qur'an regards Moses's case as the paradigm of evidence delivered in its clearest form and refused anyway.

**Why Moses After the General Law**

The placement of Moses after verses 42–44 is instructive. The general law said: messengers came in succession, each community denied its messenger, each was destroyed. Moses's story confirms the law — Pharaoh denied and was destroyed (v. 48) — but it adds two elements the law did not state. First, the *quality* of the evidence: Moses's case shows that denial persists even in the face of the most manifest authority, so that no denier can claim insufficient proof. Second, the *aftermath*: after Pharaoh's destruction, God gave Moses the Book (v. 49), so that the story does not end in ruin but in revelation. The sūrah is preparing the transition from the history of destroyed nations to the theme of scripture and community (vv. 49–53).

There is also a connection to the Prophet's own situation. The Quraysh demanded signs — *"Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"* (6:37) — as though a sufficiently spectacular miracle would compel their faith. Moses's story answers: signs of the most compelling kind were given to Pharaoh, with manifest authority, and he still refused. The problem was never the sign; it was the heart that received it. The Prophet ﷺ was given the Qur'an, which the sūrah will call *"the truth"* (v. 70) and *"their reminder"* (v. 71), and the Quraysh's rejection of it was Pharaoh's rejection of the staff — not a failure of evidence but a refusal of it.

**The Believer's Reflection**

Verse 45 teaches the believer several things about evidence and faith. It teaches that God does not send messengers empty-handed; He gives them *āyāt* and *sulṭān* — signs and the authority that signs carry. It teaches that the believer's own faith rests on evidence of this kind: the Qur'an is the *sulṭān mubīn* of this community, a clear authority that any fair reader can examine. And it teaches, by the contrast the next verses will draw, that evidence is necessary but not sufficient: the same signs produced prostration in the magicians and defiance in Pharaoh. What made the difference was not the evidence but the humility or arrogance of the one who saw it. The sūrah's opening quality — *khushūʿ*, humility (v. 2) — is thus the precondition for evidence to work at all.

**Toward Pharaoh**

The verse names the messengers and their equipment. The next verse names their audience — Pharaoh and his notables — and their response: arrogance.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:46

> **to Pharaoh and his notables. But they waxed arrogant and were a haughty people.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Audience and Its Response**

Verse 45 named the messengers and what they carried; verse 46 names to whom they were sent and how they were received: *ilā Firʿawna wa malaʾihi fa-stakbarū wa kānū qawman ʿālīn* — "to Pharaoh and his chiefs; but they were arrogant and were a haughty people." The verse is brief, but it introduces the sūrah's most concentrated portrait of the disease that underlies all the rejections it has recounted. Noah's notables were contemptuous; the second generation's were mocking and materialist; Pharaoh and his chiefs were *arrogant* — and the verse uses two words for it, as if one were not enough.

**"Pharaoh and His Notables"**

The word *Firʿawn*, Pharaoh, is a title, not a personal name — the Qur'an uses it for the ruler of Egypt in Moses's time without naming him. The Qur'an's Pharaoh is the archetype of the tyrant: he claimed divinity — *"I am your lord, most high"* (79:24); *"I have not known for you any god other than me"* (28:38) — enslaved a people, murdered their sons, and, when confronted with the clearest signs, called them sorcery. He appears in the Qur'an more than seventy times, always as the figure who took his power for godhead.

Beside him stands *malaʾihi* — "his notables," "his court." The word *malaʾ* is the same word used for the chiefs of Noah's people (v. 24) and of the second generation (v. 33). Its recurrence for the third time in the sūrah's historical section establishes that the opposition to the messengers was always an *elite* phenomenon. Pharaoh did not act alone; he was surrounded by a court that flattered him, advised him (*"Leave him and his people to a while,"* 7:127; *"Shall we believe in two human beings like us?"* 23:47), and shared his fate. The Qur'an holds the *malaʾ* responsible alongside their ruler, because power is never exercised by one man; it is exercised by a class.

**"They Were Arrogant": Istakbarū**

The first word for the response is *istakbarū* — "they were arrogant," "they sought greatness." The verb is Form X of the root *k-b-r*, "to be great," and Form X often conveys *seeking* or *claiming* a quality: *istakbara* is to consider oneself great, to claim a greatness one does not possess, to refuse to submit because submission seems beneath one. It is the word the Qur'an uses for Iblīs's refusal to prostrate to Adam: *"He refused and was arrogant (istakbara), and was among the disbelievers"* (2:34). Arrogance, in the Qur'an's diagnosis, is the *original* sin — older than humanity, the sin of the first creature to disobey — and every subsequent arrogance repeats it.

The Prophet ﷺ defined arrogance with precision:

> *"Arrogance (al-kibr) is rejecting the truth and looking down on people."* (Muslim 91)

The definition has two parts, and Pharaoh and his court exhibited both. They rejected the truth: the signs and the clear authority of verse 45. And they looked down on people: their own subjects, and above all the Israelites, whom the next verse will show them describing as *"slaves we possess."* The Prophet ﷺ also warned: *"No one who has an atom's weight of arrogance in his heart will enter Paradise"* (Muslim 91). The same ḥadīth records a Companion asking whether a man who likes his clothes and shoes to be fine is arrogant, and the Prophet ﷺ replying: *"God is beautiful and loves beauty."* Arrogance is not the enjoyment of good things; it is the refusal of truth and the contempt for persons — exactly what verse 46 names.

**"And Were a Haughty People": Qawman ʿālīn**

The second word is *ʿālīn* — "haughty," "high," "exalting themselves." The root *ʿ-l-w* means height and elevation; God is *al-ʿAlī*, the Most High, and this is precisely why human *ʿuluww* — self-elevation — is so grave a sin: it is the creature claiming an attribute that belongs to the Creator alone. The Qur'an uses this root for Pharaoh's specific crime: *"Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself (ʿalā) in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a sector among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive"* (28:4). And it states the general principle: *"That home of the Hereafter We assign to those who do not desire exaltation (ʿuluwwan) upon the earth or corruption"* (28:83).

Why two words? The commentators observe that *istakbarū* describes the *inner* attitude — the self-estimation of greatness — while *ʿālīn* describes its *outer* expression — the actual domination and oppression of others. Pharaoh and his court were arrogant in heart and haughty in conduct; they thought themselves great and they acted as though they were above every law. The phrase *kānū qawman ʿālīn* — "they *were* a haughty people" — with the verb *kāna* indicates a settled character, not a momentary reaction. Haughtiness was what they *were*, before Moses ever arrived; his coming merely exposed it.

**The Logic of Arrogance Against Evidence**

Verse 46 explains why the *sulṭān mubīn* of verse 45 failed to persuade. Arrogance is not a failure of understanding; it is a refusal of the *posture* that understanding requires. To accept a truth from a messenger, one must acknowledge that one did not know it, that another has been given what one lacks, and that one must now change. Each of these acknowledgments is an act of humility. The arrogant person cannot make them, not because he cannot follow the argument but because following it would place him beneath the one who brought it. Pharaoh could see that the staff became a serpent; what he could not do was kneel. The Qur'an describes his inner state exactly: *"They rejected them, while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance (ʿuluwwan)"* (27:14) — the same root as *ʿālīn*.

This is the deepest reason the sūrah's portrait of the believer *began* with *khushūʿ*, humility in prayer (v. 2). Humility is the faculty by which truth is received. The person who bows five times a day before God has practiced, in the body, the posture that the mind must adopt before evidence. Pharaoh, who bowed to no one and demanded that all bow to him, had no such faculty. The signs bounced off him because there was nothing in him to receive them.

**The Contrast with the Magicians**

The Qur'an sets beside Pharaoh a group who saw the same signs and responded oppositely: his own magicians. Summoned to defeat Moses, they threw their ropes and staffs; Moses threw his staff, and it swallowed their illusions; and *"the magicians fell down in prostration; they said: We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron"* (7:120–122). The magicians were experts in the very craft Pharaoh accused Moses of practicing; they knew, better than anyone, that what Moses did was not magic. And they were not arrogant — they were servants, hired men, with no throne to protect. When the evidence came, they had nothing in them to resist it, and they prostrated. Pharaoh threatened them with crucifixion; they replied: *"We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us"* (20:72). The same signs, the same day, the same court: the humble prostrated and the arrogant crucified. Verse 46 names the variable.

**Arrogance as the Sūrah's Recurring Diagnosis**

Though the word *istakbarū* appears for the first time here, arrogance has been present under other names throughout the sūrah's historical section. Noah's notables would not follow a man *"like yourselves"* (v. 24) — arrogance of class. The second generation warned against *"obeying a human being like yourselves"* (v. 34) — arrogance of rank. Pharaoh's court will refuse to believe in *"two human beings like us, while their people are slaves we possess"* (v. 47) — arrogance of power. The sūrah will apply the word to the Quraysh: *"waxing arrogant (mustakbirīn) on account thereof, talking foolishly by night"* (v. 67). In every case the obstacle to faith was not the message but the elevation of the self above the messenger. Verse 46 names the disease that all the sūrah's deniers share.

**The Believer's Examination**

Verse 46 is a mirror as well as a history. The believer is asked whether there is any *istikbār* in him — any refusal of truth because of who brought it, any looking down on people because of what they lack. The Prophet's definition makes the examination precise: Have I rejected a correction because it came from someone younger, poorer, or less educated? Have I treated anyone as beneath my notice? Have I found it hard to say "I was wrong"? Each is an atom of Pharaoh's disease, and the ḥadīth says an atom is enough to bar the Garden. The remedy is the sūrah's first quality: the daily prostration in which the forehead — the highest part of the body — is placed on the ground, and the tongue says *subḥāna rabbiya al-aʿlā*, "Glory to my Lord, the Most High." The one who says that sincerely cannot be *ʿālī* himself; he has assigned the height to its Owner.

**Toward Pharaoh's Words**

The verse has described Pharaoh's court as arrogant and haughty. The next verse will quote them, and their words will show exactly what arrogance sounds like when it speaks.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:47

> **They said, “Shall we believe in two human beings like us, while their people are slaves we possess?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Arrogance Speaks**

Verse 46 described Pharaoh and his court as arrogant and haughty. Verse 47 lets them speak, and their single sentence is the purest expression of arrogance in the sūrah: *fa-qālū a-nuʾminu li-basharayni mithlinā wa qawmuhumā lanā ʿābidūn* — "So they said: 'Shall we believe in two human beings like us, while their people are slaves to us?'" The sentence has two halves, and each is a distinct form of contempt: contempt for the messengers as mere men, and contempt for their people as mere property. Together they explain why Pharaoh could not receive the *sulṭān mubīn* of verse 45: he could not accept truth from beneath him, and everything about Moses and Aaron was, in his estimation, beneath him.

**"Shall We Believe in Two Human Beings Like Us?"**

The first half repeats, for the fifth time in the sūrah, the objection that a messenger is only human: *basharayni mithlinā* — "two humans like us." The objection was made against Noah (v. 24), against the second messenger (vv. 33, 34), and now against Moses and Aaron. But Pharaoh's court gives it a peculiar twist. Noah's notables said "a human like *you*," addressing the people. Pharaoh's court says "like *us*" — and the "us" is Pharaoh and his elite, who did not consider themselves like anyone. To say that Moses and Aaron were "like us" was, for Pharaoh, already a concession too far; the real thought was that they were *beneath* us, and the second half of the verse says so.

The interrogative *a-nuʾminu* — "shall we believe?" — is a question of indignation, not inquiry. It has the tone of "are we expected to...?" The verb *nuʾminu li-* ("believe in," "give credence to") with the preposition *li-* means to accept someone's word, to trust them. Pharaoh's court is asking, rhetorically, whether men of their station could possibly take the word of men of Moses's station. The question answers itself in their minds.

The dual form *basharayni* — "two humans" — is a small but telling detail. The objection is directed at both Moses and Aaron. The two-messenger structure that God established as a strength (v. 45) is treated by Pharaoh as a double insult: not one commoner but two presume to instruct the king.

**"While Their People Are Slaves to Us"**

The second half of the verse is the more revealing: *wa qawmuhumā lanā ʿābidūn* — "and their people are *ʿābidūn* to us." The word *ʿābidūn* is the active participle of *ʿabada*, the same root as *ʿibādah*, worship, and *ʿabd*, servant or slave. The phrase can mean, as the source notes, "their people are our slaves" — describing the literal servitude of the Israelites in Egypt — but it also carries the stronger sense of "their people *serve* us, *worship* us," reflecting Pharaoh's claim to divinity: *"I am your lord, most high"* (79:24). The source rightly observes that the word evokes both the material relationship (the Egyptians owned the Israelites) and the worshipful attitude Pharaoh expected from those beneath him. The two meanings were, in Pharaoh's system, the same: to be enslaved by Pharaoh was to be in a relationship of quasi-worship toward him.

The logic of the objection is now complete: How can we believe two men whose *own people* are our slaves? The messengers' credibility is assessed not by their message or their signs but by the social rank of their nation. Because the Israelites were at the bottom of the Egyptian order, their prophets could not, in Pharaoh's calculus, be bearers of truth. Truth, for the arrogant, flows only downward — from the powerful to the weak — and a message that flows upward is disqualified by its direction.

**The Two Contempts and Their Relationship**

The verse displays two contempts, and they are connected. The contempt for the messengers as "humans like us" is *generic* — it would apply to any human messenger. The contempt for their people as "slaves to us" is *specific* — it applies to these messengers because of who they are. The second sharpens the first: not only are they human, they are humans of the *lowest* kind. This is the layering of prejudice: species, then class, then nation. Pharaoh could not have believed any man; he especially could not believe an Israelite; and he most especially could not believe an Israelite who came to demand the freedom of the Israelites (*"So send with us the Children of Israel,"* 20:47). The message threatened the very hierarchy that made Pharaoh who he was.

**The Word ʿĀbidūn and the Irony It Contains**

There is a deep irony in Pharaoh's use of *ʿābidūn*. He complains that the Israelites are "worshippers/servants to us" — and this is precisely what Moses came to end. Moses's message was that worship (*ʿibādah*) belongs to God alone, and that no human being — not Pharaoh, not anyone — may be *maʿbūd*, an object of service in the ultimate sense. The Qur'an records Moses's charge to Pharaoh: *"And is this a favor of which you remind me — that you have enslaved (ʿabbadta) the Children of Israel?"* (26:22). Pharaoh treated the enslavement as a natural fact that disqualified the slaves' prophets; Moses treated it as the crime that his mission would abolish. The same word, *ʿ-b-d*, names the wrong that Pharaoh boasted of and the right that Moses came to restore. The sūrah's opening command — *"Worship God"* (vv. 23, 32) — is the direct negation of *"their people are worshippers to us."*

**The Source's Observation: Echoes of Noah's Notables**

The source commentary notes that the disdain in this verse echoes the words of the notables of Noah's community (v. 24) and of the second generation (v. 34). The echo is exact in structure: in each case the objection is to following someone "like us" (*mithlukum*, *mithlakum*, *mithlinā*), and in each case the real anxiety is about *rank*. Noah's notables feared that Noah wished to "set himself above you" (v. 24); the second generation's warned against "obeying" a peer (v. 34); Pharaoh's court refuses to believe men whose people are "slaves to us" (v. 47). The vocabulary of "like us" is the vocabulary of a status system under threat. Each elite understood — correctly — that the messenger's message would level the hierarchy that gave them their place, and each rejected the messenger for that reason before considering whether he was true.

**The Verse in Its Historical Truth**

The Qur'an's picture of Egyptian contempt for the enslaved Israelites is confirmed by the Qur'an's own fuller account: Pharaoh's regime *"slaughtered their sons and kept their women alive"* (28:4), imposed forced labor, and regarded the Israelites as a subject population to be managed and, when necessary, culled. From within such a system, the appearance of two Israelites claiming to speak for the Lord of the worlds was not merely implausible; it was an affront to the natural order as Pharaoh understood it. Verse 47 captures the affront in Pharaoh's own words.

**What the Verse Teaches About Prejudice and Truth**

The verse is a permanent lesson about how social prejudice blinds people to truth. Pharaoh's court did not evaluate Moses's signs; they evaluated Moses's pedigree. They asked not "is this true?" but "who is saying it?" — and having answered the second question, they never reached the first. The Qur'an teaches the opposite method: *"Say: Bring your proof, if you should be truthful"* (2:111) — truth is established by evidence, not by the status of its bearer. The Prophet ﷺ, whose earliest followers were slaves, the poor, and the young, was told by the Quraysh: *"Drive away these people, and we will listen to you"* — and God commanded: *"And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face"* (6:52). The Quraysh's demand was Pharaoh's objection in another form: how can we sit with slaves? And God's answer was the same: truth does not consult rank.

For the believer today, verse 47 is a warning against a subtle form of Pharaoh's error. It is possible to dismiss a correction because it comes from someone of lower education, poorer background, younger age, or lower social standing — to ask, in effect, "shall we believe someone like *that*?" The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Wisdom is the lost property of the believer; wherever he finds it, he has the most right to it"* (al-Tirmidhī 2687, with a weak chain but a meaning the scholars accepted). The believer takes truth from whoever carries it. Pharaoh could not, and it destroyed him.

**Toward the Consequence**

Pharaoh's court has spoken their contempt. The next verse states, in five words, what followed: they denied, and they were destroyed.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:48

> **But they denied them, and so were among the destroyed.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Shortest Account of the Greatest Downfall**

Pharaoh's court asked, with contempt, whether they should believe two men whose people were their slaves (v. 47). Verse 48 records what they did and what became of them: *fa-kadhdhabūhumā fa-kānū min al-muhlakīn* — "So they denied them both, and they were among the destroyed." Five words in Arabic. The sūrah does not narrate the plagues, the contest with the magicians, the night flight from Egypt, or the parting of the sea — all of which it tells in detail elsewhere (7:103–137; 10:75–92; 20:9–79; 26:10–68; 28:3–42). Here it gives only the two facts that matter for its argument: they denied; they were destroyed. The compression is the sūrah's method at its most severe. The reader who has followed Noah's people and the second generation knows what follows denial; the sūrah does not need to show it again.

**"They Denied Them Both": The Dual Object**

The verb is *kadhdhabūhumā* — "they called the two of them liars." The dual suffix *-humā* refers to Moses and Aaron, matching the dual *basharayni* of verse 47. Pharaoh's court rejected both messengers, and the verse holds them accountable for both rejections. The root *k-dh-b* is the same root that has marked every rejection in the sūrah: Noah's people *kadhdhabūn* (v. 26), the second generation *kadhdhabū bi-liqāʾ al-ākhirah* (v. 33) and *kadhdhabūn* (v. 39), every community *kadhdhabūhu* (v. 44), and now Pharaoh's court *kadhdhabūhumā*. The word is the sūrah's signature for the act that seals a people's fate. It is not ignorance, not doubt, not delay — it is the declaration that the truth-bearer is a liar, made in the face of *āyāt* and *sulṭān mubīn* (v. 45).

The particle *fa-* that opens the verse ("so, then") links the denial directly to the contempt of verse 47. They said "shall we believe two humans like us?" — *so* they denied. The rhetorical question was not a moment of deliberation; it was already the decision. Arrogance (v. 46) produced contempt (v. 47), and contempt produced denial (v. 48). The three verses form a single causal chain.

**"And They Were Among the Destroyed"**

The second *fa-* links the denial to its consequence: *fa-kānū min al-muhlakīn* — "so they were among the destroyed." The word *muhlakīn* is the passive participle of *ahlaka*, "to destroy," from the root *h-l-k*, perishing and ruin. The phrase *min al-muhlakīn* — "*among* the destroyed" — places Pharaoh and his court in a category that the sūrah has been populating since verse 27: the drowned people of Noah, the debris of the second generation, the "tales" of verse 44. Pharaoh joined a company. His destruction was not unique; it was the latest instance of a law.

The manner of the destruction is not stated here, but the Qur'an tells it elsewhere: Pharaoh and his army pursued the Israelites into the parted sea, and *"We drowned them all"* (17:103; 26:66). There is a precise symmetry between the first and last of the sūrah's historical accounts: Noah's people were drowned, and Pharaoh's army was drowned. The sūrah began its history with water as the instrument of judgment and closes the pattern with water again. The same element that God *"sent down in measure and settled in the earth"* (v. 18) as a mercy became, when released without measure, the instrument of justice — and the sūrah had warned: *"We are able to take it away"* (v. 18). The water that was withheld from Noah's people until the term arrived, and the water that stood aside for Moses and closed over Pharaoh, were the same water under the same command.

**Why the Verse Omits the Drama**

A reader familiar with the Exodus narrative might wonder why the sūrah passes over its most dramatic moments — the plagues, the sea, Pharaoh's last-second declaration of faith (10:90). The answer lies in the sūrah's purpose at this point. It is not telling the story of Moses; it is establishing a law of history, and Moses's case is cited as an instance. The law was stated in verse 44: messengers come, communities deny, communities are destroyed. Verse 48 shows the law operating in the most famous case of all, in the fewest possible words, so that the reader understands that even the greatest king with the largest army was not exempt. The details would distract from the point; the point is that *fa-kadhdhabūhumā fa-kānū min al-muhlakīn* is the whole of Pharaoh's story from the standpoint of eternity.

There is also a rhetorical effect in the brevity. Pharaoh was the most powerful man in the world of his time. His name filled the earth; his monuments still stand. The sūrah gives his end five words. The disproportion between his self-estimation (v. 46: *ʿālīn*, "haughty") and the sūrah's estimation of him (v. 48: *min al-muhlakīn*, "among the destroyed") is itself the lesson. The man who said "I am your lord, most high" is filed, in God's Book, as one more entry in the list of the ruined.

**The Contrast with the Magicians and the Believers**

The verse says Pharaoh's court "were among the destroyed." It does not say that everyone in Egypt was. The Qur'an records that the magicians believed and were martyred (20:70–73); that a believer from Pharaoh's own family concealed his faith and pleaded for Moses (40:28–45); that Pharaoh's wife, Āsiyah, believed and asked God for *"a house near You in Paradise"* (66:11). These were Egyptians, members of Pharaoh's court or household, who received the same signs and responded with faith. They were not among the destroyed. The verse's *min* — "among" — is a careful word: it includes those who denied and excludes those who, within the same court and the same city, believed. The line between the destroyed and the saved was not national or social; it was the line of *kadhdhaba* versus *āmana*, denial versus faith.

**Pharaoh's Last Word and Why It Did Not Save Him**

The Qur'an records that Pharaoh, as the sea closed over him, said: *"I believe that there is no deity except that in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims"* (10:90). And God's reply: *"Now? And you had disobeyed before and were of the corrupters?"* (10:91). This is the sūrah's law of the fixed term (v. 43) applied to an individual: when the *ajal* arrives, it cannot be delayed, and the faith that is offered only when the punishment is visible is not accepted — *"But their faith did not benefit them once they saw Our punishment"* (40:85). Pharaoh's story thus illustrates not only the destruction of the arrogant but the futility of the last-moment reversal, a theme the sūrah will develop at length in its closing verses (23:99–100, 107–108). The one who said *hayhāt* about the Hereafter (v. 36), or "shall we believe?" about the messengers (v. 47), and who then cries "I believe" as the water rises, is answered: *now?*

**The Believer's Reflection**

Verse 48 gives the believer the shortest possible summary of what denial costs: it places one *among the destroyed*. The believer reads it as a warning against the arrogance that produces denial — the refusal to accept truth from a source beneath one's estimation. But he also reads it as a promise: the power that opposes truth, however vast, is not permanent. Pharaoh's court asked "shall we believe two humans like us?" and the answer of history was that the two humans were right and the court was drowned. Every believer who has faced an overwhelming power in the name of a truth that power despised can take from verse 48 what the Prophet ﷺ and his persecuted Companions took from it in Makkah: the end belongs to the truth, and the powerful who deny it are filed, in the end, among the destroyed.

**Toward the Book**

The story of Moses does not end with destruction. Unlike the accounts of Noah's people and the second generation, which closed with judgment, Moses's account continues into something new: the giving of a Book. The next verse marks the transition from the history of punishment to the history of revelation.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:49

> **And indeed We gave unto Moses the Book, that haply they may be guided.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**After Destruction, Revelation**

The previous accounts ended in judgment: the Flood, the Cry, the destruction of Pharaoh. Verse 49 introduces something the sūrah has not yet mentioned in its history: *wa laqad ātaynā Mūsā al-kitāba laʿallahum yahtadūn* — "And We certainly gave Moses the Book, that they might be guided." For the first time in the historical section, the sequence does not stop at the removal of the deniers; it continues to the *gift* that followed. Moses's mission had two outcomes, not one: the destruction of Pharaoh (v. 48) and the giving of the Torah (v. 49). The verse thus turns the reader's attention from what God does to those who reject the messengers to what He does for those who follow them.

**"And Indeed We Gave": The Emphatic Formula Returns**

The verse opens with *wa laqad* — the same emphatic "and indeed, certainly" that introduced the creation of man (v. 12), the seven heavens (v. 17), and the sending of Noah (v. 23). Its return here marks the giving of the Book as an event of the same order of importance as those three: a foundational act of God. The verb *ātaynā* — "We gave, We granted" — is the verb of bestowal; the Book was not earned or discovered but *given*, as the rain was sent down (v. 18) and the gardens were produced (v. 19). Revelation is provision of a higher kind, and the sūrah uses the grammar of gift for it.

**"Moses the Book": The Torah**

The Book given to Moses is the Torah (*al-Tawrāh*), which the Qur'an names elsewhere and describes as containing *"guidance and light"* (5:44). The Qur'an refers to it repeatedly as the scripture of the Children of Israel, and it affirms its divine origin while noting that later generations altered and neglected it (2:75; 5:13). Verse 49 speaks of the Torah at the moment of its giving — pure, complete, and intended for guidance.

The source commentary draws attention to the *timing*, citing al-Rāzī's use of 28:43: *"And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the former generations, as enlightenment for the people and guidance and mercy, that they might be reminded."* The Torah was given *after* the destruction of Pharaoh, not before. This sequence has meaning. During the confrontation with Pharaoh, Moses had signs — the staff, the hand, the plagues — evidence designed to establish his authority and break the tyrant's power. Only after the Israelites were free, and had crossed the sea, and stood at Sinai, was the Book given. The signs were for the *liberation*; the Book was for the *life afterward*. A people cannot be given a law while they are slaves; first they must be freed, then instructed. The order of Moses's mission — signs, then scripture — is the order of God's dealing with any people: He removes the obstacle, then He provides the guidance.

**"That They Might Be Guided": Who Is "They"?**

The purpose clause is *laʿallahum yahtadūn* — "that they might be guided." As the source notes, "they" refers to the Children of Israel, the people to whom Moses brought the Book after the Exodus — not to Pharaoh's people, who had already been destroyed (v. 48). The Torah was given to the *saved* community, to guide them in the freedom they had been granted. The word *yahtadūn* is from the root *h-d-y*, guidance — the same root as *al-hudā*, the guidance the Fātiḥah asks for, and *al-muhtadūn*, the rightly guided. The purpose of the Book was to make the Israelites *muhtadīn* — people who know the way and walk it.

The particle *laʿalla* — "that perhaps, so that" — is the Qur'an's usual way of expressing the *purpose* of a divine act as it bears on human freedom. It does not mean that God was uncertain of the outcome; it means that the Book was given *in order that* guidance might follow, with the human response left open. The Israelites could be guided by the Book, or not; the history recorded in the Qur'an shows that they were sometimes guided and often not. The *laʿalla* preserves their responsibility.

**The Function of the Verse in the Sūrah's Argument**

Why does the sūrah mention the Torah at this point? Several reasons converge.

First, it introduces the theme of scripture, which will govern the next section. Verse 52 will declare that all the messengers formed one community; verse 53 will say that their followers *"tore their affair into pieces"* — divided into sects, each with its own book. The Torah is the first scripture the sūrah names, and its mention prepares the reader for the discussion of how scriptures were received and how their communities fragmented.

Second, it completes the pattern by showing that judgment is not the end of God's dealings with humanity. The Flood was followed by another generation (v. 31); the destruction of Pharaoh was followed by the Torah. God does not merely destroy the deniers; He guides the believers.
