The sūrah's God is not only the Judge of verses 27, 41, and 48 but the Guide of verse 49.

Third, it speaks to the Prophet's situation. The Quraysh were being told that the pattern of history — messenger, denial, destruction — applied to them. Verse 49 shows what awaited on the other side of the pattern: a Book, and a community guided by it. The Prophet ﷺ had been given the Qur'an; the sūrah will call it *"the truth"* (v. 70), *"the reminder"* (v. 71), and *"the Word"* (v. 68). The Torah was to Moses's people what the Qur'an was to Muḥammad's: the guidance given after the confrontation.

**Scripture as Guidance, Not Merely Law**

The verse describes the Torah's purpose as *guidance*, and the word deserves reflection. A book of guidance is not merely a list of rules; it is a map — a description of where one is, where one should go, and how to get there. The Qur'an describes the Torah in exactly these terms: *"Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light; the prophets who submitted judged by it for the Jews, as did the rabbis and scholars"* (5:44). Guidance (*hudā*) and light (*nūr*): the Book shows the way and illuminates it. The believer who receives scripture receives not a burden but a lamp.

This understanding of scripture is the reason the Qur'an is so severe toward those who possess a Book and do not follow it: *"The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes"* (62:5). To have a map and not consult it, to have a lamp and walk in darkness, is worse than having neither. The *laʿallahum yahtadūn* of verse 49 was a hope and a purpose; the history of the Israelites, as the Qur'an tells it, was the record of how often that purpose was frustrated by the people it was meant to serve — and, by implication, a warning to the community of the Qur'an not to repeat the pattern.

**The Believer's Relationship to His Own Book**

Verse 49 invites the believer to consider his relationship to the Book he has been given. The Torah was given *"that they might be guided"*; the Qur'an was given for the same purpose: *"This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for those conscious of God"* (2:2). The question the verse poses is whether the purpose is being fulfilled. Does the believer read the Book as a map — consulting it before decisions, measuring his life against it — or as a possession, honored on a shelf and rarely opened? The Prophet ﷺ described a coming time when *"the Qur'an will remain in name only"* (al-Bayhaqī; a report with weakness in its chain but a meaning the scholars affirmed), and the Qur'an records the Prophet's own complaint on the Day of Judgment: *"O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as a thing abandoned"* (25:30). Verse 49's hopeful *laʿalla* is a standing invitation not to be among those of whom that complaint is made.

**The Transition to Jesus and Mary**

Having named Moses and his Book, the sūrah will name, in the next verse, the last of the great messengers before Muḥammad ﷺ: Jesus, son of Mary — and it will name him together with his mother, as a *sign*. The sequence Noah, the unnamed messenger, Moses, Jesus traces the line of prophecy toward its seal, and prepares for the sūrah's declaration that all of them were one community under one Lord.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:50

> **And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We gave them refuge in a high place of stillness and a flowing spring.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Last of the Named Prophets, and His Mother**

After Moses and the Torah, the sūrah names the final great messenger before Muḥammad ﷺ: *wa jaʿalnā ibna Maryama wa ummahu āyatan wa āwaynāhumā ilā rabwatin dhāti qarārin wa maʿīn* — "And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We sheltered them on a high ground having level places of rest and flowing springs." The verse is unique in the sūrah's historical section. Every previous account concerned a messenger and a people who rejected him; this verse mentions no rejection, no notables, no punishment. It speaks only of a sign, and of refuge. The tone shifts from judgment to tenderness — a mother and child, sheltered on a hill by running water.

**"The Son of Mary": The Chosen Name**

Jesus is named here as *ibn Maryam* — "the son of Mary." The Qur'an calls him this more than twenty times, and the choice is deliberate and doctrinal. In a world where men were named after their fathers, to name Jesus after his mother was to state the central fact of his origin: he had no human father. The Qur'an describes his conception as a direct creative act: *"She said: My Lord, how will I have a child when no man has touched me? He said: Thus; God creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it 'Be,' and it is"* (3:47). The name "son of Mary" thus affirms the miracle. But it also affirms his humanity and denies his divinity: he is the *son* of a woman, born of her, nursed by her — a human being, however miraculously conceived. The Qur'an states the balance exactly: *"The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him. And his mother was a supporter of truth. They both used to eat food"* (5:75). The last phrase — "they both used to eat food" — is the Qur'an's quiet insistence that Jesus and Mary were human, using the very criterion (eating) that the notables of this sūrah used to *disqualify* messengers (v. 33). What the deniers held against prophets, the Qur'an holds as the mark of their humanity.

**"And His Mother": Mary's Rank**

The verse names Mary alongside her son — *wa ummahu*, "and his mother" — and makes them *together* a sign. Mary is the only woman named in the Qur'an, and a whole sūrah bears her name. The Qur'an describes her as chosen and purified above all women: *"O Mary, indeed God has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds"* (3:42). The Prophet ﷺ named her among the four perfected women: *"The best of the women of Paradise are Khadījah bint Khuwaylid, Fāṭimah bint Muḥammad, Maryam bint ʿImrān, and Āsiyah bint Muzāḥim, the wife of Pharaoh"* (Aḥmad; al-Ḥākim; graded ṣaḥīḥ). And al-Bukhārī and Muslim record his words: *"Many men have reached perfection, but none among women reached perfection except Āsiyah, the wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam, the daughter of ʿImrān"* (al-Bukhārī 3411; Muslim 2431). Verse 50's inclusion of Mary in the sign is thus not incidental; she is a figure of the highest rank, and her role in the miracle was not passive. She bore the child, endured the accusation of her people (19:27–28), and was vindicated when the infant spoke from the cradle (19:29–33).

**"A Sign": The Word Āyah in the Singular**

The verse says God made them *āyatan* — "a sign," in the singular, not "two signs." Mother and son together constitute *one* sign, because the miracle was one: a child born of a virgin. Neither alone is the sign; the sign is the *relationship* — a mother without a husband and a son without a father. The Qur'an uses the same expression in Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ: *"And she who guarded her chastity, so We blew into her of Our spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds"* (21:91). The source commentary notes that the sign was "through the miraculous birth of Jesus."

What does the sign signify? Like every *āyah* in the sūrah — the embryo, the rain, the cattle, the histories — it points beyond itself. The virgin birth points to God's creative freedom: He is not bound by the ordinary chain of causes. He created Adam without father or mother, Eve without a mother, Jesus without a father, and everyone else from both (3:59: *"Indeed, the example of Jesus to God is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him 'Be,' and he was"*). The sign of Mary and Jesus is thus an argument in the sūrah's ongoing case for the resurrection: the God who can produce a child without a father can produce a living body without a preceding one. Verse 14 traced the ordinary path from drop to person; verse 50 shows that God is not confined to that path.

**"And We Gave Them Refuge": Āwaynāhumā**

The second half of the verse describes an act of shelter: *āwaynāhumā* — "We gave them refuge, We sheltered them." The verb *āwā*, from the root *a-w-y*, means to take in, to shelter, to provide a haven. It is the verb the Qur'an uses for God's care of the orphaned Prophet ﷺ: *"Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge (fa-āwā)?"* (93:6). Its use here connects Jesus and Mary to a pattern of divine protection of the vulnerable. A mother alone with a child, without the shelter of a husband's house, accused by her people — this is the most vulnerable of human situations, and the verse says that God Himself was their shelter.

**"A High Ground with Rest and Flowing Springs": Rabwah, Qarār, Maʿīn**

The place of refuge is described with three terms. *Rabwah* is elevated ground, a hill — as the source notes, the same word rendered "hill" in 2:265, where the Qur'an compares charity to *"a garden on a hill (rabwah) struck by heavy rain, so it yields its fruit double."* A *rabwah* is fertile high ground, safe from flooding, open to air and light. *Dhāti qarār* — "possessing *qarār*" — means having a place of rest and settlement; *qarār* is the same word used in verse 13 for the womb as a "secure resting place" (*qarār makīn*). The hill was not merely high but *habitable* — a place where one could settle, with level ground and stability. *Maʿīn* is flowing water — a spring or stream, visible on the surface (from *ʿ-y-n*, "eye," or *m-ʿ-n*, "to flow"); the Qur'an uses it for the wine of Paradise, *"a cup from a flowing spring (maʿīn)"* (37:45; 56:18), and for the water that could be lost: *"Say: Have you considered, if your water were to sink into the ground, who could bring you flowing water (māʾin maʿīn)?"* (67:30).

Together the three words describe an ideal refuge: high (safe), settled (stable), and watered (sustaining). The commentators identified the place variously — Jerusalem, Damascus and its Ghūṭah, Ramlah in Palestine, or Egypt — and the source notes al-Rāzī's mention of the period Jesus, Mary, and Joseph spent in exile. Al-Ṭabarī transmits several identifications and, characteristically, does not insist on one. The Qur'an does not name the place, and the omission suggests that the *description* matters more than the location. Wherever it was, it was the kind of place a mother and child needed: elevated, restful, and beside running water.

**The Echo of the Womb**

The word *qarār* links this verse to verse 13, where the drop was placed in *"a secure resting place"* — the womb. The parallel is beautiful and, once noticed, unmistakable. In verse 13 God provided a *qarār* for the unborn human being inside the mother; in verse 50 He provided a *qarār* for the mother and the born child on a hill. The same divine care that prepares the womb prepares the refuge. Mary, who had been the *qarār* for Jesus before his birth, was herself given a *qarār* after it. God's provision of shelter runs from the innermost to the outermost — from the womb to the hillside — and the sūrah uses one word for both.

**The Gentleness of the Verse**

After the drownings, the Cry, and the destruction of Pharaoh, verse 50 introduces a different register. There is no denial here, no *malaʾ*, no punishment; there is a mother, a child, a hill, a spring. The verse shows the other face of the God whose judgments the sūrah has recounted: the Shelterer of the vulnerable, the Provider of rest and water. The two faces are one. The same God who removes the arrogant provides for the humble; the same *qarār* He denies to the drowned He grants to the sheltered. The sūrah's opening promised that the believers would inherit Firdaws (v. 11); verse 50 is a small earthly image of that inheritance — high ground, rest, and flowing water — given to the two human beings who most perfectly exemplified the sūrah's first quality, humility before God.

**Jesus in the Line of Messengers**

Verse 50 places Jesus in the sequence of the sūrah's prophets — Noah, the unnamed messenger, Moses, Jesus — and it prepares for the sūrah's next declaration, in verses 51–52, that all the messengers were addressed as one and formed one community. Jesus is the last named before the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ described his relationship to him in exactly the terms verse 52 will use: *"I am the closest of people to Jesus, son of Mary, in this world and the Hereafter. The prophets are paternal brothers; their mothers differ, but their religion is one"* (al-Bukhārī 3443; Muslim 2365). The son of Mary, sheltered on his hill, is a brother of Noah in his Ark and Moses at his sea — different mothers, one religion.

**Toward the Address to All Messengers**

The historical section is complete. The sūrah has named Noah, an unnamed messenger, Moses and Aaron, and Jesus and Mary; it has stated the law that governed all of them; and it has shown both the judgment on those who denied and the guidance and shelter given to those who believed. The next verse steps out of narrative altogether and addresses all the messengers at once — "O messengers!" — with a command that summarizes what every one of them was sent to do.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:51

> **O messengers! Eat of the good things and work righteousness. Truly I know what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Sudden Address to All the Prophets at Once**

The sūrah has recounted the messengers one after another — Noah, the unnamed prophet, Moses and Aaron, Jesus. Now it does something remarkable: it addresses them all together, in a single vocative: *yā ayyuhā al-rusulu kulū min al-ṭayyibāti wa-ʿmalū ṣāliḥan innī bimā taʿmalūna ʿalīm* — "O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteousness; indeed, I am Knowing of what you do." The plural *al-rusul*, "the messengers," gathers every prophet of every age into one audience, as though they stood together before their Lord and received a single instruction. The verse is the hinge between the sūrah's history and its declaration of unity: having told the messengers' stories separately, it now speaks to them as one company.

**How Can All the Messengers Be Addressed Together?**

The commentators addressed the obvious question: the messengers lived in different centuries; how could they be addressed at once? The source records al-Rāzī's two answers. First, the address is *distributive*: each messenger, in his own time, received this instruction, so that the plural summarizes what was said to each individually. Second, the address is directed to the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ but phrased in the plural to signal that the command is common to all messengers and that he stands in their line. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr note that the Prophet ﷺ is the immediate addressee — the verse comes to him in the Qur'an — but that the plural form places his mission in continuity with all those before him. Both readings converge: the instruction is universal across prophethood, and the Prophet ﷺ receives it as the last of those to whom it applies.

There is a rhetorical purpose in the plural as well. By addressing all the messengers with one command, the verse demonstrates that they shared not only a message (vv. 23, 32) and an opposition (vv. 24–25, 33–38, 47) but a *way of life*. What God required of Noah, He required of Moses and of Jesus and of Muḥammad ﷺ: eat what is good, do what is right, know that you are seen. The next verse will draw the conclusion: *"this community of yours is one community."*

**"Eat of the Good Things": The First Command**

The first command is *kulū min al-ṭayyibāt* — "eat of the good things." The word *ṭayyibāt* (singular *ṭayyib*) means things that are good, pure, wholesome, and pleasant. As the source notes, the word appears throughout the Qur'an in connection with God's blessings — the *ṭayyibāt* provided to the Israelites (2:57), permitted to the believers (5:4), and given to Moses's people (20:81). *Ṭayyib* combines two ideas: *lawful* (ḥalāl) and *good* (wholesome, clean, pleasant). The command therefore means: eat what God has permitted, and eat what is good for you.

Why is a command to *eat* addressed to the messengers? Several reasons emerge. First, it affirms the messengers' humanity, which the deniers had used against them: *"This is only a human being like you, eating of what you eat"* (v. 33). God Himself commands the messengers to eat — He does not want angels who do not eat; He wants human beings who eat *rightly*. The deniers' objection is thereby turned inside out: eating is not a disqualification from prophethood but a command within it.

Second, it rejects asceticism as a path to God. Some religious traditions taught that holiness required the mortification of the body — extreme fasting, the refusal of pleasant food, the denial of lawful enjoyment. The verse commands the *opposite*: eat the good things. The Prophet ﷺ rebuked those who wished to renounce lawful pleasures: *"By God, I am the most fearful of God among you, but I fast and I break my fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women"* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401). And the Qur'an asks: *"Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has produced for His servants, and the good things (ṭayyibāt) of provision?"* (7:32). Holiness in Islam is not the rejection of God's provisions but their grateful and lawful use.

Third, and most importantly, it connects lawful eating to righteous action. The next command is *wa-ʿmalū ṣāliḥan*, "and do righteousness," and the conjunction *wa* joins the two. The Prophet ﷺ explained the connection in one of the most important ḥadīths on the subject:

> *"O people, God is Pure (ṭayyib) and accepts only what is pure (ṭayyib). And God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, saying: 'O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteousness; indeed, I am Knowing of what you do.' And He said: 'O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided you.' Then he mentioned a man who makes a long journey, disheveled and dusty, raising his hands to the sky: 'O Lord, O Lord!' — while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he has been nourished with the unlawful. So how can he be answered?"* (Muslim 1015, from Abū Hurayrah)

The ḥadīth makes verse 51 the foundation of a doctrine: what one eats affects what one does and whether one's prayers are heard. The body nourished on the unlawful — stolen wealth, usury, fraud, forbidden food — is a body whose deeds and supplications are compromised. The messengers were commanded to eat the *ṭayyib* first, and only then to do righteousness, because the second depends on the first. This is why the scholars of the soul insisted that the purification of one's income is the beginning of the purification of one's heart.

**"And Do Righteousness": The Second Command**

The second command is *wa-ʿmalū ṣāliḥan* — "and do righteous work." The word *ṣāliḥ* means sound, whole, right, fit for purpose — a *ṣāliḥ* deed is one that is done correctly, for God, according to His law. The Qur'an pairs *"those who believe and do righteous deeds"* (*ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt*) more than fifty times; it is the standard description of the people of Paradise. The command to the messengers is thus the same command given to every believer: not merely to believe, but to *act*.

The sequence — eat, then act — is the sequence of the human being: nourishment precedes labor. But it is also a moral sequence: the quality of the nourishment shapes the quality of the labor. The source notes that *ṭayyibāt* are connected to God's blessings; the verse teaches that receiving those blessings *rightly* is the precondition of using them *rightly*. A person who eats *ṭayyib* and works *ṣāliḥ* has completed the circuit of gratitude: God gives the good thing; the servant takes it lawfully; the servant returns it as righteous action.

**"Indeed, I Am Knowing of What You Do"**

The verse closes with a reminder: *innī bimā taʿmalūna ʿalīm* — "indeed, I am Knowing of what you do." The reminder is addressed to the *messengers* — the most righteous of human beings — and this is itself instructive. Even they are told that their deeds are observed. If the messengers are reminded of divine knowledge, how much more the ordinary believer? The phrase also completes the logic of the two commands: eat the good things, do righteous work — and know that the One who commanded both sees whether you comply. The divine knowledge is the guarantor of the commands' seriousness.

The phrase echoes verse 17's *"We were not heedless of creation"* and anticipates the sūrah's closing verses, where the deniers discover that everything was seen and recorded (v. 62: *"with Us is a Book that speaks in truth"*). The messengers were told from the beginning what the deniers learn only at the end: *"I know what you do."*

**The Verse as an Argument for the Prophet's Humanity**

The sūrah's deniers said the messenger could not be genuine because he ate and drank (v. 33) and was "a human being like us" (vv. 24, 34, 47). Verse 51 is God's direct rebuttal, addressed not to the deniers but to the messengers themselves: *eat*. The command presupposes that the messengers are eating beings — human beings — and it sanctifies their eating by commanding it. The Qur'an makes the same point explicitly of the Prophet ﷺ: *"And We did not send before you any of the messengers except that they ate food and walked in the markets"* (25:20). The deniers' objection is thus not merely answered but reversed: the eating messenger is the *only* kind God sends, and He commands him to eat.

**The Verse and the Believer's Daily Life**

For the believer, verse 51 offers a complete program in a single sentence. Examine your income: is it *ṭayyib*? Examine your food: is it lawful and wholesome? Examine your deeds: are they *ṣāliḥ* — done rightly, for God? And remember, in all three, that you are seen. The Prophet's ḥadīth on the dusty traveler is the verse's practical warning: the person who neglects the first command (lawful nourishment) will find the second (righteous action) hollow and his prayers unanswered. And the person who fulfills both has done what God commanded all His messengers to do — which is the highest company a human being can keep.

**Toward the One Community**

Verse 51 addressed the messengers as one audience and gave them one instruction. The next verse will state the conclusion explicitly: they and their followers constitute one community under one Lord — and the only fitting response to that Lord is *taqwā*.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:52

> **And truly this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so reverence Me.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Conclusion the History Was Building Toward**

Every element of the sūrah's historical section has been pointing to this verse. The messengers said the same words (vv. 23, 32); they faced the same objections (vv. 24–25, 33–38, 47); they prayed the same prayer (vv. 26, 39); they were addressed together (v. 51). Now God states what all this sameness means: *wa inna hādhihi ummatukum ummatan wāḥidatan wa ana rabbukum fa-ttaqūn* — "And indeed this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me." The verse is a declaration of unity — the unity of the prophets, the unity of their religion, and the unity of the Lord who sent them — followed by the single command that this unity entails.

**"This, Your Community, Is One Community"**

The word *ummah* has several meanings in the Qur'an: a community or nation (as in 2:143), a religion or way (as in 43:22: *"we found our fathers upon an ummah"*), a period of time (12:45), and a leader or exemplar (16:120, of Abraham). Here, as the source records from al-Rāzī, the primary meaning is a *religious community* — a body of people united by a common faith. The phrase *ummatukum ummatan wāḥidatan* — "your community [is] one community" — declares that the messengers and their true followers, across all ages, constitute *one* such body.

The demonstrative *hādhihi*, "this," points to what the sūrah has just described: the chain of messengers from Noah to Jesus, all preaching *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him,"* all commanded to *"eat of the good things and do righteousness."* *This* — this line of prophets and this way they taught — is one community. The possessive *-kum*, "your," addresses the messengers (continuing the vocative of v. 51) and, through them, the Prophet ﷺ and his followers: this community of *yours* — the community you belong to — is one.

The source commentary makes an important observation, citing al-Rāzī: the unity of the community is a unity of *fundamental faith* — belief in the One God — and does not preclude differences in *sharāʾiʿ*, the specific laws and rituals (fasting, forms of prayer, dietary rules) given to different communities. The Qur'an states this explicitly: *"To each of you We prescribed a law and a method"* (5:48). The messengers agreed on the *dīn* — the religion, the core of worship and submission — while their *sharāʾiʿ* differed according to the needs of their times. The Prophet ﷺ described this precisely: *"The prophets are paternal brothers; their mothers differ, but their religion is one"* (al-Bukhārī 3443; Muslim 2365). Paternal brothers share a father — the one *dīn* — while their mothers — the particular laws — differ.

**The Parallel Verse in Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ**

The source notes that this verse is nearly identical to 21:92: *"Indeed this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me (fa-ʿbudūn)."* The only difference is the closing command: 21:92 says "worship Me," and 23:52 says "fear Me" (*fa-ttaqūn*). The two verses conclude parallel sequences of prophetic stories — Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ recounts many prophets before reaching 21:92, as this sūrah recounts several before reaching 23:52 — and the two commands are complementary. Worship (*ʿibādah*) is the positive act of devotion; *taqwā* is the protective posture of guarding oneself from what displeases God. Together they define the relationship of the one community to its one Lord: devote yourselves to Him, and guard yourselves before Him.

The choice of *taqwā* in this sūrah is fitting. *Taqwā* has been the sūrah's recurring appeal: Noah asked *"Will you not be reverent (a-fa-lā tattaqūn)?"* (v. 23), the second messenger asked the same (v. 32), and now God Himself commands it. The question the messengers asked their peoples is answered, at the level of the whole community, by the divine imperative.

**"And I Am Your Lord": The Ground of Unity**

The middle clause gives the reason for the community's unity: *wa ana rabbukum* — "and I am your Lord." The community is one because its Lord is one. Communities are constituted by what they share; nations share a land or a language or an ancestry; the community of the prophets shares a *Lord*. This is the deepest possible basis of unity, because it is not contingent on anything in the members — not their race, their era, their tongue, or their laws — but on the One they serve. Noah and Jesus had nothing in common by worldly measures: different millennia, different lands, different languages, different peoples. They had everything in common by the only measure that matters: the same *Rabb*.

The word *rabb*, as noted under verse 26, means the owner, sustainer, and caretaker who brings what he owns to its completion. To say "I am your Lord" is to say: I made you, I sustain you, I sent you, and I will bring you to your end. The community's unity is thus not a horizontal agreement among its members but a vertical dependence on a single Source. This is why the sūrah could show the messengers separated by centuries and still call them one: they were never united by contact with each other, only by relationship with Him.

**"So Fear Me": The Command That Follows**

The verse ends with *fa-ttaqūn* — "so fear Me," "so guard yourselves before Me." The particle *fa-* marks the inference: *because* you are one community and *because* I am your Lord, *therefore* have *taqwā* of Me. The command follows from the facts. If there is one Lord, there is one thing to guard against — His displeasure — and one direction in which to guard — toward Him. *Taqwā* was described under verse 23 as the careful walking of a traveler on a dangerous path; here, the verse establishes that all the messengers and their followers walk the *same* path, with the same dangers and the same Guide.

The command is in the plural, addressed to the whole community. This has a social implication that the next verse will make painfully clear: the one community was commanded to guard itself as *one*, and it instead *"tore its affair into pieces"* (v. 53). *Taqwā* was meant to be the shared discipline that kept the community whole; its neglect produced fragmentation.

**The Doctrine of the Unity of Religion**

Verse 52 is a foundational text for the Qur'anic understanding of religious history. According to this understanding, there has only ever been one true religion — *islām* in its generic sense, submission to the One God — taught by every prophet from Adam to Muḥammad ﷺ. The Qur'an states: *"Indeed, the religion in the sight of God is Islam"* (3:19); *"He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah and that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham and Moses and Jesus: to establish the religion and not be divided therein"* (42:13). The prophets did not found different religions; they renewed one religion. The differences among the communities that bear their names arose *after* them, through the fragmentation the next verse describes.

This doctrine has consequences for how the believer regards other faith communities. He honors their prophets as his own — a Muslim who denies Moses or Jesus has left Islam (2:136; 4:150–152). He recognizes that what is true in their scriptures is from the same Lord. And he understands that the disagreements between communities are not disagreements between religions God revealed but departures from the one religion He revealed. The source refers to a broader essay on this theme; the verse itself supplies its principle: one community, one Lord.

**Why Unity Is Stated Here**

The verse's placement, at the close of the historical section, is exact. The sūrah has shown the deniers of every age making the *same* objections — which proves that denial, too, is a kind of unity, a single pattern repeated. Against that unity of rejection, verse 52 sets the unity of the messengers. Two communities run through history: the community of those who said "worship God" and the community of those who said "he is only a man like you." The sūrah began by naming the first (*al-muʾminūn*, v. 1) and will end by naming the second (*al-kāfirūn*, v. 117). Verse 52 declares that the first community, across all its centuries and prophets, is *one*.

**The Verse for the Believer**

For the believer, verse 52 is a source of both belonging and responsibility. Belonging: he is a member of a community that includes Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad ﷺ, and every righteous follower of each — a community older than any nation and wider than any land. Responsibility: he is commanded, as they were, to *taqwā*; and he is warned, by the next verse, that this community has been torn before by those who forgot that its unity lay in its Lord and not in their factions. The believer who holds to the *dīn* — the core of worship and submission — and who guards himself before his Lord, keeps the community one in his own person, whatever others have done to divide it.

**Toward the Tearing**

Verse 52 stated the unity. Verse 53 will describe its rupture: *"But they tore their affair among themselves into pieces, each faction rejoicing in what it has."* The sūrah moves, without pause, from the ideal to the history of its betrayal.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:53

> **But they made their affair to be founded upon different scriptures, each party exulting in what it had.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Unity to Fragmentation**

God declared, in verse 52, that the community of the messengers was one community under one Lord. Verse 53 records what human beings did with that unity: *fa-taqaṭṭaʿū amrahum baynahum zuburan kullu ḥizbin bimā ladayhim fariḥūn* — "But they tore their affair among themselves into pieces, each faction rejoicing in what it has." The particle *fa-* ("but, then") marks the contrast with the previous verse, and the contrast is stark. God said "one"; they made it many. God said "your community"; they made it "their factions." God said "I am your Lord, so fear Me"; they made themselves judges of one another and rejoiced in their divisions. The verse is a diagnosis of what went wrong with every religious community in history, including — the Prophet ﷺ warned — the community of the Qur'an.

**"They Tore Their Affair Into Pieces": Taqaṭṭaʿū**

The verb *taqaṭṭaʿū* is Form V of the root *q-ṭ-ʿ*, "to cut." Form V is intensive and reflexive: *taqaṭṭaʿa* means to be cut into many pieces, to fragment, to sever repeatedly. The image is violent — not a single clean division but a tearing into scraps. The object is *amrahum*, "their affair" — their religion, their matter, the thing they were jointly responsible for. The phrase *baynahum*, "among themselves," specifies that the tearing was internal: no external enemy divided them; they divided themselves. The Qur'an uses the same verb in the parallel verse of Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ: *"And they tore their affair among themselves; all will return to Us"* (21:93).

The choice of *taqaṭṭaʿū* (rather than a milder word like *ikhtalafū*, "they differed") is significant. Difference of opinion within a shared framework is one thing; the *cutting* of a single body into separate pieces is another. The verse describes the second. The messengers' community was a single organism; their followers dismembered it.

**"Into Pieces / Scriptures": The Word Zubur**

The word *zuburan* has two readings, and the source commentary presents both. The first reads it as the plural of *zabūr*, meaning a written scripture or book — the same word used for the Psalms of David (*al-Zabūr*, 4:163; 17:55) and for the scriptures of earlier peoples (*"the scriptures of the former peoples,"* 26:196; *"We wrote in the Zabūr,"* 21:105). On this reading, the verse means: they divided their religion into different *scriptures*, each faction taking its own book and rejecting the others. The source records al-Rāzī's development of this reading: the root *z-b-r* also means to write and, in another usage, to fashion pieces of iron (as in 18:96: *"bring me pieces of iron — zubar al-ḥadīd"*), so that the image of scriptures scattered like iron fragments merges the two senses.

The second reading takes *zubur* as the plural of *zubrah*, "a piece, a fragment" — the same word as in 18:96. On this reading, the verse means simply: they tore their religion into pieces, into sects. Both readings describe the same historical reality from different angles: the fragmentation of the one religion into rival groups, each with its own texts and its own claims.

The two readings need not compete. The history of religious division is precisely a history of *both*: sects form, and sects produce or privilege texts — creeds, commentaries, authorities — that define them against others. The word *zubur* captures the whole process in one term: the body was cut into pieces, and the pieces became parties with their own books.

**"Each Faction Rejoicing in What It Has"**

The second half of the verse is the psychological core: *kullu ḥizbin bimā ladayhim fariḥūn* — "each faction (*ḥizb*) rejoicing in what it has." The word *ḥizb* means a party, a faction, a group defined by allegiance; the Qur'an uses it for the confederates who besieged Madinah (*al-Aḥzāb*, Sūrah 33), for the party of God (*ḥizb Allāh*, 5:56; 58:22), and for the party of Satan (*ḥizb al-shayṭān*, 58:19). Here it denotes each of the sects into which the one community was torn. The word *fariḥūn* means rejoicing, exulting, delighting — and in the Qur'an it often carries a negative sense of complacent self-satisfaction: *"Do not exult (lā tafraḥ); indeed, God does not like the exultant"* (28:76, to Qārūn).

The verse thus describes not merely division but *contentment* in division. Each faction is pleased with its own portion — its own scripture, its own interpretation, its own leaders — and this pleasure is the disease's most dangerous symptom. A divided community that grieved over its division might reunite; a divided community in which each part *rejoices* in its separateness has no motive to heal. The Qur'an repeats the diagnosis exactly in Sūrah al-Rūm: *"Of those who have divided their religion and become sects — every faction rejoicing in what it has"* (30:32). The phrase is identical, word for word, which shows that the Qur'an regards this as a fixed law of sectarianism: division breeds self-satisfaction, and self-satisfaction perpetuates division.

**Why Factions Rejoice**

What is the psychology behind *fariḥūn*? Several mechanisms combine. First, belonging: a faction gives its members identity and companionship, and human beings take pleasure in belonging regardless of what they belong to. Second, superiority: each faction defines itself as *the* true one, and its members enjoy the sense of being right while others are wrong. Third, simplification: a faction offers a bounded set of texts and authorities, relieving its members of the burden of engaging the whole truth. Fourth, and most subtly, self-worship: the faction's "what it has" becomes an idol — a possession loved for being *ours* rather than for being *true*. The Qur'an exposes this last mechanism when it describes the Jews and Christians each claiming that only they will enter Paradise (2:111) and each declaring that the other *"has nothing to stand on"* (2:113). The rejoicing is not in God but in the group.

**The Context: Who Tore the Affair?**

The immediate referent of "they" is the followers of the messengers — the communities that received the one religion and fragmented it. The source points to the Qur'an's fuller treatment of how *"each religious community split into factions after it had been given unitive knowledge"* (3:19; 6:65; 98:4). The Qur'an is explicit that the division came *after* knowledge, not from lack of it: *"And they did not become divided until after knowledge had come to them, out of jealous animosity between themselves"* (42:14). The word *baghyan* — "out of envy, rivalry, transgression" — names the cause. The community did not fragment because the truth was unclear; it fragmented because human beings envied one another and sought precedence. The verse's "each faction rejoicing in what it has" is the fruit of that rivalry.

**The Warning to the Community of the Qur'an**

Verse 53 is not only a description of past communities; it is a warning to the present one. The Prophet ﷺ foretold that his own community would follow the same path: *"The Jews split into seventy-one sects, the Christians into seventy-two, and my community will split into seventy-three, all of them in the Fire except one."* They asked which one, and he said: *"That which I and my Companions are upon"* (al-Tirmidhī 2641; Abū Dāwūd 4596; Ibn Mājah 3992; graded ḥasan). Whatever the precise significance of the numbers, the ḥadīth places the Muslim community under the same law as verse 53: it, too, would tear its affair into pieces, and the criterion of the saved faction would not be its size or its self-confidence but its fidelity to the original — "what I and my Companions are upon." The Qur'an itself commands: *"And hold firmly to the rope of God all together and do not become divided"* (3:103), and warns the Prophet ﷺ: *"Indeed, those who have divided their religion and become sects — you are not associated with them in anything"* (6:159).

The believer who reads verse 53 must therefore read it as addressed to himself. Is he a member of the *ummah wāḥidah* of verse 52, or of a *ḥizb* of verse 53? The test is not whether he belongs to a school or a community — that is inevitable and often beneficial — but whether he *rejoices* in his group's separateness, defines himself against other Muslims, treats his party's "what it has" as the whole of the religion, and forgets that the unity of the community rests in its Lord (v. 52: *"I am your Lord"*), not in any faction.

**The Verse's Logic: What Unity Requires**

Verse 52 gave the basis of unity — one Lord — and the command that maintains it — *taqwā*. Verse 53 shows what happens when the basis is forgotten and the command neglected. Unity that rests on the Lord is indestructible, because the Lord does not change; unity that rests on anything else — a leader, a text privileged over other texts, a shared grievance, a tribal identity — is a *ḥizb* waiting to form. The believer maintains the one community by orienting his loyalty upward, toward God, rather than sideways, toward the party. Ibn Masʿūd expressed the principle: *"The congregation (jamāʿah) is what accords with the truth, even if you are alone."* The one community is not the largest faction; it is the body of those who hold to what the messengers held to.

**Toward Divine Restraint**

The sūrah has described the tearing. The next verse gives God's instruction to His Prophet in the face of it — not to force unity, not to despair, but to leave those who are drowning in their heedlessness *"for a time."* The word "time" (*ḥīn*) will recall the notables' own words to Noah (v. 25), now turned back upon their descendants.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:54

> **So leave them in their heedlessness for a time.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**God's Instruction to His Prophet**

After describing how the followers of the messengers tore their religion into factions, each rejoicing in its own portion (v. 53), the sūrah turns to the Prophet ﷺ with a command: *fa-dharhum fī ghamratihim ḥattā ḥīn* — "So leave them in their confusion for a time." The verse is addressed to him directly, and its tone is one of restraint. It does not say "argue with them until they yield," nor "abandon them forever," nor "punish them." It says: leave them, in the state they are in, until a time. The verse is a lesson in the limits of a messenger's task and in the patience that God asks of those who carry the truth to people who will not hear it.

**"So Leave Them": Fa-dharhum**

The verb *dharhum* is an imperative meaning "leave them, let them be." The particle *fa-* connects it to the previous verse: *because* they have torn their affair into pieces and rejoice in their factions, *therefore* leave them. The command does not mean to cease conveying the message — the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey it until his death, and the following verses (57–77) contain some of the sūrah's most sustained arguments to these same people. It means to cease *striving to force* the outcome: to stop exhausting oneself in grief over those who have chosen their confusion, and to stop expecting that argument alone will move people who rejoice in not being moved.

The Qur'an uses this imperative in parallel contexts, as the source notes: *"Say: 'God,' then leave them (dharhum) in their discourse, playing"* (6:91); *"We shall leave them (nadharuhum) in their transgression, wandering blindly"* (6:110); *"So leave them (dharhum) to plunge and play until they meet their Day which they are promised"* (43:83; 70:42). In each case, the command comes after the people's rejection has been established and their condition described. It is God's instruction to the messenger *after* the messenger has done his part.

**"In Their Heedlessness": Ghamrah**

The word *ghamrah* is the verse's key term. As the source explains from al-Rāzī, its literal meaning is water so deep that it covers a person entirely — water over one's head. From this it came to mean any overwhelming state: the depths of confusion, the flood of heedlessness, the engulfing of a person by ignorance or error. The Qur'an uses the plural *ghamarāt* for the agonies of death, *"the depths (ghamarāt) of death"* (6:93), and for the state of the deniers: *"Rather, their hearts are in ghamrah about this"* (23:63, later in this sūrah), and *"those who are in a ghamrah, heedless"* (51:11).

The image is precise and devastating. The factions of verse 53 are not merely mistaken; they are *submerged*. They cannot see the surface because the water is over their heads; they cannot hear because their ears are full of it; they are drowning in their own confusion and do not know it, because a drowning person who has lost consciousness feels no distress. The word connects to the sūrah's water imagery: the Flood that drowned Noah's people (v. 27) and the sea that drowned Pharaoh (v. 48) were external waters; the *ghamrah* of verse 54 is an internal one — the flood of heedlessness in which a person drowns while still walking around.

The possessive *ghamratihim*, "*their* confusion," makes the state their own. It is not imposed on them; it is the condition they have chosen and in which they rejoice (v. 53: *fariḥūn*). One cannot rescue a person who is delighted to be underwater.

**"For a Time": Ḥattā Ḥīn**

The verse ends with *ḥattā ḥīn* — "until a time." The phrase is deliberately indefinite: until an appointed moment, whose arrival God knows and they do not. The commentators understood the "time" as death, or as the coming of the punishment in this world (as at Badr), or as the Day of Judgment; and the sūrah's own continuation supports all three, since it will describe the affluent seized by punishment (v. 64), death arriving (v. 99), and the final reckoning (vv. 101 ff.). Whichever moment is meant, the phrase establishes that the reprieve is temporary. The factions are left in their confusion — but not forever.

The phrase has a striking echo. In verse 25, the notables of Noah's people said of Noah: *"So wait concerning him for a time (ḥattā ḥīn)."* They thought time was on their side and that waiting would dispose of the messenger. Now God says of their spiritual descendants: *"Leave them in their confusion for a time (ḥattā ḥīn)."* The same phrase, reversed. The deniers said "wait until he is gone"; God says "leave them until they are." The notables' "time" was the time they expected to outlast the messenger; God's "time" is the time in which they will be outlasted. The sūrah's justice is again audible in its vocabulary: each side is answered in its own words.

**Why God Commands Restraint**

The command to "leave them" raises a question: does it not contradict the messenger's mission to call people to God? The classical scholars answered carefully. The command does not abrogate the duty to convey; it *regulates* the messenger's inner state and expectations. Several reasons for the restraint can be drawn from the Qur'an.

First, the limits of responsibility. *"Upon you is only the conveyance, and upon Us is the account"* (13:40). The Prophet ﷺ was not responsible for whether people accepted; his task ended at clear delivery. The command "leave them" reminds him of this boundary, which he was inclined to forget in his grief: *"Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps, if they do not believe in this message"* (18:6).

Second, the reality of choice. God has given human beings freedom, and a person who chooses confusion and rejoices in it cannot be forced out of it without destroying the freedom that makes faith meaningful. *"And if your Lord had willed, all on earth would have believed together. Then would you compel the people until they become believers?"* (10:99). To "leave them" is to respect the choice God Himself respects.

Third, the wisdom of the fixed term. The sūrah has taught that *"no community can hasten its term, nor delay it"* (v. 43). The Prophet's striving cannot advance the moment at which God will act; the command to leave them "until a time" aligns his expectation with the divine schedule.

Fourth, the messenger's own well-being. The Prophet ﷺ was a man, and the constant rejection wore on him. "Leave them" is, in part, a mercy to him — permission to lay down a burden that was never his to carry.

**Restraint Is Not Indifference**

It must be stressed that "leave them" is not a command to stop caring. The verses that follow (55–77) contain the sūrah's most extended engagement with these same people: their false confidence in wealth (vv. 55–56), the contrast with the true believers (vv. 57–61), the coming punishment (vv. 64–65), the six questions (vv. 68–70), and the argument from truth (v. 71). God tells the Prophet ﷺ to leave them and then immediately continues to address them through him. The two are compatible: the *conveying* continues; the *anguish* is set down. The believer who calls others to good must learn this balance — to keep speaking the truth while releasing attachment to the result.

**The Verse in the Believer's Life**

Verse 54 has direct application to anyone who has tried to bring a person out of a *ghamrah* — a relative sunk in sin, a friend lost in a false ideology, a community content in its factionalism — and has found the person not merely resistant but *pleased* with the water over his head. The verse gives permission to stop drowning oneself in the attempt. It does not say "give up on them"; it says "leave them in their state for a time" — keep the door open, keep speaking when there is an opening, and trust that God's "time" will come. The Prophet ﷺ modeled this: he never stopped calling the Quraysh, but after verse 54 he did not expect their conversion to depend on his exertion. Many of them did, in fact, come out of their *ghamrah* — at the Conquest of Makkah, at the "time" God had appointed — but not because he had forced them.

The verse also warns the believer against being among those left in their *ghamrah*. The factions of verse 53 were *religious* people — they had scriptures and were proud of them. Their confusion was not the confusion of the ignorant but of the self-satisfied. The believer who is certain that his party has the whole truth, who rejoices in "what it has," who feels no need to examine himself against the original — he is, by the verse's own criterion, in danger of the water rising over his head while he smiles.

**Toward the Illusion of Wealth**

The next verses will describe the specific *ghamrah* of the Makkan deniers: their conviction that the wealth and children God had given them were proof of His favor. The confusion in which they were to be left had a particular content, and the sūrah will now expose it.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:55

> **Do they reckon that, [on account of] the wealth and the children that We have provided them,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Content of Their Confusion**

God has commanded the Prophet ﷺ to leave the deniers in their *ghamrah*, their engulfing confusion (v. 54). Now the sūrah exposes what that confusion consists of: *a-yaḥsabūna annamā numidduhum bihi min mālin wa banīn* — "Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children..." The sentence is incomplete; it continues into verse 56, where the thought is finished: "...We hasten to them good things? Rather, they do not perceive." The two verses form a single question, and the source treats them together; but each half carries its own weight, and this commentary follows the sūrah's own division. Verse 55 names the premise of the deniers' error — the wealth and children they possess; verse 56 names the false conclusion they draw from it.

**"Do They Reckon": A-Yaḥsabūna**

The verb *yaḥsabūna*, from the root *ḥ-s-b*, means to reckon, to calculate, to suppose. It is the verb of estimation — of arriving at a conclusion by counting. The deniers have *calculated*: they have looked at their possessions, added them up, and reached a verdict about their standing with God. The interrogative *a-* ("do they...?") frames the calculation as a question — and, as throughout the sūrah, the question is rhetorical, expecting the answer "they should not." The Qur'an uses this construction repeatedly to expose false assumptions: *"Do they think (a-yaḥsabūna) that We do not hear their secrets?"* (43:80); *"Does man think (a-yaḥsabu) that he will be left without purpose?"* (75:36). The deniers' reckoning is about to be shown as a miscalculation.

**"What We Extend to Them": Numidduhum**

The verb *numidduhum* is from the root *m-d-d*, which means to extend, to stretch out, to supply continuously. A *madad* is reinforcement or supply; *imdād* is the act of supplying. The verb describes an ongoing provision, a stream that keeps flowing: God *keeps extending* wealth and children to them. Two things are notable. First, the subject is God — *numiddu*, "*We* extend." The deniers did not generate their wealth; it was supplied to them, day by day, from a source outside themselves. Second, the continuous tense implies that the supply is not a one-time gift but a sustained flow — and a flow can be increased, decreased, or cut, as verse 18 warned of water: *"We are able to take it away."*

The Qur'an uses this same root with a darker connotation elsewhere: *"And We will extend for them (namuddu lahum) in punishment"* (19:79); *"God mocks them and extends them (yamudduhum) in their transgression, wandering blindly"* (2:15). The extending of provision can be a mercy or a trap, depending on how it is received. The verb in verse 55 is neutral in itself; the deniers' misreading, exposed in verse 56, is what turns the mercy into a snare.

**"Wealth and Children": Māl wa Banīn**

The two things named are *māl*, wealth, and *banīn*, sons or children. These are, in the Qur'an's consistent analysis, the two great goods of worldly life and the two great tests: *"Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world; but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for hope"* (18:46). *"Your wealth and your children are only a trial (fitnah), and God has with Him a great reward"* (64:15). *"O you who believe, let not your wealth and your children divert you from the remembrance of God"* (63:9). The pairing recurs because the two together constitute what most human beings mean by "prosperity": possessions and posterity, security now and continuity after.

The Makkan elite had both in abundance. The Qur'an quotes their boast: *"We are greater in wealth and children, and we are not to be punished"* (34:35). And it records a specific instance in al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, whom God describes as one *"to whom I granted extensive wealth and children present with him, and I spread out for him everything"* — and who then *"desires that I should add more"* (74:12–15). The deniers of this sūrah are men of this type: affluent (v. 33: *"whom We had given luxury"*), and confident that their affluence proves something.

**The Structure of the Error**

Verse 55 lays out the premise from which the deniers reasoned. The premise is true: God *has* extended wealth and children to them. The error lies in what they conclude from it — and verse 56 will state the conclusion: that God is thereby "hastening good to them," rewarding them, favoring them. The logic runs: God has given us much; giving is favor; therefore God favors us; therefore our religion is correct and the messenger is wrong. Each step seems plausible; the whole is false. Verse 55 isolates the premise so that verse 56 can dismantle the inference.

The error is one of the most common in religious psychology, and it has a name in the Qur'an's vocabulary: *istidrāj* — being led on gradually by ease toward destruction. *"We will lead them on gradually (sa-nastadrijuhum) from where they do not know"* (7:182; 68:44). The source notes al-Qurṭubī's observation that worldly possessions are given to the disbeliever as a trial and serve to "entrench them in their folly." The wealth is not the reward; the wealth is the *test*, and the deniers' misreading of it is their failing of the test.

**Why Prosperity Deceives**

The deniers' reasoning deceives because it rests on an assumption that feels natural but is false: that the distribution of worldly goods tracks divine approval. The Qur'an denies this with force. *"And if it were not that the people would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful — for their houses — ceilings of silver and stairways upon which to mount"* (43:33). That is: God would give the disbelievers *even more* if it would not mislead everyone into thinking wealth signifies favor. Worldly provision is so unrelated to divine approval that God withholds its extremes from the wicked only to protect the weak from the very inference the deniers of verse 55 have drawn.

The Prophet ﷺ stated the principle in a single sentence: *"Indeed, God gives the world to those He loves and those He does not love, but He gives religion only to those He loves"* (Aḥmad; al-Ḥākim; graded ṣaḥīḥ). Wealth is distributed to believers and disbelievers alike; faith is the gift that marks favor. The deniers looked at the wrong ledger.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Opening**

Verse 55 must be read against the sūrah's beginning. Verse 1 declared: *"Truly the believers have prospered."* The word was *aflaḥa* — true, lasting prosperity. The deniers of verse 55 think *they* have prospered, on the evidence of *māl* and *banīn*. The sūrah is contrasting two definitions of prosperity: the believers', which consists in the seven qualities of verses 2–9 and ends in Firdaws (v. 11); and the deniers', which consists in wealth and children and ends — as verses 64–65 will show — in cries for help that go unanswered. The sūrah's opening word and the deniers' calculation are two answers to the same question: what does it mean to have succeeded? Verse 55 states the wrong answer in order to refute it.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 55 speaks to two kinds of believer. To the affluent believer, it is a warning: do not read your wealth and children as proof that God is pleased with you. They may be; they may equally be the *istidrāj* that lulls you. The only proof of favor is the state of your faith and deeds, which the sūrah's opening measured. To the poor believer, it is a consolation: do not read the affluence of the wicked as proof that God favors them or that your faith has failed. The Qur'an says of the worldly goods of the disbelievers: *"Let not their wealth and their children impress you; God only intends to punish them through them in worldly life"* (9:55). The ledger the deniers consult is not the ledger God keeps.

Both kinds of believer are reminded that the source of wealth and children is *numidduhum* — God's continuous extending. What is extended can be withdrawn. The person who understands this holds his wealth loosely and his children as a trust, and does not build his estimate of himself on either.

**Toward the False Conclusion**

Verse 55 has stated the premise: God extends to them wealth and children. Verse 56 will state what they wrongly conclude — and then correct it with three words: *"Rather, they do not perceive."*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:56

> **We hasten unto good for them? Nay, but they are unaware!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Completion of the Question**

Verse 55 laid out the premise of the deniers' calculation: God extends to them wealth and children. Verse 56 states the conclusion they draw and then demolishes it: *nusāriʿu lahum fī l-khayrāt bal lā yashʿurūn* — "[Do they think that] We hasten to them good things? Rather, they do not perceive." The full question, spanning both verses, reads: "Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children [means that] We are hastening good things to them?" And the answer is a single, decisive *bal* — "rather, no" — followed by the diagnosis: they do not perceive. The verse is the sūrah's most concise statement of the difference between what a thing looks like and what it is.

**"We Hasten to Them Good Things": Nusāriʿu Fī l-Khayrāt**

The verb *nusāriʿu* is from the root *s-r-ʿ*, "to be quick, to hasten." Form III (*sāraʿa*) means to race, to hurry toward, to compete in speed. The deniers imagine that God is *racing* to bring them good — that their abundance is a sign of divine eagerness to bless them. The word *khayrāt*, plural of *khayr*, means good things, benefits, blessings — and in the Qur'an it often means specifically the *true* goods, the goods of the Hereafter and of righteousness: *"They hasten (yusāriʿūna) in good deeds (al-khayrāt)"* (3:114); *"So race (fa-stabiqū) to good deeds (al-khayrāt)"* (2:148; 5:48).

The word choice is pointed, because the *same* verb and the *same* noun will describe the true believers in verse 61: *"It is those who hasten (yusāriʿūna) in good deeds (al-khayrāt), and they are foremost in them."* The deniers think God is hastening *khayrāt to* them; the believers are the ones hastening *toward khayrāt*. The deniers' *khayrāt* are wealth and children — received passively, mistaken for favor. The believers' *khayrāt* are deeds — pursued actively, with hearts that tremble (v. 60). The contrast, set up across verses 56 and 61, is one of the sūrah's finest structural touches: the same words, two opposite lives.

**"Rather, They Do Not Perceive": Bal Lā Yashʿurūn**

The particle *bal* is the Qur'an's corrective: it cancels what precedes and substitutes the truth. "Do they think We are hastening good to them? *Bal* — no; rather..." What follows is not a counter-argument but a diagnosis: *lā yashʿurūn* — "they do not perceive." The verb *yashʿurūn* is from the root *sh-ʿ-r*, which denotes perception through the senses or subtle awareness (a *shāʿir*, poet, is one who perceives what others miss; *shuʿūr* is consciousness). To say they *lā yashʿurūn* is to say that they are *unaware* — not merely mistaken in a conclusion but lacking the perception that would allow them to draw the right one. They cannot see what the wealth and children actually are.

This diagnosis links back to the *ghamrah* of verse 54. A person with water over his head does not perceive; his senses are flooded. The deniers' calculation (v. 55: *yaḥsabūna*) is done underwater. They count their possessions and reach a verdict, but the counting itself is the act of someone who cannot see the surface. God does not argue with the calculation; He names the condition that produced it.

**What the Wealth Actually Is**

If the wealth and children are not "good things hastened to them," what are they? The Qur'an gives several answers, and the sūrah's own logic supports each.

They are a test. *"Your wealth and your children are only a trial"* (64:15). The sūrah stated in verse 30 that God is *"ever testing"* (*mubtalīn*); verses 55–56 show one form the test takes. Ease tests as surely as hardship, and more subtly, because hardship at least reminds a person of his need while ease conceals it.

They are a gradual leading-on. *"We will lead them on gradually (sa-nastadrijuhum) from where they do not know (lā yaʿlamūn). And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm"* (7:182–183). The phrase "from where they do not know" is the twin of verse 56's "they do not perceive." *Istidrāj* works precisely by being imperceptible: the person receives more and more, concludes that all is well, and does not notice that each increase lengthens his fall.

They are a source of punishment in this world and the next. *"So let not their wealth and their children impress you; God only intends to punish them through them in worldly life and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers"* (9:55). The wealth is not neutral; for those who misuse it, it becomes the instrument of their loss — the object of anxiety in life, the record of misuse at the reckoning.

They are the hastened portion of a share that will otherwise be empty. *"Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world, We give him thereof, but there is not for him in the Hereafter any share"* (42:20). The Prophet ﷺ said of the disbeliever: *"As for the disbeliever, he is fed in this world for the good deeds he did, so that when he reaches the Hereafter he has no good deed for which he can be rewarded"* (Muslim 2808). The abundance of the deniers is, in this light, the *whole* of their reward, paid early — which is the opposite of "hastening good to them."

**The Correct Reading of Ease**

The Qur'an teaches the true sign of divine favor in the verses that follow (57–61): it is not what one *receives* but how one *lives* — in fear of God, faith in His signs, refusal of shirk, and giving with a trembling heart. The Companions understood this. When the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the person to whom God gives the world while he persists in disobedience, he said: *"When you see God giving a servant of this world what he loves while he persists in his disobedience, that is only istidrāj,"* and then he recited 6:44: *"So when they forgot that of which they had been reminded, We opened to them the doors of every thing, until, when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly, and they were in despair"* (Aḥmad; graded ḥasan). The rejoicing in 6:44 (*fariḥū*) is the same rejoicing as verse 53's factions (*fariḥūn*). Rejoicing in what one has — whether wealth or sect — is the posture that precedes the seizing.

**The Verse's Psychological Precision**

Verse 56's diagnosis — *lā yashʿurūn* — is more precise than a charge of dishonesty would have been. The deniers were not lying when they said their wealth proved God's favor; they believed it. Their error was perceptual, not moral, in its immediate form — though it was moral in its root, because the failure to perceive was the result of choosing not to look (v. 53: rejoicing in what they had; v. 54: their own *ghamrah*). The Qur'an distinguishes carefully between those who know the truth and deny it and those who have blinded themselves to it; the deniers of verse 56 are the second kind, and the second kind is in some ways more dangerous, because a person who does not perceive cannot be argued out of his error — he can only be awakened, and awakening comes, as verse 64 will show, from a shock.

**The Verse in Modern Life**

The reasoning verse 56 refutes is not confined to seventh-century Makkah. It is the "prosperity gospel" in every age: the belief that material success is evidence of divine approval, that the rich are blessed and the poor are cursed, that if God were displeased He would not have given so much. It appears in the confidence of nations that their power proves their righteousness, in the self-satisfaction of the comfortable who take their comfort as a verdict in their favor, and in the quiet despair of the struggling believer who wonders whether his struggle means God has turned from him. To all of these, verse 56 says: *bal lā yashʿurūn* — you are not perceiving what these things are. Wealth and children are extended (v. 55) as a test, a trust, and sometimes a trap; they are never, in themselves, a certificate of favor.

The believer's response is to measure himself by the criteria of verses 57–61, not by his bank balance or his family's size; to hold what he has as a trust that may be withdrawn; and to reserve the word *khayrāt* for what the sūrah reserves it for — the good deeds toward which he hastens, not the goods that come to him.

**Toward the True Recipients of Good**

The sūrah has shown who is *not* being hastened good. It now turns, in five verses (57–61), to those who *are* — and their portrait is the mirror image of the deniers': not those who receive and rejoice, but those who give and tremble.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:57

> **Truly those who are in awe for fear of their Lord,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Portrait of the Believers**

The sūrah opened with a portrait of the believers in seven qualities (vv. 1–9). Now, after showing the deniers' false confidence in their wealth (vv. 55–56), it draws a second portrait — four qualities in verses 57–60, with their result in verse 61 — of those who are *truly* hastening toward good. The structure is a single sentence: *"Indeed, those who [1] ..., and those who [2] ..., and those who [3] ..., and those who [4] ... — it is they who hasten in good deeds and are foremost in them."* Verse 57 gives the first quality: *inna lladhīna hum min khashyati rabbihim mushfiqūn* — "Indeed, those who, from awe of their Lord, are apprehensive."

The second portrait differs from the first in emphasis. The first was largely a portrait of *practice* — prayer, turning from vain talk, zakāh, chastity, trusts, covenants. The second is a portrait of the *inner state* that gives practice its value — fear, faith, purity from shirk, and a trembling heart. The sūrah has moved from what believers do to how they feel while doing it, and the first feeling named is a particular kind of fear.

**Two Words for Fear: Khashyah and Ishfāq**

The verse contains two terms, and the source draws on al-Rāzī to distinguish them. *Khashyah* is fear grounded in knowledge of the greatness of the one feared — reverential awe. The Qur'an makes the connection explicit: *"Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear (yakhshā) God"* (35:28). *Khashyah* is not the fear of the ignorant before an unknown threat; it is the fear of the one who *knows* how great God is and how small he is before Him. It is the fear the sūrah's opening called *khushūʿ* in its outward expression (v. 2), now named at its root.

*Ishfāq* (the participle *mushfiqūn*) is, as al-Rāzī notes, fear mixed with tenderness and care — the fear of one who is anxious about something he loves and does not want to lose. A mother is *mushfiq* over a sick child: her fear is not terror but solicitous concern. The Qur'an uses the root for the angels: *"and they, from fear of Him, are apprehensive (mushfiqūn)"* (21:28); for the believers in Paradise recalling their lives: *"Indeed, we were before, among our families, apprehensive (mushfiqīn)"* (52:26); and for those who fear the Hour: *"those who fear the Hour are apprehensive (mushfiqūn) of it"* (42:18).

The verse combines the two: they are *mushfiqūn* — anxious, caring, alert — *from khashyah of their Lord* — because of their awe at His greatness. The awe is the cause; the anxiety is the effect. They know who God is, and therefore they are never careless about where they stand with Him.

**Why Fear Comes First**

The order of the four qualities is meaningful. Fear is named first because it is the root of the others. A person who does not fear God has no motive to believe His signs, no reason to refuse shirk, and no trembling as he gives. Fear, in the sense of *khashyah*, is what makes the rest possible. The Qur'an places it at the head of the believer's inner life: *"So fear not the people but fear Me"* (5:44); *"And it is Me you should fear"* (2:40, 41). And it describes the effect of true fear on the body and heart: *"The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it; then their skins and their hearts relax at the remembrance of God"* (39:23).

There is also a contrast with the deniers just described. The deniers of verses 55–56 were *confident*: they read their wealth as proof of favor and felt secure. The believers of verse 57 are *apprehensive*: whatever they have, they do not feel secure, because they know that security before God is not something one can calculate from one's possessions. The deniers' security was the product of not perceiving (v. 56: *lā yashʿurūn*); the believers' apprehension is the product of perceiving clearly. Fear, in this sense, is a form of sight.

**Fear Is Not Despair**

The fear verse 57 describes must be distinguished from despair, which the Qur'an forbids: *"Do not despair of the mercy of God"* (39:53); *"Indeed, no one despairs of relief from God except the disbelieving people"* (12:87). *Ishfāq* is fear with tenderness — and tenderness implies hope, because one is anxious only about what one hopes to keep. The believer of verse 57 fears losing God's pleasure *because he hopes to have it*. The two emotions are inseparable, and the Qur'an consistently pairs them: *"They call upon their Lord in fear and hope"* (32:16); *"They used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear"* (21:90). The scholars described the believer as a bird flying with two wings — fear and hope — that cannot fly with one. Verse 57 names the wing of fear; verse 61's "hasten in good deeds" implies the wing of hope.

**The Prophet's Fear**

The Prophet ﷺ, who knew God better than any creature, feared Him more than any creature. He said: *"By God, I am the most fearing of God among you and the most conscious of Him"* (al-Bukhārī 5063; Muslim 1401). ʿĀʾishah reported that when he saw a cloud or wind, his face would change with concern; she asked why, since people rejoiced at clouds hoping for rain, and he said: *"O ʿĀʾishah, what would make me secure that there is no punishment in it? A people were punished by wind, and a people saw the punishment and said, 'This is a cloud bringing us rain'"* (al-Bukhārī 4829; Muslim 899). This is *ishfāq*: not panic, but the settled alertness of one who does not take God's mercy for granted. The Companions inherited it. Abū Bakr, whom the Prophet ﷺ had promised Paradise, is reported to have said: *"I would not feel secure from the plan of God even if one of my feet were in Paradise."*

**The Apparent Paradox**

Why should those who fear be described as the ones who "hasten in good deeds" (v. 61) while the confident deniers are the ones who "do not perceive" (v. 56)? Because fear of the right object is the beginning of correct action. The person who fears God does not rest on what he has done; he keeps doing more, and he examines what he has done for flaws. The person who is confident of God's favor stops. Fear moves; confidence sits. This is why the Qur'an says: *"And let them fear (yakhsha) Me"* immediately before commanding good action, and why the Prophet ﷺ described the highest level of worship — *iḥsān* — as *"to worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you"* (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). To live as one who is *seen* is to live in *khashyah*, and to live in *khashyah* is to be *mushfiq*.

**The Verse in Daily Life**

The first quality of the second portrait asks the believer a simple question: Are you *apprehensive* about your standing with God, or comfortable? Comfort is not the same as peace. The peace the Qur'an promises — *"Indeed, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest"* (13:28) — is the rest of one who has placed himself in God's hands; it is not the complacency of one who assumes God is satisfied with him. The believer of verse 57 has peace *and* apprehension: peace in God's mercy, apprehension about his own deeds. He prays and wonders whether it was accepted; he gives and wonders whether it was sincere; he fasts and wonders whether it was more than hunger. This wondering is not a defect; it is the *ishfāq* that verse 57 names and verse 60 will describe in its most vivid form — "hearts trembling."

**Toward the Second Quality**

Fear of the Lord is the root; the second quality, in verse 58, is faith in His signs. Those who fear God take His communications seriously, because one does not dismiss the words of the One before whom one trembles.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:58

> **and those who believe in the signs of their Lord,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Quality: Faith in the Signs**

The second portrait of the believers continues: *wa lladhīna hum bi-āyāti rabbihim yuʾminūn* — "and those who, in the signs of their Lord, believe." The verse is brief, but its brevity conceals a wide field. The "signs" (*āyāt*) of God include everything the sūrah has already presented as evidence: the stages of the embryo (vv. 12–14), the seven heavens (v. 17), the measured rain (v. 18), the gardens and the olive (vv. 19–20), the cattle and the ships (vv. 21–22), and the histories of the messengers (vv. 23–50). To "believe in the signs" is to accept what these things point to. The verse names as the believers' second quality the very response the sūrah has been asking for since verse 12.

**The Word Āyāt and Its Two Fields**

The word *āyah* (plural *āyāt*) means a sign, a mark, a token — something that indicates something beyond itself. The Qur'an uses it in two fields. The first is the created world: *"Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs (āyāt) for those of understanding"* (3:190). The second is revelation: each verse of the Qur'an is an *āyah*, and the Qur'an calls itself *"clear signs (āyāt bayyināt)"* (2:99). The two fields are not separate; both are communications from the same Lord, one written in matter and the other in words. The sūrah has moved between them freely, presenting the embryo and the Flood with the same word.

Verse 58's "signs of their Lord" therefore includes both. The believer believes in the *cosmic* signs — he reads the world as pointing to its Maker — and in the *revealed* signs — he accepts the Qur'an as God's word. The deniers rejected both: they looked at the world and saw only matter (v. 37: *"there is nothing but our worldly life"*), and they looked at the revelation and saw only *"a man who has invented a lie"* (v. 38). The believer's second quality is precisely what they lacked.

**Why "Their Lord" Again**

The verse repeats the phrase *rabbihim*, "their Lord," which appeared in verse 57 and will appear again in verses 59 and 60. Four times in four verses, the believers are defined by their relationship to *their Lord*. The repetition is not accidental. It fixes the source of all four qualities: the fear is fear *of their Lord*; the faith is faith *in the signs of their Lord*; the refusal of shirk is a refusal to associate anything *with their Lord*; the trembling is the trembling of those who know they will return *to their Lord*. The believers are people whose whole inner life is oriented toward a single Person. This orientation is what verse 52 called the basis of the one community — *"I am your Lord"* — and what verse 53's factions lost when they turned toward their parties.

**Faith in Signs Means Reading Them Correctly**

To believe in the signs is not merely to affirm that they exist; it is to read them as signs — to let them point where they point. The deniers of verses 55–56 *saw* their wealth and children but read them wrongly, as proof of favor rather than as tests. The believer of verse 58 reads the same phenomena correctly. He sees rain and thinks of the One who sends it *"in measure"* (v. 18); he sees his own body and remembers *"a drop in a firm lodging"* (v. 13); he sees a ruined city and remembers *"how many generations We destroyed"* (v. 42). Faith in signs is a way of seeing. The Qur'an describes its opposite: *"And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by while they turn away from it"* (12:105). The sign is there; the denier passes it; the believer stops.

This is why the verse's second quality follows naturally from its first. Fear of God (v. 57) opens the eyes; a person who is awed by God looks for Him everywhere and finds His signs everywhere. The complacent person has no motive to look. The sequence fear → faith is a psychological sequence: reverence precedes recognition.

**Believing in All the Signs**

The verse says *bi-āyāti rabbihim* — "in the signs of their Lord" — without qualification, implying *all* of them.
