This matters, because a characteristic of the factions described in verse 53 was selective belief: each took its own "piece" (*zubur*) and rejected the rest. The Qur'an condemns this partiality sharply: *"Do you believe in part of the Scripture and disbelieve in part? Then what is the recompense for those who do that among you except disgrace in worldly life, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be sent back to the severest of punishment"* (2:85). The believer of verse 58 accepts the signs whole — the ones that comfort and the ones that demand, the ones that promise Paradise and the ones that command zakāh and chastity. Partial faith is the beginning of a *ḥizb*; whole faith is the mark of the *ummah wāḥidah*.

**The Signs and the Prophet's Response**

The Prophet ﷺ modeled belief in the signs of the created world as a continuous act. When he looked at the sky, he recited the closing verses of Sūrah Āl ʿImrān — *"Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth..."* (3:190–200) — and wept (Ibn Ḥibbān; al-Bukhārī records his recitation of these verses on rising at night, 4569). Ibn Masʿūd said of him that he never passed an occasion for remembering God without taking it. To him, nothing was merely itself; everything was an *āyah*. This is the disposition verse 58 describes, and it is a disposition anyone can cultivate: to look at the ordinary — a seed, a child, a storm — and ask what it points to.

**Faith in Signs Is Not Credulity**

It should be clear that the faith verse 58 praises is not the acceptance of anything one is told. The sūrah has spent forty verses *building* the evidence: it argued from embryology, cosmology, agriculture, zoology, and history before naming faith in signs as a virtue. The believer's faith is a response to signs that have been shown, not a leap taken in the dark. The Qur'an repeatedly invites examination — *"Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?"* (88:17); *"Say, 'Travel through the land and observe'"* (6:11) — and it condemns those who believe without thought as sharply as those who deny without thought: *"the worst of creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not use reason"* (8:22). Verse 58's believer has looked, and believed because he looked.

**The Verse for the Believer**

The second quality asks: Do you believe in the signs of your Lord — all of them, in both fields, read correctly? Practically, this means: Do you read the Qur'an as God's word, accepting what it says even where it corrects you? And do you read the world as God's work, seeing in your own body, your provision, your children, and your circumstances the hand of the One who arranges them? The person who does both lives in a world that is continuously speaking, and he is continuously listening. The person who does neither lives, as verse 54 said, in a *ghamrah* — surrounded by signs and perceiving none.

**Toward the Third Quality**

Faith in the signs leads to the third quality: purity of worship. One who accepts that the signs point to *one* Lord will not give what belongs to Him to another. Verse 59 names this: *"and those who do not associate anything with their Lord."*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:59

> **and those who ascribe not partners unto their Lord,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Quality: Purity of Devotion**

The second portrait of the believers continues with its third quality: *wa lladhīna hum bi-rabbihim lā yushrikūn* — "and those who, with their Lord, do not associate [anything]." After fear (v. 57) and faith in the signs (v. 58), the sūrah names the refusal of *shirk* — the ascription of partners to God. At first reading this may seem redundant: surely one who believes in the signs of the one Lord does not associate others with Him? But the classical commentators, and al-Rāzī in particular as the source notes, understood the verse to refer not only to the gross *shirk* of idolatry but to its subtle forms — the *shirk* that can coexist with outward monotheism and that the Prophet ﷺ called "hidden." The verse is therefore not redundant but searching: it asks whether the believer's devotion is *entirely* for God, or whether something else has crept in.

**The Root of Shirk**

The verb *yushrikūn* is from the root *sh-r-k*, "to share, to be a partner." A *sharīk* is a partner; *shirk* is the act of making something a partner with God — in His lordship, His worship, or His names and attributes. The Qur'an calls *shirk* the one sin God does not forgive if a person dies in it: *"Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills"* (4:48); and it calls it *"a tremendous wrong"* (31:13), because it gives to the creature what belongs only to the Creator. The sūrah's messengers preached against it in one sentence: *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him"* (vv. 23, 32). Verse 59 names the believers as those who have taken that sentence into their hearts.

**The Grosser and the Subtler Forms**

The Makkan deniers practiced *shirk* openly: they worshipped idols alongside God, ascribed daughters to Him, and called on intermediaries. The believers of verse 59 have rejected all of that. But al-Rāzī's reading — that the verse targets *hidden* shirk — is grounded in the verse's context. It comes in a list of *inner* qualities: reverential fear, sincere faith, and (in the next verse) a trembling heart. In such a list, the mention of *shirk* naturally extends to the inner forms of it that a believer must guard against.

The Prophet ﷺ identified the primary hidden form: *"The thing I fear most for you is the lesser shirk."* They asked what that was, and he said: *"Showing off (al-riyāʾ). God will say on the Day of Resurrection, when He recompenses people for their deeds: 'Go to those for whom you used to show off in the world, and see whether you find any reward with them'"* (Aḥmad 23630; graded ṣaḥīḥ). *Riyāʾ* — performing a good deed for the sake of being seen — is *shirk* because it gives a share of the worship to the human audience. The deed is outwardly for God; inwardly it is divided.

Other subtle forms include: relying on means rather than on the One who created the means; fearing creatures as one should fear only God; loving something with the love due only to God (*"And among the people are those who take other than God as equals, loving them as they love God,"* 2:165); and obeying human authorities in what contradicts God's command (*"They have taken their scholars and monks as lords besides God,"* 9:31 — which the Prophet ﷺ explained to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim as meaning they obeyed them in permitting the forbidden and forbidding the permitted; al-Tirmidhī 3095).

**The Prophet's Prayer Against Hidden Shirk**

The Prophet ﷺ taught his Companions that hidden *shirk* is *"more subtle than the creeping of an ant,"* and he taught a supplication against it: *"O God, I seek refuge in You from associating anything with You while I know, and I seek Your forgiveness for what I do not know"* (Aḥmad 19606; al-Bukhārī, *al-Adab al-Mufrad* 716; graded ḥasan). The prayer acknowledges two levels: *shirk* one is aware of and can refuse, and *shirk* one is not aware of and can only ask forgiveness for. The believer of verse 59 is one who takes both levels seriously — who examines his motives and, finding them mixed, asks God to purify them.

**Why This Quality Follows Faith in the Signs**

The three qualities so far form a chain. Fear of God (v. 57) opens the eyes to His signs; faith in the signs (v. 58) establishes that He is one; the refusal of *shirk* (v. 59) is the *practical* consequence of that faith. A person who truly believes the signs point to one Lord cannot consistently divide his devotion. When he does — when he prays for show, or trusts his wealth more than God, or fears people more than God — he has, in that moment, stopped reading the signs correctly. Verse 59 is thus not a new subject but the test of whether verse 58's faith has taken hold.

The chain also reflects the sūrah's argument against the deniers. Their *shirk* was rooted in a failure to read signs: they saw wealth and children (v. 55) and gave those things the significance that belongs to God alone — treating them as proof of favor, as sources of security, as the measure of success. That is a form of *shirk*: attributing to created things what belongs to the Creator. The believers of verse 59 have not done this. They receive wealth and children (v. 60 will describe them *giving*) without treating them as gods.

**Sincerity as the Condition of Every Deed**

The refusal of *shirk*, in its inner form, is what Islamic scholarship calls *ikhlāṣ* — sincerity, the purification of intention so that a deed is done for God alone. The Qur'an makes *ikhlāṣ* the condition of acceptable worship: *"And they were not commanded except to worship God, sincere to Him in religion"* (98:5); *"So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate in the worship of his Lord anyone"* (18:110). The Prophet ﷺ reported God as saying: *"I am the most self-sufficient of partners. Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I abandon him and his association"* (Muslim 2985). A deed done partly for God and partly for something else is not divided between them; it is rejected entirely.

This is why verse 59 stands where it does — immediately before verse 60, which describes the believers *giving* with trembling hearts. The giving would be worthless if it were for show. Verse 59 guarantees that it is not.

**The Verse for the Believer**

The third quality asks the hardest question of the four: not "do you worship idols?" — the answer is easily no — but "is anything sharing in what you offer God?" When you pray in public, is any part of it for the eyes watching? When you give, is any part for reputation? When you speak of religion, is any part for the admiration of hearing yourself? When you trust in your savings or your connections or your skill, has any of that trust been withdrawn from God? The Prophet's teaching that hidden *shirk* is "more subtle than the creeping of an ant" means that no one can answer these questions with a confident "nothing." The believer of verse 59 is not the one who has *achieved* perfect sincerity but the one who *watches* for its failure, refuses what he catches, and asks forgiveness for what he misses.

**Toward the Trembling Heart**

Fear, faith, and sincerity now produce their characteristic act: the believers give — and their hearts tremble as they give, because they know to whom they are returning. Verse 60 describes this, and a famous exchange between the Prophet ﷺ and ʿĀʾishah explains it.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:60

> **and those who give what they give while their hearts quake with fear that they shall return to their Lord—**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fourth Quality: Giving With a Trembling Heart**

The second portrait of the believers reaches its most vivid quality: *wa lladhīna yuʾtūna mā ātaw wa qulūbuhum wajilatun annahum ilā rabbihim rājiʿūn* — "and those who give what they give while their hearts are trembling because they will return to their Lord." The three preceding qualities — fear (v. 57), faith in the signs (v. 58), and refusal of *shirk* (v. 59) — were inner states. Verse 60 shows them producing an act, and shows the state of the heart *during* the act. The believers give; and as they give, their hearts tremble. The verse is the sūrah's answer to the question raised by verses 55–56: if wealth and children are not signs of favor, what is the right relationship to what one has? The answer is: give from it, and do not feel secure even in giving.

**"They Give What They Give": Yuʾtūna Mā Ātaw**

The verb *yuʾtūna* means "they give," and *mā ātaw* means "what they give" or "what they have given." The phrasing is deliberately general. It includes charity — the *zakāh* of verse 4 and voluntary giving — but the commentators extend it to every act of worship offered to God: prayer, fasting, kindness, obedience of every kind. The believers "give what they give" means: they offer to God whatever they offer. A minority reading, *yaʾtūna mā ataw* ("they do what they do"), attributed to ʿĀʾishah and others, makes this broader sense explicit; both readings converge on the same meaning: the verse describes the believers' *deeds* in general, of which giving is the representative case.

The generality matters because it prevents a narrow reading. The verse does not say "those who give large amounts" or "those who give often." It says "those who give what they give" — whatever the amount, whatever the act — with a particular state of heart. The quality praised is not the size of the offering but the condition of the one offering.

**"While Their Hearts Are Trembling": Qulūbuhum Wajilah**

The word *wajilah* is from the root *w-j-l*, which denotes the fear that makes the heart quake — a fear felt physically, as a tremor. The Qur'an uses it for the believers' response to God's mention: *"The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble (wajilat qulūbuhum)"* (8:2); and for Abraham's guests, who reassured him: *"Do not be afraid (lā tawjal)"* (15:53). The believers of verse 60 give, and *while* giving, their hearts are in this state — not calm, not self-satisfied, but quaking.

Why? The verse explains: *annahum ilā rabbihim rājiʿūn* — "because they will return to their Lord." They know that every deed will be reviewed, and they are not certain that theirs will pass the review. The trembling is the trembling of a person handing in work to an examiner whose standards he cannot fully meet. The Qur'an describes this consciousness of return repeatedly: *"And fear a Day when you will be returned to God; then every soul will be compensated for what it earned"* (2:281); *"Indeed, to your Lord is the return"* (96:8). The believers of verse 60 hold this Day in mind at the very moment of giving — and the holding produces the tremor.

**ʿĀʾishah's Question and the Prophet's Answer**

The verse's meaning is fixed by a ḥadīth that the source rightly places at its center. ʿĀʾishah asked the Prophet ﷺ about this verse, saying: *"Is it the one who steals, fornicates, and drinks wine, while fearing God?"* She assumed — reasonably, on the surface — that a "trembling heart" belonged to the sinner who fears punishment for his sins. The Prophet ﷺ corrected her:

> *"No, O daughter of al-Ṣiddīq. Rather, it is the one who prays, fasts, and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him."* (al-Tirmidhī 3175; Ibn Mājah 4198; Aḥmad 25263; graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī)

The ḥadīth reverses the natural reading. The trembling is not the guilt of the wrongdoer; it is the humility of the *righteous* who do not presume their righteousness is enough. This is a profound psychological and theological point. The sinner's fear is about *what he has done wrong*; the believer's fear is about *whether what he has done right is acceptable*. The first is fear of consequences; the second is fear of one's own insufficiency before God's greatness. The verse describes the second, and al-Tirmidhī's version adds that the Prophet ﷺ then recited verse 61: *"It is those who hasten in good deeds."* Those who tremble over their good deeds are the same who hasten to do more — because they never feel they have done enough.

**The Contrast With the Deniers Completed**

Verses 55–56 described the deniers *receiving* wealth and children and *rejoicing* in them as proof of favor, secure and unperceiving. Verse 60 describes the believers *giving* from what they have and *trembling* over whether it is accepted. Every element is inverted: receive/give, rejoice/tremble, secure/apprehensive, unperceiving/acutely aware of the return. The deniers thought that what they *had* was good hastened to them; the believers know that what they *give* may or may not be accepted. The sūrah's structure — deniers in 55–56, believers in 57–61 — is a diptych, and verse 60 is its hinge.

**Why the Righteous Fear More Than the Wicked**

The ḥadīth raises a question: why should those who do good fear more than those who do evil? The answer lies in knowledge. The person who does good and *knows God* understands how imperfect his offering is — how mixed his intentions, how distracted his prayer, how grudging his charity — measured against the One it is offered to. The person who does evil and does *not* know God has no such standard and therefore no such fear. This is the meaning of 35:28: *"Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God."* The fear of the righteous is not neurosis; it is accuracy. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī expressed it: *"The believer combines doing good with fear; the hypocrite combines doing evil with security."*

The Companions lived this. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, promised Paradise by the Prophet ﷺ himself, is reported to have said as he lay dying: *"If I had the whole earth in gold, I would ransom myself with it from the punishment of God before I see it."* Ibn Abī Mulaykah said: *"I met thirty of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, every one of them fearing hypocrisy for himself; not one of them said that his faith was like the faith of Gabriel and Michael"* (al-Bukhārī, in the chapter heading on fear of hypocrisy). These were not people with sins to fear; they were people whose *good deeds* they did not trust. That is verse 60.

**Giving and the Sūrah's Opening**

Verse 60 recalls verse 4, where the believers were described as *"those who are active in zakāh."* There the emphasis was on the doing; here it is on the state during the doing. The two verses together give the full picture: the believer *acts* — he gives, regularly and as duty — and he acts *with a trembling heart*. Neither alone is the sūrah's ideal. Giving without trembling becomes self-congratulation; trembling without giving becomes paralysis. The believer does both at once, and verse 61 will name the result: he hastens in good deeds and is foremost in them.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 60 offers a test of one's inner state after any good deed. When you have prayed, given, fasted, or helped, what is the feeling that follows? If it is satisfaction — "that was good; I have done well" — the verse suggests something is missing. If it is a quiet unease — "I hope it was accepted; I know it was not what it should have been" — that is the *wajal* of verse 60, and the Prophet ﷺ named it as the mark of the righteous. The unease should not become despair (v. 57 taught that *ishfāq* is fear mixed with tender hope), but it should not be replaced by security either. The believer's proper state after a good deed is the state of one who has handed something to his Lord and is waiting, with a trembling heart, to learn whether it was received.

**Toward the Result**

Four qualities have been named. Verse 61 gives their consequence — and it uses the exact words that verse 56 used of the deniers, turned right side up.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:61

> **it is they who hasten toward good deeds, and are foremost in them.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Predicate of the Long Sentence**

Verses 57–60 formed the subject of a single sentence — "Indeed, those who fear..., and those who believe..., and those who do not associate..., and those who give with trembling hearts..." — and verse 61 supplies its predicate: *ulāʾika yusāriʿūna fī l-khayrāt wa hum lahā sābiqūn* — "It is they who hasten in good deeds, and they are foremost in them." The demonstrative *ulāʾika*, "those," gathers the four qualities into a single group and pronounces on them. The pronouncement is not a reward but a description: this is what such people *do*. Fear, faith, sincerity, and trembling do not produce hesitation; they produce speed. The believers race.

**The Reversal of Verse 56**

The verse's vocabulary is the sūrah's own from five verses earlier. Verse 56 asked whether the deniers thought God was *"hastening (nusāriʿu) to them good things (al-khayrāt)."* Verse 61 declares that the believers are the ones who *"hasten (yusāriʿūna) in good deeds (al-khayrāt)."* The same verb, the same noun. But the direction is reversed. The deniers imagined *khayrāt* flowing *to* them; the believers move *toward khayrāt*. The deniers' *khayrāt* were wealth and children, received passively; the believers' *khayrāt* are righteous deeds, pursued actively. The sūrah's answer to the question of verse 56 is therefore not only "no, God is not hastening good to them," but "here is what hastening in good actually looks like."

This reversal exposes the deniers' error at its root. They thought that the sign of God's favor was what one *gets*. The sūrah teaches that the sign is what one *does*. A person may receive abundantly and be under *istidrāj*; a person may have little and be *sābiq*, foremost. The measure is not the inflow but the direction of movement.

**"They Hasten": Yusāriʿūna**

The verb *yusāriʿūna*, Form III of *s-r-ʿ*, means to hurry, to race, to compete in speed. Form III carries a sense of mutual or competitive action: the believers are not merely quick but *racing* — with each other, against time, toward the good. The Qur'an commands this racing explicitly: *"So race to good deeds (fa-stabiqū l-khayrāt)"* (2:148); *"And hasten (sāriʿū) to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth"* (3:133); *"Race (sābiqū) to forgiveness from your Lord"* (57:21). The Companions understood these as literal commands to compete. The Prophet ﷺ once asked who had fasted, followed a funeral, fed a poor person, and visited a sick person that day; only Abū Bakr had done all four, and the Prophet ﷺ said: *"These are not combined in a person except that he enters Paradise"* (Muslim 1028). ʿUmar said of trying to outdo Abū Bakr in charity on the day of Tabūk — bringing half his wealth while Abū Bakr brought all of his — *"I will never compete with him in anything after this"* (Abū Dāwūd 1678; al-Tirmidhī 3675).

Why haste? Because time is short (v. 43: no one can hasten or delay his term), because the opportunity for deeds ends at death (v. 100: "send me back that I might do righteousness" — too late), and because the one who trembles over whether his deeds are accepted (v. 60) naturally tries to do as many as possible. Fear and haste are cause and effect: a person who is anxious about an approaching examination studies harder, not less.

**"And They Are Foremost in Them": Sābiqūn**

The second clause intensifies the first: *wa hum lahā sābiqūn* — "and they, for them, are foremost / outstrippers." The word *sābiq* (plural *sābiqūn*) means one who precedes, who wins the race, who arrives first. The believers do not merely hasten; they *arrive ahead*. The Qur'an gives this word a technical sense in describing the ranks of the Hereafter: *"And the foremost (al-sābiqūn), the foremost — those are the ones brought near, in the Gardens of Pleasure"* (56:10–12), and in describing the first Muslims: *"And the first forerunners (al-sābiqūn al-awwalūn) among the Emigrants and the Helpers... God is pleased with them"* (9:100). The source connects verse 61 to both passages, and rightly: the *sābiqūn* of verse 61 are the same class — those who not only do good but do it *first*, *most*, and *best*.

The preposition *lahā*, "for them" or "to them," has been read in two ways. On one reading, the believers are foremost *to* good deeds — they reach them first. On another, good deeds are *for* them — destined for them, prepared for them, such that they were always going to arrive. The second reading connects to a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that a person is guided toward the deeds for which he was created (al-Bukhārī 4949; Muslim 2647). Both readings hold: the believers race to the good, and the good was theirs to reach.

**Why Fear Produces Speed, Not Paralysis**

There is a psychological objection to verse 61 that must be answered: does not fear paralyze? Do not anxious people freeze? The sūrah's answer lies in the *kind* of fear it has described. Verse 57's fear was *ishfāq* — fear mixed with tender hope. Verse 60's trembling was over whether deeds would be *accepted*, not over whether to do them. This kind of fear is directional: it points toward more effort, better effort, purer effort. It is the fear of the athlete who wants to win and knows he might not, not the fear of the person who dares not enter the race. Paralyzing fear arises from hopelessness; the believer's fear arises from hope — and hope moves.

The Prophet ﷺ, who feared God most, was also the most active in worship. He prayed at night until his feet swelled, and when ʿĀʾishah asked why, since his past and future sins were forgiven, he said: *"Should I not be a grateful servant?"* (al-Bukhārī 4837; Muslim 2820). His fear and his haste were one thing.

**The Portrait Completed**

The second portrait of the believers is now complete, and it can be read as a unit. They fear their Lord with awe (v. 57); they believe His signs (v. 58); they give Him no partner, open or hidden (v. 59); they give what they give with hearts trembling at the thought of their return (v. 60); and therefore they race toward good and arrive first (v. 61). The portrait is entirely inward until its final line, where the inward bursts into motion. This is the sūrah's teaching on the relationship between the heart and the hand: the heart in its right state does not stay still; it drives the hand to act, and to act quickly.

Set beside the first portrait (vv. 1–9), the second explains it. The first portrait listed the deeds — prayer, turning from vain talk, zakāh, chastity, trusts, covenants, guarding the prayers. The second portrait names the inner engine that makes those deeds not merely performed but *raced toward*. A person may pray and give without racing, and the sūrah counted such a person among the believers if he was faithful; but the one who prays and gives *while trembling* and *hastening* is *sābiq*, foremost, and the sūrah reserves its highest description for him.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 61 asks: Are you hastening, or strolling? The believer who has the four qualities of verses 57–60 will find that his pace toward good deeds increases without his forcing it — because fear of God does not let him rest, faith in the signs keeps him aware of what is coming, sincerity frees him from the exhausting management of appearances, and the trembling of verse 60 keeps him from stopping to admire what he has done. If the pace is slack, the verse suggests examining the four qualities: which is weak? The sūrah's ordering implies that the remedy for slowness in good is not more resolve but more *khashyah* — more awe of the Lord to whom one returns.

**Toward the Limits of Obligation**

The portrait might seem to demand more than a human being can give. The next verse immediately reassures: *"We task no soul beyond its capacity."* The racing is asked; the impossible is not.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:62

> **And We task no soul beyond its capacity, and with Us is a Book that speaks in truth. And they shall not be wronged.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reassurance After the Demand**

Verses 57–61 have described the believers at their highest — trembling in awe, racing to good, foremost in every virtue. A reader might feel the description as a burden: who can live like that? Verse 62 answers before the question is asked: *wa lā nukallifu nafsan illā wusʿahā wa ladaynā kitābun yanṭiqu bi-l-ḥaqq wa hum lā yuẓlamūn* — "And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity; and with Us is a record that speaks with truth; and they will not be wronged." The verse has three clauses, and together they establish the framework of divine justice within which the believers' racing takes place: the demand is proportioned to ability; the account is exact; and the outcome is fair. The racing of verse 61 is not a demand for the impossible but an invitation within the possible.

**"We Do Not Burden Any Soul Beyond Its Capacity"**

The first clause is one of the Qur'an's most repeated principles. The verb *nukallifu*, from the root *k-l-f*, means to charge, to assign a task, to impose an obligation (*taklīf* is the technical term for legal and moral responsibility). The object *nafsan*, "any soul," is indefinite and universal: no soul whatsoever. The limit is *wusʿahā* — "its capacity," from the root *w-s-ʿ*, which denotes breadth, spaciousness, what one can encompass. God assigns each soul only what falls within its breadth.

The principle appears in nearly identical words at 2:286: *"God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity; it will have what it has earned, and it will bear what it has earned."* At 6:152 and 7:42 it accompanies commands about justice in measure and about the people of Paradise; at 65:7 it governs financial obligation: *"God does not burden any soul except with what He has given it."* The source notes these parallels. In the context of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn, the principle comes immediately after the portrait of the foremost, and its function is to define the terms of the race: the believers of verse 61 are not required to match each other, only to give what each is able. The one with little wealth who gives from it with a trembling heart is no less *sābiq* than the one with much.

The Prophet ﷺ applied this principle constantly. He said: *"Take on of deeds what you are able, for God does not tire until you tire"* (al-Bukhārī 43; Muslim 782), and: *"Religion is ease, and no one makes religion severe except that it overcomes him; so be moderate, approach [perfection], and give glad tidings"* (al-Bukhārī 39). When a Companion tried to fast every day and pray every night, the Prophet ﷺ forbade it and set a limit he could sustain (al-Bukhārī 1975; Muslim 1159). The racing of verse 61 is within one's capacity; going beyond it is not piety but a failure to understand verse 62.

**Capacity and Its Implications**

The principle has consequences that the scholars drew out. First, obligation is lifted or reduced by incapacity: the sick pray sitting, the traveler shortens prayer, the poor are exempt from zakāh and pilgrimage, the one who cannot fast feeds the poor instead. Second, God's commands are inherently *possible*, so no one can plead that faith or righteousness was beyond him — the deniers of the sūrah cannot say that belief was impossible for them. Third, the principle is a statement about God's *character*: He is not a tyrant who demands what cannot be given. The verse's placement after the description of those who fear Him (v. 57) is a corrective against a distorted fear: God is to be feared, but He is not to be feared as one fears an unjust master. He measures the load to the back.

There is also a hidden mercy in the phrase. "Capacity" is set by God, and He knows it better than the soul itself. A person often underestimates what he can bear — and the sūrah's believers, who "hasten" and are "foremost," are those who have discovered that their capacity is greater than they assumed. The principle does not say "do little"; it says "you will not be asked for more than you can do" — which leaves open the question of how much that is.

**"With Us Is a Record That Speaks With Truth"**

The second clause introduces the *kitāb* — the record, the book. The word is the same used for scripture, but here it means the register of deeds. Every soul's actions are written, and the book is *ladaynā*, "with Us" — in God's keeping, beyond tampering. The book *yanṭiqu bi-l-ḥaqq* — "speaks with truth." The verb *yanṭiqu*, from the root *n-ṭ-q*, means to articulate, to utter speech. The record does not merely exist; it *speaks*, and what it says is *al-ḥaqq*, the truth — nothing added, nothing omitted.

The Qur'an describes this record in several places. *"And the record will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is within it, and they will say, 'Woe to us! What is this book that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?' And they will find what they did present"* (18:49). *"This, Our record, speaks about you in truth (yanṭiqu ʿalaykum bi-l-ḥaqq). Indeed, We were having transcribed whatever you used to do"* (45:29). *"And every small and great thing is inscribed"* (54:53). The source cites 18:49 and 45:29; both establish that the record is complete and that it will testify.

The relevance to the surrounding verses is exact. The believers of verse 60 give with trembling hearts because they *"will return to their Lord."* Verse 62 tells them what awaits at that return: a truthful record. Their trembling is justified — everything is written — and also bounded — the record speaks *truth*, so nothing they did will be lost or misattributed. The deniers of verses 55–56, meanwhile, imagined that their wealth was their record of favor; verse 62 tells them that the real record is elsewhere and says something different.

**"And They Will Not Be Wronged"**

The third clause closes the verse: *wa hum lā yuẓlamūn* — "and they will not be wronged." The verb *yuẓlamūn*, from *ẓ-l-m*, means to be treated unjustly, to be given less than one's due or more than one's deserving. The passive "they will not be wronged" means: no one will be deprived of a good deed he did, and no one will be charged with an evil deed he did not do. The Qur'an repeats this promise as a fixed feature of the Judgment: *"And your Lord does not wrong anyone"* (18:49); *"Indeed, God does not wrong the people at all, but the people wrong themselves"* (10:44); *"And We place the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged at all; and if there is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth"* (21:47).

The pronoun "they" is general, covering believers and deniers alike. For the believers, "not wronged" means that every trembling gift, every raced-toward deed, is preserved and rewarded fully — and more than fully, since God multiplies good deeds (6:160). For the deniers, "not wronged" means that their punishment will be exactly what they earned, no more — which is a mercy in its precision and a terror in its accuracy.

**The Three Clauses as a System**

Read together, the three clauses describe a complete system of justice. (1) The demand is proportioned: God asks only what each can give. (2) The record is exact: everything given is written truthfully. (3) The outcome is fair: no one loses what he earned or bears what he did not. This system is the theological foundation of the believers' way of life. They can race (v. 61) because the race is within their strength (clause 1); they can tremble (v. 60) because the record is real (clause 2); and they can hope because the Judge is just (clause 3). The deniers' way of life, by contrast, denied all three: they thought God demanded nothing, recorded nothing, and had already rewarded them with wealth.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 62 is a verse for the exhausted and the anxious. To the one who feels that faith demands more than he can give, it says: God knows your capacity and asks nothing beyond it. To the one who fears that his small deeds are lost in obscurity, it says: there is a record with God, and it speaks truth. To the one who fears the Judgment as an arbitrary sentence, it says: you will not be wronged. The verse does not lower the standard of verses 57–61 — the believers are still those who fear, believe, refuse shirk, tremble, and race — but it frames that standard in mercy. The race is real; the track is fair; the judge is just; and the runner is asked only for the speed he has.

**Toward the Hearts in Confusion**

Having established justice, the sūrah returns to those who have ignored it. Verse 63 will describe the deniers' hearts as submerged in *ghamrah* — the word of verse 54 — and will say that they have deeds "other than" the good deeds of the believers, which they are busy doing.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:63

> **Nay, indeed their hearts are engrossed away from this, and they have other deeds besides which they undertake,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Return to the Deniers**

After the portrait of the believers (vv. 57–61) and the statement of divine justice (v. 62), the sūrah turns back to the deniers with the particle *bal* — "nay, rather": *bal qulūbuhum fī ghamratin min hādhā wa lahum aʿmālun min dūni dhālika hum lahā ʿāmilūn* — "Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that which they are doing." The *bal* marks a contrast with everything just said. The believers' hearts tremble (v. 60); the deniers' hearts are submerged. The believers race toward good deeds (v. 61); the deniers are busy with *other* deeds. The record speaks truth about everyone (v. 62); the deniers have not considered what it says about them. The verse is a diagnosis in two parts — the state of the heart and the direction of the hands.

**"Their Hearts Are in Confusion About This"**

The word *ghamrah* returns from verse 54, where God commanded the Prophet ﷺ to *"leave them in their ghamrah for a time."* There, the *ghamrah* was the general state of the factions; here, it is located precisely — *in their hearts* — and its object is specified — *min hādhā*, "about this." What is "this"? The commentators offer several referents, and the verse's context supports all of them: the Qur'an; the record that speaks truth (v. 62); the way of the believers just described (vv. 57–61); the reality of the return to God (v. 60). The deniers' hearts are submerged with respect to *all* of this — they cannot see the Qur'an as revelation, the record as real, the believers' way as wise, or the return as coming.

The image of *ghamrah* as water over the head was explained under verse 54. Its use here for the *heart* is precise. The Qur'an treats the heart as the organ of understanding: *"Do they not travel through the land, so that their hearts may understand?"* (22:46). A heart in *ghamrah* is a heart whose understanding is flooded — it receives the signs (v. 58) and cannot process them, because the water of heedlessness is above it. Verse 56 said the deniers *"do not perceive"*; verse 63 says why: the perceiving organ is underwater.

**"And They Have Deeds Other Than That"**

The second clause is more subtle and, in some ways, more disturbing: *wa lahum aʿmālun min dūni dhālika hum lahā ʿāmilūn* — "and they have deeds other than that, which they are doing." The word *aʿmāl*, deeds, is the same word the Qur'an uses for the believers' *ṣāliḥāt*; the deniers, too, have *aʿmāl*. But theirs are *min dūni dhālika* — "other than that," "besides that," "short of that" — that is, other than the good deeds the believers race toward. And they are actively engaged in them: *hum lahā ʿāmilūn*, "they are doers of them," a construction emphasizing continuous activity.

The commentators developed this clause in two directions, and both are sound. The first, following Ibn ʿAbbās and others: the deniers have *evil* deeds — the sins and rejections they commit — which they are busy with, and which the record (v. 62) is writing. The second: the deniers have deeds they consider good — worldly enterprises, acts of tribal generosity, the very accumulation of wealth and children that verses 55–56 described — but these deeds are "other than" what counts, because they are not done for God (v. 59) and not grounded in faith (v. 58). On this second reading, the verse is not saying only that the deniers do wrong but that even their apparently right actions fall outside the category of *khayrāt*, because the heart doing them is in *ghamrah*.

The second reading is supported by the Qur'an's general teaching: *"And We will regard what they have done of deeds and make them as dust dispersed"* (25:23); *"The example of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows forcefully on a stormy day; they are unable to keep from what they earned anything"* (14:18). The deniers are not idle; they are *busy* — but their busyness produces nothing that survives.

**Busyness as a Form of Heedlessness**

This clause exposes a truth about the human condition that the sūrah has been building toward since verse 3, where the believers were described as *"turning away from vain talk."* The opposite of righteous action is not always inaction; more often it is *other* action — the endless activity that fills a life and leaves no room for what matters. The deniers of verse 63 were not lazy men; the Makkan merchants were among the most industrious of their age. They traded, built, negotiated, raised families, defended honor. All of it was *aʿmāl*. And all of it was *min dūni dhālika* — beside the point.

The Qur'an describes this condition elsewhere as being *diverted*: *"Competition in increase diverts you (alhākum al-takāthur) until you visit the graves"* (102:1–2); *"O you who believe, let not your wealth and your children divert you (lā tulhikum) from the remembrance of God"* (63:9). The word for diversion, *lahw*, is related to the *laghw* of verse 3. The deniers of verse 63 have been diverted — not by idleness but by industry. Their hands are full, and their hearts are underwater.

**The Two Halves Connected**

The two clauses of verse 63 are cause and effect. Because the heart is in *ghamrah*, the hands do *other* deeds. A heart that perceived the return to God (v. 60) would direct the hands toward *khayrāt* (v. 61); a heart submerged in heedlessness directs them toward whatever is nearest — profit, pleasure, status, the "wealth and children" of verse 55. The sūrah's anthropology is consistent: the heart is the seat of direction, and the deeds follow. The Prophet ﷺ stated the principle: *"Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart"* (al-Bukhārī 52; Muslim 1599).

**The Pronoun "This" and the Qur'an**

If *hādhā*, "this," refers specifically to the Qur'an — a reading many commentators favored — the verse becomes a statement about the deniers' relationship to revelation. Their hearts are in *ghamrah* about *this Book*: they hear it and it does not enter, because the flood of their heedlessness keeps it out. This connects to verse 68, where the sūrah will ask: *"Have they not pondered the Word?"* The answer, supplied in advance by verse 63, is that they cannot ponder it, because pondering requires a heart above water. It also connects to the sūrah's later description of the deniers turning away from the recitation *"on your heels, in arrogance, talking nonsense by night"* (vv. 66–67). The *ghamrah* of the heart produces the turning-away of the body.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 63 is a warning against a specific and modern danger: the substitution of activity for direction. A believer can be extremely busy — with work, family, projects, even religious projects — and yet have a heart that is drifting into *ghamrah*, because the busyness has crowded out the trembling of verse 60 and the racing of verse 61. The test the verse supplies is: *What are my deeds for?* If the honest answer is "for themselves" or "for this life" or "because that is what one does," then they may be *aʿmāl min dūni dhālika* — deeds beside the point, however impressive. The remedy is not to stop working but to recover the heart: to pull it above the water by the remembrance of God, by reflection on the signs (v. 58), by the consciousness of return (v. 60) — so that the same deeds, done by a heart that is awake, become *khayrāt*.

The verse also counsels realism about others. Those in *ghamrah* are not persuaded by argument alone, because the argument does not reach a submerged heart. This is why verse 54 said "leave them for a time." The time will come — and the next verse describes it — when the water is disturbed by a shock.

**Toward the Seizing**

The deniers' hearts are underwater, their hands full of other deeds. The sūrah now describes the moment when their affluence — the very thing they read as favor — is seized, and they cry out.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:64

> **till, when We seize those of them who lived in luxury with the punishment, behold, they shall implore!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The End of the Reprieve**

Verse 54 said: *"Leave them in their confusion for a time (ḥattā ḥīn)."* Verse 64 begins with the same word — *ḥattā*, "until" — and describes the time's arrival: *ḥattā idhā akhadhnā mutrafīhim bi-l-ʿadhāb idhā hum yajʾarūn* — "Until, when We seize their affluent ones with the punishment, at once they cry out." The verse closes the arc opened ten verses earlier. The deniers were left in their *ghamrah*, busy with their other deeds (v. 63); now the *ghamrah* is broken, not by argument, but by seizure. The people who could not be reached by the Qur'an are reached by pain — and the first sound they make is a cry.

**"When We Seize": Akhadhnā**

The verb *akhadhnā* is from the root *a-kh-dh*, "to take, to grasp." God's "taking" is the Qur'an's standard word for the sudden onset of punishment: *"So each We seized (akhadhnā) for his sin"* (29:40); *"Thus is the seizure (akhdh) of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are doing wrong; indeed, His seizure is painful and severe"* (11:102). The word implies suddenness and inescapability — a hand closing on something that cannot slip out. The sūrah used the same root at verse 41: *"So the Cry seized them (akhadhathum) in truth."* The past generations were seized; now the present one is.

**"Their Affluent Ones": Mutrafīhim**

The word *mutrafīhim* is the key term. It is the plural of *mutraf*, the passive participle of *atrafa* — the verb the sūrah used in verse 33: *"whom We had given luxury (atrafnāhum) in the worldly life."* The *mutrafūn* are those made soft by ease, those steeped in luxury, the pampered elite. The Qur'an uses the word consistently for the wealthy opponents of the prophets: *"And We did not send into a city any warner except that its affluent ones (mutrafūhā) said, 'Indeed we, in that with which you were sent, are disbelievers'"* (34:34); *"And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones (mutrafīhā) and they defiantly disobey therein"* (17:16); and, of the people of the left hand: *"Indeed, they were, before that, indulging in affluence (mutrafīn)"* (56:45).

The phrase *mutrafīhim*, "*their* affluent ones," indicates that the affluent are a subset of the deniers — the leaders, the *malaʾ* of verses 24, 33, and 46, whose wealth was the very thing verses 55–56 addressed. It is these, specifically, whom God seizes. The choice is significant. The affluent were the ones who most confidently read their wealth as favor; they are the ones whose reading is most dramatically refuted. Their wealth did not protect them. The Qur'an's principle applies: *"And let not their wealth and their children impress you; God only intends to punish them through them"* (9:55).

The source notes that al-Rāzī and others identified the seizure with specific events: the famine that struck Makkah after the Prophet's prayer against the Quraysh, when they were reduced to eating carrion and bones and came to him begging for relief (al-Bukhārī 1007; Muslim 2798 — the ḥadīth of the *dukhān*, in which Ibn Masʿūd recounts the Quraysh's hunger and their appeal to the Prophet ﷺ); and the defeat at Badr, where the *mutrafūn* of Quraysh — Abū Jahl, ʿUtbah, Shaybah, Umayyah ibn Khalaf — were killed. Both are plausible instances, and the verse's wording does not restrict it to either. It describes a *pattern*: the affluent are seized, and they cry out. Whether the seizure comes as famine, as defeat, as death, or as the Judgment, the sequence is the same.

**"At Once They Cry Out": Yajʾarūn**

The word *yajʾarūn* is from the root *j-ʾ-r*, which denotes a loud, raw cry — the bellowing of cattle in distress, or the anguished shout of a person in pain calling for help. The Qur'an uses it for the human cry to God in extremity: *"And whatever you have of favor is from God; then when adversity touches you, to Him you cry out (tajʾarūn)"* (16:53). The word is not a word of dignified prayer; it is a word of visceral distress. The affluent who spoke with cool contempt of the messenger (v. 33: *"this is only a man like you"*) now bellow.

The construction *idhā hum yajʾarūn* — "at once, behold, they cry out" — uses the *idhā* of surprise: the cry is immediate, involuntary, the reflex of a person whose security has been torn away. The men who "did not perceive" (v. 56) perceive now. The *ghamrah* that argument could not penetrate is penetrated instantly by pain. This is a sober truth about human nature: many who cannot be reached by truth can be reached by loss.

**The Reversal of Verses 55–56**

Verse 64 is the direct answer to the deniers' calculation in verses 55–56. They reckoned: God gives us wealth, therefore God favors us. Verse 64 replies: God gives you wealth *and then seizes you*, and your wealth does nothing. The *mutrafūn* who thought their luxury was proof of divine haste to bless them discover that it was, at most, a reprieve — the *ḥattā ḥīn* of verse 54 — and that when the reprieve ends, the luxury is no shield. The Qur'an states the general law: *"So when they forgot that of which they had been reminded, We opened to them the doors of every thing, until, when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them (akhadhnāhum) suddenly, and they were in despair"* (6:44). Verse 64 is that verse's application to the Quraysh.

**The Cry Compared With the Believers' Trembling**

The sūrah has now presented two kinds of fear side by side. The believers' hearts *tremble* (v. 60: *wajilah*) — before any punishment, in anticipation of the return, while doing good. The deniers *cry out* (v. 64: *yajʾarūn*) — after the punishment arrives, in reaction to pain, having done nothing. The first fear is chosen and productive; the second is forced and futile. The first is the fear of one who perceives; the second is the shock of one who refused to perceive until made to. The sūrah's teaching is that every human being will fear God — either now, voluntarily, in a way that produces good deeds, or later, involuntarily, in a way that produces only a cry. Verse 60 and verse 64 are the two options.

**The Cry Is Not Repentance**

It is essential to note what the next verse will make explicit: the cry of verse 64 is *not* accepted. God will say, *"Do not cry out today; you will not be helped by Us"* (v. 65). The distinction between the cry of the seized and the repentance of the sincere is one the Qur'an draws sharply. Pharaoh's cry as he drowned — *"I believe"* (10:90) — was refused: *"Now? And you had disobeyed before"* (10:91). The cry of verse 64 is the cry of Pharaoh's type: a reaction to force, not a turning of the heart. The Qur'an explains why such a cry is worthless: *"But their faith did not benefit them once they saw Our punishment"* (40:85). Faith is meaningful only as a free choice made before the compulsion of visible punishment; once the punishment is seen, the choice is gone, and what remains is only a noise.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 64 teaches the believer two things. First, about others: do not envy the *mutrafūn*. Their ease is a reprieve, not a reward; the seizure comes; and when it comes, the ease is worthless. The Qur'an counsels: *"Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given for enjoyment to categories of them, the splendor of worldly life, by which We test them"* (20:131). Second, about oneself: fear now, so that you need not cry out later. The choice between verse 60 and verse 64 is a choice about *when* to feel the weight of the return to God — while there is time to act on it, or when it is too late. The believer who trembles at his charity is protected from the cry at his seizure, because he has already turned toward the One to whom the cry would be addressed.

There is also a lesson about wealth for the believer who has it. The *mutraf* is not defined by possessing wealth but by being *made soft* by it — by letting ease dull the heart until it sinks into *ghamrah*. A wealthy believer who trembles as he gives is not a *mutraf*; a poor man who dreams of luxury and reads comfort as God's approval may be one in spirit. The verse targets a condition of the heart, and the heart's condition is not determined by the size of the estate.

**Toward the Refusal**

They cry out. The next verse gives God's reply — and it is a closed door.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:65

> **Implore not today! Truly you will not be helped by Us!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer to the Cry**

The affluent have been seized and have cried out (v. 64). Verse 65 records God's response: *lā tajʾarū l-yawma innakum minnā lā tunṣarūn* — "Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us." The verse is short and its tone is final. There is no reproach, no argument, no recitation of their crimes — those will come in verses 66–67. There is only a refusal: the cry will not be answered. This is one of the most sobering verses of the sūrah, because it describes a moment at which the door of divine help, which the Qur'an elsewhere describes as always open — *"Call upon Me; I will respond to you"* (40:60) — is closed.

**"Do Not Cry Out Today"**

The command *lā tajʾarū* uses the same root as verse 64's *yajʾarūn* — the raw, bellowing cry of distress. God tells them to stop. The word *al-yawm*, "today," is emphatic: *this* day, the day of seizure, is not a day on which crying helps. The implication is that there *were* days on which it would have helped — the days of the messenger's call, the days of the *ḥattā ḥīn* reprieve (v. 54), the days when their hearts were in *ghamrah* and they chose to stay there (v. 63). The cry is not refused because God does not hear cries; it is refused because it comes on the wrong day.

The Qur'an marks this "today" repeatedly as the day on which pleas cease to function. To the people of Hell it will be said: *"Whether you are patient or impatient, it is all the same for you; you are only being recompensed for what you used to do"* (52:16). To those who ask for return: *"Say, 'Today you will not be ransomed, nor will you be helped'"* (cf. 57:15; 36:54). The refusal is not a change in God's mercy but a consequence of the structure of the test: the test has a term, and after the term, responses are results, not choices.

**"You Will Not Be Helped by Us": Minnā Lā Tunṣarūn**

The second clause gives the content of the refusal: *innakum minnā lā tunṣarūn* — "indeed, you, from Us, will not be helped." The word *naṣr* means help, support, victory — the aid that turns a losing situation into a winning one. The passive *tunṣarūn* means "you will be helped," and the negation with the emphatic *inna* ("indeed, you will *not* be...") shuts the door firmly. The prepositional phrase *minnā*, "from Us," is placed before the verb for emphasis: from *Us* — the only source of help that matters — no help.

The word *naṣr* has appeared in the sūrah before, from the other direction. Noah prayed: *"My Lord, help me (unṣurnī) because they have denied me"* (v. 26); the second messenger prayed the same (v. 39). Their prayers for *naṣr* were answered — the Ark was built, the Cry came, the messengers were saved. Now the deniers, in their turn, cry out for help, and the answer is: *lā tunṣarūn*. The sūrah's symmetry is exact. The help that God gave to His messengers against these people is now withheld from these people against His punishment. There is one *Nāṣir*, and He has chosen whom to help.

**Why the Cry Is Refused**

The refusal raises the question that any thoughtful reader must ask: why does the God who describes Himself as *"the Most Merciful of the merciful"* (the sūrah's own closing words, v. 118) refuse a cry for help? The classical scholars gave a set of answers grounded in the Qur'an.

First, the cry is not repentance. Repentance (*tawbah*) is a turning of the heart, made freely, accompanied by regret for the wrong and resolve to abandon it. The cry of the seized is a reaction to pain, made under compulsion, with no change of heart. Pharaoh's "I believe" while drowning (10:90) was refused for exactly this reason: *"Now? And you had disobeyed before, and were of the corrupters"* (10:91). The Qur'an states the rule: *"Repentance is not accepted of those who continue to do evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says, 'Indeed, I have repented now'"* (4:18). The affluent of verse 65 are in this category.

Second, the term has ended. The sūrah taught that *"no community can hasten its term, nor delay it"* (v. 43). Within the term, every call is answered; after it, the ledger closes. The refusal is the enforcement of a boundary that God announced in advance, through every messenger. To answer the cry would be to abolish the boundary — and with it, the meaning of the choices made within it.

Third, justice requires it. The affluent were given the messenger, the signs, the reprieve, the argument — everything verse 62 promised: no burden beyond capacity, a truthful record, no wrong done. They chose their *ghamrah*. To help them now would be to treat those who chose faith under difficulty and those who refused it under ease as the same — which would be the very injustice verse 62 denied. God's refusal of the cry is His fidelity to the believers who trembled (v. 60) when trembling was a choice.

Fourth — and this the next verses make explicit — the cry is answered with a reminder of *why*: *"My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels"* (v. 66). The refusal is not arbitrary; it has a stated cause, and the cause is their own conduct.

**The Verse Is a Mercy to Those Who Read It Now**

It might seem that verse 65 is pure severity. In fact, its presence in the Qur'an is an act of mercy — because it is addressed to the reader *before* "today" arrives. God tells the living, in advance, what He will say to the seized: "Do not cry out today; you will not be helped." The purpose is that the living will cry out *now*, while crying is answered. The verse is a warning of a closed door, delivered while the door is open. The Prophet ﷺ described this logic: *"God extends His hand by night so that the sinner of the day may repent, and extends His hand by day so that the sinner of the night may repent, until the sun rises from the west"* (Muslim 2759). The hand is extended until the sign that ends the term. Verse 65 tells us what happens after.

**The Refusal and the Believers' Security**

The verse also has a function for the believers. It tells them that the affluent oppressors who mock and persecute them will not, in the end, be rescued. The Quraysh elite who tortured Bilāl and boycotted the Muslims and scorned the Prophet ﷺ were confident that their wealth and status made them untouchable. Verse 65 tells the believers, in the middle of the Makkan persecution, that this confidence is false: a day comes on which the *mutrafūn* cry out and are told *lā tunṣarūn*. This is not vindictiveness; it is the assurance of justice, which the oppressed need in order to endure. The Qur'an gives it to them repeatedly: *"And never think that God is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only delays them for a Day when eyes will stare"* (14:42).

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 65 asks each reader to locate himself in time. Is it still the day on which crying out is answered? For the living, it is — and the verse's whole purpose is to say: *use it*. Whatever the *ghamrah* one is in, whatever the "other deeds" (v. 63) one has been busy with, the door has not yet closed; the cry raised *today*, in the reader's today, is heard. The verse is terrible only for those who hear it and wait for a later day. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"God accepts the repentance of the servant so long as the death-rattle has not reached his throat"* (al-Tirmidhī 3537; Ibn Mājah 4253; graded ḥasan). Between now and the death-rattle is the time verse 65 gives.

**Toward the Reason**

The refusal is stated. The next two verses give the reason, in God's own words to the seized: My signs were recited to you, and you turned away — arrogantly, at night, talking nonsense.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:66

> **My signs were recited unto you, but you used to turn on your heels,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason Given**

God has refused the cry of the seized (v. 65). Now, in verses 66 and 67, He tells them why. Verse 66 states the fact and their response: *qad kānat āyātī tutlā ʿalaykum fa-kuntum ʿalā aʿqābikum tankiṣūn* — "My signs were indeed recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels." The verse is a sentence of judgment with two parts: what was done *for* them (the signs recited) and what they did *in return* (turned on their heels). The refusal of help is not arbitrary; it follows from a history, and the history is stated in the most concrete terms.

**"My Signs Were Indeed Recited to You"**

The clause begins with *qad kānat*, a construction of emphasis and completion: "it *was indeed* the case that..." The signs *were* recited; there is no doubt about it, no possibility of pleading ignorance. The word *āyātī*, "My signs," with the first-person possessive, is intimate and weighty: these were not merely arguments or texts but *God's own* signs — His verses, His communications. The passive *tutlā*, "were recited," from the root *t-l-w*, denotes the recitation of scripture, and the imperfect tense (*tutlā* rather than *tuliyat*) indicates repeated, continuous action: the signs were recited *again and again*, over years, by the Prophet ﷺ in the precincts of the Kaʿbah, in the streets of Makkah, in every gathering where the Quraysh could hear.

This clause is the foundation of the justice described in verse 62. The deniers cannot say they were not warned. They were burdened with nothing beyond their capacity — only with listening to what was recited — and the record (v. 62) contains every recitation and every response. The verse establishes the *ḥujjah*, the proof against them: *"so that mankind will have no argument against God after the messengers"* (4:165).

**"But You Used to Turn Back on Your Heels": Tankiṣūn**

The response is described with an unusually physical image: *fa-kuntum ʿalā aʿqābikum tankiṣūn* — "but you used to, on your heels, turn back." The verb *tankiṣūn* is from the root *n-k-ṣ*, which means to retreat, to recoil, to go backward. The phrase *ʿalā aʿqābikum*, "on your heels," specifies the manner: not turning around and walking away, but *backing away* — retreating with one's face still toward the thing one flees, as a person recoils from something frightening or repulsive. The Qur'an uses this root for Satan at Badr, who *"turned on his heels (nakaṣa ʿalā ʿaqibayhi)"* when he saw the angels (8:48), and it uses the related image of turning "on the heels" for apostasy: *"Do you turn back on your heels (ʿalā aʿqābikum)?"* (3:144).

The image is precise for the Quraysh's behavior. They did not merely ignore the Qur'an; they *recoiled* from it. When it was recited, they backed away as from a danger — and the Qur'an records the strategy they adopted: *"Do not listen to this Qur'an and make noise during it, that perhaps you may overcome"* (41:26). They stopped their ears, raised their voices, and retreated. The recoil was continuous — *kuntum ... tankiṣūn*, "you *used to* turn back" — a habit sustained over years.

**Why "On the Heels" Is Damning**

The phrase "on the heels" carries a moral weight beyond its physical picture. To advance is to go forward, toward what one seeks; to retreat on the heels is to go backward, away from what one fears. The Qur'an is the way forward — guidance, light, *"a reminder for the worlds"* (v. 71 will call it *dhikr*) — and the deniers' response to it was to go *backward*: back to their idols, back to their forefathers' ways (v. 24: *"we never heard of this among our forefathers"*), back into the *ghamrah* (v. 63). The heel is the back of the foot; to move on one's heels is to move in the direction one's back faces. The deniers, confronted with the way forward, chose the direction of their backs.

The source connects the verse to a specific setting recorded by al-Qurṭubī: the Quraysh used to gather at night around the Kaʿbah, and there the Qur'an would be recited to them, and there they would respond with contempt and nonsense — the *sāmiran tahjurūn* of the next verse. The "turning on the heels" was thus a nightly event, in the most sacred place in Arabia, in the presence of the very House they claimed to honor.

**The Contrast With the Believers**

Verse 58 described the believers as *"those who believe in the signs of their Lord."* Verse 66 describes the deniers as those who *recoiled* from the same signs. The same *āyāt* were recited to both groups; the two responses define the two communities of the sūrah's title and its ending. The believers moved *toward* the signs — "hastening" and "foremost" (v. 61); the deniers moved *away* — on their heels. The sūrah's whole moral geography is one of direction: toward God or away from Him, forward or backward, and the recitation of the Qur'an is the moment at which the direction is chosen.

**The Signs and the Heels: An Inversion**

There is an irony in the image that the commentators noted. The word *ʿaqib*, heel, is related to *ʿāqibah*, "consequence, end, outcome" — the word the Qur'an uses for the final result of a course of action: *"See how was the end (ʿāqibah) of the deniers"* (3:137). The deniers turned on their *heels* (*aʿqāb*) and thereby determined their *end* (*ʿāqibah*). The verse that describes their retreat is spoken to them at their end. They walked backward into the very consequence they were backing away from.

**God Speaks in the First Person**

Verse 66 is the first verse in this passage where God speaks in the first person singular — *āyātī*, "*My* signs." Verses 64–65 used the plural of majesty (*akhadhnā*, "We seized"; *minnā*, "from Us"). The shift to the singular is intimate and severe: it is *I* whose signs you recoiled from; the offense was against *Me*. The Qur'an uses this shift at moments of personal reckoning: *"Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam...?"* (36:60); *"So did you deny My signs (āyātī) while you encompassed them not in knowledge?"* (27:84). The seized are being addressed by the One they turned their backs on — and He is reminding them, in His own voice, that they did.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 66 asks the believer to examine his own response to the recitation of God's signs. When the Qur'an is recited — in prayer, in a gathering, on a recording — what does the body do, and what does the heart do? Does it lean in, or does it drift back? The "turning on the heels" of the deniers was extreme, but it has milder forms: the mind that wanders when the Qur'an is read, the heart that finds a demanding verse and moves quickly past it, the habit of hearing recitation as background rather than address. The Qur'an describes the right response: *"And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and pay attention that you may receive mercy"* (7:204). The believer who listens is advancing; the one who lets it wash over him unheard is, gently, on his heels.

The verse also cautions the one who *conveys* the signs. The deniers' recoil was not the Prophet's failure; the signs were "indeed recited" — the duty was fulfilled. The one who teaches or calls others to God must do so knowing that some will turn on their heels, and that the recoil is recorded against them, not against him.

**Toward the Manner of the Retreat**

Verse 66 said they turned back. Verse 67 will describe *how* — with arrogance, in nightly gatherings, talking nonsense — and will reveal that the very House of God was the stage for their contempt.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:67

> **waxing arrogant on account thereof, talking foolishly by night.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Manner of the Retreat**

Verse 66 said that the deniers turned back on their heels when God's signs were recited. Verse 67 completes the sentence by describing *how* they turned: *mustakbirīna bihi sāmiran tahjurūn* — "being arrogant about it, [in] nightly conversation, talking nonsense." Three words, three charges. They were *mustakbirīn* — arrogant. They were *sāmir* — night-talkers, gathered in evening sessions. They were *tahjurūn* — speaking foolishly, obscenely, or abandoningly. The verse is a portrait of the Makkan elite at their nightly gatherings around the Kaʿbah, and it is the last thing God says to them before the sūrah turns to argue with them directly (v. 68).

**"Being Arrogant About It": Mustakbirīna Bihi**

The word *mustakbirīn* is from *istakbara*, the verb used of Pharaoh and his notables in verse 46: *"they were arrogant (istakbarū), and they were a haughty people."* The sūrah has thus applied to the Quraysh the same word it applied to Pharaoh — placing the merchants of Makkah in the line of the tyrant of Egypt. Arrogance (*kibr*) was defined under verse 46 by the Prophet's words: *"rejecting the truth and looking down on people"* (Muslim 91). Both halves apply here: the Quraysh rejected the truth of the recited signs, and they looked down on the Prophet ﷺ and his followers as *"the lowest among us"* (11:27, of Noah's followers; the same charge was made against the Prophet's poor Companions, 6:52).

The pronoun in *bihi*, "about it" or "by it," has several possible referents, and the commentators considered each. It may refer to the Qur'an: they were arrogant *about* the Qur'an, disdaining it. It may refer to the Sacred House: they were arrogant *by* the House — that is, they used their custodianship of the Kaʿbah as grounds for pride, believing that as its keepers they were secure from God's punishment and superior to others. Al-Qurṭubī favored this second reading and connected it to the setting of the *sāmir*, the nightly gatherings that took place in the Kaʿbah's precincts. On this reading, the verse charges the Quraysh with a specific and grotesque arrogance: they took pride in the House of God while turning their backs on the Word of God recited beside it.

The Qur'an confirms this charge elsewhere: *"And what [excuse] have they that God should not punish them while they obstruct [people] from the Sacred Mosque and they were not its [rightful] guardians? Its guardians are only the righteous"* (8:34). Custodianship of a sacred place confers no immunity; the *mutrafūn* who thought otherwise were seized.

**"In Nightly Conversation": Sāmiran**

The word *sāmir* is from the root *s-m-r*, which denotes the evening conversation held by Arabs after dark — the *samar*, the talking that fills the night. A *sāmir* is one who engages in it, and the singular here is used collectively for the gathering. The Quraysh, like other Arabs, gathered at night to talk; and their gatherings, held around the Kaʿbah, were the setting in which the Qur'an was mocked. The source records al-Qurṭubī's note that the Prophet ﷺ disliked idle conversation after the night prayer — a report preserved in al-Bukhārī (568) and Muslim (647) from Abū Barzah, that he *"disliked sleep before it [ʿishāʾ] and talk after it."* The disapproval had a general basis — the night is for rest and worship, and late talk leads to missed prayers — but it also stood in contrast to the *samar* of the Quraysh, whose nights were spent in contempt of revelation.

The night setting is significant on its own. Night is the time the Qur'an assigns to the believers' most intimate worship: *"Indeed, the hours of the night are more effective for concurrence and more suitable for words"* (73:6); the believers *"forsake their beds"* to pray (32:16). The deniers used the same hours for *samar* — talk against the truth. Two uses of the night, two communities. The sūrah will later describe the reward of those who spent their nights rightly and the fate of those who spent them in mockery.

**"Talking Nonsense": Tahjurūn**

The verb *tahjurūn* is the richest word in the verse, and the source notes that the commentators derived it from two related senses of the root *h-j-r*. The first sense is to *abandon, forsake, turn away from* — as in *hijrah*, emigration, and as in the Prophet's later complaint: *"O my Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as [a thing] abandoned (mahjūran)"* (25:30). On this reading, *tahjurūn* means "you abandon [the Qur'an]," "you turn away from it" — which continues the thought of verse 66.

The second sense is to *talk deliriously, to rave, to speak obscenely or foolishly* — as a sick person raves in fever (*hajara al-marīḍ*). On this reading, *tahjurūn* means "you rave, you talk nonsense, you speak foul words" — and the object is the Qur'an and the Prophet ﷺ, about whom the Quraysh said at their nightly gatherings that he was a poet, a sorcerer, a madman, and that the Qur'an was *"legends of the former peoples"* (v. 83). A variant reading, *tuhjirūn* (Form IV), makes the second sense explicit: "you speak obscenely."

The two senses are not in conflict; the verse likely intends both, since the Quraysh both abandoned the Qur'an and raved against it. The nonsense they talked was the *form* their abandonment took. And the word's connection to *fever-raving* is exact: the deniers' hearts were in *ghamrah* (v. 63), and the *samar* was the delirium of the submerged.

**The Three Charges as One Portrait**

Arrogance, night-gatherings, and raving: the three words together describe a specific social scene, and it is worth picturing it as the first hearers of the sūrah would have. The wealthy men of Quraysh, custodians of the Kaʿbah, reclining in its precincts after dark — proud of their lineage and their House, secure in their wealth and children (v. 55), busy with their "other deeds" (v. 63) by day and with their *samar* by night. Into this scene, the Prophet ﷺ brings the Qur'an. And the response is: recoil (v. 66), disdain, and a stream of contemptuous chatter that fills the night air beside the House of God. Verse 67 is God's description of that scene, spoken back to its participants at the moment of their seizure. *This* is what you were doing while My signs were recited. *This* is why you will not be helped.

**Arrogance as the Root**

Of the three charges, arrogance is placed first because it is the root of the other two. The Quraysh gathered at night to rave against the Qur'an *because* they were too proud to accept it — from a man of their own (v. 33's "a man like you"), from among the poor (6:52), against their forefathers (v. 24). Arrogance is the sūrah's consistent diagnosis of denial: it was Pharaoh's (v. 46), it is the Quraysh's (v. 67), and it will be the reason the deniers will give for their own damnation in the Hereafter, as the Qur'an records: *"They will say, 'Yes, a warner had come to us, but we denied'"* (67:9). The believers' portrait, by contrast, began with the opposite of arrogance: *khushūʿ*, humility, in verse 2. Humility receives the signs; arrogance recoils from them.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 67 warns against three things that remain temptations. Against *arrogance about religion* — the pride of custodianship, whether of a sacred place, a lineage, a scholarly tradition, or a community, that makes one feel secure and superior while the substance of religion is neglected. The Quraysh were the keepers of the Kaʿbah and were seized; keeping is not the same as obeying. Against *idle night-talk* — the *samar* that fills the hours God gave for rest and worship with chatter, and in modern life the endless scrolling and streaming that fills the night with noise. The Prophet's dislike of talk after ʿishāʾ is a discipline worth recovering. And against *raving about the truth* — the mockery, the flippant dismissal, the clever contempt for revelation that passes for sophistication in every age. To speak of God's word as the Quraysh spoke of it, even lightly, is to join their *samar*.

The believer's alternative is the night of the believers: *"Their sides forsake their beds; they call upon their Lord in fear and hope"* (32:16). The same darkness, used for the opposite purpose.

**Toward the Direct Challenge**

God has told the seized why they were refused. The sūrah now turns from the future scene back to the present, and addresses the Quraysh directly with a series of six questions that dismantle every excuse for their recoil. The first: *"Have they not pondered the Word?"*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:68

> **Have they not contemplated the Word, or has there come unto them that which came not unto their forefathers?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Verdict to Interrogation**

Verses 64–67 looked forward to the moment of seizure and recorded what God will say to the seized. Verse 68 returns to the present and begins a series of questions addressed *about* the Quraysh to the Prophet ﷺ — and, through him, to the Quraysh themselves: *a-fa-lam yaddabbarū l-qawla am jāʾahum mā lam yaʾti ābāʾahumu l-awwalīn* — "Have they not pondered the Word, or has there come to them what did not come to their first forefathers?" The series continues through verse 70 and considers, one by one, every excuse the deniers might offer for their recoil from the Qur'an. Each excuse is examined and dismissed. The first two are in verse 68: they did not reflect on the Word; or perhaps the message was unprecedented and therefore alarming.

**"Have They Not Pondered the Word?": Tadabbur**

The verb *yaddabbarū* is from the root *d-b-r*, "back, rear, what follows." *Tadabbur* — the Form V verbal noun — means to look at the *back* of a thing, its consequences and implications, what lies behind and beyond its surface. To *ponder* (*tadabbara*) the Qur'an is to read it for what follows from it: its meanings, its coherence, its demands, its outcomes. The Qur'an commands this reflection on itself repeatedly: *"Do they not ponder (yatadabbarūn) the Qur'an? If it had been from other than God, they would have found within it much contradiction"* (4:82); *"A blessed Book We have sent down to you, that they might ponder (li-yaddabbarū) its verses and that those of understanding would be reminded"* (38:29); *"Then do they not ponder the Qur'an, or are there locks upon hearts?"* (47:24).

The word *al-qawl*, "the Word," "the speech," refers to the Qur'an — God's speech recited to them (v. 66). The question *a-fa-lam yaddabbarū* is rhetorical and diagnostic: the reason they turned on their heels (v. 66) is that they never actually *pondered* what was being recited. They heard it — the recitation was continuous — but they did not take it to the back of things; they did not ask what it meant or where it led. Their response was immediate recoil, not delayed reflection. The first excuse the verse considers is therefore *incomprehension*, and the verse's implicit answer is: incomprehension was not the problem, because comprehension was never attempted.

This charge connects directly to verse 63. Their hearts were in *ghamrah*; and a heart underwater cannot ponder. *Tadabbur* requires a heart at the surface, receiving the words and turning them over. The Quraysh had the words — Arabic, clear, in their own dialect — and lacked only the willingness to reflect. Had they pondered, al-Rāzī argues, they would have found the Qur'an's inimitability, its coherence, its truthful accounts of past nations, its moral force — the very things the sūrah has been presenting for sixty-seven verses.

**"Or Has There Come to Them What Did Not Come to Their Forefathers?"**
