The second question considers a second excuse: perhaps the message was *unprecedented* — so novel that their alarm was understandable. *Am jāʾahum mā lam yaʾti ābāʾahumu l-awwalīn* — "or has there come to them what did not come to their first forefathers?" The Quraysh had in fact made this objection, and the sūrah recorded the same words on the lips of Noah's notables: *"We never heard of this among our forefathers of old (ābāʾinā l-awwalīn)"* (v. 24). The verse takes the objection seriously enough to state it and then, by framing it as a question, exposes its falsity.

For the message was *not* unprecedented. The sūrah has spent verses 23–52 demonstrating exactly this: Noah preached it; the messengers after him preached it; Moses and Aaron brought it; Jesus taught it. *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him"* was said to every generation. The Quraysh's own forefathers — Abraham and Ishmael, whom they claimed as ancestors and whose House they kept — were its greatest preachers. The Qur'an makes the point explicitly to Muḥammad ﷺ: *"Nothing is said to you except what was already said to the messengers before you"* (41:43), and to the Quraysh: *"[This is] a warner of the warners of old"* (53:56). Far from being unprecedented, the message was the oldest thing in the world.

There is a second layer. The commentators noted that the Quraysh, unlike the People of the Book, had not received a scripture or a messenger in their recent history — *"that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned"* (36:6). In this sense, something *had* come to them that had not come to their immediate ancestors: the Qur'an itself. But this cuts against the excuse rather than for it. A people to whom no warner had come in living memory should have *welcomed* one — as the Qur'an says they had claimed they would: *"They swore by God their strongest oaths that if a warner came to them, they would be more guided than any of the nations"* (35:42). When the warner came, they recoiled. The novelty they cited as an excuse was precisely the blessing they had asked for.

**The Structure of the Six Questions**

Verse 68 opens a set of questions that continues through verse 70, and it is useful to see the whole set. (1) Have they not pondered the Word? (2) Has something come to them unprecedented among their forefathers? (3) Do they not know their Messenger, that they should deny him? (v. 69) (4) Do they say there is madness in him? (v. 70) Then the sūrah supplies the truth: *"Rather, he has brought them the truth, and most of them are averse to the truth"* (v. 70). The questions move from the *message* (its content, its precedent) to the *messenger* (his character, his sanity) and end by locating the real cause of denial not in any of these but in the deniers' own aversion. The structure is a systematic clearing of excuses, and it mirrors the sūrah's earlier record of the four objections (human like you, seeks superiority, angels, forefathers — vv. 24, 33–34, 47) by answering each in turn.

**Why Pondering Comes First**

The first question — *tadabbur* — is placed first because it is the root of all the rest. A person who genuinely ponders the Qur'an discovers that it is not unprecedented (question 2), that its bearer is trustworthy (question 3), and that it is the opposite of madness (question 4). All the other excuses dissolve in the act of reflection. Conversely, a person who does not ponder can maintain any excuse indefinitely, because he never tests it against the text. The Qur'an's constant invitation to *tadabbur* is therefore not merely a devotional recommendation but an epistemological one: it is the method by which the Qur'an asks to be judged. The deniers refused the method and then complained about the verdict.

**The Verse and the Believers' Portrait**

Verse 58 described the believers as those who *"believe in the signs of their Lord"*; verse 68 describes the deniers as those who never pondered the Word. The contrast implies that belief in the signs is the *result* of pondering — that the believers believed because they reflected, not instead of reflecting. This is consistent with the sūrah's entire method, which argues from creation and history rather than demanding assent. The believer of Sūrah al-Muʾminūn is a person who has thought; the denier is a person who has refused to.

**The Verse for the Believer**

The command implicit in verse 68 falls on believers as much as deniers: *ponder the Word*. It is possible to be a Muslim who recites the Qur'an daily and never ponders it — who hears it, as the Quraysh heard it, without taking it to the back of things. The Prophet ﷺ described a people who would *"recite the Qur'an but it does not pass beyond their throats"* (al-Bukhārī 5058; Muslim 1066). *Tadabbur* is what carries it past the throat to the heart. Practically, it means reading slowly; asking of each verse "what does this require of me?"; noticing the connections between verses (as this sūrah's own structure rewards); and returning to the same passages until they open. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said: *"There is no good in a recitation without pondering."* The Quraysh had recitation without pondering, and it led them backward on their heels. The believer is asked to have both.

**Toward the Messenger**

Two excuses concerning the message have been examined. The next verse turns to the messenger: do they not *know* him? For the Quraysh had known Muḥammad ﷺ for forty years before he recited a single verse.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:69

> **Or do they not know their Messenger, and so deny him?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Excuse Examined**

The interrogation begun in verse 68 continues: *am lam yaʿrifū rasūlahum fa-hum lahu munkirūn* — "Or did they not know their Messenger, so that they are deniers of him?" The first two questions concerned the message — had they pondered it? was it unprecedented? This third question concerns the messenger. Perhaps, the verse proposes, they reject him because he is a stranger to them — an unknown man whose character they cannot vouch for and whose claims they therefore have reason to doubt. The question is, once again, rhetorical, and its force lies in how absurd the proposed excuse is: of all the men in Arabia, Muḥammad ﷺ was the one the Quraysh knew *best*.

**"Do They Not Know Their Messenger?": Maʿrifah**

The verb *yaʿrifū* is from the root *ʿ-r-f*, which denotes knowledge by acquaintance — recognition, familiarity, knowing a person or thing directly rather than by report. *Maʿrifah* is the knowledge one has of a face, a voice, a character encountered over time. The verse asks whether the Quraysh lacked this kind of knowledge of *rasūlahum*, "*their* Messenger" — and the possessive is pointed. He was *theirs*: of their tribe, their city, their language; born among them, raised among them, married among them, trading among them. The Qur'an elsewhere stresses this: *"There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves (min anfusikum)"* (9:128); *"a Messenger from among themselves (minhum)"* (2:129; 3:164; 62:2).

The Quraysh's knowledge of him was not superficial. As the source notes, he was known among them as *al-Amīn* — "the Trustworthy" — a title conferred not by his followers but by his opponents, before his prophethood. When the Kaʿbah was rebuilt and the clans quarreled over who would set the Black Stone in place, they agreed to accept the judgment of the next man to enter, and when Muḥammad ﷺ entered, they said: *"This is al-Amīn; we are content with him"* (Ibn Isḥāq; Aḥmad 15505). He had never lied, never broken a trust, never been seen in the idol-temples, never drunk, never quarreled dishonorably. When the emperor Heraclius questioned Abū Sufyān — then the Prophet's bitter enemy — about him, Abū Sufyān was forced to admit: *"We have never known him to lie"* (al-Bukhārī 7; Muslim 1773). And when the Prophet ﷺ first gathered the Quraysh at Mount Ṣafā to warn them, he asked: *"If I told you that horsemen were in the valley about to attack you, would you believe me?"* and they answered: *"Yes; we have never known anything but truth from you"* (al-Bukhārī 4770; Muslim 208).

**The Force of the Question**

Given this, the excuse "we do not know him" is impossible. The verse's *fa-hum lahu munkirūn* — "so they are deniers of him" — states the conclusion the excuse would have to support, and shows that the premise does not support it. If a stranger claimed prophethood, one might reasonably withhold belief. But the Quraysh were rejecting a man whose forty years of unbroken honesty they had witnessed and certified. The Qur'an makes the argument explicit in the Prophet's own words: *"I have remained among you a lifetime before it; will you not then use reason?"* (10:16). A man who never lied about a trade or a debt did not begin lying about God at forty.

The sūrah connects this to its own opening. Verse 8 described the believers as *"those who are faithful to their trusts (amānāt) and their covenant."* The Messenger was the supreme exemplar of this quality — *al-Amīn*, the trusted keeper of *amānāt*. The Quraysh's rejection therefore contradicts their own testimony: they had called him trustworthy in every matter except the one that mattered most.

**"Deniers of Him": Munkirūn**

The word *munkirūn* is from the root *n-k-r*, which is the opposite of *ʿ-r-f*: to *not recognize*, to treat as strange, to disavow. The verse plays the two roots against each other: *lam yaʿrifū* (did they not recognize?) ... *munkirūn* (they treat as unrecognized). The deniers were behaving toward a man they knew intimately as though he were a stranger — *pretending* not to know him. The word *munkir* also carries the sense of rejecting what is known to be true (*munkar* is the technical term for what is recognized as wrong), so the verse implies that their denial was a denial *against* knowledge, not from ignorance. They knew him and denied him anyway. This is the same diagnosis the Qur'an gives of the People of the Book concerning the Prophet ﷺ: *"They recognize him (yaʿrifūnahu) as they recognize their own sons, but a party of them conceal the truth while they know"* (2:146).

**Knowledge of the Messenger as Evidence**

The verse establishes a principle of religious epistemology: the *character* of a messenger is part of the evidence for his message. The Qur'an does not ask people to accept a claim in a vacuum; it points to the claimant's known truthfulness as a reason to take the claim seriously. This is why the Prophet's biography was, for the Companions, inseparable from the Qur'an — they believed the Book partly because they knew the man. Khadījah's response to his first revelation was of this kind: *"By God, God will never disgrace you. You maintain the ties of kinship, bear the burden of the weak, earn for the destitute, honor the guest, and help in the calamities of truth"* (al-Bukhārī 3; Muslim 160). She reasoned from his character to the trustworthiness of his experience. The Quraysh had the same data and reasoned the opposite way — which shows that their denial was not a failure of evidence but a refusal to follow it.

**The Excuse Behind the Excuse**

If the Quraysh knew him and knew he did not lie, why did they deny him? The sūrah has already answered: arrogance (v. 67), aversion to the truth (v. 70, coming), the *ghamrah* of the heart (v. 63), the fear of losing status (the *malaʾ*'s "seeks superiority over you," v. 24), and attachment to forefathers' ways (v. 24; v. 68). The excuse "we do not know him" was never the real reason; it was a cover. Verse 69 strips the cover away by asking the question aloud. This is the method of the whole interrogation (vv. 68–70): to name each possible excuse and show it does not hold, until the real cause — *"most of them are averse to the truth"* — is exposed.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 69 asks the believer, too, whether he *knows* his Messenger. The Quraysh knew him by acquaintance and denied him; a Muslim can affirm him and know him hardly at all — the name, the outline, a few sayings, and no living familiarity with the character that made the Quraysh call him *al-Amīn*. The remedy is the study of the *sīrah* and the *sunnah*: to come to know him as his Companions knew him, so that one's faith in his message is grounded in *maʿrifah* of the man. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"None of you truly believes until I am more beloved to him than his father, his child, and all people"* (al-Bukhārī 15; Muslim 44) — and one cannot love what one does not know.

The verse also speaks to how believers present the message. The Prophet's character was his first argument, before any verse. The believer who calls others to God carries the same responsibility: to be known, in his dealings, as trustworthy — so that when he speaks of God, no one can honestly say "we do not know this person." A Muslim who is dishonest in trade or unreliable in promises has removed from his message the evidence that verse 69 says should accompany it.

**Toward the Charge of Madness**

Three excuses have failed. The fourth and last — that the Messenger is mad — will be examined in verse 70, and the sūrah will then state, with *bal*, what is actually true.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:70

> **Or do they say, “He is possessed?” Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Last Excuse and the Real Cause**

The fourth and final question of the series is asked and answered in the same verse: *am yaqūlūna bihi jinnatun bal jāʾahum bi-l-ḥaqqi wa aktharuhum li-l-ḥaqqi kārihūn* — "Or do they say, 'In him is madness'? Rather, he has brought them the truth, and most of them are averse to the truth." The sūrah has examined whether the deniers failed to ponder (v. 68), whether the message was unprecedented (v. 68), whether they did not know the Messenger (v. 69) — and now whether they can dismiss him as insane. Having exhausted the excuses, the verse turns with *bal* to the diagnosis: the problem was never the message or the messenger; the problem was that the message was *true*, and they did not want the truth.

**"In Him Is Madness": The Old Accusation**

The phrase *bihi jinnah* — "in him is a *jinnah*," a possession by jinn, a madness — is exactly the phrase Noah's notables used of Noah in verse 25: *"He is only a man in whom is madness (bihi jinnah)."* The sūrah's deliberate repetition places the Quraysh in the line of Noah's deniers: the same accusation, word for word, a thousand years apart. The Qur'an records that every messenger received it: *"Likewise, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, 'A magician or a madman (majnūn).' Did they bequeath it to one another?"* (51:52–53). The Quraysh said of the Prophet ﷺ: *"O you upon whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad (majnūn)"* (15:6), and the Qur'an answered them: *"You are not, by the favor of your Lord, a madman"* (68:2); *"And your companion is not mad"* (81:22).

The accusation of madness was, in the Makkan context, a strategy rather than a belief. Ibn Isḥāq records that al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, when consulted by the Quraysh on what to call the Prophet ﷺ before the pilgrimage season, rejected "madman" precisely because it was unconvincing: *"He is not mad; we have seen madness and know it, and there is none of its choking or its confusion in him."* They settled on "sorcerer" as more plausible. The Quraysh themselves, in private, knew the charge was false; verse 70's question exposes it as the last resort of people who have no real argument.

**Why Madness Is Impossible Here**

The verse does not argue at length against the charge; it does not need to, because the sūrah's own content refutes it. Madness produces incoherence; the Qur'an is supremely coherent — sixty-nine verses of tightly argued, symmetrically structured, morally serious discourse have preceded this one. Madness produces contradiction; the Qur'an claims, and the deniers could not disprove, that it contains none (4:82). Madness produces no lasting change in others; the Qur'an was transforming the most stubborn people on earth. And the man himself was the *Amīn* whom the Quraysh had trusted for forty years (v. 69); madness does not descend on such a man at forty with a message of perfect moral order. The Qur'an appeals to this evidence directly: *"Do they not reflect? There is no madness in their companion; he is but a clear warner"* (7:184).

**"Rather, He Has Brought Them the Truth": Bal**

The particle *bal* cancels all four excuses at once and states what is actually the case: *jāʾahum bi-l-ḥaqq* — "he has brought them the truth." The word *al-ḥaqq* — "the truth," "the real," "what is right and due" — is one of the Qur'an's most important terms and one of God's names. It denotes not merely correct information but *reality itself*: what actually is, as opposed to what is imagined or wished. The Prophet ﷺ brought *reality* — about God, about creation, about death, about judgment — and the deniers' responses (madness, fables, sorcery) were attempts to reclassify reality as something else.

**"And Most of Them Are Averse to the Truth": The Diagnosis**

The verse's final clause is the answer to the whole interrogation: *wa aktharuhum li-l-ḥaqqi kārihūn* — "and most of them, toward the truth, are averse." The word *kārihūn* is from the root *k-r-h*, "to dislike, to hate, to find repugnant." The deniers did not reject the Qur'an because it was false, unprecedented, from an unknown man, or the product of madness; they rejected it because they *did not like the truth*. Their aversion preceded their arguments and produced them. The four excuses were the *rationalizations* of a prior dislike.

Why would anyone be averse to the truth? The sūrah has answered throughout. The truth demanded the abandonment of idols that anchored their trade and status (v. 24: "seeks superiority over you"). It demanded humility before a man of their own (v. 33: "a man like you"). It demanded that they treat the poor as equals (6:52). It demanded the surrender of ancestral ways (v. 24). It demanded chastity, honesty, charity, and prayer (vv. 2–9). And it demanded acceptance of a Resurrection at which every deed would be reviewed (v. 62). Every one of these demands cut against their interests, their pride, or their pleasures. The truth was *unwelcome*, and so they called it madness.

The Qur'an names this aversion elsewhere as the deepest cause of disbelief: *"That is because they disliked (karihū) what God revealed, so He rendered their deeds worthless"* (47:9); *"They wish to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God refuses except to perfect His light, although the disbelievers dislike it (kariha)"* (9:32). And the Prophet's definition of arrogance — *"rejecting the truth (baṭar al-ḥaqq)"* (Muslim 91), quoted under verse 46 — describes the same posture: the truth is seen and pushed away.

**"Most of Them": Aktharuhum**

The verse says *most* of them, not all. The qualification is precise and merciful. Among the Quraysh were some who were not averse to the truth and who would accept it — some already had, and many more would at the Conquest of Makkah. The Qur'an consistently refuses to condemn a people wholesale; it identifies the *majority* whose aversion set the tone, and leaves the door open for the rest. This is also a comfort to the Prophet ﷺ: not every heart in Makkah was closed. Among those who sat in the *samar* raving against the Qur'an (v. 67) were future Companions.

**The Psychology of Aversion to Truth**

Verse 70 makes a claim about human nature that deserves reflection: that people can *know* something is true and *dislike* it, and that the dislike can override the knowledge. This is not an exotic condition. It is the ordinary experience of anyone who has received a diagnosis he did not want, a criticism he knew was fair, or a demand he knew was just — and found himself reaching for reasons to dismiss it. The reasons come easily; the mind is inventive in the service of aversion. The Quraysh's four excuses are a model of the process: first "we do not understand it," then "it is unprecedented," then "we do not trust the man," then "he is mad" — each abandoned as it fails, each replaced by the next, and the aversion beneath them all unchanged.

The Qur'an's remedy for this condition is *tadabbur* (v. 68) — honest reflection that asks not "do I like this?" but "is this true?" — and *khashyah* (v. 57), the fear of God that makes one more afraid of rejecting the truth than of accepting its demands. The believers of the sūrah's portraits are people in whom the fear of God outweighed the aversion to inconvenient truth. The deniers are people in whom it did not.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 70 asks the believer to test his own relationship to unwelcome truth. When a verse of the Qur'an or a saying of the Prophet ﷺ demands something he does not want to give, what is his first move? If it is to look for an interpretation that removes the demand, to question the authenticity, to cite a scholar who softens it, to say "that was for another time" — he should recognize the pattern of verse 70. The move may sometimes be legitimate; but the *motive* must be examined. Is it the pursuit of truth, or *karāhiyat al-ḥaqq*, aversion to truth, wearing the clothes of scholarship? The honest believer asks himself the question the Qur'an asked the Quraysh, and answers it before God rather than before an audience.

**Toward the Argument From Order**

The deniers wanted the truth to conform to their desires. The next verse states what would happen if it did: the heavens and the earth would be corrupted. Truth is not adjustable to preference, and the sūrah is about to explain why.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:71

> **Were the truth to follow their caprices, the heavens and the earth and those therein would have been corrupted. Nay, We gave them their reminder, but they turned away from their reminder.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Consequence of Aversion Taken Seriously**

Verse 70 ended with the diagnosis: most of the deniers are averse to the truth. Verse 71 asks what would follow if their aversion were accommodated — if the truth were made to suit them: *wa law ittabaʿa l-ḥaqqu ahwāʾahum la-fasadati l-samāwātu wa l-arḍu wa man fīhinna bal ataynāhum bi-dhikrihim fa-hum ʿan dhikrihim muʿriḍūn* — "And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they, from their reminder, are turning away." The verse contains one of the Qur'an's most profound arguments about the nature of truth, followed by a return to the deniers' behavior. Truth cannot bend to desire without the world coming apart; and the deniers, offered the truth as a reminder, turned from it.

**"If the Truth Had Followed Their Desires"**

The word *ahwāʾ* is the plural of *hawā*, which means desire, caprice, whim, inclination — the pull of the lower self toward what it wants, regardless of what is right. The Qur'an treats *hawā* as the chief rival of revelation: *"And who is more astray than one who follows his desire (hawāhu) without guidance from God?"* (28:50); *"Have you seen the one who takes as his god his own desire (hawāhu)?"* (25:43). The Prophet ﷺ *"does not speak from desire (al-hawā); it is only a revelation revealed"* (53:3–4). The plural *ahwāʾ* here indicates that the deniers had *many* desires, pulling in different directions — which is part of the argument, as al-Rāzī noted: desires are multiple and conflicting, so a truth that followed them could not be one truth.

The hypothesis — *law ittabaʿa l-ḥaqq ahwāʾahum*, "if the truth had followed their desires" — is the deniers' implicit demand. They wanted a religion that left their idols, their trade, their status, and their pleasures intact; they wanted a truth that agreed with them. The verse takes the demand to its conclusion.

**"The Heavens and the Earth and Whoever Is in Them Would Have Been Corrupted"**

The conclusion is cosmic: *la-fasadati l-samāwātu wa l-arḍu wa man fīhinna* — the heavens, the earth, and all who dwell in them would be *corrupted*, *ruined*, *thrown into disorder* (*fasād*). Why so vast a consequence? The commentators developed the argument along several lines, and each is sound.

First, the argument from the nature of truth. Truth (*al-ḥaqq*) is what corresponds to reality; desire (*hawā*) is what the self wants. If truth followed desire, reality would be determined by wanting — and since people want contradictory things, reality would be contradictory, which is to say, no reality at all. The heavens and the earth exist by fixed truth: the sun rises where it must, water flows as it must, bodies fall as they must. A cosmos in which truth bent to whim would be a cosmos in which nothing held. Al-Rāzī connected this to the parallel verse: *"Had there been in them [the heavens and the earth] gods besides God, they would both have been corrupted (la-fasadatā)"* (21:22). Multiple gods would mean multiple wills; multiple wills would mean conflict; conflict would mean ruin. Verse 71 makes the same argument with human desires in place of rival gods: multiple desires governing truth would produce the same ruin.

Second, the argument from divine order. The heavens and the earth are sustained by God's *ḥaqq* — His truth, His right, His just ordering: *"We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth (bi-l-ḥaqq)"* (15:85; 46:3). If the truth by which they are sustained were subordinated to the caprice of creatures, the sustaining would fail. The universe is not a democracy of desires; it is a kingdom of truth, and its stability depends on that.

Third, the argument from morality. Among "whoever is in them" are human beings, whose societies are held together by truths that do not bend to individual desire: that theft is wrong, that promises bind, that the weak have rights. If moral truth followed the desires of the powerful — as the Quraysh wanted — society would dissolve into predation. The source's note that "good and evil are determined by what is true, not by what human beings want" captures this: the deniers wanted a morality tailored to their preferences, and such a morality is the end of morality.

**The Argument's Logical Shape**

Verse 71 is a *reductio ad absurdum*. Premise: the deniers demand that truth conform to their desires. Consequence: if truth conformed to desires, the world would be corrupted. But the world is not corrupted — it stands in its order, as the sūrah has displayed from verse 12 onward. Therefore truth does not conform to desires — and the deniers' demand is not merely unreasonable but incoherent. They are asking for something whose granting would destroy them along with everything else. The Qur'an frequently argues in this form, and here the argument has a moral edge: the deniers imagine that a truth suited to them would be a benefit, and the verse shows it would be a catastrophe.

**"Rather, We Have Brought Them Their Reminder"**

The particle *bal* turns from the hypothetical to the actual: *ataynāhum bi-dhikrihim* — "We have brought them *their* reminder." The word *dhikr* means reminder, remembrance, mention — and it is one of the Qur'an's names for itself: *"Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder (al-dhikr), and indeed, We will be its guardian"* (15:9). The possessive *dhikrihim*, "*their* reminder," has been read in two ways, both illuminating. It may mean the reminder *intended for them*, addressed to them, suited to their situation — the Qur'an in their language, through a man of their tribe. Or it may mean the reminder that is *their honor*, *their renown* — since *dhikr* also means "mention, fame," and the Qur'an says: *"Indeed, it is a reminder (dhikr) for you and your people"* (43:44) and *"We have sent down to you a Book in which is your mention (dhikrukum)"* (21:10). On this reading, the Qur'an was the source of the Arabs' lasting glory — the thing that would make them remembered — and they turned from it.

Both readings converge: what God brought them was *for* them, addressed to them, and honoring them. It was not the alien and unprecedented thing they claimed (v. 68). It was *theirs*.

**"But They, From Their Reminder, Are Turning Away"**

The verse ends where the whole passage has been pointing: *fa-hum ʿan dhikrihim muʿriḍūn* — "but they are turning away from their reminder." The word *muʿriḍūn*, from the root *ʿ-r-ḍ*, means to turn aside, to present one's side rather than one's face, to avert. It is a gentler word than verse 66's "turning back on the heels," but it describes the same motion: the reminder was offered, and they turned from it. The repetition of *dhikrihim* — "their reminder... their reminder" — emphasizes the ownership: it was *theirs*, and they turned away from what was *theirs*.

The structure of the verse is thus a contrast between what the deniers *wanted* — a truth that follows desire, which would destroy the world — and what they were *given* — a reminder made for them, which would save it. They rejected the second because they could not have the first. This is the tragedy the sūrah has been describing since verse 24.

**The Verse in the History of Thought**

Verse 71's argument has a permanent relevance beyond its Makkan context. Every age produces the demand that truth follow desire — that morality be whatever the individual or the culture prefers, that reality be whatever one feels it to be, that religion be edited to fit the present's inclinations. The verse's answer is unchanged: a truth that follows desire is not truth, and a world governed by such a "truth" would come apart. The stability of the cosmos, the coherence of morality, and the possibility of knowledge all depend on truth being *independent* of what anyone wants. The believer who accepts this accepts that revelation will sometimes contradict his desires — and that this contradiction is not a flaw in revelation but the proof that it is not merely his own desire reflected back.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 71 asks the believer whether he wants the truth or a truth *that follows his desires*. The two feel similar from the inside; the test is what happens when they diverge. When the Qur'an forbids what one wants or commands what one dislikes, the person who wants *the truth* submits, and the person who wants *his own truth* looks for a way around it. The sūrah has already described both: the believers who "hasten to good deeds" (v. 61) and the deniers who are "averse to the truth" (v. 70). The verse also gives the believer a reason for gratitude: the reminder is *his* — addressed to him, suited to him, honoring him. To turn from it is to turn from a gift wrapped with one's own name.

**Toward the Question of Payment**

One more excuse remains, unspoken but implied: perhaps the Messenger wanted something from them. The next verse asks it — and answers with the sūrah's characteristic phrase: *"He is the best of providers."*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:72

> **Dost thou ask any recompense of them? For thy Lord’s recompense is better, and He is the best of providers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Unspoken Excuse**

The interrogation of verses 68–70 examined the deniers' stated excuses. Verse 72 turns to one they may not have stated openly but which underlies much suspicion of religious messengers in every age: that the messenger is in it for gain. *Am tasʾaluhum kharjan fa-kharāju rabbika khayrun wa huwa khayru l-rāziqīn* — "Or do you ask them for a payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers." The verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, but its question is really about the deniers' reasoning: if they cannot object to the message (v. 68), the precedent (v. 68), the man (v. 69), or his sanity (v. 70), do they perhaps suspect his *motive*? The verse dismisses this last possibility by stating a fact the Quraysh knew: he had never asked them for anything.

**"Do You Ask Them for a Payment?": Kharj**

The word *kharj* (and its variant *kharāj*) means a payment, a tribute, a tax, a fee — something *taken out* (from the root *kh-r-j*, "to go out") of one's wealth and given to another. In later Islamic administration, *kharāj* became the technical term for land-tax; in the Qur'an's usage here, it means any remuneration demanded in exchange for a service. The question *am tasʾaluhum kharjan* — "or do you ask them for a *kharj*?" — is rhetorical and expects the answer "no." The Prophet ﷺ asked for nothing. He said, as every messenger said: *"I do not ask you for it any payment; my payment is only from the Lord of the worlds"* (26:109, 127, 145, 164, 180 — Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, and Shuʿayb each say it); *"Say, 'Whatever payment I might have asked of you — it is yours. My payment is only from God'"* (34:47); *"Say, 'I do not ask you for it any payment, and I am not of the pretentious'"* (38:86).

The absence of any fee is decisive evidence of sincerity, and the Qur'an uses it as such. A man who claimed prophethood for gain would have asked for something — wealth, position, tribute. The Quraysh in fact *offered* him these: ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah came to him with an offer of wealth, leadership, and kingship if he would stop, and he answered by reciting Sūrah Fuṣṣilat (Ibn Isḥāq; al-Bayhaqī). He refused what a fraud would have sought. His poverty was known: ʿĀʾishah reported that *"two months would pass and no fire would be lit in the houses of the Messenger of God"* — they lived on dates and water (al-Bukhārī 2567; Muslim 2972). A man living thus was not asking for *kharj*.

**The Sūrah's Recurring Charge Answered**

The verse answers an accusation the sūrah recorded at its beginning. Noah's notables said: *"He is only a man like you who wishes to seek superiority over you"* (v. 24). The charge was that the messenger sought advantage — power, precedence, gain. Verse 72 disposes of this charge for the final messenger: he asks no *kharj*. If he sought advantage, where is it? Not in wealth — he had none. Not in position — he was persecuted. Not in ease — he was driven from his city. The only "superiority" he sought was for God's word over idols, and that brought him nothing but hardship. The charge of self-interest, which has been leveled against every prophet, collapses against the facts of his life.

**"But the Payment of Your Lord Is Better": Kharāj Rabbika**

The verse's second clause supplies the reason he asks nothing: *fa-kharāju rabbika khayr* — "for the payment of your Lord is better." He does not need their *kharj* because he has a better one — from God. The word *kharāj* is used again, deliberately, for God's reward: the Prophet ﷺ is *paid*, but by a different employer. This reframing is important. The Prophet ﷺ was not working for nothing; he was working for the One whose payment exceeds any human wage. The Qur'an states the general principle for all believers: *"And whatever thing you spend, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers"* (34:39); *"Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for Paradise"* (9:111).

The comparative *khayr*, "better," is characteristically restrained. God's payment is not merely "adequate" or "also good"; it is *better* than anything the Quraysh could give — better in quantity (unlimited), in duration (eternal), in certainty (God does not default), and in kind (Paradise rather than dirhams). The comparison assumes the deniers' *kharj* has some value and then declares God's payment superior — an argument framed in the deniers' own economic terms.

**"And He Is the Best of Providers": Khayr al-Rāziqīn**

The verse ends with a divine name: *wa huwa khayru l-rāziqīn* — "and He is the best of providers." The word *rāziq* is from *rizq*, provision, sustenance — everything God gives to sustain life, from food and water to health, family, and opportunity. God is *al-Razzāq*, the Provider (51:58), and *khayr al-rāziqīn*, the best of those who provide (5:114; 22:58; 34:39; 62:11; and here). The phrase appears in the Qur'an at moments when human provision seems uncertain — when the disciples ask for a table from heaven (5:114), when believers die as emigrants (22:58), when merchants rush from the Friday sermon to a caravan (62:11). In each case, it redirects attention from the visible source of provision to the actual one.

Here, the phrase completes the argument. The Prophet ﷺ does not ask the Quraysh for *kharj* because his *rizq* comes from *khayr al-rāziqīn*. He is provided for by the best Provider, and so he can afford to ask nothing of the worst — of men who would use any payment as a lever against him.

**The Superlative Constructions of the Sūrah**

The phrase *khayr al-rāziqīn* belongs to a set of superlative divine descriptions that the sūrah uses at key moments. Verse 29: *khayr al-munzilīn*, "the best of those who bring to land" (Noah's prayer). Verse 72: *khayr al-rāziqīn*, "the best of providers." Verse 109 and verse 118: *khayr al-rāḥimīn*, "the best of those who show mercy." Each phrase names God as the *best* in a category of action that human beings also perform — landing, providing, showing mercy — and thereby situates all human action within His. Human beings provide, but He is the best provider; human beings show mercy, but He is the best at it. The construction teaches a way of seeing: every good one receives from a human hand is a small instance of a category in which God is supreme.

**The Verse and Verse 51**

Verse 72's *khayr al-rāziqīn* recalls verse 51's *kulū min al-ṭayyibāt*, "eat of the good things," addressed to the messengers. The messengers ate — the sūrah insisted on their humanity — and what they ate was *rizq* from the best Provider. The Prophet ﷺ did not need the Quraysh's payment to eat; his provision came from the same source as theirs, and would continue whether they paid him or persecuted him. The ḥadīth quoted under verse 51 about the dusty traveler whose provision was unlawful and whose prayer was therefore unanswered (Muslim 1015) has its counterpart here: the Prophet's provision was pure — he took nothing from the deniers — and his prayer was answered.

**Sincerity as Evidence: The General Principle**

Verse 72 establishes a criterion that applies beyond the Prophet ﷺ: the sincerity of one who calls to God is tested by what he asks in return. The Qur'an makes this criterion explicit in the story of the messengers to the city: *"Follow those who do not ask of you any payment, and they are rightly guided"* (36:21). The two marks go together: no payment asked, and rightly guided. The believer who evaluates religious teachers may apply the same test. Not that scholars and teachers may never be supported — the *sunnah* permits it — but that one who makes the message a means of enrichment, who tailors it to donors, who trades in religion, has failed verse 72's standard. The Prophet ﷺ asked nothing; those who follow him should be recognizable by the same freedom.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 72 asks the believer to whom he looks for his *kharāj* — his payment, his reward. If he does good for human recognition, human return, or human wages, he has chosen the lesser payer, and he will be paid accordingly — in this world, by people who forget, and not in the next. The verse invites him to make God his employer: to do what he does *for* the best Provider, and to be free of the need for any other. This freedom is practical. The person who does not need people's payment cannot be controlled by it; he can speak the truth to the wealthy (as the Prophet ﷺ did) because they hold nothing over him. *Khayr al-rāziqīn* is a name to live by: whoever believes it is provided for, and is therefore free.

**Toward the Straight Path**

The excuses have been exhausted; the Messenger's sincerity is established. The next verse states positively what he is doing: calling them to a straight path.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:73

> **Surely thou callest them unto a straight path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Positive Statement After the Negations**

Verses 68–72 cleared away every excuse for rejecting the Messenger: he brought a Word they did not ponder, a message that was not unprecedented, a character they knew, a sanity they could not deny, and a sincerity proven by his asking nothing. Verse 73 now states what he *is* doing, in the simplest possible terms: *wa innaka la-tadʿūhum ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm* — "And indeed, you are certainly calling them to a straight path." The verse is short, and its brevity is its force. After the elaborate examination of the deniers' objections, the truth is stated in a single clause with double emphasis — *inna* and the *lām* of confirmation (*la-tadʿūhum*) — as if to say: whatever they say, *this* is what is happening.

**"You Are Calling Them": Daʿwah**

The verb *tadʿūhum* is from the root *d-ʿ-w*, "to call, to invite, to summon." The verbal noun *daʿwah* has become the standard term for calling people to Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ is the *dāʿī*, the caller: *"O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness and a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and one who calls (dāʿiyan) to God by His permission, and an illuminating lamp"* (33:45–46). The verb's imperfect tense (*tadʿū*, "you are calling") indicates continuous action: he *keeps* calling, despite the recoil (v. 66), the raving (v. 67), and the aversion (v. 70). The calling does not stop because it is refused.

The object is *hum*, "them" — the very deniers whose arrogance and nonsense have just been described. The Prophet ﷺ is calling *them*, not only the receptive. This is the nature of prophetic *daʿwah*: it is addressed to all, including the hostile, and it continues even where God has said "leave them in their confusion for a time" (v. 54). The leaving concerns the *heart's attachment to results*; the calling continues regardless.

**"To a Straight Path": Ṣirāṭ Mustaqīm**

The phrase *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm* is among the most familiar in the Qur'an, prayed for in every unit of every prayer: *"Guide us to the straight path"* (1:6). The word *ṣirāṭ* means a road, a broad and clear way; *mustaqīm* means straight, upright, without crookedness — from the root *q-w-m*, "to stand." A straight path is the shortest route between two points and the one on which a traveler cannot lose his way; it has no forks to confuse him, no bends to hide the destination. The Qur'an contrasts it with the crooked paths of those who *"seek to make it crooked (ʿiwajan)"* (7:45; 11:19; 14:3), and with the *"paths (subul)"* that scatter the traveler: *"And this is My path, straight, so follow it; and do not follow the [other] paths, for they will separate you from His way"* (6:153).

The straight path in the sūrah's context is the way that leads to the destination the sūrah began by promising: *falāḥ*, success (v. 1), and Firdaws (v. 11). It is the way of the seven qualities (vv. 2–9) and the four inner states (vv. 57–60). It is straight because it goes directly to God — to *"your Lord, so fear Him"* (v. 52) — without the detours of idolatry, sectarianism (v. 53), or the "other deeds" (v. 63) that occupy those who have lost the way.

**The Path Is Objective**

Verse 73 asserts something that the preceding verse's argument makes necessary: the path is *straight* — objectively, in reality, not merely in the Prophet's opinion. Verse 71 established that truth does not follow desire; verse 73 states that the way the Prophet ﷺ calls to is *the* straight way — the one that corresponds to the truth verse 71 defended. The deniers might claim that his path was merely one option among many, no straighter than theirs. The verse denies this. There is one straight line between the human being and his Lord, and the Prophet ﷺ is calling to it. Every other path is, by geometric necessity, crooked — longer, more confusing, and not arriving.

This objectivity is why the verse is phrased as a statement of fact rather than a claim of preference. It does not say "you are calling them to a good path" or "a path you believe is right"; it says *ṣirāṭ mustaqīm* — a path that is straight. The straightness is a property of the path, verifiable by the one who walks it and arrives.

**Why the Verse Is Addressed to the Prophet**

The verse speaks to the Prophet ﷺ — "*you* are calling them" — rather than to the deniers. This is a form of consolation and confirmation. He has been called mad (v. 70), recoiled from (v. 66), mocked by night (v. 67). God tells him: you are calling them to a straight path. Whatever they say about you, this is what you are doing. The Qur'an offers this reassurance repeatedly: *"And indeed, you guide to a straight path — the path of God"* (42:52–53); *"Indeed, you are upon a straight path"* (43:43); *"So hold fast to that which has been revealed to you; indeed, you are on a straight path"* (43:43). The confirmation matters because the caller can begin to doubt himself under sustained rejection. God removes the doubt.

**The Path and the Sūrah's Believers**

The believers of the sūrah's opening are, in effect, a description of what walking the straight path looks like. Verse 73 names the path; verses 1–11 describe the walkers. The correspondence is instructive. A path is walked step by step; the believers' qualities are practices repeated daily — prayer, restraint, charity, chastity, trust-keeping. A straight path is walked without turning aside; the believers "turn away from vain talk" (v. 3), refusing the detours. A path leads to a destination; the believers "inherit Firdaws" (v. 11). The straight path is not an abstraction but the concrete way of life the sūrah has been describing.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 73 gives the believer two things. First, confidence: the way he has been called to is *straight* — not one option among equals, not a cultural preference, but the direct road to God. He need not apologize for it or doubt it because others call it crooked. Second, a standard for his own calling: he, too, is asked to call others *to a straight path* — not to himself, his group, or his opinions, but to the path. The Prophet ﷺ called to the path and asked nothing (v. 72); the believer who calls others should do the same. A call that leads people to a person or a party rather than to God has bent the path in the calling.

The verse also implies a question: if the path is straight and the call is clear, why do people not come? Verse 74 will answer: those who do not believe in the Hereafter are *deviating* from the path — and the deviation lies in them, not in the path or the caller.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:74

> **And truly those who believe not in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Deviation Located**

Verse 73 stated that the Prophet ﷺ is calling to a straight path. Verse 74 explains why some do not follow it: *wa inna lladhīna lā yuʾminūna bi-l-ākhirati ʿani l-ṣirāṭi la-nākibūn* — "And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are, from the path, certainly deviating." The two verses form a pair: the path is straight, and the deniers are off it. The verse specifies *which* deniers — those who do not believe in the Hereafter — and *what* they are doing — deviating, swerving, turning aside. The problem is diagnosed with precision: the path has not moved; they have.

**"Those Who Do Not Believe in the Hereafter"**

The verse identifies the deniers by a single characteristic: they *lā yuʾminūna bi-l-ākhirah* — "do not believe in the Hereafter." Of all the things the Quraysh denied, the sūrah selects this one as the root of their deviation. Why? Because belief in the Hereafter is what gives the straight path its point. A path is walked toward a destination; if there is no destination — no return to God, no judgment, no Paradise or Fire — then there is no reason to walk straight. One might as well wander. The deniers' materialist creed, stated in verse 37 — *"There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected"* — removed the destination, and with it the motive for the path.

The Qur'an consistently traces moral deviation to disbelief in the Hereafter. *"Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have made pleasing to them their deeds, so they wander blindly"* (27:4). *"Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with female names"* (53:27). *"Woe to those who give less [than due]... Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day?"* (83:1–5). In each case, the denial of the Hereafter is the premise, and the deviation is the conclusion. Verse 74 states the principle generally.

**"Deviating From the Path": Nākibūn**

The word *nākibūn* is from the root *n-k-b*, which means to turn aside, to swerve, to deviate from a course — as a traveler leaves the road, or as a wind shifts from its direction (a *nakbāʾ* is a wind blowing obliquely, between two quarters). The word implies not standing still off the path but *moving away* from it at an angle — a progressive divergence that grows with every step. The preposition *ʿan*, "from," reinforces the sense of departure: they are deviating *from* the path, leaving it further behind.

The image completes verse 73's geometry. There is a straight line to God. The believers walk it. The deniers, lacking belief in the destination, veer off — not necessarily in the opposite direction, but at an angle, so that the further they go, the further from the path they find themselves. A small deviation at the start becomes a great distance at the end. This is why the sūrah has described the deniers as *busy* (v. 63: "other deeds which they are doing"): they are moving, energetically, but on a line that diverges from the straight one, and their energy only increases the divergence.

**The Emphasis: Inna and Lām**

The verse is doubly emphatic, like verse 73: *inna* at the start, and the *lām* of confirmation on *la-nākibūn*. God is not tentatively suggesting that the deniers might be off course; He is declaring it with the same certainty that He declared the Prophet's path straight. The two emphatic statements together leave no middle ground: the path is straight (certainly), and they are off it (certainly). The deniers cannot claim that both paths are equally valid or that the question is open.

**Why the Hereafter Is the Hinge**

The verse's choice of the Hereafter as the diagnostic criterion deserves reflection, because it reveals the sūrah's understanding of how faith works. One might expect the root of deviation to be identified as disbelief in *God* — but the sūrah will show, in verses 84–89, that the Quraysh *did* believe in God as Creator and Lord of the heavens. What they denied was the *return* to Him. And a God from whom one will never face a reckoning is, practically, no God at all: His existence makes no difference to how one lives. Belief in the Hereafter is what turns belief in God from an abstraction into a *direction*. It is the Hereafter that makes the path matter — and it is the trembling at "return to their Lord" (v. 60) that makes the believers hasten (v. 61).

This is also why the sūrah has argued for the Resurrection so persistently — from the embryo (vv. 12–16), from the destroyed generations (vv. 42–44), from the coming seizure (vv. 64–65), and shortly from the creation of hearing, sight, and hearts (v. 78) and the alternation of night and day (v. 80). The Hereafter is the hinge on which the whole moral life turns, and the sūrah returns to it again and again because everything depends on it.

**The Path and the Fātiḥah**

Verse 74 illuminates the prayer that every Muslim recites in every prayer: *"Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor, not of those who have earned anger nor of those who are astray (al-ḍāllīn)"* (1:6–7). The *nākibūn* of verse 74 are a species of the *ḍāllīn* — those who have swerved from the road. The daily prayer is a request not to be among them: to be kept *on* the line, not veering. And the verse teaches what keeps one on the line: belief in the Hereafter, kept alive and active. The person who prays for the straight path while forgetting the destination is asking for a road while ignoring where it goes.

**Deviation Is Gradual**

The image of *nākibūn* — veering at an angle — warns that deviation is rarely a sudden reversal. No one decides, in a moment, to abandon the straight path; one drifts from it by degrees, through small compromises in which the Hereafter is momentarily forgotten. The Prophet ﷺ described the process: *"The servant commits a sin, and a black spot is placed on his heart; if he repents, it is polished away; if he returns, it increases, until it covers his heart"* (al-Tirmidhī 3334; Ibn Mājah 4244; graded ḥasan). Each spot is a small angle of deviation; the accumulated result is a heart in *ghamrah* (v. 63). The believer guards against this by returning constantly — in prayer, in remembrance, in the trembling of verse 60 — to the line, correcting the angle before it becomes a distance.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 74 asks the believer to check his heading, not merely his position. It is possible to be near the path and moving away from it; it is possible to be far from it and moving toward it. The direction matters more than the current distance. The diagnostic the verse offers is belief in the Hereafter: not the verbal affirmation, which every Muslim makes, but the *operative* belief — the degree to which the return to God actually shapes decisions. When a choice arises and the Hereafter is not in view, the angle of deviation opens, however slightly. When it is in view, the step falls on the line. The sūrah's believers were defined by exactly this: *"their hearts trembling because they will return to their Lord"* (v. 60). That trembling is what keeps a walker straight.

**Toward the Hardness of Their Hearts**

The deniers are deviating. Would mercy correct them? The next verse considers this — and its answer is one of the sūrah's most sobering observations about a certain kind of heart.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:75

> **And were We to show them mercy and remove whatever evil was upon them, they would surely persist, wandering confused in their rebellion.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Would Mercy Change Them?**

The deniers are deviating from the path (v. 74). The natural question is: could they be brought back? What if God were to treat them gently — to remove their hardships and show them mercy? Would gratitude turn them? Verse 75 answers with a hypothesis and its outcome: *wa law raḥimnāhum wa kashafnā mā bihim min ḍurrin la-lajjū fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* — "And if We had mercy on them and removed whatever harm was upon them, they would surely persist in their transgression, wandering blindly." The verse is a statement about the *kind* of heart the deniers have: a heart that reads mercy as license, that returns to its old course the moment the pressure lifts. It explains, in advance, why the seizure of verse 64 is necessary — because gentler measures have already been tried.

**"If We Had Mercy on Them and Removed the Harm"**

The hypothesis has two parts: *raḥimnāhum*, "We had mercy on them," and *kashafnā mā bihim min ḍurr*, "We removed whatever harm was upon them." The word *ḍurr* means harm, affliction, adversity — hunger, illness, loss. The commentators, as the source notes, connected this to the famine that struck Makkah after the Prophet ﷺ prayed against the Quraysh: *"O God, help me against them with seven [years of famine] like the seven of Joseph"* (al-Bukhārī 1007; Muslim 2798). The Quraysh were reduced to eating carrion and animal hides, and Abū Sufyān came to the Prophet ﷺ pleading: *"O Muḥammad, you command obedience to God and the ties of kinship; your people are perishing; pray to God for them."* He prayed, and the famine lifted — and the Quraysh returned to their denial. The source cites 43:50 for the same pattern in Pharaoh's people: *"But when We removed the punishment from them, at once they broke their word."*

The verse's hypothesis is thus not merely theoretical; it describes what *did* happen. God had mercy; the harm was removed; and they *persisted*. The verse states the general law of which the famine was an instance.

**"They Would Surely Persist in Their Transgression": Lajjū Fī Ṭughyānihim**

The verb *lajjū* is from the root *l-j-j*, which means to persist obstinately, to insist stubbornly, to keep at something despite every reason to stop. It is the root of *lujjah*, the deep of the sea (27:44), and *lajāj*, contentious insistence. The word describes a person who has dug in — who will not be moved by argument, mercy, or hardship, because his persistence has become a matter of will rather than reason. The Qur'an uses it of the deniers elsewhere: *"Rather, they persist (lajjū) in disdain and aversion"* (67:21).

The object is *ṭughyānihim*, "their transgression," from the root *ṭ-gh-y*, which means to overflow bounds, to exceed limits — as a river overflows its banks (69:11: *"when the water overflowed — ṭaghā"*), or as a ruler exceeds his authority (Pharaoh: *"Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed — ṭaghā,"* 20:24). *Ṭughyān* is the state of having broken through every restraint. The deniers, relieved of harm, would not return to bounds; they would *persist* in overflowing them.

**"Wandering Blindly": Yaʿmahūn**

The verse ends with *yaʿmahūn*, "wandering blindly," from the root *ʿ-m-h*, which denotes confusion, perplexity, groping — the state of one who cannot see where he is going and stumbles about. The Qur'an uses it as the characteristic condition of those God has left to their transgression: *"God mocks them and prolongs them in their transgression, wandering blindly (fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn)"* (2:15); *"We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly"* (6:110); *"And We have made pleasing to them their deeds, so they wander blindly"* (27:4). The phrase *fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* is a fixed Qur'anic description, and its appearance here places the Quraysh in the company of every people so described.

The combination is precise: *lajjū* (stubborn persistence) plus *yaʿmahūn* (blind wandering). They are stubborn *and* lost — insisting on a course they cannot see. This is the psychology of the *ghamrah* (vv. 54, 63): the person underwater is both unable to see and unwilling to surface.

**Why Mercy Does Not Reform Them**

The verse makes a claim that runs against a common assumption: that kindness reforms, that if only people were treated well they would respond well. The Qur'an does not deny that mercy *can* reform — it describes many who turned to God in gratitude — but it denies that mercy *necessarily* reforms, and it identifies the kind of heart on which it fails. That heart is one in *ṭughyān*, which has broken its bounds so thoroughly that it interprets every event in its own favor: hardship is an injustice to be resented, and relief is a vindication to be enjoyed. Neither moves it toward God, because it has no framework in which God is the source of either.

The Qur'an describes this heart in the account of the deniers' response to alternating blessing and hardship: *"And when We let the people taste mercy, they rejoice therein; but if evil afflicts them for what their hands have put forth, immediately they despair"* (30:36); *"And when adversity touches man, he calls upon Us... but when We bestow on him a favor from Us, he says, 'I have only been given it because of knowledge'"* (39:49). Such a heart cannot be reached by adjusting its circumstances, because it processes all circumstances through the same self-justifying lens. This is why the sūrah said "leave them in their confusion for a time" (v. 54): the confusion is not circumstantial, and changing circumstances does not cure it.

**The Verse as a Defense of Divine Justice**

Verse 75 also functions as a theodicy — an explanation of why God's severity toward the deniers is just. Someone might object: why seize them (v. 64) rather than show them more mercy? The verse answers: mercy was shown, and it did not work; if shown again, it would not work again. The severity is not God's first resort but His last, applied to hearts that have proven impervious to gentleness. The next verse will make this explicit: *"We had already seized them with the punishment, but they did not humble themselves to their Lord"* (v. 76). Both mercy and hardship have been tried; both have failed; what remains is the final seizure. The sequence is a demonstration that God exhausted the means of correction before applying the means of judgment — which is exactly what verse 62 promised: *"they will not be wronged."*

**A Contrast With the Believers**

The believers respond to mercy in the opposite way. When God removes their hardship, they *increase* in gratitude and humility; when He sends hardship, they increase in patience and turning. The Prophet ﷺ described this: *"Wondrous is the affair of the believer, for all of it is good, and that is for no one but the believer: if ease comes to him, he is grateful, and that is good for him; if harm comes to him, he is patient, and that is good for him"* (Muslim 2999). Verse 75's deniers are the inverse: ease makes them persist in transgression, and harm makes them cry out without humility (vv. 64, 76). The difference is not in what befalls them but in the heart that receives it.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 75 asks the believer how he receives *relief*. Hardship tends to turn people toward God; the truer test is what happens when the hardship lifts. Does the prayer that was fervent in illness continue in health? Does the charity that was generous in fear continue in security? Does the humility of the crisis survive the recovery? The deniers of verse 75, relieved of the famine, returned to their *ṭughyān*. The believer who notices in himself the same return — the slackening of devotion when the pressure eases — is warned by the verse to correct it before it hardens. The Qur'an commends those who remember God *"in ease and in hardship"* (3:134), not only in one.

The verse also teaches realism about others. Not everyone can be won by kindness; some hearts read kindness as weakness or as license. This does not mean kindness should be withheld — the Prophet ﷺ prayed for the Quraysh's famine to lift — but it means one should not be surprised or embittered when kindness fails. God Himself showed mercy to hearts He knew would persist. The believer shows it for the same reason: because it is right, not because it is guaranteed to work.

**Toward the Failure of Hardship**

Mercy would not have reformed them. The next verse states that hardship did not either — and names the quality they lacked: humility before their Lord.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:76

> **And We already seized them with the punishment, but they did not yield to their Lord, nor are they humble,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Hardship Has Also Been Tried**

Verse 75 said that mercy would not reform the deniers. Verse 76 states that hardship has not either: *wa laqad akhadhnāhum bi-l-ʿadhābi fa-mā stakānū li-rabbihim wa mā yataḍarraʿūn* — "And We had already seized them with the punishment, but they did not submit to their Lord, nor do they humble themselves in supplication." The verse completes a pair. Together, verses 75 and 76 establish that *neither* of the two great instruments of divine correction — ease and hardship, mercy and affliction — has moved these hearts. This is the fullest possible indictment: the deniers cannot say they were not given a chance, because they were given both kinds.

**"We Had Already Seized Them With the Punishment"**

The construction *laqad akhadhnāhum* — "We had *already* seized them" — uses the emphatic *laqad* to insist on a completed fact. This is not the future seizure of verse 64 (*ḥattā idhā akhadhnā*, "until when We seize"), which is still to come; it is a *past* seizure, already experienced. The commentators identified it with the famine described under verse 75 — the years of hunger after the Prophet's prayer, when the Quraysh saw *"a smoke"* between themselves and the sky from starvation (44:10 and the ḥadīth of Ibn Masʿūd, al-Bukhārī 4774; Muslim 2798) — and with the deaths at Badr. The source records the boycott associated with Thumāmah ibn Uthāl, the chief of Yamāmah who, after accepting Islam, cut off the grain supply to Makkah until the Quraysh begged the Prophet ﷺ to intervene (al-Bukhārī 4372; Muslim 1764). All are instances of *ʿadhāb* — punishment in this world — applied before the final reckoning.

The point is that the deniers have *tasted* punishment. It was not merely threatened; it was administered, in measured doses, as a warning. The Qur'an describes this as a deliberate divine method: *"And We will surely let them taste the nearer punishment short of the greater punishment, that perhaps they will return"* (32:21). The nearer punishment is a mercy in severe form — a small suffering meant to prevent a great one. The deniers received it.

**"But They Did Not Submit to Their Lord": Mā Stakānū**

The verb *istakānū* is from the root *k-w-n* or *s-k-n* (the grammarians differ), and in either case its meaning is to become lowly, to submit, to yield — to be brought to a state of humbled stillness. The Qur'an uses it of the steadfast believers who fought alongside earlier prophets: *"they did not weaken for what befell them in the cause of God, nor did they become feeble, nor did they submit (mā stakānū)"* (3:146) — where refusing to *istikānah* before enemies is praised. Here, the same refusal before *God* is condemned. The deniers had the fortitude not to yield — but they applied it in the wrong direction. Steadfastness against God is not strength; it is *ṭughyān* (v. 75).

The phrase *li-rabbihim*, "to their Lord," specifies the one to whom they should have yielded. The punishment was from Him; the proper response was to bend before Him. Instead they endured it as one endures a natural disaster — as bad luck, as the way of things — without connecting it to its Source or to their conduct. This is the failure the Qur'an describes in 6:43: *"Then why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hardened, and Satan made attractive to them what they were doing."*

**"Nor Do They Humble Themselves in Supplication": Mā Yataḍarraʿūn**

The second verb, *yataḍarraʿūn*, is from the root *ḍ-r-ʿ*, which denotes humbling oneself in earnest entreaty — the posture of a person who lowers himself, pleads, begs with visible humility. *Taḍarruʿ* is the supplication of the desperate and the humble: *"Call upon your Lord in humility (taḍarruʿan) and privately"* (7:55); *"And We seized them with poverty and hardship that perhaps they might humble themselves (yataḍarraʿūn)"* (6:42). The purpose of the seizing, according to 6:42, is precisely to produce *taḍarruʿ*. Verse 76 records that the purpose was not achieved: they were seized, and they did not humble themselves.

The tense shift is notable. *Mā stakānū* is past ("they did not submit") — describing their response to the past seizure. *Mā yataḍarraʿūn* is present-continuous ("they do not humble themselves") — describing their ongoing state. Even now, after the punishment has been experienced and lifted, they are not in a posture of humble supplication. The lesson did not take. This confirms verse 75: relief did not reform them either.

**Why the Deniers Did Not Humble Themselves**

One might ask how a people could be starved to eating carrion and not turn to God. The Qur'an gives the answer in the parallel verse 6:43: *"their hearts became hardened."* Hardness of heart (*qaswah*) is the condition in which suffering fails to produce softening. The Qur'an compares such hearts to stones — *"or even harder, for indeed there are stones from which rivers gush forth"* (2:74). A hardened heart experiences pain but does not *interpret* it; it suffers without learning. The deniers suffered the famine and blamed Muḥammad ﷺ for it, or bad fortune, or their gods' displeasure — anything but the truth that the One Lord was calling them to return. The Prophet ﷺ explained the danger: *"Do not talk too much without remembering God, for much talk without remembrance of God hardens the heart, and the furthest of people from God is the one with a hard heart"* (al-Tirmidhī 2411). The Quraysh's nightly *samar* (v. 67) — endless talk without remembrance — was, by this ḥadīth, the very thing that hardened them against the famine's lesson.

**Two Failures, One Heart**

Verses 75 and 76 together describe a heart on which neither carrot nor stick has any effect. This is theologically important, because it removes any suggestion that the deniers' fate is arbitrary or that God did not try. He tried mercy (v. 75); He tried hardship (v. 76). The Qur'an describes the same double method with the people of Pharaoh: *"And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of famine and a deficiency in fruits that perhaps they would be reminded. But when good came to them, they said, 'This is ours'; and if a bad condition struck them, they saw an evil omen in Moses and those with him"* (7:130–131). Good was attributed to themselves; bad was blamed on the prophet. The Quraysh reasoned identically.

**The Contrast With the Believers' Response to Affliction**

The believers of the sūrah are people whose hearts *tremble* (v. 60) *before* any punishment — they do not need to be seized to be humble. And when affliction does come to believers, they respond exactly as the deniers failed to: with *istikānah* and *taḍarruʿ*. The Prophet ﷺ, in the worst days of Ṭāʾif, did not blame God or harden; he prayed: *"O God, to You I complain of my weakness and my lack of resources and my lowliness before people... if You are not angry with me, I do not care"* (al-Ṭabarānī; Ibn Isḥāq). That prayer is *taḍarruʿ* — the humble pleading that affliction is meant to produce. The deniers were given affliction and produced none of it.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 76 asks the believer how he receives *hardship*. Verse 75 asked about relief; this verse asks about affliction — and the two together cover the whole of life. When hardship comes, does the believer *istakāna* — yield to his Lord, acknowledging that the hardship is from Him and may be a call? Does he *yataḍarraʿ* — humble himself in supplication, lowering himself before God rather than raising his voice against fate? Or does he endure with a hard heart, complaining of circumstances and blaming others, without the affliction ever becoming a conversation with God? The Qur'an's expectation is clear: *"And We seized them with poverty and hardship that perhaps they might humble themselves"* (6:42). Hardship is an invitation to humility. The deniers refused it; the believer accepts it, and finds — as the Prophet ﷺ promised — that *"no fatigue, nor disease, nor sorrow, nor sadness, nor hurt, nor distress befalls a Muslim, even the prick of a thorn, but God expiates some of his sins for it"* (al-Bukhārī 5641; Muslim 2573). The same thorn that hardens one heart purifies another.

**Toward the Gate of Severe Punishment**

Mercy failed; measured hardship failed. What remains is the unmeasured. The next verse describes the opening of a gate — and the despair behind it.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:77

> **till, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment, behold, they despair therein.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Final Stage**

Verses 75 and 76 have shown that neither mercy nor measured hardship moved the deniers. Verse 77 describes what comes after both have failed: *ḥattā idhā fataḥnā ʿalayhim bāban dhā ʿadhābin shadīdin idhā hum fīhi mublisūn* — "Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment, at once they are in despair therein." The verse is the third *ḥattā idhā* ("until, when") of this section — after verse 64 (*"until, when We seize their affluent ones"*) and verse 54's *ḥattā ḥīn* ("for a time") — and it marks the end of the reprieve. The grammar itself performs the sequence: until... until... until — and then the gate opens.

**"When We Open Upon Them a Gate": Bāb**

The image is of a *gate* (*bāb*) opened *upon* them (*ʿalayhim*). A gate that was closed held something back; its opening releases what it held. The preposition *ʿalā*, "upon," indicates that what is released comes down on them, overwhelms them — not a gate they walk through but a gate that discharges its contents onto them. The Qur'an uses the image of opened gates for both mercy and punishment: *"We opened upon them (fataḥnā ʿalayhim) the doors of every thing"* (6:44, of the *istidrāj* that precedes seizure); *"So We opened the gates of the heaven with rain pouring down"* (54:11, of Noah's Flood). The gate of verse 77 is a gate of *ʿadhāb shadīd*, "severe punishment" — and the adjective *shadīd*, "severe, intense, hard," distinguishes it from the earlier punishment (v. 76), which was severe enough to starve them but was still a warning. This is the punishment that is no longer a warning.

The word *bāb* also implies that the punishment is a *single* opening from which much pours — sudden, concentrated, and beyond the capacity to bear. The famine came gradually; the gate opens at once.

**What the Gate Is**

The commentators identified the gate with several events, and the source records the main candidates. Some, following Ibn ʿAbbās and others, identified it with the defeat at Badr, where the *mutrafūn* of Quraysh — the very elite the sūrah has been addressing — were killed in a single day: seventy dead, seventy captured, the leadership of Makkah broken. Others identified it with the conquest of Makkah, when the city's resistance collapsed and its idols were destroyed. Others identified it with death itself, the gate every denier passes through into the punishment. And others identified it with the gates of Hell on the Day of Judgment: *"And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups until, when they reach it, its gates are opened"* (39:71).

The verse's wording does not force a choice, and the pattern it describes holds at every level: when the final punishment comes — in whatever form — the deniers, who were not humbled by warning, are not humbled by it either; they are only *despairing*. Badr fits the pattern exactly: the Quraysh did not repent at Badr; they hardened and prepared for Uḥud. Death fits it: the dying denier of verses 99–100 will beg to return but will not be returned. The Judgment fits it: the people of Hell in verse 108 will be told *"be gone therein, and speak not to Me."*

**"At Once They Are in Despair Therein": Mublisūn**

The verse's key word is *mublisūn*, from the root *b-l-s*, which denotes the state of one who has lost all hope, who is struck silent and still by the realization that nothing can be done. The name *Iblīs* is, on one common derivation, from the same root — the one who despaired of God's mercy. The Qur'an uses *mublisūn* at the moment of sudden seizure: *"We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair (mublisūn)"* (6:44); and for the criminals on the Day of Judgment: *"And the Day the Hour appears, the criminals will be in despair (yublisu)"* (30:12). The word describes not active grief but a *silenced* hopelessness — the stunned recognition that the game is over.

The construction *idhā hum fīhi mublisūn* — "at once, behold, they are in it, despairing" — parallels verse 64's *idhā hum yajʾarūn* — "at once, behold, they cry out." The two responses mark two stages. At the seizure (v. 64), they *cry out* — there is still voice, still the reflex of appeal. At the gate (v. 77), they *despair* — the voice is gone; there is nothing left to say. The sequence is psychologically exact: shock produces the cry; recognition produces the silence. Verse 65 had already told them their cry would not be answered; verse 77 shows them absorbing that fact.

**Despair Versus Humility**

The verse's implicit contrast is with what the deniers *should* have done when the earlier punishment came: humbled themselves (v. 76: *istakānū*, *yataḍarraʿū*). Humility is the response of one who still has hope — who bends because he believes bending will be received. Despair is the response of one who has no hope left. The tragedy verse 77 records is that the deniers moved from hardness to despair without passing through humility. There was a stage — the measured punishment of verse 76 — at which humility was possible and would have been accepted; they skipped it, and arrived at the gate where only despair remained. The Qur'an describes this trajectory as the specific danger of the hardened heart: *"So when they forgot that of which they had been reminded, We opened to them the doors of every thing, until, when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair"* (6:44). Rejoicing → seizure → despair, with no humility between.

**The Gate and the Sūrah's Structure**

Verses 54–77 form a complete unit in the sūrah, and verse 77 closes it. The unit began with "leave them in their confusion for a time" (v. 54) and proceeds through: their false confidence in wealth (55–56), the contrast with the true believers (57–61), divine justice (62), the deniers' submerged hearts (63), the seizure and the cry (64–65), the reason (66–67), the cleared excuses (68–72), the straight path and the deviation (73–74), the failure of mercy and hardship (75–76), and now the gate and the despair (77). The arc is from reprieve to end. It is a complete moral history of a people who were warned, argued with, shown mercy, disciplined, and finally judged. And it is told *before* the end arrived — as a warning to those who could still avoid it.

**The Verse's Mercy**

Like verse 65, verse 77 is severe in content but merciful in placement. It describes the gate *before* it opens, to a people who still have time. The Quraysh who heard this verse recited had not yet been to Badr; they had not yet died; the gate was still closed. The verse's function is to make the future present — to show them the despair at the end of their road while they could still turn from the road. This is the Qur'an's consistent method: it narrates the end so that the end may be avoided. The believer who reads the verse is in the same position: the gate is described, and it is not yet open.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 77 warns the believer against the trajectory it describes: from complacency, through unheeded warnings, to a sudden end at which only despair is possible. The protection is to respond to the *earlier* stages — to let the small hardship humble, to let the near warning be enough. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"The clever one is he who takes account of himself and works for what comes after death; the weak one is he who follows his desires and then hopes in God"* (al-Tirmidhī 2459). The deniers of verse 77 followed their desires (v. 71: *ahwāʾ*) and then, at the gate, had not even hope left. The believer takes account now — in the trembling of verse 60 — so that at his gate he arrives not as *mublis*, despairing, but as one who has hoped rightly and is received.

**Toward the Signs Within**

The argument against the deniers has concluded with their end. The sūrah now begins a new argument — from the faculties God gave them: hearing, sight, and hearts. The turn is from what they will suffer to what they were given and did not use.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:78
