> **He it is Who brought into being for you hearing, sight, and hearts. Little do you give thanks!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A New Argument Begins**

Having concluded the account of the deniers' end (v. 77), the sūrah opens a fresh sequence of arguments for faith in verses 78–80. Each verse begins with *wa huwa lladhī* — "And He it is Who" — and each names an act of God that demands a response. Verse 78 names the first: *wa huwa lladhī anshaʾa lakumu l-samʿa wa l-abṣāra wa l-afʾidata qalīlan mā tashkurūn* — "And He it is Who produced for you hearing and sight and hearts; little is it that you give thanks." The argument turns from what will happen to the deniers to what has already been done for them: they were given the faculties by which truth is perceived, and they used them for everything except perceiving it.

**"He It Is Who Produced for You": Anshaʾa**

The verb *anshaʾa* is from the root *n-sh-ʾ*, which means to bring into being, to cause to grow, to originate. It is the verb the sūrah used in verse 14 for the final stage of the embryo: *"then We produced it (anshaʾnāhu) as another creation"* — and in verses 31 and 42 for the generations: *"then We produced (anshaʾnā) after them another generation."* The word implies origination from nothing and development toward a form. The hearing, sight, and hearts of verse 78 were *produced* — they did not assemble themselves; they were brought into being by an Originator and grown to their function.

The prepositional phrase *lakum*, "for you," is pointed. The faculties were produced *for* their possessors — as gifts, for their benefit, to be used. The deniers received them as anyone receives an inheritance: unearned, complete, and useful. The verse's argument begins from this gift.

**"Hearing and Sight and Hearts": The Three Faculties**

The three faculties named are *al-samʿ* (hearing), *al-abṣār* (sight, plural), and *al-afʾidah* (hearts, plural). The Qur'an names this triad repeatedly, always in this order, as the instruments of knowledge: *"And God brought you out of your mothers' wombs knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing and sight and hearts that perhaps you would be grateful"* (16:78); *"Then He proportioned him and breathed into him from His spirit and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful"* (32:9); *"Say, 'It is He who has produced you and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful'"* (67:23). The source cites the closely parallel 6:46, 32:9, and 67:23, and the repetition across sūrahs shows how central the argument is.

The order is not arbitrary. *Hearing* is named first and in the singular — the commentators noted that hearing is the faculty by which revelation is received (the Qur'an is *heard* before it is read), and that it is the first sense to function in the infant and the last to fail in the dying. *Sight* is named second and in the plural — the faculty by which the signs of creation are observed (vv. 17–22). *Hearts* (*afʾidah*, the plural of *fuʾād*) are named last and in the plural — the faculty by which what is heard and seen is *understood*. The word *fuʾād* is a specific word for the heart, related to the root for "burning" or "kindling," and it denotes the heart as the seat of reflection and emotion — the organ that takes in the data of hearing and sight and *ignites* with comprehension.

The three together constitute the complete apparatus of knowledge: reception (hearing), observation (sight), and understanding (heart). Every argument the sūrah has made — from the embryo, the heavens, the rain, the cattle, the histories, the recited Word — required these three to function. The deniers *had* them. That is the point.

**The Argument From the Faculties**

Verse 78's argument runs as follows. God gave you the instruments of knowing. With these instruments you *could* have heard the Qur'an, seen the signs, and understood their meaning. The failure to believe is therefore not a failure of equipment but of use. You have hearing and did not listen (v. 66: turned on your heels when the signs were recited); you have sight and did not look (v. 68: did not ponder); you have hearts and they were submerged (v. 63: *ghamrah*). The Qur'an makes this charge explicitly elsewhere: *"They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray"* (7:179). The faculties were given; the deniers rendered them useless by refusing to point them at the truth.

There is a second layer to the argument, which the parallel verses make clear: the faculties are themselves *signs*. Hearing and sight are extraordinary — the ear converts vibration into meaning, the eye converts light into image, and the heart converts both into knowledge. These are not things that produce themselves. The one who reflects on his own capacity to reflect finds evidence for the Originator in the very instrument he reflects with. The deniers used their eyes to count their wealth (v. 55) and never once looked at the eye.

**"Little Is It That You Give Thanks": Qalīlan Mā Tashkurūn**

The verse ends with a rebuke: *qalīlan mā tashkurūn* — "little is it that you are grateful." The word *qalīlan*, "little," is placed first for emphasis; the *mā* intensifies it. The construction has been read two ways by the grammarians: "little is your gratitude" — that is, you are scarcely grateful at all — or "for little you are grateful" — that is, your gratitude is for trivial things and not for these great ones. Both readings converge on the charge: the deniers received the faculties and did not thank the Giver.

Gratitude (*shukr*) in the Qur'an is not merely a feeling or a verbal acknowledgment; it is the *use of a gift in the way its giver intended*. To be grateful for hearing is to *listen* to the truth; to be grateful for sight is to *look* at the signs; to be grateful for the heart is to *understand*. The deniers' ingratitude was therefore not a separate sin from their denial — it *was* their denial. They took the instruments of knowing God and used them to know everything but Him. This is why the parallel verse 16:78 gives gratitude as the *purpose* of the faculties: *"He made for you hearing and sight and hearts that perhaps you would be grateful."* The purpose was gratitude, understood as right use.

**The Sequence of the Three Verses**

Verses 78–80 form a triad, and their subjects ascend. Verse 78: God gave you the faculties of knowledge (the individual's equipment). Verse 79: God spread you on the earth and will gather you to Him (the human race's origin and destination). Verse 80: God gives life and death and alternates night and day (the cosmic order). Each verse ends with a rebuke or a question: "little are you grateful" (78); "to Him you will be gathered" (79); "will you not then understand?" (80). The triad moves outward from the self to the species to the cosmos, and at each level asks the same thing: given what you have been shown and given, why do you not respond?

**The Heart as the Decisive Faculty**

Of the three faculties, the heart is decisive, because hearing and sight deliver their data to it and it decides what to do. The sūrah has been describing hearts throughout: the hearts of the believers are *wajilah*, trembling (v. 60); the hearts of the deniers are in *ghamrah*, submerged (v. 63). The same organ, in two conditions. Verse 78 names the heart as a *gift* — and thereby implies that the condition of one's heart is not fate but stewardship. The heart was given sound; it becomes submerged by neglect and hardened by refusal (v. 76). The Prophet ﷺ prayed constantly for his heart: *"O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion"* (al-Tirmidhī 2140; graded ṣaḥīḥ), and taught that hearts are between two fingers of the Merciful, turned as He wills (Muslim 2654). The gift can be kept or lost.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 78 asks the believer to take an inventory of his three faculties and their use. *Hearing*: what does he listen to, and does the Qur'an have a place among it proportionate to its worth? *Sight*: what does he look at, and does he ever look at the world *as signs* — or only as scenery, commodity, and entertainment? *Heart*: what does he understand, and does he ever turn the heart toward the meaning of what he has heard and seen? Gratitude, in the verse's sense, is not saying "thank God for my eyes" but *using* the eyes for what they were made to see. The believer who listens to the Qur'an with attention, looks at creation with reflection, and lets his heart tremble at what both reveal has given thanks in the only way that counts.

The verse also warns against the modern flood of stimulus that occupies all three faculties with *laghw* (v. 3) — endless sound, endless image, endless distraction — so that hearing, sight, and heart are perpetually full and never available for the truth. The Quraysh had their nightly *samar* (v. 67); every age has its equivalent. The faculties were given "for you"; to spend them entirely on what leaves the heart submerged is *qalīlan mā tashkurūn*.

**Toward the Scattering and the Gathering**

The individual has been addressed. The next verse widens the lens: God spread the human race on the earth — and will gather it back to Himself.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:79

> **He it is Who created you on the earth, and unto Him shall you be gathered.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second of the Three Arguments**

The triad of *wa huwa lladhī* verses continues: *wa huwa lladhī dharaʾakum fī l-arḍi wa ilayhi tuḥsharūn* — "And He it is Who scattered you upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered." Verse 78 concerned the individual's faculties; verse 79 concerns the human race as a whole — its dispersal across the earth and its destined regathering. The verse is a single sentence with two movements, outward and inward: God *scattered* you (*dharaʾa*), and to Him you will be *gathered* (*ḥashr*). The two verbs are opposites, and their pairing is the argument.

**"He Scattered You Upon the Earth": Dharaʾa**

The verb *dharaʾakum* is from the root *dh-r-ʾ*, which means to create by multiplying and spreading — to sow, to scatter, to disperse. It is related to *dharr*, the tiny particles or ants (99:7: *"an atom's weight — mithqāl dharrah"*), and *dhurriyyah*, offspring, progeny (as in the Qur'an's phrase for the descendants of Adam). The source notes that *dharaʾa* carries the sense of scattering seed — sowing it broadly over a field. The Qur'an uses it for God's creation of humankind in its multiplicity: *"He has scattered you (yadhraʾukum) therein"* (42:11); *"And We have certainly created (dharaʾnā) for Hell many of the jinn and mankind"* (7:179).

The image is of a sower broadcasting seed across a field: one hand, one motion, and the seed falls everywhere — in this valley, on that hillside, across the whole extent of the land. So God created the human race and spread it over the earth — into every climate and continent, every tribe and language, every era. The dispersal was His act. No people chose its land; no individual chose his birthplace. The Quraysh were in Makkah because they had been *scattered* there; the Persians were in Persia, the Byzantines in Byzantium, by the same sowing. The verse asks its hearers to see the whole distributed human race as the work of one hand.

**"And to Him You Will Be Gathered": Ḥashr**

The second clause reverses the motion: *wa ilayhi tuḥsharūn* — "and to Him you will be gathered." The verb *ḥashara* means to gather, to collect together, to assemble — especially to assemble a scattered multitude into one place. It is the Qur'an's standard term for the gathering of all humanity on the Day of Judgment: *"And [warn of] the Day We will gather them (naḥshuruhum) all together"* (10:28); *"And We will gather them (ḥasharnāhum) and not leave behind from them anyone"* (18:47). *Yawm al-Ḥashr*, the Day of Gathering, is one of the names of the Last Day.

The source captures the verse's logic precisely: the word *dharaʾa* implies scattering, so the verse says that God scattered human beings over the earth and will bring them all together again. What was broadcast will be collected. Every seed the Sower cast will be brought back to the Sower. The prepositional phrase *ilayhi*, "to Him," is placed before the verb for emphasis: to *Him* — not to the earth, not to oblivion, not to nowhere, but to the One who scattered.

**The Argument From Symmetry**

The verse's argument is one of symmetry, and it answers the deniers' materialist creed directly. They said: *"We die and we live, and we will not be resurrected"* (v. 37). Verse 79 replies: the One who scattered you is the One who will gather you. If scattering was possible, gathering is possible. If the seed could be sown across the whole earth by a single act, it can be collected from the whole earth by a single act. The Qur'an makes this argument repeatedly: *"Say, 'He will give them life who produced them the first time'"* (36:79); *"As We began the first creation, We will repeat it"* (21:104). The deniers accepted the first half of the verse — they could see that humanity was spread across the earth — and denied the second. The verse insists that the two are one motion, outward and back, from one Source to the same Source.

The argument also has a moral dimension. A scattering without a gathering would be purposeless — seed thrown away, never harvested. The scattering has a purpose *because* there is a gathering: humanity is spread over the earth to live, act, and be tested (v. 30), and then collected to be judged (v. 62: the record that speaks truth). Verse 115 will state the alternative and reject it: *"Did you think that We created you in play, and that to Us you would not be returned?"* Verse 79 is that verse's premise: you were scattered *on purpose*, and the purpose is completed at the gathering.

**The Earth as the Field**

The phrase *fī l-arḍ*, "upon the earth," names the field. The earth is where the seed was scattered — the place of growth, action, and testing. The sūrah has described the earth as furnished for this purpose: water sent down and lodged in it (v. 18), gardens produced from it (v. 19), the olive of Sinai growing from it (v. 20), cattle grazing on it (v. 21). The earth is not humanity's origin (that is God) or its destination (that is God); it is the *field in between* — the place where the seed grows into what it will be at harvest. The Qur'an calls the earth a *mustaqarr* (2:36), a temporary dwelling, and describes it as *"a place of living and a place of dying"* (77:25–26) — but not a place of remaining.

**Gathered Together**

The verb *tuḥsharūn* is plural and implies that the gathering is collective: *all* who were scattered are gathered *together*. The Qur'an emphasizes this totality: *"The Day when the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens, and they will come out before God, the One, the Prevailing"* (14:48); *"And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: 'You have certainly come to Us just as We created you the first time'"* (18:48). Every human being who has ever lived — from Adam to the last born — will stand in one assembly. Noah's people and the Quraysh, Pharaoh and the believer of his household, will be present in the same gathering. The sūrah's histories are not closed cases; they are pending, awaiting the *ḥashr*.

The Prophet ﷺ described the gathering: *"People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised"* — and when ʿĀʾishah asked whether men and women would then look at one another, he said: *"O ʿĀʾishah, the matter is too severe for them to look at one another"* (al-Bukhārī 6527; Muslim 2859). The gathering is total and its gravity total.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Structure**

Verse 79's motion — scattered from God, gathered to God — is the sūrah's own shape. It began with human beings as an *extract of clay* (v. 12) and will end with their standing before *"the True Sovereign"* (v. 116) to receive the verdict of heavy or light scales (vv. 102–103). Everything in between is the field. The sūrah's histories showed generations scattered and destroyed; verse 79 reminds that destruction was not their end — they, too, will be gathered. Nothing that was scattered is lost to the Gatherer.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 79 asks the believer to hold two facts together at all times: he is scattered, and he will be gathered. To be scattered is to be *here*, in this place and time, by God's placement — which means his circumstances are not accident but assignment, and his task is to grow in the field he was sown in. To be gathered is to be *going back* — which means nothing done in the field is final except its effect on the harvest. The believer who forgets the first becomes resentful of his lot; the one who forgets the second becomes absorbed in it. The verse's two clauses, held together, produce the balanced posture the sūrah praises: engaged in the earth (giving, v. 60; hastening, v. 61) and trembling at the return (v. 60).

The verse also dissolves a certain loneliness. The individual feels himself one seed in a vast field, lost among billions, unseen. Verse 79 says: the Sower who scattered you knows where every seed fell, and will gather every one. *"And not absent from your Lord is any [part] of an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven"* (10:61). No one scattered by God is lost to God.

**Toward Life, Death, and the Alternating Days**

The individual (v. 78) and the race (v. 79) have been addressed. The third verse of the triad turns to the cosmic order — life and death, night and day — and ends with a question the sūrah has asked before: *"Will you not then understand?"*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:80

> **And He it is Who gives life and causes death, and unto Him belongs the variation of the night and the day. Will you not, then, understand?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Argument: The Cosmic Rhythms**

The triad concludes: *wa huwa lladhī yuḥyī wa yumītu wa lahu khtilāfu l-layli wa l-nahāri a-fa-lā taʿqilūn* — "And He it is Who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day. Will you not then use reason?" Verse 78 argued from the faculties within the individual; verse 79 from the dispersal and gathering of the race; verse 80 argues from the two great rhythms that govern all life on earth — the alternation of life and death, and the alternation of night and day. Both rhythms are named as God's, and both point to the same conclusion: the One who governs the cycles can bring the cycle of life to its completion in resurrection.

**"He Gives Life and Causes Death": Yuḥyī wa Yumīt**

The pair *yuḥyī wa yumīt* — "He gives life and He causes death" — is one of the Qur'an's most frequent descriptions of God: *"He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned"* (10:56); *"Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and to Us is the destination"* (50:43); *"Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion... who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed"* (67:1–2). The imperfect tense (*yuḥyī*, *yumīt*) indicates continuous action: He *is* giving life and *is* causing death, now, at every moment, across the whole earth — the child born in this instant and the old man dying in it are both His acts.

The two verbs answer the deniers' creed once more. They said: *"We die and we live"* (v. 37) — as if death and life were impersonal events that simply happened. Verse 80 says: *He* gives life; *He* causes death. The verbs have a subject. Life is not a spontaneous property of matter that arises and lapses on its own; it is given and taken by a Giver and Taker. And a Giver of life who can give it once can give it again — which is the point the sūrah has been pressing since verse 16.

The order — life first, then death — reflects experience: one is born, then one dies. But the Qur'an elsewhere reverses it, *"who created death and life"* (67:2), and the reversal is instructive. From God's side, the sequence is: life given, death caused, *and life given again*. The deniers see only the first two terms and conclude the series ends. Verse 80 names the Author of the series and leaves the conclusion to the following question.

**"To Him Belongs the Alternation of Night and Day"**

The second rhythm is cosmic: *wa lahu khtilāfu l-layli wa l-nahār* — "and to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day." The word *ikhtilāf* means difference, succession, alternation — the coming of one after the other, each differing from the last. The night follows the day, the day follows the night, in an order so reliable that human beings measure time by it and never think to ask who maintains it. The verse says: it is *His* — *lahu*, "to Him belongs" — the succession is His act, His possession, His ongoing governance.

The Qur'an presents the alternation of night and day as a sign in many places: *"Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding"* (3:190); *"And He it is who made the night and the day in succession for whoever desires to remember or desires gratitude"* (25:62); *"Say, 'Have you considered: if God should make for you the night continuous until the Day of Resurrection, what deity other than God could bring you light?'"* (28:71). The alternation is a sign for several reasons that the commentators developed.

First, it is a sign of *power*: to turn the whole earth from light to darkness and back, without fail, is an act no creature can perform or interrupt. Second, it is a sign of *mercy*: the day is for work and the night for rest, and the alternation makes both possible (78:10–11). Third — and this is the reason it is paired with life and death here — it is a sign of *resurrection*. Every night, the day "dies"; every morning, it is "raised." The world goes dark and returns to light. If the deniers cannot conceive of life following death, they have only to look at what happens every twenty-four hours. Al-Rāzī and others noted that sleep and waking are a daily death and resurrection (the Qur'an says: *"It is God who takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep"* — 39:42), and the Prophet ﷺ taught the waking supplication: *"Praise be to God who gave us life after He caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection"* (al-Bukhārī 6312). The believer is reminded of resurrection every morning by the alternation verse 80 names.

**The Two Rhythms Together**

Life and death; night and day. The verse pairs the biological rhythm with the cosmic one because they are the same lesson at two scales. Both are *alternations* — one thing giving way to its opposite, then returning. Both are *governed* — neither happens by itself. And both point beyond themselves: the one who turns night into day can turn death into life. The deniers accepted the second rhythm as obvious (no one denied that morning follows night) and rejected the analogous conclusion about the first. Verse 80 sets them side by side and asks why.

**"Will You Not Then Use Reason?": A-fa-lā Taʿqilūn**

The verse ends with the question that closes so many of the Qur'an's arguments from creation: *a-fa-lā taʿqilūn* — "will you not then use reason?" The verb *taʿqilūn* is from the root *ʿ-q-l*, which originally means to tie, to bind (an *ʿiqāl* is the cord that hobbles a camel), and by extension to *bind thoughts together* — to reason, to connect premise to conclusion. The question asks the deniers to *connect* what they see: life given → life can be given again; night turned to day → death can be turned to life; alternation governed → the Governor can complete the cycle. The reasoning is not difficult. The verse does not ask for a leap of faith but for the ordinary act of binding one observation to its implication.

The sūrah asked a related question at verse 23 and verse 32 (*a-fa-lā tattaqūn*, "will you not be reverent?") and will ask another at verses 85 and 87 (*a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn*, "will you not remember?"; *a-fa-lā tattaqūn*). The sequence of questions — reason, remember, revere — describes the path from observation to faith: reason connects the signs; memory recalls what one already knew; reverence follows from both. Verse 80 asks for the first step.

**Reason and Revelation**

The verse's appeal to reason is a permanent feature of the Qur'an's method and deserves emphasis. The Qur'an does not present faith as opposed to reason or as requiring its suspension. It presents faith as the *conclusion* reason reaches when it binds observations correctly — and it presents denial as a *failure* of reason: *"the worst of creatures in the sight of God are the deaf and dumb who do not use reason (lā yaʿqilūn)"* (8:22); *"And they will say, 'If only we had listened or used reason (naʿqilu), we would not be among the companions of the Blaze'"* (67:10). The people of Hell, in this last verse, diagnose their own failure as a failure to *reason*. Verse 80's question, asked in this life, offers the chance to reason before it is too late.

**The Verse's Place in the Triad**

The three *wa huwa lladhī* verses have moved from the intimate to the universal: from the ear, eye, and heart within the body (78), to the human race spread across the earth (79), to life and death and the turning of the planet (80). At each level, the sūrah has shown God's act and asked for the appropriate response: gratitude (78), awareness of the gathering (79), reason (80). The triad is a complete case: the deniers have the instruments to know, the evidence in their own existence, and the signs in the sky above them. What remains is only to *use* what they have. The next verse will state that they did not — that they said only what those before them had said.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 80 gives the believer two daily practices of reflection. At every death he hears of, and every birth: *He* gives life and *He* causes death — nothing is random, nothing is unattended, and the One who took can restore. At every dusk and dawn: to *Him* belongs the alternation — the day that just ended was His, the night beginning is His, and the morning that will come is a small rehearsal of the Morning that will come to all. The Prophet's morning supplication — *"We have reached the morning, and the dominion belongs to God"* (Muslim 2723) — is verse 80 made into a daily habit. The believer who greets each day with it has *used reason* in the verse's sense: he has bound the sign to its meaning, and lives inside the connection.

**Toward the Repeated Words**

The three arguments have been made. The next verse records the deniers' response — and it is not an argument. It is a repetition: they say what the ancients said.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:81

> **Nay, but they say the like of that which was said by those of old.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Response to the Three Arguments**

Verses 78–80 offered three arguments for faith and resurrection — from the faculties, from the scattering and gathering, from the rhythms of life and light. Verse 81 records the deniers' response: *bal qālū mithla mā qāla l-awwalūn* — "Rather, they said the like of what the ancients said." The particle *bal* ("rather, nay") marks the failure of the expected response. They should have used reason (v. 80); instead they *repeated*. The verse is short and its judgment is devastating in its restraint: it does not accuse them of stupidity or malice, only of *unoriginality*. Confronted with fresh evidence, they produced old words.

**"They Said the Like of What the Ancients Said"**

The phrase *mithla mā qāla l-awwalūn* — "the like of what the first ones said" — identifies the deniers' response as a quotation. The Quraysh imagined themselves to be reasoning; in fact they were reciting. Their objections to resurrection were not conclusions they had reached but formulas they had inherited — the same formulas the sūrah has already recorded on the lips of the second generation after Noah: *"Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?"* (v. 35). The next two verses (82–83) will give the Quraysh's words, and they will be nearly identical to verse 35. The sūrah's structure thus makes verse 81's point visible: the reader can compare the two passages and see that they are the same words.

This is the culmination of a theme the sūrah has been developing since verse 24. The notables of Noah's people said "a man like you," "seeks superiority," "we never heard this among our forefathers." The second generation said "a man like you," "dust and bones," "far-fetched." Pharaoh said "two men like us." And now the Quraysh, presented with the final revelation, say — the same. The Qur'an states the observation directly in another sūrah: *"Likewise, no messenger came to those before them except that they said, 'A magician or a madman.' Did they bequeath it to one another (a-tawāṣaw bihi)? Rather, they are a transgressing people"* (51:52–53). The question "did they bequeath it?" is rhetorical: the deniers of different ages never met, yet their words are identical — because denial has a fixed set of moves, and every generation that refuses the truth reaches for the same ones.

**Why Denial Repeats**

Why should denial be so unoriginal? The sūrah's analysis suggests several reasons. First, because the *objections* to resurrection are few and obvious: the body decays; the dead do not return; we have not seen it. Anyone who denies will say these things, because there is little else to say. Second, because denial is not usually the product of reasoning but of aversion (v. 70: *"most of them are averse to the truth"*) — and aversion does not generate new arguments; it recycles whatever is at hand. Third, because the deniers are, by their own choice, followers of their forefathers (v. 24; v. 68) — and one who defines himself by ancestral ways will naturally speak in ancestral phrases. The Quraysh who refused to abandon their fathers' idols could hardly be expected to abandon their fathers' objections.

There is an irony here that the sūrah exploits. The deniers accused the Prophet ﷺ of bringing something *new* and *unprecedented* (v. 68: "what did not come to their forefathers"). Verse 81 turns the charge around: it is *they* who are the imitators — repeating the ancients — while the message they reject is the one thing that has come *fresh from God*. They condemned novelty and practiced repetition; they condemned the messenger for departing from the forefathers and themselves departed from nothing.

**Repetition Versus Tradition**

The verse does not condemn following the past as such. The sūrah honors the messengers of the past and declares their community one with the present (v. 52). The distinction is between *tradition* — receiving and transmitting the truth — and *mere repetition* — receiving and transmitting the refusal of it. The believers, too, say what those before them said: "Worship God; you have no god other than Him" (vv. 23, 32). The difference is that they say it because it is *true*, having pondered it (v. 68), and the deniers say what *their* predecessors said because they have *not* pondered — they have simply inherited. Verse 81's charge is not "you follow the past" but "you have never thought; you have only repeated."

**The Sūrah's Method Vindicated**

Verse 81 also justifies the sūrah's long historical section (vv. 23–50). One might have asked why the Qur'an spends so many verses on Noah and the generations after him when its audience is the Quraysh. Verse 81 answers: because the Quraysh *are* those generations, in the only respect that matters — they say what those people said. The histories were not digressions; they were mirrors. The Quraysh who heard verse 35 recited — "when we have died and become dust and bones" — and thought it was about someone else are told in verse 81 that it was about them. And verses 82–83 will prove it by putting the same words in their mouths.

**The Weight of "Those of Old"**

The word *al-awwalūn*, "the first ones, the ancients," has a double edge. It is the word the deniers themselves used with reverence: *ābāʾinā l-awwalīn*, "our forefathers of old" (v. 24), and the word they will use with contempt in verse 83: *asāṭīr al-awwalīn*, "fables of the ancients." Verse 81 uses it of the ancient *deniers* — the people whose words the Quraysh are repeating. And the sūrah has already told the reader what happened to those people: the Flood (v. 27), the Cry (v. 41), destruction generation after generation (v. 44). To say "you speak like the ancients" is therefore also to say "you are on the path of the ancients" — and the path ended in ruin. The repetition of words foretells the repetition of fate. Verse 44's *"We made them successive; whenever a community's messenger came to it, they denied him, so We made them follow one another"* is the law; verse 81 places the Quraysh under it.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 81 asks the believer to distinguish, in his own religious life, between what he has *thought* and what he has *repeated*. Faith can be inherited as thoughtlessly as denial. A Muslim who believes in the Resurrection only because his parents did, who has never let the arguments of verses 78–80 pass through his own reason, holds a belief that is true but held in the manner of the deniers — by repetition. The sūrah's ideal is the believer who has *pondered* (v. 68), *used reason* (v. 80), and *believes in the signs* (v. 58) because he has seen them. Such faith survives challenge; inherited faith often does not. The Prophet ﷺ described the person who will be questioned in the grave and will say, *"I heard the people saying something, so I said it"* — and that person fails the test (al-Bukhārī 86; Muslim 905, in the ḥadīth of the eclipse prayer). Verse 81 warns against arriving at the grave with only what one heard the people say.

The verse also gives the believer a diagnostic for the objections he encounters. When faith is challenged, the challenge is very often *mithla mā qāla l-awwalūn* — the same objections, in new vocabulary, that the Qur'an answered fourteen centuries ago and that the ancients raised before that. To recognize the repetition is to be freed from its intimidation. The sūrah has already answered "dust and bones"; it does not need to answer it again when the same words arrive in modern dress.

**Toward the Quotation**

Verse 81 said they repeat the ancients. Verses 82–83 will quote them — and the reader will hear, in the Quraysh's voice, the exact words of verse 35.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:82

> **They say, “What, when we have died and are dust and bones, are we to be resurrected?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Quotation**

Verse 81 said the deniers repeat what the ancients said. Verse 82 quotes them: *qālū a-idhā mitnā wa kunnā turāban wa ʿiẓāman a-innā la-mabʿūthūn* — "They said: 'When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?'" The reader who has followed the sūrah will recognize the words at once. In verse 35, the second generation after Noah said of their messenger: *"Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones (turāban wa ʿiẓāman), you will be brought forth?"* The vocabulary is the same — *mitnā*, *turāban*, *ʿiẓāman* — and the incredulous interrogative is the same. The sūrah has made verse 81's claim demonstrable: place verse 35 and verse 82 side by side, and the repetition is exact.

**The Structure of the Objection**

The objection has a fixed shape, and it is worth laying out because it is the *only* argument against resurrection the deniers ever produce. Premise: when we die, our bodies decompose into dust and bones. Conclusion: therefore we cannot be raised. The argument depends on an unstated assumption — that what has decomposed cannot be recomposed — and the whole force of the objection rests on the *vividness* of decomposition rather than on any reasoning about its irreversibility. The deniers point to the dust and the bones as if their mere mention settled the matter. The double interrogative — *a-idhā* ("what, when...?") and *a-innā* ("are we indeed...?") — expresses not a question but an exclamation of disbelief: *this* is what he claims? *This* rubble will stand up?

The Qur'an records this objection in many places, always in nearly the same words, which itself confirms verse 81: *"Does he promise you that when you have died and become dust and bones, you will be brought forth?"* (23:35); *"When we are dead and have become dust and bones, are we indeed to be resurrected?"* (37:16; 56:47); *"When we have died and become dust and bones, are we to be recompensed?"* (37:53); *"When we are bones and crumbled particles, will we be resurrected as a new creation?"* (17:49, 98); *"Does he promise you that when you have died... "* — the formula is fixed across sūrahs because, as verse 81 said, the deniers of every age say it.

**"Dust and Bones": Turāb wa ʿIẓām**

The two words name the two end-states of the decomposed body: *turāb*, dust, the fine earth into which flesh dissolves; and *ʿiẓām*, bones, the last solid remnant. The deniers name both to make the picture complete: nothing is left but soil and skeleton. The words are chosen for their finality. Dust is the substance of the ground, indistinguishable from any other dust; bones are inert, dry, without life. From *this*, the deniers ask, life is to return?

The Qur'an's answer, given across many verses and implied throughout this sūrah, engages the words directly. Dust: the human being was *made from* dust in the first place — *"We created you from dust"* (22:5), and this sūrah's own *"an extract of clay"* (v. 12). To return to dust is to return to the starting material, from which God made a human being once and can make one again. Bones: God asks, in the sūrah's most famous parallel, *"Who will give life to bones when they are disintegrated?"* and answers, *"Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is, of all creation, Knowing"* (36:78–79). The very things the deniers cite as proof of impossibility — dust and bones — are the things from which and around which God built them originally. The sūrah's embryology in verses 12–14 was placed early precisely so that this objection, when it arrived, would already have been answered: *"then We made the drop a clinging clot, then the clot a lump, then the lump bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh"* — bones clothed with flesh once can be clothed again.

**Why the Sūrah Repeats the Objection**

If the objection was already stated in verse 35 and already answered by the sūrah's earlier arguments, why record it again here? Several purposes are served.

First, to *prove* verse 81. The claim "they say what the ancients said" would be an assertion; verse 82 makes it a demonstration.

Second, to show that the deniers have *learned nothing* from the three arguments of verses 78–80. God gave them hearing, sight, and hearts; He scattered and will gather them; He gives life and death and alternates night and day. And their response is — the same objection they had before the arguments were made. The repetition is evidence that the arguments were not *heard*, which is what verse 66 charged: the signs were recited, and they turned on their heels.

Third, to expose the objection's *emptiness* by placing it after the answer. In verse 35, the objection came before the sūrah's fullest arguments and might have seemed weighty. In verse 82, it comes after them and sounds hollow — a formula recited by people who have been shown the alternative and did not look. The sūrah is teaching its reader to hear the objection as it really is: not an argument but an incantation.

**"Will We Indeed Be Resurrected?": Mabʿūthūn**

The verse's final word is *mabʿūthūn*, "resurrected, raised, sent forth" — from the root *b-ʿ-th*, the same root the sūrah used in verse 16: *"then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised (tubʿathūn)."* The deniers use the sūrah's own word to mock it. The sūrah stated *tubʿathūn* as a fact; the deniers repeat *mabʿūthūn* as an absurdity. The word itself is neutral; what differs is the speaker's relation to it — the believer says it with certainty and trembling (v. 60), the denier with incredulity and contempt.

**The Objection and the Faculties of Verse 78**

There is a particular irony in the deniers raising this objection immediately after verse 78 reminded them that God *produced* their hearing, sight, and hearts. The eye that looks at bones and declares resurrection impossible is itself a structure of extraordinary complexity that was assembled from nothing — from a drop, a clot, a lump (v. 14). The deniers use an organ whose existence refutes their argument to formulate the argument. This is what verse 78 meant by *"little is it that you give thanks"*: they had the instrument that proved the Maker's power and used it to deny that power.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 82 equips the believer to recognize the objection in whatever form it takes. Modern versions replace "dust and bones" with "neurons and entropy" or "information loss" or "the finality of biological death," but the structure is unchanged: the vivid description of decomposition offered as if it were an argument against recomposition. The believer who has absorbed the sūrah answers as it does: the One who assembled this from dust can reassemble it from dust; the difficulty of the second creation is, if anything, less than the first, since the first was from nothing and the second from what already existed (30:27: *"And it is He who begins creation; then He repeats it, and that is easier for Him"*). The objection has not become stronger with time; it has only acquired new vocabulary. Verse 81 named it in advance: *mithla mā qāla l-awwalūn*.

The verse also invites a quieter reflection. The believer will himself become dust and bones. The sūrah does not hide this — it said *"then indeed, after that, you will surely die"* (v. 15) with the same directness. The difference between believer and denier is not that one will decompose and the other will not; it is what each expects afterward. The believer looks at the dust and bones he will become and says, with verse 16, *tubʿathūn* — raised. The denier looks at the same dust and says *a-innā la-mabʿūthūn?* — really? The dust is the same. The reading of it is everything.

**Toward the Dismissal**

The deniers have stated the objection. The next verse completes their speech with the dismissal that always accompanies it: this was promised to our fathers too — it is only fables.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:83

> **We and our fathers were certainly warned of this before. These are naught but fables of those of old.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Completion of the Deniers' Speech**

The deniers' quoted speech, begun in verse 82, ends in verse 83: *laqad wuʿidnā naḥnu wa ābāʾunā hādhā min qablu in hādhā illā asāṭīru l-awwalīn* — "We were promised this — we and our fathers — before; this is nothing but legends of the ancients." Two sentences: an admission and a dismissal. The admission is that the promise of resurrection is not new — they and their fathers heard it before. The dismissal is that its age proves it false: an old promise unfulfilled is a legend. The verse is the deniers' final word in the sūrah's long dialogue with them, and it is self-refuting in a way the sūrah has carefully prepared the reader to see.

**"We Were Promised This — We and Our Fathers — Before"**

The first sentence is a confession the deniers do not recognize as one. *Laqad wuʿidnā*, "we were indeed promised" — with the emphatic *laqad* — acknowledges that the promise of resurrection reached them. *Naḥnu wa ābāʾunā*, "we and our fathers," acknowledges that it reached the previous generation too. *Min qablu*, "before," acknowledges that the message has a history. The deniers mean this as a complaint: the promise is stale, repeated, never delivered. But the sūrah has spent verses 23–52 establishing precisely that the same message came to every generation — and verse 52 declared that this continuity is the mark of the *one community* of God's messengers. What the deniers cite as evidence of fabrication, the sūrah has already presented as evidence of authenticity. A message that comes to every generation in the same words is not a legend spreading; it is a truth being renewed.

The admission also destroys the excuse of verse 68. There, the sūrah asked whether *"there has come to them what did not come to their first forefathers."* Verse 83 has the deniers answering, in their own words: no — our fathers were promised this too. They cannot claim the message was unprecedented and simultaneously complain that it is old. The sūrah lets them refute themselves.

**"This Is Nothing but Legends of the Ancients": Asāṭīr al-Awwalīn**

The second sentence is the dismissal: *in hādhā illā asāṭīru l-awwalīn* — "this is nothing but *asāṭīr* of the first ones." The word *asāṭīr* is the plural of *usṭūrah*, a written tale, a legend, a myth — from the root *s-ṭ-r*, "to write in lines" (as in *"by the pen and what they inscribe — yasṭurūn,"* 68:1). The word implies stories set down long ago, of the kind old men tell and children enjoy — entertaining, perhaps, but not true. The phrase *asāṭīr al-awwalīn* was the Quraysh's standard dismissal of the Qur'an, and the Qur'an records it nine times: *"And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, 'We have heard. If we willed, we could say the like of this. This is not but legends of the former peoples'"* (8:31); *"And they say, 'Legends of the former peoples which he has written down, and they are dictated to him morning and afternoon'"* (25:5); *"When Our verses are recited to him, he says, 'Legends of the former peoples'"* (68:15; 83:13). Al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who had learned Persian tales in al-Ḥīrah, was said to be the originator of the charge; he would tell the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyār and ask the Quraysh how Muḥammad's tales were any better.

**The Self-Refutation**

The verse's two sentences, placed together, form a contradiction that the sūrah has engineered the reader to notice. The deniers say: (1) this promise is *old* — our fathers heard it; and (2) this is *asāṭīr al-awwalīn* — legends of the ancients. They use the word *al-awwalīn*, "the ancients," to dismiss the message as archaic fiction. But verse 81 has just used the *same word* of the deniers themselves: *"they said the like of what the ancients (al-awwalūn) said."* The ones reciting "legends of the ancients" are themselves reciting the words of the ancients. The charge rebounds. If age discredits, it discredits their objection, which is older than they are. The sūrah noted the irony in verse 44 — that God made the destroyed generations into *aḥādīth*, tales — and the irony completes itself here: the deniers who call the Qur'an "tales" are repeating the tales of people who became tales.

There is a further layer. The message the deniers call "legends of the ancients" is the account of Noah, the generations after him, Moses, and Jesus — real histories that the sūrah has recounted. The deniers call these *asāṭīr* — myths. But the very *repetition* of the warning across generations, which they cite as evidence of myth, is evidence of history: the warnings were real, the generations were real, and the destructions were real, which is why the ruins of some of them (ʿĀd, Thamūd, Lot's people) were on the Quraysh's own trade routes (37:137–138: *"And indeed, you pass by them in the morning and at night"*). The "legend" left physical remains.

**Why "Promised" and Not "Threatened"**

The verb *wuʿidnā*, "we were promised," is from *waʿd*, promise — which in Arabic can be used for both good and bad outcomes (though *waʿīd* is specifically threat). The deniers' choice of the word implies they experienced the message as a *promise* — of resurrection, judgment, and consequence — and their complaint is that the promise was not kept: "we were promised this before, and nothing happened." This is the argument from delay, which the sūrah answered in verses 42–43: *"No community can hasten its term, nor delay it."* The delay is not evidence that the promise is false; it is the *ḥattā ḥīn*, the appointed time (v. 54), within which the promise waits. The Qur'an answers the argument from delay directly: *"And they say, 'When is this promise, if you should be truthful?'... Say, 'For you is the appointment of a Day which you will not be able to delay for an hour nor advance'"* (34:29–30). The deniers mistook patience for absence.

**The Third Recurring Objection Completed**

With verse 83, the sūrah has now shown the Quraysh reproducing all the deniers' objections that it catalogued in the historical section. "A man like you" — implied in their treatment of the Messenger (vv. 69–70). "Dust and bones" — verse 82 (matching v. 35). "Our forefathers" — verse 83's "we and our fathers" (matching v. 24's "we never heard of this among our forefathers of old"). "Fables" — verse 83's *asāṭīr* (matching v. 44's *aḥādīth*, and the general dismissal of the messengers as liars, v. 38). The pattern that verse 44 described as a *law* — each community denying its messenger in turn — has been shown operating in the present tense. The Quraysh are not observers of the histories; they are their latest instance.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 83 warns the believer against a particular intellectual posture: the assumption that *age* or *familiarity* discredits. "We have heard this before" is not an argument against a claim; it may be evidence for it. The Resurrection has been preached by every prophet because it is true, not because it is a persistent fiction; the moral law has been the same in every scripture because it comes from one Lawgiver; the account of the messengers is repeated because the messengers were real. The believer who is told that his faith is "just old stories" may answer with verse 52: yes, one community, one Lord, one message across all the ages — which is exactly what one would expect if the message were from God.

The verse also warns against the deniers' specific move of *reclassifying* truth as entertainment. To call revelation "legends" is to shift it from the category of things that make demands to the category of things that provide amusement — and once it is amusement, it need not be obeyed. This move is available in every age and is the sophisticated form of aversion to the truth (v. 70). The believer resists it by reading the accounts of the messengers as the sūrah presents them: not as tales but as *precedents* — records of what happened to people who said what the Quraysh said, and what is therefore due to happen again.

**Toward the Questions**

The deniers have spoken their last word. The sūrah now turns to a method that will expose the incoherence of their position from within: it will ask them what they themselves believe about the earth, the heavens, and the dominion of all things — and their own answers will convict them.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:84

> **Say, “Whose is the earth and whosoever is upon it, if you know?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A New Method: Interrogation From Within**

The deniers have made their last speech (vv. 82–83). The sūrah does not answer it with a fresh argument from the outside; instead, it turns to a method that will expose the incoherence of the deniers' position from within their own beliefs. Verses 84–89 are a series of three questions, each introduced by *qul*, "Say" — a command to the Prophet ﷺ — and each followed by the deniers' predicted answer and a rejoinder. Verse 84 asks the first: *qul li-mani l-arḍu wa man fīhā in kuntum taʿlamūn* — "Say: 'To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?'" The method is Socratic: the questioner already knows what the respondent will say, and the respondent's own answer becomes the premise of the argument against him.

**The Premise Behind the Method**

The method works because the Makkan deniers were not atheists. This is a point that verse 38's commentary anticipated and that these verses now make explicit. The Quraysh believed in God — *Allāh* — as the Creator of the heavens and the earth, the Sender of rain, the Lord of the Kaʿbah. The Qur'an records their belief repeatedly: *"And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, 'God'"* (31:25; 39:38; 43:9); *"And if you asked them who sends down rain from the sky and gives life thereby to the earth after its lifelessness, they would surely say, 'God'"* (29:63). Their error was not disbelief in God but *shirk* — associating others with Him in worship — and denial of the Resurrection. They believed God existed and created; they did not believe He alone deserved worship or that He would raise the dead.

The questions of verses 84–89 exploit this. If the deniers admit that God owns the earth (v. 84), rules the seven heavens and the Throne (v. 86), and holds the dominion of everything in His hand (v. 88), then their *shirk* is incoherent — why worship what does not own, rule, or hold anything? — and their denial of resurrection is incoherent — the One who owns all can surely restore what He owns. The deniers' own creed convicts them.

**"To Whom Belongs the Earth and Whoever Is in It?"**

The first question concerns *ownership*: *li-man*, "to whom belongs," "whose is." The object is *al-arḍ wa man fīhā* — "the earth and whoever is in it." The word *man*, "whoever," refers to rational beings — human beings and jinn — and the phrase encompasses the whole earth with all its inhabitants. The question asks: who is the *owner* of the ground you stand on and of you who stand on it?

The question begins with the earth because the earth is nearest and most undeniable. The deniers might argue about the heavens or the unseen; they cannot argue about the ground under their feet. And the sūrah has already described this earth as God's work: water sent down and lodged in it (v. 18), gardens brought forth from it (v. 19), the human race scattered across it (v. 79). The question invites the deniers to say what they already know about the earth's owner.

The phrase *wa man fīhā*, "and whoever is in it," is pointed. It includes the deniers themselves. The question is not only "who owns the earth?" but "who owns *you*?" If the answer is "God," then the deniers have admitted that they are owned — that they are His property, His slaves, subject to His disposal. This admission undermines their whole posture of autonomy: the *mutrafūn* who read their wealth as their own achievement (vv. 55–56) and who "tore their affair among themselves" (v. 53) as if it were theirs to tear are, by their own confession, owned.

**"If You Know": In Kuntum Taʿlamūn**

The question ends with a conditional: *in kuntum taʿlamūn* — "if you know." The phrase has two functions. First, it is a challenge: answer, if you have knowledge. It presses the deniers to commit to an answer rather than evade. Second, it is a subtle rebuke: the deniers claimed knowledge — they were confident in their objections (vv. 82–83) — and the phrase asks whether their knowledge extends to the most basic question of all. The Qur'an uses the same formula elsewhere when demanding that deniers state what they know: *"Then who is more just than God in judgment for a people who are certain?"* (5:50); *"Bring your proof, if you should be truthful"* (2:111). The deniers who "knew" that resurrection was a legend are asked whether they "know" who owns the earth.

**The Question's Place in the Series**

The three questions of verses 84, 86, and 88 ascend. Verse 84: the earth and its inhabitants — ownership of what is nearest. Verse 86: the seven heavens and the great Throne — lordship of what is highest. Verse 88: the dominion of *everything*, and protection that cannot be reciprocated — absolute sovereignty. Each question raises the scope; each expected answer is the same ("God"); each rejoinder sharpens: "will you not remember?" (v. 85), "will you not be reverent?" (v. 87), "how then are you bewitched?" (v. 89). The series moves the deniers from an admission about the earth to an admission about all existence, and shows that at every level their answer contradicts their practice.

**The Command "Say"**

Each question begins with *qul*, "Say" — God instructing the Prophet ﷺ in the exact words to use. This construction appears over three hundred times in the Qur'an, and it establishes the Prophet ﷺ as a transmitter, not an author: the questions are God's questions, put into the Prophet's mouth. In the context of the sūrah's earlier defense of the Messenger (vv. 69–72), the *qul* is significant: the man they call mad (v. 70) is being given, word for word, the argument that will silence them. The argument's power is not his but the Sender's.

**Ownership as the Ground of Worship**

The first question concerns ownership because ownership is the ground of the right to be worshipped. The one who owns a thing has authority over it; the one who is owned owes obedience. The Qur'an's word for worship, *ʿibādah*, is from the same root as *ʿabd*, slave — the one who is owned. To ask "whose is the earth and whoever is in it?" is to ask "whose slaves are you?" — and the answer determines whom you should serve. The sūrah's messengers preached: *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him"* (vv. 23, 32). Verse 84 provides the reasoning: worship the Owner, because you are owned, and no one else owns you. The idols of the Quraysh owned nothing — not the earth, not the rain, not the deniers themselves. To worship them was to serve a master who had no title.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 84 asks the believer a question he may think he has already answered: *whose is the earth and whoever is in it?* The believer says "God's" — as the Quraysh will in verse 85. But the sūrah's method applies to the believer too: does his *practice* match his answer? If God owns the earth, then the believer's property is held in trust, not owned outright — which is what the giving of verse 60 and the *zakāh* of verse 4 assume. If God owns "whoever is in it," then the believer himself is owned — which means his time, his body, his talents are not his to dispose of as he pleases but are the Owner's, on loan. The Quraysh's error was to affirm God's ownership and live as if they owned themselves. The believer who affirms it and lives accordingly has passed the test the question sets.

The verse also equips the believer for dialogue. Many who reject religion do not reject the existence of a Creator; they reject the implications. Verse 84's method — beginning from what the other person already grants and following it to its conclusion — is more effective than beginning from what he denies. The Prophet ﷺ was instructed to start with the earth, not with Paradise.

**Toward the Admission**

The question has been asked. The next verse gives the answer — the deniers' own — and the first rejoinder.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:85

> **They will say, “God’s.” Say, “Will you not, then, take heed?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Predicted Answer**

The Prophet ﷺ was told to ask whose is the earth and whoever is in it (v. 84). Verse 85 records the answer before the deniers give it: *sa-yaqūlūna li-llāh qul a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn* — "They will say, 'To God.' Say: 'Will you not then remember?'" The future tense *sa-yaqūlūna*, "they *will* say," is a prediction, and its confidence is part of the argument: God knows what the deniers believe, and He knows they will not be able to answer otherwise. When the question is put, the only honest answer available to a Qurayshī — who prayed to Allāh in storms at sea (29:65), swore by Allāh, and called the Kaʿbah the House of Allāh — is *li-llāh*, "to God." The verse records that answer and immediately draws its consequence.

**"They Will Say, 'To God'": Li-llāh**

The answer is one word: *li-llāh*, "to God," "God's" — matching the *li-man*, "to whom," of the question. The deniers concede ownership. This is not a small concession. To say the earth and all in it belong to God is to say that the deniers themselves belong to Him, that their wealth and children (v. 55) belong to Him, that the idols carved from the earth's stone belong to Him, and that the Kaʿbah they were so proud of (v. 67) belongs to Him. One word, and the whole structure of *shirk* loses its foundation.

The commentators noted that the deniers' readiness to say *li-llāh* shows that belief in God's ownership was, for them, an *inert* belief — a fact acknowledged and never acted upon. They held it as one holds a piece of information that has no bearing on life. This is the condition the sūrah has been describing since verse 63: the heart in *ghamrah*, which contains true beliefs but is submerged so that they produce nothing. The deniers *knew* God owned the earth. The knowledge lay in them like a seed in dry ground.

**"Say: Will You Not Then Remember?": A-fa-lā Tadhakkarūn**

The rejoinder is a question: *a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn* — "will you not then remember?" The verb *tadhakkarūn* is from the root *dh-k-r*, the root of *dhikr*, remembrance, reminder — the same root as *dhikrihim*, "their reminder," in verse 71, where the sūrah said God brought them their reminder and they turned from it. To *tadhakkara* is to recall what one already knows, to bring a dormant truth back to active awareness. The verb is precisely chosen. The deniers do not need to be *taught* that God owns the earth — they have just said so. They need to *remember* it — to let the truth they hold inertly become active, to draw from it the conclusions it entails.

What should they remember? The commentators drew out several implications of the admission, each of which the deniers had forgotten. If God owns the earth and all in it, then: He alone is worthy of worship, since worship is owed to the Owner and not to owned things (the idols). He has the power to resurrect, since the One who owns and disposes of everything on the earth can reassemble the dust and bones (v. 82) that are His property. He has the right to command, since an owner may direct what he owns — and so the moral demands of the Qur'an are not impositions but the Owner's instructions. And He will hold to account, since ownership implies concern for how the property is used. Each of these follows from *li-llāh*; each is what the deniers denied. The question "will you not remember?" asks them to connect the admission to its consequences — which is exactly what verse 80's *a-fa-lā taʿqilūn*, "will you not use reason?", asked, now framed as recollection rather than inference.

**Remembering Versus Learning**

The sūrah's use of *tadhakkur* here reflects a Qur'anic understanding of the human relationship to truth. The Qur'an does not present belief in God as new information that must be acquired but as knowledge already present that must be *uncovered*. Human beings were created with an innate recognition of their Lord — the *fiṭrah*: *"So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth — the fiṭrah of God upon which He has created people"* (30:30). The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Every child is born upon the fiṭrah, and it is his parents who make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian"* (al-Bukhārī 1385; Muslim 2658). And the Qur'an describes a primordial covenant in which all souls testified to God's lordship: *"Am I not your Lord? They said, 'Yes, we have testified'"* (7:172). Because of this, the Qur'an's primary self-description is *dhikr*, reminder (v. 71; 15:9; 38:1), and its characteristic question to the heedless is "will you not remember?" — not "will you not learn?" The deniers' *li-llāh* is the *fiṭrah* speaking; the *a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn* asks them to listen to it.

**The Gap Between Belief and Practice**

Verse 85 exposes a gap that is not unique to the Quraysh: the gap between what a person *affirms* and what he *does*. The deniers affirmed God's ownership and worshipped idols; affirmed His lordship and denied His power to raise the dead; affirmed that they belonged to Him and lived as if they belonged to themselves. The verse's question — "will you not remember?" — names the mechanism by which the gap is closed: *active recollection*, bringing the affirmed truth to bear on the moment of decision. The believer's practice of *dhikr* — remembrance of God in words and in heart, in prayer and outside it — is precisely this mechanism, institutionalized. The sūrah's believers are those in whom the remembrance is continuous, so that their hearts tremble (v. 60) and they hasten (v. 61); the deniers are those in whom it is absent, so that the affirmed truth stays inert.

**The Rejoinder's Gentleness**

The tone of *a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn* should be noticed. After the deniers' contemptuous dismissal of the Qur'an as legends (v. 83), one might expect a sharp reply. Instead, God instructs the Prophet ﷺ to ask, almost gently: will you not remember? The rejoinder does not accuse them of lying — their answer was true. It does not mock them. It invites them to *think*, one step further than they have. This gentleness is characteristic of the Qur'an's dialogue with those it is still trying to reach: *"Say, 'I only advise you of one thing: that you stand for God, in pairs and individually, and then give thought'"* (34:46). The three rejoinders of verses 85, 87, and 89 escalate — remember, be reverent, how are you bewitched? — but they begin with an invitation, not a condemnation.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 85 asks the believer whether the truths he affirms are active or inert. Every Muslim says *li-llāh* — "to God belongs the earth and all in it" — and recites *"to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth"* in the Qur'an regularly. The question is whether he *remembers* it at the moment it matters: when he is tempted to treat his wealth as his own, to withhold what the Owner has claimed, to fear a creature more than the Owner, to despair of a situation the Owner controls. The Quraysh had the belief and lacked the remembrance. The believer's daily *dhikr* — the *adhkār* of morning and evening, the remembrance in prayer, the *"lā ilāha illā llāh"* on the tongue — is the practice by which the belief is kept above the water, active, shaping decisions. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"The likeness of the one who remembers his Lord and the one who does not is the likeness of the living and the dead"* (al-Bukhārī 6407). The Quraysh's *li-llāh* was the speech of the living dead — a true word from a heart that had not remembered.

**Toward the Heavens**

The first question established God's ownership of the earth. The second raises the scope to the seven heavens and the great Throne — and asks not for remembrance but for reverence.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:86

> **Say, “Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the great Throne?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Question: From Earth to Throne**

The first question concerned the earth (v. 84). The second lifts the gaze as high as it can go: *qul man rabbu l-samāwāti l-sabʿi wa rabbu l-ʿarshi l-ʿaẓīm* — "Say: 'Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the great Throne?'" The question moves from ownership (*li-man*, "whose") to lordship (*man rabbu*, "who is the Lord"), and from the earth beneath the deniers' feet to the highest created things — the seven heavens and the Throne above them. The ascent is deliberate. If the deniers conceded that God owns the earth, they will find it even harder to deny that He is Lord of what is above it; and the further the scope extends, the more absurd their idols — small stones on the earth's surface — become.

**"The Lord of the Seven Heavens"**

The phrase *al-samāwāt al-sabʿ*, "the seven heavens," recalls verse 17: *"And We have created above you seven paths (sabʿa ṭarāʾiq), and never have We been heedless of creation."* The sūrah's earlier statement of the fact now becomes a question put to the deniers: who is the *Lord* of these seven? The word *rabb*, as explained under verse 26, means the owner, sustainer, and disposer who brings what he owns to its completion. To be Lord of the heavens is not merely to have made them but to hold them, maintain them, govern their motion. The Qur'an describes this maintenance: *"Indeed, God holds the heavens and the earth, lest they cease. And if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him"* (35:41).

The seven heavens were, for the Quraysh, an accepted feature of cosmology — they knew the Qur'an spoke of them and had inherited similar notions. Their answer to "who is the Lord of the seven heavens?" could only be "God"; no one attributed the heavens to al-Lāt or Hubal. The question thus extracts a second admission, larger than the first: not merely that God owns the ground, but that He rules the vault of the sky.

**"And the Lord of the Great Throne": Al-ʿArsh al-ʿAẓīm**

The second half of the question names the *ʿArsh*, the Throne — the highest of all created things, above the seven heavens. The Throne is mentioned in the Qur'an over twenty times, always as the seat of God's sovereignty: *"The Most Merciful, above the Throne, established (istawā)"* (20:5); *"And He is the Lord of the Great Throne"* (9:129); *"Owner of the Throne, the Glorious"* (85:15); *"and eight [angels] will, that Day, bear the Throne of your Lord above them"* (69:17). The Prophet ﷺ described its magnitude: *"The seven heavens compared to the Kursī are like a ring thrown in a desert, and the superiority of the Throne over the Kursī is like the superiority of that desert over that ring"* (Ibn Ḥibbān 361; al-Bayhaqī; graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī). And he taught the believers to ask for *Firdaws* because *"above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful"* (al-Bukhārī 2790, cited under verse 11).

The adjective *al-ʿaẓīm*, "the great, the tremendous," is God's own description of His Throne. It is used because the Throne is the greatest created thing, and the Lord of the greatest thing is the Lord of everything less. The argument is one of *a fortiori*: if God is Lord of the Throne, what could possibly be outside His lordship? The idols of the Quraysh, which ruled nothing — not the earth (v. 84), not the heavens, and certainly not the Throne — are, by the question's implication, exposed as nothing.

On the *istawāʾ* (God's being established above the Throne) the sound position of the early scholars, as Ibn Taymiyyah and the *salaf* consistently held, is to affirm what God affirmed of Himself without asking *how*, without likening it to creation, and without denying it. Mālik ibn Anas, when asked how God is established, answered: *"The establishment is known, the how is unknown, believing in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."* Verse 86 does not ask the deniers about the *how*; it asks them *who* — and to that they have an answer.

**Why the Throne Is Mentioned to Idolaters**

Why would the Qur'an mention the Throne — a matter of the unseen — to people who were being argued with from what they could observe? Because the Quraysh, though they did not have a revealed scripture, had inherited from the religion of Abraham fragments of true belief, including belief in a supreme God enthroned above the heavens. The Qur'an appeals to this inheritance. It also uses the Throne to extend the scope of the question to the *absolute*: the earth is the lowest level, the seven heavens are above it, the Throne is above them, and there is nothing created above the Throne. The question therefore covers the whole of creation from bottom to top, and the answer — "God" — is an admission that His lordship is total.

**Lordship and Worship**

The word *rabb* connects the question to the sūrah's central demand. The messengers preached *"Worship God"* (vv. 23, 32); God declared *"I am your Lord (rabbukum), so fear Me"* (v. 52); the believers are described four times as oriented toward *"their Lord"* (vv. 57–60). The argument of verse 86 is that lordship entails the right to worship. If God is *Rabb* of the seven heavens and the Throne, He is *Rabb* of the Quraysh, and the *Rabb* is the one to be served. The Quraysh divided these: they acknowledged God as *Rabb* in the cosmic sense and worshipped others as intermediaries — *"We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to God in position"* (39:3). The Qur'an's response, developed across many sūrahs, is that lordship and worship cannot be split: the One who is Lord of all is the only One entitled to the devotion of all.

**The Ascending Series**

Verses 84, 86, and 88 form an ascending series, and verse 86 is its middle term. Verse 84 asked about the earth — what is nearest and most tangible. Verse 86 asks about the heavens and the Throne — what is highest and most exalted. Verse 88 will ask about the *dominion of everything* and about protection — the abstract totality of sovereignty. The movement is from the concrete to the cosmic to the absolute, and at each level the deniers are made to say "God." By the third question, they have admitted that God owns, rules, and holds everything — and the sūrah will ask how, having admitted this, they can be *bewitched* into worshipping anything else.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 86 invites the believer to look up. The sūrah has directed his gaze at the embryo (vv. 12–14), the rain (v. 18), the cattle (v. 21) — things near at hand. Now it directs it at the seven heavens and, beyond what any eye can see, the Throne of the Most Merciful. The believer who reflects on the scale of what God is Lord of finds his own concerns rightly sized: the difficulties that seem vast from within are small before the Lord of the Throne, and the One who governs the heavens without effort can govern a single human life without strain. This is why the Prophet ﷺ taught, at moments of distress, the supplication: *"There is no god but God, the Great, the Forbearing; there is no god but God, Lord of the Great Throne; there is no god but God, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth and Lord of the Noble Throne"* (al-Bukhārī 6346; Muslim 2730). The words of verse 86 are, in this supplication, turned from a question to the deniers into a refuge for the believer.

**Toward Reverence**

The question has been asked. The answer will again be "God" — and this time the rejoinder will not ask for remembrance but for the response that remembrance should produce: *taqwā*.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:87

> **They will say, “God’s.” Say, “Will you not then be reverent?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Admission**

The Prophet ﷺ asked who is Lord of the seven heavens and the great Throne (v. 86). Verse 87 gives the answer and the rejoinder: *sa-yaqūlūna li-llāh qul a-fa-lā tattaqūn* — "They will say, 'To God.' Say: 'Will you not then be reverent?'" The answer is the same as verse 85's — *li-llāh* — and it is predicted with the same confidence. The deniers cannot attribute the heavens and the Throne to anyone but God. What differs is the rejoinder: verse 85 asked *"will you not remember?"*; verse 87 asks *"will you not be reverent?"* — *a-fa-lā tattaqūn*. The escalation is deliberate, and it retraces a phrase the sūrah has used before.

**The Reading "God's" and the Sense of the Answer**

The source records a matter of recitation that the commentators discuss at this verse. In verse 85 the question was *li-man*, "to whom [belongs]," and the answer *li-llāh*, "to God," matches it grammatically. In verses 86 and 88 the questions are *man rabbu*, "who is the Lord," and *man bi-yadihi*, "in whose hand" — to which the grammatically matching answer would be *Allāh*, "God," rather than *li-llāh*, "to God." The reading of Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb has *Allāh* in verses 87 and 89; the reading of the majority, including Ḥafṣ, has *li-llāh*. Al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabarī, as the source notes, all address this. The explanation for the majority reading is that the answer responds to the *sense* of the question rather than its letter: "Who is the Lord of the heavens?" means "To whom do the heavens belong?", and the answer "to God" is a natural response to that meaning. Both readings are authentic and both convey the same admission; the variation illustrates the flexibility of Arabic response and the care with which the readings were preserved.

**"Will You Not Then Be Reverent?": A-fa-lā Tattaqūn**

The rejoinder *a-fa-lā tattaqūn* is a phrase the sūrah's reader has heard twice before. Noah said it to his people: *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be reverent (a-fa-lā tattaqūn)?"* (v. 23). The messenger of the second generation said it in the same words (v. 32). And God Himself commanded it at the climax of the historical section: *"I am your Lord, so fear Me (fa-ttaqūn)"* (v. 52). Now the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to ask the Quraysh the same question. The sūrah's structure has placed the final messenger in the exact position of the first: the same demand, the same question, to the same kind of people. Verse 81 said the deniers repeat the ancients; verse 87 shows that the messengers repeat one another too — and that the repetition on the messengers' side is the one community of verse 52.

The word *taqwā*, explained under verse 23, is the protective consciousness of God — the guarding of oneself against His displeasure, the careful walking of one who knows he is watched. The rejoinder's logic is: if you admit that God is Lord of the seven heavens and the great Throne, will you not *guard yourselves before Him*? The admission should produce fear — not terror, but the reverent caution due to the Lord of everything. A person who knows he stands before the Sovereign of the heavens and does not adjust his conduct has not absorbed his own admission.

**The Escalation From Remembrance to Reverence**

The three rejoinders — remember (v. 85), be reverent (v. 87), how are you bewitched (v. 89) — form a sequence. *Remembrance* (*tadhakkur*) is the first step: bringing the dormant truth to active awareness. *Reverence* (*taqwā*) is the second: acting on the truth once remembered — letting it govern conduct. The sequence is psychologically ordered. One cannot fear what one has not called to mind; and one has not truly called to mind what one does not fear. The Qur'an regularly pairs these: *"So remember Me; I will remember you"* (2:152) leads to *"O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer"* (2:153); and the whole of the *dhikr* tradition is oriented toward producing *taqwā*. Verse 87 asks for the step that follows verse 85's.

The escalation also raises the *stakes* of the admission. Verse 85's admission (God owns the earth) invited recollection. Verse 87's admission (God is Lord of the heavens and the Throne) invites *fear* — because the Lord of the Throne is the Judge, the Sovereign, the One before whom the deniers will stand at the gathering (v. 79). To admit His lordship and not fear Him is to admit that one is subject to the King and to behave as if there were no King.

**Taqwā as the Rational Response**

The rejoinder frames *taqwā* not as an emotional demand but as the *rational* consequence of what the deniers have granted. The structure is: you say X; X entails Y; will you not do Y?
