If God is Lord of the heavens and the Throne, then He is Lord of you, He has power over you, and He will hold you to account — and the rational response to being in the power of a Sovereign who will judge is to guard oneself. Not to do so is *irrational* — which is why the third rejoinder (v. 89) will ask how they can be *bewitched*: only enchantment could explain a person who admits the premise and refuses the conclusion.

This framing matters for how the Qur'an understands *taqwā*. It is not a mood induced by threats; it is the appropriate posture of a creature who has correctly understood its position. The sūrah's believers have *taqwā* because they see clearly (vv. 57–60); the deniers lack it because they see and do not connect (v. 63: hearts in *ghamrah*). Verse 87 asks them to connect.

**The Fourth Appearance of the Question**

Verse 87 is the fourth time the sūrah has raised the demand for *taqwā* — Noah (v. 23), the second messenger (v. 32), God's own command (v. 52), and now the Prophet ﷺ to the Quraysh. The count itself is an argument. The demand has been made, across the whole of human history, by every messenger and by God directly, to every people. The deniers cannot claim it is a new demand (v. 68's excuse, already dismissed). And they cannot claim it is unreasonable, because they have just supplied the premise from which it follows. The four appearances of *a-fa-lā tattaqūn* are the sūrah's way of saying: this is the one thing that has always been asked, of everyone, on grounds that everyone concedes.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 87 asks the believer whether his admission of God's lordship has produced *taqwā*. A Muslim affirms daily that God is Lord of the heavens and the Throne — the words are in his prayers and his recitation. The rejoinder asks: *and then?* Does the affirmation make him careful — careful of what he says, earns, looks at, does in private? The Quraysh admitted the lordship and lived without care. The believer's *taqwā* is the proof that his admission is real. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb asked Ubayy ibn Kaʿb what *taqwā* was, and Ubayy asked whether ʿUmar had ever walked a path with thorns. ʿUmar said yes. Ubayy asked what he did. ʿUmar said: *"I gathered up my garment and took care."* Ubayy said: *"That is taqwā."* The believer who has said *li-llāh* and means it walks the world as ʿUmar walked the thorny path — garment gathered, attentive, because he knows whose ground he walks on and before whom he will stand.

**Toward the Absolute**

Two questions, two admissions, two rejoinders. The third question will ask about the dominion of *everything* and about the One who protects and is never protected against — and the third rejoinder will not be an invitation but an expression of astonishment.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:88

> **Say, “Who is it in Whose Hand lies the dominion of everything, who protects but is not protected against, if you know?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third and Final Question**

The series reaches its summit: *qul man bi-yadihi malakūtu kulli shayʾin wa huwa yujīru wa lā yujāru ʿalayhi in kuntum taʿlamūn* — "Say: 'Who is it in whose hand is the dominion of everything, and who protects while none can protect against Him, if you know?'" The first question concerned the earth; the second, the heavens and the Throne; the third concerns *kull shayʾ* — everything — and adds a new dimension: not only ownership and lordship but *protection*, the power to shelter and the impossibility of being sheltered from. The question is the most comprehensive of the three, and it closes with the same challenge as the first: *in kuntum taʿlamūn*, "if you know."

**"In Whose Hand Is the Dominion of Everything": Malakūt**

The word *malakūt* is, as the source notes, an intensive form of *mulk*, "dominion, kingship, sovereignty." The suffix *-ūt* in Arabic intensifies and abstracts: *jabarūt* from *jabr* (overwhelming might), *raḥamūt* from *raḥmah* (all-encompassing mercy), *malakūt* from *mulk*. Where *mulk* is kingship, *malakūt* is the *totality* and *inwardness* of kingship — sovereignty in its fullest extent and its deepest reach, including what is hidden. The Qur'an uses *malakūt* four times, and each use concerns what lies beneath or beyond the visible: *"Thus did We show Abraham the malakūt of the heavens and the earth, that he would be among the certain"* (6:75); *"Do they not look into the malakūt of the heavens and the earth?"* (7:185); *"So exalted is He in whose hand is the malakūt of everything, and to Him you will be returned"* (36:83); and here. The word denotes not only the external realm God rules but the inner reality of things — their essences, their causes, their hidden workings — all of which are "in His hand."

The phrase *bi-yadihi*, "in His hand," expresses complete control and disposal. What is in one's hand is held, directed, and cannot escape. The Qur'an uses the phrase for God's absolute power: *"Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion (bi-yadihi l-mulk)"* (67:1); *"in Your hand is all good"* (3:26). The affirmation of God's hand, like the affirmation of His establishment on the Throne (v. 86), is accepted by the *salaf* as God described it, without likening it to creation and without denying it.

*Kulli shayʾ*, "everything," leaves nothing out. The earth (v. 84) and the heavens (v. 86) were parts; this is the whole. The question asks: who holds *all of it* — every atom, every cause, every hidden reality — in His hand?

**"Who Protects While None Can Protect Against Him": Yujīru wa Lā Yujāru ʿAlayhi**

The second clause introduces the concept of *jiwār* — protection, neighborly refuge — which was central to Arabian society. In the tribal world of the Quraysh, a person in danger could seek the *jiwār* of a powerful man or clan, who would then be bound to protect him; to violate someone's *jiwār* was a grave dishonor. The Prophet ﷺ himself, returning from Ṭāʾif, entered Makkah under the *jiwār* of al-Muṭʿim ibn ʿAdī. The verse uses this familiar institution to make a point about God: *huwa yujīru* — "He grants protection" — and *lā yujāru ʿalayhi* — "and none can grant protection against Him."

The asymmetry is the argument. Among human beings, protection is reciprocal and limited: a man may protect another today and need protection tomorrow; a clan may shelter a fugitive and be overpowered by a stronger clan. But God's protection is absolute in both directions. He protects whom He wills — and no one can be protected *from* Him. There is no *mujīr*, no protector, to whom one could flee from God's decree. The Qur'an states this elsewhere: *"Say, 'Indeed, none can protect me from God, and never will I find in other than Him a refuge'"* (72:22); *"And you will not find besides Him any protector or helper"* (4:123); *"The Day they will come forth, nothing of them will be concealed from God. To whom belongs sovereignty this Day? To God, the One, the Prevailing"* (40:16).

The clause strikes directly at the Quraysh's *shirk*. They worshipped idols and intermediaries partly as *protectors* — sources of refuge, patrons who could shield them. Verse 88 asks: can any of them protect you *from God*? The answer is no; and since the only protector who cannot be overridden is God, seeking protection elsewhere is not only useless but insulting to the One whose *jiwār* alone is absolute. The Prophet ﷺ taught the believers to seek refuge in exactly these terms: *"I seek refuge in the perfect words of God from the evil of what He has created"* (Muslim 2708) — refuge in God, not from Him.

**The Three Questions as a Complete Argument**

With verse 88, the argument of verses 84–89 reaches completeness, and it is worth stating the whole. (1) God owns the earth and everyone on it — so the deniers belong to Him. (2) God is Lord of the seven heavens and the great Throne — so His rule extends to the highest of creation. (3) God holds the *malakūt* of everything and protects without being protected against — so His power is total, inward, and unopposable. From these three admissions, every element of the deniers' position collapses: *shirk* is absurd (why worship what owns, rules, and protects nothing?); denial of resurrection is absurd (the One who holds the *malakūt* of everything holds the dust and bones); and rejection of the Messenger is absurd (the One who is Lord of all has the right to send whom He wills and command what He wills). The deniers have supplied, in their own answers, the premises of the case against them.

**"If You Know": The Frame Closes**

The verse ends as verse 84 began: *in kuntum taʿlamūn*, "if you know." The repetition frames the three questions as a single test of knowledge. The deniers claimed to know that the Qur'an was legends (v. 83); the sūrah asks them to display their knowledge on the most basic questions of existence. They will pass the test — they will say "God" — and in passing it they will fail, because their answers condemn their conduct. The phrase's return also emphasizes that the knowledge being asked for is not esoteric. Anyone who *knows* anything knows that the earth, the heavens, and everything belong to God. The deniers' problem was never ignorance.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 88 offers the believer a description of God to live by. *Malakūt kulli shayʾ bi-yadihi* — the dominion of everything is in His hand: not only the outcomes he can see but the causes he cannot, the intentions of others, the turns of events, the hidden mechanisms of his own body and mind. Nothing is outside the hand. And *yujīru wa lā yujāru ʿalayhi* — He protects, and none protects against Him: the believer who is under God's protection is safe from everything, and the one who is under God's decree cannot be rescued from it by anyone. Both halves are consoling to the one who has placed himself rightly. He need not fear any creature, because no creature can protect him *against* God — and no creature can harm him *against* God's protection. The Prophet ﷺ taught this to Ibn ʿAbbās: *"Know that if the whole nation gathered to benefit you, they could benefit you only with what God has written for you; and if they gathered to harm you, they could harm you only with what God has written against you"* (al-Tirmidhī 2516). That is verse 88, taught to a boy riding behind the Prophet ﷺ.

The verse also asks the believer to examine where he actually seeks *jiwār*. In a crisis, to whom does the heart run first — to God, or to a person, an institution, a bank balance? The Quraysh ran to their idols; the believer's temptation is subtler but the same. Verse 88 corrects the direction: run to the One who protects and cannot be protected against.

**Toward Bewitchment**

The third question has been asked. The third answer will be "God." And the third rejoinder will be the sharpest: not "remember," not "be reverent," but *"how then are you bewitched?"*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:89

> **They will say, “God’s.” Say, “How then are you bewitched?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Admission and the Sharpest Rejoinder**

For the third time the deniers answer as predicted: *sa-yaqūlūna li-llāh* — "They will say, 'To God.'" And for the third time the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to respond — but this response differs in kind from the first two: *qul fa-annā tusḥarūn* — "Say: 'How then are you bewitched?'" Verse 85 asked *"will you not remember?"* — an invitation. Verse 87 asked *"will you not be reverent?"* — a summons. Verse 89 asks *"how are you bewitched?"* — an expression of astonishment at a condition that no ordinary explanation can account for. The escalation has reached its end. After three admissions that God owns, rules, and holds everything, the deniers' continued idolatry and denial can be explained only as a kind of enchantment.

**"How Then Are You Bewitched?": Tusḥarūn**

The verb *tusḥarūn* is the passive of *saḥara*, "to bewitch, to enchant, to cast a spell." The root *s-ḥ-r* denotes magic — the production of illusions that make a person see what is not there or fail to see what is. The passive voice is significant: the deniers are not accused of *practicing* sorcery but of being *subjected* to it — of being under a spell that makes them behave irrationally. The interrogative *annā*, "how? whence? from where?", expresses bewilderment: from what direction could such a spell have come? What could possibly explain a people who say "God owns everything" and then bow to stones?

The choice of *siḥr*, magic, as the metaphor is deliberate and pointed. The Quraysh had accused the Prophet ﷺ of being a *sāḥir*, a sorcerer — this was their chosen slander after they rejected "madman" as unconvincing (see the account of al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah under verse 70). They said the Qur'an was *siḥr*: *"This is nothing but magic imitated"* (74:24); *"a magician, a liar"* (38:4). Verse 89 turns the accusation around. It is not the Prophet ﷺ who is casting spells; it is *they* who are *bewitched* — because only enchantment could produce the gap between their admissions and their conduct. The magician, in their account, was the man reciting the Qur'an; in God's account, the enchanted are the men rejecting it while confessing its premises.

**The Diagnosis of Irrationality**

The three questions of verses 84–88 were designed to expose a contradiction, and verse 89 names the contradiction's only possible cause. Consider the deniers' position after their three answers. They affirm: God owns the earth and all in it, including us. God is Lord of the seven heavens and the great Throne. God holds the dominion of everything in His hand and protects while none can protect against Him. And yet they: worship idols that own, rule, and protect nothing; deny that the One who holds everything can restore the dust and bones; and reject the Messenger of the Lord they confess. This is not a position that reason can hold. A person who genuinely believed the three premises could not act as the deniers act. Therefore — the verse concludes — their reason is not functioning; something has interposed between what they know and what they do. The Qur'an's word for that something is *siḥr*: an illusion so complete that the enchanted does not know he is enchanted.

The verse thus completes the sūrah's account of the deniers' psychology. Their hearts are in *ghamrah*, submerged (v. 63). They do not *perceive* (v. 56). They do not *use reason* (v. 80). They do not *remember* (v. 85). They are *averse to the truth* (v. 70). And now: they are *bewitched* — under a spell that renders all their true beliefs inert. The spell has a name in other verses: *"Satan made attractive to them their deeds"* (6:43; 27:24); *"Their hearts are hardened"* (6:43); *"God has set a seal upon their hearts"* (2:7). Each names the same condition from a different angle: a faculty present but disabled.

**What Casts the Spell**

If the deniers are bewitched, what bewitched them? The sūrah has already given the components of the answer. *Wealth and children* (v. 55) — the *istidrāj* that lulls; the Qur'an calls this world's life *"the enjoyment of delusion"* (3:185), and delusion is a form of enchantment. *Arrogance* (v. 67) — the *kibr* that makes truth from a man like oneself unbearable. *The forefathers* (vv. 24, 68, 83) — the inherited habits that feel like reality because they were never questioned. *Aversion* (v. 70) — the dislike of what the truth demands. *Satan* (vv. 97–98 will name him directly) — whose *hamazāt*, incitements, whisper the illusions. Together these constitute the *siḥr*: not a single spell cast by a single sorcerer, but the cumulative enchantment of a life lived in the *ghamrah*, in which every true belief is present and none is operative.

**The Question as a Mercy**

Even the sharpest rejoinder retains a mercy. *Fa-annā tusḥarūn* — "how are you bewitched?" — is a question, not a verdict. A spell can be broken. The person who is told he is enchanted, and who is shown the contradiction between his beliefs and his conduct, has the possibility of waking. The sūrah's whole method in verses 84–89 has been to *awaken*: to make the deniers state aloud what they believe, so that they hear themselves say it, so that the gap between the saying and the doing becomes visible to them. The three admissions are three moments of lucidity; verse 89 asks the deniers to hold onto the lucidity long enough to notice what it implies. Many of the Quraysh did eventually wake — Khālid ibn al-Walīd, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, Abū Sufyān, and most of Makkah at the Conquest. The spell was not permanent.

**The Argument's Broader Reach**

The structure of verses 84–89 has a reach beyond seventh-century Makkah, because the condition it diagnoses is not confined to idolaters. A person may affirm every article of faith and live as though none were true; may say *li-llāh* — "to God belongs everything" — and hoard as if he owned; may confess God as Lord of the Throne and fear his employer more; may acknowledge that none can protect against God and seek his security in everything but Him. The Qur'an's question to such a person is verse 89's: *how are you bewitched?* What illusion stands between what you say and what you do? The believers of the sūrah are those in whom the spell is broken — whose admissions are active (v. 85), whose reverence follows from them (v. 87), and whose lives are the visible result (vv. 57–61). The deniers are those who have all the right answers and are enchanted nonetheless.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 89 asks the believer to search for the spells that operate in his own life — the places where a truth he affirms is disabled by an illusion he has not examined. The most common are the ones the sūrah named: the enchantment of wealth, which makes God's ownership feel theoretical; the enchantment of status, which makes humility feel like loss; the enchantment of habit, which makes the inherited feel like the true; the enchantment of desire, which makes the truth feel unwelcome. The breaking of these spells is the work of *tadabbur* (v. 68), *dhikr* (v. 85), and *taqwā* (v. 87) — the three practices the sūrah prescribes — and of the refuge-seeking the sūrah will command in verses 97–98. The Prophet ﷺ sought refuge daily from *"the evil of the whisperer"* (Sūrah al-Nās) — because he knew that enchantment is not an exotic affliction but the ordinary condition against which every believer must guard.

**Toward the Verdict**

The three questions have been asked and answered, and the deniers have convicted themselves. The next verse states the verdict in God's own voice: *"Rather, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars."*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:90

> **Nay, We brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Verdict After the Interrogation**

The three questions of verses 84–89 have extracted three admissions and delivered three rejoinders. Verse 90 pronounces the verdict: *bal ataynāhum bi-l-ḥaqqi wa innahum la-kādhibūn* — "Rather, We have brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars." The particle *bal* cancels whatever the deniers might still say in their defense and states the case plainly. Two facts: God brought them the truth; and they are liars. The verse is a judgment, and it is stated with the double emphasis of *inna* and the *lām* — *innahum la-kādhibūn* — that the Qur'an reserves for what it wishes to place beyond dispute.

**"Rather, We Have Brought Them the Truth"**

The first clause repeats, almost exactly, the clause of verse 70: *bal jāʾahum bi-l-ḥaqq* — "rather, he [the Messenger] has brought them the truth." The difference is the subject. In verse 70, the Messenger brought it; in verse 90, *We* brought it. The two are the same event described from two sides: the Messenger delivered what God sent. The repetition frames the whole passage from verse 70 to verse 90: it opened with "he brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth," and it closes with "We brought them the truth, and they are liars." Between the two lie the argument from truth's independence (v. 71), the Messenger's sincerity (v. 72), the straight path (vv. 73–74), the failure of mercy and hardship (vv. 75–77), the three signs (vv. 78–80), the deniers' repeated words (vv. 81–83), and the three questions (vv. 84–89). All of it was the *truth* being brought. Verse 90 records that it was brought — the delivery is complete — and what the deniers did with it.

The word *al-ḥaqq*, explained under verse 70, denotes reality — what actually is. The truth brought includes everything the sūrah has presented: the embryo, the heavens, the histories, the argument from the deniers' own admissions. It is *ḥaqq* because it corresponds to what is. The deniers' position, by contrast, does not correspond to what is — and that is what makes them what the second clause calls them.

**"And Indeed They Are Liars": Kādhibūn**

The second clause is the verdict proper: *wa innahum la-kādhibūn* — "and indeed they are certainly liars." The word *kādhib*, liar, is from the root *k-dh-b*, "to lie, to speak falsely, to deny." The sūrah has used the root repeatedly for the deniers' response to the messengers: *kadhdhabūhu*, "they denied him" (v. 26); *kadhdhabū bi-liqāʾi l-ākhirah*, "they denied the meeting of the Hereafter" (v. 33); *kadhdhabūhumā*, "they denied them both" (v. 48). The deniers called the messengers liars (v. 38: *"he is only a man who has invented a lie about God"*). Verse 90 delivers the counter-verdict: *they* are the liars.

In what do they lie? The commentators identified several falsehoods, each of which the sūrah has exposed. They lie in *shirk* — in attributing partners to God, which the next verse will refute in detail. They lie in denying the Resurrection — in saying "we will not be raised" (vv. 37, 82) against the evidence of their own creation. They lie in calling the Qur'an legends (v. 83) and the Messenger a madman (v. 70). And — most pointedly in the context of verses 84–89 — they lie in their *lives*: they say "God owns everything" and act as if He does not, which is a lie enacted rather than spoken. A person who affirms a truth and lives its contradiction is lying with his conduct even when his words are accurate.

**Why "Liars" and Not "Mistaken"**

The verse's choice of *kādhibūn*, liars, rather than a softer word like *mukhṭiʾūn*, mistaken, or *ḍāllūn*, astray, is deliberate and follows from the preceding verses. A person who is mistaken holds a false belief sincerely; a liar says what he knows or has reason to know is false. Verses 84–89 established that the deniers *know* the truth — they said "God" three times. Their denial is therefore not error but falsehood: the assertion of what their own admissions contradict. The Qur'an makes this distinction elsewhere in its description of the Quraysh: *"They do not call you a liar, but the wrongdoers reject the signs of God"* (6:33) — they knew he was truthful and rejected anyway; and *"they rejected them, while their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and haughtiness"* (27:14, of Pharaoh's people). Denial against inner conviction is lying, and verse 90 names it as such.

**The Symmetry of Truth and Falsehood**

The verse's two clauses set truth and lie against each other with a precision that reflects the sūrah's whole design. God brought *al-ḥaqq*; the deniers responded with *kadhib*. The structure recalls verse 71's teaching that truth does not follow desire: the deniers wanted a truth that suited them, and since the real truth did not, they substituted a falsehood that did. Every element of their creed — the idols, the denial of resurrection, the dismissal of the Qur'an — was a lie constructed to avoid a truth that made demands. And verse 62 promised that the record "speaks with truth"; verse 90 shows what the record will say of these people: liars.

**The Verdict and the Sūrah's Title**

The sūrah is named for the *believers* — *al-muʾminūn*. Verse 90 names their opposite: not merely *kāfirūn*, disbelievers, but *kādhibūn*, liars. The pairing is instructive. Faith (*īmān*) is, at its root, *truthfulness* — *taṣdīq*, affirming as true what is true. The believer is one who says "yes" to reality; the *muʾmin* is the *muṣaddiq*, the one who confirms. The opposite of *taṣdīq* is *takdhīb*, calling the truth a lie — and the one who does it is a *kādhib*. The sūrah's two communities are therefore not only believers and disbelievers but the truthful and the lying: those whose word and life correspond to what is, and those whose word and life contradict it.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 90 asks the believer to test his own relationship to *al-ḥaqq* with the same rigor the sūrah applied to the Quraysh. The question is not whether he affirms the truth — he does — but whether he *lies against it* in the sūrah's extended sense: affirming with the tongue and denying with the life. The Qur'an warns believers specifically against this: *"O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of God that you say what you do not do"* (61:2–3). The believer who says "God owns everything" and clutches; who says "God is Lord of the Throne" and fears people; who says "none can protect against Him" and seeks his safety elsewhere — has a portion, however small, of the condition verse 90 names. The remedy is the *ṣidq*, truthfulness, that the Prophet ﷺ commanded: *"Adhere to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise"* (al-Bukhārī 6094; Muslim 2607) — truthfulness not only in speech but in the correspondence between what one confesses and how one lives.

The verse also fortifies the believer against the accusation the deniers made. They called the Messenger a liar; God calls them liars. The believer who is called a liar for his faith — deluded, dishonest with himself, clinging to comforting falsehood — has the sūrah's verdict in his favor: the one who affirms the Owner of everything is the truthful one, and the one who denies Him while admitting His ownership is the liar. The names have been assigned.

**Toward the Refutation of Shirk**

The verdict has been given. The next verse turns to the central lie — the ascription of a child and of partners to God — and refutes it with an argument from the order of the universe.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:91

> **God has not taken any child, and neither are there any gods with Him, for then each god would take away what he created, and some of them would overcome others. Glory be to God above that which they ascribe!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Central Lie Refuted**

Verse 90 called the deniers liars. Verse 91 names the central lie and refutes it: *mā ttakhadha llāhu min waladin wa mā kāna maʿahu min ilāhin idhan la-dhahaba kullu ilāhin bimā khalaqa wa la-ʿalā baʿḍuhum ʿalā baʿḍin subḥāna llāhi ʿammā yaṣifūn* — "God has not taken any child, nor is there any god with Him; for then each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overpowered others. Exalted is God above what they describe." The verse contains two denials, one argument, and one doxology. The denials reject a child and rival gods; the argument shows why rival gods are impossible; the doxology declares God's transcendence above the whole description. It is the sūrah's most concentrated statement of *tawḥīd*, the oneness of God, and it is placed here because the three questions (vv. 84–89) have just established, from the deniers' own mouths, the premises it needs.

**"God Has Not Taken Any Child"**

The first denial: *mā ttakhadha llāhu min waladin* — "God has not taken any child." The verb *ittakhadha*, "to take, to adopt," and the emphatic *min* before *walad* ("any child whatsoever") make the denial total. The source notes that the immediate target is the Makkan belief that the angels were God's daughters — a belief the Qur'an refutes repeatedly: *"And they attribute daughters to God — exalted is He — while for themselves is what they desire"* (16:57); *"Has your Lord chosen you for sons and taken from among the angels daughters? Indeed, you say a grave saying"* (17:40); *"So ask them: does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?"* (37:149). The denial also encompasses the claim that Jesus, whom the sūrah named in verse 50 as *"the son of Mary"*, was the son of God: *"It is not for God to take a son; exalted is He!"* (19:35); *"Say, 'He is God, the One; God, the Eternal Refuge; He neither begets nor is born'"* (112:1–3).

The denial of a child follows from the admissions of verses 84–89. If God owns the earth and everything in it, and holds the *malakūt* of everything in His hand, then He *needs* nothing — and a child is taken by one who needs an heir, a helper, or a continuation. The Qur'an makes this argument explicit: *"They say, 'God has taken a son.' Exalted is He! He is the Free of need. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth"* (10:68). Ownership of all excludes the need that a child would satisfy. Moreover, a child is of the same kind as its parent — and nothing is of God's kind: *"There is nothing like unto Him"* (42:11). To attribute a child is to reduce the Creator to the category of created things that reproduce.

**"Nor Is There Any God With Him"**

The second denial: *wa mā kāna maʿahu min ilāhin* — "nor is there any god with Him." Again the emphatic *min* ("any god at all"). This is the denial of *shirk* in its plainest form: there is no second deity alongside God — not as equal, not as subordinate, not as intermediary. The Quraysh did not claim their idols were equal to God; they claimed they were lesser gods, partners, intercessors. The verse denies even this. *Maʿahu*, "with Him," excludes any companion in divinity of any rank.

**The Argument From Order**

Then comes the argument, introduced by *idhan*, "in that case, for then": *la-dhahaba kullu ilāhin bimā khalaqa wa la-ʿalā baʿḍuhum ʿalā baʿḍ* — "each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overpowered others." The source rightly connects this to 21:22: *"Had there been in them [the heavens and the earth] gods besides God, they both would have been corrupted (la-fasadatā)."* Verse 91 develops the same argument in more detail, and the classical theologians — al-Rāzī prominent among them — called it *dalīl al-tamānuʿ*, the argument from mutual hindrance. It runs as follows.

Suppose there were two or more gods. A god, by definition, is a creator with independent will and power. Each god would then *create* — and each would *take away what he created* (*dhahaba bimā khalaqa*): he would claim his creation as his own domain, govern it by his own will, separate it from the others'. The universe would be divided into rival realms, each under a different sovereign. But the universe is not divided; it is one — one order, one set of laws, one interlocking system in which the heavens and the earth, the rain and the plants, the cattle and the humans, all work together (vv. 17–22). The unity of the cosmos refutes the plurality of its rulers.

Further: the wills of independent gods would sooner or later *conflict* — one willing what another does not — and when wills conflict, *some would overpower others* (*ʿalā baʿḍuhum ʿalā baʿḍ*). The stronger god would prevail; the weaker would be subjected. But a subjected god is not a god — a being that can be overpowered is by definition not omnipotent, not sovereign, not divine. So either the gods never conflict (in which case there is really one will, and one god) or they do conflict (in which case the losers are not gods, and the winner is the one God). Either way, plurality collapses into unity. The argument is purely rational, and it requires no premise the deniers did not grant: they admitted the universe has a Lord who holds the dominion of everything (v. 88); verse 91 shows that "everything in one hand" is incompatible with "several hands."

**Why the Argument Is Placed Here**

The argument of verse 91 comes immediately after the three questions because it needs their admissions. The deniers said God owns the earth and all in it (v. 85), is Lord of the heavens and the Throne (v. 87), and holds the *malakūt* of everything (v. 89). If all of this is in one hand — *kulli shayʾ*, *everything* — there is nothing left for a second god to own or rule. The admission of total dominion is the admission of exclusive dominion. Verse 91 simply draws the conclusion: since everything is His, no god is *with* Him; and if any god were, the "everything" would be divided — which the deniers have just denied. The Qur'an's method here is to make the deniers refute their own idolatry by their own confession of God's sovereignty.

**"Exalted Is God Above What They Describe": Subḥāna llāh**

The verse ends with a doxology: *subḥāna llāhi ʿammā yaṣifūn* — "Glory be to God above what they describe." The word *subḥān* is from the root *s-b-ḥ*, which means to swim, to move swiftly through water or air — and by extension, to declare God far removed, to exalt Him beyond every deficiency, as a thing moving swiftly is far from where it was. *Tasbīḥ* is the declaration of God's transcendence: He is *beyond* — beyond having a child, beyond having a partner, beyond every attribute of created things that the deniers project onto Him. The verb *yaṣifūn*, "they describe," names the deniers' error precisely: they *described* God — attributed to Him daughters, partners, needs — and every description was a diminishment. God is exalted above their descriptions.

The doxology is not merely a pious flourish; it is the correct response to the argument. Having shown that God is one, the verse teaches what to *say*: *subḥāna llāh*. The Prophet ﷺ described this phrase as *"beloved to the Most Merciful, light on the tongue, heavy on the scale"* (al-Bukhārī 6406; Muslim 2694). It is the believer's reflex whenever God is described wrongly — and, in this verse, it is God's own declaration of His transcendence above the lies verse 90 named.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 91 gives the believer both a doctrine and an argument. The doctrine is *tawḥīd* in its purest statement: no child, no partner, exalted above all description. The argument is one he can use — with others and with himself. With others: the unity of the universe, its single order, its interlocking laws, is evidence that its Governor is one; a committee of gods would have produced a divided or conflicting world. With himself: the *shirk* the sūrah warned against in verse 59 — the hidden partner in one's devotion, the *riyāʾ*, the fear of creatures, the love of things as one loves God — is refuted by the same argument. If everything is in one hand, then the "partner" one serves has no power of his own; his apparent power is on loan from the one Hand. To serve him is to serve a subject as if he were the King. *Subḥāna llāhi ʿammā yaṣifūn* — and above what one's own heart secretly ascribes.

**Toward the Knower of the Unseen**

The unity of God has been demonstrated from the order of the seen world. The next verse names Him as *"Knower of the Unseen and the seen"* — and exalts Him once more above the partners they ascribe.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:92

> **Knower of the Unseen and the seen! Exalted is He above the partners they ascribe!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Seal on the Argument**

Verse 91 refuted the ascription of a child and partners to God with the argument from cosmic order. Verse 92 seals the refutation with a divine name and a second declaration of transcendence: *ʿālimi l-ghaybi wa l-shahādati fa-taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn* — "Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; so exalted is He above what they associate." The verse is short, and it functions as a coda to verses 84–91: after the three questions, the verdict, and the refutation, God names Himself by the attribute that grounds all knowledge, and declares Himself above every partner. The passage that began with *"Say: whose is the earth?"* ends with *"Knower of the unseen and the seen."*

**"Knower of the Unseen and the Witnessed": ʿĀlim al-Ghayb wa l-Shahādah**

The name *ʿĀlim al-ghayb wa l-shahādah* appears in the Qur'an ten times, and it names God as the One whose knowledge encompasses both domains of reality: *al-ghayb*, the unseen — what is hidden from creatures, whether because it is absent, future, inward, or beyond perception altogether; and *al-shahādah*, the witnessed — what is present and perceptible. The two words together mean *everything*: what can be known by anyone and what can be known by no one but Him. *"He is God, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed"* (59:22); *"Say, 'O God, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You will judge between Your servants'"* (39:46).

The grammatical form of the name here is notable: it is in the genitive (*ʿālimi*), in apposition to *Allāh* in the preceding verse's *subḥāna llāhi* — "Glory be to God... Knower of the unseen and the witnessed." The name is thus attached to the doxology: the God who is exalted above their descriptions is *the Knower*. The connection is meaningful. The deniers *described* God (v. 91: *yaṣifūn*) — attributed daughters and partners to Him — without knowledge. God is the One who *knows* — and His knowledge exposes their descriptions as fabrication. Those who speak of the unseen without knowledge are answered by the Knower of the unseen.

**Why This Name Here**

The name is chosen with precision for its position, and the commentators identified several reasons.

First, it grounds the *argument* of verse 91. The argument from cosmic order requires that the universe be one coherent system — and coherence requires a single Knower who knows the whole. A god who did not know what another god was doing could not coordinate with him; the unity of the cosmos implies a unity of knowledge behind it. God knows the unseen and the seen — all of it, at once — which is why the cosmos holds together.

Second, it answers the *lie* of verse 90. The deniers lied about God; God knows their lie. The name reminds them that their inner conviction — the *ʿilm* they had and denied (27:14) — is known to Him. They cannot hide their knowledge of the truth behind their profession of falsehood, because the Knower of the unseen sees the knowledge they conceal.

Third, it refutes the *shirk* of verse 91 from a new angle. The idols and intermediaries the Quraysh worshipped knew nothing — not the unseen, not even the seen. The Qur'an mocks this repeatedly: *"Do they associate with Him those who create nothing and they are created? And they are unable to help them, nor can they help themselves"* (7:191–192); and of the idols: *"they do not hear... and if they heard, they would not respond"* (35:14). A god who does not know cannot answer prayer, cannot judge, cannot protect. Only the Knower of the unseen and the seen can be a God. The name is therefore itself an argument against partners: whatever does not know the unseen is disqualified from divinity.

Fourth, it prepares the *next* verses. The sūrah is about to turn to the Prophet's prayers (vv. 93–98) and to the moment of death (vv. 99–100) — matters of the unseen. The name establishes that the One addressed in these prayers knows what is hidden: the punishment promised to the deniers (v. 93), the whispers of the devils (v. 97), the regret of the dying (v. 100). The believer prays to a God who knows.

**"So Exalted Is He Above What They Associate": Taʿālā**

The second half of the verse: *fa-taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn* — "so exalted is He above what they associate." The verb *taʿālā*, from the root *ʿ-l-w*, "to be high," means to be exalted, to be far above. It is the verb the sūrah's reader knows from the phrase *Allāh taʿālā*, "God, exalted is He." Verse 91 used *subḥāna*, glory; verse 92 uses *taʿālā*, exaltation — two complementary declarations of transcendence. *Subḥān* declares God free of every deficiency; *taʿālā* declares Him above every comparison. The particle *fa-*, "so," draws the exaltation as a conclusion from the name: *because* He is Knower of the unseen and the seen, He is exalted above the partners they ascribe. Knowledge of everything is incompatible with having a rival; the Knower of all is necessarily above all.

The word *yushrikūn*, "they associate," names the sin of *shirk* directly, completing the sequence of verse 91's *yaṣifūn*, "they describe." The deniers described God wrongly and associated others with Him; God is exalted above both the description and the association. The two doxologies — *subḥāna llāhi ʿammā yaṣifūn* (v. 91) and *taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn* (v. 92) — form a pair that recurs in the Qur'an as its standard response to *shirk*: *"Exalted is He and high above what they associate"* (10:18; 16:1; 30:40; 39:67).

**Knowledge and Sovereignty Together**

Verses 84–92 have established two attributes that together define divinity: *sovereignty* (ownership of the earth, lordship of the heavens and Throne, dominion of everything — vv. 84–89) and *knowledge* (of the unseen and the seen — v. 92). The two are inseparable. A sovereign who did not know could not rule; a knower who did not rule would be a spectator. God is both: He holds everything in His hand (v. 88) and He knows everything in His hand (v. 92). The idols were neither. And human beings, however powerful, are at most one — some have sovereignty over a domain — but never the other: no human knows the unseen. The verse's name thus places God in a category of His own, above every creature, which is exactly what *taʿālā* declares.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 92 gives the believer a name to hold onto in two situations. In *uncertainty*: when the future is hidden, when the outcome of an illness or a decision or a conflict cannot be known, the believer remembers that the unseen is *seen* by God — that what is *ghayb* to him is *shahādah* to his Lord — and that the One who knows it is the One who governs it. In *loneliness or injustice*: when a wrong is done in secret, when no one witnesses the truth, when one's sincerity is doubted by others, the believer remembers that the Knower of the unseen sees the secret, witnesses the truth, and knows the sincerity. The sūrah's believers, whose hearts tremble because they will return to their Lord (v. 60), tremble before the *Knower* — the One from whom nothing is hidden, so that the fear is well founded, and the One who knows their trembling is sincere, so that the hope is well founded too.

The verse also closes a door the believer must keep closed: the door of speaking about God without knowledge. The deniers *described* God with daughters and partners; the temptation for believers is subtler — to attribute to God intentions, judgments, or preferences that He has not revealed; to say "God wants" or "God will punish" about matters He has not disclosed. The Qur'an forbids this: *"And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge"* (17:36); and it lists among the gravest sins *"that you say about God what you do not know"* (7:33). The Knower of the unseen has told us what He has told us; about the rest, the believer says *subḥāna llāh* and is silent.

**Toward the Prophet's Prayer**

The argument is complete and sealed. The sūrah now turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and instructs him in a prayer — a prayer to be spared from being among the wrongdoers when their promised punishment comes.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:93

> **Say, “My Lord! If Thou showest me what they are promised,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**From Argument to Prayer**

The long argument with the deniers has concluded (vv. 84–92). The sūrah now turns inward, to the Prophet ﷺ, and instructs him in what to *say* to his Lord: *qul rabbi immā turiyannī mā yūʿadūn* — "Say: 'My Lord, if You should show me what they are promised...'" The sentence continues into verse 94, where the petition is completed: *"...my Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people."* The source treats the two verses together; this commentary honors the sūrah's division and takes verse 93 on its own, as the *condition* of the prayer — the situation the Prophet ﷺ is taught to contemplate — before verse 94 states the *request*.

The turn from argument to prayer is itself instructive. After every proof has been given and every excuse dismantled, the messenger does not gloat or rest; he prays. The one who has just been given the words that silence the deniers (vv. 84–89) is now given the words that place himself under God's protection. Victory in argument is not security before God, and the sūrah moves the Prophet ﷺ directly from the one to the other.

**"Say: My Lord": Rabbi**

The prayer opens with *rabbi*, "my Lord" — the intimate vocative, with the first-person possessive, that the Qur'an places on the lips of the prophets in their most personal petitions. Noah said *rabbi nṣurnī* (v. 26); the second messenger said the same (v. 39); the dying denier will say *rabbi rjiʿūn* (v. 99); and the sūrah will end with *rabbi ghfir wa rḥam* (v. 118). The word *rabb* — owner, sustainer, nurturer — in the possessive is the address of one who belongs to the One he addresses. The Prophet ﷺ prays not as a stranger petitioning a distant power but as a servant speaking to *his* Lord.

The address will be repeated in verse 94 — *rabbi* ... *rabbi* — and the repetition, as the commentators noted, is the mark of urgency and earnestness. One who says "my Lord, my Lord" is pleading.

**"If You Should Show Me What They Are Promised"**

The condition: *immā turiyannī mā yūʿadūn* — "if You should show me what they are promised." The grammar is emphatic: *immā* is *in* (if) plus the intensifying *mā*, and the verb *turiyannī* carries the heavy *nūn* of emphasis (*nūn al-tawkīd*). The construction expresses a real and weighty possibility: *if it should indeed happen* that You show me. What is to be shown is *mā yūʿadūn* — "what they are promised" — the punishment that the sūrah has promised the deniers throughout: the seizure of the affluent (v. 64), the gate of severe punishment (v. 77), the end that overtook every previous generation (vv. 41–44).

The verb *turiyannī*, "You show me," is precise. The Prophet ﷺ contemplates *witnessing* the punishment — being present when it falls on the people he has been sent to. This was a real possibility, and the commentators identified its historical fulfillment: the Prophet ﷺ did witness the *mutrafūn* of Quraysh cut down at Badr — Abū Jahl, ʿUtbah, Shaybah, Umayyah — and he stood over their bodies at the well and addressed them: *"Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true"* (al-Bukhārī 3976; Muslim 2875). He was shown *mā yūʿadūn*. The prayer of verses 93–94 was taught to him before that day, so that when he saw it he would be standing where he had asked to stand.

**Why the Prophet Is Taught to Contemplate This**

The instruction to contemplate witnessing the punishment serves several purposes.

First, it confirms that the punishment is real and near. God does not instruct His Prophet to prepare for a hypothetical; the prayer assumes that what the deniers are promised will come, and that the Prophet ﷺ may live to see it. The prayer is therefore itself a warning to those who hear it recited: the man you mock is being taught how to conduct himself when he watches you fall.

Second, it protects the Prophet ﷺ from two opposite dangers at that moment. One danger is *fear* — that the punishment, when it comes, might engulf him with the wrongdoers, as the Flood engulfed all but the Ark. The other, subtler danger is *exultation* — that seeing his enemies destroyed might stir something in him that God does not want in His messenger. The prayer of verse 94 will address the first explicitly ("do not place me among them"); but the humility of the whole prayer addresses the second. A man who prays "my Lord, my Lord, do not place me among them" at the moment of his enemies' fall is not gloating; he is trembling.

Third, it models the correct relationship of the messenger to the punishment. He did not cause it; he cannot control it; he is not exempt from it by his own merit but only by God's placing him outside it. The Prophet ﷺ was the best of creation, and he is still taught to pray *not to be among the wrongdoers*. If he must ask this, no one may presume.

**The Prayer and the Sūrah's Pattern**

The prayer of verses 93–94 belongs to a pattern the sūrah has established. Every messenger prayed at the moment of crisis: Noah, *"My Lord, help me because they have denied me"* (v. 26); the second messenger, the same (v. 39); and now the Prophet ﷺ, *"My Lord, if You show me what they are promised, do not place me among the wrongdoers."* The prayers differ in content — Noah asked for help; the Prophet ﷺ asks for separation — but they share a form: the messenger, having delivered the message and been rejected, turns to his Lord and hands the matter over. The prayer is the messenger's acknowledgment that the outcome is not his.

The Prophet's prayer also differs from the earlier ones in a way that reflects his position. Noah and the second messenger prayed *for help against* their people; the Prophet ﷺ prays *not to be among* his people when help against them comes. The shift is from the offensive to the protective, and it suits the mercy that characterized him. He did not pray for the Quraysh's destruction — when asked to curse them, he said: *"I was not sent as a curser; I was sent as a mercy"* (Muslim 2599). He prayed only that, if their destruction came, he would not be in it.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 93 teaches the believer to contemplate, in advance, the moment when God's promises to the wrongdoers are fulfilled — and to prepare his own heart for it. Such moments come in every life: the fall of a tyrant, the exposure of a fraud, the collapse of an arrogant enterprise, the death of one who mocked the truth. The believer's response is modeled here. Not celebration, not "I told you so," but *rabbi* — a turning to God, a recognition that what has happened is His doing, and (as verse 94 will make explicit) a plea not to be counted among those who fell. The believer who watches the wrongdoer's end and feels secure has missed the lesson; the one who watches and prays has learned it.

The verse also teaches the believer to pray *before* the crisis, not only in it. The Prophet ﷺ was taught this prayer in Makkah, years before Badr. The preparation for the moment of witnessing was made in the years of not yet witnessing. The believer who wants to stand rightly when God's promises are fulfilled — rightly humble, rightly separate from the wrongdoers, rightly under God's protection — builds that standing now, in prayers offered while the outcome is still hidden.

**Toward the Petition**

The condition has been stated: if You show me what they are promised. Verse 94 will complete the prayer with its petition — and its petition is not for triumph but for exemption.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:94

> **my Lord, then place me not among the wrongdoing people!”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Petition Completed**

Verse 93 opened the prayer with its condition: "My Lord, if You should show me what they are promised." Verse 94 completes it with the petition: *rabbi fa-lā tajʿalnī fī l-qawmi l-ẓālimīn* — "my Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people." The prayer as a whole is: *if the punishment comes while I am present, do not place me among those it strikes.* The petition is striking for what it is not. It is not a request for victory, for vindication, for the destruction of enemies, or for reward. It is a request for *separation* — that when God's judgment falls on the wrongdoers, the Prophet ﷺ not be among them. The best of creation, taught the words to say at the moment of his enemies' fall, is taught to ask only this.

**"My Lord" Repeated: The Urgency of the Plea**

The verse opens with *rabbi* for the second time in two verses. The commentators observed that the repetition of the vocative is a mark of earnest entreaty — the pleading of one who calls, and calls again, to make sure he is heard. The Prophet ﷺ is not making a formal petition; he is begging. The doubled *rabbi* also brackets the condition of verse 93: "My Lord — if You show me what they are promised — my Lord — do not place me among them." The request is wrapped in the address, as though the Prophet ﷺ were holding onto the name of his Lord on both sides of the fearful thought between.

**"Do Not Place Me Among the Wrongdoing People": Fa-lā Tajʿalnī**

The verb *tajʿalnī*, "place me, make me," is from the root *j-ʿ-l*, "to make, to put, to appoint." The petition asks God not to *put* the Prophet ﷺ in the company of the wrongdoers — not to include him in their number when the punishment comes. The phrase *fī l-qawmi l-ẓālimīn*, "among the wrongdoing people," uses the word *ẓālim*, wrongdoer, from the root *ẓ-l-m*, which means to put a thing in other than its proper place — to do injustice, to transgress. The sūrah has used the root for the deniers who ate the Prophet's food and denied his message (v. 28: *"the wrongdoing people"*, of Noah's people), and the Qur'an's supreme example of *ẓulm* is *shirk*: *"Indeed, shirk is a tremendous wrong (ẓulm ʿaẓīm)"* (31:13). The wrongdoing people are those who have put created things in God's place — exactly what verses 91–92 refuted.

The prayer asks not to be *among* them. This has two dimensions that the scholars drew out. The first is *physical*: when the punishment falls — the Flood, the Cry, the seizure — let me not be in the place where it falls. The sūrah has shown that God's punishments are precise: Noah and his family were saved while the rest drowned (v. 27); the believers with Moses were saved while Pharaoh's host drowned (v. 48). The Prophet ﷺ asks to be on the saved side of that precision. The second dimension is *moral and spiritual*: let me not be *of* them — let me not share their qualities, their arrogance, their aversion to truth, their enchantment (v. 89) — so that I am not among them because I am not like them. The prayer for physical separation rests on the prayer for moral separation, and the second is the one the believer can pray daily.

**Why the Prophet Must Ask This**

The Prophet ﷺ was sinless in the sense the scholars call *ʿiṣmah* — protected from major sin and from error in conveying revelation. Why, then, must he pray not to be placed among the wrongdoers? The commentators gave several answers, each sound.

First, the prayer is *taught*, not spontaneous — *qul*, "Say," is God's instruction — and its purpose extends beyond the Prophet ﷺ to his community. By placing these words on the Prophet's lips, God teaches every believer what to pray. If the Prophet ﷺ prays not to be among the wrongdoers, then no one may consider himself above the need for that prayer. The prayer is a lesson in humility delivered through the humblest of teachers.

Second, being *among* a punished people is not only a matter of personal guilt. The Qur'an warns: *"And fear a trial which will not strike those who have wronged among you exclusively"* (8:25). When punishment falls on a community, the righteous within it may be caught up in its outward effects — killed in the war, starved in the famine — even though their standing with God is different. Zaynab bint Jaḥsh asked the Prophet ﷺ: *"Shall we be destroyed while there are righteous among us?"* and he answered: *"Yes, when wickedness abounds"* (al-Bukhārī 3346; Muslim 2880). The prayer asks to be spared even this.

Third, the prayer is an expression of *dependence*. The Prophet ﷺ was protected from *ẓulm* — but by God's grace, not by his own power. To pray "do not place me among them" is to acknowledge that his exemption is God's doing and to ask that it continue. The saints of God do not presume on their sainthood; they ask for it again each day.

**The Prayer's Fulfillment**

The prayer was answered. When the promised punishment came to the Quraysh at Badr, the Prophet ﷺ was not among the wrongdoers — he was on the other side of the field, in the shelter built for him, praying through the night before the battle: *"O God, fulfill for me what You promised me; O God, if this band is destroyed, You will not be worshipped on earth"* (Muslim 1763). When the punishment came to Makkah in the form of conquest, he entered the city not as one of its condemned but as its conqueror, with his head bowed on his camel in humility so that his beard nearly touched the saddle. He was shown *mā yūʿadūn* (v. 93), and he was not placed among the wrongdoing people (v. 94). The prayer taught in Makkah was fulfilled in every subsequent event.

**The Spirit of the Prayer**

The prayer of verses 93–94 reveals something about the character the Qur'an cultivates. Faced with the imminent destruction of his persecutors — the people who had mocked him, tortured his followers, boycotted his clan, and plotted his murder — the Prophet ﷺ is taught to think not "let them fall" but "let me not fall with them." The focus is on his own standing, not on their fate. This is the same orientation the sūrah praised in the believers whose hearts *tremble* about their own return to God (v. 60), and it is the opposite of the deniers who *rejoice* in what they have (v. 53). The righteous person, at the moment of the wicked person's fall, thinks about his own account. The wicked person, at the moment of the righteous person's suffering, mocks (v. 110). The two responses define the two communities.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 94 gives the believer a prayer for every occasion on which he witnesses wrongdoing punished or a community brought low: *rabbi fa-lā tajʿalnī fī l-qawmi l-ẓālimīn* — "my Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people." The prayer asks for two things at once, and the believer should intend both. That he not be *caught in* the punishment — spared its outward reach, protected in the trial that does not strike the wrongdoers only. And that he not be *of* the wrongdoers — that his heart be examined and cleared of the qualities that made them what they were: the arrogance, the aversion, the busy heedlessness, the spell. The second is the deeper request, and it is the one the believer must renew constantly, because the line between the two communities runs through every heart, and no one is on the right side of it by his own guarantee.

The verse also teaches the believer what *not* to pray. Not for the destruction of enemies; the Prophet ﷺ was offered that (when the angel of the mountains asked to crush Makkah between the two hills) and declined it (al-Bukhārī 3231; Muslim 1795). Not for vindication in the eyes of people; that was never the point. Only: keep me out of their number. The believer who has this prayer in his mouth when the wrongdoer falls has the Prophet's heart in his chest.

**Toward the Assurance**

The Prophet ﷺ has been taught to pray for separation when the punishment comes. The next verse assures him — and warns the deniers — that God is fully able to show him what they are promised.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:95

> **And surely We are able to show you what We promise them.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Divine Response to the Prayer**

The Prophet ﷺ has been taught to pray: "If You show me what they are promised, do not place me among the wrongdoers" (vv. 93–94). Verse 95 is God's response — not to the petition (which is granted, as history showed) but to the *condition*: *wa innā ʿalā an nuriyaka mā naʿiduhum la-qādirūn* — "And indeed, We are certainly able to show you what We promise them." The Prophet ﷺ said "*if* You show me"; God answers: We *can*. The verse is an affirmation of power, framed with the double emphasis of *inna* and *lām* (*innā ... la-qādirūn*) that marks a solemn assurance. It addresses the Prophet ﷺ directly — *nuriyaka*, "show *you*" — and speaks of the deniers in the third person — *naʿiduhum*, "what We promise *them*." They are the subject of a promise; he is the one who will witness its fulfillment.

**"We Are Certainly Able": Qādirūn**

The word *qādirūn* is from the root *q-d-r*, which means power, ability, and also measure and decree — the same root as *qadar*, the divine decree, and as *bi-qadar*, "in measure," in verse 18 (*"We sent down water from the sky in measure"*). God is *al-Qādir*, the Able, and *al-Qadīr*, the All-Powerful. The verse's construction — *innā ʿalā ... la-qādirūn*, "We are, over [this], certainly able" — is the Qur'an's standard formula for asserting power over something the deniers doubt: *"Indeed, We are able to take it away"* (v. 18, of the water); *"Are We not able to reassemble his bones? Yes, We are able to proportion his fingertips"* (75:3–4); *"Indeed, We are able to replace them with better than them"* (70:40–41).

The assertion of *ability* answers an unspoken doubt. The deniers had lived for years hearing promises of punishment that had not yet arrived. They mocked the delay: *"When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"* (10:48; 21:38). The delay might tempt even a believer to wonder whether the promise would ever be kept. Verse 95 addresses this: the promise has not been delayed for want of power. God is *able* — fully, certainly able — to bring it, and to bring it while the Prophet ﷺ is present to see it. The delay is the *ḥattā ḥīn*, the appointed time (v. 54), not an inability.

**"To Show You What We Promise Them"**

The object of the ability is *an nuriyaka mā naʿiduhum* — "to show you what We promise them." The verb *nuriyaka*, "We show you," picks up the Prophet's own word from verse 93, *turiyannī*, "You show me." He spoke of the possibility; God confirms it as within His power. The phrase *mā naʿiduhum*, "what We promise them," uses the verb *waʿada*, promise — the same root the deniers used in verse 83 when they said *wuʿidnā*, "we were promised this before," and dismissed it as legends. God takes up their word. They said the promise was a fable; God says: We are able to show it to you — to the Messenger, in his lifetime, before their eyes.

The commentators, as the source notes, connected this to Badr. The Prophet ﷺ was shown the fulfillment of the promise on the field at Badr, and he addressed the dead of Quraysh at the well: *"O Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, O Umayyah ibn Khalaf, O ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, O Shaybah ibn Rabīʿah — have you not found what your Lord promised you to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true"* (al-Bukhārī 3976; Muslim 2875). When ʿUmar asked how he could speak to bodies without souls, the Prophet ﷺ said: *"By the One in whose hand is my soul, you do not hear what I say better than they do."* This was *nuriyaka mā naʿiduhum* — the showing of the promise.

**Why the Assurance Is Placed Here**

The verse serves three audiences at once, and its placement after the prayer of verses 93–94 allows it to address all three.

To the Prophet ﷺ, it is *comfort*. He has just been taught to contemplate the punishment and to pray for exemption from it. God assures him that the punishment is coming, that it is within His power, and — by answering the condition of his prayer — that the prayer has been heard. The messenger who prays "if You show me" is told: We can, and you will not be among them.

To the deniers, it is *warning*. They hear the Prophet ﷺ recite this verse and learn that the delay they mocked is not weakness. God is able to bring what He has promised, at a time of His choosing, and the Messenger will be there to witness it. The warning is the more pointed for being addressed to the Prophet ﷺ *about* them — as though they were already being spoken of in the past tense.

To the believers, it is *steadiness*. The persecuted Muslims of Makkah needed to know that God's promises would be kept and that their Prophet would see the vindication. Verse 95 gave them this, years before Badr. When Badr came, they recognized the fulfillment of a verse they had recited in the years of weakness.

**Ability and Wisdom**

The verse asserts God's *ability* to show the punishment, not His *obligation* to. The distinction matters. God is able to bring the punishment now, in this way, before the Prophet's eyes — and He may also, in His wisdom, delay it, bring it in another form, or defer it entirely to the Hereafter for some of them. The Qur'an makes this explicit elsewhere: *"And whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you [in death], upon you is only the notification, and upon Us is the account"* (13:40; cf. 10:46; 40:77). The Prophet ﷺ might be shown some of it or none of it; either way his task is delivery, and God's is the reckoning. Verse 95 affirms the *power*; the parallel verses affirm the *freedom* with which the power is exercised. Both are true. God showed the Prophet ﷺ some of the promise at Badr and the Conquest, and reserved the rest for the Day the sūrah will describe in verses 101–115.

**Ability as the Ground of the Whole Sūrah**

The word *qādirūn* connects this verse to the sūrah's foundational argument. The deniers' whole position rested on a denial of divine ability — specifically, the ability to resurrect dust and bones (vv. 35, 82). The sūrah has answered that denial from the embryo (vv. 12–14), from the generations (vv. 42–44), from the alternation of life and death (v. 80), and from the deniers' own admission that God holds the dominion of everything (v. 88). Verse 95 asserts ability in a nearer matter: God can bring the promised punishment in this world, before the Prophet's eyes. If the deniers doubted His ability to do the nearer thing, Badr would settle it. And the One who can do the nearer thing can do the farther: the One who fulfills a promise in this world can fulfill the promise of the next.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 95 gives the believer a settled confidence about God's promises — all of them. The believer lives, as the Makkan Muslims lived, in a world where God's promises seem delayed: the promise that the wrongdoer will be held to account, that patience will be rewarded, that the truth will prevail, that the return to God is real. The delay can feel like absence. Verse 95 says: the delay is not inability. *Innā ... la-qādirūn* — We are certainly able. The promise waits for its time; the power to fulfill it is not in question. The believer who holds this does not despair in the years before Badr — and does not gloat on the day of it, because he has also been taught the prayer of verse 94.

The verse also invites the believer to notice fulfillments when they come. God *showed* the Prophet ﷺ what He had promised; and He shows the believer, in his own life and in history, the fulfillment of promises made long before — the fall of oppressors, the vindication of the patient, the answering of prayers offered in despair. The believer who recognizes these as *nuriyaka mā naʿiduhum* — "We show you what We promised" — reads his own experience as the sūrah reads history: as the working out, in time, of what God said He would do.

**Toward the Command to Repel With What Is Better**

God is able to bring the punishment. In the meantime, how should the Prophet ﷺ conduct himself toward those who are promised it? The next verse gives one of the Qur'an's most demanding ethical instructions.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:96

> **Repel evil by that which is better. We know best what they ascribe.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Ethic of the Interval**

God has assured the Prophet ﷺ that He is able to show him the punishment promised to the deniers (v. 95). But the punishment has its appointed time, and until it comes, the Prophet ﷺ must live among the people who mock him, recoil from his recitation (v. 66), rave against him at night (v. 67), and call him mad (v. 70). How is he to treat them in the interval? Verse 96 answers: *idfaʿ bi-llatī hiya aḥsanu l-sayyiʾata naḥnu aʿlamu bimā yaṣifūn* — "Repel evil by that which is better. We know best what they describe." The verse is one of the Qur'an's most demanding ethical instructions, and its placement is precise: it comes *after* the assurance of God's power to punish and *before* the command to seek refuge from Satan. The one who knows God will deal with the wrongdoers is freed to deal with them gently himself.

**"Repel Evil by That Which Is Better": Idfaʿ bi-llatī Hiya Aḥsan**

The verb *idfaʿ* is from the root *d-f-ʿ*, "to push away, to repel, to ward off." The object is *al-sayyiʾah*, "the evil, the bad deed" — the injury, insult, or wrong done to one. The instrument is *bi-llatī hiya aḥsan* — "by that which is better," "with what is best." The construction is notable: not "repel evil with good" (*bi-l-ḥasanah*) but "repel evil with *that which is better*" (*bi-llatī hiya aḥsan*) — the comparative, the superior response, the best available. The command is not merely to refrain from retaliation, nor merely to respond with something good, but to respond with the *best* thing one can find — the response most likely to disarm, to heal, to turn the situation.

The Qur'an gives the fuller form of this command in Sūrah Fuṣṣilat, and it explains the reason: *"And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity will become as though he was a devoted friend. But none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one having a great portion"* (41:34–35). The purpose of repelling with what is better is *transformation*: the enemy becomes a friend. And the verse acknowledges the cost: it is granted only to the patient, only to those of great fortune. The command is hard; the Qur'an does not pretend otherwise.

**What "Better" Means in Practice**

The commentators, as the source notes, understood the command concretely: to meet insult with patience, ignorance with forbearance, injury with pardon, and hostility with kindness. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as *"patience in the face of anger, forbearance in the face of ignorance, and pardon in the face of injury."* The Prophet's life was the demonstration. When the man from Ṭāʾif's streets pelted him with stones, he prayed for their descendants rather than their destruction. When a Bedouin pulled his cloak so hard that it left a mark on his neck and demanded a gift, he laughed and gave the order (al-Bukhārī 3149; Muslim 1057). When he entered Makkah as conqueror and stood before the people who had persecuted him for twenty years, he asked what they expected and, hearing "good, a noble brother and son of a noble brother," said: *"Go, for you are free"* (Ibn Isḥāq; al-Bayhaqī). Each was *idfaʿ bi-llatī hiya aḥsan*: the best possible response to the worst possible treatment.

The command has limits that the scholars carefully drew. It does not forbid self-defense against violence, the enforcement of justice by legitimate authority, or the fighting that later verses of the Qur'an permitted in Madinah. It concerns the *personal* response to *personal* injury — the insult, the mockery, the slight — and it directs that response toward what heals rather than what wounds. The Prophet ﷺ never retaliated for himself; ʿĀʾishah reported: *"The Messenger of God never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant, except when fighting in the cause of God; and he never took revenge for anything done to him, unless the sanctities of God were violated, in which case he took revenge for God"* (Muslim 2328). The distinction is between one's own honor, which is repelled with what is better, and God's sanctities, which are defended.

**Why the Command Comes Here**

The placement of verse 96 after verse 95 is the key to its psychology. It is *because* God has just said "We are certainly able to show you what We promise them" that the Prophet ﷺ can repel their evil with what is better. A person who believes the wrongdoer will never be held to account is under pressure to retaliate himself — otherwise justice is never done. A person who knows that God is able, and will act at the appointed time, is *freed* from that pressure. He can afford to be gentle because the reckoning is not his responsibility. This is the sequence the Qur'an consistently teaches: *"So be patient; indeed, the promise of God is truth"* (30:60; 40:55, 77). Patience is possible because the promise is certain.

The placement *before* verses 97–98 (seeking refuge from Satan's incitements) is equally meaningful. Repelling evil with what is better is difficult precisely because the *nafs* and Satan urge retaliation — *"he insulted you; answer him"; "he mocked you; humiliate him."* These urgings are the *hamazāt al-shayāṭīn*, the incitements of the devils, against which the next verse teaches refuge. The three verses form a unit: God will handle the reckoning (95); you handle the interval with the best response (96); and when the urge to do otherwise comes, seek refuge (97–98).

**"We Know Best What They Describe": Naḥnu Aʿlamu bimā Yaṣifūn**

The verse's second clause gives the deepest reason for the command: *naḥnu aʿlamu bimā yaṣifūn* — "We know best what they describe." The verb *yaṣifūn*, "they describe," is the verb of verse 91 (*subḥāna llāhi ʿammā yaṣifūn*, "glory be to God above what they describe"). There, it denoted their false descriptions of God; here, it includes their false descriptions of the *Prophet* ﷺ — madman, sorcerer, poet, liar — and every slander in their nightly *samar* (v. 67). God says: *We know* what they say. The knowledge is *aʿlamu*, "best, most fully" — God knows their slanders better than the Prophet ﷺ does, knows the motives behind them, knows the falseness of every word.

This is a consolation and a release. The Prophet ﷺ does not need to answer every slander, because the One whose opinion matters already knows the truth. A person who is insulted feels the need to correct the record — to make sure others know the insult is false. Verse 96 tells him that the record is already correct where it counts. God knows what they describe; He knows it is false; He knows what the Prophet ﷺ actually is. The urge to retaliate is, at root, the urge to be vindicated before an audience; when the highest audience has already rendered its verdict, the urge loses its force. The believer who is slandered can repel with what is better because he is not fighting for his reputation — it is already secure with the Knower of the unseen and the seen (v. 92).

**The Command and the Believers' Portrait**

Verse 96 connects to the sūrah's opening portrait. Verse 3 described the believers as *"those who turn away from vain talk (laghw)."* The slanders of the deniers are the supreme *laghw*, and the believer's turning away from them is the first form of repelling with what is better. The Qur'an describes the servants of the Most Merciful: *"when the ignorant address them, they say words of peace"* (25:63); *"and when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity"* (25:72). The command of verse 96 is the active form of verse 3's disposition: not only turning away from the *laghw* but answering it with something that may transform its source.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 96 is among the most practically demanding verses in the Qur'an, and it applies to every believer in every relationship where injury is done — the family member who wounds, the colleague who slanders, the stranger who insults, the online voice that mocks. The command is not "endure" (though it includes endurance) but "*repel* — with the *best* thing." This requires thought: what response, in this situation, is *aḥsan* — most likely to disarm, most likely to heal, most reflective of the character God wants in His servants? Sometimes it is silence; sometimes a gentle word; sometimes an unexpected kindness; sometimes the *salām* that 25:63 prescribes. It is never the reciprocal wound.

And the verse gives the two supports that make it possible. First, the knowledge that God will handle the reckoning (v. 95): the believer does not need to be the instrument of justice against those who wrong him personally. Second, the knowledge that God knows what they describe (v. 96b): the believer does not need to defend his reputation before people, because it is already known truly before God. With these two supports, the impossible command becomes the natural response of one who trusts his Lord — and the enemy, sometimes, *"becomes as though he was a devoted friend"* (41:34). Many of the Quraysh who slandered the Prophet ﷺ became his Companions. The command worked.

**Toward the Refuge**

The command to repel with what is better will be resisted from within. The next verse teaches the prayer that guards the heart against that resistance: refuge from the incitements of the devils.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:97

> **And say, “My Lord! I seek refuge in Thee from the incitements of the satans.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Prayer That Guards the Command**

Verse 96 commanded the Prophet ﷺ to repel evil with what is better. Verse 97 teaches the prayer that makes this possible: *wa qul rabbi aʿūdhu bika min hamazāti l-shayāṭīn* — "And say: 'My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils.'" The connection is direct. The command to answer injury with the best response will be opposed — not only by the injurer, but by an inner voice that urges retaliation, resentment, and pride. That voice is the *hamz* of the devils, and against it the Prophet ﷺ is taught not to argue but to *seek refuge*. The sequence of verses 95–98 is complete: God will bring the punishment (95); respond meanwhile with what is better (96); and when the whisper urges otherwise, flee to God (97–98).

**"And Say: My Lord, I Seek Refuge in You": Aʿūdhu Bika**

The verb *aʿūdhu* is from the root *ʿ-w-dh*, "to seek protection, to take shelter, to flee to." The *istiʿādhah* — the seeking of refuge — is one of the Qur'an's fundamental acts of devotion. The Qur'an's last two sūrahs are both built on it: *"Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak..."* (113:1); *"Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind... from the evil of the retreating whisperer, who whispers in the breasts of mankind"* (114:1–5). The believer is commanded to seek refuge before reciting the Qur'an (16:98), and the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge in God at the beginning of prayer, at night, in illness, and in every circumstance of danger.

The structure of *aʿūdhu bika* — "I seek refuge *in You*" — is that of one who runs to a fortress. The one seeking refuge acknowledges two things: that there is a danger he cannot face alone, and that there is a Protector who can shelter him from it. The prayer is therefore an act of humility (I cannot do this by myself) and of trust (You can). Both are the dispositions the sūrah has praised in the believers: the trembling of verse 60 and the reliance implicit in verse 88's "He protects, and none can protect against Him."

The address *rabbi*, "my Lord," continues the intimate vocative of verses 93–94. The Prophet ﷺ is taught to bring this need, too, to *his* Lord — the same Lord to whom he prayed not to be placed among the wrongdoers now guards him from the whispers that would make him like them.

**"From the Incitements of the Devils": Hamazāt al-Shayāṭīn**

The word *hamazāt* is the plural of *hamzah*, from the root *h-m-z*, which means to prod, to goad, to pierce, to push — as a rider goads a horse with his heel, or as one jabs with a pointed instrument. The letter *hamzah* in Arabic takes its name from this root because it is a sharp, pressing sound.
