A *hamzah* of the devil is thus a *prod*, a *goad*, a *jab* — a sudden inward pressure that pushes the heart toward evil. The Qur'an uses the related word *humazah* for the slanderer who jabs at others' reputations (104:1). The devils' *hamazāt* are their goadings: the impulse to anger, the flash of pride, the urge to retaliate, the whisper of despair, the pull toward sin.

The word is exact for the context of verse 96. When one is insulted and commanded to respond with what is better, the *hamzah* comes: a jab of anger, a prod of wounded pride, a push toward the cutting reply. It is not a reasoned argument; it is a *goad* — sudden, sharp, physical in its urgency. Against such a thing, argument is too slow. The only adequate response is the reflex of refuge: *aʿūdhu bika*. The Prophet ﷺ taught this specifically for anger: when two men were quarreling before him and one grew red with rage, he said: *"I know a phrase which, if he said it, what he feels would leave him: 'I seek refuge in God from Satan the accursed'"* (al-Bukhārī 3282; Muslim 2610). The phrase is the antidote to the *hamzah*.

The plural *al-shayāṭīn*, "the devils," indicates multiplicity — not one tempter but many, each with his goad. Iblīs has his hosts (26:95), and the Prophet ﷺ taught that every person has a devil assigned to him (Muslim 2814). The plural also encompasses the *"devils of mankind and jinn"* (6:112) — human tempters as well as unseen ones, since the *hamz* can come through a companion's urging as well as through the invisible whisper. The Quraysh in their nightly *samar* (v. 67) were, in this sense, devils to one another, each goading the others' contempt.

**Why Refuge and Not Combat**

The verse teaches the Prophet ﷺ to *seek refuge* from the devils' incitements, not to *fight* them. This is a deliberate spiritual method, and the scholars explained its wisdom. Satan and his hosts are unseen; one cannot see them to strike. They are persistent; one cannot exhaust them by argument. And they are subtle; one cannot always distinguish their goad from one's own thought. Against such an enemy, the effective response is not engagement but *flight to a stronger Protector*. The Qur'an states the principle: *"And if an evil suggestion comes to you from Satan, then seek refuge in God; indeed, He is Hearing and Knowing"* (7:200; 41:36). It does not say "refute Satan" or "resist him by your strength"; it says "seek refuge in God." The one who tries to defeat the devil by his own power has already granted the devil the terms of the fight; the one who runs to God has removed himself from the field.

**The Prophet's Need for Refuge**

Why does the Prophet ﷺ — protected by God, the best of creation — need to seek refuge from the devils' goads? The commentators gave the same answer as under verse 94: the prayer is taught (*qul*, "say"), and its teaching is for the community as much as for him. If the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to seek refuge, no believer may think himself beyond the need. And the Prophet ﷺ *did* seek refuge, constantly. He said: *"There is none of you but a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him."* They asked: *"Even you, O Messenger of God?"* He said: *"Even me, except that God helped me against him, so he submitted, and he commands me only to good"* (Muslim 2814). The protection was God's help, sought and given — not an exemption from the need for it.

The verse also implies that the devils' goading is most intense against those who are doing the most good. The Prophet ﷺ was engaged in the greatest work — calling a people to God under persecution — and the devils' *hamazāt* against him would have been correspondingly fierce: goads toward despair at the rejection, toward anger at the mockery, toward the desire to see the deniers destroyed rather than guided. The prayer of verse 97 is the shield of one under heavy fire.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 97 gives the believer a prayer to keep at the ready for the moment of the *hamzah*. Every believer knows the moment: the sudden surge of anger, the flash of envy, the jab of pride, the pull toward the forbidden, the whisper that says "you have done enough" or "it is no use" or "answer him as he deserves." The moment is fast, and a slow response is no response. The prayer *rabbi aʿūdhu bika min hamazāti l-shayāṭīn* — or its shorter form, *aʿūdhu bi-llāhi min al-shayṭān al-rajīm* — must be *trained* into the reflexes, so that it arises as quickly as the goad does. The Prophet ﷺ modeled this: the *istiʿādhah* was on his tongue at the beginning of every prayer, at the recitation of every sūrah, at every stirring of anger.

The verse also relieves the believer of a burden. He is not asked to defeat the devils by his own strength, to be so pure that the goad never comes, or to win every inner battle by willpower. He is asked to *run* — to the Lord who protects and against whom none can protect (v. 88). The running is itself the victory. The Prophet ﷺ described the devil as fleeing when the believer remembers God: *"When the call to prayer is made, Satan turns and flees, breaking wind so as not to hear it"* (al-Bukhārī 608; Muslim 389). The one who seeks refuge does not need to chase the enemy; the enemy leaves.

**Toward the Second Refuge**

The first refuge is from the devils' goads. The second, in the next verse, is from something more intimate: their *presence* — that they should be near him at all.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:98

> **And I seek refuge in Thee, my Lord, lest they should be present with me.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Second Refuge: From Presence Itself**

Verse 97 sought refuge from the devils' *hamazāt*, their goadings. Verse 98 seeks refuge from something prior to the goad — their *presence*: *wa aʿūdhu bika rabbi an yaḥḍurūn* — "And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me." The first prayer asked for protection from what the devils *do*; the second asks for protection from their being *near* at all. The difference is significant. A goad presupposes a goader within reach. The second prayer asks that the reach itself be denied — that the devils not attend the believer, not stand at his side, not be present in his affairs. Together the two verses ask for a complete protection: from the attack, and from the attacker's approach.

**"And I Seek Refuge in You, My Lord": The Repetition**

The verse repeats the verb *aʿūdhu bika*, "I seek refuge in You," and the address *rabbi*, "my Lord," which appeared in verse 97. The repetition is emphatic, and the commentators noted that it mirrors the doubled *rabbi* of verses 93–94: the Prophet ﷺ is taught to *press* his prayer — to seek refuge, and seek it again, naming his Lord each time. This is the manner of the earnest supplicant, and it teaches that refuge is not sought once and assumed forever. It is sought repeatedly, because the danger is repeated. The Prophet ﷺ sought refuge at every prayer, every recitation, every sleep, and every waking; the doubled *aʿūdhu* of verses 97–98 is the pattern.

The placement of *rabbi* *after* *aʿūdhu bika* in verse 98, whereas it came before in verse 97 (*rabbi aʿūdhu bika*), is a small variation with a rhetorical effect: the name of the Lord is placed at the center of the second prayer, surrounded by the seeking of refuge on one side and the danger on the other. The supplicant holds onto the name in the middle of his plea.

**"Lest They Be Present With Me": An Yaḥḍurūn**

The verb *yaḥḍurūn* is from the root *ḥ-ḍ-r*, "to be present, to attend, to come near." *Ḥuḍūr* is presence; a *ḥāḍir* is one who is present; the opposite is *ghāʾib*, absent. The prayer asks that the devils *not be present* — not attend the believer in his affairs. The commentators drew out several contexts in which the devils' *presence* is especially feared and from which the prayer seeks protection.

In *worship*: the devil attends the prayer to distract, as the Prophet ﷺ described — *"When one of you stands to pray, Satan comes to him and confuses him until he does not know how many [units] he has prayed"* (al-Bukhārī 1231; Muslim 389). And in the recitation of the Qur'an: the *istiʿādhah* is commanded before recitation precisely so that the devil is not present to interfere (16:98). The prayer of verse 98 asks that worship be free of the attending whisperer.

In *daily affairs*: the Prophet ﷺ taught that the devil is present at meals not begun with God's name, in houses not entered with God's name, and in every occasion where God is forgotten. He said: *"When a man enters his house and mentions God at his entering and at his eating, Satan says [to his companions], 'No lodging for you and no supper.' But if he enters without mentioning God, Satan says, 'You have found lodging'; and if he eats without mentioning God, he says, 'You have found lodging and supper'"* (Muslim 2018). The prayer of verse 98 asks that the devils find no lodging.

At *death*: the commentators, following early authorities, specifically noted that the devils' presence is most dangerous at the moment of death, when they seek to unsettle the dying person's faith. The prayer *an yaḥḍurūn* thus includes the plea that they not attend one's last moments. The Prophet ﷺ taught the believers to ask for a good end and to say *"lā ilāha illā llāh"* at death, and he prayed: *"O God, I seek refuge in You from Satan's confounding me at death"* (Abū Dāwūd 1552; al-Nasāʾī 5531). This meaning connects verse 98 directly to the next verse, which describes the moment of death for the denier: *"until, when death comes to one of them, he says, 'My Lord, send me back'"* (v. 99). The believer prays that the devils not be present at his death; the denier arrives at death with only regret.

**The Logic of the Two Refuges**

The two prayers of verses 97 and 98 form an ascending pair. To seek refuge from the devils' goads (97) is to ask for protection *in* the encounter: when they jab, let me not be moved. To seek refuge from their presence (98) is to ask for protection *from* the encounter: let them not be near enough to jab. The second is the more complete protection, and it is asked for second because it is the greater request. One may be attacked and stand firm; better still is not to be attacked. The Prophet ﷺ taught a version of this in the daily *dhikr*: the believer who recites the Verse of the Throne at night *"will have a guardian from God, and no devil will come near him until morning"* (al-Bukhārī 2311). That is *an lā yaḥḍurūn* — not nearness resisted, but nearness prevented.

**Why the Prophet Is Taught This Prayer Here**

The context makes the prayer's placement exact. The Prophet ﷺ has been commanded to repel evil with what is better (v. 96) — a command that requires constant inner vigilance against the impulses the devils goad. He has been told that God knows what the deniers say about him (v. 96) — a consolation that the devils would seek to undermine by whispering resentment. And he is about to hear the sūrah's description of death and the Hereafter (vv. 99–118) — matters at which the devils' presence is most to be feared. The prayer of verses 97–98 is the Prophet's armor for all three: the interval of patient dealing with enemies, the temptation to nurse grievance, and the approach of the end. The believer who recites the sūrah is armed in the same way.

**The Presence of God as the Alternative**

The prayer against the devils' presence implies a prayer for another presence. The sūrah has described God as the One who *"holds the dominion of everything"* (v. 88), who is *"Knower of the unseen and the seen"* (v. 92), who *"was never heedless of creation"* (v. 17). God is always present; the question is whether the believer is *aware* of His presence, so that there is no room for the other. The Prophet ﷺ defined *iḥsān* as *"to worship God as though you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you"* (al-Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8). The person who lives in this awareness has, by that very awareness, denied the devils their presence — not by fighting them but by filling the space with God's remembrance. The prayer of verse 98 is the request that this filling be complete.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 98 asks the believer to think about *who is present* in his life — in his worship, his meals, his home, his work, his conversations, his solitude, and his dying. The devils seek presence wherever God is forgotten; they are excluded wherever He is remembered. The prayer *aʿūdhu bika rabbi an yaḥḍurūn* is the believer's request for a life in which the whisperer finds no lodging — and the practices that answer the prayer are the ones the Prophet ﷺ taught: God's name at entering and eating, the *istiʿādhah* before recitation and prayer, the Verse of the Throne at night, and the remembrance of God in every idle moment that would otherwise be the devil's opening. The believer who keeps these has made verse 98 a habit rather than a hope.

The verse's connection to death gives it a final urgency. The believer prays not only that the devils be absent from his living but from his dying — that at the moment when the denier of verse 99 will cry "send me back," he himself will say instead *"lā ilāha illā llāh"*, with no whisperer near to disturb it. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever's last words are 'there is no god but God' enters Paradise"* (Abū Dāwūd 3116). The prayer of verse 98 is a prayer for that ending.

**Toward the Moment of Death**

The Prophet ﷺ has been armed with two prayers of refuge. The sūrah now turns to the moment against which the second refuge was sought — the arrival of death for one who did not seek it.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:99

> **Till, when death comes to one of them, he says, “My Lord! Return me,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Moment Everything Has Been Pointing Toward**

The sūrah has argued, warned, and prayed. Now it arrives at the moment against which every warning was issued: *ḥattā idhā jāʾa aḥadahumu l-mawtu qāla rabbi rjiʿūn* — "Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, 'My Lord, send me back.'" The verse begins with the fourth *ḥattā idhā* of the sūrah's second half (after vv. 64, 77, and the *ḥattā ḥīn* of v. 54), and each has marked the end of a reprieve. This one marks the end of the reprieve that every human being has: life itself. The denier who recoiled from the recitation (v. 66), raved at night (v. 67), and called resurrection a legend (v. 83) arrives at death — and his first word is *rabbi*, "my Lord." The verse records the moment when denial ends, not because the denier has been persuaded, but because death has arrived.

**"Until, When Death Comes to One of Them"**

The phrase *jāʾa aḥadahumu l-mawt* — "death comes to one of them" — presents death as an *arrival*. It *comes*; the person does not go to it. The Qur'an consistently describes death this way: *"Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you should be in towers of lofty construction"* (4:78); *"Say, 'Indeed, the death from which you flee — indeed, it will meet you'"* (62:8). The denier who spent his life fleeing the thought of death — filling his nights with *samar* (v. 67) and his days with "other deeds" (v. 63) — is met by it. The word *aḥadahum*, "one of them," individualizes the scene: not "them" collectively but *one* — each denier, alone, at his own moment. Death is the most solitary of arrivals, and the verse frames it so.

The sūrah stated the fact of death in verse 15 with the same directness: *"Then indeed, after that, you will surely die."* Verse 99 shows the fact arriving for one who did not believe verse 16 — *"then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be raised."* He is about to discover that verse 16 is also true.

**"He Says: My Lord": The Denier's First Confession**

The denier's first word at death is *rabbi* — "my Lord." This is the word the sūrah has placed on the lips of the messengers (vv. 26, 39, 93, 94, 97, 98) and the believers (v. 109). It is the intimate address of one who acknowledges his Lord. The denier never said it in life — he said "God" only when forced to admit ownership of the earth (v. 85), and he never said "*my* Lord" as one who belonged to Him. Now, at death, he says it. The confession is genuine in the sense that it is not feigned; the veil has lifted and he sees. But it is too late to be the confession of faith, because faith is meaningful only while the unseen is unseen. The Qur'an states the rule: *"But their faith did not benefit them once they saw Our punishment"* (40:85). The denier's *rabbi* at death is not repentance; it is recognition.

**"Send Me Back": Irjiʿūn**

The petition is *irjiʿūn* — "send me back, return me." The verb is from the root *r-j-ʿ*, "to return" — the same root as the believers' awareness in verse 60 that *"they will return (rājiʿūn) to their Lord."* The believers lived knowing they would return; the denier, at the moment of return, begs to be sent back. The word is the same; the direction is opposite.

The commentators noted a grammatical peculiarity that the source records: *irjiʿūn* is a *plural* imperative — "send me back, [you all]" — though it is addressed to *rabbi*, "my Lord," in the singular. Several explanations were offered. Al-Zamakhsharī and others suggested that the plural is a plural of exaltation (*taʿẓīm*), addressing God with the majestic plural as God addresses Himself with "We." Others suggested that the dying man first addresses God (*rabbi*) and then turns his plea to the angels who have come to take his soul (*irjiʿūn*, "return me!"), as one might cry out to whoever is near. Others suggested that the plural expresses the intensity of the plea — as though the dying man were repeating "return me, return me, return me." Each explanation captures something true about the scene: it is a moment of desperate, disordered pleading, in which the dying man cries to God and to whoever is present, again and again, to undo what cannot be undone.

The Qur'an records this same plea at several points, and its consistency shows that it is the universal cry of the unprepared: *"If you could but see when the criminals are hanging their heads before their Lord, [saying], 'Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us; we will work righteousness'"* (32:12); *"And spend from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, 'My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be among the righteous'"* (63:10); *"And if you could but see when they are made to stand before the Fire and will say, 'Oh, would that we could be returned, and not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers'"* (6:27). The plea is always for *return* and always for the *deeds* that were neglected — as verse 100 will make explicit.

**Why the Plea Comes at Death**

Why does the denier, who spent his life certain that death was the end, plead at death to be returned? Because at death the *ghamrah* (vv. 54, 63) is dispelled. The water that covered his heart drains away, and he sees what the believers saw all along: that there is a Lord, that there is a return, that his deeds were "other than" what mattered (v. 63), that the promise he called a legend (v. 83) was true. The Qur'an describes this unveiling: *"You were certainly in heedlessness of this, and We have removed from you your cover, so your sight, this Day, is sharp"* (50:22). The sharpness of sight at death produces the plea — and the plea is refused, because sight given by death is not the faith that was asked for in life.

There is a painful irony that the sūrah's structure exposes. The denier said in verse 36: *"Far, far is that which you are promised!"* — meaning resurrection was impossibly distant. Now he pleads to be sent *back* — to a life that is, for him, impossibly distant in the other direction. He wanted the return to God to be far; it has come. He wants the return to life to be near; it is gone. The word *rajʿ*, return, has reversed on him.

**The Believer's Contrast**

The believers of the sūrah do not plead at death to be sent back, because they lived as those who would return (v. 60) and did what they would have wished to do (v. 61). The Prophet ﷺ, at his death, said: *"O God, [with] the Highest Companion"* (al-Bukhārī 4437; Muslim 2444) — he asked to go forward, not back. Bilāl, dying, said: *"Tomorrow I meet the beloved ones — Muḥammad and his companions"* — and when his wife cried "what grief!", he said "what joy!" The difference between *irjiʿūn* and "the Highest Companion" is the difference between a life lived in denial and one lived in awareness of return.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 99 asks the believer to imagine his own death — not morbidly, but with the purpose the sūrah intends: to make sure that his last word is not *irjiʿūn*. The test is simple. If death came now, what would he wish to have done? Whatever the answer, that is what the verse commands him to do today. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Remember often the destroyer of pleasures — death"* (al-Tirmidhī 2307; al-Nasāʾī 1824), and the purpose of the remembrance is exactly this: to bring forward, into the time of action, the clarity that the denier receives only when action is no longer possible. The believer who lives with verse 99 in view arrives at death without its plea, because he has already done what the plea would ask for.

The verse also warns against the specific delay that produces the plea. The denier did not plan to die a denier; he planned to sort things out "later." The sūrah has been dismantling "later" since verse 43 — no community can delay its term — and verse 99 shows "later" arriving as death. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Take advantage of five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your illness, your wealth before your poverty, your free time before your busyness, and your life before your death"* (al-Ḥākim; al-Bayhaqī). The fifth is verse 99's subject.

**Toward the Refusal and the Barrier**

The denier pleads to be returned so that he might do righteousness. The next verse gives God's response — a single word — and describes what stands between the dead and any return.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:100

> **that haply I may work righteousness with regard to that which I left.” Nay, indeed these are words that he speaks. And behind them is a barrier till the Day they are resurrected.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Plea Completed and Refused**

Verse 99 recorded the dying denier's cry: "My Lord, send me back." Verse 100 completes the plea and answers it: *laʿallī aʿmalu ṣāliḥan fīmā taraktu kallā innahā kalimatun huwa qāʾiluhā wa min warāʾihim barzakhun ilā yawmi yubʿathūn* — "...that I might do righteousness in what I left behind. No! It is only a word he is saying. And behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected." The verse has three parts: the stated purpose of the plea (righteous deeds), God's refusal (*kallā*), and the reason the refusal is final (the *barzakh*). It is one of the Qur'an's most important verses on what lies between death and resurrection, and it closes the account of the denier's life with the one word he never wanted to hear.

**"That I Might Do Righteousness in What I Left Behind"**

The dying man gives his reason for wanting to return: *laʿallī aʿmalu ṣāliḥan fīmā taraktu* — "that perhaps I might do righteous work in what I left behind." The phrase *aʿmalu ṣāliḥan*, "do righteous work," is the exact phrase God commanded the messengers in verse 51: *"eat of the good things and do righteousness (iʿmalū ṣāliḥan)."* The denier now asks for the chance to do what he was commanded to do all along. The phrase *fīmā taraktu*, "in what I left behind," has been read two ways. It may mean "in the world I left" — let me return to life and act rightly there. Or it may mean "with the wealth I left" — let me return and spend what I hoarded, give what I withheld. The second reading connects to 63:10, where the dying man says: *"if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity."* Both readings converge: he wants to return to the *field* (v. 79) and to the *provision* (v. 55) that he misused, and use them rightly.

The plea reveals what the dying man now knows. He knows that righteous deeds were what mattered — the very deeds he was too busy for (v. 63: "other deeds"). He knows that what he "left behind" was an opportunity, not merely an estate. He knows that the standard by which he will be judged is the one the sūrah set in verses 1–11 and 57–61. His plea is, in effect, an acknowledgment that the sūrah was right. But the acknowledgment has come at the one moment when it can no longer be acted upon.

**"No!": Kallā**

God's answer is one word: *kallā* — "No! By no means! Never!" The particle *kallā* is the Qur'an's strongest rejection; it does not merely deny but rebukes, as one might say "Certainly not!" to an impossible or improper request. It appears frequently in the Makkan sūrahs, often at exactly this kind of moment — when a false hope or a false claim is cut off: *"No! When the soul reaches the collarbones... "* (75:26); *"No! Indeed, man transgresses because he sees himself self-sufficient"* (96:6–7). Here it cuts off the plea to return. There will be no return. The sūrah has been saying this since verse 43 — *"no community can hasten its term, nor delay it"* — and *kallā* is that principle applied to the individual at the moment he most wishes it were otherwise.

**"It Is Only a Word He Is Saying"**

God then characterizes the plea: *innahā kalimatun huwa qāʾiluhā* — "it is only a word that he is the sayer of." The phrase is dismissive and diagnostic at once. The plea is *a word* — speech, not intention; sound, not resolve. The construction *huwa qāʾiluhā*, "he is its sayer," emphasizes that the saying is all there is: the man says it because the situation extracts it from him, not because a transformed will lies behind it. The commentators explained the divine judgment implied here: God knows that if the dying man *were* returned, he would return to what he was. The Qur'an states this explicitly of the people of Hell who make the same plea: *"But if they were returned, they would return to that which they were forbidden; and indeed, they are liars"* (6:28). The plea at death is the plea of a person who wants to escape the consequence, not one who has come to love the good. The Knower of the unseen and the seen (v. 92) sees the difference, and *kallā* is His verdict.

This does not mean the dying man is insincere in the ordinary sense — he means what he says at the moment he says it. It means that a resolution formed under the compulsion of visible punishment is not the free turning that constitutes faith and repentance. Faith is *belief in the unseen* (2:3); once the unseen is seen, what remains is not faith but acknowledgment, and acknowledgment is not what was asked for. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"God accepts the repentance of the servant so long as the death-rattle has not reached his throat"* (al-Tirmidhī 3537; Ibn Mājah 4253) — the door is open until the very last moment, and the man of verse 100 is past it.

**"And Behind Them Is a Barrier": Barzakh**

The verse's final clause explains why the return is impossible: *wa min warāʾihim barzakhun ilā yawmi yubʿathūn* — "and behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected." The word *barzakh* means a barrier, a partition, an isthmus — something that separates two things and prevents their mixing. The Qur'an uses it for the barrier between the two seas: *"between them is a barrier (barzakh) which they do not transgress"* (55:20); *"and placed between them a barrier (barzakh) and a prohibiting partition"* (25:53). Here it names the barrier between the dead and the living — the state between death and resurrection that Islamic theology calls, from this verse, *al-barzakh*.

The word *warāʾ* usually means "behind" but can also mean "before, in front of"; the commentators read it here as "behind them" in the sense of "beyond them, on the far side of them from the living" — the barrier stands between the dead and the world they have left. The barrier is *ilā yawmi yubʿathūn*, "until the Day they are resurrected" — it is not permanent but lasts for the whole interval of the grave, however long. During that interval, there is no crossing back. The dead cannot return to the world; the plea of verse 99 meets the *barzakh* and stops.

**The Barzakh in Islamic Belief**

Verse 100 is the foundational text for the doctrine of the intermediate state, which the ḥadīth literature develops. The *barzakh* is not unconsciousness or nonexistence; it is a state of *experience* — of reward or punishment anticipating the final Judgment. The Prophet ﷺ described the questioning in the grave by the two angels (al-Bukhārī 1338; Muslim 2870), the widening of the grave for the believer and its narrowing for the denier, the soul of the believer shown its place in Paradise and the soul of the denier shown its place in the Fire *"morning and evening"* (al-Bukhārī 1379; Muslim 2866). He said: *"The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire"* (al-Tirmidhī 2460). He sought refuge from the punishment of the grave in every prayer and taught his Companions to do so (al-Bukhārī 1377; Muslim 588). The *barzakh* of verse 100 is the setting for all of this. The denier who pleaded "send me back" enters it — and the sūrah, having named it, moves directly to the Day on which it ends.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Earlier Word**

The second generation after Noah mocked resurrection with *hayhāt hayhāt* — "far, far is what you are promised" (v. 36). The commentary on that verse noted that the deniers would learn the true meaning of distance. Verse 100 supplies it: what is *far* is not the resurrection — that is coming, *ilā yawmi yubʿathūn* — but the return to life, which lies on the other side of a *barzakh* no one crosses. The deniers measured distance wrongly. They thought the Hereafter was far and this life was securely near; in fact this life ends at a barrier, and the Hereafter waits on the far side of it with certainty.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 100 is, for the believer, the sūrah's most urgent verse on the use of time. It tells him three things. First, that the plea to "do righteousness in what I left behind" will be made by everyone who did not do it — and will be refused. The only time to do righteousness is *before* the plea. Second, that the refusal is not cruelty but consistency: God has told us, through every messenger and in this very verse, that the door closes at death; to hold Him to His word is justice, and He warned us of it in advance so that we would not need to make the plea. Third, that the *barzakh* is real and immediate: the believer will enter it, and its condition for him depends on what he brings. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"When a person dies, his deeds come to an end except three: ongoing charity, knowledge from which benefit is derived, and a righteous child who prays for him"* (Muslim 1631). These are the deeds that continue to work "in what he left behind" — the righteous person's answer to the dying denier's wish.

The believer's response to verse 100 is not fear alone but *action*: to do now what the dying will wish they had done; to leave behind what continues to earn; and to arrive at the *barzakh* not with *irjiʿūn* on his lips but with the readiness of one who has already done what he was sent to do. Then the barrier is not a wall against return but a threshold toward the Day the verse names last: *yawmi yubʿathūn*, the Day they are raised.

**Toward the Trumpet**

The barrier stands until the Day of Resurrection. The next verse describes that Day's beginning — the trumpet — and the dissolution of every human bond.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:101

> **And when the trumpet is blown, there shall be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they question one another.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Day the Barrier Ends**

Verse 100 said the barrier stands *"until the Day they are resurrected."* Verse 101 describes that Day's arrival: *fa-idhā nufikha fī l-ṣūri fa-lā ansāba baynahum yawmaʾidhin wa lā yatasāʾalūn* — "Then when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that Day, nor will they ask about one another." The *barzakh* ends with a sound, and the sound inaugurates a world in which the bonds that structured this life — lineage, family, tribe, the ties by which the Quraysh defined themselves — no longer function. The verse names two things that will be absent: kinship (*ansāb*) and mutual inquiry (*tasāʾul*). Both were central to the Makkan world; both dissolve at the blast.

**"When the Trumpet Is Blown": Al-Ṣūr**

The *ṣūr* is the Trumpet whose blowing signals the end of the world and the resurrection of the dead. The Qur'an mentions it ten times: *"And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall dead except whom God wills. Then it will be blown again, and at once they will be standing, looking on"* (39:68); *"And the Trumpet will be blown, and at once from the graves to their Lord they will hasten"* (36:51). The Prophet ﷺ described the angel Isrāfīl as having already placed the Trumpet to his lips, waiting for the command (al-Tirmidhī 2431; graded ḥasan), and when the Companions asked what they should say in the face of this, he taught them: *"Say: God is sufficient for us and the best Disposer of affairs; upon God we rely."*

The passive *nufikha*, "it is blown," leaves the blower unnamed and focuses on the event. The commentators identified this verse's blast with the *second* blowing — the blowing of resurrection — since the verse goes on to describe the resurrected in their relations to one another. The dead who were behind the *barzakh* (v. 100) are, at this blast, raised and gathered — the *ḥashr* of verse 79, *"and to Him you will be gathered."*

**"There Will Be No Kinship Among Them That Day": Lā Ansāb**

The first thing the verse says about the resurrected is that *lā ansāba baynahum* — "there is no kinship among them." The word *ansāb* is the plural of *nasab*, lineage, genealogy, blood relationship — the tie that, in Arabian society, defined a person's identity, protection, honor, and obligations. The Quraysh were obsessed with *nasab*; their poets recited genealogies; their tribes fought and allied by lineage; and their arrogance (v. 67) was in large part the arrogance of noble descent. The verse announces that on the Day of Resurrection, none of this exists. There is no *nasab* — not because families are forgotten, but because kinship *confers nothing*: no protection, no intercession, no shared fate. Each person stands alone with his deeds.

The Qur'an describes the dissolution vividly: *"On the Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his wife and his children — for every man, that Day, will be a matter adequate for him"* (80:34–37); *"O mankind, fear your Lord and fear a Day when no father will avail his son, nor will a son avail his father at all"* (31:33). The Prophet ﷺ applied this to his own family with unmistakable directness: *"O Fāṭimah, daughter of Muḥammad, ask me whatever you wish of my wealth; I cannot avail you anything against God"* (al-Bukhārī 2753; Muslim 206) — the very ḥadīth cited under verse 27, where Noah's son was excluded from the Ark despite his lineage. Verse 101 generalizes what Noah's story particularized: on that Day, no one's *nasab* will save him.

The commentators drew a fine distinction: the verse does not say that people will not *recognize* their relatives — other verses show that they will (80:34–36 presupposes recognition, since one flees from those one knows). It says there will be no *ansāb baynahum* — no *operative* kinship, no bond that functions. The relationship is remembered but powerless. This is the more painful state: to see one's father, brother, or child, and to be unable to help or be helped.

**"Nor Will They Ask About One Another": Lā Yatasāʾalūn**

The second absence is *tasāʾul*, mutual questioning — the asking after one another that is the ordinary business of a community. In this world, people ask: How is your father? What happened to your brother? Where is so-and-so? On that Day, the verse says, *lā yatasāʾalūn* — they do not ask. The commentators explained this in two ways. First, because the terror of the Day absorbs every attention, so that no one has the capacity to inquire about anyone else — *"the matter is too severe for them to look at one another,"* as the Prophet ﷺ said of the gathering (al-Bukhārī 6527; Muslim 2859). Second, because there is nothing to ask *for*: one asks after a relative in order to help or be helped, and on that Day no help passes between people, so the asking has no purpose.

The Qur'an elsewhere describes people *questioning* one another on the Day of Judgment — *"and they will approach one another, questioning"* (37:27; 52:25) — and the scholars reconciled the passages by their timing: at the first terror of the blast and the gathering, no one asks (23:101); later, in the stages of the reckoning and after entering their abodes, they turn to one another with questions and reproaches (37:27–28). The two are different moments of a long Day. Verse 101 describes the first.

**The Dissolution as Argument**

Why does the sūrah name the dissolution of kinship at this point? Because kinship was one of the deniers' chief supports. The Quraysh trusted in their lineage; they were proud of their descent from Ishmael and Abraham; they expected their tribal solidarity to protect them as it did in this world; and they assumed — as verse 55 showed — that their *children* (*banīn*) were a sign of favor. Verse 101 removes all of it. On the Day when it matters most, the *banīn* are strangers, the tribe is dissolved, the lineage is void. The only thing that remains is what the sūrah has said remains: deeds, weighed on scales (vv. 102–103). The dissolution of *nasab* is the preparation for the weighing: everything that is not one's own deed is stripped away first.

There is also a lesson for the believers, who might themselves be tempted to rely on lineage — descent from the Companions, from scholars, from the Prophet's own house. The Prophet ﷺ closed this door explicitly: *"Whoever is slowed by his deeds will not be hastened by his lineage"* (Muslim 2699). Verse 101 is the principle behind the saying.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 101 asks the believer to examine what he is relying on. If any part of his confidence before God rests on family — righteous parents, a pious spouse, a scholarly ancestor, a community of the faithful — the verse warns that on the Day it will not be *there* in any operative sense. This is not to devalue family: the Qur'an commands its care, and righteous kin are a blessing that may aid one in this life and, by God's grace, intercede in the next (as the ḥadīth of the believer's children and the *ṣāliḥ* descendants who pray for him suggest — Muslim 1631). It is to locate one's *reliance* correctly: on one's own faith and deeds, before the Lord who will weigh them. The believer's family is a trust and a help; it is not a shield.

The verse also gives urgency to relationships *now*. If the asking after one another ceases on that Day, the time to ask — to visit, to reconcile, to help, to guide toward faith — is this life. The Prophet ﷺ made the ties of kinship (*ṣilat al-raḥim*) a condition of faith: *"Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him maintain the ties of kinship"* (al-Bukhārī 6138; Muslim 47). The paradox is exact: kinship will be void on the Day, and precisely for that reason it must be honored before it.

**Toward the Scales**

Every bond dissolved, each person stands alone. The next two verses describe what happens then: the scales are set — and they come down heavy or light.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:102

> **As for those whose scales are heavy, it is they who shall prosper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Weighing**

Kinship has dissolved and each person stands alone (v. 101). Now the verdict: *fa-man thaqulat mawāzīnuhu fa-ulāʾika humu l-mufliḥūn* — "Then those whose scales are heavy — it is they who are the successful." The verse and its twin (v. 103) describe the outcome of the reckoning in the image of a balance: scales that come down heavy or light. Verse 102 is the heavy side. The word that closes it — *al-mufliḥūn*, "the successful" — is the word the sūrah opened with: *qad aflaḥa l-muʾminūn*, "truly the believers have succeeded" (v. 1). The sūrah's first word and this verse's last are the same root. What was promised at the beginning is delivered here, at the scales.

**"Those Whose Scales Are Heavy": Thaqulat Mawāzīnuhu**

The word *mawāzīn* is the plural of *mīzān* (balance, scale) or of *mawzūn* (thing weighed); the Qur'an uses it for the weighing of deeds on the Day of Judgment: *"And the weighing that Day is the truth; so those whose scales are heavy — it is they who are the successful"* (7:8); *"And We place the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be treated unjustly at all; and if there is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth"* (21:47); *"As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life; but as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be an abyss"* (101:6–9). The verb *thaqulat*, "are heavy," is from the root *th-q-l*, weight, heaviness — the root of *mithqāl*, the weight of an atom (99:7).

The scholars of the *sunnah* affirmed that the *mīzān* is real — an actual balance, whose nature is known to God, on which deeds (or the records of deeds, or the doers themselves, according to different reports) are weighed. The Prophet ﷺ described its scale: *"The Balance will be set up on the Day of Resurrection, and if the heavens and the earth were weighed in it, they would fit"* (al-Ḥākim; graded ṣaḥīḥ). And he described what weighs heavily in it: *"Two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy on the Balance, beloved to the Most Merciful: Glory be to God and with His praise; Glory be to God the Tremendous"* (al-Bukhārī 6406; Muslim 2694); *"Nothing is heavier on the Balance of the believer on the Day of Resurrection than good character"* (al-Tirmidhī 2002; Abū Dāwūd 4799); and *"Purity is half of faith, and 'praise be to God' fills the Balance"* (Muslim 223).

The plural *mawāzīn* — "scales" rather than "scale" — has been explained as a plural of magnitude (a single great balance), or as referring to the many things weighed, or as indicating that each person's deeds are weighed in their variety. The source notes the connection to 7:8–9 and 101:6–9, where the same plural is used.

**What Makes the Scales Heavy**

The verse does not specify what is weighed, and the sūrah's context supplies the answer: the deeds it has been describing. The seven qualities of verses 1–9 — humble prayer, turning from vain talk, zakāh, chastity, keeping trusts and covenants, guarding the prayers. The four inner states of verses 57–60 — awe of God, faith in His signs, refusal of shirk, giving with a trembling heart. The racing toward good of verse 61. These are what go on the heavy side. And the sūrah has also taught what *does not* weigh: wealth and children (v. 55), which the deniers thought were their credit but which are not deeds at all; the "other deeds" of verse 63, which are activity without direction; lineage (v. 101), which is not one's own doing. The scales weigh what a person *did*, with the intention he did it with — nothing else.

The ḥadīth literature adds a dimension that the sūrah's emphasis on the *heart* anticipates: what weighs is not the *size* of the deed but its *sincerity*. The Prophet ﷺ told of a man who will be brought on the Day with ninety-nine scrolls of sins, each stretching as far as the eye can see, and one card bearing the testimony *lā ilāha illā llāh* — and the card will outweigh the scrolls (al-Tirmidhī 2639; Ibn Mājah 4300; graded ṣaḥīḥ). A single sincere affirmation of faith outweighs a life of sin, because faith is the weightiest thing a human being can carry. This is why verse 60's "trembling hearts" precede verse 61's "hastening to good": the trembling is what gives the good its weight.

**"It Is They Who Are the Successful": Al-Mufliḥūn**

The verse's second half delivers the verdict in the sūrah's own vocabulary: *fa-ulāʾika humu l-mufliḥūn* — "those — they are the successful." The emphatic construction — demonstrative *ulāʾika*, pronoun *humu*, definite *al-mufliḥūn* — restricts success to them: *they*, and no others, are the successful. The word *falāḥ*, as explained under verse 1, is from the root *f-l-ḥ*, which means to cleave the earth (a *fallāḥ* is a farmer) and by extension to break through to what one seeks — to succeed after effort. The successful are those who broke through: through the *ghamrah* to clarity, through the mockery to patience, through death and the *barzakh* to the heavy scale.

The sūrah's structure comes full circle here. It opened: *qad aflaḥa l-muʾminūn* — the believers have succeeded (v. 1). It described what they do (vv. 2–9) and promised what they inherit (vv. 10–11). It then told the long story of those who did not do these things and would not inherit. Now, at the scales, it pronounces the verdict the opening announced: the heavy-scaled are *al-mufliḥūn*. And verse 117 will close the frame on the other side: *lā yufliḥu l-kāfirūn* — the disbelievers do not succeed. The word *falāḥ* brackets the entire sūrah, appearing at its first verse, at the scales, and at its penultimate verse. The whole sūrah is an account of what success is and who attains it.

**Success Defined Against the Deniers' Definition**

Verses 55–56 exposed the deniers' definition of success — wealth and children hastened to them as good things. Verse 102 gives God's definition: heavy scales. The two definitions are not merely different; they are inverted. What the deniers counted as success (accumulation, receiving) does not appear on the scales at all; what they neglected (giving, trembling, hastening) is the only thing that does. The Qur'an states the inversion elsewhere: *"And it is not your wealth or your children that bring you nearer to Us in position, but it is one who believes and does righteousness — for them there will be the double reward for what they did"* (34:37). The scales of verse 102 are the instrument by which the inversion is made final.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 102 asks the believer a question he can answer only approximately but must keep asking: *what is on my scale?* Not what is in his account, his résumé, his family, or his reputation — none of these will be weighed — but what he has *done*, with what *heart*. The sūrah's two portraits (vv. 1–9, 57–61) are the inventory. The believer who reviews them honestly will find some things heavy and some things missing, and the review is itself a mercy, because it is conducted while there is still time to add weight.

The verse also relieves an anxiety the believer might feel about the *size* of his deeds. The scales weigh sincerity, not scale. The widow's two coins, the traveler's *tasbīḥ*, the private tear of *khashyah*, the small charity given with a trembling heart — these are heavy. The Prophet ﷺ taught that *"a good word is charity,"* that *"removing something harmful from the road is charity,"* that *"your smile in your brother's face is charity"* (al-Bukhārī 2989; Muslim 1009; al-Tirmidhī 1956). Each goes on the scale. The believer who cannot do great things can do many small things sincerely, and the balance is generous: *"Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times the like thereof"* (6:160). The heavy scale is within reach of anyone who hastens toward it (v. 61).

**Toward the Light Scale**

The heavy side has been named and its outcome declared. The next verse names the other side — and its outcome is the word the sūrah used of the destroyed generations: loss.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:103

> **And as for those whose scales are light, it is they who shall lose their souls, abiding in Hell.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Other Side of the Balance**

Verse 102 gave the outcome for the heavy scale: success. Verse 103 gives the outcome for the light: *wa man khaffat mawāzīnuhu fa-ulāʾika lladhīna khasirū anfusahum fī jahannama khālidūn* — "And those whose scales are light — it is they who have lost their souls, abiding in Hell." The two verses are exact counterparts in structure: *fa-man thaqulat ... fa-ulāʾika humu l-mufliḥūn* / *wa man khaffat ... fa-ulāʾika lladhīna khasirū anfusahum*. The symmetry is deliberate. There is one balance and two outcomes; there is no third category; and the outcomes are stated in the sūrah's own recurring vocabulary — success (v. 1) against loss (v. 34).

**"Those Whose Scales Are Light": Khaffat Mawāzīnuhu**

The verb *khaffat*, "are light," is from the root *kh-f-f*, lightness — the opposite of *thaqulat*. Light scales are scales on which little of weight has been placed: few deeds, or deeds that had no weight because they lacked faith and sincerity. The Qur'an describes the deeds of the deniers as weightless in precisely this sense: *"Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in the meeting with Him, so their deeds have become worthless; and We will not assign to them on the Day of Resurrection any weight (waznan)"* (18:105). The deniers of this sūrah *"disbelieved in the meeting of the Hereafter"* (v. 33) — the same disbelief 18:105 names — and so their deeds, however many (v. 63: busy with "other deeds"), have no weight. The scale comes up light not because it is empty of activity but because it is empty of anything that counts.

The image explains something about the deniers' self-assessment. They thought they had much — wealth, children, lineage, deeds of generosity and tribal honor. They imagined a heavy scale. But the scale weighs by a standard they did not use: faith and sincerity. A person who has never learned what the scale weighs can arrive at it confident and find it light. This is the surprise the Qur'an describes: *"And there will appear to them from God that which they had not taken into account"* (39:47); *"their deeds are like a mirage in a lowland which a thirsty one thinks is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it is nothing"* (24:39).

**"It Is They Who Have Lost Their Souls": Khasirū Anfusahum**

The verdict for the light scale is not merely "they fail" but *khasirū anfusahum* — "they have lost their *selves*." The verb *khasira* is from the root *kh-s-r*, loss — the commercial term for a trade that returns less than was invested. The sūrah used it in verse 34 when the notables warned their people that following the messenger would make them *"losers"*; the commentary on that verse noted that the Qur'an's own definition of loss is the opposite. Verse 103 gives that definition. The greatest loss is not of wealth or status but of *the self* — the person's own soul, the one thing he was given to invest and could not replace. The Qur'an states this as the supreme loss: *"Say, 'Indeed, the losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss'"* (39:15); *"Say, 'Shall we inform you of the greatest losers as to deeds? Those whose effort is lost in worldly life, while they think that they are doing well in work'"* (18:103–104).

The phrase "lost their souls" is precise about the mechanism of the loss. The deniers did not lose their souls to an external thief; they *spent* them — invested them in *laghw* (v. 3), in *samar* (v. 67), in "other deeds" (v. 63), in the accumulation of what would not be weighed — and the investment returned nothing. The self that could have been placed on the heavy side was traded for what has no weight. This is the *khusrān* that Sūrah al-ʿAṣr names as the default condition of humankind: *"Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds and advise one another to truth and advise one another to patience"* (103:2–3). The exceptions are exactly the qualities on the heavy side of verse 102.

**"Abiding in Hell": Fī Jahannama Khālidūn**

The verse ends with the destination: *fī jahannama khālidūn* — "in Hell, abiding." *Jahannam* is the Qur'an's most frequent name for the Fire — the place of punishment for those who died in disbelief. The word *khālidūn*, "abiding, remaining permanently," is the same word the sūrah used of the believers in Firdaws in verse 11: *"they will abide therein forever (hum fīhā khālidūn)."* The symmetry with verse 11 is exact and intended. The believers inherit Firdaws and abide; the light-scaled enter Jahannam and abide. Both outcomes are permanent, because both are the completion of a life's direction: the believers walked the straight path (v. 73) and arrived; the deniers deviated from it (v. 74) and arrived elsewhere. Neither destination is a way station.

The sound position of the *Ahl al-Sunnah*, held by Ibn Taymiyyah and the overwhelming majority, is that the abiding of disbelievers in the Fire is eternal, as the Qur'an repeatedly states (*"they will not leave it,"* 2:167; *"the punishment will not be lightened for them,"* 2:86). For believers who enter the Fire for sins, the *khulūd* is not eternal — the Prophet ﷺ described their eventual removal through intercession and God's mercy (al-Bukhārī 7439; Muslim 183). Verse 103 concerns the light-scaled disbelievers of the sūrah — those whose scales are light because they had no faith to give their deeds weight — and for them the abiding is as permanent as the believers' abiding in Firdaws.

**The Two Verses as the Sūrah's Verdict**

Verses 102 and 103 together are the point toward which the sūrah has been moving since its first word. The sūrah opened by declaring the believers successful and describing them; it then described, at length, the deniers and the histories of their predecessors; it argued, warned, and taught prayers; and now, at the scales, it pronounces the two verdicts in a single balanced sentence. The believers' *falāḥ* (v. 1) is confirmed (v. 102); the deniers' *khusrān* — which the notables of verse 34 tried to project onto the believers — is returned to its rightful owners (v. 103). The scales are the instrument of the sūrah's justice, and they weigh exactly what the sūrah said would be weighed.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 103 is the sūrah's most direct warning to anyone who imagines his scale is heavy because his life is full. Fullness is not weight. The deniers had full lives — wealth, children, standing, activity — and light scales. The believer must ask not "how much have I done?" but "how much of what I have done has *weight*?" — that is, was done in faith, for God, with the trembling heart of verse 60. The test is uncomfortable, and it is meant to be, because the discomfort now is the only protection against the surprise later.

The verse also gives the believer the true meaning of *loss*, against which every other loss is small. To lose money, position, health, even loved ones, is grievous but recoverable — in this life or the next. To lose the *self* is the one loss for which there is no compensation, because there is nothing left to compensate. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"The clever one is he who takes account of himself and works for what comes after death"* (al-Tirmidhī 2459). The one who takes account of himself now will not be among those who *lost* themselves then. And the sūrah has told him what the account should contain: the seven qualities, the four inner states, the racing toward good. These are the weights that keep the self from being lost.

**Toward the Fire**

The light-scaled abide in Hell. The next verse describes what the Fire does to them — and the disfigurement it produces on the faces that once turned away in arrogance.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:104

> **The Fire will smite their faces, and they shall grimace therein.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Fire Described**

The light-scaled have been consigned to Hell, abiding (v. 103). Verse 104 shows what that abiding is: *talfaḥu wujūhahumu l-nāru wa hum fīhā kāliḥūn* — "The Fire will scorch their faces, and they will be in it grimacing." The verse is brief and physical. After the abstraction of scales and verdicts, the sūrah gives one concrete image: faces, fire, and the expression fire produces on them. The image is chosen with precision, because the *face* has been, throughout the sūrah, the seat of the deniers' arrogance — the faces that turned away on their heels (v. 66), that were raised in *kibr* (v. 67), that mocked the believers (v. 110). Now the Fire addresses those faces directly.

**"The Fire Will Scorch Their Faces": Talfaḥu**

The verb *talfaḥu* is from the root *l-f-ḥ*, which denotes the scorching of a hot wind or flame against the skin — the blast of heat that strikes the face when one opens an oven or stands before a blaze. A *lafḥah* is a burning gust. The word is chosen for its sensory precision: not a general burning but the specific assault of heat on the face, the most sensitive and exposed part of the body. The Qur'an uses the related verb *naḍaja* for the burning of skins (4:56) and describes the Fire *"whose fuel is people and stones"* (2:24; 66:6); *talfaḥu* adds the immediacy of the flame's breath on the face.

The object is *wujūhahum*, "their faces." The Qur'an repeatedly makes the face the site of the Day's outcomes: *"On the Day some faces will be white and some faces will be black"* (3:106); *"Faces, that Day, will be radiant, looking at their Lord; and faces, that Day, will be contorted"* (75:22–24); *"Faces, that Day, will be humbled, laboring, weary, entering a burning Fire"* (88:2–4). The face is where a person's inner state becomes visible, where honor and shame are shown, and where — in Arabian idiom — dignity resides (to "blacken the face" is to disgrace). The deniers protected their faces in this world: their pride, their standing, their public honor. The Fire strikes exactly there.

**"And They Will Be in It Grimacing": Kāliḥūn**

The word *kāliḥūn* is the verse's most vivid term. It is from the root *k-l-ḥ*, which describes the face when the lips are drawn back from the teeth in a fixed grimace — as the skin of the lips contracts and burns away, or as the face contorts in extreme pain. A *kāliḥ* is one whose face is set in this expression: teeth exposed, lips withered, the appearance of a skull. Ibn Masʿūd explained the word by comparison: *"Have you not seen a roasted head, how its lips are drawn back from its teeth?"* The commentators, including al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, recorded this explanation, and the Prophet ﷺ described the same state in a ḥadīth: *"The Fire will scorch him so that his upper lip shrinks until it reaches the middle of his head, and his lower lip hangs down until it strikes his navel"* (al-Tirmidhī 2587; Aḥmad 11065; graded ḥasan).

The word does more than describe pain. A *kāliḥ* face is a face that has lost the capacity for expression — that can no longer smile, speak clearly, or compose itself, because it is fixed in one shape. This is the exact reversal of the deniers' faces in this world. They *mocked* — and mockery lives in the face: the smirk, the raised eyebrow, the laugh (v. 110: *"you used to laugh at them"*). They *raved* by night (v. 67) — and raving lives in the mouth. They *turned away* (v. 66) — and turning away is a movement of the face. Every use they made of their faces against the truth is answered by a face that can do nothing but grimace. The Fire has taken the instrument of their contempt and fixed it in a permanent expression of agony.

**The Contrast With the Believers' Faces**

The Qur'an sets the faces of the believers against these: *"You will recognize in their faces the radiance of pleasure"* (83:24); *"Faces, that Day, will be radiant (nāḍirah), looking at their Lord"* (75:22–23). The believers' faces are *nāḍirah* — fresh, bright, moist, like a garden after rain — because they looked at their Lord; the deniers' faces are *kāliḥah* — withered, contracted, skull-like — because they turned from Him. The two states of the face on that Day are the two states of the heart in this life made visible. The sūrah described the believers' hearts as trembling in awe (v. 60) and the deniers' as submerged and hardened (vv. 63, 76). On the Day, the heart's condition surfaces on the face.

**Why the Sūrah Includes This Image**

The Qur'an's descriptions of the Fire are not gratuitous. They serve a purpose that the sūrah's own logic explains: the deniers *"did not perceive"* (v. 56), and *"their hearts are in confusion"* (v. 63), and they were *"bewitched"* (v. 89) — their faculties of perception were disabled. A verse like 104 attempts to reach a disabled perception through the most direct channel available: the imagination of physical pain in the most sensitive place. The Qur'an says of its warnings: *"Thus do We explain the signs in detail... that perhaps they will return"* (7:174). The image of the scorched, grimacing face is meant to be *felt* by one who will not *think*, in the hope that feeling will do what thought has not.

The image also enacts the justice the sūrah has promised. Verse 62 said that no one will be wronged; verse 90 called the deniers liars; verse 103 said they lost their souls. Verse 104 shows that the punishment is *fitting* — that it answers the crime in kind. The faces that mocked are the faces that burn. This correspondence is a recurring principle of the Qur'an's eschatology: *"The recompense for an evil is an evil like it"* (42:40); *"Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do"* (45:28). The punishment is not arbitrary cruelty but the shape of the crime returned.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 104 asks the believer to consider his own face — what it does, and what it will do. In this life, the face is an instrument: it can be turned toward the Qur'an or away from it; it can smile at a brother (which the Prophet ﷺ called charity) or smirk at him; it can be lowered in humility before God or raised in *kibr*. The Prophet ﷺ prayed: *"O God, You have made my form beautiful, so make my character beautiful"* (Aḥmad 3823; graded ṣaḥīḥ) — connecting the face to the conduct behind it. The believer who uses his face as the Prophet ﷺ used his — in prostration, in kindness, in the *bishr* (cheerful countenance) with which he met people — is preparing it for the radiance of 75:22, not the grimace of 23:104.

The verse also teaches the believer to take the Fire seriously without despair. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date; and if you cannot find that, then with a good word"* (al-Bukhārī 6023; Muslim 1016). The protection is within reach of everyone. The image of verse 104 is severe so that the believer will reach for the half-date, the good word, the small sincere deed that goes on the heavy side of the scale — and so that his face, on the Day, will be among those *"looking at their Lord."*

**Toward the Question**

The faces are scorched and fixed. Into this scene comes a voice — God's own — asking the question that the whole sūrah has been preparing: *"Were not My signs recited to you?"*

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:105

> **“Were not My signs recited unto you, and you used to deny them?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Question in the Fire**

Into the scene of scorched and grimacing faces (v. 104) comes a voice. It is God's, and it asks: *a-lam takun āyātī tutlā ʿalaykum fa-kuntum bihā tukadhdhibūn* — "Were not My signs recited to you, and you used to deny them?" The verse is a question, but not one seeking information. It is the question of a judge who states the charge in interrogative form so that the accused must confirm it with their own mouths. And it is a question the sūrah's reader has heard before, almost word for word: in verse 66, God said to the seized affluent, *"My signs were indeed recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels."* Verse 105 is the same charge, brought again — this time not at the moment of worldly seizure but at the final reckoning, and this time phrased as a question demanding an answer.

**"Were Not My Signs Recited to You?"**

The construction *a-lam takun āyātī tutlā ʿalaykum* — "were not My signs being recited to you?" — is a negative interrogative, which in Arabic as in English presses for the answer "yes, they were." The verb *tutlā*, in the imperfect, denotes continuous, repeated recitation — the signs were recited *again and again*, over years. The possessive *āyātī*, "*My* signs," is the intimate first person that verse 66 also used: it was *I* whose communications you received. The recitation was not an abstraction; it was the voice of the Prophet ﷺ in the precincts of the Kaʿbah, in the houses of Makkah, in every gathering where the Qur'an could be heard — the same recitation the deniers recoiled from (v. 66) and raved against (v. 67).

The question establishes the *ḥujjah*, the decisive proof. God does not punish those who were not warned: *"And never would We punish until We sent a messenger"* (17:15). The deniers in the Fire cannot plead ignorance, because the signs were recited to them — continuously, clearly, in their own tongue. The question forces them to acknowledge this. It is the fulfillment of verse 62's promise: *"with Us is a record that speaks with truth, and they will not be wronged."* The record shows the recitations; the question asks them to confirm it.

**"And You Used to Deny Them": Tukadhdhibūn**

The second half of the question names their response: *fa-kuntum bihā tukadhdhibūn* — "and you used to deny them," "call them lies." The verb *tukadhdhibūn* is from the root *k-dh-b*, the root of *kādhibūn*, "liars," in verse 90. The deniers *called the signs lies* — which is what *takdhīb* means — and God called *them* liars (v. 90). Now, in the Fire, the two are placed together: you called My signs lies, and here is the truth of what you called lies. The continuous tense — *kuntum ... tukadhdhibūn*, "you *used to* deny" — matches the continuous tense of the recitation: as often as the signs were recited, so often were they denied. The denial was a habit as sustained as the revelation.

The word *bihā*, "them," refers to *āyātī*, "My signs" — which, as under verse 58, includes both the signs of revelation (the Qur'an) and the signs of creation (the embryo, the heavens, the rain, the histories). The deniers denied both: they called the Qur'an legends (v. 83) and read the created signs wrongly, as wealth proving favor (v. 55) and dust proving finality (v. 82). The question covers the whole of their denial.

**The Parallel With Verse 66**

The near-identity of verses 66 and 105 is a structural feature the sūrah's reader should notice. Verse 66: *qad kānat āyātī tutlā ʿalaykum fa-kuntum ʿalā aʿqābikum tankiṣūn* — "My signs were recited to you, and you used to turn back on your heels." Verse 105: *a-lam takun āyātī tutlā ʿalaykum fa-kuntum bihā tukadhdhibūn* — "Were not My signs recited to you, and you used to deny them?" The first is a statement made at the worldly seizure (v. 64); the second is a question asked at the final reckoning. The two moments are linked: the worldly punishment was a warning, and the charge stated then is repeated now, when the warning has run out. The deniers heard verse 66 as a description of what God *would* say to the seized; they now hear verse 105 said to them. The sūrah warned them, in advance, of the exact words they would be asked — and they are asked them.

The difference in the verbs is also instructive. Verse 66 said they *turned on their heels* — the physical recoil. Verse 105 says they *denied* — the verbal and inward rejection. The two together describe the full response: body and tongue and heart, all turned against the recited signs.

**The Justice of the Question**

Why does God ask rather than simply sentence? The commentators explained that the question serves the perfection of justice. A just judge does not merely punish; he confronts the guilty with the evidence and gives them the opportunity to respond. The question of verse 105 does this. It states the charge — the signs were recited, and you denied them — and it waits for the answer, which verse 106 will supply. The deniers will not be able to deny the charge; they will confess it. Their own confession, extracted by God's question, is the final proof that *"they will not be wronged"* (v. 62). The Prophet ﷺ described this confrontation: *"There is none of you but his Lord will speak to him, with no interpreter between them; he will look to his right and see nothing but what he sent forth, and look to his left and see nothing but what he sent forth, and look in front of him and see nothing but the Fire before his face"* (al-Bukhārī 6539; Muslim 1016). The speaking of God to each person, without intermediary, is the setting of verse 105.

**The Verse and the Sūrah's Method**

Verse 105 vindicates the sūrah's entire method. The sūrah has been, from beginning to end, a *recitation of signs*: the embryo, the heavens, the rain, the plants, the cattle, the ships, the histories of the messengers, the three questions, the argument from order. Every one of these was an *āyah tutlā* — a sign recited. The sūrah is itself the evidence that will be cited in the question of verse 105. The reader who has recited it has had the signs recited to him; the question will one day be put to him too; and the sūrah's purpose is that his answer will not be the one verse 106 records.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 105 places before the believer the question he will be asked, and asks him to prepare his answer now. *Were not My signs recited to you?* — Yes, they were: in every prayer, every Qur'an lesson, every Friday sermon, every verse encountered in a lifetime. *And you used to...?* — The verse's ending, for the denier, is "deny them." The believer's task is to ensure that the ending, for him, is different: "and you used to *believe in them*" (the description of verse 58), "and you used to *ponder them*" (v. 68), "and you used to *tremble at them*" (v. 60). The signs are the same for everyone; the response is what the question is really asking about.

The verse also warns against a subtle form of *takdhīb*: not verbal denial but *practical* denial — hearing the signs recited and living as though they had not been. The Prophet ﷺ warned of the Qur'an that *"does not pass beyond the throat"* (al-Bukhārī 5058; Muslim 1066). A believer who hears the signs and lets them stop at the throat is, in the sūrah's extended sense, letting them be recited without response — and verse 105's question will be put to him as well. The remedy is the *tadabbur* of verse 68, which carries the recitation past the throat to the heart, where it can be answered.

**Toward the Confession**

The question has been asked. The next verse gives the deniers' answer — and it is, at last, the truth.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:106

> **They will say, “Our Lord! Our wretchedness overwhelmed us, and we were a people astray.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Confession**

God has asked: "Were not My signs recited to you, and you used to deny them?" (v. 105). Verse 106 records the answer: *qālū rabbanā ghalabat ʿalaynā shiqwatunā wa kunnā qawman ḍāllīn* — "They will say: 'Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people astray.'" The answer is a confession. There is no evasion, no excuse, no counter-argument. The people who spent their lives inventing excuses (vv. 68–70: not understood, unprecedented, unknown man, madman) have none left. They admit the charge, name the cause, and describe their condition. And they begin, as the dying denier began in verse 99, with the word they never used in life: *rabbanā*, "our Lord."

**"Our Lord": Rabbanā**

The deniers address God as *rabbanā*, "our Lord" — the possessive plural that the sūrah's believers use in their prayer (v. 109: *"Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us"*). In life the deniers acknowledged God as owner of the earth (v. 85) but never addressed Him as *their* Lord; their devotion went to idols. Now, in the Fire, the idols are gone and the address is correct. The confession of lordship is sincere in the sense that it corresponds to what they now see; but it is the recognition that comes *after* the veil is lifted, not the faith that was asked for *before*. The Qur'an describes this posthumous clarity: *"If you could but see when the criminals are hanging their heads before their Lord, [saying], 'Our Lord, we have seen and heard'"* (32:12). Seeing and hearing in the Fire is not the same as believing in the world.

**"Our Wretchedness Overcame Us": Ghalabat ʿAlaynā Shiqwatunā**

The first clause of the confession is an explanation: *ghalabat ʿalaynā shiqwatunā* — "our wretchedness overcame us." The word *shiqwah* (also read *shaqāwah*) is from the root *sh-q-w*, which denotes misery, wretchedness, ill fortune — the opposite of *saʿādah*, felicity. The Qur'an uses the pair for the two final states of humanity: *"The Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission; and among them will be the wretched (shaqiyy) and the prosperous (saʿīd)"* (11:105). To say "our *shiqwah* overcame us" is to say: the wretchedness that was in us — our disposition to misery, our fatal tendency — prevailed over us. The verb *ghalabat*, "overcame, defeated," is the language of a lost battle. Something in them fought against the signs, and it won.

The commentators discussed what *shiqwah* refers to here. Some understood it as the divine decree of wretchedness — the *qadar* by which some are destined for the Fire. Others understood it as the deniers' own inclination — their desires (*ahwāʾ*, v. 71), their arrogance (v. 67), their aversion to the truth (v. 70) — the inner disposition that they cultivated until it dominated them. The two readings are not opposed; the Qur'an teaches that God's decree operates through the choices human beings make, and that a person who chooses wretchedness repeatedly is confirmed in it: *"So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate"* (61:5). The deniers' *shiqwah* was both what God knew of them and what they made of themselves. In the Fire, they name it as the thing that defeated them.

There is a significant honesty in the phrase. The deniers do not say "You wronged us" or "the messenger failed us" or "we were not told." They say "*our* wretchedness overcame *us*" — locating the cause in themselves. The confession fulfills verse 62's promise that no one will be wronged: the punished themselves acknowledge that the fault was theirs. Verse 105's question has been answered as the Judge intended: with the accused's own admission.

**"And We Were a People Astray": Qawman Ḍāllīn**

The second clause completes the confession: *wa kunnā qawman ḍāllīn* — "and we were a people astray." The word *ḍāllīn* is from the root *ḍ-l-l*, to go astray, to lose the way, to wander from the path. It is the word of the Fātiḥah's last phrase — *"not of those who have earned anger nor of those who are astray (al-ḍāllīn)"* (1:7) — and it names the condition verse 74 diagnosed: *"those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating (nākibūn) from the path."* The deniers now describe themselves with the sūrah's own word. They were off the straight path (v. 73) — not slightly, but as *a people astray*, a whole community that had lost the way.

The confession *kunnā ḍāllīn* is remarkable because in life the deniers claimed the opposite. They said the Prophet ﷺ was astray; they said his followers were fools; they said their forefathers' way was the true one. Now they say: *we* were astray. The reversal is complete. The truth they were averse to (v. 70) is spoken by their own tongues — but in the place where speaking it changes nothing.

**Why the Confession Does Not Help Them**

The reader might ask: if the deniers confess so fully — acknowledging God as Lord, blaming themselves, admitting they were astray — why is the confession not accepted? The answer is the one the sūrah has given repeatedly (vv. 65, 100): the time for confession that *counts* was the time when the signs were being recited (v. 105), not the time when the Fire is scorching faces (v. 104). A confession extracted by punishment is not repentance; it is the recognition of fact under compulsion. The Qur'an states the rule of Pharaoh's case: *"Now? And you had disobeyed before"* (10:91); and of the people of the Fire: *"and if they were returned, they would return to that which they were forbidden"* (6:28). The confession is true, but it comes from the far side of the *barzakh* (v. 100), where nothing can be done with it. This is why the next verse's plea — "remove us from it" — will be refused (v. 108).

**The Two Confessions of the Sūrah's Ending**

The sūrah's ending contains two speeches by the deniers — verse 106 (this confession) and verse 107 (the plea to be removed) — and two speeches by God in response (verse 105's question before, verse 108's dismissal after). The structure is a trial: the charge (105), the confession (106), the plea for mercy (107), the sentence (108). The deniers are given full voice; they say everything they could say; and it is not enough, because the time when it would have been enough has passed. The trial is exhaustively fair, which is exactly the point: the sūrah wants the reader to see that no one in the Fire can say he was not heard.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 106 gives the believer a confession to make *now*, while it counts. *Rabbanā* — our Lord. *Ghalabat ʿalaynā shiqwatunā* — our wretchedness has, at times, overcome us. *Kunnā ḍāllīn* — we have strayed. Every believer can say these things truthfully about some part of his life, and saying them in this world, with the resolve to return to the path, is precisely the repentance that the deniers were offered and refused. The Qur'an teaches the believers a version of this confession as a prayer: *"Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers"* (7:23 — the words of Adam and Eve). The difference between 7:23 and 23:106 is not the content but the *timing*: Adam confessed in the world and was forgiven; the deniers confess in the Fire and are not. The believer who reads verse 106 is being shown the confession he should make today.

The verse also warns the believer about *shiqwah* as a force that can "overcome." The deniers did not decide, at a single moment, to be wretched; their disposition toward misery grew — through *laghw*, through *samar*, through aversion, through the accumulated angles of deviation (v. 74) — until it *overcame* them. The believer guards against the same growth by the practices the sūrah has prescribed: the humble prayer of verse 2, the turning from vain talk of verse 3, the trembling of verse 60, the refuge of verses 97–98. These keep the *shiqwah* from gathering strength. The Prophet ﷺ prayed: *"O God, I seek refuge in You from the burden of trial, the depths of wretchedness (darak al-shaqāʾ), the evil of decree, and the gloating of enemies"* (al-Bukhārī 6347; Muslim 2707). *Darak al-shaqāʾ* — the reaching of wretchedness — is what verse 106 records; the Prophet's prayer is the believer's protection against it.

**Toward the Plea**

They have confessed. Now they plead — for removal from the Fire, and with a promise they have made before.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:107

> **Our Lord! Remove us from it! Then if we revert, we shall be wrongdoers.”**
