**Expanded Commentary**

**The Plea After the Confession**

Having confessed that their wretchedness overcame them and that they were astray (v. 106), the people of the Fire make their plea: *rabbanā akhrijnā minhā fa-in ʿudnā fa-innā ẓālimūn* — "Our Lord, remove us from it; then if we return [to sin], we will indeed be wrongdoers." The plea has two parts: a request (take us out) and a pledge (if we relapse, we accept the name of wrongdoers). It is the last thing the deniers say in the sūrah. After it, God speaks (v. 108), and they are silenced. The plea is therefore the final statement of a people who have been speaking since verse 24 — objecting, mocking, denying, dismissing — and its content deserves careful attention, because it reveals what they have and have not understood.

**"Our Lord, Remove Us From It": Akhrijnā Minhā**

The request is *akhrijnā minhā* — "bring us out of it," *it* being the Fire. The verb *akhraja* is from the root *kh-r-j*, "to go out, to exit" — the same root as *kharj*, the payment the Prophet ﷺ did not ask for (v. 72). The deniers want to *exit* the Fire. This is the same plea, in a different setting, that the dying man made in verse 99: *irjiʿūn*, "send me back." There, the plea was to exit death and return to life; here, it is to exit the Fire and — implicitly — return to the world, since the pledge that follows ("if we return") presupposes a return to the place where sin is possible. The Qur'an records this plea from the people of the Fire elsewhere: *"Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness — other than what we were doing!"* (35:37); *"Our Lord, You have made us die twice and given us life twice, and we have confessed our sins. So is there to an exit any way?"* (40:11). The plea is universal, and so is its refusal.

The address *rabbanā* is repeated from verse 106, making three uses of "Lord" by the deniers in the sūrah's closing scenes (vv. 99, 106, 107). The people who would not say "my Lord" in life cannot stop saying it in death. The repetition is the pleading of the desperate, matching the doubled *rabbi* of the Prophet's prayer in verses 93–94 — but the Prophet ﷺ pleaded *before* the punishment not to be among the wrongdoers, and they plead *after* it to be released from being among them.

**"Then If We Return, We Will Indeed Be Wrongdoers"**

The pledge is *fa-in ʿudnā fa-innā ẓālimūn* — "then if we return [to what we were], we will indeed be wrongdoers." The verb *ʿudnā*, "we return," is from the root *ʿ-w-d*, "to go back, to return to a former state." The deniers pledge that if they are removed from the Fire and relapse into denial, they will *accept the verdict* of *ẓulm* — they will have no complaint. The pledge is meant as a guarantee: give us one more chance, and if we fail, you may call us wrongdoers with our own consent.

The pledge is revealing in two ways. First, it uses the sūrah's own word — *ẓālimūn*, wrongdoers — the word the Prophet ﷺ used in his prayer not to be placed among them (v. 94), and the word the sūrah applied to Noah's people (v. 28). The deniers now offer to accept this word for themselves *conditionally* — if they relapse. But the condition is empty: they are *already* wrongdoers, by the verdict of their own confession (v. 106) and of the scales (v. 103). The pledge offers to accept, in a hypothetical future, a name that is already theirs in the actual present.

Second, the pledge is one God has already evaluated. The Qur'an states, of exactly this kind of plea: *"But if they were returned, they would return to that which they were forbidden; and indeed, they are liars"* (6:28). The Knower of the unseen and the seen (v. 92) knows what the deniers would do if returned — and it is what they did before. The dying man's plea in verse 99 was called *"only a word he is saying"* (v. 100); this plea is the same kind of word. Its pledge is sincere in the moment of terror and worthless as a prediction, because the *shiqwah* that overcame them (v. 106) is still what they are. A person who is what he was will do what he did.

**Why the Plea Cannot Be Granted**

The commentators explained the refusal of the plea by three principles the sūrah has established. First, the *barzakh* (v. 100): there is a barrier between the dead and the world, and no one crosses it back. The request to be removed from the Fire and returned to the world asks for what the structure of reality forbids. Second, the *term* (v. 43): every community and every individual has a fixed *ajal*, and the deniers' has expired. The time for choice was the time before the term; after it, there is only consequence. Third, the *justice* (v. 62): the deniers were tested fairly, warned fully (v. 105), and confessed freely (v. 106). To grant them a second life would be to treat them differently from every other soul who had one life and was judged on it — and it would make the first life meaningless, since anyone could defer faith until after seeing the Fire. The refusal is not hardness; it is the integrity of the test.

There is a further point that the Qur'an makes in a parallel passage. In 35:37, when the people of the Fire plead *"bring us out; we will do righteousness,"* God answers: *"Did We not grant you life enough for whoever would remember therein to remember? And the warner had come to you."* The life they had *was* the second chance — and the third, and the hundredth. Every day of it was an opportunity to do what they now pledge to do. The plea to be returned asks for what they already had and wasted.

**The Contrast With the Believers' Prayer**

The sūrah will, in verse 109, quote the believers' prayer in the world: *"Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of the merciful."* Set the two prayers side by side. The believers said *rabbanā* in the world; the deniers say it in the Fire. The believers asked for forgiveness and mercy *while believing*; the deniers ask for removal *after seeing*. The believers' prayer was answered (v. 111: *"I have rewarded them this Day"*); the deniers' will be refused (v. 108). The same address, the same humility of tone — and opposite outcomes, because of *when* and *from where* the prayer was made. The sūrah wants its reader to see that the words of verse 107 are not far from the words of verse 109; what separates them is a lifetime and a barrier.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 107 gives the believer a pledge to make *now*, in the only setting where it counts. *Fa-in ʿudnā fa-innā ẓālimūn* — "if we return to what we were, we are wrongdoers." The believer who has repented of a sin can make this very pledge to his Lord as part of his repentance: I have left it; if I return, I accept the name. Made in the world, with the resolve to hold it, this pledge is the *ʿazm*, the firm intention, that the scholars named as a condition of true *tawbah*. Made in the Fire, it is only a word. The believer has the privilege of making it where it is heard.

The verse also confronts the believer with the futility of "one more chance" thinking. The deniers' plea assumes that what they needed was *more time*. The Qur'an's answer (35:37) is that they had enough. The believer who defers — who plans to pray properly later, give later, reform later, repent later — is living inside the deniers' assumption. The time he has *is* the chance; there is no supplementary one behind the barrier. The Prophet ﷺ described the person who wakes up as one who *"does not expect to reach the evening,"* and who reaches the evening as one who *"does not expect to reach the morning"* (al-Bukhārī 6416) — the posture of one who knows that the only chance is now.

**Toward the Silence**

The deniers have made their last plea. God's answer will be a command — and it will end their speaking forever.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:108

> **He will say, “Be gone therein, and speak not to Me.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Sentence**

The people of the Fire have confessed (v. 106) and pleaded (v. 107). Verse 108 gives God's answer, and it is the shortest and most final utterance in the sūrah: *qāla khsaʾū fīhā wa lā tukallimūn* — "He will say: 'Remain despised therein, and do not speak to Me.'" Two commands: stay where you are, in contempt; and be silent. The first fixes their place; the second closes their mouths. After this, the deniers do not speak again in the sūrah. The dialogue that began when Noah's notables opened their mouths in verse 24 — "he is only a man like you" — ends here, with God commanding those mouths shut.

**"Remain Despised Therein": Ikhsaʾū**

The word *ikhsaʾū* is an imperative from the root *kh-s-ʾ*, which means to drive away in contempt, to repel as one repels a dog — *ikhsaʾ* is what an Arab says to a dog to make it go away and stay away. The Qur'an uses the same root for the Sabbath-breakers turned into apes: *"Be apes, despised (khāsiʾīn)"* (2:65; 7:166), and for the sight that returns *"humbled (khāsiʾan) and fatigued"* from searching the heavens for a flaw (67:4). The word combines three meanings, all active here: *dismissal* (go away), *abasement* (in humiliation), and *silencing* (as one silences a barking dog). The command *ikhsaʾū fīhā*, "be despised in it" or "remain in it, despised," tells the deniers that their plea for removal (v. 107) is not merely refused but rebuffed with contempt — they are to stay in the Fire, and stay in it as the despised.

The commentators noted the exactness of the recompense. The deniers treated the believers with contempt — *"you took them in mockery... and you used to laugh at them"* (v. 110). They treated the messengers as dogs to be driven off: *"drive them away,"* the Quraysh said of the Prophet's poor Companions (cf. 6:52); *"he is only a man in whom is madness,"* said Noah's notables (v. 25). The word that they used, in spirit, against God's servants is the word God uses against them. *Ikhsaʾū* is contempt returned to the contemptuous.

The harshness of the word must be understood in its setting. God is *"the Most Merciful of the merciful"* (v. 118), and the sūrah will end by naming Him so. The contempt of verse 108 is not the contradiction of that mercy but its consequence when refused: mercy offered across a lifetime and mocked has a shape when it is finally withdrawn, and that shape is *ikhsaʾū*. The verse describes the end of a road; the mercy was at every point along it.

**"And Do Not Speak to Me": Lā Tukallimūn**

The second command is *lā tukallimūn* — "do not speak to Me," "do not address Me." The verb *kallama* means to speak to, to address in speech. The command forbids the deniers to address God further — no more pleas, no more pledges, no more *rabbanā*. The commentators understood this as the final severance. Ibn ʿAbbās and others said that after this word, the people of the Fire will not speak intelligibly again; their sounds will be only the *zafīr* and *shahīq* — the sighing and gasping — that the Qur'an describes: *"for them therein is sighing and gasping"* (11:106). Speech, which is the mark of the rational creature and the medium of prayer, is taken from them. They have said everything they will say.

The severity of this command is measured by what speech to God is. It is prayer, supplication, the address of the servant to his Lord — the thing the sūrah has been teaching the Prophet ﷺ to do since verse 93. To be told "do not speak to Me" is to be cut off from the one channel that remained open even in the Fire. The Qur'an describes the same severance in other words: *"God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He look at them, nor will He purify them"* (2:174; 3:77). Not to be spoken to by God, and not to be permitted to speak to Him, is a punishment beyond the physical — it is exclusion from the relationship for which the human being was made.

**Why the Refusal Is Absolute**

The commentators explained the absoluteness of verse 108 by the principle that runs through the whole sūrah. The deniers had a lifetime in which God spoke to them — through *"My signs recited to you"* (v. 105) — and they did not listen; they *"turned back on their heels"* (v. 66). They had a lifetime in which they could have spoken to God — in prayer, in repentance, in the *rabbanā* of verse 109 that the believers said — and they did not; they raved at night instead (v. 67). Now the roles are reversed with exact justice: God spoke and they would not hear; they speak and He will not hear. The Qur'an states this reversal directly of the people of the Fire: *"Indeed, there was a party of My servants who said, 'Our Lord, we have believed...' but you took them in mockery until they made you forget My remembrance"* (vv. 109–110, immediately following). They forgot God's remembrance; He now forbids them to remember Him aloud.

**The Trial Concluded**

Verses 105–108 form a complete judicial proceeding, and verse 108 is its sentence. The charge: were not My signs recited, and you denied them? (105). The confession: our wretchedness overcame us; we were astray (106). The plea: remove us; if we return, we are wrongdoers (107). The sentence: remain despised; do not speak (108). Every stage of justice has been observed. The accused were confronted with the evidence, given voice, and heard. Their plea was considered against the knowledge of the One who knows what they would do if returned (6:28). The sentence was pronounced. And the sūrah has arranged the proceeding so that the reader, having watched it, cannot say it was unfair. That is the purpose of recording it: not to satisfy a taste for severity but to establish, before the fact, that *"they will not be wronged"* (v. 62) — and to warn the living that this proceeding awaits every soul, and that the only time to prepare a defense is now.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 108 is the sūrah's darkest verse, and the believer should let it be dark. It describes the end of the possibility of speaking to God — and the believer, who speaks to God every day in prayer, who says *rabbanā* and *rabbi* as easily as breathing, should feel the weight of what it would mean to be told "do not speak to Me." The weight is the point. The Prophet ﷺ wept when he recited verses of punishment, and the Companions wept with him, not from despair but from the seriousness of what was being described. The believer who reads verse 108 with a cold heart has not read it.

But the verse is also, for the believer, an immense mercy in disguise. It tells him that the channel is *open now* — that the God who will one day say "do not speak to Me" to the despised is, today, saying *"Call upon Me; I will respond to you"* (40:60) to everyone who will call. Every prayer the believer makes is an exercise of the privilege verse 108 revokes. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Your Lord is Modest and Generous; He is shy, when His servant raises his hands to Him, to return them empty"* (Abū Dāwūd 1488; al-Tirmidhī 3556). That is the same Lord who says *ikhsaʾū*. The difference is the timing and the heart. The believer who speaks to God now, humbly, with the confession of verse 106 and the pledge of verse 107 offered *in the world*, will never hear verse 108 — because he has already said what the deniers said too late, and said it in time.

The verse also warns against treating any of God's servants with contempt — driving them away, mocking them, laughing at them — because the next verses will show that this contempt is precisely what brought the deniers to the place where contempt is returned. The believer who is tempted to despise another person for his poverty, his simplicity, or his faith should remember the word *ikhsaʾū*, and to whom it is finally addressed.

**Toward the Believers' Prayer**

God has silenced the deniers. Now He tells them why — and in doing so, He quotes the prayer of the believers whom they mocked, a prayer that the sūrah will make its own closing words.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:109

> **Verily there was a group of My servants who would say, “Our Lord! We believe; so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and Thou art the best of those who are merciful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reason for the Sentence**

God has silenced the people of the Fire (v. 108). Now He tells them why: *innahu kāna farīqun min ʿibādī yaqūlūna rabbanā āmannā fa-ghfir lanā wa rḥamnā wa anta khayru l-rāḥimīn* — "Indeed, there was a party of My servants who used to say: 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful.'" The verse introduces the believers into the scene of judgment — not in person, but through the quotation of their prayer. God recites to the deniers the words that the believers used to say in the world, and the next verse (110) will reveal what the deniers did with those words: mocked them. The sentence of verse 108 rests on this: you were silenced because you silenced, with laughter, the ones who spoke rightly.

**"A Party of My Servants": Farīq min ʿIbādī**

The believers are introduced as *farīq min ʿibādī* — "a party of My servants." The word *farīq* means a group, a portion, a party — and its indefiniteness (*a* party, not *the* majority) is honest about the believers' situation in Makkah: they were a minority, a small group, outnumbered and despised. The word *ʿibādī*, "My servants," is the term of honor. God calls them *His* servants — *ʿibād* being the plural of *ʿabd*, the one who is owned and who serves — and the possessive *-ī*, "My," places them under His direct care and ownership. The Qur'an uses *ʿibādī* for those God has taken as His own: *"O My servants who have believed, indeed My earth is spacious, so worship only Me"* (29:56); *"O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God"* (39:53); *"And My righteous servants will inherit the earth"* (21:105). To be called *ʿibādī* is to be claimed. The deniers claimed lineage (v. 101) and lost it; the believers were claimed by God and kept it.

The description recalls verse 84's question — *"whose is the earth and whoever is in it?"* — and its answer, *li-llāh*, "God's." Everyone is God's by ownership; the believers are God's by *service* as well. They are the *ʿibād* who lived as *ʿibād*. The deniers were owned and behaved as owners; the believers were owned and behaved as owned.

**"Who Used to Say": Yaqūlūna**

The verb *yaqūlūna*, "they used to say," is in the imperfect, denoting habitual action. The believers *kept* saying this prayer — it was their practice, their repeated address to God. The prayer is thus presented not as a single cry at a moment of crisis but as the steady content of a life. This distinguishes it from the deniers' *rabbanā* of verses 106–107, which was said once, in the Fire, under compulsion. The believers said *rabbanā* continuously, in the world, freely. Both groups used the same word; only one group used it *habitually*, while the saying could still shape a life.

**The Prayer Itself**

The prayer has three parts, and each connects to the sūrah's teaching.

*"Our Lord, we have believed"* — *rabbanā āmannā*. The believers begin by stating their faith — not as a boast but as the ground of their petition. The construction parallels 3:16: *"Those who say, 'Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.'"* Faith is offered as the basis for asking forgiveness, in the logic of 3:31: *"If you love God, follow me; God will love you and forgive you your sins."* The believers of verse 109 are the *muʾminūn* of the sūrah's title, and their prayer is their self-identification: we are the ones who believed.

*"So forgive us and have mercy on us"* — *fa-ghfir lanā wa rḥamnā*. The petition follows from the faith with *fa-*, "so": *because* we have believed, forgive us. What is striking is that those who believed ask for *forgiveness*. They do not say "reward us" or "we have earned Paradise." They ask to be forgiven — which presupposes that they see their faith as imperfect, their deeds as insufficient, their standing as dependent on mercy. This is the trembling of verse 60 made into words: *"those who give what they give while their hearts tremble."* The believers who tremble ask for forgiveness; the deniers who were confident (vv. 55–56) never thought to. And the pairing of *maghfirah* and *raḥmah* — forgiveness and mercy — is the Qur'an's standard pairing for what the believer needs from God: forgiveness for what he has done wrong, and mercy for everything else.

*"And You are the best of the merciful"* — *wa anta khayru l-rāḥimīn*. The prayer ends by naming God with a superlative: the *best* of those who show mercy. This is the third of the sūrah's *khayr* constructions (after *khayr al-munzilīn*, v. 29, and *khayr al-rāziqīn*, v. 72), and it is the one the sūrah will use for its final word (v. 118). To call God *khayr al-rāḥimīn* is to acknowledge that mercy exists in creatures — mothers, friends, judges show mercy — but that His is the best, the most complete, the source of all the rest. The Prophet ﷺ said that God has one hundred parts of mercy, of which He sent one to the world — by which all creatures are merciful to one another — and kept ninety-nine for the Day of Resurrection (al-Bukhārī 6000; Muslim 2752). The believers who prayed *khayr al-rāḥimīn* were appealing to the ninety-nine.

**The Prayer's Answer**

The verse does not state the prayer's answer directly, but verse 111 will: *"Indeed, I have rewarded them this Day for their patience; indeed, they are the triumphant."* The prayer was heard. The forgiveness and mercy asked for were given. The believers who said *rabbanā* in the world receive, on the Day, exactly what they asked for — while the deniers who said *rabbanā* in the Fire receive *ikhsaʾū*. The contrast is the sūrah's final teaching on prayer: the same words, addressed to the same Lord, with opposite outcomes, because one prayer was made in faith during the test and the other in terror after it.

**Why God Quotes This Prayer to the Deniers**

The rhetorical purpose of verse 109 is to confront the deniers with what they mocked. God does not merely say "you mocked My servants"; He recites the servants' words, so that the deniers hear again, in the Fire, the prayer they laughed at in the world. The words are humble, sincere, and — as the deniers now know — true. The believers said "we have believed" — and belief was right. They said "forgive us" — and forgiveness was needed. They said "You are the best of the merciful" — and mercy was real, and was withheld from none who asked for it in time. The deniers heard all this and laughed. Verse 109 makes them hear it once more, when laughter is no longer possible.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 109 gives the believer a prayer to make his own — and the sūrah will endorse it by making its last verse a variation of it (v. 118). The prayer is complete in itself: it states faith, asks forgiveness and mercy, and names God by the attribute the petition rests on. The believer who says it habitually, as the *farīq* of verse 109 did, is placing himself in their company — among "My servants," under God's claim, on the side of those who will hear verse 111 rather than verse 108.

The verse also comforts the believer who is mocked for his faith. The *farīq* of verse 109 were mocked — the next verse says so — and their prayer, to the ears of their mockers, sounded weak, superstitious, and pathetic. God calls them *ʿibādī*. The believer who is laughed at for praying, for believing, for asking forgiveness, is in the company of the sūrah's *farīq*, and the laughter is being recorded for a Day on which the prayer will be quoted back to those who laughed. This does not make the mockery pleasant; it makes it bearable. The believer can say his prayer in the face of laughter, knowing whose servants the sūrah calls those who say it.

**Toward the Mockery**

God has quoted the believers' prayer. Now He tells the deniers what they did with it — and what the doing cost them.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:110

> **But you took them in mockery, till it made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Charge Beneath the Sentence**

God has quoted the believers' prayer to the people of the Fire (v. 109). Verse 110 states what the deniers did with it: *fa-ttakhadhtumūhum sikhriyyan ḥattā ansawkum dhikrī wa kuntum minhum taḍḥakūn* — "But you took them in mockery, until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them." The verse names the sin that underlies the sentence of verse 108. The deniers were silenced not only for denying the signs (v. 105) but for what they did to the people who accepted them: they mocked them, and the mockery had a consequence the deniers did not foresee — it made them forget God. The verse is a precise account of how contempt for the believers becomes a spiritual catastrophe for the contemptuous.

**"But You Took Them in Mockery": Sikhriyyan**

The verb *ittakhadhtumūhum*, "you took them," is from the root *a-kh-dh*, "to take," in the Form VIII sense of "to adopt, to treat as, to make into." The deniers *made* the believers into an object — *sikhriyyan*, "a laughingstock, an object of ridicule." The word *sikhriyy* (read also *sukhriyy*) is from the root *s-kh-r*, to mock, to deride, to make sport of; it is the root of *istihzāʾ*'s companion *sukhriyah*, the mockery that the Qur'an forbids among believers: *"Let not a people ridicule (lā yaskhar) another people; perhaps they may be better than them"* (49:11). The deniers took the believers — the poor, the enslaved, the socially insignificant among the early Muslims — and made them into a joke.

The historical setting is documented. The Quraysh mocked Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Khabbāb, Ṣuhayb, and the other weak believers as fools and slaves who had been duped by Muḥammad ﷺ. They laughed at the Muslims' prayer, at their poverty, at their claims about resurrection. The Qur'an records their words: *"Is it these whom God has favored among us?"* (6:53) — said with contempt of the poor believers. And it records their behavior: *"Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed; and when they passed by them, they would exchange derisive glances; and when they returned to their people, they would return jesting"* (83:29–31). The *samar* of verse 67 — the nightly talk around the Kaʿbah — was the venue for much of this.

**"Until They Made You Forget My Remembrance": Ansawkum Dhikrī**

The verse's central clause is its most penetrating: *ḥattā ansawkum dhikrī* — "until they made you forget My remembrance." The grammar is striking. The subject of *ansawkum*, "made you forget," is *hum*, "they" — the believers. The believers *caused* the deniers to forget God. How? Not by any act of their own, but by being the object of the deniers' obsessive mockery. The deniers were so busy laughing at the believers that they had no attention left for God. The commentators explained: the deniers' preoccupation with ridicule *occupied* the place in their hearts and hours where *dhikr* should have been. Every evening spent mocking the Muslims was an evening not spent remembering God; every conversation about how foolish the believers were was a conversation in which God was absent — or present only as a subject of jest.

This is a precise account of a spiritual mechanism. Mockery is not merely an unkind act; it is an *occupying* act. It fills the mind with the object of contempt and with one's own sense of superiority to it. A person consumed with looking down on others has his gaze fixed downward and cannot look up. The Qur'an makes a similar point about the deniers' *wealth and children* in verse 55 and about *laghw* in verse 3: whatever fills the heart displaces God from it. In verse 110, the filler is mockery — and the tragedy is that the *objects* of the mockery were the very people whose prayer (v. 109) was the remembrance of God the deniers had forgotten. The believers were saying *rabbanā*; the deniers were laughing at them saying it; and in the laughing, the deniers forgot the One being addressed.

The phrase *dhikrī*, "My remembrance," has a double sense that the commentators noted. It can mean the deniers' remembrance *of* God — their own *dhikr*, which they neglected. Or it can mean God's *reminder* — the Qur'an, which the sūrah called *dhikrihim*, "their reminder," in verse 71. Both are true: the deniers forgot to remember God, and they forgot the Reminder He sent, because they were busy laughing at the people who had received it.

**"And You Used to Laugh at Them": Taḍḥakūn**

The verse closes by naming the act in its plainest form: *wa kuntum minhum taḍḥakūn* — "and you used to laugh at them." The verb *taḍḥakūn* is ordinary laughter — the sound of amusement — and its object is *minhum*, "at them." The continuous *kuntum ... taḍḥakūn* indicates habit: they laughed at the believers *as a practice*, over years. The word is deliberately plain. After the sophisticated diagnosis of the middle clause, the verse returns to the simple fact: you laughed. It was a joke to you. The people who said "our Lord, we have believed" were your entertainment.

The Qur'an's answer to this laughter is given in the sūrah's parallel passage: *"So today those who believed are laughing at the disbelievers, on adorned couches, observing. Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?"* (83:34–36). The laughter is returned — not as cruelty but as the exact reversal of a position. The ones who laughed become the ones laughed at; the ones on the ground become the ones on couches. And the returned laughter is not the believers' vengeance; it is the plain recognition, on the Day, of who was actually foolish.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah's Ending**

Verses 109–111 form a unit within the judgment scene, and verse 110 is its hinge. Verse 109 quoted the believers' prayer. Verse 110 shows the deniers' response to it — mockery — and the consequence — forgetting God. Verse 111 will show the outcome — the believers rewarded for their patience. The three verses together explain the sentence of verse 108. The deniers were told "do not speak to Me" because, in the world, they laughed at those who spoke to Him — and in laughing, stopped speaking to Him themselves. The silence imposed on them is the completion of a silence they chose.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 110 carries a double lesson for the believer. The first is a warning against *being* a mocker — in any form. Mockery of other people, especially of the sincere and the simple, is not a small sin; verse 110 shows it as the mechanism by which a whole people forgot God. The believer who finds himself laughing at another Muslim's piety, poverty, or earnestness — or at anyone's — should hear in his laughter the *samar* of the Quraysh. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"It is enough evil for a man that he despises his Muslim brother"* (Muslim 2564). And the Qur'an's command is direct: *"Let not a people ridicule another people; perhaps they may be better than them"* (49:11). The believers of verse 109 *were* better than their mockers, and the mockers found out too late.

The second lesson is a comfort for the believer who is *mocked*. The *farīq* of verse 109 were laughed at, and God recorded the laughter, and quoted it back to the laughers in the Fire. The believer who is mocked for his prayer, his modesty, his beliefs, or his refusal to join in what others enjoy is in the position of God's servants in verse 109 — and his mockers are in the position of verse 110. This does not license contempt in return; the sūrah has already commanded *"repel evil with what is better"* (v. 96). But it frees the believer from being wounded by laughter, because he knows whose laughter is recorded and whose will be returned. The Prophet ﷺ was mocked as a poet, a madman, a sorcerer — and he continued to pray, patiently, for the people who mocked him. Many of them later prayed beside him. The believer who endures mockery with patience is preparing for the next verse's word: *"I have rewarded them this Day for their patience."*

**Toward the Reward**

The mockery has been named. The next verse pronounces the believers' reward — and names the quality for which they receive it.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:111

> **Truly today I have rewarded them for having been patient. Truly they are the triumphant.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Reward Pronounced**

God has quoted the believers' prayer (v. 109) and named the deniers' mockery of it (v. 110). Verse 111 pronounces the outcome: *innī jazaytuhumu l-yawma bimā ṣabarū annahum humu l-fāʾizūn* — "Indeed, I have rewarded them this Day for their patience; indeed, they are the triumphant." The verse is addressed to the deniers in the Fire — it continues God's speech to them — but its subject is the believers. God tells the mockers what has become of the mocked: they have been rewarded, and they have won. The verse is the sūrah's final word on the believers before it turns to the closing questions about time and purpose, and it contains the second of the sūrah's three great words for the believers' outcome — *fāʾizūn*, the triumphant, alongside *mufliḥūn*, the successful (vv. 1, 102), and *wārithūn*, the inheritors (v. 10).

**"Indeed, I Have Rewarded Them This Day": Jazaytuhum**

The verb *jazaytuhum*, "I have rewarded them," is from the root *j-z-y*, recompense — the giving of what is due, whether good or bad. The first-person singular — *innī jazaytu*, "*I* have rewarded" — is the intimate, direct voice God used in verses 66 and 105 (*"My signs"*) and verse 109 (*"My servants"*). God Himself, not through an intermediary, has rewarded them. The perfect tense — "I *have* rewarded" — indicates completion: the reward is not promised but delivered. And *al-yawm*, "this Day," fixes it in the present of the judgment scene: today, while you burn, they are being rewarded.

The word *jazāʾ* is the same word for the deniers' recompense — the Qur'an uses it for both outcomes — and the sūrah's juxtaposition is precise. The deniers received *ikhsaʾū* (v. 108); the believers receive *jazaytuhum*. Both are recompense, exactly measured to what each did. The deniers mocked and were silenced; the believers were patient and are rewarded. Verse 62's promise — a record that speaks with truth, and no one wronged — is fulfilled on both sides at once.

**"For Their Patience": Bimā Ṣabarū**

The ground of the reward is *bimā ṣabarū* — "for what they patiently endured," "because they were patient." The verb *ṣabarū* is from the root *ṣ-b-r*, patience, steadfastness, endurance — the holding of oneself firm under pressure. Of all the qualities the sūrah has attributed to the believers — humble prayer, turning from vain talk, zakāh, chastity, trust-keeping, awe, faith in the signs, sincerity, trembling, hastening — the one named as the *ground* of the reward at this moment is *ṣabr*. Why?

Because *ṣabr* is what the mockery of verse 110 required of them. The believers were laughed at, ridiculed, made into a joke — for years, by the powerful of their society — and they did not abandon their faith, retaliate in kind, or lose the prayer of verse 109. That endurance is *ṣabr*, and it is the quality by which every other quality was preserved under pressure. A believer who prays humbly but abandons prayer when mocked has not kept the first quality; a believer who is patient keeps them all. The Qur'an describes the reward of *ṣabr* as uniquely unlimited: *"Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account"* (39:10). And it names *ṣabr* as the condition of triumph in its shortest sūrah: *"except those who believe and do righteous deeds and advise one another to truth and advise one another to patience"* (103:3).

The verse's *bimā ṣabarū* also answers the mockers' laughter directly. They laughed because the believers' patience looked like weakness — like people enduring what they could not change. Verse 111 declares that the patience was the *strength*, and that it is precisely what earned the reward. The thing the deniers found ridiculous is the thing God recompensed.

**"Indeed, They Are the Triumphant": Al-Fāʾizūn**

The verse's second half gives the believers' final designation: *annahum humu l-fāʾizūn* — "that they, they are the triumphant." The emphatic structure — *anna*, the pronoun *humu*, the definite *al-fāʾizūn* — is the same restrictive construction as verse 102's *humu l-mufliḥūn*: *they*, and no others, are the triumphant. The word *fāʾiz* is from the root *f-w-z*, which means to win, to attain what one sought, to escape what one feared — the double sense of triumph as both gaining and being saved. The Qur'an uses it for the ultimate outcome: *"Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed (fāza)"* (3:185); *"That is the great triumph (al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm)"* (a phrase repeated many times, e.g., 4:13; 9:72; 61:12).

The word completes the sūrah's vocabulary of success. *Falāḥ* (vv. 1, 102) is success as breaking through — the farmer's cleaving of the earth to reach the harvest. *Wirāthah* (vv. 10–11) is success as inheritance — receiving Firdaws as one's rightful portion. *Fawz* (v. 111) is success as triumph — winning the contest and escaping the danger. The three words describe the same outcome from three angles, and together they define what the sūrah means by "the believers have succeeded": they broke through, they inherited, they won.

The declaration is made *to the deniers*. God tells the mockers, in the Fire, that the people they laughed at are *al-fāʾizūn* — the winners. This is the final reversal of the sūrah's judgment scene. In the world, the deniers saw themselves as winners — wealthy, powerful, numerous — and the believers as losers, and verse 34 recorded their prediction that following the messenger would make one *"of the losers."* Verse 103 assigned the word *khasirū*, "lost," to the deniers; verse 111 assigns *fāʾizūn*, "triumphant," to the believers. The scoreboard the deniers read in the world has been inverted, and they are made to hear the final score.

**The Structure of the Judgment Scene Completed**

Verses 101–111 form the sūrah's judgment scene, and verse 111 closes it. The scene moved: from the Trumpet and the dissolution of kinship (101), to the scales (102–103), to the Fire and its faces (104), to the trial — charge, confession, plea, sentence (105–108) — to the believers' prayer, the mockery, and the reward (109–111). The scene began with everyone stripped of every bond and standing alone; it ends with the two groups in their final places, each hearing God's verdict. The deniers hear it as *ikhsaʾū*; the believers hear it as *jazaytuhum*. And the scene's last word about the believers — *fāʾizūn* — is the one the deniers must hear, because they need to know, finally and from God's own mouth, who won.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 111 gives the believer the name of the quality that carries all the others through to the end: *ṣabr*. The seven qualities of verses 1–9 and the four inner states of verses 57–60 describe what the believer does and feels; *ṣabr* is what keeps him doing and feeling it when it costs something — when he is mocked, when he is poor, when the wait is long, when the promise seems delayed (v. 95). The Prophet ﷺ said: *"No one has been given a gift better and more comprehensive than patience"* (al-Bukhārī 1469; Muslim 1053). Verse 111 shows why: it is the gift for which God says *jazaytuhum* — I have rewarded them — on the Day when nothing else can be added to the scale.

The verse also fixes the believer's understanding of what "winning" is. The world will tell him he is losing — losing pleasure, losing status, losing the approval of the laughing majority. The sūrah tells him that *al-fāʾizūn* is a word pronounced on the Day, by God, to the ones who laughed, about the ones who were patient. The believer who holds this does not need the world's scoreboard. He has the sūrah's, and it ends with his name on the winning side.

**Toward the Question of Time**

The believers have won and the deniers have lost. God now asks the losers one more question — about how long they think they lived — and the answer reveals how the whole of their earthly life looks from the far side of the Judgment.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:112

> **He will say, “How many years did you tarry on earth?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**A Question About Time**

The judgment has been pronounced: the believers triumphant (v. 111), the deniers silenced (v. 108). Now God asks the deniers one more question — not about their deeds but about their *time*: *qāla kam labithtum fī l-arḍi ʿadada sinīn* — "He will say: 'How long did you remain on earth, in number of years?'" The question seems, at first, to change the subject. After the trial and the sentence, why ask how many years they lived? The answer emerges over the next three verses: the question is designed to make the deniers themselves confess how *short* their earthly life was — and, by implication, how absurd it was to trade an eternity for it. The verse is the opening of the sūrah's final argument, an argument about proportion.

**"He Will Say": Qāla**

The speaker is God, continuing the direct address that began in verse 105. The verb *qāla* is in the perfect tense — "He said" — though it refers to a future event; the Qur'an frequently uses the perfect for the events of the Day of Judgment to express their certainty: what God has decreed is as good as done. Some readings have *qul*, "Say," making it a command to an angel or to the Prophet ﷺ; the majority reading *qāla* keeps the question in God's own voice. The commentators noted the tension with verse 108's *"do not speak to Me"*: if the deniers were forbidden to speak, how do they answer this question? The resolution offered by al-Rāzī and others is that verse 108's prohibition concerns *pleading* — the deniers may no longer petition for release — while the question of verse 112 is a *judicial* question, to which they are compelled to respond, as a convicted man may be made to answer the court even after sentence. Others held that the prohibition applies only after the final entry into the Fire, and this exchange precedes it. Either way, the deniers' answer in verse 113 is not a plea but a confession, extracted for the purpose the following verses reveal.

**"How Long Did You Remain on Earth?": Kam Labithtum**

The verb *labithtum* is from the root *l-b-th*, "to remain, to stay, to tarry" — to spend time in a place. The Qur'an uses it for durations: Noah *"remained among them a thousand years less fifty"* (29:14); the Companions of the Cave *"remained in their cave three hundred years"* (18:25). The question *kam labithtum*, "how long did you remain," asks for a duration. The phrase *fī l-arḍ*, "on the earth," specifies the place — the earth that was the field of their scattering (v. 79), the site of their wealth and children (v. 55), the stage of their mockery (v. 110). And the phrase *ʿadada sinīn*, "in number of years," asks for a count: not an impression but a figure.

The commentators discussed whether "on the earth" means the duration of their *lives* or the duration of their stay *in the graves* (since the earth also contains the dead). Both readings have support, and the answer in verse 113 — "a day or part of a day" — fits either: the life of the denier and his time in the *barzakh* both appear, from the Day of Judgment, as almost nothing. The primary sense, however, is the life lived — the years of denial, accumulation, and laughter — because the argument that follows (v. 115: *"did you think We created you in play?"*) concerns what they did with their *lives*, not their graves.

**Why God Asks for a Number**

The question asks for a *count* — *ʿadada sinīn*, a number of years — and the request for precision is part of the rhetorical design. In the world, the deniers counted. They counted their wealth (v. 55: *yaḥsabūna*, "they reckon"); they counted their children; they measured their years and expected many more. The Qur'an describes their attitude: *"He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal"* (104:3); *"They said, 'There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live'"* (v. 37). Now God asks them to count again — and the count, as the next verse will show, comes out shockingly small. The men who counted everything are asked for the one number that matters, and cannot give a large one.

The question also invites the deniers to *compare*. They are in the Fire, which is *khulūd*, abiding (v. 103) — endless. And they are asked how many years they spent on earth — a finite number, however large. The juxtaposition of the infinite and the finite is the question's real content. It asks, in effect: *for how many years did you purchase this eternity?* The answer, in verse 113, will be devastating in its smallness.

**The Perception of Time From the Other Side**

The question of verse 112 opens one of the Qur'an's most consistent teachings: that the earthly life, which seems long while one is in it, appears vanishingly brief from the vantage of the Hereafter. The Qur'an returns to this repeatedly. *"On the Day they see it, it will be as though they had not remained except an evening or a morning thereof"* (79:46). *"On the Day the Hour appears, the criminals will swear they had remained but an hour"* (30:55). *"As if they had not remained but an hour of the day"* (10:45; 46:35). *"They will whisper among themselves, 'You remained not but ten [days]'... the best of them in conduct will say, 'You remained not but one day'"* (20:103–104). The perception of time is relative to what surrounds it. A lifetime measured against the endless Day shrinks to an evening. The question of verse 112 makes the deniers perform this measurement themselves.

**The Verse's Place in the Sūrah's Argument**

Verse 112 begins the sūrah's closing movement (vv. 112–118), which turns from the *judgment* of the deniers to the *meaning* of the whole affair. The sūrah has established who succeeded and who lost; now it asks *why the loss was so foolish*. The answer will unfold: the earthly life was a day or less (v. 113); the deniers wasted it because they did not know its brevity (v. 114); they assumed they were created in play and would not return (v. 115); but God is the True Sovereign, and there is no god but He (v. 116); so whoever calls on another god will be held to account and will not succeed (v. 117). The question of verse 112 is the first step in this reasoning: it establishes the brevity of the life that was wasted.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 112 asks the believer to count his own years — now, while the count still matters. *Kam labithta fī l-arḍ?* How long has he been on the earth? Twenty years, forty, sixty? And how do they seem from within — long, full, substantial? The verse tells him how they will seem from the other side: as the next verse says, a day or part of a day. The believer who holds both perceptions at once — the years as they feel now and as they will look then — lives with the right sense of proportion. He does not treat the earthly life as endless, because he knows it will look like an evening; and he does not treat it as worthless, because he knows that its brief hours are the only ones in which the heavy scale (v. 102) can be filled.

The Prophet ﷺ taught this proportion with an image. He said: *"What have I to do with the world? I and the world are but like a rider who took shade under a tree, then went on and left it"* (al-Tirmidhī 2377; Ibn Mājah 4109). The shade of a tree, on a long journey — that is *kam labithtum* answered rightly. The believer who sees his life as the rider's pause does not build his house in the shade; he rests, gives thanks, and rides on toward the destination. The deniers built their houses in the shade and are now asked, in the Fire, how long the shade lasted.

**Toward the Answer**

The question has been asked. The next verse gives the deniers' answer — and it is a number so small that they immediately disown it and refer God to those who counted better.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:113

> **They will say, “We tarried a day or part of a day. But ask those who keep count.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Answer**

God asked the deniers how many years they remained on earth (v. 112). Verse 113 gives their answer: *qālū labithnā yawman aw baʿḍa yawmin fa-sʾali l-ʿāddīn* — "They will say: 'We remained a day or part of a day; but ask those who keep count.'" The answer has two parts: an estimate and a deferral. The estimate is astonishingly small — a day, or less. The deferral admits that even this estimate is uncertain and refers the question to others who kept better track. The verse records the moment at which the deniers, who once thought the earth was everything (v. 37), discover that their whole tenure on it amounts, in retrospect, to less than a single day.

**"We Remained a Day or Part of a Day"**

The estimate *yawman aw baʿḍa yawmin* — "a day or part of a day" — is the Qur'an's fixed expression for the perceived brevity of a completed span when seen from beyond it. The man who passed by the ruined town and was made to die for a hundred years said, on being raised: *"I have remained a day or part of a day"* (2:259). The Companions of the Cave, waking after three centuries, said: *"We have remained a day or part of a day"* (18:19). And of the resurrected in general: *"On the Day He will gather them, as if they had not remained but an hour of the day"* (10:45). The phrase expresses the strange collapse of duration that occurs when a span is over and one looks back on it from a wholly different scale.

The deniers' estimate is not a lie; it is their honest perception. From the Day of Judgment — which the Qur'an describes as *"a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years"* (70:4) — and from within the eternity of the Fire (v. 103), the sixty or seventy years of a human life appear as a flicker. The commentators noted a further reason for the perception: the deniers' lives were spent in *ghamrah*, heedlessness (vv. 54, 63), and heedless time leaves no substance in memory — it passes like sleep, and one wakes with the sense of having barely closed one's eyes. The believers' years were full of remembrance and deeds, and would be remembered; the deniers' years were full of *laghw* and *samar* (v. 67), and collapse to nothing. The estimate "a day or part of a day" is thus not only the effect of the Day's scale but the honest measure of a life that contained nothing lasting.

**The Contrast With Their Former Confidence**

The estimate must be set against what the deniers believed while they were alive. They said: *"There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live"* (v. 37) — the world was everything, and its span was the whole of existence. They measured their years as a possession and expected them to be many; the *mutraf* of verse 64 lived as though his ease would not end. Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, given wealth and sons and a spread-out life, *"desires that I should add more"* (74:15). Now, asked to count, they say: *a day*. The life for which they sold their souls (v. 103: *khasirū anfusahum*) was, by their own reckoning in the Fire, less than twenty-four hours. The trade is exposed in its full absurdity: an eternity in Jahannam purchased with a single day's ease.

**"But Ask Those Who Keep Count": Fa-sʾali l-ʿĀddīn**

The second half of the answer is a deferral: *fa-sʾali l-ʿāddīn* — "so ask those who count," "ask the reckoners." The word *ʿāddīn* is from the root *ʿ-d-d*, to count, to number — the same root as *ʿadad*, "number," in God's question (*ʿadada sinīn*, "number of years"). God asked for a number; the deniers cannot give one and refer Him to those who can. Who are the *ʿāddūn*? The commentators offered several identifications, all plausible. The angels who recorded their deeds and days — the *kirāman kātibīn*, "noble scribes" (82:11), who know the count exactly. Or the human beings who kept calendars and chronicles in the world. Or, in a general sense, "whoever was counting" — anyone but us, because we did not count and cannot now.

The deferral reveals a striking humility, or rather a striking loss of confidence. The men who *reckoned* everything in the world (v. 55: *yaḥsabūna*) now confess that they cannot reckon the most basic fact about themselves — how long they lived. Their confusion (*ghamrah*) has followed them into the Fire in this one respect: they are disoriented about time, uncertain whether it was a day or less, and dependent on others for the answer. The men who were sure of everything are sure of nothing, not even their own lifespan.

There is also, the commentators suggested, an element of *evasion* in the deferral. The deniers may sense where the question is leading — that their small number will be used against them (v. 114: "you remained only a little") — and prefer not to commit to a figure. "Ask the reckoners" is the answer of one who does not want to say a number that will condemn him. If so, the evasion fails: God's response (v. 114) accepts their own estimate and turns it on them.

**The Believers' Different Perception**

The Qur'an suggests that the *believers'* perception of their earthly life, from the Hereafter, is different in quality if not in duration. The best of them will also say *"you remained not but one day"* (20:104) — but for them the brevity is a relief and a wonder, not a horror: a short trial, quickly over, and then the endless reward. The Prophet ﷺ described the exchange: *"The most miserable person in the world among the people of Paradise will be brought and dipped once in Paradise, and it will be said, 'O son of Adam, have you ever seen misery?' And he will say, 'No, by God, my Lord'"* (Muslim 2807). One dip in Paradise erases the memory of a lifetime's hardship; one dip in the Fire, the same ḥadīth says, erases the memory of a lifetime's ease. For both groups, the earthly life shrinks to nothing; for one, it shrinks into eternal relief, and for the other, into eternal regret.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 113 gives the believer a measurement to live by: his life, however long it feels, will look from the other side like *a day or part of a day*. This is not a depressing thought but a clarifying one. It means that whatever hardship he is enduring — the illness, the poverty, the mockery, the long wait — is *part of a day*, and will be remembered as such. And it means that whatever he is tempted to sell his soul for — the ease, the status, the forbidden pleasure — is worth *part of a day* at most, and cannot be a reasonable price for anything eternal. The deniers' estimate in the Fire is the believer's calculation in the world: a day's ease against an eternity is a bad trade; a day's patience for an eternity is a magnificent one.

The verse also warns against arriving at the Judgment unable to account for one's time. The deniers said "ask the reckoners" because they had not reckoned. The believer is asked to be his own *ʿādd* — to count his days, to know what he did with them, to be able to answer the question of verse 112 not with confusion but with an account. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: *"Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account, and weigh your deeds before they are weighed for you."* The believer who does this will not need to say "ask those who keep count." He will have kept it.

**Toward God's Confirmation**

The deniers have estimated a day and deferred the count. God's response will accept their estimate and draw from it the lesson they should have drawn while there was time.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:114

> **He will say, “You tarried but a little, if you but knew.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Confirmation and the Lesson**

The deniers have said they remained on earth a day or part of a day, and have deferred the count to others (v. 113). Verse 114 gives God's response: *qāla in labithtum illā qalīlan law annakum kuntum taʿlamūn* — "He will say: 'You remained only a little — if only you had known.'" The response accepts the deniers' own estimate — yes, it was little — and then adds the clause that turns the estimate into an indictment: *if only you had known*. The verse is the pivot of the sūrah's closing argument. The brevity of earthly life, which the deniers have just confessed, was *knowable* in the world. They did not know it — or did not act as if they knew — and that failure is the root of everything they lost.

**"You Remained Only a Little": In Labithtum Illā Qalīlan**

The construction *in ... illā*, "not ... except," is restrictive: you remained *nothing but* a little. God confirms the smallness. The word *qalīl*, "little, few, small," is the word the sūrah used in verse 78 — *qalīlan mā tashkurūn*, "little is it that you give thanks" — and the echo is meaningful: little gratitude for the faculties, and little time in which to have shown it. The earthly life was *qalīl* in duration; the deniers' use of it was *qalīl* in substance. The two littlenesses compound each other: a short life, and almost nothing made of it.

The confirmation is important because it is God's. The deniers' estimate "a day or part of a day" might have been dismissed as the distorted perception of the terrified. God does not dismiss it; He ratifies it. From the standpoint of the Truth (v. 116: *al-Malik al-Ḥaqq*), the earthly life *is* little — not merely seems so. This is the Qur'an's consistent teaching about the world: *"Say, 'The enjoyment of this world is little (qalīl), and the Hereafter is better for he who fears God'"* (4:77); *"And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion"* (3:185); *"What is the life of this world compared to the Hereafter except [brief] enjoyment"* (13:26). Verse 114 places these teachings in God's mouth at the moment of judgment: what I told you was little was little.

**"If Only You Had Known": Law Annakum Kuntum Taʿlamūn**

The second clause is the verse's blade: *law annakum kuntum taʿlamūn* — "if only you had known." The particle *law*, "if only, had it been that," expresses a counterfactual regret — a condition that was not met and whose non-fulfillment had consequences. The verb *taʿlamūn*, "you know," is the same verb that closed God's questions in verses 84 and 88: *in kuntum taʿlamūn*, "if you know." There, the phrase challenged the deniers to display knowledge of who owns the earth; here, it laments their failure to know the one thing that would have changed everything — the brevity of their stay.

The clause has been read in two ways, and both are true. First: "You remained only a little — *if only you had known that* [in the world]." That is: had you known, while alive, that your life was a day or less, you would not have spent it as you did; you would not have traded the eternal for the momentary; you would have hastened to good (v. 61) instead of laughing at those who did (v. 110). Second: "You remained only a little — *if only you knew* [now, fully]." That is: even now you do not fully grasp how little it was; if you did, your regret would be beyond bearing. The first reading is the more prominent, because it connects to the sūrah's whole argument: the deniers were *told* — by every messenger (vv. 23–52), by the Qur'an (v. 66), by death itself (v. 15) — that life was short and the return was certain, and they did not *know* it in the sense that matters: the knowledge that shapes action.

**Knowledge That Shapes Action**

The verse raises the question of what it means to *know* something. The deniers, in one sense, knew that life was short — everyone knows this; they had buried their fathers. But their knowledge was inert, like their knowledge that God owns the earth (v. 85). They knew and did not remember (v. 85: *a-fa-lā tadhakkarūn*); knew and did not use reason (v. 80); knew and were bewitched (v. 89). Verse 114's *law annakum kuntum taʿlamūn* names the failure precisely: not ignorance of the fact, but the absence of the *operative* knowledge that lets a fact govern a life. The Qur'an distinguishes the two throughout: *"They know what is apparent of the worldly life, but they, of the Hereafter, are unaware"* (30:7). The deniers knew the apparent — how to trade, how to count wealth, how to mock — and did not know the one thing that made the apparent meaningful.

This is why the sūrah has insisted, from verse 68 onward, on *tadabbur* (pondering), *taʿaqqul* (reasoning), and *tadhakkur* (remembering). These are the activities by which inert knowledge becomes operative. A person who ponders death, reasons from the alternation of night and day (v. 80), and remembers the return (v. 60) *knows* that life is little — and lives accordingly. The deniers did none of these and so did not know, in the sense of verse 114, what they could have known.

**The Argument From Proportion Completed**

Verses 112–114 form an argument, and verse 114 completes it. God asked: how long? (112). They answered: a day or less (113). God confirmed: little — if only you had known (114). The argument's conclusion is implicit but unmistakable: *you traded an eternity for a day, and you could have known the exchange rate*. Every warning the sūrah issued — the seizure of the affluent (v. 64), the gate of severe punishment (v. 77), the death that arrives (v. 99), the barrier (v. 100), the scales (vv. 102–103) — was information about the exchange rate. The deniers had the information and treated the day as though it were everything. The Fire is not an arbitrary penalty for this; it is the other side of the exchange they chose.

**The Believers Knew**

The verse's counterfactual — "if only you had known" — implies that some *did* know. The believers of the sūrah knew that life was little. Their trembling at the return (v. 60), their hastening to good (v. 61), their patience under mockery (v. 111) — all of these are the behavior of people who *knew* that their stay was a day or less and that the Day to come was endless. They did not need to be told in the Fire; they lived as though they had already been told. The Prophet ﷺ modeled the knowledge: *"Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a traveler"* (al-Bukhārī 6416). A traveler knows he is passing through; the deniers thought they were home.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 114 offers the believer the knowledge the deniers lacked, *in time to use it*. The verse is recited to the deniers in the Fire; it is recited to the believer in the world. He can hear "you remained only a little — if only you had known" as addressed to himself *now*, and answer: I know. I know that this life is a day or part of a day. I know that the eternity on the other side is real. I know the exchange rate. And knowing, I will not trade the eternal for the momentary. This is the operative knowledge the verse names, and it is available to anyone who ponders the verse rather than merely reading it.

The verse also gives the believer a way to bear the hardships of the "little." Whatever he suffers is *qalīl* — little in duration, whatever its intensity. The Qur'an promises: *"So indeed, with hardship comes ease"* (94:5–6), and the *ease* that follows the *little* is endless. The believer who knows that his trial is part of a day, and his reward is the Day without end, has the proportion right — and having it right is exactly what verse 114 says the deniers, to their eternal cost, did not.

**Toward the Question of Purpose**

The deniers thought their brief life was everything. The next verse asks what that assumption implied about their Creator — and exposes it as the deepest error of all.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:115

> **“Did you suppose, then, that We created you frivolously, and that you would not be returned unto Us?”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Root Error Named**

God has confirmed that the deniers' earthly life was little, and lamented that they did not know it (v. 114). Verse 115 asks what assumption lay beneath their failure to know: *a-fa-ḥasibtum annamā khalaqnākum ʿabathan wa annakum ilaynā lā turjaʿūn* — "Did you then think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?" The question exposes the premise behind everything the deniers did. They lived as though life were short and meaningless — a day of play with no sequel — because they assumed, at bottom, that their creation had no purpose and no consequence. The verse names this assumption and, by framing it as an incredulous question, reveals it as the absurdity it is. It is the sūrah's most fundamental verse about *why* human beings exist.

**"Did You Then Think": A-fa-ḥasibtum**

The verb *ḥasibtum*, "you thought, you reckoned," is the verb of verse 55 — *a-yaḥsabūna*, "do they reckon?" — where the deniers miscalculated the meaning of their wealth. The same verb returns for their deepest miscalculation. The interrogative *a-* with the connective *fa-* ("did you *then*...?") links this question to the preceding verses: *given* that you lived as you did — mocking, accumulating, denying — did you *therefore* suppose that you were created for nothing? The question does not accuse the deniers of having stated this belief; few would say aloud "I was created in vain." It accuses them of having *lived* it — of conducting themselves as though it were true. Their behavior implied the premise; the verse makes the premise explicit and asks them to own it.

**"That We Created You in Vain": ʿAbathan**

The word *ʿabath* means play, idle sport, frivolity, purposeless activity — action with no aim beyond itself, like a child's fidgeting or a bored man's doodling. To create *ʿabathan* would be to create for no reason, with no design, toward no end. The Qur'an denies this of God's creation in the strongest terms: *"And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play (lāʿibīn)"* (21:16); *"And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain (bāṭilan). That is the assumption of those who disbelieve"* (38:27); *"Does man think that he will be left neglected (sudan)?"* (75:36). Each of these verses names purposelessness as the specifically *disbelieving* assumption — the belief that lies beneath the denier's way of life even when he does not articulate it.

The argument implicit in the word *ʿabath* is theological and rational at once. God is *al-Ḥakīm*, the Wise; wisdom does not act without purpose. God is *al-Malik al-Ḥaqq*, the True Sovereign (v. 116, next); a true sovereign does not create subjects and then abandon them to no end. The sūrah has displayed the *design* of creation in detail — the stages of the embryo (vv. 12–14), the measured rain (v. 18), the cattle fitted for human use (v. 21), the faculties of hearing, sight, and heart (v. 78). Design at every level, and no purpose at the summit? The very intricacy the sūrah described refutes *ʿabath*. A creation this deliberate has an aim, and the aim, as the second half of the verse states, is the return.

**"And That You Would Not Be Returned to Us": Ilaynā Lā Turjaʿūn**

The second half of the question names the consequence of the first: *wa annakum ilaynā lā turjaʿūn* — "and that you would not be returned to Us." The two clauses are linked by *wa*, "and," and they are logically inseparable. To be created in vain and to have no return are the same proposition seen from two ends. If there is no return — no reckoning, no judgment, no consequence — then the creation *was* in vain, because nothing that happened in it mattered finally. And if the creation was in vain, then there is no reason for a return. The deniers held the second (v. 37: *"we will not be resurrected"*) and thereby, without admitting it, held the first.

The verb *turjaʿūn*, "you are returned," is from the root *r-j-ʿ* — the root of the believers' *rājiʿūn*, "they will return" (v. 60), and of the dying denier's *irjiʿūn*, "send me back" (v. 99). The sūrah has used the word for the return *to God* (v. 60) and the plea to return *from death* (v. 99); verse 115 uses it for the return the deniers denied. The prepositional phrase *ilaynā*, "to Us," is placed before the verb for emphasis: to *Us* — not to dust, not to nothing, but to the One who created. The return is the completion of the creation: what came from God goes back to God, and the going-back is where the purpose is fulfilled.

**The Purpose That Replaces ʿAbath**

If human beings were not created in vain, what were they created for? The sūrah has answered throughout, and the Qur'an states it elsewhere in one sentence: *"And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me"* (51:56). The purpose is *ʿibādah* — worship, service, the recognition of the Owner by the owned (v. 84) and the corresponding life. The messengers' single sentence was this purpose stated as command: *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him"* (vv. 23, 32). The believers' portraits (vv. 1–9, 57–61) are this purpose lived. And the return (*rujūʿ*) is where the purpose is *assessed*: the scales (vv. 102–103) weigh how far each person fulfilled what he was created for. The sūrah's structure — creation (vv. 12–16), test (v. 30), history of response (vv. 23–52), judgment (vv. 101–111) — is the structure of a purposeful creation with a return. Verse 115 asks the deniers whether they really thought it was otherwise.

**The Verse as the Sūrah's Question**

Verse 115 is, in a sense, the question the whole sūrah has been asking. Every argument — from the embryo, from the heavens, from the rain, from the cattle, from the histories, from the faculties, from the alternation of night and day — was an argument that creation is *purposeful* and therefore *accountable*. Every denial — "a man like you," "dust and bones," "fables of the ancients" — was a refusal to draw the conclusion. Verse 115 states the conclusion the deniers refused and asks them, in the Fire, whether their refusal was reasonable. Did you *really* think this was all for nothing? The question needs no answer. The setting in which it is asked *is* the answer.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 115 gives the believer the foundation of meaning that the modern world most conspicuously lacks. The pervasive assumption of much contemporary thought is precisely *ʿabath*: that existence is accidental, that consciousness is an unintended byproduct, that there is no return and therefore no final significance to anything. The verse names this assumption and locates it: it is the assumption of the people in the Fire, exposed by God's incredulous question. The believer who lives by the verse has an answer to the question "what is it all for?" that the denier does not: he was created *on purpose*, by a Wise Sovereign, for worship, and he will be *returned* to the One who made him, where what he did will matter completely. This is not a consoling fiction; the sūrah has argued it from the structure of the world.

The verse also asks the believer whether his *life* reflects the belief his tongue professes. A Muslim may affirm that he was not created in vain and will be returned to God, and yet live — in his use of time, his priorities, his treatment of the "little" (v. 114) — as though *ʿabath* were true. The deniers of verse 115 did not *say* they were created in vain; they *lived* it. The believer must ensure that his life says what his creed says: that every hour is purposeful because it is heading toward a return. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"The feet of a servant will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about his life — how he spent it; his knowledge — what he did with it; his wealth — how he earned it and spent it; and his body — how he used it"* (al-Tirmidhī 2417; graded ṣaḥīḥ). Four questions, all presupposing that nothing was *ʿabath*. The believer who lives ready for them has answered verse 115 rightly.

**Toward the Sovereign**

The deniers assumed a purposeless creation and no return. The next verse states what is actually true of the One who created them — and the statement is a doxology.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:116

> **So, exalted is God, the True Sovereign; there is no god but He, Lord of the noble Throne.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Doxology After the Question**

God asked the deniers whether they thought they were created in vain and would not be returned (v. 115). Verse 116 answers with a declaration of who God actually is: *fa-taʿālā llāhu l-maliku l-ḥaqqu lā ilāha illā huwa rabbu l-ʿarshi l-karīm* — "So exalted is God, the True Sovereign; there is no god but He, Lord of the Noble Throne." The particle *fa-*, "so, therefore," draws the verse as a conclusion from the preceding: *because* creation is not in vain and the return is real, God is exalted above the deniers' assumption. The verse is a doxology — a proclamation of God's glory — placed at the end of the judgment scene as its theological summary. Everything the sūrah has argued about God is gathered here into four titles: the Exalted, the True Sovereign, the only God, the Lord of the Noble Throne.

**"So Exalted Is God": Fa-taʿālā llāh**

The verb *taʿālā*, "is exalted, is high above," is the verb of verse 92 — *fa-taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn*, "exalted is He above what they associate." There, God was exalted above the partners the deniers ascribed; here, He is exalted above the *purposelessness* they assumed. To think that God created in vain is to think of Him as a child at play or an idle man doodling — and God is *exalted* above such a conception. The word carries the sense of *transcendence*: God is not merely different from what the deniers imagined but *above* it, in a higher order altogether. The idea of *ʿabath* (v. 115) cannot reach Him.

**"The True Sovereign": Al-Malik al-Ḥaqq**

The first title is *al-Malik al-Ḥaqq*, "the True King," "the Sovereign in Truth." The word *malik*, king, sovereign, is from the root *m-l-k*, the root of *mulk* (dominion) and *malakūt* (v. 88: "the dominion of everything"). God is *al-Malik* — the King, one of His names (59:23; 62:1) — and the sūrah's three questions established the scope of His kingship: the earth (v. 84), the heavens and the Throne (v. 86), everything (v. 88). The addition of *al-Ḥaqq*, "the True," distinguishes His kingship from every other. Human kings are kings in name, by convention, for a time, over a portion; God is King *in truth* — by reality, forever, over all. The Qur'an makes the contrast on the Day of Judgment: *"To whom belongs sovereignty this Day? To God, the One, the Prevailing"* (40:16); *"The true sovereignty (al-mulk al-ḥaqq), that Day, is for the Most Merciful"* (25:26).

The title answers verse 115's *ʿabath* directly. A *true* King does not create subjects in vain. Kingship implies governance, law, accountability, reward and punishment — everything the deniers denied. To say God is *al-Malik al-Ḥaqq* is to say that creation is a *kingdom*, ordered by a real Sovereign, in which every subject will be called to account. The judgment scene the sūrah has just described (vv. 101–111) is the King's court in session. And the word *al-Ḥaqq* echoes the sūrah's insistence that God brought the deniers *the truth* (vv. 70, 90) and that truth does not follow desire (v. 71). The King is the Truth; His kingdom runs on it.

**"There Is No God but He": Lā Ilāha Illā Huwa**

The second title is the *kalimat al-tawḥīd*, the sentence of divine unity: *lā ilāha illā huwa* — "there is no god but He." It is the sūrah's messengers' message stated in its canonical form. Noah said: *"Worship God; you have no god other than Him (mā lakum min ilāhin ghayruhu)"* (v. 23); the second messenger repeated it (v. 32); and now, after the argument from cosmic order (v. 91) and the three admissions (vv. 85, 87, 89), the sentence is stated by God Himself as the settled truth. *Lā ilāha illā huwa* — the negation of every false god and the affirmation of the one true One — is the thing every messenger came to say and the thing the deniers refused. The verse places it at the sūrah's summit.

The Prophet ﷺ described this sentence as the best thing he and the prophets before him ever said: *"The best of what I and the prophets before me have said is: there is no god but God alone, without partner"* (al-Tirmidhī 3585; Mālik). It is the key to Paradise, the word by which a person enters Islam, the last thing the believer hopes to say before death (Abū Dāwūd 3116), and the card that outweighs the ninety-nine scrolls (al-Tirmidhī 2639). Its appearance in verse 116 is the sūrah's affirmation that everything it has argued reduces to this.

**"Lord of the Noble Throne": Rabb al-ʿArsh al-Karīm**

The third title is *rabb al-ʿarsh al-karīm* — "Lord of the Noble Throne." The Throne appeared in verse 86 as *al-ʿarsh al-ʿaẓīm*, "the Great Throne"; here it is *al-karīm*, "the Noble, the Generous, the Honored." The two adjectives complete each other. *ʿAẓīm* names the Throne's magnitude — the greatest of created things; *karīm* names its dignity and its bounty — the seat from which all good descends. The word *karīm* is also one of God's own names (*al-Karīm*, the Generous, 82:6), and its application to the Throne suggests that the Throne is the source of generosity because its Lord is generous. The sūrah, which is about to end with a prayer for mercy (v. 118), names the Throne *karīm* as the place from which the mercy comes. The Prophet ﷺ taught the believers to ask for Firdaws because *"above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful"* (al-Bukhārī 2790, cited under verse 11): the Throne is the roof of the believers' reward and the seat of the Most Merciful. That is why it is *karīm*.

The title also completes the sūrah's cosmology. Verse 17 named the seven paths above; verse 86 named the seven heavens and the Great Throne; verse 116 names the Noble Throne as the seat of the True Sovereign. From the extract of clay (v. 12) to the Lord of the Noble Throne (v. 116), the sūrah has traced the whole span of existence, and it places God at the summit — as King, as the only God, and as Lord of the highest created thing.

**The Four Titles as a Summary**

The four titles of verse 116 summarize the sūrah's theology in order. *Taʿālā*: God is transcendent, above the deniers' conceptions — above partners (v. 92) and above purposelessness (v. 115). *Al-Malik al-Ḥaqq*: God is the real Sovereign, whose kingdom is ordered and accountable — the ground of the judgment scene (vv. 101–111) and the answer to *ʿabath*. *Lā ilāha illā huwa*: God is one, without partner — the messengers' message (vv. 23, 32) and the conclusion of the argument from order (v. 91). *Rabb al-ʿarsh al-karīm*: God is the Lord of the highest, the source of all generosity — the seat from which the believers' reward (v. 11) and the sūrah's final mercy (v. 118) descend. A reader who has understood these four titles has understood what the sūrah has been saying about God from its first verse.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 116 gives the believer a creed in one sentence and a sanctuary in one recitation. The Prophet ﷺ taught that a specific supplication for distress includes exactly these titles: *"There is no god but God, the Great, the Forbearing; there is no god but God, Lord of the Great Throne; there is no god but God, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth and Lord of the Noble Throne (rabb al-ʿarsh al-karīm)"* (al-Bukhārī 6346; Muslim 2730). The words of verse 116 are, in this ḥadīth, the words of the believer in trouble — because to remember that God is the True Sovereign, the only God, and the Lord of the Noble Throne is to remember that nothing in the trouble is outside His kingdom, and that the seat from which help comes is *karīm*, generous.
