The verse also settles the believer's understanding of his own purpose, against the *ʿabath* of verse 115. He is the subject of a True King — not a stray particle in a purposeless cosmos but a servant in a kingdom, with a Sovereign who sees, a law to keep, and a court to which he will be summoned. This is a dignifying thought. To be created in vain is to be nothing; to be created by *al-Malik al-Ḥaqq* is to be someone whose life matters to the King. The believer who says *lā ilāha illā huwa* with understanding has placed himself in that kingdom, under that Throne, and can live with the seriousness and the hope that the position deserves.

**Toward the Final Warning and the Final Prayer**

God has been exalted as the True Sovereign. Two verses remain. The first will state the consequence for anyone who calls on another god beside Him — and will close the frame the sūrah opened with its first word. The second will give the sūrah's last prayer.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:117

> **Whosoever calls upon another god along with God, for which he has no proof, his reckoning is with God. Truly the disbelievers will not prosper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Frame Closes**

The sūrah opened with a declaration: *qad aflaḥa l-muʾminūn* — "Truly the believers have succeeded" (v. 1). Its penultimate verse closes the frame with the declaration's mirror: *innahu lā yufliḥu l-kāfirūn* — "Truly the disbelievers will not succeed." The same root — *f-l-ḥ* — the same emphatic construction, the same word *falāḥ* that named the sūrah's subject at its first breath. Between the two declarations lie 115 verses that have shown what success is, who attains it, who forfeits it, and why. Verse 117 is the sūrah's judgment stated as a general law: *man yadʿu maʿa llāhi ilāhan ākhara lā burhāna lahu bihi fa-innamā ḥisābuhu ʿinda rabbihi innahu lā yufliḥu l-kāfirūn* — "And whoever calls upon another god with God, for which he has no proof — his account is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed."

**"Whoever Calls Upon Another God With God"**

The verse begins with a universal conditional: *man yadʿu*, "whoever calls upon." The verb *yadʿū* is from the root *d-ʿ-w*, "to call, to invoke, to pray to" — the root of *duʿāʾ*, supplication, and of *daʿwah*, the call to God (v. 73: *"you are calling them to a straight path"*). To *call upon* a god is to direct one's prayer, hope, and dependence toward it — the essential act of worship. The object is *ilāhan ākhara maʿa llāh* — "another god *with* God." The phrase does not describe the atheist who denies God altogether but the *mushrik* who acknowledges God and adds another beside Him — exactly the position of the Quraysh, who said "God" when asked who owns the earth (v. 85) and then called on al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā. The word *maʿa*, "with," is the word of *shirk*: association, the placing of a partner *alongside*.

The verse thus returns, at the sūrah's close, to its central charge. The messengers said: *"you have no god other than Him"* (vv. 23, 32). The argument from order proved: *"nor is there any god with Him (maʿahu)"* (v. 91). The doxology declared: *"there is no god but He"* (v. 116). Verse 117 states the consequence for whoever ignores all of this and calls on another god *maʿa llāh*.

**"For Which He Has No Proof": Lā Burhāna Lahu Bihi**

The parenthetical clause *lā burhāna lahu bihi* — "he has no proof for it" — is a description, not a condition. It does not mean "if he happens to have no proof" (as though some might); it means that *no one* who calls on another god has proof, because there is none to have. The word *burhān*, proof, demonstration, decisive evidence, is the Qur'an's term for the argument that settles a matter: *"Say, 'Bring your proof (burhānakum), if you should be truthful'"* (2:111; 27:64); *"Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say, 'Bring your proof'"* (21:24). The Qur'an issues the challenge repeatedly and records that it is never met. The sūrah itself has shown why: the three questions (vv. 84–89) established that the deniers' own beliefs contradict their idolatry; the argument from order (v. 91) established that a second god is impossible. There is no *burhān* for *shirk* because *shirk* is false, and falsehood has no proof.

The clause also contrasts with the believers' position. The sūrah's faith is *grounded*: it has argued from the embryo, the heavens, the rain, the histories, the faculties, and the deniers' own admissions. The believers believe *with* proof — the *āyāt*, signs (v. 58), which are *bayyināt*, clear proofs. The *mushrik* believes *without* proof. The verse's *lā burhāna lahu* is therefore not a minor observation but the epistemological summary of the whole sūrah: one side has evidence and the other does not, and the side without evidence is the one that laughed (v. 110).

**"His Account Is Only With His Lord": Ḥisābuhu ʿinda Rabbihi**

The consequence is stated with restraint: *fa-innamā ḥisābuhu ʿinda rabbihi* — "then his account is only with his Lord." The word *ḥisāb*, reckoning, account, is from the root *ḥ-s-b*, the root of *yaḥsabūna*, "they reckon" (v. 55), and *ḥasibtum*, "you thought" (v. 115). The deniers *reckoned* wrongly about their wealth and their purpose; now their *reckoning* is with God. The restrictive *innamā*, "only," and the phrase *ʿinda rabbihi*, "with his Lord," together convey that the *mushrik*'s account is God's affair alone — no one else will settle it, no one else can intervene, and no one else needs to. The verse does not describe the punishment in detail; it says only that the account will be rendered, and to whom. The sūrah has already shown what the account contains (vv. 101–111); verse 117 states the principle that produces it.

The phrase *ʿinda rabbihi*, "with *his* Lord," retains the possessive even for the *mushrik*: God is *his* Lord, whether he acknowledged it or not. The man who called on another god still has one Lord, and it is that Lord who will take his account. The possessive is a small reminder of the ownership established in verse 84: whoever is on the earth is God's, and the account is with the Owner.

**"Indeed, the Disbelievers Will Not Succeed": Lā Yufliḥu l-Kāfirūn**

The verse and the sūrah's argument end with the sentence that mirrors verse 1: *innahu lā yufliḥu l-kāfirūn* — "Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed." The pronoun *innahu*, "indeed it [is the case that]," introduces the statement as a settled fact. The verb *yufliḥu*, "succeed, prosper," is the verb of verse 1's *aflaḥa* and verse 102's *mufliḥūn*. The subject is *al-kāfirūn*, "the disbelievers" — the sūrah's title's opposite. *Al-muʾminūn* succeed (v. 1); *al-kāfirūn* do not (v. 117). The sūrah is bracketed by the two sentences, and everything between them is the explanation of the difference.

The word *kāfir* is from the root *k-f-r*, "to cover, to conceal" — a farmer who covers seed is a *kāfir* in the root sense (57:20). The disbeliever is one who *covers* the truth: the truth of God's ownership that he admits (v. 85) and hides beneath idolatry; the truth of the return that he knows (v. 115) and hides beneath denial; the truth of his own brief life (v. 114) that he covers with the illusion of permanence. *Falāḥ*, by contrast, is from the root that means to *cleave open* the earth. The two words are, at the level of their roots, opposites: the *kāfir* covers; the *mufliḥ* breaks open. One buries the truth; the other breaks through to it. The sūrah's first and last declarations are built on this opposition, and the whole of it is contained in the two roots.

**The Sūrah's Argument in One Verse**

Verse 117 gathers the sūrah's teaching into a single sentence. *Shirk* — calling on another god with God — is the central error (vv. 23, 32, 59, 91, 116). It has no proof (vv. 84–91). Its account is with God alone (vv. 62, 101–111). And its outcome is the opposite of *falāḥ* (v. 1 ↔ v. 117). A reader who remembers only this verse remembers the sūrah's structure: the believers succeed, the disbelievers do not, and the difference is whether one called on God alone.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 117 asks the believer, one final time, whether he calls on *another god with God*. The gross form of the question is easily answered; the subtle form — the *shirk* of verse 59, the hidden partner in devotion — is not. Whom does he *call upon*, in the sense of *duʿāʾ* — direct his hope toward, depend on, fear, love as one loves God? If the honest answer includes anything *maʿa llāh*, "alongside God" — a person, a possession, a position, the self — the verse's *lā burhāna lahu bihi* applies: there is no proof for it, no justification, no argument that could stand before the True Sovereign (v. 116). The believer's response is the one the sūrah has taught throughout: *subḥāna llāh* (v. 91), refuge (vv. 97–98), and the return of all calling to the One who alone answers.

The verse also gives the believer the confidence of the sūrah's frame. He is among *al-muʾminūn* who *aflaḥa* — if he holds to what the sūrah has described. The disbelievers *lā yufliḥūn* — whatever their wealth, numbers, or laughter. The two sentences are God's, stated at the sūrah's two ends, and they will not be revised. The believer who is mocked, poor, or outnumbered can hold verse 117 against verse 1 and know which side he is on.

**Toward the Final Prayer**

The argument is complete; the frame is closed. One verse remains, and it is not an argument but a prayer — the prayer of the believers from verse 109, given now to the Prophet ﷺ and to every reader as the sūrah's last word.

---
## Sūrah al-Muʾminūn 23:118

> **Say, “My Lord! Forgive and show mercy, for Thou art the best of those who are merciful.”**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Last Word Is a Prayer**

The sūrah has argued for 117 verses. It has described the believers and the deniers, recounted the histories of the messengers, dismantled every objection, conducted the trial of the people of the Fire, pronounced the believers triumphant, and closed its frame with the declaration that the disbelievers will not succeed. Now, with everything said, it ends not with a final argument or a final warning but with a prayer, placed on the Prophet's lips by divine command: *wa qul rabbi ghfir wa rḥam wa anta khayru l-rāḥimīn* — "And say: 'My Lord, forgive and have mercy, for You are the best of the merciful.'" The sūrah that began with *falāḥ* ends with *raḥmah*. The success it promised at its first verse is, at its last, asked for as a mercy.

**"And Say": Wa Qul**

The command *qul*, "say," has governed the sūrah's closing section: *"Say: whose is the earth?"* (v. 84); *"Say: who is the Lord of the seven heavens?"* (v. 86); *"Say: who holds the dominion of everything?"* (v. 88); *"Say: my Lord, if You show me what they are promised"* (v. 93); *"Say: my Lord, I seek refuge"* (v. 97). Each *qul* placed words in the Prophet's mouth — first arguments, then prayers. This final *qul* gives him the last words of the sūrah, and they are the simplest. After the questions that silenced the deniers and the refuges that guarded against the devils, the Prophet ﷺ is told to say what every servant must say in the end: forgive me, and have mercy.

The command is to the Prophet ﷺ, and through him to every believer. He was the best of creation; he had just been given, in this very sūrah, the arguments that exposed the deniers' folly and the assurance of God's power to punish them (v. 95). And he is told to end by asking forgiveness. If the Prophet ﷺ asks forgiveness, no one may end his prayers with anything less.

**"My Lord": Rabbi**

The address is *rabbi*, "my Lord" — the intimate vocative the sūrah has given to Noah (v. 26), to the second messenger (v. 39), to the Prophet ﷺ (vv. 93, 94, 97, 98), and — too late — to the dying denier (v. 99). The sūrah ends with the word said rightly: by the Messenger, in the world, in humility. The whole sūrah has been, among other things, a lesson in *when* to say *rabbi*: the believers said it in life (v. 109) and were rewarded; the deniers said it at death (v. 99) and in the Fire (vv. 106–107) and were refused. The final *rabbi* is the sūrah's model — the word said while it counts.

**"Forgive and Have Mercy": Ighfir wa Rḥam**

The petition is two imperatives: *ighfir*, "forgive," and *irḥam*, "have mercy." The pairing is the same as in the believers' prayer of verse 109 — *fa-ghfir lanā wa rḥamnā*, "forgive us and have mercy on us" — and the sūrah's ending deliberately echoes that prayer. What the *farīq min ʿibādī*, "the party of My servants" (v. 109), used to say in the world, the Prophet ﷺ is now commanded to say. The believers' prayer, quoted by God to the people of the Fire as the prayer they mocked, becomes the sūrah's own closing words. The mocked prayer is vindicated by being made the Qur'an's last word on the subject.

The two petitions are complementary, and the commentators explained their order. *Maghfirah*, forgiveness, is from the root *gh-f-r*, which means to cover, to shield, to protect — a *mighfar* is a helmet. To forgive is to cover the sin so that it does not harm: to remove it from the record and shield the sinner from its consequence. *Raḥmah*, mercy, is from the root *r-ḥ-m*, related to *raḥim*, the womb — the tender, encompassing, nourishing care of the one who bears. To have mercy is to give what the servant needs beyond the removal of harm: guidance, provision, ease, Paradise. Forgiveness clears the past; mercy furnishes the future. A servant needs both, and the prayer asks for both in two words.

The petitions are stated without objects — not "forgive *me*" or "have mercy on *me*" but simply "forgive, have mercy" — and the commentators noted that this absoluteness widens the prayer. It asks for forgiveness and mercy without specifying for whom, so that it encompasses the one praying and, implicitly, all who join him. The Prophet ﷺ was told to say it; every believer who recites the sūrah says it after him; and the unbounded petition covers them all.

**"For You Are the Best of the Merciful": Khayr al-Rāḥimīn**

The prayer closes with the ground on which it rests: *wa anta khayru l-rāḥimīn* — "and You are the best of the merciful." This is the sūrah's final *khayr* construction, completing a series that traced the sūrah's movement. *Khayr al-munzilīn*, "the best of those who bring to land" (v. 29) — Noah's prayer at his deliverance. *Khayr al-rāziqīn*, "the best of providers" (v. 72) — the answer to the deniers' suspicion that the Messenger sought payment. *Khayr al-rāḥimīn*, "the best of the merciful" (vv. 109, 118) — the believers' prayer and the sūrah's last word. Deliverance, provision, mercy: the three things a servant most needs, and God is the *best* source of each.

The phrase's logic is the logic of every petition to God: the petitioner asks for mercy *because* God is the best at giving it. The ground of hope is not the servant's merit — the prayer has just asked for *forgiveness*, which presupposes fault — but God's character. The Prophet ﷺ taught that God's mercy exceeds all creaturely mercy: when a captive woman was seen searching for her child and nursing it, he asked the Companions whether she would throw her child into a fire, and when they said no, he said: *"God is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child"* (al-Bukhārī 5999; Muslim 2754). That is *khayr al-rāḥimīn*: better than the best mercy we can see. The prayer ends by naming the reason it can be made at all.

**Why the Sūrah Ends Here**

The commentators reflected on why a sūrah of such argumentative force should end with so gentle a prayer, and their answers illuminate the whole.

First, because the sūrah's severity was in the service of mercy. Every warning — the seizure, the gate, the Fire, the silencing — was issued *so that* the reader would turn to God while turning was possible. The sūrah's last verse shows the turn: this is what the warnings were for. The reader who has felt the weight of verses 99–115 is meant to arrive at verse 118 ready to say it.

Second, because the sūrah is named for *the believers*, and this prayer is theirs. Verse 109 quoted it as the prayer of God's servants; verse 118 gives it to the Prophet ﷺ and to everyone who follows him. The sūrah ends by placing its readers in the company of the *farīq* it praised — if they will say what that party said.

Third, because *falāḥ* is a mercy. The sūrah began by declaring the believers successful; it ends by asking for the mercy that success depends on. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds."* They asked: *"Not even you, O Messenger of God?"* He said: *"Not even I, unless God envelops me in His mercy"* (al-Bukhārī 5673; Muslim 2816). The believers of verse 1 succeed; verse 118 explains that their success is *raḥmah*, and asks for it.

Fourth, because the prayer answers the sūrah's title. *Al-Muʾminūn* — the believers — are those who say *rabbi ghfir wa rḥam* and mean it. To end the sūrah with these words is to end it with the believers' voice, which is where it began.

**The Verse for the Believer**

Verse 118 gives the believer his last word, for every day and for his life. It is a prayer to say after every prayer, at the end of every day, at the close of every reading of the Qur'an, and — God willing — at the end. The Prophet ﷺ, when he had recited the whole Qur'an or finished a gathering of remembrance, would ask forgiveness; and his last words on earth included a prayer for forgiveness and mercy (al-Bukhārī 4440: *"O God, forgive me and have mercy on me, and join me with the Highest Companion"*). Verse 118 is that prayer's source.

The believer who has read the sūrah has been shown what success is (vv. 1–11), how the world was made to point to God (vv. 12–22), how every messenger said the same thing (vv. 23–52), how the deniers of every age recoiled from it (vv. 53–92), how the Prophet ﷺ was taught to pray through the interval (vv. 93–98), how death and judgment arrive (vv. 99–115), and who God is (vv. 116–117). Having been shown all this, he is told what to say: *rabbi ghfir wa rḥam wa anta khayru l-rāḥimīn*. My Lord, forgive and have mercy, for You are the best of the merciful. Nothing else needs to be added. The sūrah of the believers ends with the believers' prayer, and the reader who says it has become one of them.

---
**[End of the commentary on Sūrah al-Muʾminūn]**
